idea.title: Lithium voidage swap: CO2 replaces spent-brine reinjection in Smackover lithium/bromine fields
idea.one_line: Gulf Coast lithium and bromine brine producers must create pore-space voidage, and CO2 storage needs pressure relief, the failure that limited Gorgon. Matching the two lets each tonne of CO2 replace 1.74 m3 of withdrawn brine worth $9-59 of lithium, and turns a lithium plant into a Mt-scale storage site.
idea.conventional_core: Saline-aquifer CO2 storage with active brine extraction for pressure management: Buscheck et al. 2012 ACRM; the DOE Brine Extraction Storage Test; Gorgon's produced-water handling.
idea.graft: Direct lithium extraction (DLE) from oilfield and bromine brines (Smackover; Standard Lithium/Equinor, ExxonMobil, Albemarle). The brine that storage must remove becomes a mineral feedstock.
idea.mechanism:
Smackover brines in southern Arkansas exceed 400 mg/L Li (USGS, Knierim 2024). DLE projects plan to produce brine, strip the Li, and reinject the spent brine into the Smackover for pressure support. Bromine producers already do the same.

The swap: CO2 from Gulf Coast ammonia, gas-processing and hydrogen plants (separation floor about 0.002-0.007 GJ/t) is injected into the Smackover down-dip, below the Buckner anhydrite seal, as the pressure-support fluid. The spent brine goes to a shallower disposal zone or to treatment.

The result: storage gets continuous pressure relief, and the lithium operation gets pressure maintenance plus a storage-fee revenue line. Injection must stay out of hydrocarbon-bearing compartments, with no EOR.
idea.target: The approximately 25 Mt/yr of Gulf Coast concentrated industrial CO2 within reach of the Smackover trend (Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, East Texas). Also the profitability gap of first-wave Arkansas DLE projects, which Malone et al. (2026) find unprofitable at 2025 lithium prices.
idea.quantitative_claims:
Computed with CoolProp in subsurface_ideas.py.

Per tonne of CO2:
- CO2 density at Smackover conditions (100-130 C, 250-320 bar) is 575-588 kg/m3, so the voidage is 1.70-1.74 m3/t.
- Lithium in that voidage, at 80% DLE recovery (assumption): 0.21-0.56 kg Li, or 1.1-3.0 kg LCE, worth $9-59/t CO2 at $8-20k/t LCE (150-400 mg/L).
- Equivalently, 337-900 t of CO2 storage per t of LCE.

System scale:
- The three initial Arkansas DLE projects (about 53,100 t/yr LCE, Malone 2026) imply about 42 Mm3/yr of brine (about 716 kbbl/d) at 300 mg/L. That is voidage for about 24 Mt CO2/yr.
- One 25 kt/yr LCE plant at 400 mg/L gives about 8.4 Mt/yr.
- Brine already handled in 2022 (5,000 t Li brought to surface, USGS) gives 8-14 Mt/yr of voidage at 200-350 mg/L.

Costs and energy:
- Disposing spent brine elsewhere costs $5.5-11/t CO2 at $0.5-1/bbl.
- Added energy is only CO2 compression (floor 0.28 GJ/t to 150 bar). Brine lift is already paid by the DLE plant.

Side check (negative result for the map's 'storage plus produced-brine geothermal' open problem): the heat in the voidage brine is 0.33 GJ_th/t, about 9 kWh_e/t at 10% binary efficiency, against about 120 kWh/t of compression.
idea.who_gains: S3 and S4 (ExxonMobil, Equinor/Standard Lithium, Albemarle, Lanxess; Gulf Coast ammonia and hydrogen emitters needing storage). S7 (US critical minerals plus CCS; Arkansas and Louisiana revenue). S6 (south Arkansas oilfield workforce as legacy production declines). S10 (de-risks DLE economics). S1, cautiously: dedicated storage with no oil EOR, plus battery minerals.
idea.who_loses: Hard-rock and evaporite lithium producers (Australia, Chile and Argentina, which matters for S8) and Chinese processors, through added competition. S11 in south Arkansas, from brine-spill, CO2-pipeline (Satartia-type) and water concerns. Part of S1 may see 'CO2 injected to push out brine' as EOR-like. Fossil CO2 sources benefit, which is S1's subsidy concern. Bromine operators bear CO2-breakthrough risk to their brine supply.
idea.closest_known_work: Buscheck et al. 2012 (Int J GHG Control, 214 citations): active CO2 reservoir management with brine extraction, desalination and geothermal. Rock Springs Uplift pressure-management field demonstration (2017). DOE BEST brine extraction test (2022). Huang et al. 2026: review of lithium plus geothermal co-production in the Smackover. Malone et al. 2026: scoping review of Arkansas oilfield-brine DLE, which finds the first projects greenfield and unprofitable at 2025 prices. Liu et al. 2026 (Chem Eng J): surface CO2 mineralization plus Li from produced water.
idea.why_different: ACRM-type schemes treat extracted brine as a cost (desalination or disposal), and DLE schemes treat reinjection as a cost. This idea makes the two flows each other's solution, a two-way pore-space swap in which lithium pays for pressure relief and CO2 provides pressure support. I found no paper coupling DLE voidage to CO2 storage capacity (OpenAlex title searches only; absence of evidence in a quick search is weak).
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test:
Simulation (2-4 weeks, open-source OPM Flow or MRST): a line-drive or 5-spot Smackover sector model using published porosity, permeability and Li data. Compute the time to CO2 breakthrough at brine producers against well spacing, the pressure-relief fraction, and the cumulative Li value per t stored. Kill if breakthrough comes in under 10 years at economic spacing, or if under 50% of injected volume is offset by production.

Bench (4 weeks): Li uptake of a commercial Li-Al-LDH or ion-sieve sorbent from synthetic Smackover brine pre-equilibrated with CO2 (lower pH). Kill if uptake falls more than 30% and pH correction costs more than about $10/t CO2.
idea.family: CO2 as voidage-replacement fluid in lithium/bromine brine fields (Smackover): brine production for DLE doubles as storage pressure relief

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: CN103603642B (China University of Geosciences, Wuhan; priority 2013): Method of using CO2 to displace high-salinity brine deep in the formation
closest.overlap: This is the core mechanism, already patented. Captured CO2 is compressed to supercritical and injected into a deep high-salt brine layer while extraction wells produce the brine. The brine goes to 'deep processing and purification', meaning mineral and salt recovery, and any CO2 that breaks through is separated and reinjected. It claims explicit relief of pressure build-up and salt precipitation compared with injecting CO2 alone. It is generic (no lithium, DLE or Smackover) but is the same two-way swap: CO2 as the voidage fluid, produced brine as the mineral feedstock.

closest.title: CN103603639B (CUG Wuhan, 2013): System for exploiting deep high-salinity brine and using its heat via CO2 injection
closest.overlap: A closed loop of CO2 injection wells and brine extraction wells, recovering the brine's salts plus geothermal heat, with pressure maintenance and CO2 storage. It covers the heat side-branch the idea tests and finds negative.

closest.title: Fang et al. 2017, Environ Earth Sci: Pure brine recovery vs CO2-enhanced brine recovery, a case study of potassium-rich brine recovery in the Jianghan Basin
closest.overlap: A peer-reviewed field-specific study of 'CO2-enhanced brine recovery', in which CO2 replaces voidage in a mineral-brine (potash) operation, including leakage risk. It is the same concept applied to K-rich brine instead of Li.

closest.title: Li Qi et al. 2015, J Clean Prod: CO2-EWR, a cleaner solution for coal chemical industry in China (75 citations); also the Eastern Junggar CO2-EWR field test, Ma et al., Fuel 2026/27
closest.overlap: The established Chinese 'CO2-enhanced water recovery' framework: inject CO2 and produce deep saline water for use, with concentrated industrial (coal-chemical) CO2 as the source, plus a field test. It pairs a high-purity cheap CO2 source with brine production. It focuses on water and general brine resources rather than lithium DLE economics.

closest.title: Hamdi, Clarkson and Zirbes 2025, SPE ATCE 228170: Geothermal and lithium recovery potentials of a small-scale CO2-saturated brine injection in the Leduc aquifer, Alberta
closest.overlap: The closest lithium-specific work. A doublet produces Li brine (79 mg/L) for DLE, and the spent brine is saturated with CO2 from a nearby gas plant and reinjected, so storage is co-located with DLE to offset injection costs. The difference is that CO2 is stored dissolved in the reinjected spent brine at a few t/day; free-phase CO2 does not replace the brine voidage, so the scale is not Mt/yr.

closest.title: Buscheck et al. 2012, Active CO2 Reservoir Management (CMTC 151746 / IJGGC); Buscheck 2016, pre-injection brine production (IJGGC); DOE BEST brine extraction test (2022)
closest.overlap: Brine production to relieve CO2-storage pressure, with 'beneficial utilization of produced brine'. ACRM also names pore-space competition with neighbouring subsurface activities. The produced brine is treated as water or heat, not lithium. The idea already cites this.

closest.title: Liu, Wang and Zhang 2026, Chem Eng J 174444: Integrated critical minerals recovery from produced water and CO2 sequestration; Bang and Jiang 2026 (Water Sci Technol); Jiang and Zhang 2024 (GSC Open File): DLE on CO2-mineralization-treated Montney brine
closest.overlap: Combines Li and critical-mineral recovery from produced brine with CO2 capture. That capture happens by surface mineralization, not by subsurface voidage replacement.

closest.title: TETRA Technologies: Arkansas Smackover brine unit (Li/Br, MoU with ExxonMobil's Saltwerx, 2023) and MoU with CarbonFree on CCUS (2021)
closest.overlap: A Smackover bromine and lithium operator that has also pursued CCUS. The CarbonFree tie-up was surface mineralization (SkyMine-type). I found no announcement of CO2 as the Smackover pressure-support fluid.

art.what_is_new:
Prior work already has the general mechanism: injecting CO2 to displace and produce deep mineral brine, with the brine processed for salts and CO2 storage gaining pressure relief. That is patented in CN103603642B (2013) and studied as CO2-EWR and CO2-enhanced potassium brine recovery (Li et al. 2015; Fang et al. 2017, Jianghan). The 'two-way pore-space swap' framing is therefore not new in principle, and the idea's claim that no work couples brine-mineral extraction to CO2 storage is wrong. Hamdi et al. (2025) also co-locate DLE with CO2 storage in Alberta's Leduc aquifer, but as dissolved CO2 in reinjected spent brine at a few t/day.

Not found, and plausibly new:
(1) Applying it to lithium DLE specifically, with free-phase CO2 replacing the spent-brine reinjection that DLE and bromine projects plan for pressure support, so CO2 takes the place of the reinjectate rather than being added to it.
(2) The Smackover and Gulf Coast setting: Arkansas DLE brine units, the Buckner anhydrite seal, high-purity ammonia, hydrogen and gas-processing CO2, no EOR, and Class VI plus brine-unit regulation.
(3) Quantified voidage-to-lithium economics ($9-59 of Li per t CO2; about 24 Mt/yr of voidage from the first Arkansas DLE projects), used to close the DLE profitability gap.
(4) The specific risks: CO2 breakthrough into DLE and bromine producers, and Li sorbent performance on CO2-acidified brine.

The novelty is therefore in the application and system integration, not in the mechanism.

Caveat: the web-search budget was exhausted, so this used Crossref, Semantic Scholar, Google Patents and TETRA's IR feed only. Industry announcements, such as ExxonMobil, Standard Lithium/Equinor or Chevron pairing Smackover CCS with lithium, or Arkansas Class VI and brine-unit pore-space disputes, could not be checked and may narrow the novelty further.

phys.assumptions:
All numbers below are as printed by graft_subsurface_2.py. Labels: [src] = sourced; [recall] = pre-cutoff knowledge not re-verified this session; [assume] = my assumption. The web-search budget was exhausted, so only USGS MCS 2026 (lithium) and the EPA Class VI primacy page were fetched this session.

FLOORS (verifier, ideal gas)
- Ammonia/SMR process CO2 at 98%: separation floor 0.0025 GJ/t.
- Gas-processing acid gas at 95%: 0.0065 GJ/t.
- The idea's claimed 0.002-0.007 GJ/t is consistent with these.
- Ideal isothermal compression from 1 to 150 bar: 0.282 GJ/t. This is not a separation floor but is unavoidable.

VOIDAGE (CoolProp Span-Wagner)
- Density: 588 kg/m3 at 100 C/250 bar, 575 kg/m3 at 115 C/280 bar, 578 kg/m3 at 130 C/320 bar.
- That gives a voidage of 1.699-1.740 m3/t, which confirms the claim.
- CO2 viscosity is about 0.046 cP. Assuming brine at 0.45 cP, the brine/CO2 viscosity ratio is 9.9.

LITHIUM PER TONNE (80% DLE recovery [assume])
- 150 mg/L: 1.11 kg LCE/t, worth $10/t at the 2025 US average of $9k/t LCE, or $22/t at $20k/t.
- 300 mg/L: 2.22 kg LCE/t, worth $20/t or $44/t.
- 400 mg/L: 2.96 kg LCE/t, worth $27/t or $59/t.
- That is 337-900 t CO2 per t LCE.
- [src] USGS MCS 2026: the 2025 US contract average for battery-grade Li2CO3 was $9,000/t; China spot rose from about $9,300 (Jan) to $10,300 (Nov). The claim's $20k/t upper bound is therefore optimistic versus 2025 prices.

ENERGY (GJ/t)
- Compression at 95/115/140 kWh/t (0.342/0.414/0.504) [recall, NETL/IEAGHG ranges].
- Plus dehydration 0.005-0.02.
- Plus pumping spent brine to a new zone at 30-100 bar ΔP (0.007-0.027).
- Plus recycle of breakthrough CO2 at 0-3% of compression.
- Totals: low 0.354, base 0.443, high 0.566. Base is 1.57x the compression floor; nothing falls below a floor.
- Brine lift is treated as already paid by the DLE plant, as the idea states.

COST ($/t; capex annualised with CRF(8%, 20 yr) = 0.1019 plus O&M) [assume]
- Inputs: power at $45/65/90 per MWh; compressors at $1.5k/2.5k/3.5k per kW; pipelines of 50/150/300 km at $1.0/1.5/2.0M per km carrying 5/3/1.5 Mt/yr; 1/2/3 Class VI injectors per Mt/yr at $10/15/25M each; MRV $3/5/10; spent-brine disposal at $0.5/0.75/1.0 per bbl; recycle $0/1/3; dehydration $1/2/3.
- Low $19.1/t: compression 6.8, pipeline 1.3, wells 1.5, brine disposal 5.5.
- Base $42.9/t: compression 12.6, dehydration 2.0, pipeline 9.5, wells 4.6, MRV 5.0, spent-brine disposal 8.2, recycle 1.0.
- High $110.4/t: dominated by $50.7/t of pipeline for a small source 300 km away.
- The swap-specific increment over a plain Class VI site is $5.5/9.2/13.9 per t.
- Margin against 45Q at $85/t [recall: retained in the July 2025 OBBBA]: +$66, +$42 and -$25 per t.
- If the storage site were pressure-limited, the avoided cost of dedicated ACRM brine extraction is $6.2/10.3/15.8 per t. That is roughly the same size as the swap's added disposal cost.

SCALE
- First-wave Arkansas DLE (53,100 t/yr LCE, a Malone 2026 figure not verified here): 41.6 Mm3/yr of brine at 300 mg/L, matching 23.9 Mt CO2/yr; at 400 mg/L, 17.9 Mt/yr.
- One 22.5 kt/yr plant at 437 mg/L ([recall] Standard Lithium SWA DFS): 6.9 Mt/yr. One 25 kt/yr plant at 400 mg/L: 8.4 Mt/yr.
- Brine handled in 2022 (5,000 t Li): 8-14 Mt/yr.
- Global ceiling: if all 2025 lithium demand (263 kt Li, [src] USGS) came from 300 mg/L brine with CO2 voidage replacement, that is 0.63 Gt/yr, or 1.7% of fossil CO2.
- If 5-15% of 2.5x-2025 lithium demand came from such fields: 0.079-0.236 Gt/yr [assume].
- The reported 0.025 Gt/yr is the realistic US Gulf Coast scale.

RESOURCES
- At 25 Mt/yr: 11.1 PJ/yr, which is 0.0018% of world primary energy or 0.0103% of world electricity. It also means 43 Mm3/yr (0.75 Mbbl/d) of spent brine needing a new disposal zone.
- No water is consumed. Land is limited to pads and pipeline right-of-way.

RESERVOIR SCREENING [assume: 100 mD, 17% porosity, 40 m net, ct 1e-9/Pa]
- Pressure diffusion length: 12.8 km after 1 yr, 57.4 km after 20 yr (D = 1.31 m2/s).
- Plume radius over 20 yr: 1.8-2.9 km at 0.5 Mt/yr, 4.0 km at 1 Mt/yr.
- Breakthrough, with breakthrough at 3-5% of pattern pore volume and 0.5 Mt/yr per injector:
  - 1.0 km spacing: 0.7 yr
  - 1.5 km: 2.8 yr
  - 3.0 km: 11.1 yr
  - 5.0 km: 30.7 yr
- Buoyant up-dip creep is only 7-21 m/yr, so dip direction matters less than viscous drive and gravity override.
- Dissolved CO2 at saturation (115 C, 280 bar, NaCl-proxy TDS 200-300 g/L): 20.8-29.1 kg/m3. Recycle is at most 36-51 kg per t stored (3.6-5.1%) if produced brine were saturated.
phys.violations:
There are no thermodynamic violations. Every energy figure is above the separation and compression floors. There are three framing or accounting errors and one design risk:

1. ATTRIBUTION ERROR, the largest. The headline "each tonne of CO2 replaces 1.74 m3 of brine worth $9-59 of lithium" is a co-location ratio, not a credit per tonne of CO2. The lithium is produced whether the voidage is filled by CO2 or by spent brine. The only incremental revenue is the storage fee (in practice 45Q), offset by the cost of disposing spent brine elsewhere ($5.5-13.9/t including recycle). Also, the claim's $59/t uses $20k/t LCE, while the 2025 US average was $9k/t; at that price the figure is $10-27/t.

2. PRESSURE RELIEF IS RELOCATED, NOT CREATED. Spent brine (1.7 m3/t) must still go to a "shallower disposal zone", so basin-scale pressure relief is zero unless that zone is open or underpressured. The value to storage is about the avoided ACRM extraction cost ($6.2-15.8/t), and only at pressure-limited sites. Most Gulf Coast Class VI sites are not pressure-limited.

3. "PRESSURE MAINTENANCE FOR THE DLE PLANT" IS NOT NEW. Spent-brine reinjection already provides it. The genuine reservoir benefit, which the idea missed, is avoiding Li-depleted brine recirculating to the producers and diluting their grade. That benefit is unquantified here.

4. DESIGN RISK. The kill criterion (breakthrough in under 10 yr) is met at well spacings under about 3 km: 0.7 yr at 1 km and 2.8 yr at 1.5 km. The idea is viable only with injector-producer spacing of at least 3-5 km. That is achievable, because pressure reaches about 13 km in 1 yr, but it changes the geometry from a line-drive or 5-spot to distant pressure-connected injection.

Economics: the swap is profitable mainly because of 45Q at $85/t (margin +$42/t base). The same high-purity CO2 would be profitable in a plain Class VI site. The lithium coupling adds about +/-$10/t, so it is not what makes the project pay.
phys.resource_needs:
At 25 Mt/yr (base 0.443 GJ/t, mostly compression electricity):
- Energy: 11.1 PJ/yr, which is 0.0018% of world primary energy or 0.0103% of world electricity (about 2.9 TWh).
- Brine: 43 Mm3/yr (0.75 Mbbl/d) of spent brine needs a new disposal formation.
- Pore space: 1.7 m3 per t CO2 in the Smackover.
- Water: none consumed.
- Land: well pads and CO2 pipeline right-of-way. Pipeline lengths are 50-300 km depending on source; that is the dominant cost in the high case.
- Wells: 1-3 Class VI injectors per Mt/yr, plus spent-brine disposal wells (about 4,700 m3/d per Mt/yr).
- Materials: conventional steel for wells, pipe and compressors, nothing critical.
- Other: a recycle compressor for CO2 that degasses from produced brine after breakthrough (at most 3.6-5.1% of stored CO2 if the brine were saturated).
phys.key_uncertainties:
1. Breakthrough geometry. It needs a sector simulation (OPM Flow/MRST) with real Smackover heterogeneity. Smackover grainstones are layered, and high-permeability streaks could cut the screened 11-31 yr breakthrough times at 3-5 km. Gravity override was not modelled.

2. Disposal zone. Does a shallower zone in south Arkansas have the capacity and injectivity to take 0.75 Mbbl/d at 25 Mt/yr, and will regulators accept moving a Li-depleted brine stream to it? This determines whether any net pressure relief exists.

3. Hydrocarbon compartments and legacy wells. South Arkansas has about a century of legacy oil and gas penetrations. Class VI area-of-review costs and leakage risk could dominate. Injection must avoid oil-bearing compartments (EOR optics).

4. Unverified source figures, since the search budget ran out:
   - About 25 Mt/yr of concentrated Gulf Coast CO2 "within reach": source distances are 100-400 km, and pipeline cost scales strongly with distance and volume (pipeline cost ranges from $1.3/t in the low case to $50.7/t in the high case).
   - The Malone 2026 figure of 53,100 t/yr LCE and the USGS figure of 5,000 t Li brought to surface in 2022.
   - The [recall] SWA DFS figures (22.5 kt/yr, 437 mg/L).
   - The 45Q rate of $85/t after OBBBA.
   - Arkansas Class VI primacy status. Texas primacy (Nov 2025) was confirmed this session; Arkansas was not.

5. Brine chemistry. CO2-acidified brine (lower pH) may cut Li-Al-LDH or ion-sieve uptake; that bench test is still needed. CaCl2-rich Smackover brine salts CO2 out more than the NaCl proxy assumes, so recycle may be lower than 3.6-5.1%.

6. Lithium price path. The 2025 average was $9k/t. First-wave DLE profitability, and so whether brine production happens at all, governs the scale. If DLE plants are not built, there is no voidage.

7. Bromine operators (Lanxess, Albemarle) may treat CO2 near their brine units as a threat to supply, which would limit sites to new DLE units.

Evidence weighting: CO2 storage and brine reinjection are realized and measured technologies. ACRM is at field-demo level (BEST 2022, Rock Springs). Commercial oilfield-brine DLE is at demo or first-plant stage. The combination exists only on paper (TRL about 3).

stances.evidence:
Climate Action Network's Jan 2021 position on CCUS sets the red lines. It calls for phasing out public support for fossil-linked technologies 'including CCS', opposes EOR/EGR as 'dangerously at odds with any climate action', and warns that storage liability is likely to shift to the public sector (point 9). Its objection to industrial CCS rests on evidence ('no definitive evidence'), not on principle. What favours this idea: dedicated saline storage with no oil production, process CO2 from ammonia and gas processing, and battery minerals.

What counts against it, from my calculation (stake_lithium_swap.py):
- At $85/t, 45Q is worth $28.6k-76.5k per t LCE. That is 1.4-9.6x the lithium value at $8-20k/t LCE.
- So economically this is a federally subsidised fossil-CO2 storage project, and the lithium is a by-product.
- The gas-processing CO2 in the source pool is stripped so that natural gas can be sold.

In Louisiana's Class VI primacy rulemaking (FR 2024-00044, effective 5 Feb 2024), EPA received 41,622 comments (36,151 of them mass mailings). Environmental-justice and civil-rights groups raised enforcement history, staff capacity, the state taking on liability, and overburdened communities. Expect the same organisations in the Arkansas, Louisiana and East Texas parts of the Smackover trend.
stances.red_line_hit: Public subsidy for fossil-linked CCS (CAN red line 3). Displacing a fluid to produce a resource looks like EOR (red line 7) even though no oil is produced. Long-term storage liability moves to the state (red line 9).

stances.evidence:
IPCC AR6 WGIII C.4.4 and COP28 1/CMA.5 para 28(e) back CCS 'particularly in hard-to-abate sectors'. Ammonia, hydrogen and gas-processing CO2 is the most concentrated stream there is: the separation floor is about 0.002-0.007 GJ/t, against 0.47 GJ/t for DAC (OptiLex verifier). Brine extraction for pressure management is an established research line: Buscheck et al. 2012 ACRM, the DOE Brine Extraction Storage Test (2022) and the Rock Springs Uplift demonstration (2017). It is not a fringe idea.

Scientists will make their support conditional on three open questions: (1) when CO2 breaks through at the brine producers, (2) induced seismicity when injection and production run at the same time, and (3) how storage permanence is accounted for while the same formation is still being produced. Mitigation deterrence is a weaker concern here than for DAC or BECCS, because this is point-source abatement, not offsetting removal. In Baum et al. 2024, the high moral-hazard ratings fell on engineered CDR.
stances.red_line_hit: None categorical. Credibility depends on the reservoir simulation (breakthrough time, pressure-offset fraction) and on MRV for storage inside a formation that is still being produced.

stances.evidence:
The incumbents' interests line up directly.
- Equinor co-owns Smackover Lithium with Standard Lithium. The JV finalised a $225M DOE grant on 16 Jan 2025 and won AOGC royalty approval on 29 May 2025. It received more than $1bn in project-finance indications on 9 Dec 2025 and signed an LG Energy Solution offtake on 31 Aug 2026 (all from Standard Lithium press releases).
- In 2021 Standard Lithium started an Arkansas carbon-capture pilot at Mission Creek's Dorcheat Macedonia gas-processing plant, using the CO2 'to optimize its process' and possibly for sequestration. So capturing gas-processing CO2 is already on a DLE developer's agenda.
- ExxonMobil runs a Smackover lithium programme. It also owns the former Denbury Gulf Coast CO2 pipeline network, which it acquired in 2023; this is from my own knowledge and was not re-verified this session.
- Under OBBBA, 45Q pays $85/t, indexed, and gives EOR parity.

One tension: because EOR now earns the same 45Q credit plus oil revenue, S3 has an incentive to send scarce concentrated CO2 to EOR rather than to lithium-field storage. The idea's 'no EOR' covenant costs S3 an option and does not reduce its credits.
stances.red_line_hit: None. A per-tonne fee is not involved. There is a commercial risk that CO2 breaks through into brine or hydrocarbon units that S3 operates.

stances.evidence:
Gulf Coast ammonia, hydrogen and chemical emitters need storage that has its pressure managed. The cement and chemicals roadmaps (GCCA) and the Carbon Capture Coalition show that S4 relies on CCUS for process emissions. One local fit is the El Dorado, Arkansas ammonia complex (LSB Industries), which sits on the Smackover trend and earlier announced a CCS project with Lapis Energy. That is from my own knowledge, not verified this session; if true, the CO2 would need little pipeline.

There is a split inside S4. The bromine producers (Albemarle, Lanxess) are chemical incumbents whose brine supply would carry the risk of CO2 breakthrough and a lower pH, and Lanxess has been Standard Lithium's host and partner at El Dorado. Expect them to support the idea only if CO2 is kept out of their brine units, or if they share in the storage revenue.
stances.red_line_hit: For bromine and lithium brine operators, contamination or dilution of the brine resource by injected CO2. Emitting S4 firms have no red line.

stances.evidence: Not directly involved. Gas-turbine flue CO2 (separation floor 0.22 GJ/t at 4%) is far more expensive to capture than the ammonia and gas-processing streams the idea targets, so utilities are unlikely early suppliers. The 45Q and Carbon Capture Coalition alignment means utilities would not oppose. They could benefit later from storage capacity with managed pressure.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: The Carbon Capture Coalition describes itself as a 'nonpartisan collaboration of companies, unions, conservation and environmental policy organizations', and backs 45Q and carbon-management infrastructure. South Arkansas' legacy oil and brine workforce maps onto drilling, injection, brine handling and DLE operations as conventional production declines. The jobs are real but modest: three DLE plants plus injection wells.
stances.red_line_hit: None. Only positive: it keeps oilfield skills in use.

stances.evidence:
Several government signals point the same way.
- Federal critical-minerals policy: the $225M DOE grant (Jan 2025) and Priority Critical Mineral Project designation for the South West Arkansas project (Apr 2025). The project completed federal permitting for a 22,500 t/yr Li2CO3 plant in May 2026 (Wikipedia, Smackover Formation).
- Arkansas state: the AOGC unanimously approved a 2.5% gross lithium royalty on 29 May 2025, the first ever.
- Federal fiscal: OBBBA kept and strengthened 45Q but phases out the 45X critical-mineral production credit to 75/50/25/0% for 2031-2033 (HR1 text, Sec. 45X(b)(3)(C)). A 45Q storage revenue line would therefore backfill DLE economics just as 45X disappears.
- Primacy: EPA granted Louisiana Class VI primacy (effective 5 Feb 2024) and Texas (7 Nov 2025). I could not verify Arkansas' Class VI primacy status this session (no Federal Register record found), so Arkansas wells may still need EPA Region 6 permits.

On cost, the 45Q outlay would be about $0.7bn/yr at 8.4 Mt and about $2.0bn/yr at 24 Mt (my calculation). Fiscal watchdogs such as Taxpayers for Common Sense have objected to 45Q generosity.
stances.red_line_hit: Fiscal cost of 45Q and the state taking on post-closure liability (raised in the Louisiana primacy comments). There is no energy-security red line, since it adds domestic lithium supply.

stances.evidence:
Lithium Triangle governments are trying to capture more lithium rent. Chile announced plans to nationalise lithium in April 2023 (affecting SQM and Albemarle), Bolivia has pushed OPEC-like regional coordination, and Argentina competes with low royalties (Wikipedia, Lithium Triangle). Subsidised US brine lithium adds competing supply. At the scale of the first three projects (about 53 kt/yr LCE), it is a modest share of the world market. This mirrors the documented objections by S8 trade partners to unilateral measures such as CBAM; those objections were not re-verified this session.

Climate-justice advocates have generally opposed fossil-linked CCS subsidies (the CAN line). On the other side, there is no Global South land take, and DLE avoids evaporation ponds. Water depletion is the Likan Antay (Atacama) community's main grievance against brine mining, but saying US DLE eases that pressure would be speculative.
stances.red_line_hit: Competition from subsidised Northern supply for Global South mineral exporters. Fossil CCS subsidies in the North, seen as delaying mitigation.

stances.evidence: There is no visible consumer price. The cost falls on federal taxpayers through 45Q, not on fuel or power bills. Canada (2025) shows invisible industrial mechanisms survive where visible consumer charges were repealed. Cheaper domestic lithium could slightly lower battery costs, but the effect is diffuse. Pew (May 2024): 65% of US adults prioritise renewables over fossil fuels. That survey gives no direct signal on this mechanism.
stances.red_line_hit: None: no price rise visible to consumers.

stances.evidence:
Malone et al. 2026 find the first-wave Arkansas DLE projects unprofitable at 2025 lithium prices. A contracted storage-fee line would de-risk the project finance: more than $1bn of finance interest (Dec 2025) and binding offtakes (Mar and Aug 2026) show the market is already engaging. Per tonne of CO2, 45Q revenue is larger than lithium revenue, so lenders would underwrite the project mostly as a storage asset.

Insurers and lenders will price three new risks: cross-unit CO2 breakthrough between brine owners, measurement and verification of storage in a formation still being produced (a 45Q recapture risk), and pipeline liability.
stances.red_line_hit: Uninsurable liability or a 45Q recapture event if storage security cannot be demonstrated while the formation is still producing brine.

stances.evidence:
Negative precedents:
- Satartia, Mississippi (Feb 2020): a Denbury CO2/H2S pipeline ruptured less than half a mile from town, and about 300 people (42 residents plus about 250 nearby) were evacuated. PHMSA proposed a $3.87M penalty in 2022. That pipeline network is now ExxonMobil's (not re-verified).
- Louisiana's Class VI primacy drew 41,622 comments, including concerns about environmental justice, enforcement and liability.
- Lake Maurepas storage was contested locally (C&EN, 'The battle for Lake Maurepas', Apr 2023). I could not retrieve the details.

Mitigating factors: south Arkansas has a century of oil and bromine brine industry, and the AOGC approved the lithium royalty unanimously with no objections reported. Brine owners would get only about $0.23-1.48 per t CO2 from the 2.5% lithium royalty (my calculation), so pore-space compensation for the CO2 would be the real local economic lever, and that is unresolved.

CO2 sourced locally, such as an ammonia plant near El Dorado, reduces pipeline exposure. Gulf Coast CO2 piped hundreds of km to the Smackover increases it.
stances.red_line_hit: CO2 pipeline safety, as at Satartia. Brine spills and groundwater. Pore-space rights and possible eminent domain for pipelines. Distrust of state enforcement capacity.

stake.coalition_notes:
The idea fits the existing 45Q coalition: S3, S4, S6, S7 and S10, which is the Carbon Capture Coalition pattern, plus the COP28 'hard-to-abate' framing. That gives broad but conventional support. The lithium story adds critical-minerals hawks in S7 and, potentially, battery-minded parts of S1. It is the only new coalition lever.

The key fact from the calculation (scratchpad/climate/stake_lithium_swap.py) is that 45Q at $85/t is worth 1.4-9.6x the lithium value per tonne stored. Lithium contributes about $9-59/t CO2. Honestly framed, this is a subsidised storage project with lithium as a by-product. S1 and fiscal watchdogs will frame it that way, so presenting it as a lithium project will not win S1 over.

Ways to widen the coalition:
(1) Prioritise local process CO2, such as ammonia on the Smackover trend (the El Dorado complex is unverified), over long pipelines from Gulf Coast gas processing. This lowers the S11 Satartia-type risk and the S1 fossil-gas objection.
(2) Commit to no EOR and no injection into hydrocarbon compartments. OBBBA's EOR parity means S3 gives up an option but no credit value.
(3) Use operator-funded long-term liability bonds rather than transfer to the state. This answers CAN red line 9 and the Louisiana primacy comments.
(4) Pay a pore-space or throughput fee to plume-area owners. The 2.5% lithium royalty is worth less than $1.50/t CO2, so it is not enough on its own.
(5) Give bromine incumbents (Albemarle, Lanxess) a revenue share, or exclude their units, to neutralise the main dissent within S4.
(6) Time the storage revenue to replace 45X as it phases out in 2031-2033. That is a fiscal argument for S7.

Remaining opposition: most of S1 and climate-justice parts of S8 on subsidies for fossil-linked CCS, Lithium Triangle exporters on supply competition, and S11 near pipelines.

Evidence gaps: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so I relied on direct fetches. Not verified this session: Arkansas Class VI primacy status, Arkansas pore-space law, ExxonMobil's lithium timeline and Denbury network, the LSB/Lapis El Dorado CCS project, and details of Louisiana local moratoria. Verified primary sources: Federal Register 2024-00044 (Louisiana primacy, comment counts); Standard Lithium press releases (royalty 2.5%, 29 May 2025; DOE $225M; financing; LG offtake; 2021 CO2 capture pilot); the HR1 text (45X critical-mineral phase-out 2031-2033); Wikipedia (Satartia; Smackover Formation; Lithium Triangle); the CAN 2021 PDF (local copy).

critic.fatal_flaw: None. The physics, scale and stakeholder red lines can all be designed around. Without the swap framing, what remains is high-purity point-source Class VI storage in the Smackover under the Buckner seal. Its floor is 0.0025 GJ/t, its base cost is $43/t and it has positive 45Q margin. That works whether or not lithium is involved. The swap fails as a claim of value creation: it adds no pressure relief and no lithium credit. It does not fail as a project.
critic.top_fixable_flaw: Injecting free-phase CO2 into live lithium-producing patterns hurts the lithium owner. My calculation is in scratchpad/climate/critic_li_swap.py. CO2 is an immiscible displacing fluid, so it leaves brine behind at residual saturation (Swr 0.25-0.45). Per tonne stored, that strands 0.57-1.41 m3 of full-grade brine that later CO2 cannot recover. At 150-400 mg/L, 80% recovery and $9k/t LCE, the stranded lithium is worth $3-22 per t CO2 undiscounted. The lithium in the voidage itself is worth $10-26/t, so up to about 80% of the headline lithium figure is lost. Spent-brine reinjection is miscible and eventually sweeps that lithium, diluted. This is resource loss for Smackover brine-unit royalty owners, which is a correlative-rights problem for S11 and for operators in S3/S4. It sits on top of the breakthrough risk at under 3 km spacing and the need for a new shallower disposal zone (0.25 Mbbl/d per 8.4 Mt/yr, 0.74 Mbbl/d at 25 Mt/yr). That disposal zone moves the pressure perturbation closer to underground drinking-water sources, through weaker seals and past more legacy wells, which is worse than leaving it under the Buckner. The "CO2 replaces the reinjectate" geometry is the wrong design. Valued honestly, the lithium-CO2 coupling is near zero or negative.
critic.suggested_patch:
The patch is a pattern-sequencing and siting rule. It drops "CO2 replaces spent-brine reinjection" and the pressure-relief claim.

(1) Near term (2028-2035): put CO2 injectors only in Smackover compartments down-dip or outside the unit. These should be below the economic lithium cut-off (about 150 mg/L or less) or outside the brine-unit boundary, at least 5 km from producers. Pressure diffusion (about 13 km/yr) still connects them hydraulically to the unit, but the plume does not reach producers for more than 25 years. Spent brine is reinjected inside the unit exactly as already permitted, so there is no new shallow disposal zone and no grade dilution change.

(2) Later: roll storage into patterns already flushed with spent brine (grade 30% of original or less) once their lithium is mostly recovered. The displaced low-grade brine goes through DLE once more before reinjection. Stranded lithium then falls to about $1-5/t, and breakthrough no longer threatens live producers.

(3) Rename the coupling. The DLE operator sells three things: the brine unit's existing unitization (pore-space aggregation, the main Class VI bottleneck), its wells, core and seismic data, and its legacy-well inventory for the area of review. Value these as avoided Class VI pore-space and characterization cost, not as lithium per tonne.

(4) Add kill metrics to the OPM/MRST test: stranded lithium under $2/t CO2 at an 8% discount rate; no CO2 at producers within 25 years; avoided pore-space and characterization cost over $5/t. If the avoided cost comes in under $5/t, report this as plain Class VI storage that happens to sit next to a DLE unit, and fold it into the generic point-source storage family.

patched_idea.title: Lithium-unit storage sequencing: Class VI CO2 storage sited and phased around Smackover lithium/bromine brine units
patched_idea.one_line: Gulf Coast concentrated CO2 is stored in the Smackover below the Buckner seal, in compartments down-dip of or outside lithium brine units, and only later in patterns already flushed of their lithium. The DLE operator sells its unitized pore space, wells, data and legacy-well inventory as avoided Class VI cost, not as 'lithium per tonne'. The coupling is honest only if that avoided cost exceeds about $5/t; otherwise this is plain Class VI storage that sits next to a DLE unit.
patched_idea.conventional_core: High-purity point-source saline-aquifer CO2 storage (Class VI) in the Smackover below the Buckner anhydrite, with pressure and plume management. Precedents: Buscheck et al. 2012 ACRM, the DOE Brine Extraction Storage Test, and Gorgon's produced-water lessons.
patched_idea.graft: Direct lithium extraction (DLE) from Smackover oilfield and bromine brines (Standard Lithium/Equinor, ExxonMobil, Albemarle, Lanxess). The graft is reframed. What the brine unit offers storage is (a) existing unitization, i.e. pore-space aggregation, the main Class VI bottleneck, (b) wells, core, logs and seismic, (c) a mapped legacy-well inventory for the area of review, and (d) at end of life, lithium-depleted patterns that can be stored in without stranding grade.
patched_idea.mechanism:
Phase 1 (about 2028-2035), siting rule:
- CO2 from Gulf Coast ammonia, gas-processing and hydrogen plants (separation floor about 0.002-0.007 GJ/t) is injected into Smackover compartments that are down-dip of or outside the lithium brine unit, below the economic lithium cut-off (about 150 mg/L or less) or outside the unit boundary.
- Stand-off is at least 7 km from active producers, or injection rates are capped so the modelled plume edge stays more than 2 km from the nearest producer after 25 years.
- The plume does not reach live patterns. Pressure diffusion (roughly 8-22 km in the first year) still connects the two hydraulically, so any pressure interaction is monitored, not claimed as a benefit.
- Spent brine is reinjected inside the unit exactly as already permitted. There is no new shallower disposal zone and no change in grade dilution.

Phase 2 (later), sequencing rule:
- Storage rolls into patterns that spent-brine reinjection has already flushed to 30% or less of original grade.
- Brine the CO2 displaces there is run through DLE once more before reinjection.
- Stranded lithium at residual saturation then becomes small, and breakthrough no longer threatens live producers.

Throughout:
- Injection stays out of hydrocarbon-bearing compartments, with no EOR.
- Bromine and lithium operators hold a contractual veto on any pattern still above cut-off.
- The commercial coupling is a pore-space and data licence from the brine unit to the storage operator, valued as avoided Class VI pore-space aggregation and characterization cost.
patched_idea.target:
Roughly 25 Mt/yr of Gulf Coast concentrated industrial CO2 within reach of the Smackover trend (Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, East Texas). Phase-2 capacity is limited by how fast patterns get flushed and by the Smackover's storage capacity below the Buckner, not by DLE brine voidage.

A secondary target is a modest non-lithium revenue line (pore-space and data licence) for first-wave Arkansas DLE projects. Malone et al. (2026) find these projects unprofitable at 2025 lithium prices.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
Computed in scratchpad/climate/critic_li_swap.py (critic) and patch_li_swap.py (this patch). Subsurface parameters are assumed literature-range values, not site data.

Dropped headline claims:
- The original '$9-59/t CO2 lithium in the voidage' credit is withdrawn.
- The '24 Mt/yr from DLE voidage' scale claim is withdrawn.
- The 'continuous pressure relief' claim is withdrawn.

Why the original geometry fails: CO2 is immiscible, so it strands residual brine of 0.57-1.41 m3 per t stored. At full grade (150-400 mg/L, 80% recovery, $9k/t LCE) that is $3-22/t of lithium lost, against $10-26/t in the voidage itself.

Phase-2 stranding: in patterns flushed to 30% of original grade, stranded lithium falls to $1.0-6.5/t undiscounted, and is about $1-2.4/t at 150 mg/L original grade. The patch metric needs under $2/t at 8% discount. Since PV factors are 0.15-0.32 at years 15-25, Phase-2 stranding should pass.

Plume stand-off (volumetric cylinder with a gravity-override multiplier):
- 0.5 Mt/yr per injector: 1.1-4.5 km after 10-25 years.
- 1.0 Mt/yr per injector: 1.6-6.4 km after 10-25 years.
- In the thin-reservoir, strong-override case (30 m thick, Sg 0.3, plume reach doubled), 1 Mt/yr reaches 6.4 km in 25 years. So the critic's 5 km stand-off is not safe there; the patch sets at least 7 km or a rate cap.

Pressure diffusion reach in the first year (sqrt(4Dt), k 50-300 mD): 8-22 km. The compartments are hydraulically connected to the unit.

Avoided-cost coupling (order-of-magnitude assumptions):
- Avoided characterization and pore-space aggregation of $15-60M per site spread over 15-30 Mt gives about $1-4/t undiscounted.
- That is likely below the $5/t kill threshold unless unitized pore space carries a large legal premium (for example, avoiding years of Class VI delay).

Unchanged from the original:
- CO2 density at reservoir conditions: 575-588 kg/m3.
- Compression floor: about 0.28 GJ/t to 150 bar.
- The base case as plain Class VI storage: about $43/t, with a positive 45Q margin (critic's estimate).
- Side check (negative result): the voidage brine's heat is worth about 9 kWh_e/t, against about 120 kWh/t of compression.
patched_idea.who_gains:
S3 and S4: Gulf Coast ammonia, hydrogen and gas-processing emitters get Smackover storage with faster pore-space access. DLE and bromine operators (ExxonMobil, Equinor/Standard Lithium, Albemarle, Lanxess) get a licence revenue line with no grade loss in live patterns and an end-of-life use for flushed patterns.

S7 gets US critical minerals plus CCS, and Arkansas and Louisiana revenue. S6 gets south Arkansas oilfield workforce reuse. S10 gets risk spread across DLE and CCS.

S1 is cautiously positive: storage is dedicated, with no EOR, and is separated from lithium production. S11 avoids a new shallow disposal zone near drinking-water sources.
patched_idea.who_loses:
Hard-rock and evaporite lithium producers (Australia, Chile and Argentina, which matters for S8) see only marginal effect, since lithium output is unchanged by the patch. S11 in south Arkansas still faces CO2-pipeline risk (Satartia-type) and brine-handling concerns. Part of S1 objects that fossil point sources gain storage subsidies (45Q).

Unit royalty owners must agree to Phase-2 storage in flushed patterns. Residual correlative-rights exposure is about $1-6/t undiscounted.
patched_idea.closest_known_work: Buscheck et al. 2012 (Int J GHG Control): active CO2 reservoir management with brine extraction. Rock Springs Uplift pressure-management field demonstration (2017). DOE BEST brine extraction test (2022). Huang et al. 2026: review of lithium plus geothermal co-production in the Smackover. Malone et al. 2026: scoping review of Arkansas oilfield-brine DLE. Liu et al. 2026 (Chem Eng J): CO2 mineralization plus lithium from produced water. Arkansas and Louisiana brine-unitization and CO2-storage pore-space statutes, which are the legal substrate for the licence.
patched_idea.why_different:
ACRM treats extracted brine as a cost, and DLE treats reinjection as a cost. The original 'two-way swap' was physically wrong: CO2 strands lithium. This version couples the two through space and time instead.

Storage avoids live lithium patterns until they are depleted, and the brine unit's already-solved pore-space aggregation, data and legacy-well mapping are transferred to storage. The novelty is the siting and sequencing rule plus the licence, and it is modest.

No paper coupling DLE units to CO2 storage phasing was found (OpenAlex title searches only; weak evidence). The patch's own estimate puts the coupling's value at about $1-4/t, so the honest prior is that this folds into generic point-source Class VI storage.
patched_idea.cheapest_falsifying_test:
Simulation (2-4 weeks, OPM Flow or MRST): a Smackover sector model with a DLE line-drive and spent-brine reinjection, plus a down-dip CO2 injector, using published porosity, permeability and lithium data. Kill or fold if any of the following holds:
(a) CO2 reaches any active producer within 25 years at 7 km stand-off and 0.5-1 Mt/yr.
(b) Phase-2 stranded lithium is $2/t CO2 or more at an 8% discount rate.
(c) The pressure rise from the CO2 injector cuts DLE producer deliverability or raises reinjection pressure beyond permitted limits.

Desk study (2 weeks): price the avoided Class VI pore-space aggregation, characterization wells, seismic and AoR legacy-well work for a unitized versus a greenfield Smackover site, from Class VI permit dockets and Arkansas Oil and Gas Commission unit orders. If the avoided cost is under $5/t, report the idea as plain Class VI storage next to a DLE unit and merge it into the point-source storage family.

The bench test on lithium uptake from CO2-equilibrated brine applies only to Phase-2 re-processing. Kill that step if uptake drops more than 30% and pH correction costs more than about $2/t CO2.

fix.change_summary:
I applied the critic's patch. Storage siting and phasing now follow two rules. Phase 1 puts CO2 injectors in compartments down-dip of or outside the lithium unit, below the cut-off. Phase 2 stores only in patterns already flushed to 30% or less of original grade, and re-runs the displaced brine through DLE. Spent brine is reinjected inside the unit as already permitted, so the new shallow disposal zone is gone.

The '$9-59/t lithium in the voidage', '24 Mt/yr voidage scale' and 'continuous pressure relief' claims are withdrawn. The coupling is renamed as a pore-space and data licence valued as avoided Class VI cost, with the critic's kill metrics added.

My own calculations (scratchpad/climate/patch_li_swap.py) changed two things. First, the critic's 5 km stand-off is not safe in a thin reservoir with gravity override: at 1 Mt/yr the plume reaches about 6.4 km in 25 years, so I tightened the rule to at least 7 km or a rate cap. Second, Phase-2 stranded lithium comes to $1-6.5/t undiscounted, which should pass the under-$2/t test once discounted.

I also estimated the avoided-cost coupling at only about $1-4/t (order-of-magnitude assumptions). That is below the $5/t threshold, so the idea is now stated as likely to fold into generic point-source Class VI storage unless the desk study finds a large premium for unitized pore space.

The conventional core (Smackover saline storage with brine management) and the DLE graft are kept. The mechanism did change, from 'CO2 replaces the reinjectate' to spatial and temporal separation plus a pore-space licence.

phys2.assumptions:
All numbers below are exactly as the script printed them. Subsurface values are assumed literature ranges, not site data. Labels: [src] sourced; [recall] from pre-cutoff knowledge, not re-verified; [assume] my assumption.

FLOORS
- Separation floor from the verifier: ammonia/SMR process CO2 (98%) 0.0025 GJ/t; gas-processing acid gas (95%) 0.0065 GJ/t.
- Ideal isothermal compression from 1 to 150 bar: 0.282 GJ/t (78 kWh/t).
- CO2 at 115 C and 280 bar (CoolProp): 575 kg/m3, 1.740 m3/t.
- The card's figures of 0.002-0.007 GJ/t and about 0.28 GJ/t are confirmed.

ENERGY (low / base / high)
- Totals: 0.351 / 0.440 / 0.596 GJ/t, i.e. 97 / 122 / 166 kWh/t. That is 1.24x / 1.56x / 2.11x the compression floor.
- Compression: 95 / 115 / 140 kWh/t [recall, NETL/IEAGHG ranges].
- Dehydration: 0.005-0.02 GJ/t.
- Pipeline boosting: 2-5 kWh/t per 100 km over 50 / 150 / 400 km [assume].

COST, plain Class VI (2025$; capex at CRF 8%/20 yr = 0.1019; characterization and legacy-well work annualized over the site's injection life)
- Totals: low $16.1/t, base $42.0/t, high $163.5/t.
- Base breakdown: compression 12.6, boosting 0.3, dehydration 2.0, pipeline 9.5, injectors 4.6, MRV 5.0, characterization 3.1, AoR corrective action 1.5, pore lease 1.5, permit/financial-responsibility/PISC 2.0.
- Cost inputs [assume/recall]:
  - Gulf Coast power $45-90/MWh.
  - Compressors $1.5-3.5k/kW.
  - Pipeline $1-2.5M/km over 50-400 km.
  - Injectors $10-25M each.
  - MRV $3-10/t.
  - Greenfield characterization $15-60M per site.
  - 20-400 legacy wells at $75-300k each.
- The high case is dominated by pipeline cost ($84.6/t): 400 km at 1.5 Mt/yr. It is a deliberate worst-case stack.

COUPLING (triangular Monte Carlo, N = 200k)
- Avoided cost undiscounted: P50 $0.73/t (P5-P95 0.40-1.23).
- Avoided cost per discounted tonne: P50 $1.56/t.
- Value of a 0-2 yr permitting speed-up: P50 $2.28/t.
- Total: P50 $3.92/t (P5-P95 2.06-6.79). P(total > $5/t) = 26%.
- Coupled cost = plain cost minus coupling value: $12.1 / $38.1 / $163.5 per t.

45Q [recall: $85/t, 12-year credit period, construction must start before 1 Jan 2033]
- Margin during the credit window: low +$69/t, base +$43/t, high -$78/t.
- After year 12 the base case loses $42/t unless another carbon price exists.

SCALE
- The 25 Mt/yr target is 0.067% of fossil CO2.
- I report 0.01 Gt/yr as realistic, because pressure limits it (see violations).
phys2.violations:
No claim falls below a thermodynamic floor. Several claims are inconsistent with the card's own rules or overstated.

1. The 7 km stand-off does not meet the 2 km plume margin in every case. In the thin-reservoir, strong-override case at 1 Mt/yr, the plume edge reaches 6.4 km at 25 years, leaving 0.6 km. In that case only the rate cap works; "7 km OR rate cap" should read "7 km AND the margin check". Thief-zone cases give 2.3-4.7 km at 25 years, so they pass.

2. The Phase-2 stranding discount is mis-timed. The card applies PV factors of 0.15-0.32 counted from today, but the CO2 tonnes are stored at that same future date. Discounted like-for-like, stranding is $1.13-6.49/t, not under $2/t. Phase 2 still passes, for a different reason: flushed grade is 45-120 mg/L, below the card's own 150 mg/L cut-off, so the stranded lithium has roughly zero economic value. At $20k/t LCE and a cut-off that falls below 120 mg/L, stranding could reach up to $14.41/t.

3. The coupling largely contradicts Phase-1 geometry. By the card's own rule the plume sits outside or down-dip of the brine unit, so the unit's pore-space aggregation does not cover it. Only part of the data, the legacy-well inventory (not the plugging cost) and DLE wells used as pressure monitors carry over. Undiscounted, that is P50 $0.73/t, below the card's $1-4/t. The coupling clears $5/t (26% probability) only if it speeds up permitting by more than a year. That is doubtful in Arkansas: EPA's list fetched 2026-10-05 shows Class VI primacy only in AZ, LA, ND, TX, WV and WY, so Arkansas permits go through EPA Region 6 whatever the brine unit offers.

4. The 25 Mt/yr target is limited by pressure, not by flushing. Theis model, 40 bar cap at 5 km after 25 years:
- Per-hub caps: 0.8 Mt/yr at 50 mD, 1.8 at 100 mD, 6.6 at 300 mD.
- Hubs needed for 25 Mt/yr: 33 / 14 / 4.
- Pressure reach after 25 years is 48-102 km, so hubs must be spaced about twice that apart.

5. Phase 2 adds only 0.42-0.94 Mt/yr of capacity per DLE plant, decades from now. The target is therefore almost entirely plain Phase-1 Class VI storage.

6. Pressure at DLE producers 7 km away is not negligible. At 1 Mt/yr after 25 years it is 5.3 bar at 300 mD, 19.3 bar at 100 mD and 44.0 bar at 50 mD. This bears directly on kill criterion (c), the limit on reinjection pressure.

7. The licence revenue is too small to change DLE economics. At $1-5/t and 1-2 Mt/yr it brings $1-10M/yr, which is 0.4-4.4% of a 25 kt/yr LCE plant's revenue of $225M/yr at $9k/t. It cannot fix the unprofitability Malone et al. report.
phys2.resource_needs:
At 25 Mt/yr and 0.44 GJ/t:
- **Energy:** 11.0 PJ/yr. That is 0.00177% of world primary energy, or 0.0102% of world electricity if all electric.
- **Wells:** 25-50 injectors at 0.5-1 Mt/yr each.
- **Plume footprint:** about 7,996 km2 after 25 years, at 2% storage efficiency, 40 m thickness and 17% porosity (3 Mt/yr: about 960 km2; 10 Mt/yr: about 3,198 km2).
- **Area of review:** pressure fronts of 48-102 km, and many hubs at 4-33 for 25 Mt/yr.
- **Water:** none consumed.
- **Land:** well pads plus pipeline right of way.
- **Materials:** steel for 50-400 km of pipeline per hub, plus the wells.
phys2.key_uncertainties:
1. **Speed-up from the brine unit's legal and data assets.** Whether they actually shorten Class VI permitting by more than a year is the only route to a coupling worth more than $5/t. Arkansas has no primacy, and a lithium brine unit is legally distinct from CO2 pore-space rights. Pore-space ownership and compulsory-pooling rules were not verified this session.

2. **Smackover reservoir properties near sites.** Permeability, thickness, compartmentalization and high-permeability streaks control plume reach (1.1-6.4 km), pressure at producers (2.2-44 bar) and hub capacity (0.8-6.6 Mt/yr). Fault-bounded blocks would be worse than the infinite-acting Theis model assumes.

3. **Concentrated CO2 actually within reach.** The Smackover trend lies roughly 150-400 km from the Mississippi River industrial corridor [assume]. Coastal emitters can store more cheaply in Miocene/Frio sands nearby. Local sources such as Haynesville gas treating, south Arkansas ammonia and refining, and East Texas plants may total well under 25 Mt/yr. This was not verified, and pipeline cost dominates the high case.

4. **Policy timing.** Under current law [recall], 45Q requires construction to start before 2033 and pays for 12 years. Phase 1 straddles that deadline, and Phase 2 (about 2045-2055) has no 45Q.

5. **Long-term buoyant drift up-dip.** Free-phase CO2 drifts 3-61 m/yr toward the brine unit and the structural oil traps (1-18 km over 300 years, before trapping). This enlarges the area of review and the post-injection monitoring liability.

6. **Lithium price and cut-off.** The $9k/t LCE price is the 2025 US average [src: earlier OptiLex script, USGS]. At $20k/t, and with a lower cut-off, Phase-2 stranding could matter again.

7. **Monte Carlo inputs.** The avoided-cost ranges in the Monte Carlo are order-of-magnitude assumptions. The web-search budget was exhausted this session; only the EPA primacy page was fetched.

Bottom line: the storage physics and economics hold up as generic point-source Class VI storage, at about $42/t base with a positive 45Q margin. The DLE coupling is worth about $1-4/t and most likely folds into the point-source storage family, as the card's own kill rule anticipates.

idea.title: Dissolve AGRU vent CO2 into produced water already going down saltwater-disposal wells (Permian)
idea.one_line: The Permian already pumps roughly a cubic kilometre of brine underground each year. Dissolving the basin's vented gas-processing CO2 into that stream, Carbfix-style, stores CO2 as dense, non-buoyant dissolved carbon without new water, new wells or a buoyant plume.
idea.conventional_core: Oilfield produced-water gathering and Class II saltwater disposal (SWD) wells, operated by majors and water midstream firms. Gas-plant amine units (AGRU) already separate near-pure CO2 that is often vented.
idea.graft: Carbfix's in-well dissolution: CO2 is released down a dip-tube below about 350-1,000 m, where hydrostatic pressure dissolves it in the down-flowing water before it reaches the formation. Burton & Bryant's 2009 surface-dissolution concept is the related method.
idea.mechanism:
1. Dehydrate and compress AGRU off-gas (more than 95% CO2) to about 35-100 bar.
2. Release it into the tubing of selected deep SWD wells at a depth where it dissolves fully. Water velocity of about 6 m/s in 3.5-inch tubing at 20k bbl/d far exceeds the bubble rise speed of about 0.2-0.3 m/s.
3. The CO2-charged brine is denser than formation brine and sinks. No free-phase plume forms, so no perfect caprock is needed.
4. Limit design loading to about 70-80% of saturation at the dissolution point, so no free gas can exsolve downstream where pressure only rises.
5. Use only deep disposal zones with verified containment (not over-pressured shallow zones).
idea.target: The 5-15 Mt/yr of processing-plant CO2 in the Permian and other shale basins, plus any basin where disposal water and concentrated CO2 are co-located.
idea.quantitative_claims:
All figures are my calculations from the same script.

CO2 solubility (Spycher 2003 equilibrium constant, PR fugacity, Sechenov salting-out 0.10-0.12 kg/mol):
- Check against pure water: 1.17 mol/kg at 25C and 50 bar (literature about 1.25); 1.10 at 50C and 100 bar (literature about 1.05-1.1).
- In 1.5-4 molal NaCl brines: 12-26 kg CO2 per t water at 30C and 35 bar; 14-31 at 40C and 60 bar; 17-36 at 45C and 100 bar.
- Design loading is therefore 10-25 kg/m3, depending on salinity and dissolution depth: 40-100 t of carrier water per t CO2 (Carbfix uses about 25 t/t).
- Added volume from dissolved CO2 is only about 0.8 m3 per t, so disposal pressure is essentially unchanged.

Scale and source match:
- Permian disposal of 12-20 MMbbl/d (assumed; industry estimates put total Permian produced water above 20 MMbbl/d, not re-verified) is 0.70-1.16 km3/yr. That supports 7-29 Mt CO2/yr.
- That matches the basin's gas-processing CO2 of 8-16 Mt/yr (my estimate: 27 Bcf/d raw gas at an assumed 1.5-3% CO2; part already goes to EOR or acid-gas injection).

Energy:
- Compression floor 0.20 GJ/t to 35 bar and 0.26 to 100 bar, against 0.28 for supercritical injection at 150 bar. Separation is about 0 for AGRU off-gas.
- Scale check: 25 Mt/yr at 0.25 GJ/t is 6 PJ/yr (0.001% of world primary energy).

Cost claim: below $35/t (compression about $10-15/t, plus dip-tube, corrosion-resistant tubing and monitoring retrofits), against 45Q $85/t. This is an assumption to test.
idea.who_gains:
S3 Permian operators and gas processors (Oxy, Exxon, Chevron, and water midstream such as Aris and WaterBridge): 45Q income on CO2 they now vent, using wells and water they already handle.
S6 Permian workers.
S7: no new water use in an arid basin.
S1/S2: storage without EOR, no added oil, and a non-buoyant storage form.
S11: CO2 vents near gas plants are eliminated.
idea.who_loses:
S11 if containment fails. Texas regulators have curtailed deep disposal in seismic response areas, and shallow disposal zones have over-pressured, with brine breakouts at the surface. CO2-charged brine reaching the surface would degas (a CO2 hazard), so only proven-containment deep zones qualify.
SWD operators bear corrosion and retrofit cost.
Regulatory risk: Class II wells would need Class VI permitting or an equivalent ruling to earn 45Q.
idea.closest_known_work:
- Carbfix (Iceland): in-well dissolution into basalt, measured more than 95% mineralised within 2 years (Matter et al. 2016).
- Burton & Bryant (2009, SPE): surface dissolution of CO2 into extracted aquifer brine, with a cost assessment.
- 'Dissolved-water CO2 injection' studies (Energy & Fuels, about 2024-25).
- Permian acid-gas injection (AGI) wells: free-phase, not dissolved.
- A Crossref search found no deployment that dissolves CO2 into oilfield disposal water.
idea.why_different: Carbfix's binding constraint is water: about 25 t per t, or 25 km3/yr per Gt. This idea uses water that is already being lifted, treated and pumped underground for disposal, in wells that already exist, next to concentrated CO2 that is already separated and vented. The carrier water's marginal cost is zero, and the storage form is dissolved and sinking rather than a buoyant plume.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test:
1. Desk study (about 1 month): pull Texas RRC disposal-well volumes and injection pressures, plus produced-water chemistry from the USGS Produced Waters Database. Compute well by well the deliverable dissolved CO2 at 80% saturation with PHREEQC or the script above.
   - Kill criterion: fewer than 3 Mt/yr of CO2 can be carried by deep wells that have verified containment and lie outside seismic response areas.
2. Bench test (about 2 months): corrosion coupons in CO2-saturated Permian brine.
   - Kill criterion: the retrofit cost per well exceeds about $5/t over 10 years.
idea.family: Dissolve concentrated CO2 (gas-plant/AGRU vent) into produced water already going down Permian saltwater-disposal wells (Carbfix-style dissolved storage)

art.label: IMPORT

closest.title: DOE NETL 'Carbonated Brine Injection' (CBI) programme: Xiong, Belarbi, Thomas et al., 'Assessment of Carbonated Brine Injection as Low-risk Strategy for Geologic Carbon Storage' (2023, OSTI 2204489)
closest.overlap: This is the idea under another name. The programme is DOE FECM/NETL-funded and dissolves CO2 into produced water, then injects it down saltwater-disposal (SWD) wells at an operating SWD facility: the BEST site near Watford City, Williston Basin. It concludes that 'CO2 dissolved in produced water can be injected without appreciably increasing subsurface pressure or leakage risks'. It also finds that dissolution trapping is immediate, which avoids buoyant migration, and that the dissolved-CO2 limit depends on salinity, pressure and temperature. These are the idea's core claims.

closest.title: NETL / Univ. North Dakota / NGL Energy Partners: 'Carbonated Brine Injection Pilot Plan' (2024, OSTI 2427261) and 'CBI for a Pilot Site ... Pena Creek, Dimmit County TX, Edwards Limestone' (2024, OSTI 2446568)
closest.overlap: A three-year effort to plan a pilot of CBI, in partnership with NGL Energy Partners, one of the largest Texas and Permian SWD/water-midstream operators. The site is a Texas SWD location. The work covers geomodelling, dissolved-CO2 molality and pressure modelling, wellbore corrosion, and the reactive-transport fate of the dissolved CO2. That is essentially the idea's 'desk study + corrosion' falsification plan, already done by DOE with an incumbent water-midstream partner.

closest.title: Belarbi et al., 'Investigation of Scale Deposition and Wellbore Corrosion in Carbonated Brine Injection' (CCUS 2024, OSTI 2323923); Xiong et al., 'CBI ... Inyan Kara Sandstone' (OSTI 2323919)
closest.overlap: Defines CBI as dissolving CO2 in produced water and injecting it into deep reservoirs to 'leverage the existing saltwater disposal infrastructure'. Covers Class II well material compatibility, scale and corrosion. States explicitly that the opportunity is to work with industry on 'CBI using existing Class II wells to gain CO2 tax credits', which is the idea's 45Q business case.

closest.title: Hydrozonix LLC patent US12246975B2, 'Carbon sequestration systems with oil and gas operations' (priority Jan 2018, granted Mar 2025)
closest.overlap: A patent held by a Permian water-management firm. It claims treating produced water, supersaturating it with CO2 (as nanobubbles) and injecting it into Class II disposal wells, frac wells or EOR wells to sequester carbon. It covers the produced-water + SWD + dissolved-CO2 combination, so freedom to operate needs checking.

closest.title: Eke, Naylor, Haszeldine & Curtis, 'CO2/Brine Surface Dissolution and Injection: CO2 Storage Enhancement' (SPE 124711, 2009/2011); Burton & Bryant (2009) surface dissolution
closest.overlap: Engineering and cost basis for dissolving CO2 into brine at the surface and injecting it as carbonated brine: energy balance, equipment sizing, materials and mixing costs. These papers predate the SWD-specific framing.

closest.title: Carbfix (Matter et al. 2016; Sigfusson et al. 2015): in-well dissolution via a dip-tube
closest.overlap: Source of the downhole-dissolution mechanism: CO2 released below about 350 m into down-flowing water. The idea grafts this onto SWD tubing. Carbfix itself uses dedicated water and basalt, not oilfield disposal water.

closest.title: Dissolved-water CO2 injection (Energy & Fuels 2025, doi 10.1021/acs.energyfuels.4c05249; EAGE 2025)
closest.overlap: Recent saline-aquifer studies of injecting CO2 pre-dissolved in water, framed around salt-precipitation mitigation. Same storage form, different motivation.

art.what_is_new:
The core concept already exists in published DOE work. Dissolving CO2 into oilfield produced water and injecting it down existing Class II saltwater-disposal wells, to get non-buoyant dissolved storage and 45Q credits, is the subject of NETL's 'Carbonated Brine Injection' (CBI) programme, 2023-2024. That programme was run with the University of North Dakota and NGL Energy Partners, a major Texas and Permian SWD operator. It already covers simulation, corrosion and scale, reactive transport, and a pilot plan for a Texas SWD site (Pena Creek, Dimmit County). Hydrozonix (a Permian water firm) also holds a granted patent, priority 2018, on CO2-supersaturated produced water injected into Class II disposal wells. The idea's own 'closest known work' missed both, and its claim that 'no deployment dissolves CO2 into oilfield disposal water' is true only in the narrow sense that I found no commercial field deployment. A pilot is planned, and the concept is published and patented.

Possibly new, but these are engineering refinements, not a new concept:
1. Dissolving the CO2 downhole, Carbfix-style, through a dip-tube in the SWD tubing. The NETL abstracts I could read do not say whether mixing is at the surface or downhole. Burton & Bryant and Eke et al. assume surface mixing.
2. Pairing CBI specifically with gas-processing (AGRU) vent CO2 as the source.
3. Sizing it at Permian basin scale, roughly 0.7-1.2 km3/yr of disposal water against 8-16 Mt/yr of CO2, plus the 70-80% saturation design rule.

Recommendation: do not build this as an original idea. Read the NETL CBI reports, especially the Pena Creek and BEST pilot plans and the corrosion study. Contact NETL (Wei Xiong) and NGL about the pilot's status, and check whether Hydrozonix's patent blocks it. The cheapest test the idea proposes has largely been done already.

Caveat: the session's WebSearch budget was used up. This search ran through the OSTI API, Crossref and Google Patents only, so recent 2025-26 trade-press deployments, such as any Permian SWD operator CBI announcement or a Texas Railroad Commission (RRC) ruling, may have been missed.

phys.assumptions:
All figures below are as printed by the script.

FLOORS
- Separation floor: upgrading AGRU off-gas from 96% to 99.9% CO2 costs 0.0081 GJ/t. The separation energy is already spent in the AGRU, so the binding floor is compression.
- Compression floor, real-gas isothermal (Redlich-Kwong fugacity, inlet 1.5 bar, 35C):
  - 0.174 GJ/t to 35 bar
  - 0.198 to 60 bar
  - 0.210 to 100 bar
  - 0.217 to 150 bar
- The idea's figures (0.20 / 0.26 / 0.28 GJ/t) are ideal gas from 1 bar. They are slightly conservative, not below the floor.

ENERGY (floor divided by isothermal efficiency, plus auxiliaries)
- Low: 35 bar, efficiency 0.75 = 0.243 GJ/t (67 kWh/t)
- Base: 60 bar, efficiency 0.65 = 0.325 GJ/t (90 kWh/t)
- High: 100 bar, efficiency 0.55 = 0.422 GJ/t (117 kWh/t)
- These match the NETL/IEAGHG order of magnitude for CO2 compression (about 90-120 kWh/t to about 150 bar). Not re-fetched this session.

SOLUBILITY (Spycher et al. 2003 with RK fugacity; Sechenov ks 0.10-0.12; NaCl 1.5-4 molal)
- Validation in pure water:
  - 25C, 50.7 bar: 1.220 mol/kg (literature about 1.2-1.3)
  - 50C, 101.3 bar: 1.144 mol/kg (literature about 1.07; the model runs about 7% high because it sets phi_H2O = 1)
- Saturation in brine, kg CO2 per m3:
  - 30C / 35 bar: 11.4-25.5
  - 40C / 60 bar: 13.9-31.0
  - 45C / 100 bar: 16.2-36.1
- Water needed at 75% of saturation:
  - 52-117 m3/t (35 bar)
  - 43-96 m3/t (60 bar)
  - 37-82 m3/t (100 bar)
- For comparison, Carbfix uses about 25 t water per t CO2 (Matter et al. 2016, fresh water; per the Wikipedia summary fetched this session).
- Fluid volume added: 0.75 m3/t dissolved, against 1.30 m3/t free-phase at 250 bar and 60C. That is about half the pore volume, but disposal-zone overpressure is driven by the water itself.

STABILITY OF THE DISSOLVED CO2 (loading = 0.34 mol/kg)
- It stays dissolved going down: saturation is 0.64 / 0.71 / 0.80 mol/kg at 1,500 / 3,000 / 4,000 m.
- It comes out of solution if the brine rises to about 150 m (saturation 0.27) or 50 m (0.11). A leak to the surface would therefore degas.

TUBING HYDRAULICS (20,000 bbl/d)
- Water velocity and friction over 3,000 m:
  - 3.5in tubing: 8.11 m/s, 260 bar friction
  - 4.5in: 4.64 m/s, 62 bar
  - 5.5in: 3.03 m/s, 21 bar
  - 7in: 1.84 m/s, 6 bar
- The idea's '6 m/s in 3.5in' detail is wrong; real wells at that rate use 4.5-7in tubing. Even there, the 1.8-4.6 m/s velocity still exceeds bubble slip (about 0.2-0.35 m/s), so the mechanism survives.
- Release depth below the liquid level: 324 m for 35 bar, 556 m for 60 bar, 927 m for 100 bar.

SCALE: SOURCE (27 Bcf/d Permian gas, an EIA order of magnitude not re-fetched; CO2 content 1.5-3%, assumed)
- Raw CO2 in the gas: 7.8-15.6 Mt/yr. This matches the idea's 8-16.
- Only CO2 above pipeline or cryogenic spec is removed (50/70/90%), and part already goes to acid-gas injection or EOR (vented share 40/60/80%).
- Ventable AGRU CO2: 1.6 / 4.4 / 11.2 Mt/yr. Not verified against EPA GHGRP Subpart W.

SCALE: SINK (12/16/20 MMbbl/d of disposal water = 0.70/0.93/1.16 km3/yr; assumed, not re-verified)
- Qualifying share (deep, contained, outside seismic response areas): 20/35/50%
- Uptime match between water flow and CO2 supply: 60/75/85%
- Loading: 10/15/25 kg/m3
- Capacity: 0.8 / 3.7 / 12.3 Mt/yr. The idea's 7-29 Mt/yr assumes all disposal water qualifies.
- Permian deliverable, min(source, sink): 0.8 / 3.7 / 11.2 Mt/yr.
- Global, assuming about 250 MMbbl/d of produced water (commonly cited order of magnitude), 20-40% of it disposed, and 10/25/50% co-located with concentrated CO2: 0.003 / 0.016 / 0.073 Gt/yr.

COST (one gas-plant hub of 0.3 Mt/yr)
- Assumptions, low / base / high:
  - Electricity: $40 / 60 / 90 per MWh
  - Compression capex: $2,000 / 3,000 / 4,500 per kW
  - Per-well water: 30k / 20k / 15k bbl/d
  - Well retrofit (CRA tubing, dip-tube string, packer, wellhead, MIT and cement logs): $0.8M / 2M / 4M per well
  - Spur pipelines: 1.5 / 2.5 / 4 km per well at $0.25M / 0.4M / 0.7M per km
  - Trunk pipeline: 5 / 10 / 20 km at $0.6M / 1.0M / 1.5M per km
  - MRV capex: $3M / 10M / 25M
  - MRV opex: $0.3M / 1M / 2.5M per year
  - O&M: 2.5 / 3.5 / 5% of capex
  - Chemicals: $0.5 / 1 / 3 per t
  - Capital recovery: 6% over 25 yr / 8% over 20 yr / 10% over 12 yr (12 years = the 45Q credit period)
- Results:
  - Low: 37.0 kt/yr per well, 9 wells, capex $22M, $11.7/t
  - Base: 13.1 kt/yr per well, 23 wells, capex $99M, $55.0/t (capital $33.7, electricity $5.4, O&M $11.6, MRV $3.3, chemicals $1.0)
  - High: 5.2 kt/yr per well, 58 wells, capex $469M, $329.8/t
- The high case compounds every pessimistic assumption, so it is a corner case.

SIMPLE BASELINE (dedicated free-phase injection to 150 bar, AGI or Class VI style; 1/2/3 new wells at $6M / 12M / 25M each)
- Cost: $11.3 / 35.4 / 119.9 per t.
- 45Q pays $85/t (statutory value, unverified this session; it should include the 2025 law's EOR parity).
- Texas Class VI primacy: EPA final rule signed 7 Nov 2025 (EPA UIC page, fetched).
phys.violations:
No claim falls below a thermodynamic floor, so nothing is physically impossible. The idea contains these errors or overstatements:

1. **Tubing.** '6 m/s in 3.5-inch tubing at 20k bbl/d' is wrong. The script computes 8.11 m/s and about 260 bar of friction over 3,000 m, which is not operable. With 4.5-7 inch tubing (1.8-4.6 m/s) the mechanism still works.
2. **Permian capacity.** The 7-29 Mt/yr claim assumes all disposal water qualifies. After restricting to deep, contained wells outside seismic response areas, and allowing for uptime matching, the deliverable is 0.8 / 3.7 / 11.2 Mt/yr. The base is limited by sink capacity.
3. **Ventable source CO2.** The 8-16 Mt/yr figure counts all raw CO2 in the gas. AGRUs remove only the CO2 above spec, and some already goes to AGI or EOR. Base ventable CO2 is 4.4 Mt/yr (range 1.6-11.2).
4. **Cost.** '<$35/t' holds only in the low case: $12 low, $55 base, $330 high. In the base case the idea costs more than the simple dedicated-well baseline ($35/t). Water flow caps each well's CO2 throughput at about 13 kt/yr in the base case, so a 0.3 Mt/yr plant needs about 23 retrofitted wells, where 1-2 dedicated wells would do. Base cost is still below 45Q's $85/t.
5. **Global scale.** About 0.016 Gt/yr base (0.003-0.073), a Mt-scale niche rather than a Gt lever.
6. **Minor.** The compression floors (0.20 / 0.26 / 0.28 GJ/t) are ideal gas from 1 bar. The real-gas values are 0.174 / 0.210 / 0.217, so the idea's floors are slightly high (conservative), not wrong in the dangerous direction.
phys.key_uncertainties:
1. **Deep-well liquid level.** Many deep Permian disposal wells (Ellenburger, Devonian) take water on vacuum, so the liquid level inside the tubing can sit far below surface. The CO2 release point must be 324-927 m below that level, which means longer dip-tubes. This has not been checked well by well.
2. **Eligible disposal water.** The 20-50% eligible share is assumed. Texas RRC has cut or suspended deep disposal in the Northern Culberson-Reeves, Stanton and Gardendale seismic response areas; for example, all 23 deep disposal permits in Northern Culberson-Reeves were suspended in January 2024 (RRC page, fetched). That removes some of the deep-zone capacity the idea relies on. Shallow zones are excluded for overpressure.
3. **Source CO2 is unverified.** The vented AGRU CO2 is an estimate. It needs checking against EPA GHGRP Subpart W acid-gas-removal vent data. Many Permian streams are sour (CO2 plus H2S) and already go to AGI or thermal oxidisers.
4. **Regulation.** If storage is the primary purpose, Class II wells likely need Class VI, or Subpart RR MRV, to earn 45Q. Texas holds Class VI primacy (final rule signed 7 Nov 2025), so the Railroad Commission (RRC) decides. The required MRV and monitoring-well burden drives the cost range.
5. **Chemistry and corrosion.** Effects of CO2 plus H2S in high-TDS brine are not quantified. The bench test is the real kill criterion. Acidified brine reacting with carbonate disposal zones could change injectivity either way.
6. **Does the brine sink?** Dissolved CO2 adds only about 0.3-1% density. Salinity and temperature contrasts between injected and formation brine may dominate, so 'sinks' is not guaranteed. The real security gain is the absence of a buoyant free phase. A wellbore or fault leak that brought the brine to about 150 m would still degas.
7. **Input data not re-verified this session.**
   - Permian disposal volume (12-20 MMbbl/d) and global produced water (about 250 MMbbl/d).
   - Well retrofit, spur pipeline and MRV costs: engineering estimates, not quotes.
8. **Solubility model.** It is about 7% high against Bamberger 2000 at 50C and 100 bar.

**Evidence weighting.** Carbfix's dissolution and mineralisation are realised results, but in basalt with fresh water. In sedimentary disposal zones with high-TDS brine, mineralisation should not be assumed; storage there is solubility trapping only.
phys.resource_needs:
- **Energy:** 0.243 / 0.325 / 0.422 GJ/t of electricity. At 25 Mt/yr that is 6.1 / 8.1 / 10.5 PJ/yr, or 0.00098-0.0017% of world primary energy, which is negligible.
- **Compression:** about 2.6-4.5 MW per 0.3 Mt/yr hub.
- **Water:** no new water. It uses 37-117 m3 of existing disposal brine per t CO2 (base 15 kg/m3 = about 67 m3/t). In the Permian base case that is about 0.25 km3/yr of disposal water carrying CO2.
- **Materials:** corrosion-resistant (CRA or lined) tubing and spur pipelines. The base case needs 23 wells and about 58 km of spurs per 0.3 Mt/yr hub, plus monitoring wells and AoR modelling for Class VI-equivalent permitting.
- **Land:** existing well pads and pipeline right-of-way only.

stances.evidence: CAN's 2021 position (1,300+ NGOs) has red line 3, which phases out public support for fossil-linked tech 'including CCS', and red line 7, which opposes EOR. This idea avoids EOR, but it is paid through 45Q and it extends the life of gas processing. NGOs that back CCS sit in the Carbon Capture Coalition with industry and unions, and its self-description includes 'conservation and environmental policy organizations'. Texas-focused environmental and civil-rights groups ran mass comment campaigns against EPA giving Texas Class VI primacy. They cited the RRC's 'insufficient enforcement of violations associated with Class II injection wells' and its lack of independence from industry (EPA final rule, FR 2025-19898, 14 Nov 2025; 7,534 written comments). Wikipedia's CCS article cites critics who see CCS as perpetuating fossil dependence, and it records that gas-processing CCS has underperformed: Shute Creek vented about half its captured CO2 when EOR sales were unprofitable, and at Gorgon two-thirds could not be injected in one year. Expect mainstream NGOs to oppose, with a minority (CATF, EDF type, not verified this session) open to it if there is no EOR and MRV is transparent.
