Sources: CAN 2021 PDF (map); https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-11-14/html/2025-19898.htm; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_capture_and_storage
stances.red_line_hit: Public subsidy for fossil-linked CCS (CAN red line 3) and fossil lock-in or mitigation deterrence for Permian gas. Distrust of the RRC as regulator. The EOR red line is NOT hit unless operators divert the CO2 to EOR, which OBBBA's 45Q parity makes financially attractive.

stances.evidence: IPCC AR6 WGIII C.4.4 backs CCS where it abates emissions. Inherent CO2 from gas processing is the lowest-cost capture: the verifier gives a separation floor of about 0 for AGRU off-gas, against 0.47 GJ/t for air. Carbfix's dissolved storage has measured results: 95% mineralised within 2 years in the 2016 basalt pilot, using about 25 t water per t CO2 (Matter et al. 2016, as summarised by Wikipedia). The scientific caveats are two. First, Permian sedimentary disposal zones are not reactive basalt, so mineralisation will be slow and security rests on dissolution and density, not on rock formation. Second, induced seismicity is documented: the RRC suspended 23 deep disposal permits in Northern Culberson-Reeves after M3.6-5.2 quakes (Dec 2023), and the 2022 Gardendale quake was M5.4. Expect scientists to support it conditionally, given MRV of dissolved CO2 and siting outside seismic response areas. Sources: IPCC SPM (map); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbfix; https://www.rrc.texas.gov/oil-and-gas/applications-and-permits/injection-storage-permits/oil-and-gas-waste-disposal/injection-disposal-permit-procedures/seismicity-review/seismicity-response/
stances.red_line_hit: None categorical. MRV and seismicity are conditions.

stances.evidence: OBBBA kept 45Q at $85/t and made it transferable for cash (GCCSI, map), and gas-processing CO2 is already a core 45Q source. Texas lobbied for and won Class VI primacy: EPA approved it on 7 Nov 2025, and industry commenters praised the RRC's experience with CO2 injection in Class II EOR. Majors already have Permian decarbonisation pledges (OGCI and OGDC methane and flaring targets, map; ExxonMobil's Permian net-zero-by-2030 pledge, from memory, page not retrievable). Three frictions matter. (a) Since OBBBA, EOR earns the same $85/t, so any operator with access to a Permian CO2-EOR market gets the same credit plus a CO2 sale price. Dissolved SWD storage only wins where there is no EOR outlet, or where the operator wants storage that does not produce oil. (b) A 45Q claim for non-EOR storage needs compliance with UIC rules, which in practice means a Class VI permit (26 CFR 1.45Q-3 does not itself name the well class). Water midstream firms may resist putting high-volume Class II disposal wells under Class VI area-of-review, monitoring and post-closure financial assurance. (c) Seismic curtailments already constrain disposal capacity, and operators will not add CO2 to wells they need for water. Sources: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/1.45Q-3; govinfo FR 2025-19898; GCCSI 45Q page (map)
stances.red_line_hit: Class VI regulatory burden and long-term liability on business-critical disposal wells. Any risk to produced-water disposal capacity. A per-tonne charge would be a red line, but none is proposed (the WEC precedent).

stances.evidence: Steel, cement and chemicals are not directly affected. Indirectly, a success would demonstrate low-cost dissolved storage, which could be reused near other co-located sources. Fermentation and ethanol CO2, which has a verifier floor of about 0, are a closer analogue than cement. S4 groups the 45Q and Carbon Capture Coalition (map), so they would not oppose. No documented S4 position on dissolved storage in oilfield water was found.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: There is no direct effect on power. Compression load, about 0.25 GJ/t (verifier), totals about 6 PJ/yr at 25 Mt, a small new load for Permian utilities. Utilities are part of the 45Q coalition (map). No documented position.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: Unions are in the Carbon Capture Coalition, which describes itself as including 'companies, unions, conservation and environmental policy organizations' (https://carboncapturecoalition.org/). The idea adds retrofit, compression and monitoring work in the Permian and threatens no existing jobs. It shares the pattern of OBBBA's surviving credits, all of which protect incumbent workforces (map).
stances.red_line_hit: None. Job losses would only follow if seismic or containment incidents curtailed disposal and therefore oil production.

stances.evidence: Texas state government actively sought Class VI primacy: the Governor and state legislators commented and EPA approved it in Nov 2025 (FR 2025-19898). 45Q was the only carbon-specific IRA credit the 2025 Congress strengthened, with bipartisan support (map). COP28 decision 1/CMA.5 para 28 endorses CCUS and 'abatement' (map). The idea also uses no new water in an arid basin. Fiscal watchdogs such as Taxpayers for Common Sense (map) object to 45Q windfalls. If retrofit costs really are below $35/t against an $85/t credit, the margin of roughly $50/t is an obvious target for that criticism. This is an S7 fiscal caveat inside overall support.
stances.red_line_hit: Fiscal: a 45Q windfall on cheap, already-separated CO2. If the full credit is claimed while capture costs about $0 and storage under $35/t, expect scrutiny of whether the same CO2 would have gone to EOR or acid-gas injection anyway (additionality).

stances.evidence: Climate-justice advocates in CAN (including its Southern members) oppose fossil-linked CCS subsidies (CAN 2021 red lines 3 and 6, map). The Baum et al. 2024 30-country survey found Global South publics more supportive of every technology but more worried that they undermine mitigation (map). Global South governments signed COP28 para 28, which includes CCUS 'particularly in hard-to-abate sectors' (map). Gas processing is fossil production, not a hard-to-abate industrial sector, so it falls outside that qualifier. Effects on S8 are indirect, as this is a US basin. It could lower the carbon intensity of LNG exports, a selling point for importers and arguably a lock-in for exporters.
stances.red_line_hit: Mitigation deterrence and fossil lock-in. The idea falls outside the COP28 'hard-to-abate' qualifier.

stances.evidence: The idea has no effect on consumer prices. It is funded through the tax credit rather than through a visible charge, which is the pattern that survives politically, as in Canada 2025 (map). No documented consumer position on gas-processing CCS was found.
stances.red_line_hit: None. Avoiding a visible price is its advantage.

stances.evidence: Investors: 45Q's cash transferability (map) makes the credit a bankable cash flow, and water midstream is an investable sector. Insurers and lenders face uncapped long-term liability. CAN red line 9 says storage liability is 'likely to shift to the public' (map), and Class VI requires post-injection site care and financial assurance. Seismicity in Permian disposal zones is a documented operating risk: the RRC suspended 23 deep disposal permits in Dec 2023. No documented insurer position on CO2 dissolved in disposal water was found. The main deal risk is permitting: whether a Class II disposal well can earn 45Q without a full Class VI conversion.
stances.red_line_hit: Unpriced long-term liability and seismic or containment exposure. Regulatory uncertainty over whether co-injecting CO2 with disposal water qualifies.

stances.evidence: For: venting of AGRU CO2 ends, and there are no new pipelines if sources and wells are co-located. Against: Permian communities already live with disposal-induced seismicity. RRC records show the M5.4 Gardendale quake (Dec 2022), with all deep disposal wells there shut in; M3.6-5.2 quakes in Northern Culberson-Reeves, with 23 permits suspended in Jan 2024; and repeated curtailments in Stanton (RRC seismic response page). The Texas Class VI primacy process drew 7,534 written comments, many from mass campaigns citing the RRC's 'inabilities to inspect wells' (FR 2025-19898). The CO2 hazard is precedented: the 2020 Satartia pipeline rupture evacuated about 200 people and hospitalised 45 (Wikipedia CCS). By my own arithmetic, brine charged to the design load of about 20 kg CO2/m3 would release roughly 10-11 m3 of CO2 gas per m3 if it degassed at the surface during a breakout. That turns the existing problem of brine breakouts into an asphyxiation hazard in low-lying areas. Local opposition also hit the closest analogue, Carbfix's Coda Terminal. Wikipedia places it at Straumsvík (the Hafnarfjörður area) and does not mention opposition; reports of resident opposition there are from memory and NOT verified this session.
stances.red_line_hit: Local safety: seismicity, surface breakouts of CO2-charged brine, and distrust of the RRC as regulator. Siting must exclude seismic response areas and over-pressured shallow zones, as the idea itself proposes.

stake.coalition_notes:
Likely coalition: support from S3 (gas processors and SWD operators), S6, S7 (Texas and federal bipartisan 45Q) and S2 (conditional). Neutral: S4, S5, S9. Split: S1, S8, S10, S11. This is the existing 45Q / Carbon Capture Coalition alliance, and the idea gains two pieces of support it otherwise lacks: S2 (non-buoyant storage with no new water) and moderate S1 (no EOR).

Key findings that change the picture:

(1) 45Q EOR parity (OBBBA 2025) works against this idea. A Permian processor with access to CO2-EOR gets the same $85/t plus a CO2 sale price. Dissolved storage therefore only wins where there is no EOR outlet, or as a deliberate no-oil choice. Commercial uptake may be lower than the physics suggests, and S1's 'no EOR' approval is fragile unless there is a binding no-EOR commitment.

(2) The real gate is regulatory, not technical. A 45Q claim for non-EOR storage requires UIC compliance (26 CFR 1.45Q-3), which in practice means Class VI. Texas has had Class VI primacy since EPA's final rule (signed 7 Nov 2025, FR 14 Nov 2025). That makes an RRC ruling on co-injecting CO2 into disposal wells feasible within one state, but SWD operators may resist putting disposal wells under the Class VI regime.

(3) S11 and S1 distrust of the RRC is documented: 7,534 comments, enforcement and inspection concerns. Seismic curtailments, including the Dec 2023 suspension of 23 deep disposal permits in Northern Culberson-Reeves, constrain both the qualifying well pool and public trust.

Design features that would widen the coalition:
- Exclude seismic response areas and shallow over-pressured zones.
- Publish monitoring data openly.
- Commit to no EOR diversion and no voluntary-offset sales (removes CAN red lines 4 and 7).
- Pair it with an OGDC-style methane and flaring commitment, the broadest documented overlap.
- Address the windfall of roughly $50/t (about $85 credit against under $35 cost, an assumption) to pre-empt the fiscal-watchdog and additionality critique.

Not verified this session: the ExxonMobil Permian 2030 pledge, the Hafnarfjörður opposition to Coda, the membership lists of the Carbon Capture Coalition and the RRC's 2025 Permian disposal-rule details. The web search budget was exhausted, so evidence came from fetches of known primary pages plus the supplied map.

critic.fatal_flaw:
None found. The three things that look fatal at first are not.

1. **Physics holds.** Compression is about 0.24-0.42 GJ/t against a 0.17 GJ/t real-gas floor, and nothing falls below a floor. The gas-to-water volume ratio at a 60 bar release is about 0.12, so the dip-tube dissolution mechanism works in 4.5-7 inch tubing.

2. **Wells that take water on vacuum are fixable.** For an under-pressured zone at 3,500-4,000 m (0.35-0.43 psi/ft), the static liquid level sits about 300-1,000 m below surface. The release point must then be at about 620-1,580 m. That means a longer dip-tube, and possibly a backpressure choke that holds the liquid level and stops CO2 when water flow stops. It is not a dead end.

3. **The prior-art result (IMPORT) does not kill the climate case.** The NETL/UND/NGL carbonated-brine-injection pilot work and the Hydrozonix patent kill the idea as an original invention. For the user's goal, they are evidence that the idea is buildable and that the incumbents already want it. The recommendation therefore changes from "invent" to "accelerate, or license, and site".

One near-fatal item cannot be resolved on paper: whether 45Q can be claimed at all on CO2 dissolved into Class II disposal water.
- The Treasury rule 26 CFR 1.45Q-3 requires compliance with the injection-well (UIC) rules.
- The EPA rule 40 CFR 144.19 makes Texas's Railroad Commission (RRC), which now has Class VI primacy, decide whether a disposal well must convert to a Class VI CO2-storage well.

If every well must convert, see the fixable flaw below. If the RRC refuses Class II treatment and Class VI construction standards cannot be met by retrofitting (corrosion-resistant casing and cement through drinking-water aquifers, 40 CFR 146.86), the idea collapses to "drill new wells". That is the simple baseline, and the idea then has no edge.
critic.top_fixable_flaw:
**The idea sizes the CO2 source first and then looks for water to carry it. Water flow caps throughput at about 13 kt of CO2 per year per disposal well, so a 0.3 Mt/yr gas plant needs about 23 retrofitted wells.** Each of those wells then becomes a CO2-storage well with its own area-of-review modelling, monitoring, financial assurance and liability. That is exactly the S3 red line (Class VI burden on business-critical disposal wells) and the S10 red line (unpriced long-term liability). It also makes the idea lose to the simple baseline of 1-2 dedicated wells.

My re-run of the TEA (critic_ia3.py), 0.3 Mt/yr hub:

| Extra per-well Class VI permitting and monitoring | Cost |
|---|---|
| None | $63/t |
| $2M per well | $84/t |
| $4M per well | $105/t |

The dedicated-well baseline is $35/t, and the 45Q credit is $85/t. With realistic per-well regulatory costs the margin over 45Q disappears.
critic.suggested_patch:
**Turn the siting around: start from the water.** Restrict the idea to high-rate commercial disposal pads, meaning multi-well pads that take 40-60k bbl/d per well into deep zones with verified containment, outside the seismic response areas. Pair each pad with a small CO2 vent of 0.05-0.2 Mt/yr within about 3 km. Dissolve the CO2 at one point, the pad, and seek one Subpart RR monitoring plan and one RRC ruling (or Class VI permit) per pad, not per well.

My re-run of the TEA (base assumptions: 8% over 20 years, $60/MWh, $2M retrofit per well, plus $0.1M per well per year of monitoring):

| Case | Idea (no extra permit / $2M permit per well) | Dedicated new well |
|---|---|---|
| 0.05 Mt/yr, 2 wells at 40k bbl/d | $58 / $69 per t | $76/t |
| 0.10 Mt/yr, 2 wells at 60k bbl/d, 20 kg/m3 | $34 / $40 per t | $44/t |
| 0.20 Mt/yr, 4 wells at 60k bbl/d | $27 / $32 per t | $28/t |

So the honest niche is small vented sources, under about 0.15 Mt/yr, next to big disposal pads. That is where a dedicated well does not pay, and it is roughly the shape of the existing NGL/NETL pilot.

Supporting changes:
1. **Make non-buoyant storage the regulatory argument.** Model the area of review for dissolved storage, which is about pressure footprint only and has no plume. Show that it is smaller than for free-phase CO2, and ask the RRC to approve a reduced area of review and less monitoring on that basis. That is the only lever that brings the monitoring cost below the baseline's.
2. **Change the desk-study kill criterion.** The proposed test is "under 3 Mt/yr basin-wide". Replace it with a pad-level test: fewer than 10 pads where a vent of at least 50 kt/yr sits within 3 km of at least 80k bbl/d of contained deep disposal. Check the vent side against EPA GHGRP Subpart W acid-gas-removal vents, not against estimates from raw CO2 content.
3. **Stop running a parallel R&D effort.** Contact NETL (Xiong) and NGL about the status of the Pena Creek pilot, and check freedom to operate against Hydrozonix US12246975B2 before spending on corrosion coupons.
4. **Add a binding no-EOR and no-offset-sale commitment.** Because EOR now earns the same 45Q credit, CO2 can easily be diverted to oil recovery. Without this commitment the moderate climate-NGO (S1) support evaporates.

patched_idea.title: Dissolve small gas-plant CO2 vents into high-rate Permian saltwater-disposal pads, permitted once per pad
patched_idea.one_line: Start from the water, not the CO2. A small vented gas-plant CO2 stream (about 0.05-0.15 Mt/yr) is paired with a nearby high-rate commercial disposal pad and dissolved, Carbfix-style, into brine the basin already pumps underground. Dissolved, non-buoyant storage is used to win one reduced-scope permit per pad. This is the niche where a dedicated CO2 well does not pay.
patched_idea.conventional_core: Oilfield produced-water gathering and Class II saltwater disposal (SWD), run by majors and water midstream firms (Aris, WaterBridge, NGL and similar). The focus is high-rate multi-well commercial pads taking 40-60k bbl/d per well into deep zones. Gas-plant amine units (AGRU) already separate near-pure CO2, which small plants often vent because a dedicated acid-gas or Class VI well does not pay at their scale.
patched_idea.graft: Carbfix's in-well dissolution: CO2 is released down a dip-tube below the depth where hydrostatic pressure dissolves it in the down-flowing water before it reaches the formation. Burton & Bryant (2009, SPE) describe the related surface-dissolution method.
patched_idea.mechanism:
Siting rule (water first):
- Select high-rate commercial SWD pads: multi-well pads taking 40-60k bbl/d per well, injecting into deep zones with verified containment, outside Texas RRC seismic response areas and away from over-pressured shallow zones.
- Pair each pad with an AGRU vent of 0.05-0.2 Mt/yr within about 3 km. Vent size comes from EPA GHGRP Subpart W acid-gas-removal reports.
- Each pad gets one pipeline, one compression skid and one permitting unit.

Process:
1. Dehydrate and compress AGRU off-gas (more than 95% CO2) to about 35-100 bar. Pipe it to the pad.
2. Release it into the tubing of 2-4 pad wells through a dip-tube at a depth where it dissolves fully.
   - At 60k bbl/d, 5.5-7 inch tubing gives 5.6-9 m/s, far above the bubble rise speed of about 0.2-0.3 m/s.
   - For under-pressured zones that take water on vacuum, the static liquid level sits about 300-1,000 m below surface. The release point then moves deeper, to about 620-1,580 m. A backpressure choke holds the liquid level, and an interlock cuts CO2 whenever water flow stops.
3. The CO2-charged brine is denser than formation brine and sinks, so no free-phase plume forms.
4. Limit design loading to about 70-80% of saturation at the dissolution point, so no free gas can exsolve downstream, where pressure only rises.

Permitting:
5. Seek one Subpart RR monitoring plan and one RRC ruling (or Class VI permit) per pad, not per well.
6. Model the area of review for dissolved storage as a pressure footprint only, with no plume. Show it is smaller than the area of review for free-phase CO2 injection, and ask the RRC for a reduced area of review and less monitoring on that basis.

Commitment:
7. Make a binding contractual commitment: no diversion to EOR and no resale as offsets. Credits are claimed only as 45Q geologic storage.
patched_idea.target:
Small vented AGRU and processing-plant CO2 sources (about 0.05-0.15 Mt/yr each) in the Permian and other shale basins that sit within about 3 km of high-rate deep disposal pads. Below about 0.15 Mt/yr, a dedicated CO2 well loses to the pad option.

Larger sources (more than about 0.2 Mt/yr) are left to dedicated AGI/Class VI wells. Those wells cost about the same per tonne and carry less regulatory novelty.

The basin-wide 8-16 Mt/yr figure is now an upper bound, not the target. The addressable volume is set by pad-vent pairs that pass the desk study.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
Unless noted, figures are my calculations. Per-well throughput and tubing velocities were re-run in patch_ia3.py.

Solubility (unchanged):
- Spycher 2003 equilibrium constant, PR fugacity, Sechenov coefficient 0.10-0.12 kg/mol.
- Checks against pure water: 1.17 mol/kg at 25C and 50 bar (literature about 1.25); 1.10 at 50C and 100 bar (literature about 1.05-1.1).
- In 1.5-4 molal NaCl brines: 12-26 kg/t at 30C and 35 bar; 14-31 at 40C and 60 bar; 17-36 at 45C and 100 bar.
- Design loading is 10-20 kg/m3. Dissolved CO2 adds about 0.8 m3 of volume per t.

Per-well capacity (bbl = 0.159 m3):

| Rate per well | Capacity at 10-20 kg/m3 |
|---|---|
| 20k bbl/d | 12-23 kt/yr (critic's figure: about 13 kt) |
| 40k bbl/d | 23-46 kt/yr |
| 60k bbl/d | 35-70 kt/yr |

A 0.05 Mt/yr vent therefore needs 1-2 pad wells, 0.1 Mt/yr needs 2-3, and 0.2 Mt/yr needs 3-6. A 0.3 Mt/yr plant on ordinary 20k bbl/d wells would need about 23 wells, which is why it is excluded.

Tubing velocity at 60k bbl/d: 24 m/s in 3.5-inch, 14 in 4.5-inch, 9.1 in 5.5-inch and 5.6 in 7-inch tubing. All are far above bubble rise.

Energy (unchanged):
- Compression is about 0.24-0.42 GJ/t, against a 0.17-0.26 GJ/t floor. Separation is about 0 for AGRU off-gas.

Cost (critic's TEA re-run; modelled, not measured; 8% over 20 years, $60/MWh, $2M retrofit per well, $0.1M per well per year of monitoring):

| Case | Pad, no extra permit cost | Pad, $2M per-well permit | Dedicated new well |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.05 Mt/yr, 2 wells at 40k bbl/d | $58/t | $69/t | $76/t |
| 0.10 Mt/yr, 2 wells at 60k bbl/d, 20 kg/m3 | $34/t | $40/t | $44/t |
| 0.20 Mt/yr, 4 wells | $27/t | $32/t | $28/t |

All cases sit below 45Q's $85/t. The edge over the baseline exists only below about 0.15 Mt/yr, and only if permitting is per pad. Per-well Class VI at $2-4M on a 23-well hub gives $84-105/t, which is why that configuration is excluded.
patched_idea.who_gains:
S3: small gas processors that now vent CO2 earn 45Q where a dedicated well does not pay. Water midstream pad owners (Aris, WaterBridge, NGL) earn a new CO2 tipping fee on existing pads.
S6: Permian field and midstream jobs.
S7: no new water use in an arid basin.
S1/S2: dedicated storage with a binding no-EOR, no-offset-resale commitment, and a non-buoyant storage form.
S11: CO2 vents near small gas plants are eliminated.
S10: liability is concentrated in a few pads with one monitoring plan each, rather than spread across dozens of wells.
patched_idea.who_loses:
S11 if containment fails. Texas has curtailed deep disposal in seismic response areas, and over-pressured shallow zones have produced surface brine breakouts. CO2-charged brine reaching the surface would degas, so only deep pads with verified containment qualify.
Pad operators bear the cost of corrosion-resistant retrofits and the downhole interlock.
Regulatory risk: if the RRC requires full Class VI conversion and well construction to 40 CFR 146.86 that cannot be met by retrofit, the idea collapses to the dedicated-well baseline.
Licence or royalty exposure to the Hydrozonix patent (US12246975B2) if freedom to operate is not clear.
patched_idea.closest_known_work:
- Carbfix (Iceland): in-well dissolution into basalt. More than 95% was measured as mineralised within 2 years (Matter et al. 2016, field result).
- Burton & Bryant (2009, SPE): surface dissolution into extracted brine, with a cost assessment.
- NETL / UND / NGL carbonated-brine injection pilot work (Pena Creek). This is the closest analogue and roughly the pad-plus-small-vent shape; its status needs confirming.
- Hydrozonix patent US12246975B2: CO2 dissolved into produced water for disposal.
- 'Dissolved-water CO2 injection' studies (Energy & Fuels, about 2024-25).
- Permian acid-gas injection (AGI) wells: free-phase storage, not dissolved.

After the critic's prior-art findings, the idea is no longer an original invention. Its role is accelerate, license and site: choose pad-vent pairs and win the per-pad, reduced-area-of-review regulatory treatment.
patched_idea.why_different:
The idea's edge is narrow and specific. For small vents below about 0.15 Mt/yr, a dedicated Class VI or AGI well has fixed permitting, drilling and monitoring costs that cannot be spread over enough tonnes. A high-rate disposal pad already has the wells, the water, the containment data and an operator.

Dissolved storage is non-buoyant and plume-free. That makes the regulatory argument for a smaller, pressure-only area of review, which is the lever that lets the pad beat the dedicated-well baseline.

Carbfix's binding constraint, about 25 t of water per t of CO2, is met by water already being disposed of at zero marginal cost.
patched_idea.cheapest_falsifying_test:
1. Prior-art and status check (about 2 weeks, nearly free; do this before any lab spend):
   - Contact NETL (Xiong) and NGL about the Pena Creek pilot's status and results.
   - Run a freedom-to-operate review against Hydrozonix US12246975B2.
   - Kill or pivot criterion: if the pilot has already de-risked the method and the patent blocks the work, pivot to a licensing and siting role only.

2. Pad-level desk study (about 1 month):
   - Match EPA GHGRP Subpart W acid-gas-removal vent reports against Texas RRC disposal volumes and pressures, and USGS produced-water chemistry.
   - Kill criterion: fewer than 10 pads where a vent of at least 50 kt/yr sits within 3 km of at least 80k bbl/d of contained deep disposal, outside seismic response areas.

3. Regulatory test (in parallel):
   - Seek an informal RRC pre-application opinion on one pad: does it allow a single permitting unit and a reduced, pressure-only area of review for dissolved storage?
   - Kill criterion: per-well Class VI conversion is required, at about $2M or more per well.

4. Bench corrosion test (only if steps 1-3 pass): coupons in CO2-saturated Permian brine.
   - Kill criterion: retrofit cost above about $5/t over 10 years.

fix.change_summary:
I applied the critic's patch without changing the core mechanism. CO2 is still released through a dip-tube in Carbfix style, so it dissolves in the produced water already going down saltwater-disposal (SWD) wells, held below saturation. The graft and the underlying physics are unchanged.

What changed:
- **Siting is now water-first.** The idea targets high-rate commercial SWD pads (40-60k bbl/d per well, deep zones with verified containment, outside seismic response areas). Each pad is paired with a small AGRU vent of 0.05-0.2 Mt/yr within about 3 km. Permitting covers one pad at a time, with one Subpart RR plan and one RRC ruling per pad, not one per well.
- **Target narrowed.** The aim is vents below about 0.15 Mt/yr, where the critic's techno-economic re-run shows the pad beating a dedicated well ($34-40/t vs $44/t at 0.1 Mt/yr). Above about 0.2 Mt/yr the pad loses its edge, and the basin-wide 8-16 Mt/yr is now only an upper bound.
- **Regulatory lever made explicit.** Dissolved storage forms no plume, which supports asking the RRC for a smaller area of review based on pressure footprint alone.
- **Critic's mechanical fixes added.** For wells that take water on vacuum, the release point moves deeper (about 620-1,580 m), with a backpressure choke and an interlock that cuts CO2 when water flow stops.
- **Binding commitment added.** CO2 cannot be diverted to EOR or resold as offsets.
- **Prior art reframed.** The NETL/NGL Pena Creek pilot and the Hydrozonix patent make this an "accelerate, license and site" play rather than an invention.
- **Falsifying test reordered.** Step 1 is now a cheap prior-art, status and freedom-to-operate check. The basin-wide kill criterion is replaced by a pad-level one: fewer than 10 pads with a vent of at least 50 kt/yr within 3 km of at least 80k bbl/d, checked against Subpart W reports. An RRC pre-application test is added.

I re-ran per-well throughput and tubing velocity in a scratch script (patch_ia3.py). At 10-20 kg/m3 a well carries 12-23 kt/yr at 20k bbl/d and 35-70 kt/yr at 60k bbl/d. The 3.5-inch tubing figure is corrected from about 6 m/s to 8.1 m/s at 20k bbl/d, and at 60k bbl/d 5.5-7 inch tubing gives 5.6-9 m/s. All figures stay far above bubble rise speed.

idea.title: Refinery-style fenceline monitoring network at every HCFC-22 plant to close the HFC-23 gap
idea.one_line: Adapt the US refinery benzene fenceline rule to HFC-23. Run a continuous canister network with public action levels around each HCFC-22 plant, so plant-level non-destruction is visible within weeks. Destruction is already required under Kigali and costs under $1/t CO2e.
idea.conventional_core: HFC-23 thermal destruction at HCFC-22 plants. It is TRL 9, and Kigali requires it 'to the extent practicable' from 2020.
idea.graft: From refining: the US EPA Refinery Sector Rule fenceline programme (40 CFR 63.658, 2015, from my own knowledge; not re-fetched). It uses time-integrated samplers on the perimeter, a numerical action level, a mandatory root-cause analysis when the level is exceeded, and public data. Here the benzene tubes are replaced by time-integrated whole-air canisters, because HFC-23 is too volatile for passive sorbent tubes. Analysis uses preconcentration GC-MS, the same method AGAGE uses for flasks.
idea.mechanism: Place 8-12 perimeter canister samplers around each HCFC-22 plant (weekly or two-weekly integration), plus a short annual tracer-release calibration as in Rust et al. 2024. A plant at the practicable abated emission factor gives a small downwind signal; a plant venting its HFC-23 gives a signal 5-15x larger. An exceedance triggers root-cause analysis and incinerator inspection under the national regulator, with data shared to the Montreal Protocol bodies. This replaces regional inversions, which cannot name a plant, with plant-level attribution.
idea.target: HFC-23 by-product from HCFC-22 production (F-gases). The binding constraint is MRV and compliance, not technology.
idea.quantitative_claims: (a) Gap size, my calculation from map figures: measured global HFC-23 was 14.0 Gg/yr in 2023, against about 2.8 Gg implied by reports. The 11.2 Gg gap is about 163 Mt CO2e/yr at GWP100 14,600. Rust et al. (Nature 2024, measured at one facility with regional observations and a tracer) found an abated emission factor of 0.19% (0.13-0.24%) of HCFC-22 produced. They extrapolate that proper destruction could cut global emissions by at least 84%. (b) Detectability, my Gaussian plume calculation (Briggs rural class D, u = 4 m/s, ground release, 100 kt/yr HCFC-22 plant). At EF 0.19% the centreline is about 19,000 ppt at 2 km. At EF 1% it is about 100,000 ppt. A two-week mean at 15% of the time downwind is about 2,900 ppt versus about 15,000 ppt, against a background of about 37 ppt (assumed). Detection is therefore not the limit; quantification needs the tracer calibration. (c) Cost: assumed $0.15-0.4M per plant per year across an assumed 25-40 plants comes to $4-16M/yr, or $0.02-0.10 per t CO2e of the gap. Destruction itself is assessed at well under $1/t CO2e; that is my recollection of CDM-era literature, not verified this run. No energy claim, because thermal destruction is a small fuel load.
idea.who_gains: S1 and S2: a verifiable cut of up to about 160 Mt CO2e/yr at the lowest cost per tonne in this map. S4: compliant fluorochemical producers that already destroy HFC-23 (Rust et al. measured one such plant) get a level playing field against non-compliant competitors. S7: Montreal Protocol parties and national regulators get evidence that holds up in enforcement. S8: no cost burden; Multilateral Fund support is possible.
idea.who_loses: S4: non-compliant HCFC-22 plants must run incinerators they may be bypassing, at a small cost. S7, specifically China: a sovereignty concern. The design must therefore be operated nationally, with data shared, not imposed from outside. S11: near-zero effect.
idea.closest_known_work: Rust et al., Nature 2024 (doi 10.1038/s41586-024-07833-y). This was a one-off, research-grade facility-level quantification with regional stations and a deliberately released tracer at one European HCFC-22/fluoropolymer plant. Regional inversions such as Communications Earth & Environment 2024 cannot attribute emissions to a plant.
idea.why_different: This idea turns that one-off research measurement into a routine compliance instrument with action levels, modelled on the refinery fenceline rule that already survives in the US regulatory system. The novelty is the institutional graft, not the measurement physics.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test: For 3 months, run 6-8 weekly canisters around one HCFC-22 plant with a known emission factor, ideally the Rust et al. facility or a cooperating Western plant, plus one tracer release. Then blind-test whether the fenceline-only inference separates EF 0.2% from 1% and recovers the emission rate within ±50%. The idea fails if the weekly inference uncertainty exceeds about ±50%, or if site geometry (stack heights, neighbouring HFC sources in chemical parks) causes misattribution. Cost is about tens of thousands of dollars.
idea.family: Plant-level verification/enforcement of existing HFC-23 destruction at HCFC-22 plants (fenceline monitoring; feed interlocks with signed analysers)

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: Rust D., Vollmer M.K., Henne S., Frumau A., van den Bulk P., Hensen A., ... Reimann S. 'Effective realization of abatement measures can reduce HFC-23 emissions', Nature 2024
closest.overlap: High on the physics; none on the institution. This is a one-off research measurement of the emission factor at one European HCFC-22 plant, using regional stations plus a tracer (the TNO co-authors use near-source tracer methods). It found an EF of 0.19% and estimated that global destruction would cut emissions by at least 84%. The abstract proposes no routine monitoring regime, action level or compliance instrument. Confirmed via the Europe PMC abstract.

closest.title: US EPA Petroleum Refinery Sector Rule fenceline monitoring, 40 CFR 63.658 (2015)
closest.overlap: This is the institutional template being grafted: passive benzene samplers on the perimeter, two-week integration, an action level of 9 ug/m3, root-cause analysis and public data. It applies to benzene at refineries only, not to F-gases. I could not re-fetch it this run because eCFR blocked the request; details are from my own knowledge.

closest.title: US EPA 2024 HON / SOCMI NESHAP amendments: fenceline monitoring at chemical plants
closest.overlap: Closest precedent for moving the refinery fenceline rule to chemical plants with canister sampling. My recollection is that it uses canister sampling (Method 327) for ethylene oxide and chloroprene, plus action levels and root-cause analysis. It was placed under reconsideration in March 2025 (confirmed on the EPA page). It does not cover HFC-23 or HCFC-22 plants. The canister and action-level details are not verified this run.

closest.title: Adam B. et al. 'Emissions of HFC-23 do not reflect commitments made under the Kigali Amendment', Communications Earth & Environment 2024
closest.overlap: Establishes the gap: 14.0 ± 0.9 Gg/yr in 2023, five times the 2021 reported value, with the discrepancy concentrated in eastern China. It uses regional inversion and cannot attribute emissions to a plant. It motivates the idea but proposes no facility monitoring.

closest.title: Stanley K.M. et al. 'Increase in global emissions of HFC-23 despite near-total expected reductions', Nature Communications 2020
closest.overlap: Earlier evidence of the gap between top-down and reported emissions. Same limitation: global and regional scale, no plant attribution.

closest.title: Mobile tracer gas dispersion method (Mønster 2015, Waste Management; Fredenslund 2019 validation)
closest.overlap: A validated, routinely used method for quantifying site-level emissions with a co-released tracer, used for methane at landfills, farms and industrial sites. Its validated uncertainty is relevant to the idea's ±50% falsification threshold. It has not been applied as a routine F-gas compliance check at HCFC-22 plants.

closest.title: Zhao et al. 'By-production, emissions and abatement cost-climate benefit of HFC-23 in China's HCFC-22 plants', Advances in Climate Change Research 2023
closest.overlap: Plant-level bottom-up inventory and abatement costs for China, relevant to the idea's cost claim of under $1/t CO2e. It is not a measurement or verification scheme.

closest.title: Measurement-based MRV precedents: EU Methane Regulation 2024/1787 and OGMP 2.0 site-level reconciliation; China MEE 2021 notice on controlling by-product HFC-23 (my recollection, not verified this run)
closest.overlap: These show regulators already require measurement-based or online monitoring of facility emissions. The China notice reportedly bans venting and requires monitoring at the destruction unit, a process-side measurement rather than ambient perimeter attribution. I could not fetch the MEE page (404), so this is unconfirmed.

art.what_is_new:
Every component already exists:
- The refinery fenceline rule, with action levels, root-cause analysis and public data.
- Its 2024 extension to chemical plants using canisters (HON).
- Research-grade quantification of HFC-23 at one facility using a tracer and regional stations (Rust et al. 2024).
- Validated tracer-dispersion methods for quantifying site emissions.
- Regional inversions showing the gap, about 14 Gg/yr measured in 2023 against about 5x less reported (Adam et al. 2024).

I found no precedent for combining them: a routine, regulatory, perimeter-canister network with numerical action levels at HCFC-22 plants, tracer-calibrated for HFC-23 and linked to Kigali Article 2J(6) compliance and Montreal Protocol reporting. As the idea itself says, the novelty is the institutional graft, not the measurement physics.

Caveats:
1. **Search was cut short.** The session's WebSearch budget ran out, so I searched only through Europe PMC and Crossref APIs plus direct fetches.
2. **Unchecked sources:**
   - Montreal Protocol MOP decisions and Multilateral Fund Executive Committee documents on HFC-23 monitoring (MOP-35/36/37, ExCom 9x).
   - EIA advocacy reports.
   - The text of China's MEE 2021 HFC-23 notice.
   - Chinese-language studies of measurements near fluorochemical parks.
   Any of these could hold a near-identical proposal, so the label should stay PARTIAL until they are checked.
3. **Details from memory.** The HON canister and action-level details and the refinery-rule details are from my own knowledge, not re-verified this run.

phys.assumptions:
PRIMARY SOURCES CHECKED THIS RUN (abstracts via Europe PMC/Crossref; eCFR text via Cornell LII):
- Comms Earth & Env 2024 (doi 10.1038/s43247-024-01946-y), measured by atmospheric inversion: global HFC-23 was 14.0 ± 0.9 Gg/yr in 2023, down from a 17.3 Gg peak in 2019. The paper says emissions remained "five times higher than reported in 2021", which implies about 2.8 Gg reported.
- Rust et al., Nature 2024 (doi 10.1038/s41586-024-07833-y), measured at one European plant with regional stations and a released tracer: EF 0.19% (0.13-0.24%). The paper extrapolates that destruction could cut global emissions by at least 84% (69-100%), or 14 (12-16) Gg/yr.
- 40 CFR 63.658: 14-day samples; a benzene action level of 9 µg/m3 on the annual average of delta-c (highest site minus lowest site); root-cause analysis starts within 5 days and must be done within 45. The idea's description of the graft is therefore accurate.

ASSUMPTIONS (modelled, not measured):
- GWP100 for HFC-23 is 14,600 (AR6). The AR5 value of 12,400 gives about 15% fewer tonnes.
- Fuel for thermal destruction: 20/60/150 GJ per t HFC-23. This is a kinetic need, not a thermodynamic one.
- HF neutralisation: 1.6 t lime per t HFC-23 at $0-250/t lime.
- Incinerator capex of $5/10/20M per unit (the high case adds a redundant unit to cover downtime), needed at 30/50/80% of plants. Fixed O&M is 4% of capex; finance is 8% over 15 years.
- Monitoring at $0.23/0.51/0.95M per plant per year: 12-16 samplers, 26 periods, specialist preconcentration GC-MS at $400-1,500 per sample, plus an annual tracer, staff and sampler capex.
- 25/35/60 plants worldwide.
- 30/70/95% of the gap is actually closed by the compliance response.
- Plume model: Briggs rural Gaussian, 100 kt/yr plant, u = 4 m/s, background 37 ppt.
- Monte Carlo: 336 hourly met steps per 2-week period; a mix of stability classes B-E; 3 vents within 150 m at 0-30 m height; inference uses a single ground-level class-D point source with a delta-c background, as in 63.658.

SCRIPT OUTPUTS (exactly as printed):
- Gap: 11.20 Gg/yr = 163.5 Mt CO2e (range 142.2-176.7; AR5 138.9). The idea's 163 Mt is confirmed. Caveat: this compares measured 2023 with reported 2021.
- Floor: destroying CHF3 has dH = -275 kJ/mol (exothermic), so the floor is 0. Concentrating HFC-23 from a 50% vent needs 3.34 kJ/t CO2e.
- Contrast: removal from air at 37 ppt costs 215.6 GJ/t CO2e in fan work alone, so source prevention is the only physical route.
- Energy: 0.00137/0.00411/0.01027 GJ/t CO2e. CO2 from the fuel is 0.008-0.058% of the abated amount.
- Cost: $0.081/0.444/4.970 per t CO2e. Monitoring alone is $0.035/0.155/1.331 per t. The idea's $0.02-0.10/t for monitoring is optimistic by about 1.5-2x in the base case, but still trivial.
- Plume at 2 km: 19,104 ppt (EF 0.19%) and 100,546 ppt (EF 1%), matching the idea's 19,000 and 100,000. A two-week sector average (15% frequency) gives 1,336 vs 7,030 ppt. The idea's 2,900 vs 15,000 is about 2x high, but either way the signal is far above the 37 ppt background.
- Monte Carlo, idealised flat terrain: without a tracer, median 0.70 and 91% within ±50%, so it is biased. With the tracer and a 500 m ring, median 1.00, 5-95% range [0.51, 1.98], 78% within ±50%. With the tracer and a 1,500 m ring, [0.72, 1.30], 100% within ±50%. With an unmodelled neighbour source at 1.5 km, 84%.
- Telling EF 0.2% from 1%: 3.0% false alarms and 1.5% missed violations.
- Implication: a ring close to a multi-vent plant, calibrated by a single-vent tracer, can fail the idea's own ±50% test. Samplers should sit about 1-1.5 km out, or the tracer should be released at several vents.

No claim falls below a physical floor, and none needs heroic assumptions. The verdict is strong on physics and techno-economics. Delivery is institutional.
phys.resource_needs: Energy is 0.175/0.470/0.690 PJ/yr, which is 2.8e-7 to 1.1e-6 of world primary energy. Lime is about 12.5 kt/yr, or none if HF is recovered as a product. The network needs about 12,740 canister samples per year, roughly 5 instrument-years of preconcentration GC-MS (assuming 2,500 runs per instrument-year). Specialist lab capacity of the AGAGE/Medusa class is a real bottleneck, because commodity TO-15 labs are not set up for ppt-level HFC-23. Land is under 1 ha per plant and water use is negligible (scrubber only). It also needs one tracer release per plant per year, met stations, and, for the high-cost case, new or redundant incinerators at up to 80% of plants (about $150M/yr annualised).
phys.violations:
None physical. Destruction is exothermic, so the thermodynamic floor is 0, and every energy figure sits far above it. Minor overstatements in the idea:
- **Two-week mean plume concentrations:** about 2x higher than my sector-averaged calculation (2,900 vs 1,336 ppt at EF 0.19%). This does not change detectability.
- **Monitoring cost:** $0.02-0.10/t looks optimistic. The script gives $0.035/0.155/1.331 per t for monitoring alone, because specialist GC-MS costs more per sample than commodity analysis.
- **"Destruction under $1/t":** this was unverified recollection. The modelled total base case is $0.444/t, but $4.97/t in a pessimistic case with many new redundant incinerators and only 30% of the gap closed.
- **The ±50% inference claim:** it holds only with sampler geometry about 1-1.5 km out or multi-vent tracer calibration. A 500 m ring with a single-vent tracer gave only 78% of periods within ±50%.
phys.key_uncertainties:
1. **Political, the binding constraint.** China, the largest HCFC-22 producer, may not accept monitoring; it has to be nationally operated with shared data. And Kigali's "to the extent practicable" wording gives regulators leeway not to act on an exceedance.
2. **Attribution of the gap.** CEE 2024 says non-HCFC-22 sources explain only a minor but highly uncertain fraction. Unreported production or feedstock HCFC-22 lines would also be caught by fenceline monitoring, but would shift who is liable.
3. **Year mismatch.** The gap compares 2023 measured with 2021 reported, and Rust et al.'s 84% extrapolation used a different base year.
4. **The Monte Carlo is modelled, not measured.** It uses Gaussian plumes over flat terrain. Real chemical parks (buildings, stack downwash, coastal or complex terrain, neighbouring fluorochemical plants and R-23 storage or handling) will widen errors. The proposed 3-month blind test against a plant with a known EF is the right falsifier, at a cost of tens of thousands of dollars.
5. **Behavioural precedent, from memory and not re-fetched this run.** Venting reportedly resumed after CDM HFC-23 credits ended (around 2013), which suggests compliance follows incentives and enforcement, not technology.
6. **Measurement capacity.** Cost and capacity of specialist ppt-level GC-MS analysis.
7. **GWP choice.** AR6 vs AR5 GWP moves the tonnes by about 15%. The GWP20 view is smaller (0.097 Gt base) because HFC-23 lasts about 228 years.
8. **Scale is small.** About 0.04-0.17 Gt CO2e/yr, or 0.08-0.32% of global GHG. This is a cheap, high-certainty niche lever, not a primary climate solution.

stances.evidence: The idea triggers none of CAN's (2021) red lines: it is not CCS, EOR, an offset or a removal. It enforces destruction that is already mandated. US environmental-justice groups have long used fenceline data as an advocacy tool. The Environmental Integrity Project analysed refinery benzene fenceline data at 100+ refineries and found 10 above the 9 ug/m3 action level in Q3 2019 (https://environmentalintegrity.org/reports/monitoring-for-benzene-at-refinery-fencelines/). NRDC endorsed the AIM Act HFC phasedown (map). One historical warning applies: under the CDM, HFC-23 destruction projects earned 38% of all CERs issued by June 2013. The Carbon Trust warned this could lead makers to produce by-product just to destroy it, and the EU banned HFC-23 credits from the ETS from 1 May 2013 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clean_Development_Mechanism). S1 support therefore depends on keeping this a compliance instrument, not a credit-generating one.
stances.red_line_hit: None as designed. If it were monetised as offsets or credits (the CDM HFC-23 precedent), it would hit CAN red line (4) on offsets and revive the perverse-incentive scandal.

stances.evidence: The idea comes from the atmospheric-measurement community. In Rust et al., Nature 2024 (doi 10.1038/s41586-024-07833-y), facility-level measurement at one plant found an abated emission factor of 0.19%, and the authors argue proper destruction could cut global emissions by at least 84%. Regional inversions cannot attribute emissions to a plant. Wikipedia's Fluoroform summary of the 2024 research says the HFC-23 decrease is 'much less than has been reported' and misses the Kigali 2020 target. The CFC-11 precedent shows atmospheric detection leading to enforcement: Montzka et al. 2018 found unexpected emissions, attributed to eastern China, and they had largely reversed by 2019 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichlorofluoromethane). S2 would want the falsification test (±50% recovery) published before it is used for enforcement.
stances.red_line_hit: None. Methodological caveat: S2 will reject enforcement claims built on uncalibrated plume inference, especially in chemical parks that hold several fluorochemical sources.

stances.evidence: Oil and gas has no direct economic stake in HCFC-22 production. Refiners have operated under the 2015 Refinery Sector Rule's benzene fenceline programme, which reported data via EPA CEDRI from 2018 (https://www.epa.gov/stationary-sources-air-pollution/petroleum-refinery-sector-risk-and-technology-review-and-new-source). That shows the instrument is livable, but an exceedance record also creates litigation and PR exposure. The only plausible S3 concern is precedent: plant-level atmospheric attribution for HFC-23 strengthens the case for the same method on methane. The map shows S3 accepts direct methane regulation but treats a per-tonne fee as a red line.
stances.red_line_hit: None directly. Indirect precedent risk: fenceline attribution could later underpin per-tonne methane charges, which is S3's documented red line (WEC disapproved under the CRA in 2025).

stances.evidence: Winners: compliant fluorochemical producers. Incumbent chemical makers backed the AIM Act through the Alliance for Responsible Atmospheric Policy and AHRI (map, Kigali/AIM Act entry). A producer that already destroys HFC-23, like the plant Rust et al. measured, gains a level playing field. Losers: non-compliant HCFC-22 plants, concentrated where most HCFC-22 is now made. Wikipedia says developing countries have become the largest producers. The cost is less trivial than 'under $1/t CO2e' implies. My calculation (scratchpad climate/hfc23_stake.py) assumes a raw co-production of 1.5-3% HFC-23 and destruction at $0.1-1/t CO2e. That gives $22-438 per t HCFC-22, about 1-30% of an assumed $1.5-3k/t HCFC-22 price. The upper end is a plausible motive for bypassing incinerators. Documented S4 hostility to fenceline monitoring as an instrument: the 2024 HON rule extended fenceline requirements to US chemical plants. A 17 Jul 2025 presidential proclamation then gave 25 chemical facilities 2 more years. It asserted 'The technology to implement the HON Rule is not available' (https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/07/regulatory-relief-for-certain-stationary-sources-to-promote-american-chemical-manufacturing-security/). The proclamation does not name fenceline monitoring specifically. The ACC position is from my own knowledge and was not re-verified.
stances.red_line_hit: Public, continuous fenceline data with action levels; the US chemical sector fought this in the HON rule. Compliance cost for non-compliant plants: possibly 7-30% of HCFC-22 price at upper-bound assumptions.

stances.evidence: Power utilities have no exposure to HCFC-22 production and no documented position on HFC-23. The measure affects no electricity prices, assets or obligations.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: The measure creates no plant closures or job losses. Incinerators already exist or are required under Kigali, and running them adds a small amount of operator and monitoring work. I found no documented union position on HFC-23 or fenceline monitoring, and S6 has no reason to mobilise either way.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: Collective support is formal. Kigali requires by-product HFC-23 destruction 'to the extent practicable' from 2020 (map), and China accepted Kigali on 17 Jun 2021 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kigali_Amendment). The CFC-11 episode shows China acting on atmospheric evidence: emissions fell by 20,000 US tons between 2018 and 2019 (Wikipedia Trichlorofluoromethane). That is the best precedent that atmospheric attribution changes state behaviour without a trade fight. The idea's claim that China issued a 2021 national notice requiring HFC-23 destruction is my own recollection and was not verified. Friction: (a) sovereignty, since externally run monitoring around Chinese or Indian plants would be resisted, so the design must be nationally operated with data shared; (b) the US executive in 2025 moved against fenceline-style requirements (HON proclamation), so US leadership on the instrument is unlikely before 2029, although the US remains bound through its 2022 Kigali ratification (not re-verified).
stances.red_line_hit: Sovereignty: monitoring imposed from outside on producer states (China, India). In the US in 2025-26, new fenceline mandates on chemical plants run against current executive policy.

stances.evidence: Climate-justice advocates support enforcement against large industrial emitters and get a cheap, verifiable cut without burdening poor consumers. Global South producer governments hold the non-compliant capacity, and some argue that unilateral measures are discriminatory (map, CBAM objections from India and South Africa, not re-verified). The Montreal Protocol model that brought S8 in, with slower Article 5 schedules and Multilateral Fund payments, is the documented route to acceptance. Funding the monitoring, and incinerator operation where needed, through the MLF would follow that model. Baum et al. 2024 (map) is the closest public-opinion evidence: Global South publics support climate technologies but worry about unequal burdens. It surveyed CDR and SRM, not monitoring, so it is only weakly relevant here.
stances.red_line_hit: Seen as Northern-imposed surveillance of developing-country industry if it is not MLF-funded and nationally operated.

stances.evidence: Consumers would see no visible price effect. Much HCFC-22 is now fluoropolymer feedstock, and its emissive refrigerant use is being phased out under the Montreal Protocol. Even an upper-bound cost of up to $438/t HCFC-22 (my calculation, assumptions above) is spread across fluoropolymer value chains. The map's Canada 2025 evidence shows visible consumer prices get repealed, but this measure has no visible consumer price.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: Investors have minor exposure through listed fluorochemical producers, which face compliance-cost and reputational risk if fenceline data show venting. For carbon-market investors, the CDM HFC-23 history (EU ban from 2013) is a negative memory, so a compliance-only design avoids the credit-integrity controversy. Insurers have no material stake. I found no documented investor position.
stances.red_line_hit: None. Reputational and disclosure risk for holders of non-compliant producers.

stances.evidence: Fenceline monitoring with public data is a long-standing demand of communities living next to facilities: the 2015 refinery rule's public data, EIP's analysis, and the general fenceline-community literature calling for 'increased monitoring, reporting' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenceline_community). HFC-23 has low local toxicity, so salience is low. The samplers and public data could, however, become a local transparency asset in chemical parks. Physical footprint is minimal: 8-12 samplers and an annual tracer release, with an inert, non-toxic tracer assumed.
stances.red_line_hit: None, provided the tracer-release calibration uses an inert, non-toxic, low-GWP tracer, with that disclosed.

stake.coalition_notes:
This is one of the broadest, lowest-conflict ideas so far. It enforces an obligation all parties already accepted (Kigali by-product destruction) and triggers none of CAN's carbon-management red lines (CCS, EOR, offsets, CDR). Supporters are S1, S2 and S11, plus compliant S4 producers. S3, S5, S6, S9 and S10 are neutral.

Real opposition is concentrated in two places:
- **Non-compliant HCFC-22 producers and their host states (S4/S7/S8).** Their objections are cost and sovereignty.
- **The 2025-26 US executive and parts of the US chemical sector.** They fought fenceline-style requirements: the 17 Jul 2025 HON proclamation exempted 25 facilities for 2 years.

**Correction to the idea's framing.** The idea calls destruction a 'small cost'. On my calculation (raw co-production 1.5-3%, $0.1-1/t CO2e) it is $22-438 per t HCFC-22, roughly 1-30% of an assumed HCFC-22 price at the upper end. That plausibly explains bypassing and should be stated honestly.

**Design rules for coalition fit:**
1. Make it a compliance instrument, never a credit. The CDM HFC-23 scandal (38% of CERs; EU ban 2013) is the strongest documented way this could flip S1 to oppose.
2. Operate it nationally, share the data with Montreal Protocol bodies, and fund it plus incinerator O&M through the Multilateral Fund. That is the Kigali model that brought S8 and S7 producers in.
3. Frame it on the CFC-11 precedent: atmospheric detection led to domestic enforcement, and emissions fell within about a year.
4. Validate first. S2 will not back enforcement before the cheapest falsifying test shows ±50% recovery and no misattribution in multi-source chemical parks.

**Evidence limits.** The web search budget was exhausted this session, so several positions rest on fetched secondary pages or my own knowledge:
- The Rust et al. figures come from the map; the Nature page was paywalled.
- These are unverified: ACC's HON stance, China's 2021 HFC-23 notice, the AIM Act HFC-23 provisions, and US Kigali ratification details.
- The HCFC-22 price and destruction-cost ranges are assumptions.

Calculation script: climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/hfc23_stake.py

critic.fatal_flaw: None. The physics holds: destruction is exothermic, and the fenceline signal is 35-190x the background even on the critic's lower sector-averaged figure. The cost is cents per tonne, and no stakeholder red line rules it out once it is designed as a compliance instrument rather than a credit. The scale ceiling (about 0.1-0.16 Gt CO2e/yr) makes this a niche lever rather than a primary climate solution. That limits it but does not kill it.
critic.top_fixable_flaw:
The proposal has a principal-agent hole. Its own sovereignty fix ("operated nationally, with data shared") gives the measurements to the same reporting chain whose numbers are already about 5x below the atmosphere (CEE 2024: 14.0 Gg measured in 2023 against about 2.8 Gg implied by reports).

The refinery fenceline rule works because a third party with an incentive to act holds the data: EPA, EJ NGOs such as EIP, and courts. In a producer state where the regulator is part of the under-reporting, a nationally run canister network gives no independent assurance. Canisters are physical samples that can be swapped, diluted or simply not taken.

The idea's backstop is a consistency check: plant estimates should add up to the regional inversion. That check is too coarse to replace the missing independence. In the critic's script (critic_hfc23_recon.py; 25-60 plants, per-plant lognormal error from the 500 m-ring Monte Carlo, top-down 14.0 ± 0.9 Gg), a 2 Gg/yr (about 29 Mt CO2e) missing or falsified source is flagged only 10-14% of the time, and a 3 Gg one only 29-43%. A few large plants dominate the bottom-up error.

Two further gaps follow from this:
1. **Unregistered capacity.** Undeclared or feedstock-only HCFC-22 lines are not on the 25-40-plant list, so they are never ringed.
2. **No enforceable threshold.** Kigali's "to the extent practicable" wording means an exceedance has no numeric legal trigger.
critic.suggested_patch:
Add the network to the Multilateral Fund's existing production-sector verification audits (from memory: independent audits of HCFC production in Article 5 countries; check against ExCom documents). Do not set it up as a new national programme. Concretely:

1. **Split samples with chain of custody.** Every canister period gets a duplicate, sealed and logged with GPS and time, then shipped to an independent lab (an AGAGE/Medusa-class lab, or a lab in another Party). Each year 10-20% of duplicates are selected at random for analysis. If national and independent results differ by more than ±20% (or than the stated lab uncertainty), a full audit follows. Data stays nationally owned, which meets S7/S8's sovereignty condition, while the independence is real. The cost is about 10-20% extra on top of the $0.15-0.95M per plant per year monitoring budget.

2. **Unannounced auditor visits.** One mobile tracer-dispersion survey (Mønster/Fredenslund method) per plant per year, at an unannounced time and run by the MLF verifier. Bias in the static network then becomes detectable.

3. **Numeric "practicable" standard.** Ask the Parties (a MOP decision, or ExCom guidance) to define "practicable" as an annual emission factor: for example 0.3% of HCFC-22 production, the upper end of Rust et al.'s measured 0.13-0.24% plus margin. Set the action level on the tracer-calibrated annual emission rate against declared production. A mismatch between emissions and declared production then also flags under-declared production.

4. **Reconciliation as a coarse backstop only.** Publish bottom-up plant sums against the eastern-China inversion each year. State plainly that this catches only gaps of about 3-5 Gg or more, and treat a persistent unexplained residual as grounds to search for unregistered lines, for example with mobile surveys in fluorochemical parks.

5. **Revised falsifying test.** Run the cheapest falsifying test at the 1-1.5 km ring geometry and with multi-vent tracer release, since the 500 m single-vent case failed the ±50% bar 22% of the time. Add a falsification check: the independent lab must recover a spiked or blinded canister within ±20%.

Minor cost note: fenceline excess is about 1-7 ppb, so a TO-15-type preconcentrator with a trap that retains CHF3 (boiling point -82 °C) may be enough. Commodity labs might then replace specialist ppt-level analysis, which would ease the 12,740-samples-a-year capacity bottleneck. This needs a lab check.

patched_idea.title: Refinery-style fenceline monitoring with independent split-sample audit at every HCFC-22 plant, to close the HFC-23 gap
patched_idea.one_line: Adapt the US refinery benzene fenceline rule to HFC-23: a continuous perimeter canister network with a numeric action level around each HCFC-22 plant. The network sits inside the Multilateral Fund's production-sector verification rather than a stand-alone national programme. Sealed duplicate canisters go to an independent lab, and the auditor runs unannounced tracer surveys. Plant-level non-destruction becomes visible within weeks, and the check does not depend on the reporting chain that is already about 5x below the atmosphere. Destruction is already required under Kigali and was assessed in CDM-era literature at well under $1/t CO2e (recollection, not re-verified).
patched_idea.conventional_core: HFC-23 thermal destruction at HCFC-22 plants. It is TRL 9, and Kigali requires it 'to the extent practicable' from 2020.
patched_idea.graft: From refining: the US EPA Refinery Sector Rule fenceline programme (40 CFR 63.658, 2015, from my own knowledge; not re-fetched). It uses time-integrated perimeter samplers, a numerical action level, a mandatory root-cause analysis when the level is exceeded, and public data. The benzene tubes are replaced by time-integrated whole-air canisters, because HFC-23 is too volatile for passive sorbent tubes. Analysis uses preconcentration GC-MS (the AGAGE flask method, or possibly a TO-15-type preconcentrator whose trap retains CHF3; this needs a lab check). The graft is unchanged. The patch only adds what made the refinery rule work: a party independent of the plant that holds and can act on the data.
patched_idea.mechanism:
Unchanged core: 8-12 perimeter canister samplers around each HCFC-22 plant (weekly or two-weekly integration), placed on a ring of about 1-1.5 km rather than 500 m, plus a tracer-release calibration with release points at multiple vents, as in Rust et al. 2024. A plant at the practicable abated emission factor gives a small downwind signal; a plant venting its HFC-23 gives a signal 5-15x larger. Patched governance and independence layer:

(1) Host. The network runs inside the Multilateral Fund's existing production-sector verification audits of Article 5 HCFC producers. This is from memory and must be checked against ExCom documents. For non-Article-5 producers it runs under the equivalent national or regional regulator. It is not a new national programme.

(2) Split samples with chain of custody. Every canister period produces a duplicate, which is sealed and logged with GPS position and time, then held. Each year a random 10-20% of the duplicates go to an independent lab: an AGAGE/Medusa-class lab or a lab in another Party. If the national and independent results differ by more than ±20% (or by more than the stated combined lab uncertainty), a full audit follows. The data stays nationally owned, which meets the S7/S8 sovereignty condition, but the samples cannot be quietly swapped, diluted or skipped without the random draw exposing it.

(3) Unannounced auditor surveys. The MLF verifier runs one mobile tracer-dispersion survey (Mønster/Fredenslund method) per plant per year, at a time not announced in advance. This makes bias in the static network detectable.

(4) Numeric 'practicable' standard. The Parties are asked, through a MOP decision or ExCom guidance, to define 'practicable' as an annual emission factor, for example 0.3% of HCFC-22 production. That is the top of Rust et al.'s measured 0.13-0.24% range plus a margin. The action level applies to the tracer-calibrated annual emission rate against declared production. An exceedance triggers root-cause analysis and incinerator inspection. Persistent emissions that do not fit declared production also flag under-declared production.

(5) Reconciliation as a coarse backstop only. Bottom-up plant sums are published each year against the eastern-China (and global) inversions. The proposal says plainly that this check catches only gaps of about 3-5 Gg/yr or more. A persistent unexplained residual triggers mobile surveys of fluorochemical parks to look for unregistered or feedstock-only HCFC-22 lines, which the plant-list ring cannot see. Plant-level attribution replaces regional inversions, which cannot name a plant; the inversions are kept only as this backstop.
patched_idea.target: HFC-23 by-product from HCFC-22 production (F-gases). The binding constraint is MRV, independence of verification and an enforceable threshold, not technology.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
(a) Gap size, my calculation from map figures: measured global HFC-23 was 14.0 Gg/yr in 2023, against about 2.8 Gg implied by reports (CEE 2024). The 11.2 Gg gap is about 163 Mt CO2e/yr at GWP100 14,600. Rust et al. (Nature 2024) measured one facility using regional observations and a tracer and found an abated emission factor of 0.19% (0.13-0.24%) of HCFC-22 produced. They extrapolate that proper destruction could cut global emissions by at least 84%.

(b) Detectability, my Gaussian plume calculation (Briggs rural class D, u = 4 m/s, ground release, 100 kt/yr HCFC-22 plant). At EF 0.19% the centreline is about 19,000 ppt at 2 km; at EF 1% it is about 100,000 ppt. A two-week mean at 15% of the time downwind is about 2,900 ppt versus about 15,000 ppt, against an assumed background of about 37 ppt. On the critic's lower sector-averaged figure the excess is about 1-7 ppb, 35-190x background. Detection is not the limit; quantification needs the tracer calibration.

(c) Independence (from the critic's reconciliation Monte Carlo, critic_hfc23_recon.py; not re-run by me). Bottom-up against top-down reconciliation (25-60 plants, top-down 14.0 ± 0.9 Gg) flags a missing or falsified 2 Gg/yr source only 10-14% of the time, and a 3 Gg source only 29-43%. This is why the patch rests independence on split samples and unannounced surveys rather than reconciliation. The patch claims no detection rate for the split-sample scheme; that is set by the random-draw fraction and is to be modelled.

(d) Cost, all assumptions: base monitoring $0.15-0.4M per plant per year. The critic's own range runs to $0.95M and should be treated as the upper bound. The independence layer adds about 10-20% for duplicates and independent analysis, plus an assumed $50-100k per unannounced tracer survey. Across an assumed 25-40 plants that is about $5.5-23M/yr, or about $0.03-0.14 per t CO2e of the 163 Mt gap. Using the critic's $0.95M upper bound it is about $45-50M/yr, or about $0.3/t. Destruction itself is assessed at well under $1/t CO2e (my recollection of CDM-era literature, not verified this run).

(e) Threshold: at 0.3% EF, a 100 kt/yr plant may emit about 300 t HFC-23/yr (about 4.4 Mt CO2e). Plants above that trigger action. No energy claim, because thermal destruction is a small fuel load.

(f) Possible lab capacity relief: if a TO-15-type preconcentrator retains CHF3 (boiling point -82 °C), commodity labs could analyse the roughly 12,740 samples a year instead of specialist ppt-level labs. This is unverified.
patched_idea.who_gains: S1 and S2: a verifiable cut of up to about 160 Mt CO2e/yr at the lowest cost per tonne in this map. The verification is now independent of the reporting chain. S4: compliant fluorochemical producers that already destroy HFC-23 (Rust et al. measured one such plant) get a level playing field against non-compliant competitors. S7: Montreal Protocol parties get evidence that holds up in enforcement and a numeric standard to enforce. Producer states keep ownership of their data. S8: no cost burden; Multilateral Fund support is possible, and the audit runs inside an existing MLF mechanism rather than an external imposition.
patched_idea.who_loses: S4: non-compliant HCFC-22 plants must run incinerators they may be bypassing, at a small cost. Plants with undeclared production lose cover, because emissions are checked against declared output. S7, specifically China: a sovereignty concern. It is mitigated because data stays nationally owned and audits run through the existing MLF framework, but independent analysis of split samples and unannounced visits still need political consent. That consent is the main adoption risk. S11: near-zero effect.
patched_idea.closest_known_work: Rust et al., Nature 2024 (doi 10.1038/s41586-024-07833-y). This was a one-off, research-grade facility-level quantification with regional stations and a deliberately released tracer at one European HCFC-22/fluoropolymer plant. Regional inversions such as Communications Earth & Environment 2024 cannot attribute emissions to a plant. Mobile tracer-dispersion surveys (Mønster/Fredenslund) are established for landfill and industrial methane. The MLF production-sector verification audits are an existing institutional host; their scope is to be confirmed against ExCom documents.
patched_idea.why_different: This idea turns that one-off research measurement into a routine compliance instrument with a numeric action level, modelled on the refinery fenceline rule. Unlike a plain national fenceline network, it reproduces the feature that makes the refinery rule work: a party independent of the plant holds verifiable samples, and an auditor shows up unannounced. Both sit inside an existing Montreal Protocol mechanism, so no new external regime is needed. The novelty is the institutional graft, not the measurement physics.

fix.change_summary: I kept the core (HFC-23 thermal destruction) and the graft (a refinery-style fenceline canister network with an action level and root-cause analysis) unchanged. I patched the principal-agent hole the critic found. The network now sits inside the Multilateral Fund's existing production-sector verification audits rather than a new national programme; this hosting is from memory and is flagged for checking against ExCom documents, since no web check was possible this run. I added four further pieces. First, sealed, GPS- and time-logged duplicate canisters, of which a random 10-20% go each year to an independent AGAGE-class or other-Party lab, with a full audit on a discrepancy above ±20%. Second, one unannounced mobile tracer-dispersion survey per plant per year by the MLF verifier. Third, a proposed numeric 'practicable' standard of about 0.3% EF, checked against declared production, which also flags under-declared output. Fourth, the bottom-up against top-down reconciliation is demoted to an explicitly coarse backstop (it catches only gaps of about 3-5 Gg or more), with mobile park surveys to look for unregistered lines. I moved the falsifying test to a 1-1.5 km ring with multi-vent tracer release and added a ±20% blinded-canister check. Costs are updated: about $5.5-23M/yr, or $0.03-0.14/t CO2e, rising to about $0.3/t at the critic's upper monitoring cost. These are assumptions, not measured. I also noted the unverified commodity-lab (TO-15-type) option for lab capacity. Political consent to independent analysis is now named as the main adoption risk.

idea.title: Enclosed degassing weir: capture reservoir methane that degasses below tropical hydro dams and oxidise it like VAM
idea.one_line: Below tropical dams, methane dissolved in deep reservoir water degasses after the turbines. Enclosing the existing kind of aerating weir and drawing a controlled air sweep through it concentrates that methane to 0.4-4% in air, which a regenerative thermal oxidiser can destroy autothermally.
idea.conventional_core: Hydropower tailrace aerating or regulating weirs (as at Petit Saut and Nam Theun 2), which are already built to oxygenate the turbined water.
idea.graft: The VAM regenerative thermal oxidiser (RTO), plus air stripping from water treatment. The weir becomes an enclosed stripping cascade whose exhaust is treated as ventilation-air methane.
idea.mechanism: Turbined hypolimnetic water flows over a cascade inside an enclosure. A fan draws air through it at about 0.13 m3 per m3 of water (stripping factor about 4), which strips about 75% of the dissolved CH4. The exhaust, at 0.4-4% CH4 and kept below 25% of the lower explosive limit by extra dilution, feeds an RTO or a nearby boiler. The cost is 2-4 m of head, plus a bypass in low-methane months.
idea.target: Downstream degassing at young or deep-intake tropical reservoirs in Brazil, Laos, West Africa and Guyana. At Nam Theun 2 this was 10-30% of reservoir CH4 (measured), concentrated in a few months.
idea.quantitative_claims:
Calculated in scratchpad/climate/sysint/idea5_hydro_weir.py, assuming a dimensionless Henry coefficient of about 30 for CH4.
(1) At 2 mg/L CH4 and 1,000 m3/s, the sweep air carries 1.7% CH4, above the 0.18-0.2% RTO autothermal threshold. Recovering 75% gives about 47 kt CH4/yr, or 1.3 Mt CO2e at GWP100 (biogenic factor 27), if it ran all year.
(2) Energy: a 2-4 m head loss forgoes 18-35 MW, which is 0.44-0.88 GJ/t CO2e ($6-12/t at $50/MWh). At 0.5 mg/L it rises to 2.6 GJ/t ($37/t); at 5 mg/L it falls to 0.26 GJ/t ($4/t). For comparison, the verifier puts fan work alone for removing methane from ambient air at 8.8 GJ/t CO2e (GWP100).
(3) Capex for the RTO plus enclosure is about $44M (MATEC RTO unit cost plus an assumed $30M structure). That is $3.5/t CO2e at full-year operation, or about $10-14/t if the plant only runs seasonally: Nam Theun 2 measured 80% of downstream emissions within 2-4 months.
(4) Measured context from Deshmukh et al. 2016: hypolimnetic CH4 reached 1,000 µmol/L (about 16 mg/L). Turbulence at the intake shifted emissions upstream and cut downstream emissions by at least 40% through enhanced oxidation.
idea.who_gains: S5: hydro utilities defend the 'clean hydro' label and earn methane credits. S8: Brazil, Laos and African host countries. S7: methane-pledge accounting. S1/S2: a measurable methane cut. S11: downstream oxygenation continues. No industry is harmed.
idea.who_loses: Hydro output falls by 0.5-3% during operating months. Some operators resist measuring reservoir emissions at all, for reputational reasons. Hydro projects counted as zero-emission in carbon markets could face scrutiny once the methane is measured.
idea.closest_known_work: Bambace et al. 2007, Energy, doi 10.1016/j.energy.2006.09.008: proposed recovering methane from turbined water at tropical dams. The Petit Saut aerating weir, which degasses methane but vents it. Nam Theun 2 measurements and intake design (Deshmukh et al. 2016, Biogeosciences 13:1919). Lake Kivu methane extraction, which deals with natural, far higher concentrations. VAM RTOs.
idea.why_different: Bambace proposed extracting and enriching the methane for fuel, which is hard at mg/L concentrations. This idea skips enrichment: it reuses an aerating weir, which already exists or is cheap, as the stripping contactor, and treats the dilute exhaust with mature VAM oxidiser hardware. The simple baseline to beat is Nam Theun 2's intake-turbulence and selective-withdrawal approach.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test: (1) Desk compilation: published dissolved CH4 in turbined water, with discharge time series, for 5-10 tropical reservoirs. Compute annual capturable kt CH4 and the seasonal capacity factor, and compare with intake-design mitigation. (2) A bench cascade flume, 1-5 m, using CH4-spiked water, to measure stripping efficiency against air-to-water ratio. Kill the idea if most large dams have turbined-water CH4 below about 0.5 mg/L for most of the year, or if intake-mixing or selective-withdrawal designs achieve similar cuts at under $5/t.
idea.family: Capture of methane degassing below tropical hydro dams (enclosed tailrace/weir) and oxidation in a VAM-type RTO

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: Bambace, Ramos, Lima & Rosa 2007, 'Mitigation and recovery of methane emissions from tropical hydroelectric dams', Energy 32 (doi 10.1016/j.energy.2006.09.008), with follow-ups Lima et al. 2008 'Methane emissions from large dams as renewable energy resources: a developing nation perspective', Mitig Adapt Strateg Glob Change 13:193-206 (doi 10.1007/s11027-007-9086-5), and Ramos et al. 2009 'Methane stocks in tropical hydropower reservoirs as a potential energy source', Climatic Change 93 (doi 10.1007/s10584-008-9542-6)
closest.overlap: Same target: methane dissolved in hypolimnetic or turbined water at tropical dams, recovered before it degasses downstream, as a mitigation measure. Their framing is energy recovery: the methane is extracted and used as fuel. I could not read the abstracts (paywalled, with null abstracts in OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar), so how much of the mechanism overlaps is only partly verified.

closest.title: Quaranta & Muntean 2022/23, 'Wasted and excess energy in the hydropower sector: A European assessment of tailrace hydrokinetic potential, degassing-methane capture and waste-heat recovery', Applied Energy (doi 10.1016/j.apenergy.2022.120213)
closest.overlap: Explicitly treats 'degassing-methane capture' at hydropower tailraces as a retrofit category. Estimates about 5,950 t CH4/yr is capturable in principle across Europe, and says this is limited by technology and high installation cost. No specific design for the contactor or the oxidiser.

closest.title: Choi et al. 2025, 'Techno-economic and environmental assessment of hydrogen production utilizing captured methane from hydropower reservoirs', Int J Hydrogen Energy 176:151547 (doi 10.1016/j.ijhydene.2025.151547)
closest.overlap: A recent techno-economic analysis that assumes methane captured from hydropower reservoirs, upgrades it by water scrubbing, and reforms it to H2. This is the enrichment-and-use route the idea deliberately avoids. Full text not read.

closest.title: Petit Saut aerating weir (French Guiana) and Nam Theun 2 regulating dam and aeration structures; Descloux et al. 2015, 'Efficiency of the Nam Theun 2 hydraulic structures on water aeration and methane degassing', Hydroecol. Appl. 19:63-86 (doi 10.1051/hydro/2015002); Deshmukh et al. 2016, Biogeosciences 13:1919
closest.overlap: These are the conventional core: weirs and cascades built and measured specifically to oxygenate turbined water. In doing so they strip most of the dissolved CH4, which is vented to the atmosphere (some is also oxidised downstream).
