The stripping contactor already exists and has been characterised; none of these papers enclose it or treat its exhaust.

closest.title: Desorption chambers for dissolved CH4 in anaerobic (UASB) sewage effluent, with off-gas treated by biofilter or combustion: e.g. Brandt/Chernicharo group 2018 'Control of dissolved CH4 in a municipal UASB reactor effluent by means of a desorption-biofiltration arrangement', J Environ Manage (doi 10.1016/j.jenvman.2017.06.061); 2022 spray-nozzle recovery (doi 10.2166/wst.2022.028); 2021 technical note on desorption chambers (doi 10.5327/276455760102002); 2026 reuse of desorption-chamber gas (doi 10.1590/s1413-4152031s104)
closest.overlap: Practised precedent for the same physical combination: air-stripping mg/L dissolved CH4 from flowing water in an enclosed chamber, then destroying the dilute off-gas. This is done at wastewater flow scale with biofilters or flares, not RTOs, and not at hydropower scale (around 1,000 m3/s).

closest.title: Coal-mine ventilation-air-methane (VAM) regenerative thermal oxidisers (e.g. MEGTEC VOCSIDIZER, and Biothermica units used at a Vale coal mine), plus low-concentration catalytic gas turbines for VAM
closest.overlap: A mature oxidiser for 0.2-1% CH4 in air, autothermal above about 0.2%. The graft uses it unchanged.

art.what_is_new: Every component exists, and the goal (recovering degassing methane from turbined water at tropical dams) has been proposed since Bambace et al. 2007 and Lima et al. 2008. In 2022 it was named as a retrofit category for European hydropower (Quaranta & Muntean). What I found no precedent for is the specific combination. It (a) encloses the existing oxygenation weir or cascade (Petit Saut, Nam Theun 2 type) and uses it as an air-stripping contactor at a low air-to-water ratio. (b) It deliberately does not enrich the methane to fuel grade, which is the route taken by Bambace/Lima and by Choi et al. 2025 (water scrubbing, then reforming to H2). (c) It treats the 0.4-4% CH4 sweep as ventilation-air methane, destroying it autothermally in a stock VAM RTO or co-firing it in a boiler. (d) It sizes the plant around the measured seasonality of downstream degassing (about 80% of downstream emissions within 2-4 months at Nam Theun 2). The closest operating analogue for 'strip, then oxidise the dilute off-gas' is the UASB-effluent desorption chamber with biofilter or flare in Brazilian sewage plants. It runs at orders of magnitude smaller flow, which is useful as a bench-scale validation reference. I found no pilot, patent or company doing enclosed tailrace or weir capture at a dam. Caveats: the WebSearch budget for this session was already exhausted, so the hunt relied on Crossref and OpenAlex citation-graph and keyword queries (OpenAlex then rate-limited), plus metadata fetches. Patent databases (Google Patents) could not be queried. Bambace 2007, Lima 2008, Ramos 2009 and Choi 2025 were not read in full. A Brazilian INPE patent filing on reservoir methane recovery is plausible and should be checked before claiming novelty. The idea's own baseline still applies, and is not prior art for this mechanism: intake or selective-withdrawal design that shifts emissions upstream and enhances oxidation (Nam Theun 2).

phys.assumptions:
All numbers below are as printed by systems_5.py, which imports climate/physics.py. Costs and energy are per t CO2e at GWP100 (biogenic CH4, 27.0) unless marked otherwise.

MEASURED site data (primary sources read this session):
- Nam Theun 2, Lao PDR (Deshmukh et al. 2016, Biogeosciences 13:1919). Downstream CH4 fell from 10 Gg/yr after commissioning (2010) to 2 Gg/yr four years after impoundment (2012). 80% of it fell within 2-4 months. In the 2010 peak month, degassing was 385 Mg/month at the powerhouse, 1240 at the regulating dam and 756 at the aeration weir, so the weir's share was 32%. The open weir's degassing efficiency was "up to 99%". Turbined CH4 at TRC1 averaged 117±71 µmol/L in 2010, then 33 (2011) and 9.8 (2012).
- Petit Saut (Abril et al. 2005, GBC, doi 10.1029/2005GB002457). CH4 emissions were 0.07 Mt C/yr in 1994-96 and 0.016 Mt C/yr from 2000. The aerating weir accounts for about 70% of the CH4 flux.
- Balbina (Kemenes et al. 2007, GRL, doi 10.1029/2007GL029479). Downstream emissions were 39 Gg C/yr, about 52 kt CH4/yr, measured in 2004-06.

ASSUMED (from memory, not verified this session): head and mean flow at each site (NT2 about 350 m and 240 m3/s; Petit Saut about 32 m and 260 m3/s; Balbina about 22 m and 600 m3/s). These change only the head-loss penalty.

Stripping and RTO inputs:
- Henry's coefficient Hcc(CH4, 28 C) = 30.0, computed from Sander's Hcp of 1.4e-5 with a 1600 K temperature dependence. This matches the idea's ~30.
- Kremser analysis: at S=4, a single stage gives 80% and a two-stage counter-current cascade gives 95%. The idea's 75% recovery is achievable.
- The sweep is capped at 1.0% CH4, the VAM RTO ceiling (about 1-1.2%, and 25% of LEL is 1.25%).

Cost model, low/base/high:
- Pressure drop across RTO beds, ducting and enclosure: 2/3/5 kPa; fan efficiency 0.7.
- Incremental head: 0 / 1 / 4 m. Retrofitting an existing weir costs about 0-1 m; a new weir costs 2-4 m.
- Value of lost power: $40/60/90 per MWh.
- RTO capex: $70k/105k/200k per m3/s of air. MATEC's VAM unit at €9.5M per 100 m3/s is about $103k per m3/s.
- Enclosure capex: $10/30/60M per 1000 m3/s of water, scaled with exponent 0.7. This is an assumption; no costed design exists.
- O&M 3-6% of capex per year; MRV $0.3-1M per year; WACC 8%; 20-year life.
- Optimistic tonnage is paired with optimistic costs, and pessimistic with pessimistic.

Results (base case unless noted):
- Balbina: 26 kt CH4/yr, $12/t, 0.22 GJ/t.
- Petit Saut (2026 decline assumed): 7.5 kt/yr, $19/t, 0.26 GJ/t; range $5-90/t and 0.016-1.64 GJ/t.
- NT2 in its 2010 commissioning pulse, all three degassing sites enclosed: 7 kt/yr, $20/t.
- NT2 at 2012 levels, weir only: 0.6 kt/yr, $171/t, 1.38 GJ/t. The pessimistic tail is $731/t and 8.5 GJ/t.
- The idea's generic case (1000 m3/s, 2 mg/L, all year): $10.5/t and 0.242 GJ/t. Its head-loss arithmetic reproduces (2 m: 17.7 MW, 0.44 GJ/t; 4 m: 35.3 MW, 0.87 GJ/t).
- Costs at GWP20 are about 3x lower; for example, Petit Saut base is $6/t.

Scale (bottom-up, assumed):
- Low: 15 dams × 3 kt = 0.001 Gt CO2e/yr.
- Base: 40 dams × 8 kt = 0.009 Gt CO2e/yr (0.026 at GWP20). This is 0.016% of 53 Gt and uses 2.28 PJ/yr, or 0.00037% of world primary energy.
- High: 100 dams × 15 kt = 0.041 Gt CO2e/yr (0.12 at GWP20).
- Top-down cross-check: 5-10% of the modelled 10-18 Tg CH4/yr from global reservoirs gives 0.013-0.049 Gt CO2e/yr. Those reservoir totals are not verified this session.
phys.violations:
No thermodynamic violation. The separation floor is 0 GJ/t because the water is supersaturated. At 2 mg/L the equilibrium gas-phase CH4 is 9.2%, about 47,917x ambient air, so stripping into a 1% sweep releases 5.6 kJ/mol. Oxidation is exothermic. The energy cost is hydraulic, not separative.

Claims that need correcting:
(1) The sweep concentration of 1.73% at 2 mg/L and S=4 is above the ~1-1.2% VAM-RTO ceiling and the 1.25% (25% LEL) limit. Keeping the sweep at or below 1% needs 231 m3/s of air instead of 133 (S=6.9), and 577 m3/s at 5 mg/L. That means about 1.7x the claimed RTO capacity, although it also improves stripping.
(2) The generic 47 kt CH4/yr all-year case is not representative of measured sites:
   - Nam Theun 2's entire downstream emission was 2 Gg/yr by 2012 (measured), and the weir handled only about 32% of degassing. Much of it degasses at the powerhouse tailrace and the regulating dam, upstream of the weir.
   - Petit Saut's weir flux was about 15 kt CH4/yr in the 2000s (70% of 0.016 Mt C/yr) and is likely lower now.
   - Only Balbina-type sites approach the idea's tonnage, and that is based on 2004-06 data.
(3) The claim that output falls only 0.5-3% holds only for high-head plants. A 2-4 m head loss is 0.6-1.1% at NT2 (~350 m head) but 6-13% at Petit Saut (~32 m) and 9-18% at Balbina (~22 m).
(4) The $3.5/t capex figure assumes full-year, high-tonnage operation. At a mature, low-emission site such as NT2 in 2012, the cost rises to $171-731/t.
(5) Additionality: for a NEW weir, some of the CH4 it strips would otherwise have been oxidised in the river. At NT2, river CH4 returned to background within 30 km. Net avoided emissions are therefore less than captured; only retrofits of existing aerating weirs, as at Petit Saut, are about 100% additional.
(6) Safety: the equilibrium headspace is about 9% CH4 at 2 mg/L (inside the flammable range) and 74% at 16 mg/L. The enclosure needs a forced sweep and LEL interlocks. This is solvable with VAM practice but is not trivial.

Nothing requires heroic assumptions, so the verdict is not 'implausible'. However, global scale is tiny: base 0.009 Gt CO2e/yr.
phys.resource_needs:
Per site, for the base cases:
- Sweep air of 55-231 m3/s (Petit Saut 55, Balbina 153, generic 231).
- Fans of 0.23-1.0 MW.
- Lost hydro output of 0-9 MW for a retrofit (1 m base) and up to 35 MW for a new 4 m weir at 1000 m3/s.
- Capex of $14-60M (Petit Saut $17M, Balbina $37M, generic $54M).
- Steel and concrete for the enclosure, RTO ceramic beds, LEL monitoring, and about 1-3 ha at an existing dam site (assumed).
- Water: none consumed, and downstream oxygenation is preserved.

Globally (base: 40 dams): 2.28 PJ/yr, or 0.00037% of world primary energy. Total capex is about $1-2B across 40 dams (inferred from the per-site figures).

It needs continuous dissolved-CH4 monitoring at the turbine outlet to support methane credits, and a bypass in low-CH4 months.
phys.key_uncertainties:
(1) How much CH4 is in turbined water today. Emissions decay with reservoir age: NT2 fell 5x in 4 years, and Petit Saut fell about 4x by 2000. The site list and current dissolved-CH4 data in 2026 (now 32 years for Petit Saut and 39 for Balbina) are the main cost driver, and the desk compilation the idea proposes is the right first test.
(2) Where degassing happens. At NT2 only about 32% occurred at the weir; the rest was at the tailrace and regulating dam. Capturing it may require enclosing the draft-tube outlet or tailrace, not just the weir, which is harder and raises capex.
(3) Enclosure capex. The $10-60M per 1000 m3/s figure is entirely assumed; no costed design for enclosing a large open-channel weir exists.
(4) Hydraulic data for each site (head and flow) are from memory and unverified.
(5) Counterfactual oxidation for new weirs.
(6) The alternative baseline: NT2's intake-mixing design cut downstream emissions by at least 40% at near-zero marginal cost, but it applies to new builds only.
(7) G-res global degassing totals were not verified this session (Harrison et al. 2021 was paywalled).
(8) Whether carbon markets will credit avoided reservoir CH4 that is not counted in any baseline inventory.

Note on evidence: the site emissions are measured, the cost inputs are modelled or assumed, and the scale is a bottom-up assumption.

stances.evidence: Methane cuts get broad S1 support: Sierra Club backed the US Waste Emissions Charge, per the IEA policy page in the map. But the hosts are large tropical dams that S1 has fought. International Rivers documented at Nam Theun 2 (NT2) that compensation and replacement land were 'inadequate, unfair or non-existent' (Wikipedia, Nam_Theun_2_Dam). Jirau, an Amazon dam with documented indigenous-consultation disputes and labour riots, was registered under the CDM as 'the largest renewable energy plant' to earn credits (Wikipedia, Jirau_Dam). CAN (2021) rejects offsets 'as an alternative' to cuts. Expected result: S1 backs measurement and abatement at existing dams, and opposes anything that relabels dams as clean or helps finance new ones.
stances.red_line_hit: Greenwashing that legitimises large dams, including new builds that cite the fix. Offsets sold against continued emissions. Displacement and land conflicts at the host projects.

stances.evidence: Deemer et al. 2016 (BioScience) put reservoir-surface emissions at 0.8 (0.5-1.2) Pg CO2e/yr, mostly CH4, and flagged degassing and downstream emissions as under-counted. The IPCC 2019 Refinement (Vol 4, Ch 7) now gives inventory methods for downstream CH4. Its default ratio of downstream to surface CH4 is a median of 0.09 (95% CI 0.05-0.22, n=36 reservoirs). The idea's own reference, Deshmukh et al. 2016 (an NT2 measurement study co-authored by the operator), shows the science community engaging with degassing. S2 support depends on beating the simple baseline. IPCC Tier 2 treats downstream emissions as zero when water is withdrawn from the oxic layer. At NT2, intake turbulence cut downstream emissions by at least 40%.
stances.red_line_hit: None categorical. S2 would reject crediting that ignores the selective-withdrawal baseline or the decline in flux as a reservoir ages.

stances.evidence: No oil and gas assets are affected. OGCI and OGDC methane commitments (in the map) cover only fossil operations. I found no documented S3 position on reservoir methane.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: Steel, cement and chemicals are not touched. The idea uses existing VAM regenerative thermal oxidiser (RTO) hardware, which could be a small sales market for equipment suppliers. I found no documented position.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: IHA presents hydro as low-carbon, noting 'only wind and nuclear power have lower median lifecycle' emissions (23 gCO2e/kWh). It built the G-res tool to estimate net reservoir emissions but gives no methane-mitigation guidance (hydropower.org page on greenhouse gas emissions). Some operators engage: NTPC co-authored the NT2 degassing measurements. The idea itself lists operators who resist measurement for reputational reasons. Credits are unlikely to come through the renewable route: ICVCM rejected grid-connected renewable methodologies in Aug 2024. It approved methane-destruction categories (landfill gas, Jun 2024; mine methane, VCS ACM0008, May 2026), but no methodology yet covers reservoir degassing.
stances.red_line_hit: Disclosure that weakens the 'clean hydro' claim, or puts existing hydro credits and green-bond eligibility under scrutiny. Hydro output falls 0.5-3% during the operating months.

stances.evidence: No high-carbon jobs are lost. The only employment is small-scale construction and operations at remote dam sites. I found no documented union position.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: The Global Methane Pledge has 159 countries plus the EC, including Brazil, and targets a 30% global cut from 2020 levels by 2030. Its six pathways do not mention reservoirs (globalmethanepledge.org). The IPCC 2019 Refinement gives an inventory method, so abatement could count in national inventories. But measuring and reporting downstream CH4 raises reported national totals for hydro-heavy countries (Brazil, Laos) before any abatement shows. The Jirau CDM registration shows that host governments have marketed big hydro as clean.
stances.red_line_hit: Larger reported national inventories. Any challenge to hydro's role in energy-security and decarbonisation plans.

stances.evidence: Host governments (Brazil, Laos, West Africa, Guyana) could gain climate finance. In Baum et al. 2024 (N=30,284, 30 countries), Global South publics were more supportive of every climate technology. Climate-justice advocates and affected communities have documented grievances against the same dams. At NT2, International Rivers reported inadequate compensation. Downstream on the Xe Bang Fai, 40,000-150,000 people faced flooding, poorer water quality and fishery losses (Wikipedia, Nam_Theun_2_Dam).
stances.red_line_hit: Legitimising dams with unresolved displacement and livelihood harms. Revenue going to operators rather than affected communities.

stances.evidence: The cost is 2-4 m of head, or 0.5-3% of hydro output, in the operating months only. That is negligible at grid level, and I found no documented consumer position.
stances.red_line_hit: None. This would change only if the lost output were passed through in tariffs at small isolated grids.

stances.evidence: Methane destruction is an integrity-approved credit category under ICVCM (landfill gas 2024; mine methane May 2026), while renewable-energy credits were rejected (Aug 2024). However, no reservoir-degassing methodology exists. I checked the economics against measured NT2 data (Deshmukh 2016): downstream emissions fell from 10 kt CH4/yr after commissioning to 2 kt/yr four years after impoundment. Capturing 75% of the year-4 flux gives about 40 kt CO2e/yr (AR6 GWP100 of 27). On the idea's $44M capex, that is $87-141/t for capex alone, at capital recovery factors of 0.08-0.13. In the first year it is $17-28/t. The idea's 47 kt CH4/yr case is 23x NT2's measured year-4 flux (scratchpad/climate/stake_hydro_nt2.py).
stances.red_line_hit: Methodology risk and a flux that declines as the reservoir ages, which strands capex. Reputational exposure from controversial host dams.

stances.evidence: This is inferred from documented local grievances, not from a stated position. NT2's downstream Xe Bang Fai communities documented water-quality and fishery harm. The enclosed weir keeps the existing oxygenating function and removes CH4 that would otherwise degas locally. No community position on this specific idea exists.
stances.red_line_hit: Local safety from a combustible air stream and an oxidiser near settlements (the design dilutes it below 25% of the lower explosive limit). Any change to the downstream flow regime or dissolved oxygen. Noise and access restrictions at the enclosed weir.

stake.coalition_notes:
Opposition is low because no major industry is harmed (S3, S4, S6 and S9 are neutral), but the coalition is narrow and the money at stake is small.

The real contest is S1 and S8 justice advocates against S5 operators and S7 hydro-heavy governments, over whether measuring and abating reservoir methane relabels controversial dams as clean.

Scale findings that weaken the case:
- Measured data from Nam Theun 2 (Deshmukh et al. 2016, Biogeosciences 13:1919) show downstream CH4 fell from 10 to 2 kt/yr within 4 years of impoundment.
- Downstream emissions were only 10-30% of the reservoir total.
- The intake design alone cut downstream emissions by at least 40%.
- IPCC 2019 Refinement Tier 2 sets downstream emissions to zero for withdrawal from the oxic layer, and its default ratio of downstream to surface CH4 is a median of 0.09 (n=36).
- The idea's headline 47 kt CH4/yr is therefore an optimistic young, deep-intake case. At NT2's year-4 flux, capex alone costs $87-141/t CO2e.

A credible pitch would:
1. Target only young, deep-intake reservoirs with high flux, in the first 3-5 years after impoundment.
2. Be benchmarked against selective withdrawal.
3. Earn revenue through a new methane-destruction methodology (an ICVCM-approved category type) rather than renewable-energy credits (rejected in Aug 2024).
4. Be explicitly barred from use to justify new dams. This would neutralise S1's greenwashing objection.

Evidence limits: the web search budget was exhausted, so International Rivers' own pages (fetched URLs returned 404) and any Brazilian government or Eletrobras statements were not retrieved. Their positions above rest on Wikipedia summaries and inference.

Sources: hydropower.org/greenhouse-gas-emissions; bg.copernicus.org/articles/13/1919/2016; IPCC 2019 Refinement Vol4 Ch7 (Table 7.10, Tier 2 text); academic.oup.com/bioscience/article/66/11/949/2754271; icvcm.org/assessment-status; globalmethanepledge.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nam_Theun_2_Dam; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jirau_Dam.

critic.fatal_flaw:
Not fatal to the idea as a whole, but fatal to its headline target ("young or deep-intake tropical reservoirs", Nam Theun 2-type pulse). At NT2, downstream CH4 fell from 10 Gg/yr (2010) to 2 Gg/yr (2012), an e-folding time of 1.24 yr (measured, Deshmukh 2016). Integrating that decay at 75% capture (critic_systems_5.py, undiscounted, optimistic because it assumes the whole downstream flux is captured, not just the weir's 32% share):
- Built at impoundment: 9.3 kt CH4 lifetime (0.25 Mt CO2e), so the $44M capex alone is at least $175/t.
- Built 1, 2 or 3 years later: at least $391, $874 or $1,955/t.
A retrofit of a weir enclosure plus an RTO cannot be permitted and built in under about 2 years, so it misses the pulse it was sized for. The only way to catch the pulse is to build the plant with the dam. That makes it a feature of new dams, which hits S1's and S8's red line (legitimising new large dams), and the TEA/stakeholder coalition patch explicitly bars that use. The young-reservoir case therefore fails on both cost and stakeholder grounds and should be dropped. The idea survives only at old, persistently emitting reservoirs (see fixable flaw).
critic.top_fixable_flaw:
The conventional core, an existing aerating weir to enclose at 0-1 m extra head with about 100% additionality, exists at only about two dams (Petit Saut and NT2), and both have already decayed: NT2 is at 2 Gg/yr total downstream, of which the weir is about 32%. The sites that still emit decades after impoundment are Balbina-type: shallow, warm, large flooded area, low head (about 22 m, from memory). Balbina's 52 kt/yr is measured, but in 2004-06. These sites have no aerating weir, so the plan becomes a new structure there, and both its additionality and its head penalty are worse than claimed.

Recomputed for a Balbina-like site (Q 600 m3/s, 26 kt CH4/yr captured, $60/MWh, critic_systems_5.py):
- Head penalty: each metre of new head costs about 5% of plant output. A 2-4 m weir costs 9-18%, which is a real S5 red line, not 0.5-3%.
- Counterfactual oxidation: a new contactor strips CH4 that the river would partly have oxidised. With an assumed river-oxidation fraction of 0.4 (my assumption, not verified this session), net abatement drops from 0.70 to 0.42 Mt CO2e/yr.
- Lost-power cost: rises to $13-26/t, before capex.
critic.suggested_patch:
1. Drop the young-reservoir and new-weir case, and say so explicitly. This also settles the S1 objection: the plant is never a feature of a new dam.

2. Retarget to persistent emitters, using a desk screen: reservoirs more than 15 years past impoundment whose currently measured turbined-water CH4 is at least 0.5 mg/L for at least 6 months a year. Candidates to check are Balbina, Petit Saut, Samuel, Curuá-Una and Tucuruí. Use post-2020 measurements only.

3. Change the contactor from "enclose a weir" to "hood the turbulence that already exists": the draft-tube outlet, tailrace boil or spillway stilling basin, where turbined water already degasses. Make zero added head the base case and at most 1 m the cap. Low-head plants lose about 5% of output per metre, so treat head as a hard design constraint and score sites on the measured fraction of CH4 that degasses in the hooded zone. NT2's split was powerhouse 15%, regulating dam 49%, weir 32%. Bench-test what a hood can capture against a cascade.

4. Report net abatement as captured × (1 − f_ox), where f_ox is the measured river-oxidation fraction for that site, and require it in the methane-destruction methodology the coalition notes propose.

5. Kill criterion: fewer than 10 sites worldwide meet the screen in step 2 with net abatement above 0.1 Mt CO2e/yr and total cost below $30/t.

patched_idea.title: Hooded tailrace degassing at old, persistently emitting tropical reservoirs: capture the methane that already degasses below the turbines and oxidise it like VAM
patched_idea.one_line: At tropical reservoirs that still emit methane more than 15 years after impoundment, put a hood over the turbulence that already exists below the powerhouse (draft-tube outlet, tailrace boil, spillway stilling basin). A controlled air sweep under the hood holds the degassed CH4 at about 1% in air, and a VAM-type regenerative thermal oxidiser destroys it. The base case adds no head, and the plant is never built as part of a new dam.
patched_idea.conventional_core: The turbulent degassing zones that existing hydropower plants already have: the draft-tube outlet, the tailrace boil and the spillway stilling basin. At Nam Theun 2 the measured split of downstream degassing was 15% at the powerhouse, 49% at the regulating dam and 32% at the aerating weir (Deshmukh et al. 2016). Existing aerating weirs (Petit Saut, NT2) stay eligible where they still emit.
patched_idea.graft: Unchanged: the VAM regenerative thermal oxidiser (RTO), plus the air-sweep and off-gas handling used in water-treatment air stripping. The hooded degassing zone's exhaust is handled as ventilation-air methane.
patched_idea.mechanism: A hood or enclosure covers a degassing zone the plant already has. A fan holds the hood slightly below atmospheric pressure and draws a sweep at roughly 1% CH4 (20% of the lower explosive limit; the RTO's autothermal threshold is about 0.2%). For example, 45 m3/s of air carries about 0.3 kg/s of CH4. The exhaust goes to an RTO, or to a nearby boiler as combustion air. No water is pumped and no cascade is added. The base case uses only the degassing that already happens in the hooded zone, so added head is 0 m, capped at 1 m: at a low-head plant of about 22 m, each metre costs about 4.5% of output, so head is a hard constraint. Low-methane months are bypassed (the fans and RTO idle). The plant is a retrofit at old reservoirs only, never part of a new dam. Net abatement = captured × (1 − f_ox), where f_ox is the site's measured fraction of that CH4 the river would otherwise have oxidised. f_ox should be low for CH4 that already degasses in the hooded turbulence, but it must be measured, not assumed.
patched_idea.target: Old reservoirs that emit persistently: more than 15 years past impoundment, with post-2020 measured turbined-water CH4 of at least 0.5 mg/L for at least 6 months a year. Candidates for the desk screen are Balbina, Petit Saut, Samuel, Curuá-Una and Tucuruí (Brazil and French Guiana), plus any comparable shallow, warm reservoirs with large flooded areas in West Africa and Southeast Asia. The young-reservoir and new-weir case is explicitly dropped. At NT2 the downstream pulse decayed with an e-folding time of about 1.24 years (measured, 10 Gg/yr in 2010 to 2 Gg/yr in 2012). A plant built one or more years after impoundment would therefore cost at least $390/t on capex alone, and the only way to catch the pulse is to build the plant with the dam, which crosses the S1/S8 red line against legitimising new dams.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
Calculated in scratchpad/climate/sysint/idea5_patch_hood.py for a Balbina-like site. The Q of 600 m3/s and 22 m head are the critic's figures; the head is unverified, as are the post-2020 concentrations. Inputs: $60/MWh; RTO at the MATEC unit cost (360,000 m3/h for EUR 9.5M) plus an assumed $15M for hood and ducting; 8% over 20 years; GWP100 for biogenic CH4 = 27. phi is the share of dissolved CH4 that degasses inside the hooded zone, the key unknown.
(1) Zero added head: energy is fan work only (500 Pa, 60% efficiency), 0.01-0.07 MW, under $0.2/t CO2e. That is far below both the original 2-4 m weir penalty and the verifier's 8.8 GJ/t CO2e for ambient-air methane removal. Capex is about $20-24M.
(2) Net abatement and total cost with f_ox = 0.4, the critic's assumption and conservative for already-degassing CH4:
- 1 mg/L, phi 0.3, 12 months: 0.09 Mt CO2e/yr at $22/t.
- 1 mg/L, phi 0.5, 12 months: 0.15 Mt/yr at $14/t.
- 2 mg/L, phi 0.5, 6 months: 0.15 Mt/yr at $16/t.
- 2 mg/L, phi 0.5, 12 months: 0.31 Mt/yr at $8/t.
- 0.5 mg/L, phi 0.15, 6 months: 0.011 Mt/yr at about $180/t, which fails.
(3) Adding 1 m of head (the cap) adds about 5.3 MW of lost output, $9-120/t depending on the case. So the zero-head design is what makes this work, not an option.
(4) Screen condition: at Q = 600 m3/s and f_ox = 0.4, reaching 0.1 Mt CO2e/yr net needs c × phi ≥ 0.33 mg/L at year-round operation, or ≥ 0.65 mg/L at 6 months.
(5) Measured context: Balbina's 52 kt CH4/yr total emissions date from 2004-06 and are not current. NT2's hypolimnetic CH4 reached about 16 mg/L in its early years (Deshmukh 2016), but that was the decaying young-reservoir pulse and is not used as a target here.
patched_idea.cheapest_falsifying_test: (1) A desk screen of post-2020 measurements: for each candidate reservoir, turbined-water CH4 and its seasonality, discharge, head, and the measured split of degassing between the powerhouse outlet, spillway and river, from which phi is estimated. Compute net kt CO2e/yr at measured or bounded f_ox. (2) A bench or pilot test: a hood over a turbulent jet or stilling basin in a flume with CH4-spiked water, measuring the fraction of dissolved CH4 the hood captures at zero added head, compared with a forced cascade. (3) Kill the idea if fewer than 10 sites worldwide pass the screen with net abatement of at least 0.1 Mt CO2e/yr at under $30/t; or if the measured phi in hooded zones is below about 0.15 at typical post-2020 concentrations (under about 1 mg/L), because those cases cost more than $45/t; or if intake-mixing or selective-withdrawal retrofits achieve similar net cuts at old reservoirs for under $5/t.
patched_idea.who_gains: S5: hydro utilities at old reservoirs cut a measured liability with no loss of output (zero added head) and could earn methane-destruction credits. S8 and S7: Brazil and other host countries gain methane-pledge accounting, and the plan does not legitimise new dams. S1 and S2: a measurable cut in methane at existing assets, with a net-of-oxidation methodology. S11: downstream water quality is unaffected, because the plant changes no flow or head. No industry is harmed.
patched_idea.who_loses: Hydro operators who prefer not to measure reservoir emissions, for reputational reasons, and old hydro projects currently counted as zero-emission in carbon markets, which face scrutiny once their methane is quantified. Plant output falls only if a site uses the 1 m head cap (about 4.5% per metre at about 22 m head), and that case usually fails on cost. Proponents of new dams lose a possible 'methane-managed' green label, because the idea explicitly excludes them.
patched_idea.closest_known_work: Bambace et al. 2007 (Energy, doi 10.1016/j.energy.2006.09.008) proposed recovering methane from turbined water for fuel. Petit Saut's aerating weir degasses methane but vents it. Nam Theun 2 measurements and intake design: Deshmukh et al. 2016, Biogeosciences 13:1919. Lake Kivu extraction deals with natural, far higher concentrations. VAM RTOs.
patched_idea.why_different: Bambace extracts and enriches methane for fuel, which is hard at mg/L concentrations. The original version of this idea added a stripping weir and paid for it in head. The patched version adds neither enrichment nor head: it puts a hood over degassing that existing powerhouses and spillways already perform and passes the dilute sweep to mature VAM oxidiser hardware. It also scores sites on measured net abatement, captured × (1 − f_ox). The simple baseline to beat is intake-mixing or selective-withdrawal retrofits.

fix.change_summary: I applied the critic's five-part patch. (1) The young-reservoir, new-weir and new-dam case is dropped and stated as excluded: NT2's measured 1.24-year e-folding decay makes late-built capture cost $390/t or more on capex, and building the plant with the dam crosses the S1/S8 red line. (2) The target is now old reservoirs that still emit, defined by a post-2020 desk screen (more than 15 years since impoundment, at least 0.5 mg/L for at least 6 months a year; candidates Balbina, Petit Saut, Samuel, Curuá-Una, Tucuruí). (3) The contactor is no longer an enclosed stripping weir. It is now a hood over turbulence the plant already has (draft-tube outlet, tailrace boil, stilling basin), with zero added head as the base case and a 1 m cap; at a 22 m head each metre is about 4.5% of output. (4) Net abatement is now reported as captured × (1 − f_ox), with f_ox measured on site. (5) The critic's kill criterion is adopted: fewer than 10 sites with at least 0.1 Mt CO2e/yr net under $30/t, plus a new kill threshold on the hood capture share phi. All numbers were recomputed in scratchpad/climate/sysint/idea5_patch_hood.py. At zero head the energy cost falls to under $0.2/t, and total cost is capex-dominated at $8-22/t where c × phi is at least 0.33 mg/L year-round, but above $45/t at low concentration or small phi. The old figures (2-4 m head, 1.3 Mt/yr, 16 mg/L pulse) were removed as headline claims. The Balbina head and current concentrations are unverified, because the web-search budget was exhausted this session. The VAM-RTO graft is unchanged. mechanism_changed=true because the forced-stripping cascade (stripping factor about 4) is replaced by passive capture under a hood. The enclose-existing-degassing-plus-sweep-plus-RTO architecture is preserved.

phys2.assumptions:
Script: systems_5_patched.py (run with the repo .venv; imports climate/physics.py). Numbers below are as the script printed them. GWP100 for biogenic CH4 is 27 (AR6). Water temperature is 28 C. CH4 Henry constant is 1.4e-5 mol/(m3 Pa) at 298 K with d ln H/d(1/T) = 1600 K (Sander compilation, from memory).

Site and sweep inputs:
- Balbina-like site: Q = 600 m3/s and 22 m head. Both are the critic's figures and unverified, though they are self-consistent with the 250 MW installed capacity and a capacity factor of about 0.47.
- Hood: well-mixed sweep at y = 1% CH4. Water leaves the hood at c_eq + (c − c_eq)(1 − phi_open).

Summary case (c = 1 mg/L, phi = 0.3, 12 months): net 0.133 Mt CO2e/yr in all three cost cases.

| | Low | Base | High |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cost ($/t CO2e) | 8.0 | 23.9 | 68.6 |
| Energy (GJ electricity per t CO2e) | 0.0107 | 0.0214 | 0.0357 |
| Capex ($M) | 8.0 | 20.0 | 48.0 |

What sets each cost case:
- **RTO capex per m3/s of sweep:** $70k / $103k / $300k. The base derives from the idea's MATEC figure (EUR 9.5M per 100 m3/s, unverified). The high case is a judgement for fully installed VAM projects.
- **Minimum RTO unit:** $3M / $5M / $8M.
- **Hood:** $5M / $15M / $40M, for about 5,000 m2 of flood-rated, corrosion-proof enclosure over moving water (judgement).
- **O&M:** 2% / 3% / 5% of capex per year.
- **MRV:** $0.2M / $0.5M / $1.0M per year.
- **Electricity:** $40 / $60 / $90 per MWh.
- **Total pressure drop (hood + duct + RTO beds):** 1,500 / 3,000 / 5,000 Pa, with 70% fan efficiency.
- **Capital recovery:** 6% / 8% / 10% over 20 years.

Corrections to the idea's own model:
- The idea's table reproduces exactly: 0.092 Mt at $22/t; 0.153 at $14; 0.153 at $16; 0.307 at $8; 0.011 at $178. Its one-m-head and screen arithmetic is also correct: 5.30 MW lost, 4.5% of output, $2.78M/yr.
- **Suppression is missing from the idea's model.** A 1% sweep holds the water under the hood at c_eq = 0.2157 mg/L. Captured CH4 as a share of open-air degassing is therefore:

| c (mg/L) | Captured / open-air at y = 1% |
|---|---|
| 0.5 | 0.57 |
| 1 | 0.78 |
| 2 | 0.89 |

- **The (1 − f_ox) haircut points the wrong way** for CH4 that degasses inside the hood, because that CH4 would have degassed there anyway. Net/captured = 1.00 at f_ds 0, 1.11 at 0.4 and 1.22 at 0.8.
- The two corrections partly cancel. Corrected base results:

| Case | Net (Mt CO2e/yr) | Base cost ($/t) |
|---|---|---|
| c 1, phi 0.3, 12 mo | 0.133 | 23.9 |
| c 1, phi 0.5, 12 mo | 0.222 | 14.5 |
| c 2, phi 0.5, 6 mo | 0.239 | 15.3 |
| c 2, phi 0.5, 12 mo | 0.478 | 7.8 |
| c 0.5, phi 0.15, 6 mo | 0.014 | 221.2 |

- **Optimal sweep fraction:** y of about 0.5% gives $22.6/t, against $23.9 at 1% and $27.6 at 0.25%.
- **Corrected kill-screen threshold** (net ≥ 0.1 Mt and < $30/t, base costs): c·phi ≥ 0.25 mg/L year-round or ≥ 0.46 mg/L for 6 months. With high costs the year-round threshold is 0.78 mg/L, and the 6-month case never passes up to c·phi = 2.

Measured anchors:
- **Balbina** (Kemenes et al. 2007 GRL, 2004-06 data): 39 Gg C/yr downstream = 52 kt CH4/yr, plus 34 Gg C/yr from the reservoir surface = 45 kt CH4/yr. The idea mislabels the 52 kt as total emissions; it is the downstream share. At Q = 600 this implies the turbined water lost a mean ≥ 2.75 mg/L in 2004-06.
- **Petit Saut** (Abril et al. 2005 GBC): 21.4 kt CH4/yr in 2000-03, about 70% of it at the aerating weir. That is 15.0 kt CH4 = 0.40 Mt CO2e/yr, after a 4.4x decline from 1994-96. A Petit Saut-like weir case (Q = 250, phi = 0.7) gives:

| c (mg/L) | Net (Mt CO2e/yr) | Base cost ($/t) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.130 | 24.5 |
| 0.5 | 0.055 | 57.1 |
| 0.3 | 0.025 | 123.6 |

- **Nam Theun 2** (Deshmukh et al. 2016 BG 13:1919, peak months of 2010): degassing split 16% at the powerhouse, 52% at the regulating dam and 32% at the weir. This roughly matches the idea's 15/49/32 when computed from peak-month values. The concentration below the turbines fell from 117 to 1.55 µmol/L over a 30 km channel.

Energy floor: there is no separation work. The water is supersaturated about 24,022x relative to ambient air at 1 mg/L, so moving CH4 into a 1% sweep releases energy (dG = −3.84 kJ/mol at 1 mg/L; −0.0089 GJ/t CO2e). The floor is 0 for any c > 0.2157 mg/L. Fan work is 0.0040 GJ/t CO2e at 500 Pa and 0.0242 at 3,000 Pa, against the verifier's 8.84 GJ/t CO2e for removing methane from ambient air.

Scale: the headline figure of 0.0015 Gt/yr assumes 15 sites at 0.1 Mt each. The range is 0.0003 Gt (5 sites × 0.05 Mt) to 0.0060 Gt (30 sites × 0.2 Mt), which is 0.000 to 0.011% of global GHG emissions. The GWP20 equivalent of the 15-site case is 0.0044 Gt.
phys2.violations:
None of the claims is below the thermodynamic floor: the separation is spontaneous and fan work is far above zero. The arithmetic needs no heroic assumptions, but several input and modelling errors were found:

1. **Suppression is omitted.** A hood held at 1% CH4 sets dissolved-CH4 equilibrium at 0.2157 mg/L. At 0.5 mg/L this cuts capture to 0.57 of the open-air value, and at 1 mg/L to 0.78, so the low-concentration cases are overstated.
2. **The (1 − f_ox) haircut is the wrong sign of correction** for in-zone degassing, which would have degassed there anyway. Net abatement is at least the captured amount. The idea's method is conservative here, but it is scientifically mis-specified as a basis for MRV methodology.
3. **Balbina's 52 kt CH4/yr is the downstream share, not the total.** The total is 97 kt (Kemenes 2007). The data are from 2004-06, so they are not post-2020.
4. **The capex excludes O&M and MRV.** Including them roughly doubles the cost at small sites.
5. **The RTO unit cost (MATEC, EUR 9.5M per 100 m3/s) is unverified.** It may be the low end compared with fully installed VAM projects.
6. **Hooding spillway stilling basins is probably not practical.** They run during floods at thousands of m3/s, so in practice only the tailrace boil and the aerating weirs are hoodable.
7. **At NT2, only about 16% of downstream degassing happened at the powerhouse.** The rest happened at the downstream structures, and degassing below the boil is spread over km. A hood over the boil alone may therefore reach phi < 0.15 at sites without a weir.
phys2.resource_needs: Energy is fan electricity only: 0.0107–0.0357 GJ/t CO2e, which is 0.0161 PJ/yr for a 0.75 Mt/yr fleet, or 2.59e-08 of world primary energy. Water pumping is zero, and so is added head in the base case; each metre of head would cost 5.30 MW (4.5% of output) at Q = 600. Per-site materials (judgement): a hood of about 5,000 m2 using about 500 t of steel or FRP, plus an RTO sized for a sweep of about 20–80 m3/s; land about 0.5 ha; no water consumed. Capex is $8–48M per site. MRV also needs continuous CH4 and flow monitoring, plus measurement of phi and downstream oxidation.
phys2.key_uncertainties:
1. **Post-2020 turbined-water CH4 concentrations at the candidate sites.** The only measured anchors are dated: Balbina 2004-06 (implying ≥ 2.75 mg/L), Petit Saut 2000-03 (about 15 kt CH4/yr at the weir), and the NT2 young-reservoir pulse. Petit Saut's emissions fell 4.4x within about 6 years of impoundment.
2. **phi, the share that degasses inside a hoodable footprint.** At NT2 the powerhouse share was only 16%, while existing aerating weirs reach about 70% (Petit Saut). Sites with weirs therefore look much better than tailrace-only sites.
3. **RTO and hood installed costs**: whether a hood over flowing water can be flood-rated and kept safe at 20% of the lower explosive limit (1% CH4).
4. **Global scale.** I could not source a global figure for reservoir degassing. The G-res 2021 abstract says degassing is "much larger than previously recognized" but the abstract gives no number. My bracket of 1–3 Tg CH4/yr is unsourced and gives a ceiling of 0.005–0.016 Gt CO2e/yr, and the 0.0003–0.006 Gt bottom-up range is small either way.
5. **Carbon-credit eligibility and baseline rules** for methane from hydropower that is currently counted as zero-emission.
6. **The simple baseline**: intake mixing retrofits. At NT2, mixing at the intake (built into the original design) cut emissions by ≥ 40% (Deshmukh 2016). The cost of retrofitting this at old dams is unknown.
7. **Interpretation.** The concept is cheap per tonne ($8–69/t at c·phi = 0.3 mg/L) and physically sound, but tiny in scale. It is a niche, credit-funded methane cut, not a climate-scale solution.

Web search budget was exhausted; sources came from the fetched NT2 PDF and from OpenAlex abstracts.

idea.title: Sulfate-recharged AWD: gypsum plus alternate wetting and drying in rice
idea.one_line: Add a small dose of gypsum (clean FGD gypsum, or phosphogypsum within a contaminant cap) to alternate-wetting-and-drying rice. Sulfate-reducing bacteria then outcompete methanogens, and each drying cycle should re-oxidise sulfide back to sulfate, so the small dose keeps working.
idea.conventional_core: Alternate wetting and drying (AWD): TRL 9 agronomy, credited under Verra VM0051, cutting rice CH4 by 30-50% and saving about 30% of water (map).
idea.graft: Thermodynamic competitive exclusion, as in marine sediments: when sulfate is present, sulfate reducers outcompete methanogens for H2 and acetate.
idea.mechanism: Each mole of sulfate diverts the electrons of about one mole of CH4 (acetate + SO4 to 2 HCO3- + HS-; or 4 H2 + SO4). Under continuous flooding the sulfate is consumed once. Under AWD the drying phase lets O2 in, re-oxidising FeS and H2S to sulfate, so the same sulfur can suppress methanogenesis again in the next flood. This is the hypothesis under test. Many South Asian rice soils are short of sulfur, so the dose may also raise yields.
idea.target: Paddy rice CH4, assumed about 30 Mt CH4/yr: 0.81 Gt CO2e at GWP100 or 2.4 Gt at GWP20, using the verifier's biogenic GWPs. Starting point: irrigated systems where AWD is feasible, in India, Bangladesh, Vietnam and China.
idea.quantitative_claims:
(1) Measured (Malyan et al. 2021, Agric. Ecosyst. Environ., irrigated rice in India, lab plus field). Four amendments cut cumulative CH4 by 9.3-27.5%. Phosphogypsum had the largest GWP reduction (23.6%), so I infer it was near the top of that range. Grain yield rose 3.1-11.2%, and GHG intensity fell from 0.309 to 0.212 kg CO2e/kg grain.
(2) Stoichiometry (my calculation). Assume 100-250 kg CH4/ha/season emitted, with emissions equal to 30-60% of production. Diverting 20-40% of production then needs 0.4-3.6 t gypsum/ha/season without recycling, or 0.1-1.2 t if AWD drying recycles sulfate 3x (assumed).
(3) Savings: 0.54-2.7 t CO2e/ha/season (GWP100 biogenic 27.0). Gypsum at 0.7-2 t/ha, $15-40/t plus $10/ha spreading (assumed), costs $20-90/ha, or about $7-170/t CO2e before any yield credit. A 5% yield gain on 5 t/ha at $300/t is worth about $75/ha and would pay for the gypsum. Confound: the yield gain may come from sulfur nutrition, not from methane suppression.
(4) Scale: 10-30% adoption times an extra 10-25% cut beyond AWD alone gives 8-61 Mt CO2e/yr (GWP100), or about 3x that at GWP20.
(5) Energy: negligible; there is no separation step.
idea.who_gains: S8 smallholders: yield and sulfur nutrition, plus a credit stacked on AWD's water saving. S4 phosphate-fertiliser industry: phosphogypsum is a large stacked waste and liability that becomes a product, and FGD gypsum sellers also benefit. S7 India, Bangladesh and Vietnam: methane cuts using an input their extension systems already handle (India supports gypsum for sodic soils; from memory, unverified). S2: a clear mechanism that is easy to test. S1: supportive if contaminant limits hold.
idea.who_loses: S11 and S9 consumers carry a food-safety risk. Sulfate reducers methylate mercury, and rice accumulates MeHg. Phosphogypsum carries Ra-226, fluoride and cadmium. Iron-poor soils risk H2S toxicity, and sulfate can leach to groundwater. S10 credit buyers distrust rice MRV after Verra suspended its CDM rice methodology (4.56M credits). Natural-gypsum suppliers may face competition from subsidised waste gypsum.
idea.closest_known_work: Malyan et al. 2021 (doi 10.1016/j.agee.2021.107545) on phosphogypsum and other CH4-mitigating chemicals in rice. Kumar et al. 2020, Chemosphere (doi 10.1016/j.chemosphere.2019.124824), a review of fly ash, steel slag and phosphogypsum for paddy GHG mitigation. Many sulfate-in-paddy studies. AWD under Verra VM0051 (map).
idea.why_different: Prior work treats gypsum and AWD as separate options. This idea sizes the gypsum dose around sulfate recycling during drying cycles, so a fraction of the stoichiometric dose lasts the season. It also routes industrial gypsum through fertiliser channels under an explicit contaminant and MeHg cap.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test: A 10-week pot or microcosm trial with four arms: continuous flood, AWD, flood plus gypsum, and AWD plus gypsum, at 0.3-1 t/ha equivalent. Measure CH4 flux by chamber, porewater sulfate after each drying, and soil and grain MeHg. Falsified if any of these holds: (a) AWD plus gypsum beats AWD alone by less than 10 percentage points of CH4; (b) porewater sulfate does not rebound after drying; (c) MeHg rises more than 50% above control. Cost about $15-30k at a university greenhouse.
idea.family: Gypsum sulfate dosing combined with AWD so drying re-oxidises sulfide and sulfate suppression recurs

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: Liu Q, Romani M, Wang J, Planer-Friedrich B, Pausch J, Dorodnikov M (2021). Alternating Wet-Dry Cycles Rather than Sulfate Fertilization Control Pathways of Methanogenesis and Methane Turnover in Rice Straw-Amended Paddy Soil. Environ. Sci. Technol.
closest.overlap: Closest precedent. It tests the idea's exact 2x2 design (continuous flood vs AWD, each with and without sulfate) in straw-amended Italian paddy mesocosms. AWD cut porewater CH4 from 51 to 0.04 mg C/L at flowering, while 'sulfate addition had no significant effect on CH4 concentration'. The authors attribute this to abundant organic substrate removing the competitive advantage of sulfate reducers. So the combination is not new, and the one direct test is a NEGATIVE result for the extra effect of sulfate on top of AWD, at least on high-straw soils. This study effectively runs the idea's falsification test (a) already, though with sulfate fertiliser rather than gypsum and without tracking sulfate rebound per cycle.

closest.title: From substrate limitation to competition control: straw input regulates sulfate-mediated suppression of methanogenesis in paddy soils. Soil Biology and Biochemistry (2026)
closest.overlap: Studies the same mechanism and its boundary condition. Straw or organic-substrate input decides whether sulfate suppresses methanogenesis, which explains the Liu 2021 null. It implies that sulfate dosing works only on low-organic-input soils, a constraint the idea's scale estimate (10-30% adoption across irrigated Asia) does not include. I found only the title and metadata, not the full abstract.

closest.title: Malyan SK et al. (2021), Agric. Ecosyst. Environ.; Effect of phosphogypsum on reduction of methane emission from rice paddy soil, Korean J. Environ. Agric. (2007); Theint EE et al. (2016), Influence of gypsum amendment on methane emission from paddy soil affected by saline irrigation water, Front. Environ. Sci.; Kumar et al. (2020), Chemosphere review
closest.overlap: Gypsum and phosphogypsum as a paddy CH4 amendment are well established and include the industrial-waste (phosphogypsum) channel. These studies used continuous flooding or unspecified water regimes. Older field work such as Denier van der Gon & Neue (1994, Global Biogeochem. Cycles; cited from memory, not re-verified) reported large CH4 cuts from gypsum in wetland rice.

closest.title: Kim H, Park JH (2026). Stimulating sulfate reducing bacteria by sulfate-based amendments to reduce methane emissions and immobilize arsenic in paddy soils. EGU26-10550
closest.overlap: In anaerobic lab incubations only, ammonium sulfate and potassium sulfate cut CH4 by about 95-100% and also immobilised arsenic. It supports the mechanism but includes no wet-dry cycling, no gypsum and no test of re-oxidation. A lab-incubation magnitude should not be read as a field effect.

closest.title: Peatland drought and rewetting sulfate-regeneration literature (e.g. Knorr & Blodau 2009; Estop-Aragones et al. 2013; cited from memory, not re-verified this session)
closest.overlap: Already establishes the 'graft' mechanism: drying re-oxidises reduced sulfur to sulfate, which then suppresses methanogenesis after rewetting, giving a recurring, recharged sulfate pool. This is known biogeochemistry, transferred here from peat to paddy.

closest.title: Tanner KC et al. (2018), Alternate Wetting and Drying Decreases Methylmercury in Flooded Rice Systems, SSSAJ; Mercury and Sulfur Redox Cycling Affect Methylmercury Levels in Rice Paddy Soils across a Contamination Gradient, Environ. Sci. Technol. (2023); Seyfferth et al. (2025), GeoHealth
closest.overlap: Covers the MeHg co-risk. AWD on its own lowers MeHg, and sulfur redox cycling drives MeHg in paddies, so the idea's MeHg cap measures a known interaction rather than a new one. The real question is whether gypsum erodes AWD's MeHg benefit.

closest.title: Larazo NA et al. (2026), Managing yield and soil trace gas fluxes in rice through furrow irrigation and sulfur-enriched urea, J. Environ. Qual.
closest.overlap: A three-year field factorial of water-saving irrigation by sulfur-containing fertiliser. Furrow irrigation cut CH4 by 90-100%, and S-urea mainly affected N2O. This is further evidence that once water management is aggressive, there is little CH4 left for sulfate to remove.

art.what_is_new:
Not new: the gypsum/sulfate x AWD combination and the drying re-oxidation mechanism. Liu et al. 2021 (ES&T) ran the exact four-arm design and found that sulfate adds no significant CH4 reduction on top of AWD in straw-amended soil. A 2026 Soil Biology and Biochemistry paper explains the null: organic-substrate (straw) input controls whether sulfate suppression works. Sulfate regeneration on drying is established in peatland biogeochemistry. Gypsum and phosphogypsum as paddy CH4 amendments go back decades, and Malyan 2021 and a Korean 2007 study already cover phosphogypsum.

Possibly new, and narrow:
(1) Sizing the dose explicitly on per-cycle sulfate recycling and measuring porewater sulfate rebound after each drying. I found no paddy study that quantifies this.
(2) Restricting the target to low-organic-input, sulfur-deficient irrigated soils, where the Liu null may not apply.
(3) Routing phosphogypsum through fertiliser channels under an explicit Ra-226/Cd/F and MeHg cap, bundled into AWD carbon-credit MRV.

Implication: the idea's falsification arm (a) is already partly falsified in the literature for high-straw systems. The marginal CH4 benefit beyond AWD may be small, because AWD already removes most of the methanogenesis that sulfate would compete for. Any revised pitch should lead with sulfur-deficiency yield gains plus the use of waste gypsum, not with the size of the CH4 cut. The 8-61 Mt CO2e/yr estimate should be cut to account for the substrate condition.

Caveat: WebSearch budget was exhausted, so this search ran on the Crossref and Europe PMC APIs only. I did not check patents or the DOE/ARPA-E/ARIA programmes. The Denier van der Gon and peatland citations are from memory.

phys.assumptions:
Script: graft_bio_3.py (imports climate/physics.py; GWP100 biogenic CH4 27.0, GWP20 79.7). All numbers below are as the script printed them.

FLOOR. There is no gas separation, so the separation floor does not apply (floor_gj_per_t = 0). The binding limit is electron-balance stoichiometry: one SO4 replaces one CH4, so diverting 1 kg of CH4 needs 10.73 kg of gypsum. One tonne of gypsum, used once, can avoid at most 93.2 kg CH4, which is 2.52 t CO2e at GWP100 (7.43 t at GWP20). Gypsum is 18.6% S.

CLAIM 2 (stoichiometry). Re-derived and correct: 0.36-3.58 t gypsum/ha used once, or 0.12-1.19 t with 3x recycling.

CLAIM 3 (savings and cost).
- The pairings need recycling to be real. Claimed savings of 2.7 t CO2e/ha at a 0.7 t dose need a recycling factor of at least 1.53, even at 100% electron efficiency, because the single-use cap at that dose is 1.76 t CO2e/ha.
- The 0.54-2.7 t CO2e/ha range applies the cut to the continuously flooded baseline. Stacked on AWD, only the AWD residual (IPCC 2019 multiple-drainage scaling factor 0.55) is left to cut.
- Measured cross-check: Hu et al. 2018 (Huan Jing Ke Xue, PMID 29998699; FGD gypsum, Chongqing paddy, static chambers) found that 2, 4, 8 and 16 t/ha cut mean CH4 flux by 31.6%, 57.3%, 83.6% and 90.7%. That implies 25-68% of the stoichiometric maximum at 2 t/ha, assuming a 150-400 kg/ha baseline; the baseline itself is not available to me.

PER-HECTARE SCENARIOS (gypsum on top of AWD). Shared cost assumptions: haul $0.06/t-km; depot capex $15 per t/yr of throughput, annualised at 10% over 10 years.
- Low: baseline 250 kg CH4/ha; AWD residual 150 kg; an extra 40% cut avoids 60 kg CH4 = 1.62 t CO2e (GWP100). Dose 0.5 t/ha at $15/t, 50 km haul, MRV $3/ha. This needs 129% electron efficiency used once, so it only holds if the recycling hypothesis is true. Result: $11/t CO2e, or -$17/t after a $45/ha yield credit; 0.065 GJ/t.
- Base: baseline 150 kg; AWD residual 82 kg; an extra 25% cut avoids 20.6 kg CH4 = 0.56 t CO2e (0.54 net). Dose 0.75 t/ha at $25/t, 200 km haul, MRV $8/ha; needs 30% efficiency. Result: $48/ha, which is $89/t at GWP100 or $29/t at GWP20; 0.498 GJ/t.
- High: baseline 100 kg; AWD residual 55 kg; an extra 10% cut avoids 5.5 kg CH4. Dose 1.5 t/ha at $40/t, 500 km haul; 0.07 t CO2e/ha net of 76 kg/ha of transport CO2. Result: $1870/t (GWP100), $309/t (GWP20); 14.129 GJ/t.
- Energy basis: diesel truck 1.2 MJ/t-km, processing 0.05 GJ/t, spreading 0.05 GJ/ha, embodied 74.1 kg CO2/GJ.

YIELD CREDIT. The agronomic S dose for S-deficient soils is about 20-40 kg S/ha, i.e. 0.11-0.21 t gypsum. The methane doses above supply 93-279 kg S/ha. A sulfur-nutrition yield gain therefore pays only for the first ~0.1-0.2 t; the claim that a 5% yield gain pays for the whole dose holds only in the low case.

SCALE. Rice CH4 assumed at 30 Mt/yr = 0.81 Gt CO2e (GWP100) or 2.39 Gt (GWP20); 165 Mha harvested; implied mean 182 kg CH4/ha/yr.
- Low: 5% adoption × 15% of the AWD residual = 3.3 Mt CO2e/yr.
- Base: 15% × 25% = 16.7 Mt CO2e/yr (49.3 Mt at GWP20); needs 18.6 Mt gypsum/yr.
- High: 30% × 40% = 58.3 Mt CO2e/yr; 24.8 Mt gypsum/yr.
- Claim 4's arithmetic (8-61 Mt) is correct.
phys.resource_needs:
Energy is negligible: 2.8-9.7 PJ/yr, under 0.002% of world primary energy, almost all of it diesel for hauling gypsum. Haul distance dominates; past ~500 km the high case loses about half its gross benefit to transport.

Gypsum: 8-25 Mt/yr across the scenarios (base 18.6 Mt). That is within supply as I recall it, which I could not verify: phosphogypsum about 150-280 Mt/yr globally (India about 10-15 Mt), FGD gypsum over 100 Mt/yr, plus natural gypsum.

No land or extra water is needed; AWD saves water. Sulfur loading of 93-279 kg S/ha/season is 2-7x the crop's need, which means sulfate leaching to groundwater and accumulating sulfur.

Monitoring: soil Hg screening before enrolling fields; MeHg testing of grain; Ra-226, Cd and F certification of phosphogypsum batches. My recollection is a US EPA limit of 10 pCi/g Ra-226 for agricultural phosphogypsum, unverified. Plus CH4 MRV, which is the weak point for credits.
phys.violations:
There are no thermodynamic violations; the idea is not physically impossible.

Heroic or unsupported assumptions:
(a) The low/optimistic case needs more than 100% single-use electron efficiency (129%), so it rests entirely on the untested sulfate-recycling hypothesis. Claim 3's pairing of 2.7 t CO2e/ha at a 0.7 t dose needs at least 1.53x recycling.
(b) Claim 3 computes savings against the flooded baseline, but the idea is stacked on AWD, which already removes about 45% of emissions. Per-ha savings are about 0.55-0.6x what is stated, and cost per tonne is correspondingly higher.
(c) The yield credit covering the whole dose only holds for doses near the agronomic S rate (about 0.1-0.2 t/ha), not 0.7-2 t.
(d) Direct counter-evidence on the core graft:
- Liu et al. 2021 (ES&T 55:12075, PMID 34409832): rice mesocosms in straw-amended soil, flooded or with two wet-dry cycles. Sulfate fertilisation did not lower soil CH4 concentrations; AWD alone took CH4 from 51 to 0.04 mg C/L. The authors' explanation is that ample organic substrate relaxed the competition between sulfate reducers and methanogens. The confound is that this was straw-amended soil, but straw incorporation is common in Asian rice systems.
- Tang et al. 2022 (J Environ Sci 119:166, PMID 35934461): lab incubation of sulfur-amended paddy soils. Rising redox re-oxidised reduced sulfur to sulfate, which raised MeHg 10.9-35.2% and MeHg phytoavailability by up to 75%. The drying-phase sulfate recharge this idea depends on is therefore the same process that raises MeHg.
phys.key_uncertainties:
1. Does sulfate recycle under real AWD drying, and is the extra CH4 cut beyond AWD worth having? This decides both cost (base $89/t versus high $1870/t) and scale. Liu 2021 found sulfate added nothing measurable in straw-amended mesocosms, and AWD already suppresses most methanogenesis, so the residual left to target is small. A 2026 EGU abstract (Kim & Park, anaerobic 10 g incubations, no AWD) reports 81-96% CH4 cuts from sulfate salts, but that is a lab upper bound, not a field result.
2. MeHg trade-off. Tang 2022 suggests the recycling mechanism itself raises MeHg, so the falsification threshold (c) of MeHg up 50% may trip in Hg-impacted soils. Hg-contaminated regions would have to be excluded.
3. Unverified items:
- Malyan et al. 2021: the citation exists (AGEE, Oct 2021; Malyan, Bhatia ... Pathak), but the abstract is paywalled, so I could not check the 9.3-27.5% figure, the 23.6% figure, the dose or the yield numbers.
- The Verra CDM-rice suspension figure (4.56M credits) and India's gypsum subsidy are unverified; the web-search budget was exhausted.
- Rice CH4 of about 30 Mt/yr: the bottom-up Global Methane Budget range is about 25-38 Mt.
4. MRV. CH4 savings stacked on AWD at 0.07-1.6 t CO2e/ha are hard to measure and credit separately from AWD. Buyers (S10) may discount them.
5. Prior art is denser than the idea suggests. Hu 2018 FGD dose-response, Wörner 2016 (gypsum and S-cycling microbes), Liu 2021 (sulfate × AWD directly) and the Kumar 2020 review all exist. The actual novelty is narrower: dose sizing on the assumption of recycling, plus a contaminant cap. The proposed $15-30k pot trial is the right cheap test and should include straw-amended arms and soil Hg screening.

stances.evidence: The idea avoids S1's fossil-specific red lines: there is no EOR, no fossil lock-in, and no CCS subsidy (CAN 2021 position paper, red lines 3 and 7). Agricultural methane cuts fit the COP28 GST call (1/CMA.5 para 28f) to substantially reduce methane by 2030. The split comes from two places. (a) Phosphogypsum is a campaign target. Wikipedia's Piney Point article reports that the Center for Biological Diversity and Sierra Club petitioned EPA in Feb 2021 for stronger stack protections. EPA approved TFI's request to put phosphogypsum in roads on 14 Oct 2020 and withdrew the approval on 30 Jun 2021, citing an incomplete application (EPA phosphogypsum page). The page does not name any NGO challenger, and I could not verify one. (b) If the cuts are sold as voluntary offsets, CAN red line 4 applies (no 'negative emissions or offsets as an alternative to stringent emission reductions'). Expect support for a clean FGD or natural gypsum variant framed as a farm practice, and opposition to a phosphogypsum variant that generates offsets.
stances.red_line_hit: Phosphogypsum radioactivity and contaminants (Ra-226, Cd, F). Offsets substituting for cuts (CAN 2021 red line 4).

stances.evidence: Support is for the falsification trial, not yet for deployment. The mechanism, sulfate reducers outcompeting methanogens, is textbook. PNAS 2004 (doi 10.1073/pnas.0404412101) modelled sulfur-deposition suppression of wetland CH4, and the measured trial is Malyan et al. 2021 (CH4 cut 9.3-27.5%, yield up 3.1-11.2%). S2 will ask for co-measurement of food-safety outcomes, because the mercury literature points the other way. Guo et al. 2024 (J Hazard Mater, doi 10.1016/j.jhazmat.2024.135049) found sulfate-reducing bacteria cut soil MeHg production by about 22% and 17% in two soils but raised grain MeHg by about 55% and 99%. Li et al. 2023 (J Hazard Mater, doi 10.1016/j.jhazmat.2023.131602) found sulfur or sulfate at 1000 mg/kg raised grain MeHg by 269-444%, with smaller effects at 500 mg/kg. Confound: my calculation puts the proposed 0.3-1 t/ha gypsum at only about 21-72 mg S/kg in a 20 cm plough layer, 14-47x below Li's high dose, so field-rate dose-response is unknown. A GeoHealth 2025 study (doi 10.1029/2025gh001410) found less flooding cut CH4, grain As, Hg and MeHg, but raised grain Cd by 50-97% above the CODEX limit and cut yield by up to 40% in the driest regime. AWD therefore carries its own trade-off, which the idea's falsification test should also measure (Cd).
stances.red_line_hit: None categorical. Deployment is conditional on MeHg and Cd staying within limits.

stances.evidence: No direct stake. The idea neither threatens nor helps upstream oil and gas: no fee, no EOR, no storage obligation. The only touchpoint is S3 companies as possible credit buyers. OGCI and OGDC methane commitments cover their own operations (map), so rice credits would not count toward them. There is a mild reputational risk if bought as offsets. I found no documented S3 position on rice methane.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: The phosphate-fertiliser industry has a documented, sustained effort to find phosphogypsum outlets. EPA records show TFI's 2020 request for road use, approved then withdrawn in 2021, and a Dec 2024 approval for a Mosaic private-road pilot in Florida. US law already permits agricultural use when stack Ra-226 averages at most 10 pCi/g, with certification (40 CFR 61.204). Turning a stacked liability into a fertiliser product is a direct S4 win. The Piney Point failure (Mar-Apr 2021: about 480M gallons of wastewater, 316 households evacuated, $100M state closure funding) shows the size of the stack liability. FGD-gypsum sellers, an S5 by-product, also gain.
stances.red_line_hit: None for S4. The risk for S4 is regulatory: a contaminant cap stricter than 10 pCi/g, or Cd limits, would shrink the eligible supply.

stances.evidence: Utilities' only stake is as sellers of FGD gypsum, a modest by-product revenue. Agricultural FGD gypsum is an established US outlet (USDA NRCS gypsum practice standard; from memory, not re-verified this session). No cost or obligation falls on S5. I found no documented position.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: No job losses in high-carbon regions. There could be small employment gains in gypsum logistics and agricultural extension. Unlike the Carbon Capture Coalition alignment on 45Q (map), there is no union constituency built around it. I found no documented position.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: Governments of major rice producers are divided on agricultural methane. Bangladesh, Vietnam, Indonesia, the Philippines and Pakistan are Global Methane Pledge participants; India, China and Thailand are not. These come from the participant list on globalmethanepledge.org, fetched 2026-10-05, which counts 159 countries plus the EC. India's stated reason, protecting smallholder agricultural emissions, comes from my memory and was not verified this session. All parties nonetheless agreed the COP28 methane language. Agriculture ministries are drawn to a yield-raising sulfur input delivered through existing fertiliser channels; India's use of gypsum on sodic soils is the idea's own claim and was not verified. Food-safety regulators are a counterweight on MeHg, Cd and Ra-226. In the US, the phosphogypsum road approval reversed within 8 months (2020-2021), which shows the regulatory volatility.
stances.red_line_hit: For non-GMP states (India, China): any framing as a binding agricultural methane commitment. For all states: food-safety exceedances.

stances.evidence: On the benefit side, there is no land grab, smallholders gain yield (Malyan 2021: +3.1-11.2%) where soils are sulfur-deficient, and Baum et al. 2024 (N=30,284, 30 countries, 2022) found Global South publics more supportive of every climate technology. On the cost side, the same survey found Global South respondents more worried about mitigation deterrence and unequal risk. Putting abatement onto smallholders through offsets bought by Northern emitters triggers the CAN offset objection. AWD needs controlled irrigation, so rainfed and the poorest farmers are excluded. Farmers would bear the contaminant risk from industrial waste routed onto their fields, a classic environmental-justice concern.
stances.red_line_hit: Offsetting Northern emissions with smallholder abatement. Contaminated industrial waste on poor farmers' fields.

stances.evidence: There is no price rise; if yields rise, rice supply could grow slightly. The red line is food safety. Rice is a MeHg exposure route: sulfate-reducer activity raised grain MeHg by 55-99% (Guo 2024), and high sulfur doses by 269-444% (Li 2023, at doses far above the proposal). AWD can raise grain Cd by 50-97% (GeoHealth 2025), and phosphogypsum adds more Cd. My worst-case calculation assumes phosphogypsum Cd of 0.5-5 mg/kg, a literature range I did not verify. That adds 0.35-10 g Cd/ha/season at 0.7-2 t/ha. Consumers are neutral if grain monitoring shows no exceedances, and opposed if it does.
stances.red_line_hit: Food-safety exceedances (MeHg, Cd, Ra-226 in grain).

stances.evidence: Credit buyers face a rice MRV credibility problem. Verra inactivated the CDM rice methodology AMS-III.AU in March 2023 (Verra VM0051 page). VM0051 v1.0 became active on 27 Feb 2025 and v1.1 on 14 Jul 2026, but it covers 'improved water and crop management' and does not mention amendments. The extra gypsum cut is therefore probably not creditable today without a methodology revision. The idea's figure of 4.56M suspended credits was not verified. Insurers and lenders would see contaminant liability in phosphogypsum distribution, which Piney Point illustrates. Impact investors in agriculture may back the yield case.
stances.red_line_hit: Weak MRV (cuts from a soil amendment are hard to verify per field). Contaminant liability.

stances.evidence: There are two different communities. Those near phosphogypsum stacks may gain if stacks are drawn down, given Piney Point's 2021 evacuations and Tampa Bay discharge. Those near the fields carry the soil contamination. My calculation: at the 10 pCi/g cap, 0.7-2 t/ha/season adds about 0.10-0.28 Bq/g Ra-226 to a 20 cm plough layer each season, against a typical soil background of about 0.03-0.04 Bq/g. That is a worst case at the cap; actual Ra-226 varies by stack and some phosphogypsum is far lower. The total accumulates over 2-3 seasons a year. Sulfate leaching to groundwater and H2S near iron-poor fields are local risks. FGD or natural gypsum largely removes the radiological concern.
stances.red_line_hit: Radioactive or heavy-metal soil build-up near homes and water sources (phosphogypsum variant).

stake.coalition_notes: Overall: the idea sidesteps every fossil-sector fight on the map (EOR, storage liability, consumer carbon prices, per-tonne fees on S3), so S3/S5/S6 are neutral rather than opposed. S4 (phosphate) is the only strong industrial supporter. The contested ground is food safety and waste-to-field, not climate politics. Narrowest broad coalition: (1) default to clean FGD or natural gypsum, allowing phosphogypsum only under a stricter Ra-226/Cd cap than the US 10 pCi/g, with grain MeHg/Cd/Ra monitoring as a condition of payment. This removes the S1/S11 red line at the cost of S4's main prize. (2) Frame it as a sulfur fertiliser plus water practice delivered through national extension and results-based finance in Global Methane Pledge countries (Bangladesh, Vietnam, Indonesia, Philippines, Pakistan), not as voluntary offsets. This avoids CAN red line 4 and India/China sensitivity over agricultural commitments. (3) Credit only after a VM0051 revision covering amendments, with a direct-measurement MRV component, to address S10's distrust after AMS-III.AU was inactivated (Mar 2023). Key evidence gap that decides S2/S9/S11: MeHg dose-response at field rates. The adverse MeHg results come from doses about 5-47x higher (Li 2023: 1000 mg/kg vs the proposal's ~21-72 mg S/kg at 0.3-1 t/ha), or from SRB inoculation rather than sulfate dosing (Guo 2024). AWD drying itself lowered grain MeHg but raised Cd (GeoHealth 2025), so the falsification trial should add grain Cd and Ra-226 to its kill criteria. Caveats: WebSearch budget was exhausted this session. Positions come from fetched primary pages (EPA phosphogypsum page, 40 CFR 61.204 via Cornell LII, the Verra VM0051 page, globalmethanepledge.org, Europe PMC abstracts, Wikipedia's Piney Point article) plus the supplied map. India's stated reason for staying out of the GMP, the NRCS gypsum standard, the phosphogypsum Cd range and the 4.56M-credit figure are unverified. I found no documented position from S3, S5 or S6 on rice methane. Calculation script: climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/gypsum_stakeholder.py

critic.fatal_flaw: None found. There is no physics violation. The scale is small (base about 17 Mt CO2e/yr, about 0.03% of global emissions), but that limits the idea to an add-on rather than killing it. Every stakeholder red line can be designed around: drop phosphogypsum, screen out mercury-impacted soils, and do not sell the cuts as offsets. The serious threat is empirical, not fatal. The marginal methane cut on top of AWD may be close to zero across much of the target area, and a cheap trial can settle that.
critic.top_fixable_flaw:
The target and the falsification trial are not conditioned on the substrate (straw) regime, which decides whether the 1-to-1 electron diversion can happen at all. My electron budget (critic_gypsum_awd.py, same scratchpad folder):
- **Straw.** 3-6 t/ha of incorporated straw, half degraded in season, supplies about 200-400 kmol of electrons/ha.
- **Gypsum.** A 0.75 t/ha dose takes up only about 35 kmol of electrons per pass.
- **The CH4 left after AWD.** The residual is 27-75 kmol of electrons, i.e. 55-150 kg CH4.
- **Iron.** Native Fe(III) re-oxidised in each AWD drying returns about 1-23 kmol of electrons per cycle. AWD therefore already performs the "recharged electron acceptor" trick with iron, and the extra sulfate is comparable in size, not dominant.

What follows from this:
- When donor (straw) is in excess, sulfate reducers and methanogens both get fed. Sulfate becomes a parallel sink rather than a diversion, which is exactly Liu 2021's null.
- The idea's own 4-arm pot trial, run on a typical straw-incorporated soil, will probably repeat that null. Run on a low-organic soil, it will give a positive that cannot be extrapolated.
- The 10-30% adoption estimate assumes donor-limited soils across irrigated Asia.
- India's push to replace stubble burning with in-situ straw incorporation is reducing the low-straw niche over time. This is a policy trend I recall, not verified this session.
- Recycling sulfate 3x does not help unless donor is limiting. The recycling hypothesis is therefore secondary to the substrate condition.
critic.suggested_patch:
Replace the 4-arm trial with an 8-arm factorial, all under AWD, plus a flooded control at the high-straw level:
- **Straw:** removed vs. 5 t/ha incorporated.
- **Gypsum:** none, an agronomic dose of 0.15 t/ha (about 28 kg S), and a methane dose of 0.75 t/ha.

Do not use phosphogypsum in the trial; use FGD or natural gypsum only. Screen soils for Hg first.

Isolate recycling directly. Measure, before and after each drying cycle:
- porewater SO4
- 0.5 M HCl-extractable Fe(II)/Fe(III)
- acid-volatile sulfide

Add 34S-labelled gypsum in one replicate block if budget allows, roughly $5k extra.

Restate the kill criteria in transferable units:
- (a) Falsified if the marginal CH4 avoided is under 0.3 mol CH4 per mol of added SO4 in the low-straw arm. That is an efficiency below 30%, the level the base-case TEA needs.
- (b) Falsified if net SO4 regenerated per drying cycle is under 25% of the added SO4.
- (c) Falsified if grain MeHg or Cd rises more than 20% above AWD-alone. AWD lowers MeHg, so the comparator must be AWD, not flooding.

Deployment change:
- Default to the agronomic S dose sold as sulfur fertiliser, which the yield gain pays for.
- Count methane only as a measured co-benefit, and only in mapped donor-limited soils: straw removed or exported, and low soil organic carbon.
- Re-scope the scale estimate to that soil class before claiming any Mt figure.

patched_idea.title: Sulfate-recharged AWD: gypsum plus alternate wetting and drying in rice, scoped to donor-limited soils
patched_idea.one_line: Add a small dose of clean gypsum (FGD or natural; no phosphogypsum) to alternate-wetting-and-drying rice. Sulfate reducers then outcompete methanogens, and each drying cycle should re-oxidise sulfide back to sulfate. The default is a sulfur-fertiliser dose that the yield gain pays for; methane is counted only as a measured co-benefit, and only on mapped soils where electron donor (straw, organic carbon) is limiting.
patched_idea.conventional_core: Alternate wetting and drying (AWD): TRL 9 agronomy, credited under Verra VM0051, cutting rice CH4 by 30-50% and saving about 30% of water (map). Gypsum as a sulfur fertiliser is likewise conventional agronomy.
patched_idea.graft: Thermodynamic competitive exclusion, as in marine sediments: when sulfate is present, sulfate reducers outcompete methanogens for H2 and acetate. Unchanged from the original.
patched_idea.mechanism:
Each mole of sulfate diverts the electrons of up to about one mole of CH4 (acetate + SO4 to 2 HCO3- + HS-; or 4 H2 + SO4). Under continuous flooding the sulfate is consumed once. Under AWD the drying phase lets O2 in and re-oxidises FeS and H2S to sulfate, so the same sulfur can suppress methanogenesis again in the next flood. This is the hypothesis under test.

Applicability condition (added by the patch). The diversion is 1-to-1 only when electron donor is limiting. Incorporated straw at 3-6 t/ha supplies about 200-400 kmol of electrons/ha per season. A 0.75 t/ha gypsum dose takes up only about 35 kmol per pass (critic_gypsum_awd.py). Where donor is in excess, sulfate reducers and methanogens are both fed, so sulfate is a parallel sink rather than a diversion (consistent with the null in Liu 2021, as cited by the critic). Native Fe(III), re-oxidised each AWD drying, already returns about 1-23 kmol of electrons per cycle. AWD therefore already performs a recharged-acceptor effect with iron, and added sulfate is comparable in size to it, not dominant.

The mechanism is therefore claimed only for donor-limited soils: straw removed or exported, and low soil organic carbon. Many South Asian rice soils are short of sulfur, so the agronomic dose may also raise yields; that is the deployment default.
patched_idea.target: Paddy rice CH4, assumed about 30 Mt CH4/yr: 0.81 Gt CO2e at GWP100 or 2.4 Gt at GWP20, using the verifier's biogenic GWPs (27.0 and 79.7). The patch re-scopes the addressable target to AWD-feasible irrigated rice on donor-limited soils (straw removed or exported, low SOC) in India, Bangladesh, Vietnam and China. On assumed shares this is about 1.9-9.3 Mha of the ~96 Mha harvested area (assumptions listed under quantitative claims). Mapping this soil class is a prerequisite before any Mt figure is claimed.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
(1) Measured (Malyan et al. 2021, Agric. Ecosyst. Environ., irrigated rice in India, lab plus field). Four amendments cut cumulative CH4 by 9.3-27.5%. Phosphogypsum had the largest GWP reduction (23.6%), so I infer it was near the top of that range. Grain yield rose 3.1-11.2%, and GHG intensity fell from 0.309 to 0.212 kg CO2e/kg grain. Confound: the straw/organic-matter regime of those plots was not used to condition the result here, so it may not transfer to straw-incorporated soils.

(2) Electron budget (critic's calculation, critic_gypsum_awd.py, modelled):
- Straw: 3-6 t/ha incorporated supplies 200-400 kmol e-/ha per season.
- Residual CH4 after AWD: 55-150 kg, i.e. 27-75 kmol e-.
- Gypsum: 0.15 t/ha is about 7 kmol e- per pass; 0.75 t/ha about 35.
- Native Fe(III) recharge: 1-23 kmol e- per drying cycle.
Sulfate can be a diversion only where donor is limiting.

(3) Per-hectare co-benefit (patch_gypsum_awd.py, modelled). Avoided CH4 is capped at 40% of the AWD residual (an assumption).
- Agronomic dose, 0.15 t/ha gypsum (871 mol SO4, 28 kg S):
  - At the kill threshold (0.3 mol CH4 per mol SO4, single pass): 4.2 kg CH4 = 0.11 t CO2e (GWP100), 0.33 t (GWP20).
  - At full efficiency with 3 passes: up to 42 kg CH4 = 1.13 t CO2e (GWP100).
- Methane dose, 0.75 t/ha: 21-60 kg CH4 = 0.57-1.62 t CO2e (GWP100), limited by the residual cap.

(4) Economics (assumed prices: gypsum $15-40/t, spreading $10/ha). The agronomic dose costs about $12-16/ha. A 3.1% yield gain (the low end in Malyan) on 5 t/ha at $300/t is worth about $46/ha, so sulfur nutrition pays for the dose and methane comes as a free co-benefit. Confound: the yield gain may come from sulfur nutrition rather than methane suppression, which is why methane is not sold on its own.

(5) Re-scoped scale (assumptions, unverified this session):
- Harvested area about 96 Mha: India 47, China 30, Bangladesh 11.5, Vietnam 7.2 (FAO order of magnitude, from memory).
- 65% of that area irrigated.
- 30-50% of irrigated area AWD-feasible.
- 10-30% of that donor-limited.
- 10-30% adoption.
Result: about 0.02-3.2 Mt CO2e/yr (GWP100), or 0.06-9.4 Mt (GWP20). This replaces the original 8-61 Mt figure, which assumed donor-limited soils across irrigated Asia. The upper end is plausibly shrinking where policy pushes in-situ straw incorporation instead of stubble burning (the critic's recollection of Indian policy, not verified).

(6) Energy: negligible; there is no separation step.
patched_idea.who_gains: S8 smallholders: a sulfur-fertiliser dose that pays for itself through yield, with a measured methane co-benefit and AWD's water saving. S4 FGD-gypsum producers (utilities and industry): a by-product becomes fertiliser. The phosphate industry no longer gains, because phosphogypsum is excluded.
