S7 India, Bangladesh and Vietnam: an input their extension systems already handle (India supports gypsum for sodic soils; from memory, unverified). S2: a cleanly conditioned, testable mechanism. S1: supportive because there is no phosphogypsum, Hg-impacted soils are screened out, and no offsets are sold on unmeasured cuts.
patched_idea.who_loses: S11 and S9 food-safety concerns, now mitigated rather than eliminated. Sulfate reducers methylate mercury, and rice accumulates MeHg; the patch requires Hg screening and a 20% MeHg/Cd ceiling against AWD-alone. Iron-poor soils risk H2S toxicity, and sulfate can leach to groundwater. S10 credit buyers: the patch drops the stand-alone offset claim, given distrust of rice MRV after Verra suspended its CDM rice methodology (4.56M credits). Phosphogypsum stack owners lose the outlet they would have had in the original idea. Natural-gypsum suppliers may face competition from FGD gypsum.
patched_idea.closest_known_work: Malyan et al. 2021 (doi 10.1016/j.agee.2021.107545) on phosphogypsum and other CH4-mitigating chemicals in rice. Kumar et al. 2020, Chemosphere (doi 10.1016/j.chemosphere.2019.124824), a review of fly ash, steel slag and phosphogypsum for paddy GHG mitigation. Liu 2021 (as cited by the critic): a null result for sulfate under substrate excess. Many sulfate-in-paddy studies. AWD under Verra VM0051 (map).
patched_idea.why_different:
Prior work treats gypsum and AWD as separate options and does not condition on substrate. This idea:
- Sizes the dose around sulfate recycling during AWD drying cycles.
- Restricts the methane claim to donor-limited soils, using an explicit electron budget (straw vs SO4 vs Fe(III)).
- Tests recycling directly, with porewater SO4, AVS and Fe(II)/Fe(III) measured before and after each drying, plus optional 34S labelling.
- Routes clean industrial gypsum through sulfur-fertiliser channels, with an Hg screen and a MeHg/Cd cap.
patched_idea.cheapest_falsifying_test:
A 10-week pot or microcosm trial on Hg-screened soil with FGD or natural gypsum only (no phosphogypsum). Design: an all-AWD factorial of straw (removed vs 5 t/ha incorporated) by gypsum (none, 0.15 t/ha agronomic dose of about 28 kg S, and 0.75 t/ha methane dose), plus a continuously flooded control at the high-straw level.

Measurements:
- CH4 flux by chamber.
- Before and after each drying cycle: porewater SO4, 0.5 M HCl-extractable Fe(II)/Fe(III), and acid-volatile sulfide.
- Grain and soil MeHg and Cd.
- Optionally, 34S-labelled gypsum in one replicate block (about $5k extra).

The idea is falsified if any of these holds:
- (a) In the low-straw arm, marginal CH4 avoided is below 0.3 mol CH4 per mol of added SO4.
- (b) Net SO4 regenerated per drying cycle is below 25% of the added SO4.
- (c) Grain MeHg or Cd rises more than 20% above AWD-alone.

A null in the high-straw arm together with a positive in the low-straw arm confirms the substrate condition rather than falsifying the idea. Cost about $20-35k at a university greenhouse.

fix.change_summary:
I applied the critic's patch and kept the core mechanism (sulfate re-oxidised during AWD drying and reused against methanogens) and the graft (competitive exclusion by sulfate reducers) unchanged.

- **Applicability condition.** The patch adds an explicit condition: the 1-to-1 electron diversion is claimed only on donor-limited soils (straw removed or exported, low SOC). This follows the critic's electron budget: straw supplies 200-400 kmol e-/ha, a 0.75 t gypsum dose about 35, and the AWD Fe(III) recharge 1-23 per cycle.
- **Trial.** The 4-arm trial becomes an 8-arm design: an AWD factorial of straw (removed vs 5 t/ha) by gypsum (0, 0.15, 0.75 t/ha), plus a flooded high-straw control. It uses FGD or natural gypsum only and Hg-screened soils. Porewater SO4, AVS and Fe(II)/Fe(III) are measured before and after each drying, with optional 34S labelling.
- **Kill criteria.** These are restated in transferable units: (a) below 0.3 mol CH4 avoided per mol SO4 in the low-straw arm; (b) below 25% SO4 regenerated per drying cycle; (c) MeHg or Cd more than 20% above AWD-alone.
- **Deployment default.** Deployment now defaults to the agronomic sulfur dose: about $12-16/ha against roughly $46/ha of yield value at a 3.1% gain. Methane counts only as a measured co-benefit and is not sold as an offset.
- **Recalculated figures.** I recalculated per-hectare and scale figures in patch_gypsum_awd.py, run with the verifier's GWPs. The co-benefit is 0.11-1.13 t CO2e/ha/season (GWP100) at the agronomic dose. Scale falls from 8-61 to about 0.02-3.2 Mt CO2e/yr (GWP100) on 1.9-9.3 Mha of assumed donor-limited AWD area; those area shares are flagged as unverified assumptions.
- **Stakeholder lists.** Excluding phosphogypsum moves the phosphate industry out of the gainers list.

Scripts: climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/patch_gypsum_awd.py (new) and critic_gypsum_awd.py (critic's).

idea.title: Store heat, not the loaded sorbent: grid-charged hot-water storage so DAC regenerates 24/7
idea.one_line: To use cheap-hour electricity without leaving capital idle, charge a pressurised hot-water store (12-16 h) during the cheapest hours and regenerate continuously. Storing heat costs ~$9-25 per t/yr of capacity, against ~$550-1,660 for storing loaded sorbent (the map's 'store the swing' proposal).
idea.conventional_core: Solid-sorbent temperature-swing DAC kept at a high capacity factor.
idea.graft: Power-to-heat with large pressurised hot-water storage, from Danish and German district heating.
idea.mechanism:
DAC cost is capital multiplied by utilisation. Running only on curtailed power raises the capital charge from $274/t at 95% capacity factor to $788/t at 33%, at Stratos-like $2,600 per t/yr.

Heat is the largest energy term, and it can be time-shifted cheaply in water at 100-120 C. The electric loads (fans, vacuum) stay continuous.

Storing the swing (loaded sorbent) needs extra sorbent inventory at $20-40/kg, which is 20-70x dearer than storing the heat. Storing the swing makes sense only for very cheap sorbents such as CaO.
idea.target: Regeneration energy cost versus capacity-factor trade-off (intermittency), a bottleneck named in the verified map.
idea.quantitative_claims:
Modelled; script thermo_ideas.py §3.

- **Heat storage:** a 100 kt/yr plant needs 22.8 MW_th (7.2 GJ_th/t). A 16 h store holds 365 MWh_th, which is ~6,300 m3 of water at ΔT 50 K. At $150-400/m3 that costs $0.9-2.5M, or $9-25 per t/yr.
- **Storing loaded sorbent instead:** 16 h is 183 t of CO2, which needs 2,770-4,150 t of sorbent (1.0-1.5 mmol/g) costing $55-166M, or $553-1,660 per t/yr.
- **Heat cost, air-source heat pump at COP 2.2:** $55/t at a $60/MWh average price, versus $18/t if bought in the cheapest 8 h at an assumed $20/MWh. That saves ~$36/t.
- **Heat cost, electric boiler:** $120/t versus $40/t on the same assumptions.
- **Charging equipment:** must be rated at 3x the average load (31 MWe of heat pump or 68 MWe of e-boiler for 8 h/day of charging).
idea.who_gains:
- **S5:** a large flexible load that absorbs midday solar and wind surplus.
- **S10:** the capacity factor stays high.
- **S7:** grid balancing.
- **S9:** slightly lower curtailment costs.
idea.who_loses:
- **S3 gas-heat suppliers.**
- **DAC designs marketed as 'runs only on curtailed power'.**
- **Heat-pump buyers:** charging hardware must be rated at 3x the average load.
idea.closest_known_work:
- **Fan & Xu 2026, ES&T:** CSP plus sand storage for DAC, above 80% capacity factor.
- **District-heating power-to-heat with storage:** Denmark.
- **Antora and Rondo:** thermal batteries for higher-temperature industrial heat.
- **The verified map's open problem 'store the swing':** this calculation shows it is 20-70x more expensive for amine sorbents.
idea.why_different: It is a quantitative correction to a popular proposal: buffer the heat, not the loaded sorbent. It is grid-charged and uses the cheapest storage medium at the temperature the sorbent needs.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test:
1. **Desk test (days):** take 2025 hourly wholesale prices for ERCOT, DE-LU, Nord Pool SE3 and CAISO. Compute the heat cost of charging in the cheapest 8-12 h, with 2-5%/day storage loss, against flat purchase.
2. **Falsified if** the saving is below $15/t in every target market, i.e. the mean of the cheapest 8 h sits within ~$15/MWh of the daily mean.
idea.family: Grid-charged pressurised hot-water storage so DAC regenerates 24/7 on cheap-hour power

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: Mohan, Konuru, Luo & Jenkins (2025), 'Direct air capture with thermal energy storage: process design and electricity system impacts', J. Phys.: Energy 8(1) 015011
closest.overlap: This is the core concept, already published. It models solid-sorbent DAC regenerating at 100-120 C with heat from grid-charged thermal storage, so the plant runs baseload while the heat is bought when wind and solar are available. The model leaves capacity factor unconstrained apart from 2 weeks of maintenance, and the DAC runs baseload because capital is expensive. It compares four set-ups at 5 Mt/yr: heat pump only, heat pump plus TES, TES only, and TES plus a steam turbine. The storage is resistive-charged firebrick at 200-1200 C ($19/kWh-th, $109/kW-e charge). Gross removal costs are within 3% of each other (~$570-585/t). Net cost after grid-emission effects is ~11-13% lower with TES only than without storage (~$515 vs ~$570/t), and ~$200/t lower than heat pump only (~$715/t). The authors say they are the first to combine TES with DAC. Caution for the idea's ~$36/t saving claim: in this model the storage barely changed facility-level gross cost (<3% spread).

closest.title: Fan & Xu (2026), 'Design Optimization and Global Impact Assessment of Solar-Thermal Direct Air Carbon Capture', Environ. Sci. Technol. (PMID 42260897)
closest.overlap: Thermal storage (sand) buffers regeneration heat so a sorbent DAC plant reaches a capacity factor above 80%. A 6,000 t/yr module costs $160-200/t (core technology) and ~$300-350/t (deployment-adjusted). The heat source is concentrated solar, not grid power or a heat pump, and the storage medium is sand, not water.

closest.title: Arwa & Schell (2024), 'Batteries or silos: Optimizing storage capacity in direct air capture plants to maximize renewable energy use', Applied Energy 122345
closest.overlap: This is the 'store the swing' alternative for liquid-solvent DAC. The model stores the solid CaCO3/CaO intermediates in silos (660 t and 370 t over a 336-h profile) instead of a 355 MWh / 65 MW battery, and finds silos cheaper. It does not consider heat storage. It supports the idea's caveat that storing the swing pays only with cheap solids such as CaO; it does not cover amine sorbents.

closest.title: Prats-Salvado, Monnerie & Sattler (DLR): 'Solar-Powered Direct Air Capture' ES&T 2024 (10.1021/acs.est.3c08269) and the review 'Powering DAC: ... overlooked role of concentrated solar thermal' (2025, 10.1007/s40518-025-00255-y)
closest.overlap: Dispatchable stored heat for DAC, framed around concentrated solar, which they call the cheapest dispatchable renewable heat. I could not access the ES&T paper's full text, so I have not confirmed whether it compares a PV-plus-heater-plus-storage option.

closest.title: Fasihi, Efimova & Breyer (2019), 'Techno-economic assessment of CO2 direct air capture plants', J. Cleaner Production
closest.overlap: Low-temperature sorbent DAC powered by hybrid wind, solar and battery systems for high full-load hours, with heat supply as a major cost lever. From memory, not verified in the abstract: the LUT models supply DAC heat with heat pumps and heat storage.

closest.title: Klockow, Mader & Linder (2024), 'Combining DAC and long-term energy storage: renewable heating with CO2 capture', SSRN 5020898
closest.overlap: Couples a CaO/Ca(OH)2 thermochemical heat store with CO2 capture: 480 kWh of heat per t CO2, with the discharged slaked lime used as the sorbent. It combines heat storage with capture, but through a different chemistry.

closest.title: Danish and German district-heating power-to-heat with large pressurised or unpressurised hot-water accumulators
closest.overlap: The grafted component is a mature, commercial technology: large heat pumps and e-boilers charge cheaply in low-price hours and store heat in tanks at roughly 90-120 C. No cited DAC paper uses it, but the hardware and its economics are standard.

art.what_is_new:
Not new: grid-charged thermal storage that lets solid-sorbent DAC regenerate baseload on cheap or intermittent power. Mohan, Konuru, Luo & Jenkins (Princeton ZERO Lab, 2025) published this, including heat-pump-plus-TES and TES-only set-ups. Fan & Xu (2026) did the same with concentrated solar and sand storage, above 80% capacity factor.

What remains new is incremental:
1. **The storage medium.** Pressurised hot water at 100-120 C, charged by a heat pump at COP ~2.2, matches the sorbent's regeneration temperature. Mohan et al. used resistive-charged firebrick at 200-1200 C, costing $19/kWh-th plus $109/kW-e. Water at $150-400/m3 and 50 K ΔT works out to ~$2.6-6.9/kWh-th, so the specific claim is a cheaper store at matched temperature with heat-pump charging. The hardware itself is mature district-heating practice.
2. **The 'store heat, not loaded amine sorbent' cost comparison.** It puts storing loaded amine sorbent at 20-70x dearer than storing the heat. I found no paper making this comparison for amine sorbents. Arwa & Schell (2024) stored CaO/CaCO3 solids for liquid-solvent DAC and compared only against batteries.

Before the desk test: Mohan et al. found storage changed facility-level gross cost by under 3%. The benefit showed up mainly in system-level net cost through grid-emission effects, with TES only ~11-13% cheaper. That makes the idea's claimed ~$36/t saving the claim to check.

Search limits: the web-search budget was exhausted, so this used the Crossref, PubMed, OpenAlex and IOP pages directly. Company announcements pairing Antora, Rondo or similar thermal batteries with DAC were not checked. A DuckDuckGo fallback returned a CAPTCHA, which I did not attempt.

phys.assumptions:
The script was run with the OptiLex verifier. Price and generation-mix data are real 2025 hourly series from SMARD (Bundesnetzagentur), downloaded 2025-10-05 into scratchpad/climate/smard/. Everything else is labelled as an assumption in the script.

**Plant basis.** A 100 kt/yr solid-sorbent TSA plant at a capacity factor of 0.95. Regeneration heat is 5.5/7.2/9.0 GJ_th/t; the base value is Climeworks Gen2 nominal, about 2,000 kWh_th/t, as the idea uses. Fans, vacuum and auxiliaries take 0.5/0.65/0.8 MWh_e/t and run continuously. Regeneration is at about 100 C.

**Equipment and grid costs (low/base/high).**
- Capital recovery factor (CRF): 0.08/0.10/0.12, plus 2%/yr O&M on heat equipment.
- High-temperature heat pump: $600/900/1,500 per kW_th.
- Electrode boiler: $60/100/200 per kW_e.
- Pressurised hot-water tank: $150/400/1,000 per m3, cycling from 150 C to 105 C.
- Storage loss: 0.5/1/3% per cycle.
- German-style network charges: EUR 0/15/30 per MWh, plus a capacity charge of EUR 0/40/100 per kW/yr. The low case represents an interruptible tariff.
- Exchange rate: USD 1.13 per EUR.

**Heat-pump COP.** 1.5/1.8/2.5. The 2.5 case is only reachable with a waste-heat source at about 50 C.

**Whole-plant cost.** Capex of $1,500/2,600/4,000 per t/yr; the base is the Stratos proxy the idea uses, with O&M at 4%/yr. Sorbent replacement costs $20/50/100 per t. CO2 transport and storage are excluded.

**Bundling and scale.** Low/base/high are applied jointly as favourable, central and unfavourable bundles. The scale figure of 0.3 Gt/yr is an assumed 2050 base for DAC using this heat route; 0.05 is the low case and 1.0 the high case. It is not a calculated limit: about 0.01 Mt/yr operates in 2025, and IEA NZE-type pathways reach about 1 Gt/yr by 2050 (modelled).

**What the reported numbers are.** The energy figures (7.30/9.54/11.88 GJ/t) are the all-electric e-boiler route. The cost figures ($352/673/1,151 per t) are gross per tonne captured, using DE-LU 2025 prices with stored e-boiler or heat-pump heat. They are not costs per net tonne; see the uncertainties.
phys.violations:
Nothing falls below the thermodynamic floor. The air-capture floor is 20.5 kJ/mol = 0.465 GJ/t (129 kWh/t). The all-electric route uses 7.30/9.54/11.88 GJ_e/t, a second-law efficiency of 6.4%/4.9%/3.9%. The idea's arithmetic reproduces exactly: 22.8 MW_th, 365 MWh_th and 6,292 m3, costing $9-25 per t/yr against $553-1,660 per t/yr for a loaded-sorbent buffer. The capital charge is $274/t at a capacity factor (CF) of 95% and $788/t at 33%. "Store heat, not sorbent" holds by more than 20x even at $1,000/m3 pressurised tanks.

The following errors in the idea change its conclusion.

**1. Temperature infeasibility as written.** A 50 K swing at about 100-120 C puts the bottom of the swing (e.g. 120 to 70 C) below the roughly 100 C regeneration temperature. A valid store runs from 150 to 105 C (4.7 bar abs, 6,734 m3), from 130 to 105 C (12,236 m3), or as a cascade. The store stays cheap in every case.

**2. Overstated heat-pump COP.** The idea assumes an air-source COP of 2.2 to 100 C, which is 57% of Carnot. At a feasible 150 C store top, 50% of Carnot gives COP 1.51 from 10 C air and 1.36 from -5 C air. COP above 2 needs a waste-heat source at about 50 C, which gives 2.12 at 150 C.

**3. Omitted costs of 3x-rated charging hardware and grid capacity.** The idea's "~$36/t saving" is gross energy only. With equipment capex and capacity charges, the levelised regeneration-heat cost in $/t is:

| Market (2025 prices) | Case | Best flat option | Best stored option | Saving |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DE-LU | low | 114 | 92 | +21 |
| DE-LU | base | 163 | 164 | -1 |
| DE-LU | high | 212 | 269 | -58 |
| DK1 | low | 104 | 84 | +21 |
| DK1 | base | 153 | 155 | -3 |
| DK1 | high | 202 | 262 | -59 |
| FR | low | 81 | 63 | +18 |
| FR | base | 128 | 137 | -9 |
| FR | high | 180 | 245 | -65 |

- The base-case breakdowns explain the result. The e-boiler with 8 h charging costs energy 151, grid capacity 33 and capex plus O&M 12.1. The heat pump with 8 h charging has capex plus O&M of 81. Oversizing the heat pump 3x cancels its arbitrage.
- In base and high cases the best option is a flat-running heat pump, not storage.
- By the idea's own falsification line (a saving below $15/t in every market), the claim fails at base in all three markets measured. It passes only in the favourable bundle: interruptible grid tariff, cheap heat pump and low CRF.

**4. Price spread data is not the problem.** In 2025 the cheapest 8 h/day averaged EUR 50.7 against a mean of 89.3 in DE-LU (spread 38.7; 573 negative hours). DK1 averaged 45.4 against 81.1 (spread 35.7). FR averaged 33.8 against 61.1 (spread 27.2). These match the idea's assumed $40/MWh spread.
phys.key_uncertainties:
**1. Grid CO2 erodes net removal.** In DE 2025, production-based mean generation intensity was 0.316 t/MWh, and 0.241 in the cheapest 8 h. A grid-charged e-boiler DAC plant therefore emits 0.53/0.70/0.88 t CO2 per t captured. That leaves a net removal of 0.47/0.30/0.12, which turns into $752/$2,221/$9,518 per net tonne. The intensity estimate ignores imports, life-cycle emissions and marginal-versus-average effects; marginal intensity would be worse. The idea only works with dedicated low-carbon supply or in very clean grids, and France's intensity was not computed.

**2. Grid tariff design decides the result.**
- The capacity charge on the 3x connection alone is $33/t in the base e-boiler case.
- Interruptible or flexible-load tariffs, such as Danish e-boiler tariffs or German atypical-use discounts, flip the result to about +$18-21/t.
- The tariff values are assumptions from memory, not fetched.

**3. Markets not tested.** ERCOT, CAISO and SE3 are untested because no data was fetched. ERCOT's 4CP and CAISO's midday negative prices could change the sign.

**4. Cost assumptions taken from memory.** Heat-pump, e-boiler and tank costs are Danish Energy Agency-range values from memory, not checked against the primary catalogue this session; the web-search budget was exhausted. Pressurised-tank cost at 150 C is the least certain, but it never decides the result.

**5. Hybrid dispatch not modelled.** A flat heat pump plus a small e-boiler and store used only in negative or near-zero hours was not modelled and could beat both options by a few $/t.

**6. Wrong proxy for the capital charge.** The $2,600 per t/yr capex is a Stratos (KOH plus calciner) proxy, not a solid-sorbent TSA plant. Real-plant heat duty and capacity factor are confounded by early-plant underperformance.

**7. The store does not make capture cheaper.** Even in the low case, the store moves total cost from $374 to $352 per gross tonne, about 6%. Gross DAC stays at $352-1,151/t.
phys.resource_needs:
**Per Gt/yr of DAC on this heat route (low/base/high):**
- **Storage water:** 51/67/84 million m3 of pressurised hot water (16 h store, 150 to 105 C). That is minor in water and steel terms.
- **Charging capacity:** 523/685/856 GW_e of e-boiler, rated at 3x the average load. This is the binding resource: grid connections at that scale.
- **Electricity, e-boiler route:** 2,043/2,670/3,325 TWh, which is 6.8%/8.9%/11.1% of world electricity (30,000 TWh).
- **Electricity, heat-pump route:** 1,519/1,761/1,800 TWh, which is 5.1%/5.9%/6.0% of world electricity.
- **Energy:** 7.3/9.5/11.9 EJ of final energy, which is 1.18%/1.54%/1.92% of world primary energy (620 EJ). Final energy is compared to primary here, so this understates the primary-equivalent share.

**Other inputs:**
- **Land:** footprint of the tanks plus the DAC contactors. Not computed beyond the tank volume.
- **Water:** only fill and make-up water for the store. Sorbent-process water is not computed.

stances.evidence: Most stakeholders will react to this as a DAC project; the hot-water storage graft barely registers. CAN (Jan 2021, 1,300+ NGOs) says DACCS has 'no place' in steep-reduction scenarios and it opposes negative emissions or offsets used as an alternative to cuts. CIEL (ciel.org/issue/carbon-capture-and-storage, fetched 2026-10-05) calls carbon capture a 'license to pollute indefinitely' and notes DAC 'depends on CCS or CCUS'. Frontier-style durable-removal supporters are the pro side, so the map records S1 as split. One marginal point helps: the graft replaces fossil heat with grid power plus storage, and 1PointFive's Stratos uses a natural-gas calciner (1pointfive.com, fetched 2026-10-05). It removes one concrete S1 objection without touching the core one.
stances.red_line_hit: Mitigation deterrence and offsets (CAN red lines 4 and 8). EOR applies if the CO2 goes to EOR: after OBBBA (Jul 2025), 45Q pays EOR the same as storage, which hits CAN red line 7.

stances.evidence: IPCC AR6 WGIII treats CDR as needed for residual emissions. The idea is a cost and efficiency improvement that does not dispute the physics. The OptiLex verifier puts the DAC floor at 0.47 GJ/t, with real plants at 5-10+ GJ/t; this idea leaves the energy use unchanged and only cuts its cost and carbon intensity by charging in low-price hours. Scientists' concern about DAC's energy scale still applies. Wikipedia's DAC article (fetched 2026-10-05) cites a 2026 study: 2 Gt/yr would need more than half of 2024 US electricity generation (modelled). Expect support for R&D and for the desk test, with a 'residuals only' caveat.
stances.red_line_hit: None for this idea. Generic DAC energy-scale scepticism applies.

stances.evidence: S3 has two interests here and they partly cancel. Occidental acquired Carbon Engineering (Nov 2023, $1.1bn), Stratos holds a Class VI permit (Apr 2025) and stores in saline formations, and 45Q DAC at $180/t survived OBBBA with EOR parity. Any cut in DAC operating cost helps S3 DAC owners. Against that, the idea's own 'who_loses' names gas-heat suppliers, and it does not apply to Stratos-type liquid-solvent DAC, which needs about 900 C calcination. Hot water at 100-120 C serves only solid-sorbent DAC. My own arithmetic, not the verifier: even 1 Gt/yr of DAC heat at 7.2 GJ/t is about 7 EJ, roughly 5% of world gas use, and at realistic 2030s DAC scale the displaced gas is negligible. No documented S3 position on electrified DAC heat was found.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: This does not touch steel, cement or chemicals processes. Indirectly, cheaper DAC removals could become a compliance or offset option for residual process emissions, which S4 would welcome. That is the same mechanism S1 objects to. Point-source capture at kilns has a lower floor (0.11 GJ/t, verifier) and is S4's documented route (GCCA roadmap, Brevik), so DAC is a complement rather than a substitute.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: The idea gives utilities a large, schedulable, flexible load that absorbs surplus solar and wind; it is the Danish/German district-heating power-to-heat model (precedent cited in the idea, not re-verified this session). Texas SB 6, signed 20 Jun 2025 and effective immediately, adds a demand-reduction service for customers of 75 MW and above, with 24-hour notice and continuous curtailment during energy emergencies. It also makes large loads pay at least $100,000 for screening studies (capitol.texas.gov, fetched 2026-10-05). A 100 kt/yr plant needs 31-68 MWe of charging equipment plus fans, so it sits near the 75 MW line. A load that can stop charging for 8-16 h without losing output fits this regime well; a flat 24/7 DAC load does not.
stances.red_line_hit: None if the load is genuinely interruptible. The charging hardware is rated at 3x the average load, so it can add to the connection costs a utility must recover.

stances.evidence: Unions belong to the Carbon Capture Coalition, which describes itself as companies, unions and NGOs advocating for 45Q, and which welcomed the 45Q safe-harbour extension (14 Aug 2026). Cheaper DAC means more 45Q-backed construction (sorbent contactors, pressure vessels, heat pumps, Class VI wells). The graft itself has no documented union position, and its job effect is small and positive. Low confidence: this is inferred from the coalition, not stated about the idea.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: 45Q DAC at $180/t was kept and inflation-indexed in OBBBA (Jul 2025), the only carbon-specific IRA credit that the 2025 Congress strengthened. COP28 decision 1/CMA.5 para 28 names 'removal technologies' and asks parties to triple renewables, and a flexible load helps integrate them. The SB 6 regime (Jun 2025) shows state governments want large loads to be interruptible and to pay for their own interconnection, and this design meets both conditions. The fiscal counterpoint: Taxpayers for Common Sense opposes 45Q expansions, and DAC claims the highest per-tonne credit. I could not verify the 2025-26 status of the DOE Regional DAC Hubs: the DOE page shows only a $1.8bn Dec 2024 funding notice.
stances.red_line_hit: Fiscal cost per tonne ($180/t 45Q) for fiscal hawks. No energy-security red line.

stances.evidence: Baum et al. 2024 (N=30,284, 30 countries, fielded 2022, online quota samples) found Global South publics more supportive of every technology, but more worried that the technologies undermine mitigation and spread risk unequally. Both North and South rated DACCS/BECCS the highest moral-hazard risk. Climate-justice advocates align with CAN and CIEL ('license to pollute'). The idea adds no land-grab risk; its footprint is a water store of about 6,300 m3 per 100 kt/yr. The DAC-specific concern that low-carbon power used for removal in rich countries could otherwise displace fossil generation applies to DAC in general, not specifically to this idea.
stances.red_line_hit: Mitigation deterrence, where DAC removals let Northern emitters delay cuts.

stances.evidence: Consumers do not pay for DAC directly; 45Q or voluntary buyers do. Baum 2024 found government funding the most popular policy type. The visible-price evidence (Canada scrapping the consumer carbon charge, Mar 2025) does not apply, because the idea adds no consumer price. On the plus side, charging in surplus hours can modestly reduce curtailment and negative-price costs. On the risk side, large new loads can push network upgrade costs onto ratepayers, which is the concern SB 6's fee and cost provisions address. Net effect is small either way.
stances.red_line_hit: Price rises only if grid-connection costs are socialised to ratepayers.

stances.evidence: Investors and insurers gain on two counts. On cost, utilisation drives DAC capital charge (modelled: $274/t at 95% capacity factor against $788/t at 33%), and the graft keeps utilisation high at $9-25 per t/yr of extra capital. On delivery, the realised market shows a large gap: cdr.fyi (fetched 2026-10-05) reports 50.5 Mt contracted against 1.7 Mt delivered, at an average $337/t. A press report adds one realised failure: Heimildin (May 2025, via Wikipedia) found Climeworks Mammoth (36 kt/yr nameplate, geothermal-powered) capturing far below capacity. That report does not link the shortfall to heat supply or intermittency, so it is not evidence for or against this graft. Pressurised hot-water storage is mature district-heating hardware, so it should be easy to finance and insure.
stances.red_line_hit: None. Durability and delivery risk of the DAC core remains.

stances.evidence: Hot water at 100-120 C under pressure is standard district-heating practice and a lower local hazard than amine solvents. It does not add the CO2-pipeline risk that DAC hubs bring: my own knowledge, not fetched this session, is that the Feb 2020 Satartia, Mississippi CO2 pipeline rupture led to dozens of hospitalisations. Stratos uses brackish non-potable water in a closed loop (1pointfive.com), which addresses one water concern. Local reaction will follow the hub's pipeline and Class VI well siting and its noise from fans, not the heat store. I could not fetch documented community positions on the Louisiana and Texas DAC hubs this session.
stances.red_line_hit: Local safety from CO2 transport and injection, inherited from DAC hubs, not from the heat store. Pressure-vessel safety is minor.

stake.coalition_notes:
How to read this: nearly every stance is inherited from DAC itself. The graft (grid-charged hot-water storage) moves only a few groups at the margin, and the moves are positive. It removes fossil process heat, an S1 objection that applies to gas-calciner designs such as Stratos. It also makes the plant an interruptible large load, which S5 and S7 want and which Texas SB 6 (Jun 2025) now rewards. A grid-charged solid-sorbent DAC load is still only as clean as the hours it charges in.

Likely coalition: S2 (R&D), S5, S6, S7 and S10 support; S3, S4, S9 and S11 are neutral; S1 and S8 are split, and their objection is to DAC (mitigation deterrence and offsets), not to the heat store.

Three conditions would widen the coalition:
1. **Dedicated geologic storage only, with EOR excluded.** OBBBA's EOR parity under 45Q otherwise lets DAC CO2 hit CAN red line 7.
2. **Residual-emissions framing.** Matching COP28's 'particularly in hard-to-abate sectors' and the IPCC language keeps the S2 and moderate-S1 position available.
3. **A tariff with no cost shift for flexible load.** Large-load interconnection costs should not fall on ratepayers.

Scope limit: the hot-water store works only for low-temperature solid-sorbent DAC, not 900 C liquid-solvent DAC (Oxy/CE), so the main S3 DAC player is unaffected.

Evidence gaps: the web-search budget was exhausted, so evidence comes from the provided map plus direct fetches (CIEL, 1PointFive Stratos, Wikipedia on DAC and Climeworks, cdr.fyi, Texas SB 6 text). The following are not verified this session:
- the DOE DAC hub status after 2025;
- the Danish power-to-heat precedent;
- documented community positions near the hubs.

The Mammoth underperformance figure is a press report with no stated cause, and should not be used as evidence about intermittency.

critic.fatal_flaw:
None on physics, scale or a stakeholder red line. Every energy term is above the 0.465 GJ/t floor. The store is small: about 67 Mm3 of water per Gt/yr. No stakeholder group objects to the heat store itself; the S1/S8 objections are about DAC in general.

The idea is close to non-viable as an engine output for two reasons:
- **Prior art:** grid-charged TES for solid-sorbent DAC, including a heat-pump+TES set-up, is already published (Mohan, Konuru, Luo & Jenkins 2025, J. Phys.: Energy).
- **It fails its own falsification line:** at base assumptions the saving is below $15/t in all three markets with measured data (DE-LU, DK1, FR 2025). The three markets the idea named (ERCOT, CAISO, SE3) are untested, so it is not formally falsified.

Treat it as a marginal, incremental refinement, not a new solution.
critic.top_fixable_flaw:
**The value case is measured against a strawman and on gross tonnes.**

1. **Wrong baseline for capacity factor.** The $274 vs $788/t capital-charge argument compares against a plant that runs only on curtailed power (33% CF). A flat 24/7 grid-fed heat pump already gets 95% CF with no store. So the store adds no utilisation. It only adds energy arbitrage, and the 3x-rated heat pump's capex wipes that out (verifier base saving: -1/-3/-9 $/t).

2. **The real cost driver is unpriced: grid CO2.** My check (critic_bt4_hybrid.py, DE-LU 2025 SMARD data, direct-combustion intensity, which is a lower bound):
   - Even the best heat route (flat heat pump, COP 1.8) emits 0.37 t CO2 per t captured from heat, plus 0.21 t from fans and vacuum. That is about 0.58 t/t, so net removal is about 0.42.
   - This multiplies $/net t by about 2.4x, which dwarfs any arbitrage.
   - The cheapest 8 h average 0.241 t/MWh, not much cleaner than the 0.316 mean, so storage charged that way barely helps.
   - Only negative-price hours are clean (0.100 t/MWh), and there were only 573 of them in 2025.

patched_idea.title: Store heat, not the loaded sorbent: a hybrid hot-water buffer for low-carbon-grid DAC
patched_idea.one_line: In solid-sorbent DAC, buffer the regeneration heat in pressurised hot water rather than buffering loaded amine sorbent (the map's 'store the swing' idea). Heat storage costs ~$9-25 per t/yr of capacity, against ~$550-1,660 for sorbent. Charge it with a hybrid: a 1x flat heat pump plus a cheap interruptible electrode boiler. The plant is sited only on grids or PPAs below ~0.05 t CO2/MWh. Honest value: ~$10-12 per gross t (~1.5-2% of cost), plus about 24 h of interruptibility that grid operators can pay for.
patched_idea.conventional_core: Solid-sorbent temperature-swing DAC kept at a high capacity factor, as in the parent work (Mohan, Konuru, Luo & Jenkins 2025, J. Phys.: Energy, grid-charged TES and heat pump for solid-sorbent DAC).
patched_idea.graft: Power-to-heat with large pressurised hot-water storage, as in Danish and German district heating. Their pattern: an electrode boiler on interruptible, network-charge-exempt tariffs next to a base-load heat source, with a tank in between.
patched_idea.mechanism:
1. **The capacity-factor argument is dropped as a selling point.** A flat 24/7 grid-fed heat pump already runs at ~95% CF without any store. The store adds only (a) energy arbitrage and (b) interruptibility.

2. **What to buffer.** Heat is the largest energy term (~7.2 GJ_th/t) and can be time-shifted cheaply in water at 100-120 C. Buffering the swing instead (loaded amine sorbent at $20-40/kg) costs 20-70x more per unit of capacity. That makes sense only for very cheap sorbents such as CaO, the only case covered by Arwa & Schell 2024.

3. **Hybrid charging** replaces the 3x-rated design:
   - a 1x-rated high-temperature heat pump runs flat, on a ~50 C waste-heat source where possible (COP ≥ 1.8-2);
   - a 2x-rated electrode boiler (~$100/kW_e) on an interruptible tariff fires only when price is below ~EUR 10-20/MWh, covering demand and charging a 16 h store;
   - the heat pump throttles while the store discharges.
   Fans and vacuum stay continuous.

4. **Carbon rule.** Every result is reported per net tonne, net of grid emissions from heat and auxiliary loads. Siting is restricted to grids or dedicated PPAs below ~0.05 t CO2/MWh, for example the Nordics or Québec, or France after checking its intensity. Charging is also gated on intensity as well as price, but this gate is a safeguard, not the fix: on a fossil-heavy grid it cannot clean the supply.

5. **Grid service.** The store is sized so the plant can drop its heat-pump and boiler load for up to ~24 h, matching large-load demand-response and curtailment programmes such as Texas SB 6-type rules. This is the value grid operators and utilities (S5/S7) actually pay for.
patched_idea.target: The trade-off between regeneration energy cost, grid carbon and capacity factor for intermittent-power DAC, a bottleneck named in the verified map.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
All figures are modelled, for a 100 kt/yr plant at 95% CF. Scripts: thermo_ideas.py §3, critic_bt4_hybrid.py and patch_bt4_net.py. Prices are DE-LU 2025 hourly data from SMARD. Grid intensity is a direct-combustion lower bound.

**Store sizing (unchanged):**
- Heat demand is 22.8 MW_th (7.2 GJ_th/t, 15x the 0.465 GJ/t floor).
- A 16 h store holds 365 MWh_th, ~6,300 m3 of water at ΔT 50 K.
- At $150-400/m3 it costs $0.9-2.5M, or $9-25 per t/yr.
- Buffering 16 h of loaded sorbent instead (183 t CO2, 2,770-4,150 t of sorbent at 1.0-1.5 mmol/g) costs $55-166M, or $553-1,660 per t/yr.

**Heat cost on DE-LU 2025:**

| Configuration | Heat cost ($/t) | Saving vs flat heat pump ($/t) |
|---|---|---|
| Flat heat pump, COP 1.8 (energy 138, capex 26, capacity 6) | 170 | — |
| Hybrid, 2x boiler, charge below EUR 10/MWh (25% boiler share) | 161 | ~9 |
| Hybrid, 2x boiler, charge below EUR 20/MWh | 158 | ~12 |
| Hybrid, 1x boiler | 174-175 | none (worse) |
| Original 3x-rated, 8 h charging design | — | -1 to -9 (negative) |

The ~$10-12/t saving is ~1.5-2% of the ~$673/t gross cost. The earlier $36/t claim is withdrawn.

**Net removal:** electricity is ~1.76 MWh_e per gross t (1.11 for heat plus 0.65 auxiliary).

| Grid intensity (t CO2/MWh) | Net removal (t per gross t) | Cost per net t |
|---|---|---|
| 0.316 (DE-LU mean) | 0.44 | ~$1,520 |
| 0.10 | 0.82 | ~$820 |
| 0.05 | 0.91 | ~$740 |
| 0.02 | 0.96 | ~$700 |

On DE-LU this route is worse than point-source capture.

**Carbon gating on DE-LU does not help.**
- The cheapest 8 h average 0.241 t/MWh, against a 0.316 mean.
- Only the 573 negative-price hours are clean (0.100).
- Gating at below 0.10 t/MWh cuts boiler share to 7-10% and removes the saving ($171-173/t). Heat CO2 stays ~0.372 t/t because the COP-1 boiler loses to the COP-1.8 heat pump.
- Hence siting, not gating, is the carbon fix.

**Falsification status:** the base saving is below $15/t in DE-LU, DK1 and FR (2025, critic's check). ERCOT, CAISO and SE3 are untested; the local SE3 price file failed to download (HTTP 503).
patched_idea.who_gains:
- **S5 utilities and S7 governments:** a ~33-70 MWe interruptible load per 100 kt/yr that can drop for ~24 h. It also absorbs negative-price hours.
- **S10 investors:** the plant keeps a high CF and gains a demand-response revenue line. The arbitrage gain itself is modest.
- **S1/S2:** honest per-net-tonne reporting and a siting rule on low-carbon grids, which removes the 'DAC on a fossil grid' objection for this design.
- **S9 consumers:** marginally less curtailment, and the plant adds grid flexibility.
patched_idea.who_loses:
- **S3 gas-heat suppliers:** DAC regeneration heat is electrified.
- **DAC projects on fossil-heavy grids:** the siting rule excludes them, as do designs marketed as 'runs only on curtailed power'.
- **Developers expecting large arbitrage profits:** the value is ~$10-12/t, not ~$36/t.
patched_idea.closest_known_work:
- **Mohan, Konuru, Luo & Jenkins 2025, J. Phys.: Energy (the parent work):** grid-charged TES for solid-sorbent DAC, including a heat pump + TES set-up.
- **Fan & Xu 2026, ES&T:** CSP plus sand storage for DAC, above 80% CF.
- **Arwa & Schell 2024:** storing the swing with CaO.
- **Danish and German district heating:** electrode boilers plus pressurised tanks.
- **Antora and Rondo:** high-temperature thermal batteries.

Citations are as given by the critic. They were not re-verified in this patch because the web-search budget was exhausted.
patched_idea.why_different:
This is an incremental refinement of Mohan et al. 2025, not a new solution. It adds three things:
- **(a) The quantitative correction:** buffer the heat, not loaded amine sorbent. This is 20-70x cheaper per unit of capacity, and prior 'store the swing' work covered only CaO.
- **(b) District-heating hybrid charging:** a 1x heat pump plus a cheap interruptible boiler, instead of an over-rated heat pump.
- **(c) A store sized for ~24 h interruptibility, with net-tonne and siting rules.** This turns a marginal arbitrage play into a large-load demand-response asset.

fix.change_summary:
I applied the critic's patch and kept the core (solid-sorbent TVSA DAC at high capacity factor) and the graft (district-heating power-to-heat with a pressurised hot-water store) unchanged.

**What changed:**
- **Charging design:** the 3x-rated heat pump or boiler charging in the cheapest 8 h is replaced by the critic's hybrid. That is a 1x flat high-temperature heat pump, a 2x interruptible electrode boiler firing below EUR 10-20/MWh, and a 16 h store. This configuration comes from district-heating practice, so it sharpens the graft rather than replacing it.
- **Baseline:** the capacity-factor argument against curtailed-only plants was a strawman and is dropped.
- **Value claim:** cut from $36/t to the reproduced $10-12 per gross t (DE-LU 2025: $158-161 versus $170 for a flat heat pump, about 1.5-2% of cost).
- **Net-tonne reporting:** added. Net removal is 0.44 t/t on the DE-LU mean grid against 0.91 at 0.05 t/MWh, so siting is restricted to grids or PPAs below 0.05 t/MWh.
- **Contribution:** reframed as an increment on the parent, Mohan et al. 2025. It adds the store-heat-not-amine-sorbent correction (20-70x cheaper per unit of capacity) and ~24 h interruptibility for large-load demand response.
- **Falsification test:** moved to ERCOT, CAISO and SE3, with demand-response revenue counted and measured per net tonne.

**New finding:** my patch_bt4_net.py check showed that the critic's suggested carbon gate does not work on DE-LU. Gating below 0.10 t/MWh wipes out the saving ($171-173/t), and heat CO2 stays at ~0.372 t/t, because the COP-1 boiler loses to the COP-1.8 heat pump. So the idea now says siting is the carbon fix and gating is only a safeguard.

**Not done:**
- The SE3 price file in scratch is an HTTP 503 page, so SE3 stays untested.
- The web-search budget was exhausted, so the Mohan et al. and Texas SB 6 citations are as given by the critic and not re-verified.

The idea remains marginal: an incremental refinement, not a new solution.

idea.title: Solar collector-adsorber DAC: one passive capture-release cycle per day
idea.one_line: A glazed solar panel packed with sorbent sheets loads CO2 from night air with a ~10 Pa breeze. By day it is sealed and steam-swept at 1 atm by its own solar heat, so all regeneration heat is free, there is no vacuum pump and no large contactor, and purchased electricity falls to compression only (~130 kWh/t, against the 650 kWh/t Climeworks states).
idea.conventional_core: Mass-manufactured glazed and evacuated-tube solar-thermal collectors (the solar-water-heater supply chain), plus existing DAC sorbents: supported amine on silica, or K2CO3 on carbon.
idea.graft: The sorption cycle used in atmospheric-water harvesters and solar adsorption ice makers: the sorbent adsorbs at night and is desorbed by sunlight inside the same enclosure (Pons & Guilleminot zeolite/carbon ice makers, 1980s; Kim et al. 2017 Science, MOF-801 water harvester).
idea.mechanism:
Night: louvres open, and air passes at 1.2-2.5 cm/s through a 3-5 cm layer of sorbent sheets. Each m2 must process 529-1,059 m3 of air per night for 0.3-0.6 kg CO2 at 75% capture (verifier air volume). Wind or a ~10 Pa fan is enough: 0.03 GJ/t by the verifier fan formula. Cool, humid night air raises sorbent capacity.

Day: louvres close and residual air is purged. The panel heats to ~105 C (amine variant). Co-adsorbed and injected water flashes to steam, which sweeps CO2 out at 1 atm to a condenser, and the water is recycled. A glazed flat box cannot hold process vacuum (1 atm is ~10 t of force per m2), so the design is atmospheric steam sweep by construction.

K2CO3 variant: thermochemistry (NBS data) gives a night equilibrium pCO2 of 3.5e-6 bar at 25 C and pH2O 0.01 bar, far below the 4.2e-4 bar in air, so loading is strongly favoured. Release needs >=110 C at 0.2 bar total or >=141 C to self-pressurise to 1 atm, so this variant needs evacuated-tube-class collectors.

What the panel replaces: purchased regeneration heat, the fan and contactor ductwork, vacuum pumps, and the separate heat plant. Heating happens after O2 has been purged, which should slow oxidative degradation.

With one cycle per day, the binding parameter becomes sorbent inventory and calendar life. That is why the cheap strong sorbent can win here: K2CO3's 140 kJ/mol is 7x the floor, but when heat is free and ample per m2, enthalpy costs only collector area.
idea.target: DAC regeneration heat source, fan/contactor work, vacuum-pump electricity and separate contactor capex, using free diurnal temperature, humidity and solar gradients.
idea.quantitative_claims:
All figures are modelled; assumptions are labelled; scripts are scratchpad/climate/thermo_ideas.py and thermo_ideas2.py.

- **Solar heat delivered:** 6.9-12.6 MJ/m2/day, from 5.5-7 kWh/m2/day on the tilted aperture at 35-50% daily collector efficiency (assumed).
- **Heat demand, all solar:** amine variant (1.2 mmol/g, 75 kJ/mol, 1.5+1.5 mol H2O/mol, dT 80 K) 314 kJ/mol = 7.1 GJ_th/t. K2CO3 variant (0.8 mmol/g, 140 kJ/mol, dT 120 K) 424 kJ/mol = 9.6 GJ_th/t.
- **Heat-limited ceiling:** 1.25 and 0.97 kg CO2/m2/day. The design target of 0.3-0.6 kg/m2/day uses 24-62% of the solar heat.
- **Purchased electricity:** 0.46 GJe/t (129 kWh/t): compression 1 to 150 bar at 65% efficiency (floor 0.28 GJ/t) plus a 10 Pa fan. That is 20% of the 2.34 GJe/t Climeworks Gen2 states, and 0.4% of world electricity per Gt/yr.
- **Productivity:** 90-180 kg CO2/m2/yr over an assumed 300 sunny days, i.e. 5.6-11 m2 of aperture per t/yr. Land is 11,000-22,000 km2 per Gt/yr at twice the aperture area.
- **Sorbent inventory:** 63 kg (amine) or 95 kg (K2CO3) per t/yr of capacity.
- **Sorbent cost per tonne over 3,000 daily cycles (10 yr):** $126/t for amine at an assumed $20/kg, and $28/t for K2CO3 at an assumed $3/kg.
- **Capex:** $840-3,500 per t/yr, assuming panels at $100-200/m2 installed. Stratos is ~$2,600 per t/yr.
- **Rough levelised cost of removal (CRF 0.10, O&M 4%/yr, electricity at $60/MWh, transport and storage $25/t):** $150-230/t for the K2CO3 variant at 0.6 kg/m2/day, and $290-520/t for the amine variant. For comparison, Fan & Xu 2026 model $160-200/t core and $300-350/t deployment-adjusted for CSP plus sand storage.
idea.who_gains:
- **S7 and S8 in sunny regions with storage** (Oman/UAE peridotite, Saudi Arabia, US Southwest, India): local manufacture of glass-and-steel hardware, and removal that does not compete for grid power.
- **S3 NOCs and majors:** land host and storage operator role.
- **S10:** modular, factory-built, low grid exposure.
- **S5:** neutral to slightly positive (small load).
- **S1 and S2:** no fossil energy input and a transparent energy budget. S1's general DAC moral-hazard concern remains.
idea.who_loses:
- **S11 desert land users and ecology:** 11-22 km2 per Mt/yr.
- **Grid-powered DAC developers:** compete for the same offtake buyers.
- **Water:** none on net, since condensate is recycled. In the K2CO3 variant, night humidity is a reactant.
idea.closest_known_work:
- **Kar et al. 2025, Nature Energy (Reisner lab):** a lab dual-bed reactor that captures at night and uses concentrated light by day to release CO2 and convert it to syngas.
- **Fan & Xu 2026, ES&T:** CSP plus sand storage feeding a conventional sorbent DAC. Above 80% capacity factor, $160-200/t core cost (modelled), 6,000 t/yr in <1 km2.
- **Kim et al. 2017, Science:** MOF water harvester, the source of the graft.
- **Heirloom:** fan-free passive trays, but an electric kiln for release.
- **Qi et al. 2026, ACS Sust Chem Eng:** solar-driven regenerative sorbent from wood waste (abstract not read).
- **Search limit:** prior-art search was cut short because the web search budget was exhausted, so an unseen close match is possible.
idea.why_different:
- The panel is non-concentrating and at atmospheric pressure, and it is contactor, regenerator and heat source in one.
- It is steam-swept, with no vacuum and no fans.
- The CO2 product goes to storage rather than conversion.
- It deliberately picks a cheap strong sorbent because heat is free and plentiful per m2, while sorbent inventory is the cost driver at one cycle per day.
idea.family: Passive solar collector-adsorber DAC panel, one night-load/day-steam-sweep cycle

art.label: IMPORT

closest.title: Wang, Qu, Ding, Webley & Li (Univ. Melbourne / Monash / Tianjin Univ.), 'Distributed direct air capture of carbon dioxide by synergistic water harvesting', Nature Communications 15 (2024); companion patent application PCT/AU2023/050429 (filed 22 May 2023)
closest.overlap: This is essentially the same core idea, already built and tested outdoors. The adsorbent column is black-coated and double-glazed with a transparent vacuum jacket, like an evacuated tube, with a low-ratio parabolic concentrator (CR 1.9). Photothermal efficiency is 63.1%. The column serves as air contactor, regenerator and solar heat source in one. Amine resin plus silica gel take up CO2 and water from ambient air. Solar heating to about 100-110 C then flashes the co-adsorbed water into an in-situ vapour purge at ambient pressure. The paper stresses that this needs no vacuum pump and no steam boiler, and that the vapour displaces air so the amine is less exposed to oxidation. It reports 97.7-99% CO2 purity, about 98% recovery at 600 W/m2, and condensate water recovered. Measured regeneration heat is 10.3-10.4 MJ/kg CO2 (amine resin). Outdoor solar runs took place in Tianjin in May 2022. Working capacity was stable at 0.9-1.0 mmol/g over 9 cycles (electrically heated runs). Their conceptual 'solar DAC farm' (Fig. 5e) loads from natural wind and switches between adsorption and regeneration by shading or exposing the columns to sun. Their modelled total cost is $111-313/t. Every element of the idea's amine variant is in this paper: integrated glazed solar collector-adsorber, wind-fed loading, solar-heated steam sweep at 1 atm with no vacuum, purge of O2 before heating, and condensate recycle. The idea's 'graft' (the adsorb-then-solar-desorb water-harvester cycle) is exactly how this paper frames itself.

closest.title: Kar et al. (Reisner lab, Cambridge), 'Direct air capture of CO2 for solar fuel production in flow', Nature Energy (2025)
closest.overlap: A dual-bed flow reactor: a silica-amine bed captures CO2 from air, and concentrated light then releases it onto a photocatalyst that makes syngas. The authors explicitly propose a diurnal cycle, with capture at night and release under sunlight by day. That is prior art for the night-load/day-release schedule. The differences are that it uses concentrated light and is aimed at conversion, not storage.

closest.title: Fan & Xu, 'Design Optimization and Global Impact Assessment of Solar-Thermal Direct Air Carbon Capture', Environmental Science & Technology (2026)
closest.overlap: A modelled system feeding concentrated solar heat plus sand thermal storage to conventional sorbent DAC. It gives $160-200/t core cost and $300-350/t deployment-adjusted cost, above 80% capacity factor, with a 6,000 t/yr module on under 1 km2. It notes that short-cycle sorbents matched to solar availability work best. This overlaps the idea's economics and site logic (sunny regions over storage basins), but the heat source is separate rather than built into the panel.

closest.title: Qi et al., 'Upcycling Wood Waste into Solar-Driven Regenerative Sorbent for Direct Air Capture', ACS Sustainable Chemistry & Engineering (2026)
closest.overlap: An amine-functionalised wood-derived sorbent in which retained lignin acts as the photothermal absorber. Under one-sun illumination it releases 50% of its CO2 in 22 minutes at 67 C, and humidity raises uptake (1.84 mmol/g at 25 C). It shows that sunlight alone can regenerate a sorbent in situ at material level, but it describes no panel or process system.

closest.title: Kim et al. 2017 (Science, MOF-801 water harvester) and Pons & Guilleminot solar adsorption ice makers (1980s)
closest.overlap: These are the idea's own graft sources. A glazed enclosure adsorbs at night and is solar-desorbed by day. Wang et al. 2024 already carried this cycle over to CO2 DAC, together with water co-harvesting.

closest.title: Distributed direct air capture by carbon nanofiber air filters, Science Advances (2025); Wang et al., 'Solar-Powered CO2 Capture and Release Using Amine-Functionalized Plasmonic TiN Nanoparticles', JACS Au (2025)
closest.overlap: Further examples of sorbents regenerated by solar heat or photothermally (a CNF filter at 4 mmol/g, solar-thermal regenerable, $209-668/t including storage; TiN-APTES tested on simulated flue gas). These are partial overlaps at component level only.

closest.title: Heirloom (passive limestone trays, electric kiln) and passive wind contactors such as Spiritus and Lackner's moisture-swing 'mechanical trees'
closest.overlap: Prior art for the passive, fan-free loading half of the idea. Their regeneration is not done by solar heat inside the same enclosure.

art.what_is_new:
The core concept already exists for the amine variant. Wang et al. (Nature Communications, 2024) built and tested outdoors a glazed, vacuum-insulated solar collector-adsorber. It is wind-fed, uses an in-situ water-vapour (steam) sweep at ambient pressure around 100-110 C, needs no vacuum pump or boiler, displaces O2 before heating and recovers condensate. The work is covered by a Melbourne patent application (PCT/AU2023/050429). Kar et al. (2025) separately proposed the night-capture/day-sunlight-release schedule.

What remains new is a set of design and economic variations, not a new mechanism:
1. **K2CO3-on-carbon variant.** I found no precedent for solar-collector regeneration of an alkali-carbonate DAC sorbent inside the same enclosure. Its feasibility hinges on two untested points: release at 110-141 C, needing evacuated-tube-class collectors, and deliquescence above about 43% RH.
2. **Non-concentrating flat-plate format.** A glazed flat box with sorbent sheets, versus Wang's tubular column with a CR 1.9 concentrator. This is mostly packaging, and evacuated tubes are what the idea's own K2CO3 variant needs.
3. **Once-daily cycle as an explicit design constraint.** The idea treats sorbent inventory and calendar life as the binding cost, and argues for picking a cheap high-enthalpy sorbent because solar heat per m2 is surplus. Wang et al. instead optimise working capacity and heat per kg.
4. **Storage-oriented accounting.** Compression to 150 bar is the only purchased electricity (about 130 kWh/t, modelled), versus Wang's utilisation framing and Kar's syngas.

Recommendation: treat the amine panel as IMPORT and build on Wang et al. Their 10.3 MJ/kg measured regeneration heat is above the idea's assumed 7.1 GJ/t (7.1 MJ/kg), so per-m2 productivity should be re-derived from their number. Their resin also lost more than 20% capacity over 6 cycles at 110 C in air, while vapour-purged runs were stable over 9 cycles. That makes the 3,000-cycle life the critical unknown. Only the K2CO3 sub-variant is a genuinely open PARTIAL-level question.

Search limitations: the session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted and OpenAlex was rate-limited, so I searched with Europe PMC and fetched full text from PMC. Patent databases (Google Patents, Espacenet) and company sites were not searched directly, so a close patent or startup match may have been missed.

phys.assumptions:
All results are modelled (my script plus the verifier). None are measured. The web search budget was exhausted this session, so literature values are quoted from memory and not re-verified; the script labels each one [lit], [claim] or [eng].

**What the script does differently from the proposer's script**
- It simulates the collector hour by hour, instead of assuming a 35-50% daily efficiency:
  - The day is a half-sine from 06:00 to 18:00, at 5.5/6.5/7.0 kWh/m2/day on the tilted aperture (the claim's range).
  - Ambient is 30 C and the bed starts at 20 C.
  - The panel follows an EN 12975-style efficiency curve. The selective flat plate uses eta0 0.75-0.80 and a1 3.5-4.5 W/m2K. The deep louvred box is assumed to lose more heat than a standard collector. The K2CO3 low case uses an evacuated tube (0.65/1.2) and its base case a double-glazed plate (0.72/2.8).
  - The whole panel's thermal mass warms up first (casing 5/8/12 kJ/K/m2). Desorption then runs at the regeneration temperature (T_reg).
- Sorbent mass per m2 is solved together with the daily loading, because more loading means more sorbent and more heat.
- Sorbent is capped by the claimed 3-5 cm bed depth: 15/10/7.5 kg/m2.

**Chemistry assumptions (low/base/high)**

| Parameter | Amine | K2CO3 |
|---|---|---|
| Working capacity (mmol/g) | 1.2/0.8/0.5 | 0.8/0.6/0.35 |
| Regeneration temperature (C) | 100/105/110 | 130/140/150 |
| Water per CO2 (mol/mol) | 3/5/8 total desorbed plus sweep | 0.5/1.5/3 extra |
| Desorption enthalpy (kJ/mol) | 70-80 | 140 |

- Amine working capacity is reduced because regeneration at 1 atm, with no vacuum, leaves a higher residual loading.
- The K2CO3 enthalpy of 140 kJ/mol is recomputed from NBS data.
- Purge steam is 2/3.5/5 mol per m2 per day.

**Electricity**
- Compression from 1 to 150 bar: the isothermal floor is 0.282 GJ/t, at 70/65/60% efficiency.
- Fan: none (wind only), 10 Pa at 50%, or 15 Pa at 30%.
- Air-cooled condenser: 1-2% of the latent heat rejected.
- Auxiliaries: 0.02-0.05 GJ/t.

**Cost inputs (low/base/high)**

| Item | Low | Base | High |
|---|---|---|---|
| Panel, installed ($/m2), amine | 120 | 200 | 350 |
| Panel, installed ($/m2), K2CO3 | 150 | 250 | 400 |
| Field balance of plant (manifolds, condenser, compressor at ~35% capacity factor, controls), $ per t/yr | 150 | 350 | 700 |
| Panel life (years) | 25 | 20 | 15 |
| Discount rate | 6% | 8% | 10% |
| O&M (% of capex per year) | 2% | 3% | 5% |
| Electricity ($/MWh) | 40 | 60 | 80 |
| Transport and storage ($/t) | 15 | 25 | 40 |
| Amine price ($/kg) / life (years) | 10 / 10 | 20 / 5 | 50 / 2 |
| K2CO3 composite price ($/kg) / life (years) | 2 / 15 | 4 / 8 | 8 / 3 |
| Productive days per year | 330 | 300 | 270 |
| Land (multiple of aperture) | 2.0 | 2.2 | 2.5 |

**Reported figures**
- Energy figures are solar heat plus purchased electricity:
  - low: 8.6 GJ_th + 0.45 GJe (amine);
  - base: 14.5 GJ_th + 0.58 GJe (amine), or 15.8 + 0.53 (K2CO3);
  - high: 42.5 GJ_th + 0.85 GJe (amine).
- Cost low is K2CO3 at $137/t. Amine low is $158/t.
- Cost base is K2CO3 at $584/t. Amine base is $805/t.
- Cost high is the "moderate-high" case: pessimistic chemistry and costs, but the base collector and 6.5 kWh of sun. It comes to $3,289/t for K2CO3 and $5,830/t for amine. In the fully pessimistic case the K2CO3 panel never reaches 150 C, so there is no output; amine falls to 0.06 kg/m2/day at $9,283/t.
- The scale of 0.05 Gt/yr is my judgement of a realistic 2050 ceiling, set by manufacturing and sorbent supply rather than by physics.
phys.violations:
There are no thermodynamic violations.

**Floor check**
- The separation floor for air at 420 ppm, 75% capture and 99% purity is 0.465 GJ/t (129 kWh/t).
- The claimed purchased electricity is 0.46 GJe/t, which sits below that floor. This is legitimate, because the separation work comes from the exergy of the solar heat:
  - 2.61 to 9.43 GJ/t across the amine cases;
  - 5.01 GJ/t for K2CO3 low and 4.74 GJ/t for K2CO3 base;
  - second-law efficiency on heat exergy is 5-18% for amine and 9-10% for K2CO3.
- The claimed electricity is confirmed: 0.45 GJe/t (low), 0.53-0.58 (base), 0.85 (high). That compares with the 2.34 GJe/t Climeworks states for Gen2, which is a company figure, not a measurement.
- The K2CO3 thermochemistry is confirmed: dH is -140.1 kJ/mol, and night equilibrium pCO2 is 3.54e-06 bar, so loading is favoured. Release needs at least 140 C self-pressurised, 136 C with steam sweep at pCO2 0.2, 130 C at pCO2 0.1, and 110 C only at 0.2 bar total.

**Claims flagged as optimistic or implausible**

1. **Collector efficiency.** The claim assumes 35-50% daily efficiency. The simulation gives 23% (amine base, 105 C) and 19% (K2CO3 base, 140 C). It reaches 40-44% only with a best-in-class collector, 7 kWh of sun and 100-130 C. The claimed heat-limited ceilings (1.25 and 0.97 kg/m2/day) reproduce only with the claim's own parameters (1.05 and 1.12), which leave out casing thermal mass and purge steam. At base they fall to 0.39 (amine) and 0.31 (K2CO3).

2. **The bed depth binds before heat does.** A 3-5 cm layer holds about 7.5-15 kg of sorbent per m2. That gives 0.35 kg/m2/day for amine base and 0.26 for K2CO3 base, so the 0.6 kg/m2/day design point does not fit the stated geometry at base capacity. The optimistic case reaches only 0.79 (amine) and 0.53 (K2CO3).

3. **The K2CO3 variant has no workable panel design.**
   - Release at 1 atm needs at least 130-140 C even with steam sweep (the 110 C figure requires 0.2 bar total, which the vacuum-free design excludes).
   - A good single-glazed selective flat plate at 140 C gives only 0.19 kg/m2/day.
   - Evacuated tubes are sealed vacuum annuli. They are geometrically incompatible with cross-flow of night air through a 3-5 cm sorbent layer, and no such design is known.
   - At 150 C with a double-glazed plate and 5.5 kWh, the panel never reaches regeneration temperature.

4. **Sorbent economics dominate at one cycle per day.**
   - The claim's $126/t amine sorbent charge assumes a 10-year, 3,000-cycle life.
   - At 0.8 mmol/g the base amine sorbent charge is $474/t (5-year life, $20/kg). It is $282/t at 10 years and $1,062/t at 2 years.
   - Re-costing the claim's own design points with the base cost stack gives amine $542-689/t and K2CO3 $292/t, against the claimed $290-520/t and $150-230/t.

5. **The panel box must be well insulated.** A non-selective single-glazed box, or a leaky louvred box (a1 of about 6 W/m2K), gives 0.00-0.05 kg/m2/day. A selective absorber, or double glazing, plus tight louvre seals are mandatory.

6. **"Free heat" is not free.** Heat use is 8.6-15.8 GJ_th/t at base and optimistic values, against the claim's 7.1-9.6. That heat costs collector area, which is the dominant capex.
phys.resource_needs:
Resource needs are given per 1 Gt CO2/yr, from the script.

**Aperture and land**
- Aperture is 9.5 billion m2 (amine base) or 12.6 billion m2 (K2CO3 base). In the optimistic cases it is 3.8 and 5.7 billion m2.
- That equals 128-421 years of today's solar-thermal collector output, taken as about 30 million m2/yr new. This output figure is approximate, from memory of IEA SHC data.
- Land is 20,829 km2 (amine base) and 27,771 km2 (K2CO3 base), or 7,651-11,476 km2 in the optimistic cases. The claim was 11,000-22,000 km2.

**Materials**
- Cover glass is 38-126 Mt, which is 0.5-1.6 years of world flat-glass output (about 80 Mt/yr, approximate).
- Frame, absorber and louvre metal is 46-151 Mt.
- Sorbent inventory is 57-126 Mt. That is far above present production, all approximate:
  - amine-functional resin, on the order of 0.1-1 Mt/yr;
  - K2CO3, about 2 Mt/yr;
  - activated carbon, about 3 Mt/yr.

**Energy and water**
- Electricity is 0.40-0.54% of world electricity per Gt/yr at the low and base cases, and 0.79% at amine high. It is daytime only, so it can be matched to PV.
- Solar heat is about 9-16 GJ_th/t, collected on site.
- Water: the system is a net producer, since night air co-adsorbs water and condensate is recycled. However, the condenser must reject about 2-5 GJ/t of latent heat during desert daytime.

**Realistic scale**
About 0.01-0.05 Gt/yr by 2050. The limits are glazed-collector and sorbent manufacturing, desert sites near CO2 storage, and cost competitiveness, not physics.
phys.key_uncertainties:
1. **Working capacity under realistic conditions.** It is unknown what working capacity is achieved in a 10-12 h night at 10-25 C and 20-60% relative humidity, with regeneration at 1 atm and no vacuum. The residual loading at 105 C under steam and CO2 has not been measured for this cycle. This is the bench test the idea proposes, and it is the right first test.

2. **Steam and co-adsorbed water per mole of CO2 for atmospheric steam stripping.** Base is 5 mol/mol. At 8 mol/mol, heat per tonne roughly doubles and productivity collapses.

3. **Real heat-loss coefficient of a louvred, gas-tight, 3-5 cm deep sorbent box at 105-140 C.** Neither a selective absorber in contact with the sorbent nor tight louvre seals has been demonstrated. The economics swing from about $140/t to no output on this one parameter (a1 of 3.5 versus 6 W/m2K).

4. **Sorbent calendar and cycle life under daily heating and humid nights.**
   - The claimed amine life of 10 years is versus a base of 5.
   - Oxidation is possible if the O2 purge is incomplete or the louvres reopen while the panel is still warm.
   - K2CO3 deliquesces above about 43% RH, forms hydrates, and loads slowly at ambient temperature.

5. **Panel cost.** At $120-400/m2 installed, the panel includes louvres, seals, steam injection and a CO2 manifold. Solar-water-heater prices are only a lower bound.

6. **Field balance-of-plant cost.** This covers gathering wet CO2 at 1 atm across km2 of panels, and compression at a capacity factor of about 35%.

7. **Night wind.** Desert night winds are often calm under inversions, so 10-15 Pa fans are likely needed. Their energy is negligible (0.03-0.09 GJ/t), but they add capex.

8. **Source verification.** Literature inputs could not be re-verified this run: collector coefficients, Lewatit or amine isotherms, sorbent prices and world production figures were all quoted from memory. The Climeworks 2.34 GJe/t is a company-stated figure, and Fan & Xu 2026 is a modelled result.

9. **Simple baseline.** Conventional DAC powered by PV with a heat pump in the same desert spends only about $41-74/t on energy. The panel therefore wins only if panel plus sorbent capex at one cycle per day beats a conventional contactor's capital charge, and the base case ($584-805/t) does not show that.

stances.evidence: Closest comparable is DAC/DACCS generally. CAN (2021, 1,300+ NGOs) says DACCS has 'no place' in scenarios built on early, steep cuts, and it opposes negative emissions or offsets used 'as an alternative to stringent emission reductions'. CIEL calls CCS-dependent DAC a 'license to pollute indefinitely' and notes that almost all existing CCS is tied to EOR (ciel.org/issue/carbon-capture-and-storage). Critics cited on Wikipedia's DAC page (e.g. Jonathan Foley) call DAC a 'greenwashing exercise', and the same page reports Occidental's $1.1bn Stratos purchase (Nov 2023) being read as extending the life of fossil fuels. Point in favour: the panel uses no fossil heat and little grid power (129 kWh/t modelled), which answers the energy-diversion criticism of grid-powered DAC. Moderate NGOs that back durable removal for residual emissions (the Frontier-aligned camp) would be more favourable. Net effect: the anti-CCS/EJ wing (CAN, CIEL) opposes, while removal-for-residuals groups conditionally support. The design does not change that split, because the objection is about substitution, not energy source.
stances.red_line_hit: Mitigation deterrence/offsets (CAN red lines 4 and 8). It becomes a hard red line if the captured CO2 goes to EOR (CAN red line 7), which 45Q's 2025 EOR parity makes financially tempting for an S3 storage partner. It also hits the storage-liability transfer concern (CAN red line 9).

stances.evidence: IPCC AR6 WGIII says CDR is needed to counterbalance residual emissions in net-zero pathways. Its C.4.4 also warns that CCS can prolong fossil use. The physics fits S2 expectations: the verifier floor is 0.47 GJ/t at 420 ppm, and the design's solar-thermal heat demand (7.1-9.6 GJ_th/t, modelled) is plausible next to real DAC at 5-10+ GJ/t. Scientists would want measured data, not models: Heimildin (May 2025, via Wikipedia's Climeworks page) reported Climeworks capturing 'only a fraction' of nameplate, so S2 will demand measured MRV. Support is for research and field trials; Baum et al. 2024 found small field trials the most supported activity.
stances.red_line_hit: None categorical. Credibility red line: claims of $150-230/t are modelled only, and S2 would reject removal claims without measured 30-day+ performance and independent MRV.

stances.evidence: Occidental/1PointFive bought Carbon Engineering and Stratos ($1.1bn, Nov 2023, per Wikipedia DAC page) and frames DAC as future-proofing its industry. 45Q pays $180/t for DAC in geologic storage, and OBBBA (2025) gave EOR parity. ADNOC appears among 44.01's listed partners (4401.earth logos), so Gulf NOCs are engaging with mineral storage. A low-electricity DAC that sells storage and land-host services to NOCs fits that strategy. Caveat from the scale script: modelled LCOR of $150-230/t (K2CO3) straddles the $180/t credit (margin +30 to -50 $/t). The amine variant ($290-520/t) fails without voluntary buyers, so S3 support depends on the cheap variant working.
stances.red_line_hit: None for S3 itself. Its preferred use, pairing DAC with EOR for 'net-zero oil', crosses S1's red line, and any mandate or per-tonne fee attached to removal would cross S3's (precedent: Waste Emissions Charge disapproved Mar 2025).

stances.evidence: Heavy industry's documented priority is point-source CCUS for process emissions (GCCA roadmap; Brevik cement CCS), where the verifier floor is far lower (0.11 GJ/t cement vs 0.47 GJ/t air). DAC does not abate S4's emissions directly. S4's interest would be as a buyer of removals for residuals under future compliance schemes. Steel and glass makers could gain supply contracts (glass, steel frames, collectors). There is mild concern that DAC credits compete for the same 45Q or public budgets as industrial CCS, but there is no documented opposition.
stances.red_line_hit: None. A possible concern is that public money for DAC crowds out industrial CCS or CCfD support.

stances.evidence: Small grid load. By the scale script, 1 Mt/yr needs 0.13 TWh against about 0.7 TWh electric (plus heat) for grid DAC at Climeworks' stated 650 kWh/t, so it neither competes heavily for capacity nor offers a big new load customer. Utilities in the Carbon Capture Coalition back 45Q mainly for point-source capture. Utilities that hoped to sell DAC loads (grid-DAC hubs) gain less here. No documented utility position on solar-thermal DAC.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: Unions are in the Carbon Capture Coalition, which backs 45Q including the DAC rate, and DAC hub proposals were pitched on construction and pipeline jobs. This design moves the labour to factory-built glass and steel panels plus field installation in sunny regions. For US workers that means jobs in the Southwest/Gulf, not necessarily in coal and steel regions. If panels are imported (the solar-water-heater supply chain is China-dominated), union support weakens, although OBBBA's foreign-entity-of-concern limits on 45Q partly address this. Few permanent operating jobs per tonne, since the plant is passive. Unions support it if domestic-content/prevailing-wage rules are attached; otherwise neutral.
stances.red_line_hit: Offshored manufacturing or a low-wage, low-job passive plant does not deliver the job promise. No direct job losses.

stances.evidence: Sunny, storage-rich governments are plausible champions. Oman/UAE entities (ADNOC, Masdar, Oman's MEM) appear as 44.01 partners. Saudi Arabia and other COP28 parties endorsed 'removal technologies' (1/CMA.5 para 28e). US: 45Q DAC at $180/t survived OBBBA, so the federal tax credit is bipartisan, but the DOE DAC-hub grant programme ($3.5bn, energy.gov) has an unverified 2025-26 status, so I cannot verify continued grant support. Fiscal hawks (Taxpayers for Common Sense) object to 45Q costs. At the ~$180/t credit, 1 Gt/yr would cost about $180bn/yr in public money, which is the fiscal red line at scale.
stances.red_line_hit: Fiscal cost at scale: open-ended per-tonne subsidy. Energy security is not an issue, since the plant is self-powered for heat.

stances.evidence: Baum et al. 2024 (N=30,284, 30 countries): Global South publics were more supportive of every technology, but more worried about mitigation deterrence and unequal risk; both North and South rated engineered CDR (DACCS) the highest moral-hazard risk. The idea's own who-gains list puts India, Oman and Saudi Arabia as hosts, which offers local manufacturing and removal revenue. Climate-justice advocates (CAN's land-conflict red line for BECCS, CIEL's EJ focus) will scrutinise 11-22 km2 per Mt/yr of land in host countries used to offset Northern emissions. Credits mostly flow to Northern buyers (Frontier, Microsoft).
stances.red_line_hit: Land grabs and carbon colonialism: large desert or rangeland areas in Global South hosts used to offset rich-country emissions. Moral hazard (Baum 2024).

stances.evidence: Funding comes from voluntary buyers (Frontier AMC, $1.8bn) and the 45Q tax credit, so there is no visible consumer price, which fits the Canada 2025 lesson that visible consumer carbon prices fail. Andre et al. 2024: 69% globally willing to contribute 1% of income, so latent support exists. Pew 2024: 65% of US adults prefer renewables. Baum 2024 shows public wariness of engineered CDR vs afforestation. Consumers become a negative force only if costs pass through via a takeback obligation or compliance mandate.
stances.red_line_hit: Price rises, but only if funded through a fuel or product mandate rather than tax credits or voluntary purchase.

stances.evidence: Frontier members (Stripe, Google, Shopify, JPMorgan and others) are pre-committing $1.8bn to durable removal, targeting <$100/t, and value low-grid-exposure modular designs. Investor caveats from realised outcomes: Heimildin (May 2025) reported Climeworks' Icelandic plants capturing a fraction of nameplate, so buyers now discount nameplate claims. The idea's falsification thresholds (>=0.15 kg/m2/day measured, >90% purity, <20% capacity loss over 30 cycles) are the kind of de-risking investors require. Insurers would want storage-liability clarity.
stances.red_line_hit: Delivery risk: paying for undelivered tonnes. Storage liability and reversal risk.

stances.evidence: Land use is the main local issue. By the scale script, 11-22 km2 per Mt/yr is about 0.8-1.5 times the 14.2 km2 Ivanpah solar plant. Ivanpah's construction was halted in 2011 over desert-tortoise habitat and relocation concerns. Ivanpah's bird deaths (3,500-6,000/yr) came from concentrated solar flux, which does not apply to non-concentrating panels, so that mechanism is not transferable. Downstream storage infrastructure carries documented safety concerns: the Satartia, Mississippi CO2 pipeline rupture (Feb 2020) evacuated about 300 people (42 residents plus about 250 nearby), and PHMSA proposed a $3.87M penalty. CIEL documents EJ opposition to CCS sited in pollution-burdened communities such as Louisiana's 'Cancer Alley'. Benefits: no combustion, low noise (10 Pa fans), and no net water use. Siting next to storage (on-site mineralisation or injection) avoids pipelines and would help.
stances.red_line_hit: Desert land and ecology (habitat, rangeland); CO2 pipeline safety if product is piped; EJ siting in already-burdened communities.

stake.coalition_notes: Likely coalition: S3 (Oxy/1PointFive, Gulf NOCs as storage and land hosts), S10 (Frontier-type durable-removal buyers), S2 (support for research and field trials), sunny storage-rich S7 (Gulf, US Southwest), and S6 conditional on domestic manufacturing. Main opposition: the anti-CCS/EJ wing of S1 (CAN, CIEL), plus S8 and S11 over land and moral hazard. The idea's distinctive features improve its standing on two documented objections: grid-energy diversion (129 vs ~650 kWh/t electric, modelled) and fossil heat use. They do NOT address the core S1/S8 objection, which is about substitution for emissions cuts and applies to all DAC. To widen the coalition: (1) bar EOR use and commit to dedicated storage or mineralisation only. This removes CAN's red line 7 but costs S3 the OBBBA EOR-parity upside, a real trade-off. (2) Market it explicitly for residual or historical emissions, not offsets for ongoing fossil use. (3) Co-site panels with storage (e.g. Oman peridotite, Class VI wells) to avoid pipelines (Satartia precedent). (4) Site on degraded or already-disturbed land with community benefit agreements, avoiding Ivanpah-style habitat fights. (5) Domestic-content and labour standards for S6. Economic fragility: modelled LCOR of $150-230/t (K2CO3 variant) straddles 45Q's $180/t DAC credit (margin +30 to -50 $/t); the amine variant ($290-520/t) needs voluntary buyers, so S3 and S10 support is contingent on the bench and outdoor falsification tests. Evidence limits: the WebSearch budget was exhausted this session, so I could not verify the 2025-26 status of the DOE DAC hubs, Project Cypress community engagement, Climeworks' 2025 layoffs or Oxy's latest Stratos statements; the stances above for those points rest on the provided map positions plus fetched Wikipedia, CIEL, energy.gov and 4401.earth pages.
