critic.top_fixable_flaw:
The dominant cost term is never tested, and the kill criteria let through designs that cost more than $10,000/t.

Sorbent cost per tonne is price divided by (working capacity × lifetime cycles). Per tonne it does not depend on cycles per day if degradation is per cycle. For amine at $20/kg and 0.8-1.0 mmol/g (modelled):
- 1,500 cycles gives $303-379/t;
- reaching $100/t or less needs 4,500-5,700 cycles.

The proposed thresholds are far too loose:
- **Fade:** 20% loss over 30 cycles means replacement at about 45 cycles, roughly $14,800/t in sorbent.
- **Uptake:** at 0.15 kg/m2/day, capital plus O&M alone is $632/t (base stack: $200/m2, $350 per t/yr BOS, 8% over 20 years, 3% O&M).

The once-daily cycle also helps only if life is calendar-limited, and in that case it is the wrong choice. Wang's measured cycle is about 3 h of adsorption and 40 min of solar vapour-purge desorption. Running 3-4 cycles a day would cut the base amine sorbent charge from $474/t to $119-158/t.

Wang's resin lost more than 20% over 6 cycles at 110 C in air, but stayed stable over 9 vapour-purged cycles. That is too few cycles to tell which degradation regime applies.
critic.suggested_patch:
Start from Wang et al.'s 2024 vapour-purge column. Check freedom to operate against PCT/AU2023/050429, or license it.

Replace test step 2 with a two-arm ageing test of 6-8 weeks on the amine sorbent:

1. **Cycle arm:** Wang-style 105 C in-situ vapour purge, 6-8 cycles per day, at least 300 cycles.
2. **Calendar arm:** sorbent held through the real once-daily temperature and humidity profile with oxygen exposure, including the louvre-reopening transient after sunset.

Set cost-anchored kill criteria:
- **Fade:** kill if extrapolated fade exceeds about 5% per 1,000 cycles. At least about 4,500 cycles are needed for a sorbent charge of $100/t or less.
- **Uptake:** sustained uptake below 0.35 kg CO2/m2/day.
- **Heat:** measured regeneration heat above about 10 MJ/kg CO2 (Wang measured 10.3).

Choose the operating mode from the result:
- If degradation is calendar- or time-at-temperature-limited, switch to 3-4 short cycles per day with shading. Shading adds capex but divides sorbent inventory by 3-4.
- If degradation is per cycle, the inventory argument does not apply. Then compare the design directly against PV plus heat-pump conventional DAC (energy about $41-74/t).

Drop the flat-plate K2CO3 variant. Retest K2CO3 only in an evacuated tubular column at 140 C or above, and add a deliquescence and hydrate test above 43% RH.

patched_idea.title: Solar collector-adsorber DAC panel (amine): passive night loading, solar vapour-purge release in the same glazed enclosure, cycle count chosen by measured sorbent ageing
patched_idea.one_line: A glazed solar panel packed with amine sorbent sheets loads CO2 from night air with a ~10 Pa breeze. By day it is sealed and its own solar heat releases the CO2 by an in-situ water-vapour purge at 1 atm, so there is no purchased regeneration heat and no vacuum pump, and purchased electricity is ~130 kWh/t, mostly compression. Whether to run one cycle a day or 3-4 shaded cycles a day is set by a two-arm ageing test with kill criteria tied to cost, and the flat-plate K2CO3 variant is dropped.
patched_idea.conventional_core: Mass-manufactured glazed and evacuated-tube solar-thermal collectors (the solar-water-heater supply chain), plus existing amine DAC sorbents: a primary-amine-grafted resin or amine on silica. The closest measured basis is Wang et al. 2024, Nat Commun: in-situ vapour-promoted desorption (VPD) of an amine resin with a silica-gel water buffer, measured at bench and prototype scale. Before any build, check freedom to operate against PCT/AU2023/050429 (University of Melbourne, filed 22 May 2023), or license it.
patched_idea.graft: The sorption cycle used in atmospheric-water harvesters and solar adsorption ice makers: the sorbent adsorbs at night and sunlight desorbs it inside the same enclosure (Pons & Guilleminot zeolite/carbon ice makers, 1980s; Kim et al. 2017 Science, MOF-801 water harvester).
patched_idea.mechanism:
Night (base mode): louvres open and air passes at 1.2-2.5 cm/s through a 3-5 cm layer of amine sorbent sheets interleaved with a silica-gel water buffer. Each m2 processes ~0.5-1.1 thousand m3 of air per night for 0.35-0.6 kg CO2 at 75% capture (verifier air volume). Wind or a ~10 Pa fan is enough: 0.029 GJ/t by the verifier fan formula. Cool, humid night air raises amine capacity and refills the water buffer.

Day: louvres close and residual air is purged. Solar heat brings the bed to about 100-105 C. Co-adsorbed water flashes to vapour and lowers CO2 partial pressure in situ, which is Wang's VPD. CO2 leaves at 1 atm to a condenser, and the condensate is recycled. Wang measured 97.7% purity, over 99% peak, at 10.3 MJ/kg of solar-derived heat. A glazed flat box cannot hold process vacuum (1 atm is ~10 t of force per m2), so the design is atmospheric vapour purge by construction. Heating happens after O2 has been purged. Wang's resin lost >20% capacity over 6 cycles when desorbed at 110 C in air, but was stable over 9 vapour-purged cycles. Whether that holds for thousands of cycles is the central open question.

The operating mode is set by the measured degradation regime, not assumed:
- **Calendar- or time-at-temperature-limited:** run 3-4 short cycles per day using shading or louvre cooling between solar desorptions, as in Wang's ~3 h adsorption plus ~40 min desorption. This divides sorbent inventory by 3-4 at the cost of shading capex.
- **Per-cycle limited:** cycles per day do not change sorbent cost per tonne. Keep once-daily operation for its passive simplicity, and benchmark it directly against PV plus heat-pump conventional DAC.

What the panel replaces: purchased regeneration heat, the fan and contactor ductwork, vacuum pumps, steam boilers and the separate heat plant.

Dropped: the flat-plate K2CO3 variant. In 2KHCO3 -> K2CO3 + CO2 + H2O, steam is a reaction product, not an inert sweep gas. At 1 atm total that needs ~31 mol steam per mol CO2 at 120 C and ~100 at 110 C, or self-pressurisation at 141 C or above, which a flat plate gives only ~0.19 kg/m2/day (critic, modelled). K2CO3 is kept only as a later, separate test in an evacuated tubular column at 140 C or above.
patched_idea.target: DAC regeneration heat source, fan/contactor work, vacuum-pump electricity and separate contactor capex, using free diurnal temperature, humidity and solar gradients. The binding cost driver, sorbent cost per tonne (price divided by working capacity times lifetime cycles), is now the first thing measured.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
All figures are modelled unless marked measured. Scripts: scratchpad/climate/thermo_ideas.py, thermo_ideas2.py, critic_bt1_solarpanel.py and patch_bt1_solarpanel.py.

- **Solar heat delivered:** 6.9-12.6 MJ/m2/day, from 5.5-7 kWh/m2/day on the tilted aperture at 35-50% daily collector efficiency (assumed).
- **Regeneration heat:** 10.3 MJ/kg CO2, measured by Wang et al. 2024 for solar VPD on a lab and prototype scale with amine resin. It replaces the earlier modelled 7.1 GJ/t. The heat-limited ceiling is therefore 0.67-1.22 kg CO2/m2/day.
- **Design target and heat use:** 0.35-0.6 kg/m2/day. At the low-irradiance end, 0.6 kg/m2/day is reachable only if heat is 11.5 MJ/kg or less.
- **Purchased electricity:** 0.46 GJe/t (129 kWh/t): compression 1 to 150 bar at 65% efficiency, plus a 10 Pa fan at 0.029 GJ/t. That is ~20% of the 2.34 GJe/t Climeworks Gen2 states.
- **Productivity:** 105-180 kg CO2/m2/yr over an assumed 300 sunny days, i.e. 5.6-9.5 m2 of aperture per t/yr. Land is ~11,000-19,000 km2 per Gt/yr at twice the aperture area.
- **Sorbent charge:** $20/kg at 0.9 mmol/g working capacity (Wang measured 0.9-1.0) with 90% mean capacity:
  - 1,500 cycles: $374/t
  - 3,000 cycles: $187/t
  - 4,500 cycles: $125/t
  - 6,000 cycles: $94/t
  - Fade of 5% per 1,000 cycles reaches 20% loss at ~4,000 cycles, about $140/t. ≤$100/t needs about 5,600 cycles.
- **Mode effect if life is calendar-limited (5-year life, 8%, at 0.6 kg/m2/day):** sorbent inventory is 84 kg per t/yr once daily ($422/t), and 21-28 kg per t/yr at 3-4 cycles per day ($105-141/t). Shading at an assumed $30/m2 adds ~$26/t.
- **Capex:** $560-2,250 per t/yr: panels $100-200/m2, with $0-350 per t/yr BOS. Stratos is ~$2,600 per t/yr.
- **Rough levelised cost, amine only, at 4,500 lifetime cycles:** includes electricity at $60/MWh and $25/t transport and storage. The flat-plate K2CO3 sub-$200/t case is withdrawn.
  - $245-350/t at 0.6 kg/m2/day;
  - $307-457/t at 0.35 kg/m2/day;
  - $494-707/t if life is only 1,500 cycles.
- **Comparators:** Fan & Xu 2026 model $160-200/t core for CSP plus sand storage feeding conventional DAC. The critic models an energy-only cost of $41-74/t for PV plus heat-pump conventional DAC.
- **Scale:** a residual-removal niche of about 0.01-0.05 Gt/yr, not a climate fix.
patched_idea.who_gains:
- **S7 and S8 in sunny regions with geological storage** (Oman/UAE peridotite, Saudi Arabia, US Southwest, India): local manufacture of glass-and-steel hardware, and removal that does not compete for grid power.
- **S3 NOCs and majors:** land host and storage operator role. Dedicated storage, not EOR, to keep S1 on side.
- **S10:** modular, factory-built hardware with low grid exposure, and a test plan whose kill criteria cap the downside early.
- **S5:** neutral to slightly positive (small load).
- **S1 and S2:** no fossil energy input and a transparent, measured energy budget. S1's general DAC moral-hazard concern remains.
patched_idea.who_loses:
- **S11 desert land users and ecology:** ~11-19 km2 per Mt/yr.
- **Grid-powered DAC developers:** compete for the same offtake buyers.
- **IP holders, or the developer:** freedom to operate around PCT/AU2023/050429 may require a licence.
- **Water:** none on net, since condensate is recycled.
patched_idea.closest_known_work:
- **Wang et al. 2024, Nat Commun (Melbourne/Tianjin/Monash):** read in full. Solar-powered in-situ vapour-promoted desorption of an amine resin with a silica-gel buffer, run as a column and a solar prototype. Measured 10.3 MJ/kg, 97.7% purity, 3.7-3.9 kg CO2/h/m3 resin, and 9 stable cycles. This is the base this design starts from. Patent application PCT/AU2023/050429.
- **Kar et al. 2025, Nature Energy (Reisner lab):** a lab dual-bed reactor that captures at night and uses concentrated light by day to release CO2 and convert it to syngas.
- **Fan & Xu 2026, ES&T:** CSP plus sand storage feeding conventional sorbent DAC. $160-200/t core cost, modelled.
- **Heirloom:** fan-free passive trays, but an electric kiln for release.
- **Kim et al. 2017, Science:** MOF water harvester, the source of the graft.
- **Search limit:** the web search budget was exhausted before this patch, so a 2025-26 field-scale solar VPD panel could exist unseen.
patched_idea.why_different: Wang et al. demonstrated the chemistry and a solar-heated column. The added step here is packaging it into the mass-produced glazed solar-collector form factor: a non-concentrating, atmospheric-pressure panel that is contactor, regenerator and heat source in one, with passive or wind-driven night loading. The operating mode (one cycle per day versus 3-4 shaded cycles per day) is chosen from a measured ageing regime rather than assumed. The novelty is now packaging and operation, not the chemistry. The earlier cheap-strong-sorbent (K2CO3 flat-plate) differentiator is withdrawn as thermodynamically unworkable at 1 atm.
patched_idea.cheapest_falsifying_test:
1. **Bench uptake (2 weeks):** TGA or fixed-bed measurement of 10-12 h uptake at 420 ppm, 10-25 C and RH 20-60%, on amine resin or amine-silica sheets with a silica-gel buffer. Drop the design if working capacity is below 0.7 mmol/g.
2. **Two-arm ageing test (6-8 weeks, amine only):**
   - **Cycle arm:** Wang-style 105 C in-situ vapour purge, 6-8 cycles per day, at least 300 cycles.
   - **Calendar arm:** sorbent held through the real once-daily temperature and humidity profile with O2 exposure, including the louvre-reopening transient after sunset.
3. **Outdoor panel check (~$15-30k, 30 days):** one or two 1 m2 panels outdoors or under a solar simulator, with inlet/outlet CO2 analysers, a condenser and a gas meter.

Cost-anchored kill criteria; the idea is killed if any of these hold:
- extrapolated fade above ~5% per 1,000 cycles (about 4,000 cycles to 20% loss, or a sorbent charge above ~$140/t);
- sustained uptake below 0.35 kg CO2/m2/day;
- measured regeneration heat above ~11.5 MJ/kg CO2, above which 0.6 kg/m2/day is unreachable at 6.9 MJ/m2/day (Wang measured 10.3);
- product purity below 90%.

Mode decision:
- Calendar-limited ageing: switch to 3-4 shaded cycles per day.
- Per-cycle-limited ageing: compare directly against PV plus heat-pump conventional DAC, and abandon the panel if it does not beat that on $/t.

K2CO3 is retested only later, in an evacuated tubular column at 140 C or above, with a deliquescence and hydrate test above 43% RH.

fix.change_summary:
I applied the critic's patch. The core mechanism stays: a glazed solar collector-adsorber that loads CO2 at night and releases it by day at 1 atm using its own solar heat, with no vacuum. The graft also stays: the night-adsorb, solar-desorb cycle of water harvesters and ice makers. The changes:

1. **K2CO3 variant dropped.** The flat-plate K2CO3 variant is removed. Steam is a product of KHCO3 decomposition, so at 1 atm it needs 31-100 mol steam per mol CO2. K2CO3 is deferred to a later tubular-column test at 140 C or above, with a deliquescence check. This also withdraws the sub-$200/t headline and the cheap-strong-sorbent differentiator.
2. **Rebased on Wang et al. 2024.** The design now builds on Wang et al. 2024 Nat Commun (in-situ vapour-promoted desorption), which I read in full. Its measured values replace modelled ones: 10.3 MJ/kg heat, 0.9-1.0 mmol/g working capacity, 97.7% purity, and its degradation data. A freedom-to-operate and licence step for PCT/AU2023/050429 is added. Wang is now listed as the closest work, and the novelty claim is narrowed to packaging and operation.
3. **Sorbent cost and cost range recomputed** (scratchpad/climate/patch_bt1_solarpanel.py). Sorbent cost is now price divided by working capacity times lifetime cycles: $374/t at 1,500 cycles, $125/t at 4,500 cycles, and about 5,600 cycles for ≤$100/t. The levelised cost of removal for the amine variant is now $245-350/t at 0.6 kg/m2/day and 4,500 cycles, rising to $494-707/t if life is 1,500 cycles. The earlier $150-230/t claim is withdrawn.
4. **Test plan replaced.** The loose 30-day test is replaced by a two-arm ageing test: a cycle arm of at least 300 vapour-purge cycles, and a calendar arm on the once-daily temperature, humidity and O2 profile. The kill criteria are now tied to cost:
   - fade above 5% per 1,000 cycles;
   - uptake below 0.35 kg/m2/day;
   - regeneration heat above 11.5 MJ/kg. The critic proposed ~10 MJ/kg; I set 11.5 because that is the limit for 0.6 kg/m2/day at low irradiance, and 10 would kill Wang's own measured 10.3.
   - purity below 90%.
5. **Operating mode decided by the test.** If ageing is calendar-limited, run 3-4 shaded cycles per day: inventory falls from 84 to 21-28 kg per t/yr, at about +$26/t for shading. If it is per-cycle-limited, benchmark directly against PV plus heat-pump DAC.

The web search budget was exhausted, so I could not run a fresh 2025-26 prior-art search.

idea.title: Repair-cycle DAC sorbent: wash out and reload the oxidised amine in place
idea.one_line: Photosystem II repairs itself by swapping out only its damaged D1 protein. Copy that: build solid-amine DAC contactors so the oxidised amine is flushed and re-impregnated in place, while the costly support and structure stay.
idea.conventional_core: Solid-amine temperature-vacuum swing DAC (Climeworks type; PEI-class amines on silica or laminate supports), regenerated at about 80-100 C.
idea.graft: The photosystem II D1 repair cycle. The FtsH protease degrades photodamaged D1, and a new D1 is made and reassembled into the PSII complex, whose other parts are kept (Zhang et al. 2026, New Phytologist).
idea.mechanism: Oxidative degradation attacks the amine, not the inorganic support. Physically impregnated amine (rather than covalently grafted) can be washed out with a solvent, and fresh amine solution can re-coat the same structured support inside the contactor. The sorbent becomes a permanent scaffold plus a consumable amine, and the design goal shifts from 'make the amine last' to 'make the amine cheap to replace'.
idea.target: Sorbent lifetime and replacement cost. The map flags this as the main materials lever at gigatonne scale: no public field-lifetime data exist, and TEA needs 1e4 to 1e5 cycles. The target plants are Mammoth-class and later solid-sorbent plants.
idea.quantitative_claims:
(1) Parametric (my calculation): sorbent replacement costs $69-1,038/t CO2. Inputs are a working capacity of 1-1.5 mol/kg, 3-6 cycles/day, 1-2 yr life and $20-50/kg for structured sorbent, which gives 48-289 kg CO2 per kg of sorbent over its life. In-place reload cuts this by 46-54%, or $33-560/t depending on the case. Reload assumptions: amine is 20-30% of sorbent cost, the support is reused 5-10 times, and process overhead is 10-15%.
(2) Material flow: replacement mass falls from 3.5-21 Mt/yr of sorbent per Gt CO2 to mostly amine, at 1.4-8.3 Mt/yr per Gt (40 wt%). Amine supply, the Deutz and Bardow concern, is not solved.
(3) Reload energy, assuming 2 kg methanol evaporated per kg sorbent per reload, is 0.008-0.046 GJ/t CO2. That is under 1% of real DAC energy (5-10 GJ/t) and at most 10% of the 0.465 GJ/t floor (verifier).
(4) Degradation is fast enough to test in days. In an accelerated test (Thakkar et al. 2024, ACS Omega), PEI-silica lost about 94% of its capacity within 24 h at 120 C in air with 21% O2.
idea.who_gains: S10 DAC buyers and investors get a lower, more predictable cost per delivered tonne. Solid-sorbent DAC operators gain, including S3/S4-backed ones such as Shell- and Mitsubishi-backed Avnos. S4 amine and chemical makers sell a recurring consumable. S1 and S8 gain cheaper durable removal, reserved for residual emissions.
idea.who_loses: Sorbent and contactor suppliers whose revenue comes from replacing whole modules. S1 critics who see cheaper DAC as moral hazard. S11, if the solvent handling during reload (methanol VOCs, spent amine waste) is poorly contained.
idea.closest_known_work: Climeworks' sorbent and filter upgrades at Mammoth (map). Thakkar et al. 2024 accelerated PEI-silica testing (doi 10.1021/acsomega.4c05639). Zhao et al. 2025 PEI on layered double hydroxide, which resists oxidation (doi 10.1002/advs.202507756). Han et al. 2026, epoxide-functionalised amines stable in O2 and humidity (Adv. Sci.). The antioxidant-additive literature.
idea.why_different: Existing work tries to make the amine last longer. This idea accepts degradation and makes the amine cheap to replace in place without dismantling the contactor. I found no published wash-and-reload study for DAC laminates, but my literature search was cut short by the search budget, so prior art may exist.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test: A 4-6 week bench loop needing only a TGA and an oven. Age PEI/silica powder and a PEI-coated laminate coupon at 100-120 C in air to about 50% capacity loss. Wash with water and methanol, re-impregnate, then re-measure CO2 capacity at 400 ppm and BET surface area. Repeat 5 times. Falsified if recovered capacity is below 80% of fresh after the second reload, or if BET area falls more than 10% per cycle (oxidation products bonding to silica or blocking pores). Cost under $10k.

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: Li W., Stevens L., ... Fabbri D., Snape C.E. (2026). Toward Sustainable Adsorbents for CO2 Capture: Reuse of Silica from Spent Silica-Polyethylenimine. Energy & Fuels 40(15), 8222-8228
closest.overlap: Very close to the core concept. The authors recover the silica support from spent silica-(alkoxylated) PEI adsorbent and re-impregnate it with fresh PEI. Optimal loading was 45 wt% against 47 wt% fresh, and CO2 capacity was about 10% below fresh. Two differences from the idea: the spent amine was removed by 1- or 2-stage pyrolysis at 500-600 C, not a solvent wash, and this caused about 13% mesopore contraction and about 10% pore-volume loss. The work used powder, was done ex situ, ran only one reuse cycle (the authors call multi-cycle work future study) and was framed for post-combustion rather than DAC.

closest.title: Coralli I., Giuri D., ... Stevens L.A., Snape C.E., Fabbri D. (2023). Valorization Strategies in CO2 Capture: A New Life for Exhausted Silica-Polyethylenimine. Int. J. Mol. Sci. 24, 14415
closest.overlap: Uses the idea's proposed wash-out step itself: methanol solvent extraction to recover degraded PEI and silica from used Si-PEI CO2 sorbents, plus characterisation of the degradation products (urea and carbamate). The aim was valorisation of the spent PEI (pyrolysis to alkylpyrazines), not re-impregnation of the support, and the work was on powder and done ex situ.

closest.title: Industrial analogue: SCR deNOx catalyst rejuvenation (washing out poisons and re-impregnating active vanadium/tungsten on the same TiO2 honeycomb, done commercially, sometimes on site)
closest.overlap: An established commercial practice of keeping a costly structured support and replacing only the active phase by wash and re-impregnation. It is the same scaffold-plus-consumable business logic in a different chemistry. This is background knowledge; I did not re-verify it in this session because the search budget was exhausted.

closest.title: Thakkar et al. 2024, ACS Omega (accelerated oxidative ageing of PEI-silica) and Shu/Lively et al. 2025, Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 'Performance Degradation of Amine-Infused Fiber Sorbents for DAC: Mechanisms and Solutions'
closest.overlap: Degradation-mechanism work on DAC amine sorbents. The fiber-sorbent paper addresses degradation by pre-treating the support or swapping materials, not by re-infusing amine. Both confirm that the field's focus is 'make the amine last' or 'make the support compatible', not in-place reload.

closest.title: Climeworks Mammoth sorbent and filter upgrades; stability-focused DAC sorbent work (Zhao et al. 2025, PEI-modified AMO-LDH, Adv. Sci. doi 10.1002/advs.202507756; epoxide-functionalised amines)
closest.overlap: Commercial and academic practice here is whole-sorbent or filter replacement plus more oxidation-resistant amines. I found no public description of in-contactor amine wash-out and reload.

art.what_is_new:
The core chemistry is already published, so it is not novel: strip spent PEI from silica with methanol (Coralli et al. 2023) and re-impregnate the recovered support with fresh PEI at about 90% of fresh capacity (Li et al., Energy & Fuels 2026, via pyrolysis). The commercial logic of keeping the costly support and replacing only the active phase also exists in SCR catalyst rejuvenation. What I found no precedent for:
(1) Doing the strip and reload in place, inside a structured DAC contactor (laminate or monolith), without unloading the sorbent.
(2) A solvent-only strip feeding directly into a re-coat over multiple cycles. The published reuse used 500-600 C pyrolysis, gave only one cycle, and caused about 13% mesopore contraction, which bears directly on the idea's BET falsification criterion. Pyrolysis would also destroy polymer or cellulose laminates, so the solvent route is required for DAC structured supports.
(3) Applying it to air-capture conditions, where oxidative degradation dominates, rather than flue gas, and framing it as cutting sorbent-replacement cost per tonne in DAC TEA.

Revise 'closest_known_work' and 'why_different': the claim that no one has published wash-and-reload is only true for in-place DAC laminates; ex situ silica support recovery and reimpregnation is published. The falsifying test should cite Li et al. 2026 as its baseline (about 10% capacity loss after one pyrolysis-based reuse) and show that solvent washing does better over 5 cycles.

Search limitations: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, and Google Patents, OpenAlex and DuckDuckGo were unavailable (503, 429 and a CAPTCHA). The search relied on Crossref and Europe PMC. Patents (for example Climeworks, Global Thermostat/Corning and Svante filings on sorbent refurbishment) were not checked, so an in-situ reload patent may exist.

phys.assumptions:
The script ran successfully. Every number below is quoted as the script printed it. Labels: [verifier] means OptiLex physics.py. [idea] means the idea's own inputs. [mem] means a literature value recalled from memory and not re-checked, because the session's web-search budget (200/200) was used up before this run. [assume] means my judgement.

FLOOR: 20.47 kJ/mol = 0.465 GJ/t (129 kWh/t) for air at 420 ppm, 75% capture, 99% purity [verifier]. At real solid-sorbent DAC energy of 5, 7 and 10 GJ/t, second-law efficiency is 9.3%, 6.6% and 4.7%. The 5-10+ GJ/t range is [mem], from the McQueen et al. 2021 review: about 5.4-11.9 GJ/t, mostly modelled or pilot data, and heat-dominated. The reload step is not a separation, so it adds energy above the floor and cannot breach it.

CLAIM 1 (sorbent cost) reproduces exactly:
- 48.2 kg CO2 per kg sorbent (1.0 mol/kg, 3 cycles/day, 1 yr = 1,095 cycles) gives $1,038/t at $50/kg.
- 289.1 kg/kg (1.5 mol/kg, 6 cycles/day, 2 yr = 4,380 cycles) gives $69/t at $20/kg.
- My base case of 120.5 kg/kg (1.25 mol/kg, 4 cycles/day, 1.5 yr) gives $291/t at $35/kg.
- The idea's 1-2 yr lifetimes are below the TEA target of 1e4 cycles, which is 4.6-9.1 yr at 3-6 cycles/day.

RELOAD SAVINGS: I modelled the cost of a reload, as a fraction of new sorbent price, as f = a + (1-a)/N + proc. Here a is the amine's share of sorbent cost, N is how many times the support is reused, and proc is the reload process overhead.
- On the idea's own inputs the saving is 41-62%. The idea claims 46-54%, which falls inside this range.
- Stress cases: a=0.5 and N=5 saves 25%. If the support degrades so N=2, the saving is 20%. With a=0.7 and N=3 the saving is 0%.
- Effect on sorbent cost in $/t: $1,038 falls to $394-612, $291 to $110-171, and $69 to $26-41.

CLAIM 3 (reload energy) holds, assuming latent heat plus 30% losses [assume]:
- Methanol at 2 kg per kg sorbent: 0.010-0.059 GJ/t.
- Methanol at 4 kg/kg, covering wash plus impregnation solution: 0.020-0.119 GJ/t.
- Water at 4 kg/kg: 0.041-0.244 GJ/t, which is at most 3.48% of 7 GJ/t.
- The idea's claim of 0.008-0.046 GJ/t is consistent with this. Energy is not the binding constraint.

FULL DAC COST (gross $/t, CRF annualisation, all inputs [assume] with [mem] anchors):
- Low: capex $500 per t/yr at 6% over 25 yr; heat 4 GJ at $4/GJ; electricity 1 GJ at $40/MWh; T&S $10. Cost falls from $160 to $118 with reload, a 26.6% cut. Sorbent was 43.1% of cost.
- Base: capex $1,500 at 8% over 20 yr; heat 5.5 GJ at $8/GJ; electricity 1.5 GJ at $60/MWh; T&S $20. Cost falls from $592 to $474, a 20.0% cut. Sorbent was 49.0%.
- High: capex $3,000 at 10% over 15 yr; heat 8 GJ at $15/GJ; electricity 2.5 GJ at $100/MWh; N=2; T&S $40. Cost falls from $1,811 to $1,607, an 11.3% cut. Sorbent was 57.3%.
- Reload downtime of 2 days per reload [assume] costs 0.27-0.55% of capacity.
- The model lands in the [mem] band from Young et al. 2023 and the 2024-25 DAC offtake prices of roughly $400-1,000/t.

Energy figures are total DAC energy plus reload energy: low 5.0+0.010, base about 7.0, high 10.5+0.119 GJ/t.

SCALE: the idea is a cost lever on solid-sorbent DAC, not a new removal pathway. I used 0.5 Gt/yr as the realistic 2050 value. That is a judgement within IEA NZE's roughly 1 Gt DAC by 2050 [mem]. Realized DAC today is about 0.01-0.02 Mt/yr [mem]. Energy share of world primary: 0.5 Gt at 7 GJ/t needs 3.5 EJ (0.56%). 1 Gt at 7 GJ/t needs 7.0 EJ (1.13%), and at 10 GJ/t, 10.0 EJ (1.61%).
phys.resource_needs:
Energy: about 7 GJ/t, mostly heat at 80-100 C. That is 3.5 EJ (0.56% of world primary energy) at 0.5 Gt/yr and 7.0 EJ (1.13%) at 1 Gt/yr; reload adds only 0.01-0.24 GJ/t.

Materials per Gt CO2/yr:
- Without reload, sorbent use is 3.5-20.8 Mt/yr (base 8.3).
- With reload, amine make-up is 1.4-8.3 Mt/yr (base 3.3), and support make-up is 0.2-2.5 Mt/yr at N=5-10.
- That amine demand is 2-14x today's global ethyleneamines market (about 0.6 Mt/yr [mem]); the reload does not reduce amine demand.
- Embodied CO2 of the amine, at 2-4 kg CO2e per kg [assume], is 0.28-3.32% of the CO2 captured.

Solvent and waste: methanol VOC losses are 0.14-4.15 Mt/yr per Gt, assuming 1-5% loss per reload and 4 kg solvent per kg sorbent. Spent oxidised amine becomes an on-site liquid waste stream of the same Mt scale.

Land and water [mem]: the plant footprint is small, about 0.1-1 km2 per Mt excluding the energy supply. Water balance under steam-assisted TVSA depends on climate.
phys.violations:
I found no thermodynamic violations: nothing is claimed below the 0.465 GJ/t floor, and the reload energy is additive. The arithmetic in claims 1 and 3 checks out. The 46-54% saving in claim 1 is, if anything, conservative on the idea's own inputs (41-62%).

Four issues stop short of 'implausible' but limit the idea:

(a) The mechanism needs physically impregnated amine. Climeworks' original sorbent is aminosilane covalently grafted onto cellulose [mem, Gebald et al.], so the 'Climeworks-type / Mammoth' framing may not apply. The idea fits PEI-impregnated monoliths and laminates (Global Thermostat-type) better.

(b) The saving depends on the expensive part of the sorbent being the support and not the amine (a = 0.2-0.3). At bulk PEI prices of about $3-10/kg [mem], that holds only for costly structured supports. With cheap precipitated silica, a rises and the saving falls toward 0-25%.

(c) Support reuse of N = 5-10 is unproven. Oxidised PEI may crosslink or bond to silica, and silica ages hydrothermally under steam. At N=2 the saving is only 20%.

(d) Claim 4 (94% capacity loss in 24 h at 120 C in air; Thakkar 2024) was not re-verified here. 120 C ageing may not reproduce the degradation chemistry of humid field operation at 80-100 C.
phys.key_uncertainties:
1. Removability: whether oxidised and urea-linked PEI can actually be washed off the support with water or methanol, or instead fouls the pores. This decides N and is the idea's cheapest falsifying test.

2. Cost split: whether the amine or the structured support dominates sorbent cost. This sets the saving at anywhere from 0% to 62%.

3. Field sorbent data: no public field data on lifetime or working capacity exist. Sorbent cost spans $69-1,038/t across plausible inputs, so it can be anywhere from a minor to the dominant cost line.

4. Sorbent improvements may overtake the idea. If oxidation-resistant amines (Zhao 2025, Han 2026) or newer sorbent generations reach about 1e4 cycles, the sorbent cost share drops and the reload's value shrinks to about $28-43/t.

5. Solvent risk: handling methanol inside air contactors brings flammability, VOC emissions and spent-amine waste (an S11 issue). A water-only wash avoids VOCs but doubles reload energy, which is still negligible.

6. Prior art: search for wash-and-reload of supported amines was incomplete in both the idea's run and this one. The concept of re-impregnating spent sorbents may exist in the lab literature.

7. Sourcing: every [mem] value (PEI price, ethyleneamines market size, McQueen energy range, Young et al. costs, capex) needs a primary source before it is quoted externally.

stances.evidence: S1's stance follows from its position on DAC itself; how the sorbent is maintained barely matters to it. CAN (Jan 2021, 1,300+ NGOs) says DACCS has 'no place' in scenarios built on early, steep reductions. It will not support negative emissions or offsets 'as an alternative to stringent emission reductions', and it wants public support for CCS-linked technologies phased out. CIEL (fetched 2026-10-05) groups DAC with CCS/CCUS because it 'depends on CCS or CCUS' and so carries the same pipeline and storage hazards. Moderate NGOs and the conservation members of the Carbon Capture Coalition accept durable removal reserved for residual emissions. Frontier's buyers are framed that way, and S1 is split on it in the map. The idea itself frames its benefit as removal reserved for residuals, which is the only framing moderate S1 accepts. Net: the CAN/CIEL wing opposes and the moderate wing is neutral to mildly supportive. A process-efficiency improvement does not move either wing on its own.
stances.red_line_hit: Mitigation deterrence: cheaper DAC strengthens the 'removal instead of reduction' argument, which is CAN red line (4) and red line (8) on DACCS. EOR is a second red line, conditional: if reloaded contactors are deployed at Occidental-type plants that send CO2 to EOR, now at 45Q parity since OBBBA 2025, CAN red line (7) applies. Any public subsidy for the R&D also falls under red line (3).

stances.evidence: IPCC AR6 WGIII (C.4.4 and the CDR sections) treats CDR, including DACCS, as necessary to counterbalance residual emissions in net-zero pathways. It also warns that CCS can prolong fossil use. Oxford Net Zero (Allen and Jenkins, Joule 2021, carbon takeback) treats durable storage as a required backstop. On realised outcomes, S2 has documented that DAC underdelivers. Orca averaged about 600 t/yr against a 4,000 t/yr nameplate (Wikipedia, citing reporting, measured), and cdr.fyi shows 50.5 Mt of durable CDR contracted but only 1.7 Mt delivered (trailing 24 months, fetched 2026-10-05). S2 would therefore support a cheap, falsifiable bench test that targets an unmeasured cost driver: no public data exist on sorbent field lifetime. S2 would reject any claim that this changes DAC's role beyond residual emissions. The reload energy is under 1% of DAC's real 5-10 GJ/t, so the climate-relevant cost lever is materials, not energy.
stances.red_line_hit: None, provided claims stay within the bench data. S2 objects to unverified cost claims: the $33-560/t saving is a parametric model with no field data. It also objects to framing DAC as a substitute for reductions.

stances.evidence: Occidental, through 1PointFive and its $1.1bn purchase of Carbon Engineering in Nov 2023, is the largest DAC developer and sells removal into the Frontier and Microsoft AMCs. Wikipedia reports Oxy views carbon removal as 'a sort of future-proofing for its industry'. From my own knowledge, not re-verified this session: Oxy CEO Hollub said in 2023 that DAC gives the industry a 'license to continue to operate'. The idea names Avnos, which is backed by Shell and Mitsubishi, per the idea text (not re-verified). OBBBA 2025 kept DAC at $180/t under 45Q and gave EOR and utilisation parity, which S3 supports through the Carbon Capture Coalition. A lower sorbent cost per tonne raises DAC margins under a fixed credit. Caveat: Oxy's Stratos uses liquid-solvent (KOH/calcium-loop) DAC, not solid amine, so this idea does not help Oxy's own technology directly. It helps solid-sorbent DAC as a technology class, including S3-backed solid-sorbent players. S3's support for DAC as a sector is documented; support for this specific idea is inferred.
stances.red_line_hit: None for S3. The idea imposes no fee, mandate or production limit, and S3's documented red line is a per-tonne charge, such as the Waste Emissions Charge repealed in 2025.

stances.evidence: Two sub-groups gain. (a) Chemical and amine makers gain a recurring consumable. My calculation from the idea's ranges is 1.4-8.3 Mt/yr of amine per Gt CO2. That is roughly 2-13x current global ethyleneamines output, against my unverified recollection of about 0.65 Mt/yr for that output, so at scale it is a new bulk market. It is also a supply-chain bottleneck (the Deutz and Bardow concern the idea admits it does not solve). (b) Cement, steel and chemicals plants that need durable removals for residual process emissions (GCCA roadmap; COP28 1/CMA.5 para 28(e): 'particularly in hard-to-abate sectors') gain cheaper offsets for the residue. VCI's documented stance on German CCfDs ('no panacea', wants lower energy prices) shows S4 supports cost-cutting tools that do not raise its own costs. This idea raises none. Contactor and sorbent-module suppliers whose revenue comes from replacing whole modules lose, as the idea itself notes, so S4 equipment makers are a small dissenting segment.
stances.red_line_hit: None for chemical makers. A minor one for sorbent and contactor suppliers: lost revenue from replacing whole modules.

stances.evidence: DAC is a large flexible electricity and heat load (real systems run at 5-10 GJ/t), so utilities gain demand. Utilities' documented support for 45Q comes through the Carbon Capture Coalition. Sorbent reload changes materials cost, not the energy draw: reload energy is 0.008-0.046 GJ/t CO2, under 1% of DAC energy, per the verifier-checked idea claim. There is no documented utility position on DAC sorbent chemistry. A modest positive tilt exists if cheaper DAC means more plants and more load sales.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: S6 unions (for example USW and building trades) are members of the Carbon Capture Coalition, which backs 45Q including DAC at $180/t. They support carbon-management infrastructure as job-preserving for high-carbon regions. In-place reload is a maintenance-process change. It adds some recurring O&M labour (wash and re-impregnation cycles) and avoids module-replacement shipments, so the effect on jobs is near zero to slightly positive and local. There is no documented union position on sorbent maintenance. The stance is mildly positive on DAC deployment generally and indifferent to this specific idea.
stances.red_line_hit: None, unless solvent-handling safety becomes a workplace issue. Methanol is toxic and flammable, so worker-exposure controls would matter to unions.

stances.evidence: OBBBA (signed 4 Jul 2025) kept 45Q DAC at $180/t while cutting credits for new entrants. That is the only major carbon-specific IRA credit the 2025 Congress strengthened, and support was bipartisan. COP28 1/CMA.5 para 28(e) names 'removal technologies such as carbon capture and utilization and storage' among the technologies all parties accept. The EU NZIA sets a 50 Mt/yr injection-capacity objective for 2030. For governments paying per tonne, a lower cost per tonne for DAC lowers the fiscal cost per tonne removed, or raises tonnes removed per dollar of credit. The DOE invested $1.2bn in the Texas and Louisiana DAC hubs under the BIL. Their 2025-26 status was not verified this session, and I could not confirm whether they were cut. That is a confound: S7 support for DAC grants may be weaker than support for the 45Q credit.
stances.red_line_hit: Fiscal: if credits are paid per tonne, cost reductions accrue to developers unless credit levels fall. Taxpayers for Common Sense already opposes 45Q EOR parity. No new red line from the idea itself.

stances.evidence: Baum et al. 2024 (Nature Communications; N=30,284; 30 countries; fielded 2022) found Global South publics more supportive of all climate-intervention technologies. They were also more worried that these technologies undermine mitigation and spread risk unequally. North and South both rated engineered CDR (DACCS, BECCS) the highest mitigation-deterrence risk. Climate-justice advocates align with CAN's red lines against offsets substituting for cuts. S8 governments would welcome cheaper durable removal only if it is paid for by historical emitters rather than used to delay their reductions. The idea names S8 as gaining 'cheaper durable removal', but that holds only if removal funding is additional. Unlike land-based CDR, solid-sorbent DAC causes no land conflict, which removes the BECCS red line (CAN red line 5).
stances.red_line_hit: Mitigation deterrence and offsets: cheaper DAC could let Northern emitters delay cuts. Siting DAC and storage in poorer regions is also a concern: objectors have said they feel 'experimented on' (Wikipedia, DAC community-opposition section).

stances.evidence: The idea creates no consumer-facing price change: no fuel charge, no tariff and no mandate. Canada's 2025 removal of the consumer fuel charge and Washington's 2024 retention of cap-and-invest show S9 reacts to visible costs. This idea imposes none. Andre et al. 2024 (Nature Climate Change; 125 countries; N=129,902) found 69% willing to contribute 1% of income. Baum 2024 found government funding of research and small field trials the most popular policy types. Publics rate engineered CDR highest for moral hazard, so salience is low and sentiment ambivalent.
stances.red_line_hit: None. There is no price rise, unless a future carbon-takeback obligation passes DAC costs into fuel prices, in which case cheaper DAC lowers the pass-through.

stances.evidence: S10 is the demand side for durable CDR. Frontier is a $1.8bn advance market commitment (AMC) to 2040 targeting <$100/t, with members including Stripe, Google, Shopify, Anthropic, JPMorgan and Salesforce. cdr.fyi (fetched 2026-10-05) shows 50.5 Mt contracted against 1.7 Mt delivered over the trailing 24 months, a delivery gap of about 30x. That gap is the investor risk this idea targets. A modelled 46-54% cut in sorbent-replacement cost ($33-560/t, parametric, no field data) also makes cost per tonne more predictable because replacement becomes a routine operating cost. Insurers and investors would want field-lifetime data before pricing it in. The proposed 4-6 week bench test for under $10k is the kind of cheap de-risking investors fund. Orca's underperformance (about 600 t/yr against 4,000 t/yr nameplate, measured) makes buyers wary of claims based on nameplate capacity.
stances.red_line_hit: None. Reputational risk exists if DAC purchases are seen as greenwashing, which is the S1 moral-hazard critique, but that applies to DAC generally, not to this idea.

stances.evidence: Communities near DAC hubs have objected that projects are 'always developed in poor areas' and that they feel 'experimented on' (Wikipedia DAC article, community-opposition section). CIEL points to pipeline and storage hazards. This idea adds a new on-site chemical handling step. Using the idea's own assumptions, I calculated that a 1 Mt/yr plant would cycle about 7-42 kt/yr of methanol, about 19-114 t/day evaporated and presumably mostly recovered. It would also generate about 1.4-8.3 kt/yr of spent, oxidised amine waste. Whole-module replacement creates solid waste shipped off-site; in-place reload replaces that with liquid VOC handling and hazardous-waste streams on-site. A switch to a water or ethanol wash would reduce the concern; using methanol was the idea's assumption, not a requirement. Local stance depends on whether the solvent loop is closed and permitted.
stances.red_line_hit: Local safety and pollution: methanol VOC emissions, flammable solvent storage and spent-amine liquid waste (oxidation products may include ammonia or nitrosamine precursors, which the idea has not assessed). It adds to existing siting-justice and CO2 pipeline-safety concerns.

stake.coalition_notes: How this idea sorts stakeholders: it is a component-level cost improvement to solid-sorbent DAC. Stakeholders' stances therefore follow their position on DAC, and the specific mechanism hardly shifts them. Likely supporters: S2 (as a cheap falsifiable test of an unmeasured cost driver), S3 and S4 (chemical makers gain a recurring bulk amine market; S3 gains as a DAC sector developer, though Oxy's own liquid-KOH process is not helped), S7 (lower fiscal cost per tonne under 45Q's $180/t, kept by OBBBA 2025) and S10 (Frontier/AMC buyers facing a 50.5 Mt contracted vs 1.7 Mt delivered gap per cdr.fyi). S5, S6 and S9 are neutral because the idea creates no price, job or load shock. S1 and S8 are split, and their red lines come from DAC generally: mitigation deterrence, offsets, and EOR if deployed via Oxy-type plants, which have had 45Q EOR parity since OBBBA. S11 is split because the idea introduces a new on-site risk: methanol handling (about 19-114 t/day cycled at a 1 Mt/yr plant, my calculation from the idea's assumptions) and spent-amine liquid waste. Three design choices would widen the coalition at no cost to the core idea. (1) Use a water or ethanol wash with a closed solvent loop and characterise the spent-amine waste, which neutralises S11 and S6 safety concerns. (2) Commit to dedicated geologic storage only, not EOR, which removes CAN red line (7) and the S1/S8 EOR objection. (3) Frame the output strictly as removal for residual emissions alongside reductions, consistent with COP28 1/CMA.5 para 28(e) and the IPCC, which keeps moderate S1 and S8 neutral rather than opposed. Unresolved tension: amine demand at Gt scale (1.4-8.3 Mt/yr per Gt, about 2-13x my unverified estimate of current ethyleneamines output) is a supply bottleneck S4 would profit from but which could raise amine prices for other users. Caveats: WebSearch was exhausted this session, so the following are from documented positions in the map, two WebFetch pages (CIEL CCS page and cdr.fyi, both fetched 2026-10-05; the Wikipedia DAC article was also fetched) or flagged own-knowledge. The 2025-26 status of the DOE DAC hubs is unverified, as are Mammoth's measured output, Hollub's 2023 'license to operate' quote and the Avnos backers. No stakeholder has a documented position on sorbent reload specifically; every stance is inferred from positions on DAC, 45Q and CDR markets.

critic.fatal_flaw: None found. The physics holds: reload energy is additive and below 1% of DAC energy, and nothing is claimed below the 0.465 GJ/t floor. The stakeholder red lines (mitigation deterrence, EOR) come from DAC in general and can be designed around by committing to geologic storage only and framing the output as removal for residual emissions. Two issues narrow the idea without killing it. First, 'Climeworks-type/Mammoth' is probably the wrong target: Gen-1/2 Climeworks used covalently grafted aminosilane on cellulose, which cannot be washed out, so the idea applies only to physically impregnated PEI on structured supports (Global Thermostat/Corning-type monoliths and laminates). Second, the novelty is now only the in-place step: Coralli 2023 published the methanol strip, and Li 2026 published re-impregnation of recovered silica at about 90% of fresh capacity.
critic.top_fixable_flaw:
The proposed falsifying test checks only the published part of the idea and leaves out the new claim. Ageing PEI/silica powder, washing it with methanol and re-impregnating it in an oven/TGA loop repeats Coralli 2023 and Li 2026 ex situ. It says nothing about whether a fouled structured contactor can be stripped and re-coated in place to a uniform, full-capacity amine loading. Yet in-place re-coating is where the value either survives or disappears.

My check script (critic_graft_bio_4.py) shows the saving depends more on recovered working capacity (cap_ret) than on the amine cost share. Take the idea's mid inputs (a=0.25, N=5, overhead 12%). The saving is 48% at full recovery, 42% at 90%, 35% at 80% and 26% at 70%. If the support survives only N=3 reloads, the saving falls to 31%, 23% and 11% at 90%, 80% and 70% recovery.

In-place wet impregnation of a laminate or monolith risks:
- uneven amine loading along the flow path and from wall to centre;
- amine migrating to the outer surface as the solvent dries, which blocks pores and raises pressure drop;
- solvent pooling at the bottom of the vacuum chamber.

Any of these would push cap_ret into the 70-80% range, where the idea stops being worth doing. The amine cost share itself is not the risk. At 40 wt% PEI costing $5-20/kg in a $20-50/kg structured sorbent, a = 0.04-0.40, mostly at or below the idea's assumed 0.2-0.3, which favours the idea.

Separately, ageing in dry air at 100-120 C does not reproduce field degradation. In humid TVSA service at 80-100 C, CO2-driven urea crosslinking and steam effects on the support act together. Urea-linked PEI is the fraction least likely to wash out.

patched_idea.title: Repair-cycle DAC sorbent: strip and re-coat the oxidised amine in place on impregnated-PEI structured contactors
patched_idea.one_line: Photosystem II repairs itself by swapping out only its damaged D1 protein. Copy that in DAC contactors built with physically impregnated PEI: flush out the oxidised amine with solvent and re-coat fresh amine inside the sealed contactor, over several cycles, while the costly structured support stays in place.
patched_idea.conventional_core: Solid-amine temperature-vacuum swing DAC using physically impregnated PEI-class amines on structured supports, such as the Global Thermostat/Corning-type monoliths and laminates. These are regenerated at about 80-100 C. Covalently grafted aminosilane sorbents, such as Climeworks Gen-1/2 aminosilane on cellulose, are out of scope because grafted amine cannot be washed out.
patched_idea.graft: The photosystem II D1 repair cycle. The FtsH protease degrades photodamaged D1, and a new D1 is made and reassembled into the PSII complex, whose other parts are kept (Zhang et al. 2026, New Phytologist).
patched_idea.mechanism: Oxidative degradation attacks the amine, not the inorganic support. In impregnated (not grafted) PEI sorbents, the oxidised amine can be removed by flowing solvent through the contactor: water first, then ethanol. Fresh PEI solution is then flowed through and vacuum-dried inside the same housing. The sorbent becomes a permanent scaffold plus a consumable amine, and the design goal shifts from 'make the amine last' to 'make the amine cheap to replace without dismantling the contactor'. The value depends on two quantities. The first is recovered working capacity, r, the share of fresh capacity regained after each in-place reload. The second is N, the number of reload cycles the support survives.
patched_idea.target: Sorbent lifetime and replacement cost for plants using impregnated-PEI structured contactors (monolith or laminate). No public field-lifetime data exist, and TEA needs 1e4 to 1e5 cycles. Mammoth-type grafted-cellulose sorbents are not targets.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
(1) Parametric sorbent replacement cost, from my calculation: $69-1,038/t CO2. Inputs: working capacity 1-1.5 mol/kg, 3-6 cycles/day, 1-2 yr life, and $20-50/kg for structured sorbent, which gives 48-289 kg CO2 per kg of sorbent over its life.

The saving is now reported as a function of r and N, replacing the earlier flat 46-54%. Model: relative cost = ((1-a)/N + a + o)/r, where a is the amine share of sorbent cost and o = 0.12 is process overhead (script patch_graft_bio_4.py; it reproduces the critic's figures).
- At a = 0.25 and N = 5, the saving is 48% at r = 1.0, 42% at 0.9, 39% at 0.85, 35% at 0.8 and 26% at 0.7.
- At a = 0.25 and N = 3, it is 38%, 31%, 27%, 23% and 11% at the same r values.
- With PEI at $5-20/kg in a $20-50/kg sorbent, a = 0.04-0.40. At a = 0.04, N = 5 and r = 0.85 the saving is 59%. At a = 0.40, N = 3 and r = 0.85 it is only 15%.
- Breakeven r ranges from 0.35 (a = 0.04, N = 5) to 0.72 (a = 0.40, N = 3).
- In dollars, at a = 0.25 and r = 0.85 the saving is $27-403/t for N = 5 and $19-281/t for N = 3. At r = 1.0 and N = 5 it is $33-498/t.

(2) Material flow: replacement mass falls from 3.5-21 Mt/yr of sorbent per Gt CO2 to mostly amine, at 1.4-8.3 Mt/yr per Gt (40 wt%). If r < 1, more amine is used per tonne, scaling as 1/r. Amine supply, the Deutz and Bardow concern, is not solved.

(3) Reload energy, assuming 2 kg of solvent evaporated per kg sorbent per reload: 0.008-0.046 GJ/t CO2. This was computed for methanol; ethanol has a similar latent heat per kg. It is under 1% of real DAC energy (5-10 GJ/t) and at most 10% of the 0.465 GJ/t floor (verifier).

(4) Accelerated ageing works within days: PEI-silica lost about 94% of its capacity within 24 h at 120 C in air with 21% O2 (Thakkar et al. 2024, ACS Omega). Dry-air ageing does not reproduce field degradation, though. In humid TVSA service, CO2-driven urea crosslinking and steam effects on the support act together, and urea-linked PEI is the fraction least likely to wash out. The test therefore includes humid cyclic ageing.
patched_idea.who_gains: S10: DAC buyers and investors get a lower, more predictable cost per delivered tonne. Operators of impregnated-PEI structured-contactor DAC gain. S4: amine and chemical makers sell a recurring consumable. S1 and S8 gain cheaper durable removal, reserved for residual emissions and committed to geologic storage only. S6 and S11 face lower solvent hazard because methanol is replaced by water and ethanol.
patched_idea.who_loses: Sorbent and contactor suppliers whose revenue comes from replacing whole modules. S1 critics who see cheaper DAC as moral hazard. S11, if spent wash (oxidised amine, ethanol) is poorly contained or disposed of.
patched_idea.closest_known_work:
These two citations come from the critic and I have not verified them independently:
- Coralli 2023 published the methanol strip of PEI from silica.
- Li 2026 published re-impregnation of recovered silica at about 90% of fresh capacity, ex situ.

Other related work:
- Thakkar et al. 2024, accelerated PEI-silica degradation (doi 10.1021/acsomega.4c05639).
- Zhao et al. 2025, PEI on layered double hydroxide that resists oxidation (doi 10.1002/advs.202507756).
- Han et al. 2026, epoxide-functionalised amines (Adv. Sci.).
- The antioxidant-additive literature.
- Climeworks' sorbent upgrades at Mammoth. These are a different sorbent class, grafted rather than impregnated.

Before spending on Arm B, a patent search for sorbent refurbishment or in-situ regeneration is needed, covering Global Thermostat/Corning, Climeworks and Svante.
patched_idea.why_different: The strip-and-re-impregnate chemistry has already been published ex situ (Coralli 2023; Li 2026). The novelty claimed here is narrower: stripping with solvent only and re-coating inside an intact structured contactor, over several cycles, with uniform loading and no rise in pressure drop. It is that in-place step that turns a lab recycling route into an operating practice that avoids dismantling. I found no published in-place multi-cycle study for DAC monoliths or laminates. My search was incomplete and the patent search is still outstanding.
patched_idea.family: In-place wash-out and re-impregnation of oxidised amine on DAC sorbent supports

fix.change_summary:
I applied the critic's patch and kept the core mechanism (strip the oxidised amine with solvent and re-impregnate it while keeping the support) and the PSII D1 repair-cycle graft.

- **Target:** moved from Climeworks/Mammoth, whose grafted aminosilane on cellulose cannot be washed out, to impregnated-PEI structured contactors such as Global Thermostat/Corning-type monoliths and laminates.
- **Prior art:** added Coralli 2023 and Li 2026, both ex-situ. I have not verified these two critic-supplied citations myself. The novelty is now restated as solvent-only, in-place, multi-cycle stripping and re-coating inside an intact contactor.
- **Solvent:** replaced methanol with water then ethanol, for S6 and S11 safety.
- **Saving:** the flat 46-54% figure is replaced by a function of recovered capacity r and support reuse count N. I recomputed it with a script that reproduces the critic's numbers (scratchpad/climate/patch_graft_bio_4.py). Example: at a = 0.25, the saving is 48/42/35/26% at r = 1/0.9/0.8/0.7 for N = 5, and 38/31/23/11% for N = 3. Breakeven r ranges from 0.35 to 0.72.
- **Ageing caveat:** dry-air ageing does not reproduce urea crosslinking in humid service.
- **Falsifying test:** the powder-only test is replaced by a two-arm test. Arm A is a Li 2026 powder baseline. Arm B is an in-place flow-cell test on a structured coupon with humid TVSA ageing, sliced axial loading, pressure-drop, BET and wash-nitrogen measurements, and kill criteria derived from the cost model.
- **Patent search:** added a Global Thermostat/Corning, Climeworks and Svante patent search as a gate before Arm B.

idea.title: An AEC-Q100 for carbon removal: semiconductor-style mechanism-matched accelerated qualification of DAC sorbents, gating offtake contracts
idea.one_line: Before any DAC plant is bought from, require a sorbent and contactor qualification report built the way carmakers qualify chips: mechanism-specific highly accelerated stress tests calibrated against field data. Sorbent lifetime alone swings cost by $10-1,100/t, and no field-lifetime data are public.
idea.conventional_core: Solid-amine temperature-vacuum-swing DAC (Climeworks Gen2/Gen3 class, TRL 7-8).
idea.graft: Semiconductor reliability engineering. JEDEC-style stress-test-driven qualification (HAST, temperature-humidity bias, Arrhenius-Peck acceleration models; failure-mechanism-specific per JESD47/JEP122) with a buyer council setting the gate, as the Automotive Electronics Council's AEC-Q100 does for chips (founded by US carmakers in the 1990s; recalled).
idea.mechanism: Stress matrix: temperature 80-120°C, O2 21-100%, RH 0-80%, plus ozone at 100 ppb and SO2/NO2 spikes. Capacity fade is fitted to Arrhenius-Peck models. Acceleration factors are accepted only when the stress degradation-product fingerprint (FTIR carbonyl, imine and urea bands; N loss) matches field-aged samples, the semiconductor 'same failure mechanism' rule. The dominant buyers (Frontier and Microsoft, about 80-90% of DAC demand) then require a qualified lifetime of at least N cycles before prepaying. This prices delivery risk, which the map shows is the binding constraint (Mammoth at 3.75% of nameplate).
idea.target: DAC utilisation and delivery risk, sorbent oxidative degradation, and the map's finding that no public field-lifetime data exist for any commercial DAC sorbent.
idea.quantitative_claims:
My calculations:
- **Sorbent cost per tonne:** C/(0.044 x q x N), where C is sorbent price, q working capacity and N cycles. At q = 1-2 mmol/g and $20-50/kg:
  - N = 1,000: $227-1,136/t
  - N = 5,000: $45-227/t
  - N = 20,000: $11-57/t
  - N = 100,000: $2-11/t
- **Acceleration:** 100->120°C gives 2.7-4.4x at an ASSUMED activation energy of 60-90 kJ/mol. Adding pure O2, if degradation is first-order in O2, gives 13-21x. One week of stress then equals about 3-5 months of 100°C regeneration exposure, so a full qualification fits in 4-8 weeks.
- **Utilisation lever:** capital charge per tonne scales with 0.9/utilisation, which is 24x at Mammoth's 3.75% and 3.3x at Orca's ~27%.
- **Energy:** none. This is a test protocol.
idea.who_gains: S10: buyers and insurers can price and underwrite delivery risk. S1/S2: removal claims become more credible. Robust-sorbent suppliers and DAC developers can differentiate on qualified lifetime. S7: DOE and the EU CRCF can reference a standard. S3: Oxy, Shell/Avnos and others selling DAC get a credible quality signal.
idea.who_loses: Vendors with fragile sorbents are exposed earlier. Startups face 1-2 months of extra qualification time and about $0.1-0.3M of cost. No major industry loses.
idea.closest_known_work: NETL 'Amine Degradation Experiments on a Polymer Supported Molecular Amine DAC Sorbent' (2024, OSTI 2429563). Jones group, ACS AMI 2023 (contributions of CO2/O2/H2O to oxidative stability of solid amine DAC sorbents). Jamdade, Cai & Sholl 2024 (J Phys Chem C, ozonolysis degradation, DFT-based with no field validation). Sayari group oxidation studies. Open DAC 2025 (screening, no lifetime). Climeworks' internal upgrades (unpublished).
idea.why_different: Existing work is per-paper degradation chemistry with no agreed acceleration model and no field calibration. The graft adds two things: a mechanism-matched, field-calibrated acceleration standard, and a buyer-council gate that ties it to money, which is the way semiconductors turned reliability into a purchasing condition.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test: About 6 months for about $50-150k. Take two commercial sorbents (Lewatit VP OC 1065 and a PEI/silica). Run 4-6 stress cells for 1-4 weeks, plus an outdoor real-air TVSA cycling rig for 6 months. The idea is falsified if the fitted Arrhenius-Peck model mispredicts 6-month field capacity fade by more than ±30%, or if the stress-aged FTIR or N-loss fingerprint differs from field-aged material (a mechanism change, so no valid acceleration exists).
idea.family: Mechanism-matched accelerated lifetime qualification of DAC sorbents gating offtake contracts

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: Thakkar, Ruba, Matteson, Dugas, Singh (LANL), 'Accelerated Testing of PEI-Silica Sorbent Pellets for Direct Air Capture', ACS Omega 9(46):45970, 2024
closest.overlap: This is an explicit accelerated-testing protocol for a DAC sorbent, and its stress matrix is nearly the one proposed: regeneration at 80, 100 and 120°C under N2, ambient air (21% O2), and dry or 75% RH CO2, with 100 h runs mapped to cycle equivalents (33/100/100 cycles). It found about 94% degradation within 24 h at 120°C in air. It has no field calibration, no Arrhenius-Peck acceleration factor tied to real-plant fade, and no purchasing role.

closest.title: Si, Yang, Yu, Lei, Zhu, 'Deactivation Kinetics of Polyethylenimine-based Adsorbents Used for the Capture of Low Concentration CO2', ACS Omega, 2019
closest.overlap: This is the Arrhenius part of the idea, already measured. It fits a parallel thermal and oxidative deactivation kinetic model for PEI sorbents: thermal is first-order with Ea about 81 kJ/mol, and O2-induced is second-order with Ea about 74 kJ/mol. Those values fall inside the idea's assumed 60-90 kJ/mol, so its 2.7-4.4x acceleration estimate has a published empirical anchor. The data are lab-only (50-80°C) with no field validation. The second-order O2 dependence also means pure-O2 acceleration would be stronger than the idea's first-order assumption.

closest.title: Muldoon, Sekizkardes, Sorescu, Steckel (NETL), 'Accelerated Aging of a Polymer-Supported Molecular Amine Direct Air Capture Sorbent: Experiments and Theory', 2024 (OSTI 2426375; the brief also cites the related OSTI 2429563)
closest.overlap: Accelerated aging with in situ ATR-FTIR tracking of degradation products while temperature and humidity are varied, plus DFT mechanisms. This is the spectroscopic fingerprinting part of the idea. It reports no acceleration factors and no comparison with field-aged material.

closest.title: Varni, Braunecker, Calegari Andrade et al. (NREL/LLNL and others), 'Understanding and mitigating degradation in amine-based sorbents for CO2 direct air capture', Chem 12(3), 2026 (OSTI 3024224); and Fakhraddinfakhriazar, Molina-Fernandez, Leonard, 'Stability of Adsorbents for DAC: Challenges and Perspectives', Energy & Fuels, 2026
closest.overlap: Two 2026 reviews of DAC sorbent degradation. Both say limited lifetime drives cost and that stability is 'often overlooked'. The Varni review says accelerated testing is 'beginning to illuminate' mechanisms and lists knowledge gaps. Neither abstract proposes a standard, field-calibrated acceleration factors or plant-aged data. They confirm the gap the idea targets rather than filling it.

closest.title: Ozone/NOx, trace-metal and humidity degradation studies: Zorrilla-Valtierra, Lively, Walton et al., Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2026 (ozone and NOx on MOF-supported amines); Kuspangaliyeva, Lively, Jones, ES&T 2025/26 (Cu and Fe at about 4 ppm cause deactivation); Carneiro ... Jones (Georgia Tech with Global Thermostat), Angew. Chem. 2023 (water's role in radical auto-oxidation)
closest.overlap: These cover the rest of the proposed stress matrix (ozone and NOx spikes, humidity) and the mechanism chemistry. The Carneiro paper has an industrial co-author (Global Thermostat), but the results are still lab-only and published one paper at a time, as the idea says.

closest.title: Deep Sky Alpha (Innisfail, Alberta; construction from Aug 2025, now operating) and NCCC's DAC RECO2UP solid-amine field unit (DOE)
closest.overlap: These are real-air field-testing infrastructure. Deep Sky Alpha runs multiple vendors' DAC units side by side, year-round, with standardised instrumentation, and benchmarks their operational data. It could supply the field-aged reference data the idea needs. Its public page does not mention sorbent-lifetime or degradation metrics, any acceleration model, or a qualification gate for buyers.

closest.title: Frontier offtake structure (pay-on-delivery offtakes; low-volume prepurchases for early suppliers) and Kita non-delivery / project-failure insurance for carbon removal
closest.overlap: This is the money side. Buyers and insurers already price delivery risk through supplier diligence, pay-on-delivery contracts and non-delivery insurance, but nothing public ties this to a sorbent qualification test. Caveat: Frontier's large offtakes already pay only on delivery, so a gate 'before prepaying' mainly affects prepurchases and insurer underwriting, not most of the dollars.

closest.title: Cross-industry precedent for the graft: IEC 61215 PV module qualification (damp heat 85°C/85% RH, thermal cycling) with the PVEL/Kiwa PV Module Reliability Scorecard used by lenders for bankability; DOE Hydrogen Program accelerated stress test protocols for PEM fuel cells; lab-vs-pilot degradation correlation for post-combustion amine solvents
closest.overlap: Qualification standards gating finance have already been carried from semiconductors into energy hardware. PV is the closest case: lenders and buyers require accelerated-stress qualification and a scorecard before financing. This is recalled background, not sourced in this search. The template is therefore not new to energy, only absent from DAC sorbents.

art.what_is_new:
Every technical part already exists, mostly for DAC sorbents themselves:
- **Accelerated aging** at 80/100/120°C in air and O2 with humidity (LANL 2024).
- **Arrhenius deactivation kinetics** with Ea of about 74-81 kJ/mol (Si 2019).
- **FTIR degradation fingerprinting** (NETL 2024).
- **Ozone, NOx and trace-metal stress studies** (Lively, Walton and Jones groups, 2023-26).
- **Real-air side-by-side field testing** (Deep Sky Alpha, NCCC).
- **Buyer and insurer mechanisms for delivery risk** (Frontier pay-on-delivery offtakes and prepurchases; Kita non-delivery insurance).

The graft template, an accelerated-stress qualification standard that gates financing, is also established in energy through IEC 61215 and the PVEL scorecard for PV and DOE's fuel-cell accelerated stress tests. That point is recalled background, not sourced in this search.

Three things appear new; no precedent turned up in this search:
1. **A field-calibrated acceleration standard for DAC sorbents.** Stress-test fade would be checked against plant-aged or outdoor-aged material, with a "same failure mechanism" rule based on matching degradation-product fingerprints. None of the lab studies or reviews found reports a comparison with field-aged sorbent, and the 2026 reviews (Varni et al., Chem; Fakhraddinfakhriazar et al., Energy & Fuels) present accelerated testing as still emerging.
2. **A standards-body or buyer-council qualification**, in the AEC-Q100 mould, specific to DAC sorbents and contactors.
3. **Making qualified lifetime a condition of offtake, prepurchase or insurance.**

Caveats that affect value rather than novelty:
- **Prepayment gate.** Frontier's large offtakes already pay on delivery, so a gate before prepaying would mostly bind prepurchases and insurers.
- **Pure-O2 acceleration.** Si 2019 measured second-order O2 kinetics, so pure-O2 acceleration may be larger than the idea's first-order estimate and more prone to changing the failure mechanism. That raises the stakes on the fingerprint-matching rule.
- **Search coverage.** The web-search budget had run out, so this search used Crossref, Europe PMC, OSTI and direct page fetches. Patent databases, ISO/TC 265 work items and DOE prize or test-centre protocol documents were not checked directly, and an unpublished industry or DOE standard effort may exist.

phys.assumptions:
Nature of the idea: it is a test protocol plus a buyer-side purchasing gate, and it removes 0 t of CO2 itself. The cost and energy figures reported here are for the solid-amine TVSA direct air capture (DAC) it gates, taken from the script's levelised-cost model. The protocol's own incremental cost is reported separately.

**Thermodynamic floor:** air at 420 ppm, 75% capture, 99% purity gives 20.47 kJ/mol = 0.465 GJ/t (129 kWh/t). Real plants at 5/7/10 GJ/t run at a second-law efficiency of 9.3/6.6/4.7%.

**Sorbent arithmetic.** The claim's formula C/(0.044·q·N) reproduces exactly: $227-1,136/t at N=1,000; $45-227 at 5k; $11-57 at 20k; $2-11 at 100k.
- I flag the claimed working capacity q=1-2 mmol/g as optimistic. Humid 400 ppm cyclic capacity of 0.5-1.5 mmol/g is the assumed literature range.
- With the wider range (q 0.5-2, C $10-50/kg), N=1k gives $114-2,272/t.
- Cycle length is assumed at 2-6 h at 90% uptime. On that basis N=5,000 is 1.3-3.8 years of operation and N=20,000 is 5.1-15.2 years.

**Acceleration claims.** Both reproduce, given the assumed activation energy (Ea) of 60-90 kJ/mol and degradation first-order in O2.
- 100 to 120°C gives 2.67-4.37x.
- Adding pure O2 gives 12.7-20.8x.
- One week of stress then equals 2.9-4.8 months at 100°C in air. The claim said 3-5 months.

**Levelised cost of DAC model (all inputs assumed ranges spanning the literature).**
- Capex: $1,000/2,500/5,000 per t/yr. That spans modelled NOAK (~$0.7-1.5k) to the FOAK cost implied by public Climeworks/1PointFive figures (reported, not audited).
- Finance: discount rate 6/8/10% over 25/20/15 years.
- Utilisation: 0.9/0.8/0.6.
- Heat: 4.5/6/8 GJ/t at $4/8/12 per GJ.
- Electricity: 0.35/0.5/0.8 MWh/t at $40/70/100 per MWh.
- Sorbent: $10/30/50 per kg, q 1.5/1.0/0.7, N 20k/5k/1k.
- O&M: 3/4/5% of capex per year.

The results are:

| Case | Capital | O&M | Energy | Sorbent | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Low | 87 | 33 | 32 | 8 | $160/t |
| Base | 318 | 125 | 83 | 136 | $663/t |
| High | 1,096 | 417 | 176 | 1,623 | $3,311/t |

These are gross figures with no LCA penalty. Realized 2024-25 contract prices are roughly $400-1,000+/t (reported).

**Sorbent lifetime lever in the base case:**

| N (cycles) | Total | Sorbent share |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | $1,208/t | 56% |
| 5,000 | $663/t | 21% |
| 20,000 | $560/t | 6% |
| 100,000 | $533/t | 1% |

**Utilisation lever in the base case (capital + O&M only):** $9,457/t at u=0.0375, $1,313/t at u=0.27 and $394/t at u=0.9. The claimed 0.9/u ratios of 24x and 3.33x are arithmetically correct.

**The protocol's own cost.** A qualification of $0.15-0.6M amortised over 1 Mt to 10 kt of a vendor's deliveries comes to $0.15-60/t. A standards body at $2-5M/yr over a DAC market of 10 to 0.1 Mt/yr adds $0.2-50/t. In today's kt-scale market the overhead per tonne is high.

**Scale (assumed).** For DAC that this gate enables by about 2035, I assumed 0.001-0.05 Gt/yr and used 0.01 Gt/yr as the base. At 6 GJ/t that is 0.06 EJ/yr = 0.010% of world primary energy. At 1 Gt/yr it would be 6 EJ = 0.968%.

**Prior art.** NETL's 2024 OSTI 2429563 record is confirmed only as a conference summary stating that DAC cost is sensitive to sorbent lifetime. It discloses no rates.
phys.violations:
There are no physics violations. Nothing goes below the 0.465 GJ/t floor, and the protocol itself uses roughly zero energy. All of the idea's stated arithmetic reproduces.

Some assumptions are heroic, or rest on an unverified premise:

1. **The field baseline is probably wrong.** The claim treats the field case as 100°C regeneration in air. But Climeworks-class TVSA desorbs under vacuum or steam with little O2, and most of the cycle is spent at ambient temperature.
   - Assumption used to test this: the sorbent is hot for 15-30% of the cycle, with 0.1-1.05% absolute O2 while hot.
   - On that basis, the 120°C, 100% O2 stress cell runs 735x to 22,805x faster than the field, not 13-21x.
   - 4-8 weeks of stress would then represent 56 to 3,496 plant-years. This is an extrapolation across a gap of more than 100x, where a change of mechanism is likely.
   - Air ingress at hot/cold transitions probably dominates real oxidation, and no data on it are public.
2. **Extrapolation needs very tight activation-energy knowledge.** A ±30% prediction requires Ea known to:
   - ±16.0 kJ/mol for the 120 to 100°C extrapolation;
   - ±2.7 kJ/mol for 120 to 25°C.
   - Ea uncertainty of 60-90 kJ/mol alone spreads the 120 to 25°C acceleration factor from 347 to 6,456 (18.6x).
3. **The Peck humidity term may have the wrong sign.** For amines, water generally suppresses urea formation. The semiconductor model form cannot be imported; it has to be fitted.
4. **Claimed working capacity q=1-2 mmol/g is optimistic.** About 0.5-1.5 mmol/g is more realistic.
5. **Utilisation premise is unverified.** The claim that Mammoth runs at 3.75% of nameplate is reported, not verified. More importantly, there is no evidence that sorbent fade causes the under-delivery; commissioning, engineering and energy supply are the more likely causes. The gate addresses only one of these causes.
phys.resource_needs:
**The protocol itself:**
- 4-6 stress cells, FTIR and elemental N analysis, and one outdoor real-air TVSA rig.
- About $50-150k per falsification test, and $0.1-0.3M per vendor qualification (the idea's own figures).
- A standards or buyer-council body, assumed at $2-5M/yr.
- Negligible energy, land and water.

**The DAC it gates, at the 0.01 Gt/yr base:**
- 0.06 EJ/yr, which is 0.010% of world primary energy (at 6 GJ/t, mostly heat at about 100°C).
- About 0.05 Mt/yr of replacement sorbent at N=5,000 and q=1.0.

**At 1 Gt/yr:**
- 6 EJ, or 0.968% of world primary energy.
- Sorbent replacement of 4.54 Mt/yr at N=5k, or 1.14 Mt/yr at N=20k. At that scale amine supply is material, and the lifetime the standard certifies becomes a materials-supply lever.
- Land: an assumed ~0.1-1 km2 per Mt/yr.
- Water: site-dependent and unknown; humid TVSA can be a net producer or a net consumer.
phys.key_uncertainties:
1. **Whether stress-aged and field-aged sorbent share a degradation mechanism.** This is the idea's own falsifier. It is now the central test, because the true acceleration gap is 10^2 to 10^4, not about 20x. Oxidation under 100% O2 may switch to a different radical-chain pathway.
2. **Real O2 exposure during the hot step and at hot/cold transitions in commercial plants.** These are proprietary, and they set the field degradation rate.
3. **Activation energy and O2 reaction order for commercial sorbents.** The Ea of 60-90 kJ/mol was assumed, not measured. The protocol's ±30% target needs Ea to within about ±3 kJ/mol if it extrapolates to ambient temperature.
4. **Non-chemical failure modes the matrix does not cover:** contactor fouling, attrition, PEI leaching or pore collapse under steam, and dust.
5. **Whether sorbent fade drives the low utilisation at Mammoth and Orca at all.** The 3.75% and 27% figures are reported and unverified. If commissioning and engineering are the cause, the utilisation lever (24x) cannot be attributed to this idea.
6. **Buyer-council feasibility.** The 80-90% demand concentration (Frontier and Microsoft) is the idea's claim and unverified here. Buyers may also prefer to use delivery-contingent payment rather than a qualification gate. That is a simpler baseline that already prices delivery risk.
7. **Field-lifetime data.** None are public, so the base N=5,000 is an assumption. In the base case, sorbent is $136/t of the $663/t total. The lifetime lever matters strongly only if the true N is below about 5k; at N≥20k it is 6% or less of the cost.
8. **Search coverage.** My web search budget was exhausted, so I could not check existing ASTM or ISO DAC sorbent test-method efforts, or Climeworks Gen3 durability claims, as prior art.

stances.evidence: Climate Action Network (Jan 2021 position, 1,300+ NGOs) says DACCS has 'no place' in scenarios built on early, steep cuts, and will not support negative emissions or offsets 'as an alternative to stringent emission reductions'. That makes CAN-aligned groups at best neutral toward anything that helps sell DAC tonnes. The idea, though, adds no subsidy, no EOR and no new offset category. It is an integrity measure that exposes underperformance, which is the critics' own complaint. In May 2025 Heimildin reported that Mammoth captured 105 t in its first 10 months, per verifier Puro.Earth, and quoted critics calling Climeworks' operations scam-like (saved notes, scratchpad/climate/frontier/h.txt). CDR-quality NGOs (the Carbon180/CATF type; specific positions not re-verified this session) would likely back a public performance standard. The Wikipedia DAC article's section on environmentalist opposition records the view that DAC sustains the emitters.
stances.red_line_hit: Indirect only: it is infrastructure for a removal/offset market (CAN red line 4, mitigation deterrence). It does not touch the EOR, public-subsidy or BECCS land red lines.

stances.evidence: The closest prior work is S2's own: NETL's 2024 amine-degradation experiments (OSTI 2429563), the Jones group in ACS AMI 2023, Jamdade/Cai/Sholl 2024 and the Sayari group. IPCC AR6 WGIII treats CDR as needed for residual emissions, and a measured-lifetime standard matches the field's preference for executed data over modelled claims. Dissent: Mark Jacobson-type critics, quoted in Heimildin 2025, say carbon capture delays the transition. That objection is to DAC itself, not to testing it. Confound for S2 to flag: no public evidence yet shows that sorbent degradation causes DAC delivery shortfalls. My calculation: Mammoth's 105 t is 0.35% of 10-month nameplate and still only 1.1-2.1% of the 12-24 machines then installed, and the cause is unpublished.
stances.red_line_hit: None. S2 would object if acceleration factors were accepted without field calibration, and the idea's own falsification test addresses that.

stances.evidence: Low stakes. Occidental/1PointFive's Stratos uses Carbon Engineering's liquid KOH solvent and calciner, not solid amine, so a solid-amine sorbent standard would not cover its main DAC asset unless widened to solvents. Shell/Avnos and others selling DAC would gain a quality signal. S3's documented interests are 45Q ($180/t DAC, with EOR parity after OBBBA 2025) and EOR offtake, and the idea leaves both alone. S3 would turn negative only if the standard became a condition for 45Q DAC credits, which the idea does not propose.
stances.red_line_hit: None. A regulatory mandate tied to 45Q eligibility would become one, as an added compliance cost.

stances.evidence: Steel and cement are unaffected. The chemicals sub-sector may gain: Lanxess makes the Lewatit VP OC 1065 benchmark sorbent named in the falsifying test, and robust-sorbent makers could compete on qualified lifetime. AEC-Q100 is the precedent: it became a purchasing condition that suppliers able to meet it used as a selling point (recalled, not re-verified). S4's documented priorities (CBAM protection, CCfDs, energy prices; VCI called CCfDs 'no panacea') are not touched.
stances.red_line_hit: None

stances.evidence: No documented utility position on DAC sorbent testing. Utilities are affected only indirectly, as power and heat suppliers to DAC plants. At Mammoth, Climeworks' CEO cited 5,000-6,000 kWh/t (Nikkei, via Heimildin 2025), so higher DAC utilisation would mean more electricity sales. The idea itself uses no energy.
stances.red_line_hit: None

stances.evidence: No job effect at plant scale.
