Unions in the Carbon Capture Coalition (70+ companies, unions and NGOs) back carbon-management deployment and independent-engineer certification for 45Q integrity (CCC statement on the 45Q safe-harbour extension). A 1-2 month qualification delay at startups is immaterial to employment. A gate that filters out fragile projects could marginally slow DAC-hub build-out, but it could also prevent stranded-hub layoffs.
stances.red_line_hit: None

stances.evidence: Governments bear capex risk on DAC through grants (the US DOE DAC hubs under the 2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law; reported 2025 cancellations not re-verified this session), while 45Q pays per stored tonne and so leaves delivery risk with developers. A referenceable lifetime standard protects grant money and could feed the EU CRCF DACCS certification methodologies. Isometric DAC protocol v1.3 already counts sorbent replacement as embodied emissions, but it does not require lifetime testing. It asks for re-testing only when sorbent formulations or operating conditions change substantially (registry.isometric.com, fetched 2026-10-05), so there is a gap a government standard could fill. Salience is low.
stances.red_line_hit: None. Caution: a buyer council in which Frontier and Microsoft jointly set purchase conditions may draw competition-law scrutiny (an AEC-type standards body would need antitrust structuring).

stances.evidence: Baum et al. 2024 (N=30,284, 30 countries) found Global South publics more supportive of every climate technology, but both North and South rated engineered CDR (DACCS) the highest moral-hazard risk. A qualification gate set by a Northern buyer council echoes S8's documented objection to CBAM as unilateral standard-setting (India and South Africa; documented in the map, not re-verified). The $0.1-0.3M qualification cost could fall hardest on Global South DAC startups. Climate-justice groups' DAC 'false solution' framing applies to DAC itself, not to its testing.
stances.red_line_hit: Possible: a Northern-set technical barrier to market entry (CBAM-like). It is avoidable with open protocols and subsidised test access.

stances.evidence: No consumer price effect: this is a voluntary-market purchasing condition, not a tax or levy, and it avoids the visible-consumer-price trap documented in Canada (consumer fuel charge removed 1 Apr 2025). The roughly 21,000 Climeworks retail subscribers reported by Heimildin 2025 are consumers who benefit from verified delivery. Andre et al. 2024 found 69% of 129,902 people willing to give 1% of income, which suggests demand for credible removal, but that finding is not specific to this idea.
stances.red_line_hit: None

stances.evidence: Buyers and insurers are the main beneficiaries. cdr.fyi (data to about Aug 2026) shows 50.5 Mt durable CDR contracted against 1.7 Mt delivered (3.4%); the gap is partly confounded because most contracts are for future years. Frontier already uses 60+ technical reviewers. Its offtakes are paid 'if and when delivered', so delivery risk on offtakes already sits with suppliers, and the gate adds most value for prepurchases, project lenders and delivery insurers that need loss data. Heimildin 2025 reports that a third of Mammoth's 25-year credits were pre-sold and that Climeworks wrote down Orca by $1.4M in 2023. That is exactly the exposure a qualified-lifetime metric prices. The idea's claim that Frontier and Microsoft hold 80-90% of DAC demand is unverified.
stances.red_line_hit: None. Possible antitrust exposure for a coordinated buyer gate.

stances.evidence: Communities near DAC sites have documented air-quality concerns and a sense of being 'experimented on' (Wikipedia, Direct air capture: environmentalist opposition, citing Batres et al. and Blaeser). The idea's degradation fingerprint (amine N-loss, imine/urea and degradation products) could double as a characterisation of local emissions. That would fit Isometric v1.3's environmental-safeguarding re-testing requirement and could win S11 support if results were public. The idea says nothing about siting, which is S11's main issue.
stances.red_line_hit: None. Siting and local safety are left unaddressed rather than worsened.

stake.coalition_notes: This idea has low salience and low conflict. No group's documented red line is hit directly: there is no EOR, no new subsidy, no consumer price and no land use. S10 and S2 support it, S7 supports it at low salience, and S3/S4/S5/S6/S9 are neutral because their documented interests (45Q, CBAM, CCfDs, energy prices) are untouched. The only real split is S1. The idea inherits DAC's mitigation-deterrence baggage (CAN: DACCS has 'no place'; Baum 2024: engineered CDR is rated the highest moral-hazard risk in both North and South), but it is also an integrity measure that answers the critics' own complaint, Mammoth's 105 t in its first 10 months (Puro.Earth via Heimildin, May 2025). That gives it a rare critic-plus-buyer overlap. Four caveats limit its coalition value. (1) Premise: there is no public evidence that sorbent degradation drives the delivery shortfall. By my calculation, Mammoth reached only 1.1-2.1% even of its installed machines, with the cause unpublished, so commissioning or engineering issues are an uncontrolled confound. (2) Frontier offtakes already pay only on delivery, so the gate matters mainly for prepurchases, lenders, insurers and DOE grant capex, not offtakes. (3) Scope: Oxy's Stratos uses a liquid KOH solvent, so a solid-amine standard misses the largest S3 DAC asset unless it is widened to solvents and contactors. (4) A buyer council that jointly gates purchases needs antitrust structuring, and an open protocol with subsidised test access would head off an S8 objection to Northern standard-setting. Ways to win S1 and S11: publish qualification results and degradation-emission fingerprints openly, and keep the standard decoupled from offset claims. The burden on suppliers is small: amortised over 10 years at a 36 kt/yr plant, qualification costs $0.3-0.9/t at 90% utilisation and $7-22/t at Mammoth-like 3.75% (script: scratchpad/climate/aecq_stakeholder_calc.py). The web search budget was exhausted this session, so several positions rely on the map, saved notes and three fetches (cdr.fyi, frontierclimate.com, the Isometric DAC v1.3 protocol, the Carbon Capture Coalition 45Q statement), and I could not re-verify them.

critic.fatal_flaw: No fatal flaw. The idea is a test protocol, so it cannot breach the 0.465 GJ/t separation floor, and no stakeholder red line is hit that cannot be designed around. The S8 risk of Northern-set standards and the antitrust risk of a buyer council are both structural choices that can be changed. The value case is weaker than pitched, though, for two reasons. First, there is no public evidence that sorbent fade causes the shortfall at Mammoth, so the 24x utilisation lever cannot be credited to this idea. Second, Frontier offtakes already pay only on delivery, so a gate "before prepaying" binds only prepurchases, lenders, insurers and DOE grant capex. Both points shrink the idea's impact; neither breaks it.
critic.top_fixable_flaw:
The calibration step, which is the core of the "same mechanism, field-calibrated" graft, cannot work as specified. There are two separate problems.

(1) The stress-to-field gap is 10^2-10^4x, not 13-21x. TVSA desorbs at low O2, and the sorbent is hot for only 15-30% of each cycle. Extrapolating that far needs the activation energy known to about ±3 kJ/mol. A 120°C, pure-O2 cell is also the condition most likely to switch the degradation mechanism, because Si 2019 found O2 kinetics are second-order.

(2) The proposed 6-month outdoor rig cannot measure field fade precisely enough to test a ±30% prediction. My script (scratchpad/climate/critic_aecq.py) defines end-of-life as 20% capacity loss at N cycles and assumes 90% uptime. On that basis, 6 months is 657-1,971 cycles, so field fade is only:
- 2.6-7.9% at N = 5,000
- 0.7-2.0% at N = 20,000

With capacity-measurement repeatability of ±2-3% (an assumed figure), the 1-sigma relative error on that fade is:
- 36-161% at N = 5,000
- 144-646% at N = 20,000

The falsification test therefore cannot pass or fail for exactly the sorbents that matter: those with N of at least 5,000, where sorbent cost is 21% or less of $/t. It only resolves for sorbents with N around 1,000 or fewer, which would fail the gate anyway.
critic.suggested_patch:
Swap the borrowed AEC-Q absolute-lifetime extrapolation for an approach in three parts. Two come from the same reliability toolkit; the third is an O&G import.

(a) **Field coupons.** Install sacrificial sorbent coupons inside operating contactors, the way corrosion coupons sit in oil and gas pipelines. Candidate sites are Deep Sky Alpha's multi-vendor site, NCCC and vendors' own plants. Pull coupons at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months. Each pulled coupon gets two measurements:
- FTIR (carbonyl, imine and urea bands) and elemental nitrogen loss, which detect chemical change far more precisely than a 1-8% capacity difference;
- equilibrium capacity on a TGA under one fixed protocol.
This gives field-aged reference material at kilotonne scale, with no extra rig to build.

(b) **Stress conditions bounded to the plant.** Run stress tests at the plant's own hot-step O2 partial pressure, set by measuring air ingress during desorption and at the hot/cold transitions. Use step-stress at 100, 110 and 120°C. Do not use pure O2. Cap the accepted acceleration factor at about 50x. Above that cap, report a qualified lower bound on lifetime rather than an extrapolated N.

(c) **A gate that ranks rather than certifies, tied to the money that is actually exposed.** The gate output should be a relative ranking of sorbents within a matched mechanism, plus a lower-bound N. It should not certify an absolute lifetime.
- Tie it to delivery-insurance pricing (for example Kita), lender covenants, DOE/EU grant milestones and Frontier prepurchases only. Leave it off pay-on-delivery offtakes, which already price delivery risk.
- Publish the protocol and all coupon data openly through a neutral standards body (ASTM or ISO TC 265), not a Frontier/Microsoft buyer council. This removes the antitrust exposure and the S8 objection, and it gives S1 and S11 their transparency.

**Revised falsifier, at about the same cost of $50-150k:** the stress model's predicted ratio of 6-month to 12-month fingerprint growth must match the coupon data within ±30%, and the rank order of the two sorbents must be preserved.

patched_idea.title: An AEC-Q100 for carbon removal: semiconductor-style, mechanism-matched, coupon-calibrated qualification of DAC sorbents that gates delivery-risk money
patched_idea.one_line: Before lenders, insurers, grant programmes or prepurchasers put money into a DAC plant, require a sorbent qualification report built the way carmakers qualify chips. It would use mechanism-matched step-stress tests run at the plant's own oxygen conditions, calibrated against sorbent coupons aged inside operating contactors. Sorbent lifetime alone swings sorbent cost from $2 to $1,136/t, and no field-lifetime data are public.
patched_idea.conventional_core: Solid-amine temperature-vacuum-swing DAC (Climeworks Gen2/Gen3 class, TRL 7-8). Unchanged.
patched_idea.graft:
Semiconductor reliability engineering, unchanged as the single import. It brings three practices:
- JEDEC-style qualification that is specific to each failure mechanism (JESD47/JEP122): HAST, temperature-humidity bias, Arrhenius-Peck acceleration models, and the rule that an acceleration factor is valid only if the stress produces the same failure mechanism as the field.
- The reliability toolkit's own controls on extrapolation: step-stress testing, capped acceleration factors, and lower-bound lifetime claims when extrapolation runs out.
- Calibration against field-returned and in-situ monitored parts.
The governance pattern is still AEC-Q100: a document drafted by the buyers and published openly, which purchasers then cite. The physical way of getting in-situ field samples copies corrosion coupons in oil and gas pipelines. That is a hardware precedent for the calibration step, not a second imported mechanism.
patched_idea.mechanism:
1. **Stress matrix, bounded to the plant (patched).** Step-stress at 100, 110 and 120°C. O2 is held at the plant's measured hot-step O2 partial pressure, set by measuring air ingress during desorption and at the hot/cold transitions, never pure O2. RH runs 0-80%, with ozone at about 100 ppb and SO2/NO2 spikes as separate cells. Acceleration comes from (a) temperature, through Arrhenius-Peck fits, and (b) duty-cycle compression, because the stress cell stays hot all the time while the plant sorbent is hot for only 15-30% of each cycle. The accepted total acceleration factor is capped at about 50x. Beyond the cap, the report states a qualified lower bound on N rather than an extrapolated N.

2. **Same-mechanism rule (kept).** An acceleration factor counts only if the stress degradation-product fingerprint matches field-aged material. The fingerprint is FTIR carbonyl, imine and urea bands plus elemental N loss.

3. **Field calibration by in-situ coupons (patched; replaces the outdoor rig).** Sacrificial sorbent coupons go inside operating contactors. Candidate sites are Deep Sky Alpha's multi-vendor site, NCCC and vendors' own plants. Coupons are pulled at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months. Each pulled coupon gets two measurements:
   - FTIR plus N loss, the primary and more precise signal;
   - TGA equilibrium capacity under one fixed protocol, as a secondary signal.
   The plant's logged temperature and O2 histories are fed into the stress model. Its predicted absolute fingerprint growth is then compared with the coupons. Coupons also catch oxidation during cold, ambient-air adsorption steps, which step-stress cannot compress.

4. **Gate output (patched).** The output is a rank order of sorbents within a matched mechanism, plus a lower-bound N. It is not an absolute lifetime certificate.

5. **Who uses the gate (patched).** The gate binds only the money actually exposed to delivery risk:
   - delivery-insurance pricing (for example Kita);
   - lender covenants;
   - DOE and EU grant milestones;
   - Frontier/Microsoft prepurchases.
   It does not bind pay-on-delivery offtakes, which already price delivery risk.

6. **Governance (patched).** A buyer, insurer and developer working group drafts the protocol inside a neutral standards body (ASTM, or ISO TC 265), as AEC-Q100 is drafted by buyers but published openly. The protocol and the coupon data for each qualified product are published openly.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
My calculations (scratchpad/climate/patch_aecq.py; critic's critic_aecq.py). End-of-life is defined as 20% capacity loss at N cycles, with 90% uptime.

- **Sorbent cost per tonne (unchanged):** C/(0.044 x q x N), at working capacity q = 1-2 mmol/g and sorbent price $20-50/kg:
  - N = 1,000: $227-1,136/t
  - N = 5,000: $45-227/t
  - N = 20,000: $11-57/t
  - N = 100,000: $2-11/t

- **Acceleration (corrected):**
  - Thermal only, 100->120°C at the plant's O2 level: 2.7-4.4x at an ASSUMED activation energy of 60-90 kJ/mol (1.7-2.1x for 100->110°C).
  - Duty-cycle compression (hot fraction 15-30%): 3.3-6.7x.
  - Combined: about 9-29x, inside the 50x cap. The earlier 13-21x pure-O2 factor is withdrawn, because O2 kinetics may be second-order and pure O2 risks switching the degradation mechanism.

- **Qualification time:** A full-life demonstration fits in 12 weeks or less only for N of about 5,000 with short cycles (2-12 weeks of stress across the cases).
  - At N = 20,000, 8-80 weeks of stress would be needed (plant life 5-15 years at 2-6 h cycles), so in most cases the report gives a lower bound on N.
  - The earlier claim that a full qualification fits in 4-8 weeks is withdrawn.

- **Coupon resolution at 12 months:** The ASSUMED precision is ±2.5% absolute for capacity and ±0.3% of amine N for N loss and FTIR.
  - Field fade is 1.3-15.8%.
  - The 1-sigma relative error on fade is 22-269% from capacity but 3-32% from N loss and FTIR.
  - Only the chemical fingerprint can test a ±30% prediction for sorbents with N of at least 5,000.

- **Falsifier design:** The ratio of 6-month to 12-month growth is about 0.50 for linear kinetics, 0.71 for diffusion-limited (t^0.5) and 0.25 for autocatalytic (t^2). The ratio therefore checks the model's time dependence, but a model that is linear in time passes it automatically. So the absolute predicted growth must also be tested.

- **Utilisation:** Capital charge scales with 0.9/utilisation, which is 24x at Mammoth's 3.75% and 3.3x at Orca's ~27%. This is context only and is NOT credited to this idea.

- **Energy:** none. This is a test protocol.
patched_idea.who_gains:
- **S10 (investors and insurers):** lenders, insurers and prepurchasers can price delivery risk using an open, field-calibrated lower bound on lifetime.
- **S1/S2 (activists and scientists):** removal claims rest on public coupon data, not vendor assertions.
- **S11 (local communities):** the published data give them transparency on plant performance.
- **S8 (Global South):** the standard is set by a neutral standards body that any country or developer can join, not a Northern buyer cartel.
- **S7 (governments):** DOE grant milestones and the EU CRCF can reference an ASTM/ISO standard.
- **S3 (oil and gas):** DAC sellers such as Oxy and Shell/Avnos get a credible quality signal.
- **Suppliers:** robust-sorbent suppliers can differentiate on qualified lifetime.
patched_idea.who_loses:
- **Vendors with fragile sorbents** are exposed earlier.
- **Developers** must host coupons and disclose degradation data, a cost in confidentiality.
- **Startups** face 2-12 weeks of stress testing and about $0.1-0.3M of cost. A lower-bound N, not a full lifetime, may initially raise their cost of capital.
- No major industry loses. Pay-on-delivery offtakes are untouched.
patched_idea.closest_known_work:
Degradation chemistry:
- NETL, 'Amine Degradation Experiments on a Polymer Supported Molecular Amine DAC Sorbent' (2024, OSTI 2429563).
- Jones group, ACS AMI 2023 (contributions of CO2, O2 and H2O to oxidative stability of solid amine DAC sorbents).
- Jamdade, Cai & Sholl 2024 (J Phys Chem C; DFT ozonolysis, no field validation).
- Sayari group and Si 2019 oxidation-kinetics studies.
- Open DAC 2025 (screening, no lifetime).
- Climeworks' internal upgrades (unpublished).

Precedents for the patch:
- corrosion-coupon monitoring in oil and gas pipelines;
- JEDEC step-stress and field-return calibration practice;
- carbon-removal delivery insurance (for example Kita).

fix.change_summary:
I applied the critic's three-part patch and kept the core (solid-amine TVSA DAC) and the single graft (JEDEC/AEC-Q mechanism-matched reliability qualification).

**(1) Stress conditions.** Stress tests now run as 100/110/120°C step-stress at the plant's measured hot-step O2 partial pressure. Pure O2 is dropped, and accepted acceleration is capped at about 50x, with a lower bound on N reported beyond the cap. My recalculation (scratchpad/climate/patch_aecq.py) gives:
- **Acceleration:** about 9-29x in total (2.7-4.4x thermal times 3.3-6.7x duty-cycle compression), replacing the withdrawn 13-21x pure-O2 figure.
- **Full-life demonstration:** fits in 12 weeks only for N of about 5,000. At N = 20,000 it would need 8-80 weeks, so the claim that qualification takes 4-8 weeks is withdrawn and the lower-bound output is required.

**(2) Field calibration.** The 6-month outdoor rig is replaced by in-situ sorbent coupons in operating contactors, pulled at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months. I framed this as the reliability toolkit's own field-return and in-situ monitoring practice, with oil and gas corrosion coupons as the hardware precedent, so it does not add a second graft. N loss and FTIR become the primary signal. At assumed precisions, their 12-month relative error is 3-32%, against 22-269% for capacity.

**(3) Gate.** The gate now outputs a rank order plus a lower-bound N, not a certified lifetime. It is tied to prepurchases, debt, insurance and grants, not to pay-on-delivery offtakes, and it is published through ASTM/ISO TC 265 instead of a Frontier/Microsoft council. That keeps the AEC-Q pattern of buyer-drafted, openly published standards while removing the antitrust and S8 problems.

**Utilisation claim.** The 24x Mammoth lever is relabelled as context and not credited to the idea.

**One fix beyond the critic.** The critic's ratio-only falsifier is passed automatically by any model that is linear in time (ratio 0.50). So the falsifier now also requires the absolute predicted fingerprint growth to match the coupons within ±30%. The test now runs for 12 months rather than 6.

The mechanism's core logic (stress, same-mechanism fingerprint rule, field calibration, gate on money) is unchanged. The changes are bounds on its parameters and on whom it gates, so mechanism_changed is false.

idea.title: Forced-aeration of ultramafic tailings with the mine's own power-station exhaust (heap-leach practice)
idea.one_line: Build brucite-bearing nickel tailings into agglomerated, aerated heaps, as copper bioleach heaps are built, and blow the mine's gas-engine or turbine exhaust (about 5% CO2) through them. This removes the CO2-supply limit that holds passive carbonation at Mt Keith to about 11% of mine emissions.
idea.conventional_core: Passive carbonation of ultramafic tailings (Mt Keith: about 39.8 kt CO2/yr, 11% of the mine's emissions; measured by Wilson et al. 2014).
idea.graft: From mining hydrometallurgy: heap-leach construction. Fines are agglomerated for permeability, stacked in lifts, aerated from below with low-pressure blowers through perforated pipe (an ASTM F2987 heap-leach aeration specification exists), and drip-irrigated to control moisture.
idea.mechanism: Fresh tailings with brucite (Mg(OH)2) are agglomerated and stacked 6-10 m high over aeration pipe. Exhaust from the mine power station (about 5% CO2, cooled) is blown through the stack, and drip irrigation keeps the pores moist without flooding them. CO2 reacts with brucite to form hydromagnesite and nesquehonite. Passive tests show the reaction is limited by CO2 supply (Energy Procedia 2017: CO2 diffusion slower than reaction). Treated exhaust leaves through the top of the heap. The result is a permanent mineral store of the mine's own fossil CO2. This is an emissions reduction, not a removal.
idea.target: Mine-site Scope 1 CO2, through mineral storage in tailings at nickel, chrysotile, diamond and PGM mines.
idea.quantitative_claims: (a) Capacity, my stoichiometry with an assumed 11 Mt/yr of tailings and 0.5-3 wt% brucite: full brucite carbonation stores 33-199 kt CO2/yr. That is 9-55% of an approximately 360 kt/yr mine, against the 11% achieved passively. (b) Gas-phase delivery is necessary, because dissolved delivery fails on water. Carbonated water at pCO2 0.05 atm holds 0.07 g/L, which needs 1,337 Mm3 of water per 100 kt CO2. At 1 atm pure CO2 it still needs 67 Mm3. (c) Blower work, my Darcy calculation for 100 kt/yr over a 2 km2 pad 8 m high with 5% CO2 and 30-60% uptake. Permeability of 1e-11 m2 gives 0.013-0.05 GJ/t. 1e-12 m2 gives 0.13-0.52 GJ/t. 1e-13 m2 (silty, unagglomerated) gives 1.3-5.2 GJ/t, which is unworkable, so agglomeration is required. Air-fed aeration (420 ppm) would cost 27-27,000 GJ/t, far above the DAC fan figure of 0.29 GJ/t at 100 Pa. The graft only works with a concentrated source. (d) Removal versus reduction: the CO2 is fossil from the power station, so it is reduction. Background atmospheric carbonation continues on the heap surfaces.
idea.who_gains: S4: miners (BHP Nickel West-type, Anglo, chrysotile and diamond operators) cut Scope 1 by tens of percent with equipment they already know. S11: carbonate cementation stabilises tailings and reduces dust, and possibly lowers the risk of tailings-dam failure. S1: permanent mineral storage with no pipeline or injection well. S7: Western Australia and Canada can claim a 'carbon-neutral mine' story.
idea.who_loses: Few. S10 and S4 take on blower and agglomeration opex (binder cost is unquantified here). S6: neutral. MRV across heterogeneous tailings is hard, which is a risk for S1/S2 trust if the tonnes are sold as credits. Projects should claim Scope 1 reduction, not credits, until this is resolved.
idea.closest_known_work: Harrison, Power & Dipple, 'Accelerated carbonation of brucite in mine tailings for carbon sequestration', ES&T 2013 (doi 10.1021/es3012854). This was a bench study with CO2-enriched gas; I did not retrieve the rate numbers this run. Wilson et al. 2014 (Mt Keith, passive). Energy Procedia 2017 (supply-limited, watering frequency matters). The map mentions BHP and Anglo American accelerated-carbonation trials with Isometric, and Arca's tailings-tilling approach (my recollection, unverified).
idea.why_different: The prior work shows the chemistry at bench scale and the supply limit in the field. This idea imports a proven field-scale gas-delivery and stacking practice from heap leaching to feed concentrated CO2 at depth. The calculation shows permeability, not CO2 chemistry, is the go/no-go variable.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test: Column test, about 3 months: 1-2 m columns of real brucite-bearing tailings, agglomerated and not, fed humidified 5% CO2 against an air control. Measure gas permeability, inlet and outlet CO2 (uptake), and total inorganic carbon by depth over time. It fails if agglomerated permeability is under about 1e-12 m2, or if brucite conversion stalls below about 30% from surface passivation.
idea.family: Forced aeration of brucite-bearing ultramafic tailings heaps with mine power-station exhaust

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: Harrison, Power & Dipple, 'Accelerated carbonation of brucite in mine tailings for carbon sequestration', ES&T 2013 (PMID 22770473, doi 10.1021/es3012854)
closest.overlap: The abstract was verified. It already makes the idea's core claim. Brucite carbonation to nesquehonite rises linearly with pCO2, and CO2 uptake into solution limits the rate. Feeding CO2-enriched gas to Mt Keith tailings could offset about 22-57% of annual mine emissions. That is essentially the idea's 9-55% capacity claim and its supply-limit rationale. The paper has bench-scale data only, with no field gas-delivery engineering.

closest.title: Hamilton, Wilson, Morgan, Harrison, Turvey, Paterson, Dipple & Southam, 'Accelerating Mineral Carbonation in Ultramafic Mine Tailings via Direct CO2 Reaction and Heap Leaching...', Economic Geology 115(2):303-323, 2020 (doi 10.5382/econgeo.4710)
closest.overlap: The abstract was verified via Crossref. The authors reacted partially saturated ultramafic (Woodsreef chrysotile) tailings in columns with synthetic flue gas (10% CO2 in N2). In 4 weeks, minerals stored double the CO2 that three decades of passive carbonation had stored. Separately, they ran simulated heap leaching with 0.08 M H2SO4 (about 21.2 kg CO2/m2/yr in MIN3P modelling). They aim for field deployment using 'conventional technology'. So flue gas plus heap-leach thinking on tailings already exists. Their heap element is acid irrigation for cation release, not forced gas aeration through agglomerated lifts.

closest.title: Power, McCutcheon, Harrison, Wilson, Dipple, Kelly, Southam & Southam, 'Strategizing Carbon-Neutral Mines: A Case for Pilot Projects', Minerals 4:399, 2014 (doi 10.3390/min4020399)
closest.overlap: This review sets out acceleration strategies for tailings carbonation, including CO2-enriched gas and bioleaching or heap-style approaches, and argues for mine-site pilots. The full text was not retrieved (HTTP 403). From my recollection, it discusses supplying CO2 from point sources such as power plants to tailings; this is unverified this run.

closest.title: Assima, Larachi, Beaudoin & Molson, 'Dynamics of carbon dioxide uptake in chrysotile mining residues - effect of mineralogy and liquid saturation', IJGGC 12:124-135, 2013 (doi 10.1016/j.ijggc.2012.10.001), plus related Larachi-group fixed-bed work
closest.overlap: This is forced gas-phase flow of CO2-bearing gas through packed beds of brucite-bearing ultramafic residues, with liquid saturation as a controlling variable. It is the bench analogue of the aerated heap, and it already identified the moisture window that the idea's drip-irrigation step targets. The abstract was not retrieved; my description comes from recollection.

closest.title: Wilson et al. 2014, Mt Keith passive carbonation (IJGGC); Power et al. 2021 ES&T 'Carbonation, cementation, and stabilization of ultramafic mine tailings'
closest.overlap: Wilson et al. is the baseline (about 39.8 kt/yr, about 11% of emissions). Power et al. 2021 already backs the S11 co-benefit: carbonate cementation stabilises tailings and reduces dust.

closest.title: Arca (with BHP, IGO, EV Nickel and others): carbon mineralization at an active mine, 18-month demo completed 2025, about 10x the baseline mineralization rate, about 300 kt CDR offtake with Microsoft
closest.overlap: Field-scale acceleration of tailings carbonation at an active mine is now commercial. Arca's site does not say whether it uses air or concentrated CO2 ('Smart Churning'). It appears to be air-based removal with mechanical turnover, not flue gas forced through engineered heaps. It is a competing route to the same Scope 1 and CDR value.

closest.title: Gagné et al., 'CO2 Direct-Air Capture Combined with Mine Tailings Carbonation System', SSRN 2022 (doi 10.2139/ssrn.4286306)
closest.overlap: This couples a concentrated CO2 source to on-site tailings carbonation (Quebec chrysotile, 50 kt/yr case). It delivers the CO2 dissolved in water, the route the idea's calculation (b) argues against.

art.what_is_new: Most of the idea already exists. Harrison et al. 2013 proposed feeding CO2-enriched gas to Mt Keith brucite tailings to remove the CO2-supply limit, estimating a 22-57% offset. Hamilton et al. 2020 ran 10% CO2 synthetic flue gas through tailings columns and also proposed heap leaching. What appears new is the field engineering from copper heap-leach practice: agglomerating tailings fines for permeability, stacking 6-10 m lifts over low-pressure perforated aeration pipe, and controlling moisture with drip irrigation. The other new part is the Darcy blower-energy analysis, which makes gas permeability (around 1e-12 m2 or better, so agglomeration is required) the go/no-go variable instead of the chemistry. It also shows that air-fed aeration would not work, so the graft needs a concentrated source. I found no published field pilot that forces power-station exhaust through an engineered, aerated tailings heap. That claim is weak because the search budget was exhausted mid-run, so BHP or Anglo industry trials and ARPA-E MINER projects could not be checked. The novelty is in engineering and deployment, not in concept. The idea should cite Harrison 2013 and Hamilton 2020 as the conceptual origin and present itself as the heap-construction implementation. Its decisive test stays the agglomerated-column permeability and passivation test.

phys.assumptions:
Script: climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/graft_near_5.py (uses climate/physics.py). Numbers below are as the script printed them.

THERMODYNAMIC FLOOR. The reaction brucite + CO2 + 2H2O -> nesquehonite has dG0 = -21.6 kJ/mol at 1 atm (approximate tabulated thermochemistry; nesquehonite is the least certain value). dG is -14.2 kJ/mol at pCO2 0.05, -11.9 at 0.02 and -2.3 at 420 ppm. It is spontaneous in all cases, so the floor for capture into the mineral is <= 0 (reported as 0). The only energy needed is for transporting gas, solids and water. Reference only: the floor for separating CO2 from 5% exhaust (40% capture, 99% purity) is 0.178 GJ/t, but it does not apply because no CO2 is purified. The reaction releases heat: dH = -87.4 kJ/mol, or 1.99 GJ/t.

CLAIM (a), CAPACITY: confirmed. 11 Mt/yr of tailings with 0.5 / 1.5 / 3% brucite can store, as hydromagnesite, 33.2 / 99.6 / 199.2 kt/yr (9 / 28 / 55% of the 362 kt/yr mine total implied by 39.8 kt being 11%). As nesquehonite it can store 41.5 / 124.5 / 249.0 kt/yr. This agrees with the bench study of Harrison, Power & Dipple (ES&T 47:126, 2013). That study found the rate rises linearly with pCO2 and that CO2 uptake into solution stays rate-limiting. The authors estimated offsets of about 22-57% of Mt Keith emissions; that is the authors' estimate, not a field result.

CLAIM (b), DISSOLVED DELIVERY: arithmetic confirmed. Delivering 100 kt as dissolved CO2(aq) needs 1,337 Mm3 of water at 0.05 atm and 67 Mm3 at 1 atm. Caveat: pore water buffered by brucite carries dissolved inorganic carbon mostly as HCO3-/CO3--, probably around 10-100x more (my estimate). The claim is therefore directionally right but overstates the water penalty.

CLAIM (c), BLOWER WORK: confirmed. Case: 100 kt/yr, 2 km2 x 8 m pad, 5% CO2, viscosity 1.8e-5 Pa s, 60% blower efficiency.
- Heap pressure drop only: 0.054 / 0.540 / 5.399 GJ/t at k = 1e-11 / 1e-12 / 1e-13 m2 with 30% uptake, and 0.013 / 0.135 / 1.350 GJ/t with 60% uptake.
- Adding 1.5 kPa for ducts and distribution (needed for even flow): 0.061-0.634 GJ/t.
- Air-fed version on the same pad: 191-76,521 GJ/t. This confirms the graft only works with a concentrated CO2 source.
- DAC fan reference: 0.29 GJ/t.

ENERGY (low / base / high): 0.18 / 1.09 / 9.72 GJ/t stored.
- Blower: 0.072 / 0.298 / 0.184 GJ/t.
- Tailings handling (filtering, agglomeration, conveyor stacking): 0.5 / 1.5 / 4 kWh/t tailings, which is 0.11 / 0.80 / 9.54 GJ/t CO2.
- Handling dominates, not the blower. Handling energy scales with the tailings tonnage, and dividing by the brucite grade turns it into energy per tonne of CO2.

COST. Capex annualised at 8% over 15 years (CRF 0.117). Inputs (low / base / high):
- Fixed capex for ducts, quench and blowers: $10 / 25 / 60M.
- Sacrificial aeration pipe on each new pad: 0.86 km2/yr of new pad, pipe spacing 3 / 2 / 1.5 m, $4 / 8 / 15 per m.
- Incremental tailings filtering, agglomeration and stacking over slurry disposal: $0.5 / 2 / 5 per t of tailings. This is my assumption at the order-of-magnitude level of filtered-tailings literature.
- Cement binder: 0 / 0.5 / 1.5 wt% at $150-200/t, with 0.8 t CO2 per t of cement.
- Electricity: $80 / 120 / 180 per MWh, from on-site gas at 0.45 t CO2/MWh.
- MRV: $5 / 15 / 30 per t.
- Water: 0.82 t/t, from the reaction stoichiometry plus half the reaction heat going to evaporation.
- Supply cap (my assumption): the power station supplies about 50% of mine CO2.

COST RESULTS:
- Low: 180.9 kt stored, 176.8 kt net, $53/t stored, $54/t net.
- Base: 74.7 kt stored, $543/t stored. Of that, tailings handling is $294/t and binder is $110/t. Net is only 20.5 kt/yr after the binder's 44.0 kt and the energy's 10.2 kt of emissions, which makes $1,977/t net.
- High: 16.6 kt stored, $6,759/t stored (= $112.2M/16.6 kt), and net NEGATIVE (-135.6 kt/yr).
- If dry stacking is already justified for dam safety or water reasons, the base cost falls to $248/t stored.

GLOBAL SCALE: 0.0003-0.0121 Gt/yr, from 0.2-1.0 Gt/yr of ultramafic tailings, 0.5-2% brucite and 40-80% conversion. The central figure is 0.002 Gt/yr, which is 0.005% of fossil CO2. The tailings tonnage is my estimate, not sourced this run.
phys.violations:
No thermodynamic violation: the chemistry is exergonic and no claim falls below a floor. Claims (a), (b) and (c) reproduce. Problems the idea omits:

1) Kinetics on a single pad. A 2 km2 x 8 m pad holds 25.6 Mt, about 2.3 years of tailings. Storing 100 kt/yr there requires 35%/yr brucite conversion at 1.5% brucite, 17%/yr at 3%, and 104%/yr at 0.5%. The 0.5% case is impossible on this pad.

2) Aeration flux. The design needs 0.215 m3/m2/h, which my recollection puts at 2-20x typical copper bioleach aeration (unsourced). The heap-leach graft is therefore being pushed beyond its proven practice.

3) Binder. Copper heaps are agglomerated with acid curing, and acid would dissolve brucite, so the graft needs a different binder. A cement binder at 0.5-1.5 wt% emits 44-132 kt/yr, enough to cancel most or all of the storage (base net is 20.5 of 74.7 kt). A binder-free method, or agglomerates cured by carbonation, is a hidden go/no-go condition.

4) Tailings handling. Filtering and dry-stacking about 30 kt/d of fine, serpentine-rich tailings is the dominant cost ($294/t of the $543/t base) and the dominant energy use (0.80 of 1.09 GJ/t). The idea does not account for it.

5) Pore clogging. Nesquehonite has about 3x the molar volume of brucite, so uniform conversion cuts permeability to 0.78x (1.5% brucite) or 0.60x (3%). Crusting at the gas front would be worse.

Verdict: plausible but only marginally so at the base case. It is not implausible, because the low case needs no heroic assumptions if the brucite grade is high (about 3%) and agglomeration works without a binder.
phys.resource_needs:
Energy: 0.18-9.72 GJ/t stored (base 1.09). At a global scale of about 6 Mt/yr this is 6.6 PJ/yr, or 0.00106% of world primary energy, which is negligible.

Water: about 0.82 t/t CO2, which is 61 kt/yr at the base case. The source is the hydration water in nesquehonite plus evaporation driven by the reaction heat. That is small against the site's hypersaline borefield supply, but this is an arid site.

Land: about 0.86 km2/yr of new 8 m pad for 11 Mt/yr of tailings. This replaces the slurry tailings dam area rather than adding to it.

Materials:
- Sacrificial perforated pipe of about 290-570 km/yr, from 0.86 km2 at 3-1.5 m spacing.
- Large low-pressure ducting, about 3 m diameter for 60-120 m3/s.
- An exhaust quench or cooler.
- A tailings filter plant and agglomeration drums.
- Possibly binder at 0-1.5 wt%, which is 0-165 kt/yr of cement.

CO2 supply: the design depends on an on-site fossil power station. Mines that move to renewables or the grid lose the CO2 source.
phys.key_uncertainties:
1) Brucite grade and how reactive it is. Grade drives everything from $53/t to net-negative. Mt Keith's own distribution of brucite content was not re-verified this run.

2) Agglomerate permeability under an 8 m load once wetted. Above about 1e-11 m2 the design is fine; at 1e-12 it is marginal (0.18-0.63 GJ/t); at 1e-13 it fails. Fine serpentine and clay particles may not agglomerate without a binder.

3) Binder choice and its CO2 cost. This is the hidden go/no-go condition, since cement cancels most of the benefit.

4) The incremental cost of filtering and dry-stacking 11 Mt/yr of fine tailings. It may be partly justified anyway by the Global Industry Standard on Tailings Management (GISTM) and dam-safety rules; if so, the base drops to $248/t.

5) Field conversion rate and passivation at 5% CO2. The evidence is bench only: Harrison 2013 found a linear pCO2 dependence and remained limited by uptake into solution. Preferential flow and channeling are known problems in heap aeration.

6) Moisture control: drying out from the exothermic heat versus flooding.

7) CO2 supply share. I assumed 50% of mine CO2 comes from the power station. Confound, my recollection and unverified this run: BHP placed Western Australia Nickel, including Mt Keith, into temporary suspension from late 2024, and it has been adding renewable power. If so, the reference site may not currently have the exhaust stream the idea relies on.

8) The status of the BHP/Anglo trials with Isometric and of Arca was not verified; my search budget was exhausted.

9) Global ultramafic tailings tonnage is my order-of-magnitude estimate (0.2-1 Gt/yr).

10) The thermochemistry values for nesquehonite are approximate, but the sign of dG is robust.

stances.evidence: The closest documented position is CAN's 2021 CCUS paper (1,300+ NGOs), supplied in the map. The idea avoids most of CAN's red lines: there is no EOR (red line 7), no offsets if tonnes are claimed only as Scope 1 (red line 4), no geological storage liability shifted to the public (red line 9), and carbonate storage is permanent. It does hit red line 3, which opposes public support for fossil-linked capture 'including CCS'. The CO2 here is captured from a fossil gas power station, so a subsidy or credit for it is fossil-linked capture. It also raises a mitigation-deterrence risk: a mine could keep running its gas engines instead of electrifying with renewables. Expect mainstream NGOs to tolerate it as industrial process abatement. The ones that already oppose CCS will object if it is used to justify new gas generation or sold as credits. Baum et al. 2024 found engineered approaches carry the highest perceived moral-hazard risk. No NGO statement specifically on tailings carbonation was found this session, because the search budget was exhausted, so this stance is inferred from analogous positions.
stances.red_line_hit: Possible: fossil-linked capture (CAN red line 3) and mitigation deterrence if it replaces electrification. It becomes an offsets red line (CAN 4) if the tonnes are sold as credits rather than claimed as Scope 1.

stances.evidence: Carbonation of ultramafic tailings is a well-established research line in the peer-reviewed literature the idea cites: Wilson et al. 2014 measured passive carbonation at Mt Keith (~39.8 kt/yr); Harrison, Power & Dipple, ES&T 2013 did bench work on accelerated brucite carbonation; Energy Procedia 2017 found the field process limited by CO2 supply. Researchers would endorse a column test that is designed to falsify the idea. The IPCC AR6 WGIII text in the map backs CCS/CDR in hard-to-abate sectors. Scientists' support would depend on MRV, since total inorganic carbon is heterogeneous across a heap, and on honest labelling as reduction rather than removal, which the idea already does. Wikipedia's carbon sequestration entry describes ultramafic tailings as 'a readily available source' of reactive oxides. That is low-grade corroboration; the primary sources were not re-fetched this session.
stances.red_line_hit: None if the tonnes are labelled as reduction. Overclaiming 'removal' or weak MRV would be one.

stances.evidence: Oil and gas firms are not directly affected. The idea needs no pipeline, injection well or EOR, so the map's documented S3 interests in 45Q, EOR parity and storage revenue do not apply. At most it gives gas-fired off-grid generation an 'abatable' story, which suits the COP28 'transitional fuels' framing, and it adds a little gas demand at remote mines. Gas marketers have no documented position on tailings carbonation.
stances.red_line_hit: None. It involves no per-tonne fee and no restriction on gas.

stances.evidence: The beneficiaries are miners, who have already invested in this area. The map notes BHP and Anglo American accelerated-carbonation trials with Isometric. From recollection, not verified this session: De Beers/Anglo's 'Project CarbonVault' on kimberlite tailings, and BHP-funded tailings carbonation research with UBC. The equipment, heap stacking and aeration blowers, is standard in mining. There are two confounds. First, cost: blower and agglomeration opex, with binder cost unquantified. The idea's own calculation makes permeability the go/no-go variable, from 0.013-0.05 GJ/t at 1e-11 m2 to 1.3-5.2 GJ/t at 1e-13 m2. Second, BHP announced in 2024 that its Western Australia Nickel operations, which include Mt Keith, would be temporarily suspended because nickel prices had collapsed. That is my recollection and was not re-verified. The flagship site may therefore not be operating, so near-term appetite for capex at nickel mines is weak, and PGM, diamond and active ultramafic operations are better first hosts.
stances.red_line_hit: Cost: added opex in a depressed commodity market. There is no regulatory red line.

stances.evidence: The power stations at remote mines are usually captive or owned by independent power producers, not grid utilities. The idea uses their exhaust as feedstock and asks nothing of utilities beyond the ducting and gas-quality data they would provide. Utilities have no documented position.
stances.red_line_hit: None

stances.evidence: The idea neither cuts nor shifts mining jobs. It may add a few heap-construction and operating roles and could extend a mine's social licence. Unions joined the Carbon Capture Coalition (from the map) in support of capture that preserves jobs, which points toward mild support. However, no union position on tailings carbonation exists, and the scale is too small to be salient. Worker-safety caveats apply: exhaust gas brings CO/NOx and CO2 accumulation risk in enclosed areas near heaps, and fibres at chrysotile sites.
stances.red_line_hit: Occupational exposure at chrysotile (asbestos) sites.

stances.evidence: The policy fit is good. Australia's Safeguard Mechanism, as reformed in 2023, requires covered facilities above 100 kt CO2e/yr to cut baselines about 4.9% a year to 2030, so on-site Scope 1 reductions have compliance value. That figure is my recollection and was not re-verified. Canada's Clean Technology and CCUS investment tax credits, the COP28 decision's endorsement of abatement 'particularly in hard-to-abate sectors', and the critical-minerals strategies of WA and Canada all favour a 'low-carbon nickel' story. The OBBBA natural experiment in the map shows that credits for incumbent constituencies survive. The idea needs no new subsidy class, which lowers its fiscal exposure.
stances.red_line_hit: None. Governments would need MRV rules before letting the tonnes count toward compliance.

stances.evidence: Several target sites are in the Global South: PGM mines in South Africa, diamond mines in Botswana and South Africa, and chrysotile mines in Brazil, Zimbabwe and Kazakhstan. The idea involves no land acquisition, since it uses existing tailings, and no imported offsets if it is claimed as Scope 1, so the main climate-justice triggers in Baum et al. 2024 (unequal risk spread, mitigation deterrence) are weak. It could help exporters meet embedded-emissions rules. CBAM does not currently cover nickel or PGMs, so that benefit is indirect. Risk: if Northern buyers purchase the tonnes as credits from Southern mines, the offset and justice critiques apply. Chrysotile remains contested because many Global South health advocates campaign for asbestos bans.
stances.red_line_hit: Offsets, if credits are exported; asbestos at chrysotile sites.

stances.evidence: The price effect is negligible. The cost falls on mine opex for nickel, PGMs and diamonds, a tiny share of consumer prices. The Canada 2025 and Washington 2024 cases in the map show that consumers only engage with visible price signals, and this has none.
stances.red_line_hit: None

stances.evidence: Investors and insurers value Scope 1 cuts and tailings risk reduction. Since Brumadinho (Vale, 25 Jan 2019, 270 dead, from Wikipedia this session), investors have pushed for the investor-co-convened Global Industry Standard on Tailings Management (UNEP/ICMM/PRI, 2020; from recollection, the source page was unreachable). Carbonate cementation that reduces dust and possibly increases stability is attractive to insurers, but the stability benefit is unproven, and the 'possibly' in the idea should stay. Durable-CDR buyers (Frontier and others in the map) are not natural buyers, because these tonnes are a reduction rather than a removal. Support is conditional on the column test, as opex in a weak nickel market is the key risk.
stances.red_line_hit: Unquantified opex. There is also greenwashing and credit risk if MRV is weak and tonnes are marketed as removal.

stances.evidence: The local benefits are reduced tailings dust and possibly more stable tailings. The local concerns are reshaping tailings into 6-10 m aerated heaps, which changes a tailings facility under GISTM and touches the sensitivity heightened after Brumadinho; venting cooled exhaust (NOx, CO, residual CO2) through heap tops; and above all disturbing chrysotile tailings, which would release asbestos fibres during agglomeration and stacking. Canada banned asbestos in 2018, and legacy chrysotile tailings such as those at Thetford Mines are a known community health issue (from recollection). Many ultramafic mines, such as Mt Keith in WA, are remote, which lowers exposure, but the land may carry native-title interests that require consent processes. That last point is my recollection and was not verified.
stances.red_line_hit: Local safety: asbestos fibre release at chrysotile sites, plus changes to tailings facilities and venting of exhaust near communities.

stake.coalition_notes: The coalition is broad but low-salience: no group is strongly against it, and only S4 (miners), S2 (researchers) and S7 (governments) care much. It avoids the main sources of conflict in the map: no EOR, no pipeline or injection liability, no consumer price, no land grab, and no new subsidy class. The tonnes are claimed as Scope 1 reduction rather than as credits. Five conditions keep it that way: (1) Claim Scope 1 reductions under compliance schemes such as Australia's Safeguard Mechanism, not voluntary credits or 'removal', until MRV across heterogeneous heaps is proven. This keeps it clear of CAN red line 4 and S8 offset concerns. (2) Frame it as abatement of a residual source alongside, not instead of, electrifying mines with renewables, so that S1 cannot read it as gas lock-in or mitigation deterrence. (3) Drop chrysotile sites from the target list, or treat them separately, because asbestos fibre release is a hard S11/S6/S8 red line. Start with PGM, diamond and active nickel sites. (4) Run it under GISTM tailings governance with community consent, especially where native title applies. (5) Confound for S4/S10 appetite: BHP's WA nickel operations, including the Mt Keith reference site, were reportedly suspended from 2024 by low nickel prices (my recollection, not re-verified). The first host may need to be a different mine, and the business case depends on the column test showing permeability of at least 1e-12 m2. Evidence limits: this session's web search budget was exhausted and several primary sources (GISTM, ES&T 2013, Arca) could not be fetched. The stances for S1, S6 and S11 are therefore inferred from analogous documented positions (CAN 2021, Carbon Capture Coalition, Baum 2024, Brumadinho/GISTM), and items marked 'recollection' still need verification.

critic.fatal_flaw: None that cannot be designed around. The chemistry runs downhill and the blower work holds up once permeability reaches about 1e-12 m2. The low case does not need heroic assumptions. Two limits stop short of fatal but cap the idea. (1) Scale: about 0.002 Gt/yr globally, or 0.005% of fossil CO2. This is niche Scope 1 abatement for a few mines, not a climate solution, and should be ranked that way. (2) The CO2 source shrinks over time. The design needs a captive fossil power station, and remote mines are moving to renewables, so the source is a fading asset. Push hard on that and it collides with S1's lock-in concern. The reference site is also confounded: BHP's WA Nickel suspension, which the reports recalled but did not re-verify, means Mt Keith may not have an exhaust stream now.
critic.top_fixable_flaw:
The net-benefit accounting leaves out the counterfactual. Heaping and forcing exhaust through the tailings uses up the brucite that would otherwise carbonate passively from air in the slurry tailings dam. Mt Keith's measured 39.8 kt/yr, the idea's own "conventional core", is exactly that baseline atmospheric uptake. It is not extra. My script (scratchpad/climate/critic_graft_near_5.py, using the TEA's case outputs) recalculates net incremental storage, after subtracting binder and energy emissions and a lost passive baseline of 0, 20 and 39.8 kt/yr:
- Base case: net falls from +20.5 kt/yr to +0.5 kt/yr, then to -19.3 kt/yr. That is net-negative at roughly $41M/yr.
- Low case (3% brucite, no binder): 177, 157 and 137 kt/yr, at $54, $61 and $70 per tonne of incremental CO2. It survives.
- Base case with no binder and dry-stacking already justified: $287, $416 and $750 per tonne of incremental CO2.
So whether the idea pays off depends on three things together: the binder, the brucite grade, and the counterfactual. The headline "9-55% of mine emissions versus 11% passive" overstates the gain by up to the whole passive baseline.

Moisture is a secondary point. Forced flow of saturated exhaust that warms by 10 C inside the heap carries away about 0.84 t of water per tonne of CO2 stored (5% CO2, 30% uptake). Drying is therefore set by the gas flow, not only by reaction heat, so drying fronts and crusting at the inlet are likely.
critic.suggested_patch:
1) Accounting rule: report only incremental tonnes, meaning stored CO2 minus the measured passive atmospheric uptake those tailings would have achieved in the existing facility, minus binder and energy emissions. Claim them as Scope 1 reduction, as the stakeholder report already recommends.
2) No cement binder. Agglomerate with water only and cure the pellets in the agglomeration drum or first lift using the same exhaust. Nesquehonite and hydromagnesite cementation is documented (Power et al. 2021, ES&T), so the carbonation reaction does the binding. If that fails, skip agglomeration and use only tailings that are already filtered or dry-stacked for dam-safety or water reasons (GISTM), where the TEA base falls to about $248/t stored.
3) Site gate before any pilot: brucite of at least about 2-3 wt%, measured from the site's own XRD or TGA data; a captive gas power station expected to run at least 10 more years; and a measured passive baseline. Exclude chrysotile sites.
4) Extend the 3-month column test with two arms:
   (i) binder-free, carbonation-cured agglomerates under an 8 m-equivalent load, wetted;
   (ii) the same tailings left as a surface-exposed slurry with air only, to measure the counterfactual.
   Pass/fail: incremental net uptake above zero, permeability of at least 1e-12 m2 after 3 months of carbonation (because nesquehonite swelling reduces permeability), and drying-front depth controlled by recirculating or rehumidifying the gas.
5) Present Harrison 2013 and Hamilton 2020 as the concept's origin, and position the idea as the heap-engineering implementation.

patched_idea.title: Forced-aeration of ultramafic tailings with the mine's own power-station exhaust (heap-leach practice), scored on incremental tonnes only
patched_idea.one_line: Build brucite-bearing nickel tailings into binder-free, carbonation-cured agglomerate heaps, as copper bioleach heaps are built, and blow the mine's gas-engine or turbine exhaust (about 5% CO2) through them. This removes the CO2-supply limit on passive carbonation. Only the tonnes above the tailings' own measured passive uptake count, net of energy emissions, and they are claimed as Scope 1 reduction.
patched_idea.conventional_core: Passive carbonation of ultramafic tailings. At Mt Keith, Wilson et al. 2014 measured about 39.8 kt CO2/yr, or 11% of the mine's emissions. That passive uptake is the counterfactual baseline the heap must beat, not a gain it can claim.
patched_idea.graft: From mining hydrometallurgy: heap-leach construction. Fines are agglomerated for permeability, stacked in lifts, aerated from below with low-pressure blowers through perforated pipe (an ASTM F2987 heap-leach aeration specification exists), and drip-irrigated to control moisture.
patched_idea.mechanism: Fresh brucite-bearing (Mg(OH)2) tailings are agglomerated with water only, with no cement binder. The pellets are cured in the agglomeration drum or the first lift using the same exhaust, so nesquehonite and hydromagnesite cementation does the binding (Power et al. 2021, ES&T, cited by the critic and not re-retrieved here). Pellets are stacked 6-10 m over aeration pipe. Cooled exhaust from the mine power station (about 5% CO2) is blown through the stack. Drip irrigation keeps pores moist without flooding them, and the gas is partly recirculated or rehumidified to limit drying fronts at the inlet. CO2 reacts with brucite to form hydromagnesite and nesquehonite. Passive tests show the reaction is limited by CO2 supply (Energy Procedia 2017). Treated exhaust leaves through the top. Fallback if binder-free pellets fail: no agglomeration at all, used only on tailings the site already filters or dry-stacks for dam-safety or water reasons (GISTM), so stacking costs are not charged to carbon. Accounting rule: incremental tonnes = CO2 stored in the heap - measured passive atmospheric uptake those tailings would have reached in the existing facility - blower, agglomeration and any binder emissions. These are claimed as Scope 1 reduction, not removal credits. Site gate before any pilot: (a) brucite of at least about 2-3 wt%, measured from the site's own XRD or TGA data; (b) a captive gas power station expected to run at least 10 more years; (c) a measured passive baseline; (d) no chrysotile sites.
patched_idea.target: Mine-site Scope 1 CO2 at gated nickel, diamond and PGM mines (chrysotile excluded), through mineral storage in tailings, while a captive fossil power station is still running.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims: (a) Gross capacity (my stoichiometry, 11 Mt/yr of tailings, 0.5-3 wt% brucite): full brucite carbonation stores 33-199 kt CO2/yr. Net of a passive baseline of up to 39.8 kt/yr, the incremental gain is roughly -7 to +159 kt/yr before energy. The site gate of at least 2-3 wt% brucite removes the low end. The earlier headline of '9-55% vs 11% passive' overstated the gain by up to the whole passive baseline. (b) Gas-phase delivery is necessary. Carbonated water at pCO2 0.05 atm holds 0.07 g/L, which needs 1,337 Mm3 of water per 100 kt CO2. At 1 atm pure CO2 it still needs 67 Mm3. (c) Blower work (my Darcy calculation: 100 kt/yr, 2 km2 pad, 8 m high, 5% CO2, 30-60% uptake). Permeability of 1e-11 m2 gives 0.013-0.05 GJ/t. 1e-12 m2 gives 0.13-0.52 GJ/t. 1e-13 m2 gives 1.3-5.2 GJ/t, which is unworkable. At 420 ppm air feed it costs 27-27,000 GJ/t, so the graft only works with a concentrated source. (d) Incremental economics. These are modelled numbers from the critic's script (scratchpad/climate/critic_graft_near_5.py, using TEA case outputs), re-run this pass. Passive baseline lost is 0 / 20 / 39.8 kt/yr in each case. Low case (3% brucite, no binder, about $9.6M/yr): net 177 / 157 / 137 kt/yr at $54 / $61 / $70 per incremental tonne. Base case with binder-free carbonation-cured pellets or existing dry-stack (about $18.5M/yr at $248/t stored): net 64.5 / 44.5 / 24.7 kt/yr at $287 / $416 / $750 per tonne. The superseded base case with cement binder nets +20.5 / +0.5 / -19.3 kt/yr at about $40.6M/yr, which is why the binder is dropped. (e) Moisture: saturated 5% CO2 exhaust at 30% uptake that warms 30 to 40 C in the heap removes about 0.84 t of water per t CO2 stored (0.37 t/t for a 5 C rise, 1.73 t/t for 25 to 45 C). Drying is therefore set by the gas flow, which is why recirculation or rehumidification is in the design. (f) Scale: about 0.002 Gt/yr globally (critic's estimate), which is niche Scope 1 abatement, not a climate-scale lever. (g) The CO2 is fossil, so this is reduction, not removal.
patched_idea.who_gains: S4: gated miners (Nickel West-type, Anglo, diamond and PGM operators) with high-brucite tailings and a long-lived captive gas plant cut Scope 1 by an incremental tonnage of perhaps 10-45% of a roughly 360 kt/yr mine in the low case, using equipment they already know. S11: carbonate cementation stabilises tailings and reduces dust; this is strongest where tailings are already dry-stacked. S1: permanent mineral storage with no pipeline or injection well, and conservative incremental-only accounting. S7: Western Australia and Canada get a measured abatement story.
patched_idea.who_loses: S4 and S10 pay blower and agglomeration opex ($287-750 per incremental tonne in the binder-free base case), which is uneconomic except at high-brucite or dry-stack sites. S1 objects to lock-in, because the design depends on a captive fossil power station that remote mines are replacing with renewables. The CO2 source is a fading asset, which caps project life. MRV across heterogeneous tailings is hard, so no credits are sold until the passive baseline and incremental tonnes are measured. S6: neutral.
patched_idea.closest_known_work: Harrison, Power & Dipple, 'Accelerated carbonation of brucite in mine tailings for carbon sequestration', ES&T 2013 (doi 10.1021/es3012854), is the origin of the concept, a bench study with CO2-enriched gas. Hamilton et al. 2020, cited by the critic and not re-retrieved here, is follow-on accelerated tailings carbonation work. Others: Wilson et al. 2014 (Mt Keith, passive baseline); Energy Procedia 2017 (supply-limited, watering frequency matters); Power et al. 2021 (carbonate cementation of tailings). Also BHP and Anglo American accelerated-carbonation trials with Isometric, and Arca's tailings-tilling approach (my recollection, unverified). Confound: BHP's WA Nickel suspension, also unverified, may mean Mt Keith has no running exhaust stream now.
patched_idea.why_different: The concept of accelerating brucite carbonation with concentrated CO2 is not new (Harrison 2013; Hamilton 2020). This idea's contribution is the heap-engineering implementation. It imports field-scale heap-leach stacking and forced aeration to deliver exhaust CO2 at depth, uses binder-free carbonation-cured agglomerates, and accounts only for incremental tonnes against a measured passive baseline. The calculation shows the go/no-go variables are permeability after carbonation, brucite grade and the counterfactual, not the CO2 chemistry.
patched_idea.cheapest_falsifying_test: Column test, about 3 months, three arms on the same real brucite-bearing tailings. (i) Binder-free, carbonation-cured agglomerates in 1-2 m columns under an 8 m-equivalent load, wetted, fed humidified 5% CO2 with recirculation or rehumidification. (ii) The same tailings as surface-exposed slurry, air only, to measure the counterfactual passive uptake. (iii) Unagglomerated tailings fed 5% CO2. Measure gas permeability over time, inlet and outlet CO2, total inorganic carbon by depth, and drying-front depth. The test fails if: incremental net uptake ((i) minus (ii), minus energy) is at or below zero; permeability falls below about 1e-12 m2 after 3 months of carbonation (nesquehonite swelling); brucite conversion stalls below about 30%; or the drying front cannot be controlled by gas rehumidification. Pre-test gate: site XRD or TGA shows at least 2-3 wt% brucite, and the captive gas plant has at least 10 years of remaining life.

fix.change_summary: I applied the critic's five-part patch and kept the core mechanism (forced aeration of stacked ultramafic tailings with captive power-station exhaust) and the graft (heap-leach construction and aeration). Changes: (1) Accounting now counts only incremental tonnes: stored CO2 minus the measured passive atmospheric uptake the same tailings would have reached, minus energy and any binder emissions, claimed as Scope 1 reduction and not as credits. The old headline of '9-55% vs 11% passive' is withdrawn as overstated. (2) The cement binder is replaced by water-only agglomerates cured with the same exhaust, so carbonate cementation does the binding (Power et al. 2021). The fallback is to use only tailings already filtered or dry-stacked for GISTM reasons. (3) A site gate is added: at least 2-3 wt% brucite from site XRD or TGA, a captive gas plant with at least 10 years of remaining life, and a measured passive baseline; chrysotile sites are excluded. (4) Gas recirculation or rehumidification is added, because forced flow removes about 0.84 t of water per t CO2. (5) The column test gains a binder-free loaded arm and an air-only slurry counterfactual arm, with pass/fail on incremental net uptake above zero and permeability of at least 1e-12 m2 after carbonation. (6) Harrison 2013 and Hamilton 2020 are now presented as the concept's origin, with this idea as the heap-engineering implementation. I re-ran the critic's script (scratchpad/climate/critic_graft_near_5.py), and the incremental numbers match: low case $54-70 per incremental tonne; binder-free base case $287-750 per tonne; the cement-binder base case could turn net-negative. I also added the critic's scale limit (about 0.002 Gt/yr), the fading fossil-source and lock-in risk, and the unverified Mt Keith exhaust confound. Hamilton 2020 and Power 2021 were not re-retrieved this run.

idea.title: Fracture-stimulated mineralization doublets in hot olivine-rich rock
idea.one_line: Apply Fervo-style horizontal, multistage-stimulated well pairs to hot peridotite or ultramafic rock. CO2-charged water circulates in a closed loop and turns CO2 into carbonate permanently. Kinetics put the viable window at rock of 90 C or hotter, at roughly 3 km or deeper on a normal gradient.
idea.conventional_core: In-situ CO2 mineralization in reactive rock: Carbfix (basalt) and 44.01 (Oman peridotite, about 88% mineralized in 45 days in a 2025 pilot).
idea.graft: Shale/EGS completion technology: long horizontal laterals, 40-stage stimulation, and an injector-producer doublet as at Fervo Project Red/Cape. It is used to create reactive surface area and to recirculate the carrier water.
idea.mechanism:
Natural fractures limit the area current mineralization pilots can reach, and freshwater supply limits scale (Carbfix uses about 25 t water per t CO2).

A stimulated horizontal doublet in hot olivine-rich rock creates about 8x10^5 m2 of fracture face per well. Water is carbonated at about 60 bar, pumped through the fracture network, produced, re-carbonated and reinjected, so freshwater use is about zero. Heat can be co-produced.

The chemistry: forsterite dissolution consumes CO2 to make magnesite. The reaction's volume increase can either clog the rock or propagate cracks (Kelemen's 'reaction-driven cracking'). Whether permeability survives is the central uncertainty.
idea.target: Large ophiolite and ultramafic bodies near CO2 sources or DAC: Oman/UAE (Samail; ADNOC/44.01), plus US and other ultramafic and basalt provinces. Durable storage that needs no caprock, about 1.6 Gt olivine per Gt CO2.
idea.quantitative_claims:
Computed with Palandri and Kharaka (2004) forsterite kinetics in subsurface_ideas.py.

Stoichiometry: 1.60 t forsterite per t CO2 at most.

Reaction rate and surface area needed:
- For 0.1 Mt CO2/yr per doublet, reactive area needs are:
  - 1.5x10^10 m2 at 40 C, pH 5 (about 18,600x the geometric fracture face; the wall rock would need to react to 1.9 m depth at 10^4 m2/m3 grain area)
  - 3.1x10^9 m2 at 60 C (39 cm)
  - 4.1x10^8 m2 at 90 C, pH 5 (5 cm)
  - 1.5x10^8 m2 at 90 C, pH 4 (1.8 cm)
  - 1.7x10^7 m2 at 150 C (0.2 cm)
- Conclusion: shallow, cool peridotite cannot reach 0.1 Mt/yr per well, while rock at 90 C or hotter plausibly can.
- The reaction front advances about 8.6 cm/yr into each fracture face (about 69,000 m3 of rock per year at 70% olivine).

Water and energy:
- Carrier water is 25-38 t per t CO2 (0.6-0.9 mol/kg), about 44-65 kbbl/d per doublet, recirculated.
- Circulation pumping takes 0.19-0.38 GJ/t (5-10 MPa loop pressure drop). CO2 compression to about 60 bar adds 0.35 GJ/t. The total of about 0.55-0.73 GJ/t is about 1-2% of world electricity per Gt/yr.
idea.who_gains: S3 and S7 in Gulf states with ophiolites (Oman, UAE): a storage business using frac and EGS skills. S6 (frac crews during shale downturns). S4 Gulf industry (ammonia, steel, cement) needing storage. S1 and S2: mineral permanence over more than 10,000 yr, no caprock dependence and no EOR. S8 host countries, if benefit-sharing is designed in.
idea.who_loses: S11 near sites: induced seismicity from stimulation and water handling. The anti-fracking part of S1, which may reject 'fracking for carbon' framing despite the climate benefit. Basalt and saline-aquifer storage competitors lose some share. Clogging risk falls on S10 investors.
idea.closest_known_work: Kelemen and Matter 2008 (PNAS): in-situ carbonation of peridotite, explicitly proposing hydraulic fracturing plus heating. Kelemen et al. 2011 (Annu Rev): recipes for enhanced in-situ storage. 44.01 Oman pilot (Nature 2025, about 88% in 45 days). Carbfix (Matter 2016). Nguyen et al. (ARMA 2026, LANL): induced shear fractures raise peridotite permeability up to 5 orders of magnitude and sustain carbonation. Dai et al. 2026: thermo-hydro-chemical model of fractured peridotite for H2 plus heat. Fervo Cape and Project Red horizontal EGS (drilling time down about 75%, S-1/A 2026).
idea.why_different: Kelemen proposed fracturing in 2008, before horizontal multistage EGS was demonstrated (Fervo, 2023-26). This idea is an engineering realization: closed-loop doublets that remove the freshwater bottleneck. It comes with an explicit kinetic design rule (rock at 90 C or hotter) that rejects shallow, cool targets. It is not a new concept, and the novelty is modest.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test:
Bench (2-3 months, LANL-type triaxial rig or a university lab): flow CO2-charged water (60 bar pCO2) through a saw-cut or shear-fractured dunite core at 90 C and at 150 C for 60-90 days. Track permeability, carbonate yield (TGA/XRD) and reacted-rim thickness. Kill if permeability falls more than 10x within 30 days at both temperatures, or if the reacted rim grows under about 0.5 cm/yr equivalent at 90 C.

Desk: fit the 44.01 Oman pilot mass balance to the same kinetic model to calibrate the reactive area per fracture.
idea.family: Fracture-stimulated horizontal doublets for in-situ CO2 mineralisation in hot peridotite

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: Kelemen & Matter 2008, 'In situ carbonation of peridotite for CO2 storage', PNAS
closest.overlap: This is the core concept. The abstract (verified via Crossref) says peridotite carbonation can be accelerated by drilling, hydraulic fracturing and elevated temperature, with the exothermic reaction keeping the rock hot at depth. It projects more than 1 Gt CO2/yr in Oman. The paper predates horizontal multistage completions and does not specify an injector-producer recirculation doublet.

closest.title: Kelemen et al. 2011, 'Rates and mechanisms of mineral carbonation in peridotite: natural processes and recipes for enhanced, in situ CO2 capture and storage', Annu Rev Earth Planet Sci; and Kelemen et al. 2020, 'Engineered carbon mineralization in ultramafic rocks for CO2 removal from air', Chem Geol 550
closest.overlap: These papers expand the 2008 recipes: fracturing, heating to near the olivine-carbonation rate optimum (about 185 C), reaction-driven cracking, and pumping CO2-bearing fluid through peridotite. The idea's temperature-window logic follows this line. The full text was not retrievable this run (publisher returned 403), so the details come from known content.

closest.title: Clark et al. 2020, 'CarbFix2: CO2 and H2S mineralization during 3.5 years of continuous injection into basaltic rocks at more than 250 C', GCA (Hellisheidi)
closest.overlap: This is operating precedent for the carrier-water loop. Gas is dissolved into produced geothermal water and reinjected into a hot (above 250 C) reactive reservoir at a working geothermal plant, so heat co-production and no external freshwater already exist together, in basalt. It uses no horizontal multistage stimulation and no peridotite. Cited from memory, not re-fetched this run.

closest.title: Carrington 2026, 'CO2 Plume Geothermal (CPG) With In-Situ Mineralization for Combined Heat Extraction and Permanent Storage', SSRN 7313760 (posted 20 Aug 2026)
closest.overlap: This is the closest conceptual twin found: combined heat extraction and permanent mineral storage in mafic and ultramafic formations, using coupled reactive-transport, geomechanics and THM modelling. It differs in using supercritical CO2 rather than carbonated water as the working fluid. It names no Fervo-style horizontal multistage doublet and gives no explicit at-least-90 C kinetic siting rule. It is a preprint and modelling only.

closest.title: Dai et al. 2026, 'Thermo-hydro-chemical coupled numerical modeling of hydrogen-thermal co-development in hydraulically fractured peridotite', Advances in Geo-Energy Research 20(2):145-162
closest.overlap: This models EGS-style hydraulically fractured peridotite with heat co-production. The target product is H2 from serpentinization, not CO2 mineralization. The abstract could not be retrieved, so the well geometry is unknown.

closest.title: Nguyen et al. (LANL) 2026, 'In Situ Shearing Experiments Reveal How Fractures Enhance and Sustain Carbon Mineralization in Altered Peridotite', ARMA 2026-0720
closest.overlap: Lab evidence for the idea's central uncertainty: induced shear fractures raised permeability by up to 5 orders of magnitude, and carbonation proceeded with supercritical CO2. It is essentially the proposed falsifying bench test, but with supercritical CO2 and short durations rather than 60-90 days of carbonated water at 90 C and 150 C.

closest.title: Novakowski (Queen's) with Deep Sky: EGU25-14364 and EGU26-15459, hydrogeological challenges, fractures and matrix diffusion for carbon mineralization in terrestrial mafic and ultramafic rock
closest.overlap: These abstracts identify fracture-limited injectivity and pore volume as the commercial bottleneck. EGU26 explicitly points to geothermal-industry hydraulic stimulation (without proppant) of healed fractures as the remedy, which is the same diagnosis and graft direction as this idea. Neither abstract mentions horizontal wells, recirculation or temperature targeting.

closest.title: Soltanov, Matter et al. 2026, 'Rapid CO2 Mineralization in Oman's Peridotite Formation: Insights from Reactive Transport Simulation', SPE (Oman Petroleum & Energy Show) 232354
closest.overlap: This is a reactive-transport fit to the Oman pilot (10 days of injecting CO2-dissolved water, then 50 days of incubation), which converts more than 50% of the CO2 to carbonate, mostly hydromagnesite. It is the ready-made calibration target for the idea's desk test. It covers single-well injection only, with no stimulation or doublet.

closest.title: 44.01 Oman/UAE (Project Hajar, with ADNOC) field pilots; Matter et al. Goldschmidt 2025 'CO2 Mineralization in Ultramafic Rocks: Learnings from Field Demonstration Projects'
closest.overlap: These are commercial in-situ peridotite mineralization projects with ADNOC, the stakeholder set the idea targets. The public material describes shallow injection of carbonated water, with no horizontal multistage EGS completions or recirculation doublets disclosed.

closest.title: Eden GeoPower (ARPA-E MINER 2022, ARPA-E geologic-hydrogen awards 2024); Goldschmidt 2025 'Hydrogen Generation in Peridotite Cores Fractured by Electrical Reservoir Stimulation'
closest.overlap: Eden is developing stimulation of ultramafic and other reactive rock to create reactive surface area, for stimulated H2 and mineral recovery. This is the same graft (EGS-type permeability creation in reactive rock) aimed at a different product. No CO2-mineralization doublet was disclosed.

closest.title: Fervo Project Red / Cape horizontal multistage EGS; Utah FORGE 2024 stimulation campaign (SPE 223519, 223576)
closest.overlap: This is the source of the graft: horizontal laterals, multistage stimulation and injector-producer doublets in hot crystalline rock. It has never been applied to carbonation, and the rock is granite, not peridotite.

art.what_is_new:
The concept is not new. Kelemen and Matter (2008) already proposed drilling, hydraulically fracturing and heating peridotite for in-situ carbonation. Carbon storage with heat co-production in mafic and ultramafic rock was proposed in Carrington's 2026 CPG-mineralization preprint, which uses supercritical CO2. Fractured peridotite with heat production has been modelled for H2 by Dai et al. (2026). Reusing produced geothermal water as a CO2 carrier into hot reactive rock already runs at CarbFix2/Hellisheidi (basalt, above 250 C), so the "freshwater near zero" component is not novel. Geothermal-style hydraulic stimulation was explicitly suggested in 2026 as the fix for permeability-limited ultramafic mineralization (Novakowski with Deep Sky, EGU26).

What I found no precedent for is the specific engineering package:
- Fervo-style horizontal, multistage (about 40-stage) injector-producer doublets completed in peridotite.
- Carbonated water (about 60 bar pCO2) recirculated through the stimulated fracture network, rather than one-pass injection or supercritical-CO2 CPG.
- An explicit kinetic siting rule (rock of at least 90 C, about 3 km or deeper) derived from forsterite rate laws and fracture-face area, which rules out shallow, cool ophiolite targets of the kind current pilots use.

That is a modest integration-and-design-rule novelty, not a new mechanism; the idea's own "why_different" assessment is accurate.

Evidence from 2026 reshapes the falsification plan:
- Nguyen et al. (LANL, ARMA 2026) already provides lab evidence that induced fractures raise peridotite permeability by up to 5 orders of magnitude and sustain carbonation. That covers the short-term part of the bench test, though not the 60-90-day permeability survival question in carbonated water at 90 C and 150 C.
- Soltanov, Matter et al. (SPE 2026) already fit a reactive-transport model to the Oman pilot (more than 50% mineralized in 60 days, mostly hydromagnesite). The desk calibration should build on that model, not start from scratch.

Coverage limits: the session's WebSearch budget was exhausted. Google Patents and FreePatentsOnline were unreachable (503/403), and DuckDuckGo returned a CAPTCHA, which I did not attempt. ARPA-E project lists were not retrieved. The search therefore relied on Crossref, EGU abstracts and company sites, and patents are effectively unchecked. A patent sweep (for example 44.01, ADNOC, Fervo, Eden or Vema assignees, and "stimulated mineralization doublet") is the main remaining gap before the PARTIAL label can be considered firm.

phys.assumptions:
Scope: storage only. The CO2 arrives high-purity at about 1 bar, and capture and transport are excluded. They are added back at the end, with Gulf high-purity CO2 assumed to cost $15-30/t to capture [recall] and $10/t to transport.

Thermodynamics:
- Formation data are from Robie & Hemingway [recall].
- For Mg2SiO4 + 2CO2 -> 2MgCO3 + SiO2, dH = -88.2 kJ/mol CO2 and dG = -36.5 kJ/mol CO2. The storage step is exergonic and releases 2.00 GJ_th per t CO2.
- The only unavoidable work is dissolving the CO2. The isothermal compression floor is 0.192 GJ/t to 30 bar and 0.231 GJ/t to 60 bar.
- Separation floors are upstream of this idea: 0.465 GJ/t from air and 0.0065 GJ/t from a 95% CO2 stream.

Kinetics: Palandri & Kharaka (2004) forsterite parameters [recall]. They reproduce all of the idea's numbers:
- 1.598 t forsterite per t CO2.
- Area needed: 1.5e10 m2 at 40 C, 3.1e9 at 60 C, 4.1e8 at 90 C pH 5, 1.5e8 at 90 C pH 4, 1.7e7 at 150 C.
- Geometric fracture area of 8e5 m2 per well, from 40 stages x 100 m half-length x 50 m height.
- A required front advance of 8.6 cm/yr into each face (69,194 m3/yr of rock at 70% olivine and 3.3 t/m3).

Transport check (new): zero-order reaction-diffusion, optimistic because it applies the inlet-pH rate everywhere and ignores silica passivation.
- Diffusivity: D_CO2 scaled from 1.91e-9 m2/s by Stokes-Einstein with CoolProp viscosity. Effective diffusivity follows Archie's law, D_eff = D x phi^2.
- Inputs: C0 = 800 mol/m3, grain area 1e4 m2/m3, and a shrinking-core front through an open reacted rim.
- CO2 uptake capacity of the rock is 1.45 t CO2/m3.

Water and energy:
