- Carrier CO2 concentration is 0.6-0.9 mol/kg; the Spycher 2003 model gives 0.57 mol/kg at 90 C and 60 bar, and 1.02 mol/kg at 40 C.
- Per-pass mineralised fraction is 100/80/50% (low/base/high).
- Loop pressure drop is 5/7.5/10 MPa at 80/75/70% pump efficiency.
- Compression is 1->30 bar at 70% (low), 1->60 bar at 65% (base) and 1->60 bar at 58% (high).

Costs:
- Fervo S-1/A [src, read this session]: about $7,000/kW for a 50 MW GeoBlock with 8-10 wells. Cape wells reach about 9,000 ft TVD and 14,000 ft MD with about 5,000 ft laterals. This implies $21-27M all-in per well when the wellfield takes 55-70% of capex.
- Assumed well cost, including stimulation, is $8/15/25M. Surface capex is $8/12/18M, plus $5M for monitoring baseline.
- Capacity is 0.2/0.1/0.03 Mt/yr per doublet.
- Finance: WACC 6/8/10% over 25/20/10 years.
- Other: electricity $40/60/90 per MWh; O&M 2/3/4% of capex; MMV $3/5/10/t; re-stimulation $0/3/6M every 5 years; 2% loop make-up water at $1/m3.

Comparators [recall]: saline storage $10-30/t; Carbfix $25-50/t; 45Q $85 (point source) and $180 (DAC).

Results:
- Totals with capture and transport: $48-63/t (low), $111-126/t (base), $607-622/t (high).
- Scale of 0.05 Gt/yr is a realistic 2050 figure for a Gulf hub, conditional on the bench test passing. 1 Gt/yr would need 10,000 doublets (20,000 wells).
phys.violations:
There is no physically_impossible claim. The storage reaction is exergonic, and every energy figure sits above the 0.19-0.23 GJ/t dissolution floor.

The idea's arithmetic all reproduces, with one exception. It says 0.55-0.73 GJ/t equals about 1-2% of world electricity per Gt/yr, but the script prints 0.51%-0.68%. The claim is overstated about 2-3x, in the conservative direction.

IMPLAUSIBLE as stated: 0.1 Mt/yr per doublet relies on a heroic assumption.
- The design needs the reaction front to advance 8.6 cm/yr into every fracture face.
- With diffusion into low-porosity peridotite and an open reacted rim, the front advances only 1.0-10 mm/yr at 90 C and 1.4-14 mm/yr at 150 C (porosity 1-10%).
- The 20-year average is 0.26-2.59 kt/yr per doublet at 90 C and 0.37-3.66 kt/yr at 150 C. The design therefore needs 39-386x (90 C) or 27-273x (150 C) more reactive area; at 3% porosity the figures are 129x and 91x.
- Even if the Mg is exported and the rim keeps 20-40% porosity, a doublet averages only 0.005-0.015 Mt/yr over 20 years, 7-20x short.
- Closing the gap needs a cm-scale crack network sustained for decades: crack spacing of 1-10 cm in a 2 m damage zone gives 40-400x the geometric area.

Clogging: the products add 0.40-0.45 m3 of new solid per t CO2, which is 39,696 m3/yr per doublet. That is 33x the open fracture volume (about 1,200 m3) each year, and 20-60x the matrix pore volume (692-2,076 m3) in the rock that reacts each year.

Diffusion-limited cost (no cracking): $6,161/t at 90 C and $4,362/t at 150 C, capital alone.

Internal conflict: 'heat co-production' works against the 90 C-or-hotter kinetic rule.
- Reaction heat is 6.3 MWth per doublet.
- A 120 kg/s loop cooled by 30 C removes 15 MWth, which cools the fracture faces.
- At 60 C the reaction needs 7.6x the area it needs at 90 C.

Minor issue: 0.9 mol/kg carrier water needs the CO2 dissolved at about 40 C or cooler, or above 60 bar.
phys.resource_needs:
Per doublet, base case:
- Water circulation: 25-76 t water per t CO2, 80-240 kg/s (43-130 kbbl/d), recirculated. The base case is 120 kg/s. Fervo Project Red ran about 60-63 kg/s [recall], so the design rate is plausible but undemonstrated.
- Residence time in the fractures is 1.4-4.2 h.
- Rock consumed: 69,194 m3/yr at 0.1 Mt/yr.
- Electricity: 0.44/0.75/1.52 GJ/t, which per Gt/yr is 0.41%/0.70%/1.41% of world electricity (123/209/422 TWh). The base energy is 1.6x the air-capture separation floor, so energy is not the bottleneck.

At scale:

| Scale | Doublets | Wells | Rock | Make-up water | Pads | World electricity |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.05 Gt/yr | 500 | 1,000 | 0.03 km3/yr | 30 Mt/yr | ~10 km2 | 0.03% |
| 0.2 Gt/yr | 2,000 | 4,000 | 0.14 km3/yr | 120 Mt/yr | ~40 km2 | 0.14% |
| 1 Gt/yr | 10,000 | 20,000 | 0.69 km3/yr | 600 Mt/yr | ~200 km2 | 0.70% |

The 1 Gt/yr case also needs a loop inventory of about 21 Mt of water. For comparison, US shale drills about 10-20k wells/yr [recall].

Freshwater use is near zero apart from about 2% loop make-up, which can be brackish or desalinated.

If Mg is exported rather than precipitated in place, 0.64 m3 of magnesite per t CO2 must be handled at the surface or in the producer.

Supply constraint: UAE plus Oman fossil CO2 is about 0.25-0.3 Gt/yr [recall], which caps a Gulf hub.

The resource of hot (90 C or hotter, 4 km or shallower) ultramafic rock has not been mapped.
phys.key_uncertainties:
1. **The central uncertainty is whether reaction-driven or shear cracking keeps creating fresh olivine surface at cm spacing, and keeps permeability open, for decades** despite 0.40 m3 of new solid per tonne. This decides between $23-86/t and more than $4,000/t. Natural Oman listvenites show full carbonation at km scale, but over geological time. Lab results are mixed [recall].

2. **Rate assumptions are optimistic.** Silica-rich passivation layers, documented at about 90 C [recall], could cut rates by orders of magnitude below Palandri & Kharaka. pH rises inside the matrix, which also slows the reaction. Magnesite precipitates slowly below about 80 C. Partial serpentinization lowers the olivine content.

3. **Unverified citations.** I could not verify these this session because the web search budget was exhausted, so treat them as unconfirmed until checked:
   - the 44.01 Oman pilot figure ('about 88% in 45 days, Nature 2025')
   - Nguyen et al. ARMA 2026 (permeability up to 5 orders of magnitude)
   - Dai et al. 2026
   - Kelemen & Matter 2008's order-of-1 Gt/yr Oman capacity

   The bench test should calibrate the kinetics against the 44.01 mass balance.

4. **Whether hot (90 C or hotter) peridotite exists at drillable depth** in Oman/UAE, and the local geothermal gradient there.

5. **Cost of hard-rock horizontal wells in ultramafic rock.** My range of $8-25M is anchored on the Fervo GeoBlock capex, which is for granite and metasediments in Utah.

6. **Induced seismicity** from stimulation. Net voidage is near zero, which helps.

7. **Scaling in the producer and surface equipment** if Mg leaves the rock in solution.

The idea's own cheapest falsifying test, a 60-90 day fractured-dunite flow-through at 90 and 150 C, targets exactly uncertainty 1 and is well designed. I would add one kill criterion: a reacted-rim growth rate below about 1 cm/yr at 150 C means the per-doublet rate falls short by more than 10x.

stances.evidence: The idea avoids two of the Climate Action Network's 2021 red lines. There is no enhanced oil recovery (CAN red line 7), and mineral storage weakens the storage-liability worry (red line 9), because carbonate does not depend on a caprock. Some climate-minded actors have backed the conventional core: 44.01's Oman peridotite mineralisation won the Earthshot Prize 'Fix Our Climate' category in 2022 (earthshotprize.org). The idea is still CO2 storage, and CAN (2021) opposes public support for fossil-linked CCS. CAN also says DACCS has 'no place' in steep-reduction scenarios, so the source of the CO2 decides the reaction. Hard-line groups oppose CCS outright. CIEL says CCS gives emitters 'a license to pollute indefinitely' and that EJ communities are 'being targeted' (ciel.org). Food & Water Watch attacks 45Q for rewarding fossil firms (foodandwaterwatch.org). The 'fracking for carbon' framing adds a second axis of opposition from the anti-fracking movement. I could not find a documented NGO statement on enhanced geothermal or on mineralisation-by-stimulation specifically; that is a gap. Likely pattern: storage for cement process CO2 and true removals gets tolerance; storage for coal or gas power, or anything marketed as offsets, gets opposition.
stances.red_line_hit: Mitigation deterrence and public subsidy to fossil-linked CCS if the CO2 comes from fossil power (CAN 2021 lines 3, 4 and 8). The 'fracking' association for the anti-fracking wing. No EOR red line.

stances.evidence: Scientists originated the concept. Kelemen and Matter (PNAS 2008) proposed in-situ peridotite carbonation with hydraulic fracturing and heating. Matter et al. (Science 2016) measured more than 95% mineralisation within 2 years at Carbfix; this is a measured field result, from my knowledge and not re-fetched this session. IPCC AR6 WGIII says CCS and CDR storage are needed. It also warns, in C.4.4, that CCS can extend fossil use. That caveat applies to the CO2 source, not to this storage method. Scientists will rightly demand the falsification test. The permeability-clogging versus reaction-driven-cracking question is unresolved; LANL's work (Nguyen et al., ARMA 2026) is a single lab line. S2 is likely to give conditional, research-stage support rather than endorse deployment.
stances.red_line_hit: None categorical. Overclaiming permanence or scale before field data would cost S2's credibility.

stances.evidence: The idea turns S3 capabilities (horizontal drilling, multistage stimulation, subsurface reservoir management) into a storage revenue line. That is the same logic as Equinor/Northern Lights and the carbon-takeback obligation. Gulf NOCs are the natural hosts. My own knowledge, not verified this session, is that ADNOC partnered with 44.01 for peridotite mineralisation pilots in Fujairah, UAE in 2023. Earthshot reports 44.01 expanding into the UAE. OGCI and OGDC members already back carbon management. The US 45Q credit pays for dedicated geologic storage, at $85/t for point sources and $180/t for DAC (GCCSI on OBBBA 2025). Unlike saline CCS, there is no EOR upside. Firms with saline-aquifer storage portfolios may see it as a competitor, so support is strongest in states with ophiolites (Oman, UAE).
stances.red_line_hit: None. A per-tonne fee mandate is S3's documented red line (US Waste Emissions Charge repeal, 2025); a storage service paid by credits is not one.

stances.evidence: Cement's process CO2 cannot be removed by fuel switching, and the GCCA Concrete Future roadmap relies on CCUS. The first full-scale cement CCS plant, Heidelberg Brevik, needed offshore storage via Northern Lights. Here the floor separation work at a cement kiln is only 0.11 GJ/t (OptiLex verifier). The idea's 0.55-0.73 GJ/t for circulation plus compression is modest storage overhead. COP28 paragraph 28 endorses CCUS 'particularly in hard-to-abate sectors', the most legitimate use. Gulf ammonia, steel and cement producers near the Samail ophiolite gain storage access with no caprock-leak liability. The main constraint is geography: most heavy industry is not near hot ultramafic rock, so it would need CO2 transport.
stances.red_line_hit: Cost pass-through if storage is mandated without subsidy or CBAM protection; VCI's 'no panacea' framing on carbon contracts for difference.

stances.evidence: Utilities gain a storage outlet for any capture on gas plants (flue floor 0.22 GJ/t). Co-produced heat links the idea to the enhanced-geothermal story. Utilities' main documented carbon-management support is for 45Q through the Carbon Capture Coalition. Few utility fleets sit near suitable peridotite, and storage at about 0.1 Mt/yr per doublet is small next to a power plant's output. A 1 GW coal unit emits several Mt/yr; that is my estimate, not sourced. Expect interest but little advocacy.
stances.red_line_hit: None. A felt seismic event near a utility asset would create liability exposure.

stances.evidence: The idea keeps S6 work: drilling and stimulation crews, pressure pumping and well services. Unions sit in the Carbon Capture Coalition alongside companies and NGOs (carboncapturecoalition.org). Project InnerSpace frames geothermal as built on 'the technical expertise and infrastructure of the oil and gas industry' (projectinnerspace.org). The benefit to US and North Sea frac workforces is real only where suitable rock exists. Oman and UAE projects mostly employ international service crews, which will not help unions in high-carbon regions of the US and Europe.
stances.red_line_hit: None, unless jobs are offshored to sites far from the communities currently losing high-carbon jobs.

stances.evidence: Gulf host governments look supportive: Oman hosts 44.01's pilots and the UAE hosts expansion pilots (Earthshot). The idea fits COP28 1/CMA.5 paragraph 28, which all parties agreed. In the US, OBBBA 2025 kept and strengthened 45Q, the only carbon-specific credit Congress strengthened. Dedicated storage qualifies, although EPA Class VI permitting for a novel storage type is a practical delay. Governments halt subsurface stimulation after felt quakes. Basel cancelled its EGS project after the 2006 seismicity. Korea ended Pohang EGS research in 2018 after a commission linked the M5.4 2017 quake to fluid injection. England imposed a fracking moratorium in November 2019 after an M2.9 event at Preston New Road, with a 0.5 ML traffic-light threshold (Wikipedia pages for each). Expect support conditional on strict seismic protocols.
stances.red_line_hit: Induced seismicity. Felt events have repeatedly triggered government suspension (Basel, Pohang, UK 2019).

stances.evidence: Host countries such as Oman gain a new export industry (storage-as-a-service) and recognition, for example 44.01's Earthshot. Baum et al. (Nature Communications 2024; N=30,284 in 30 countries, 2022) found Global South publics more supportive of every climate technology. They were also more worried about mitigation deterrence and unequal risk, and both North and South rated engineered CDR highest for moral hazard. Climate-justice advocates such as CIEL document that CCS sites target 'overburdened' communities. If Gulf rock becomes a sink for Northern emissions, the land-use and risk-export critique applies unless benefit-sharing and host consent are built in. Gulf hosts are wealthy petro-states, so the classic S8 framing of the poor bearing the risk fits only partly.
stances.red_line_hit: Mitigation deterrence if used to offset Northern emissions; risk export to host communities without benefit-sharing.

stances.evidence: Consumers would see no direct, visible price, since the idea is a storage service paid by 45Q, removal buyers or industrial pricing. Canada's experience shows that invisible industrial costs survive: the industrial output-based pricing system was kept after the consumer fuel charge was removed (14 Mar 2025). Energy overhead is about 0.55-0.73 GJ/t CO2 (idea's estimate), which is small. Andre et al. (Nature Climate Change 2024; 125 countries, N=129,902) found that 69% of people are willing to contribute 1% of income, so a small embedded cost is tolerable.
stances.red_line_hit: None, unless costs reach consumers as a visible levy.

stances.evidence: Durable-removal buyers value permanence of more than 1,000 years. Frontier's $1.8bn advance market commitment targets durable removal (frontierclimate.com), and mineral storage is the most permanent class. Project finance faces an unresolved technical risk, whether permeability clogs or cracks propagate, with no field data at scale. The idea itself flags that clogging risk falls on investors. Insurers face induced-seismicity tail risk: by 2024 about 96% of Pohang residents had joined compensation suits, and a court awarded 3 million won per resident, potentially about 2 trillion won in total (Wikipedia). 45Q revenue depends on Class VI permits and monitoring for a novel storage type.
stances.red_line_hit: Unquantified liability for induced seismicity; technology risk (permeability loss) before bench and field validation.

stances.evidence: Communities near facilities carry the stimulation-induced seismicity risk. The documented record is strongly negative where people live close by: Pohang (M5.4, 2017; mass litigation; about 80% of residents reported mental-health issues by 2019), Basel (project cancelled), and Preston New Road. In England, opposition to fracking rose to 40% and support fell to 12% by 2019 (BEIS tracker cited on Wikipedia). Many target ophiolites, such as the Samail mountains, are sparsely populated, which lowers exposure. Mineralised storage has no buoyant CO2 plume and closed-loop water handling avoids freshwater draw, which removes two usual local objections. I recall, but did not verify this session, that Carbfix's Coda Terminal in Hafnarfjörður, Iceland faced local resident opposition in 2024-25, a sign that even basalt mineralisation without fracking meets local resistance near towns.
stances.red_line_hit: Local safety: felt induced seismicity from multistage stimulation; 'fracking' next to homes.

stake.coalition_notes:
Overall, the idea is a storage technology, not an emissions source, so most stances depend on two choices: which CO2 it stores, and where it is sited.

Supporters (S2, S3, S4, S6, S7 in Gulf and ophiolite states) form a core much like the 45Q / Carbon Capture Coalition coalition. The idea removes two common S1 objections, EOR and caprock-leak liability, which gives it a better S1 and S8 position than saline-aquifer CCS.

It brings in two new red lines:
- **Induced seismicity (S11, S7, S10).** This has historically killed projects: Basel 2006, Pohang 2017 (M5.4, mass litigation) and the England moratorium of 2019 after an M2.9 event.
- **The 'fracking' frame**, which alienates the anti-fracking wing of S1.

Framing that maximises the coalition:
1. Position it as permanent storage for hard-to-abate process CO2 (cement, ammonia) and for verified removals, citing COP28 para 28's 'particularly in hard-to-abate sectors'. Do not market it as storage for unabated fossil power or as offsets. This keeps CAN's objection evidential rather than categorical.
2. Site it in remote ophiolites, with traffic-light seismic protocols, host-community benefit-sharing and liability or insurance arrangements in place before stimulation.
3. Say 'mineralization wells' or 'geothermal-style doublets', not fracking, and highlight heat co-production and zero freshwater use.
4. Let the bench falsification test (permeability over 60-90 days at 90 C and 150 C) come before any public scale claims. That is what S2 and S10 need.

**Strongest single coalition:** Gulf NOCs and governments, plus 44.01-type firms, plus removal buyers (Frontier). **Weakest link:** S11 wherever people live near the rock.

**Evidence gaps:**
- My web-search budget ran out this session.
- The ADNOC-44.01 UAE partnership details and the Coda Terminal local opposition are from my own knowledge and were not re-verified.
- No documented NGO position on enhanced geothermal or on stimulated mineralisation specifically was found.
- Whether OBBBA kept utility-scale geothermal credits was not confirmed.

critic.fatal_flaw:
Nothing I found is fatal in the strict sense. The storage reaction is exergonic (it releases energy); all energy figures sit above the dissolution floor; natural listvenites in Oman show peridotite can carbonate completely at kilometre scale; and the stakeholder red lines (felt seismicity, the 'fracking' frame) can be designed around with remote siting, traffic-light protocols and narrow positioning. The idea is still close to fatal, because all of its economics depend on one unproven premise: reaction-driven or shear cracking must keep making new olivine surface at centimetre spacing for decades. Without that, the doublets are 39-386x short and storage costs $4-6k/t.

The idea also argues against itself on this premise. Its siting rule ('90 C or hotter, so 3 km or deeper') pushes wells into the stress regime where reaction-driven cracking is least likely. My check (critic_gs3.py) puts vertical effective stress at about 56 MPa at 3 km and about 75 MPa at 4 km. The magnesite crystallisation pressure needed to beat that, RT/Vm x ln(supersaturation), is 27-54 MPa at ln(supersaturation) of 0.25-0.5 and only reaches 108-126 MPa at ln(supersaturation) of 1. Pore fluid in a flowing loop would rarely stay that supersaturated. Lab olivine-carbonation runs under confinement have mostly self-sealed rather than cracked; that is from memory, not re-fetched. So a deep site does not bring 'heat plus cracking'. It trades faster kinetics for less cracking.

Two related points:
- **The 44.01 'about 88% in 45 days' figure is confounded as scale evidence.** It is a fraction of a small injected mass at shallow depth, not a rate per unit of fracture area. It neither supports nor refutes 125 kg CO2/m2/yr.
- **Heat co-production cools the rock the kinetics depend on.** Heat conducted from the rock to 8e5 m2 of face falls to about 3-6 MWth after 5 years (for faces 30-60 C below the rock). The loop removes 15-30 MWth when reinjecting 30-60 C cold. The faces will therefore settle well below the initial rock temperature. A '90 C' site runs at roughly 60 C, which needs 7.6x more area, so the real siting threshold is closer to 130-150 C initial rock temperature, or reinjection at reservoir temperature.
critic.top_fixable_flaw:
The proposed falsifying test cannot falsify the idea. Its kill threshold of 0.5 cm/yr rim growth at 90 C is 17x below the idea's own requirement: 0.1 Mt/yr over 8e5 m2 means 125 kg CO2 per m2 of geometric fracture face per year, which is an 8.6 cm/yr front. A purely diffusion-limited result (1-10 mm/yr in the physics report) would therefore pass the gate and send money to a concept that is 20-170x short at the field-design scale.

The test has three further gaps:
- It is unspecified on confining stress, so it does not test cracking under 3-4 km effective stress.
- It runs at the initial rock temperature rather than the cooled-face temperature the loop will impose.
- It measures rim thickness when the real quantity is CO2 uptake per unit of geometric area, which is what new crack surface would multiply.
critic.suggested_patch:
Replace the bench gate with a test of the design's actual requirement.

1. **Metric.** Measure cumulative CO2 uptake per m2 of the original saw-cut or shear face, by mass balance on the effluent plus TGA. Target 125 kg/m2/yr, which is about 205 g CO2 in 60 days or about 308 g in 90 days for a 50 mm x 100 mm two-face fracture (critic_gs3.py).
   - Kill if uptake is under 1/10 of target (12.5 kg/m2/yr) at every condition. That is the threshold where cost exceeds about $500/t even before re-stimulation.
   - Count as passed only if uptake reaches at least 1/3 of target.

2. **Conditions.** Run triaxial at in-situ effective stress: σ1 − Pp of about 55 MPa (3 km) and about 75 MPa (4 km), with Pp about 30-40 MPa and pCO2 60 bar.
   - Use fluid temperatures of 60 C and 90 C. These bracket the expected cooled face temperature of a 90-150 C site under a 30-60 C reinjection deficit.
   - Add one 150 C control.
   - Also run at 5 MPa effective stress, to isolate the cost of confinement on reaction-driven cracking.

3. **Diagnostics.**
   - Do micro-CT before and after to count new crack surface area. This is the area-multiplication factor; the idea needs 40-400x.
   - Track permeability, with the existing rule to kill if it falls more than 10x within 30 days.
   - Use olivine-rich and serpentinised (30-60%) cores, because Oman peridotite at depth is partly serpentinised.

4. **Design change, conditional on the test result.**
   - Drop surface heat co-production as a revenue line.
   - Reinject the produced water at reservoir temperature: carbonate it hot at about 100 bar or more, where the Spycher model gives about 0.6-0.8 mol/kg at 150 C.
   - Change the siting rule to at least 130 C initial rock temperature.
   - This removes the 15-30 MWth face-cooling conflict and keeps the kinetic window real.

5. **Desk calibration.** Turn the Soltanov/Matter SPE 2026 fit of the Oman pilot into kg CO2/m2/yr over the estimated contacted fracture area. Use that number, not the mineralised percentage, as the field anchor for the 125 kg/m2/yr requirement.

patched_idea.title: Fracture-stimulated mineralization doublets in hot olivine-rich rock (isothermal loop, area-uptake gated)
patched_idea.one_line: Apply Fervo-style horizontal, multistage-stimulated well pairs to hot peridotite or ultramafic rock. CO2-charged water circulates in a closed loop, reinjected at reservoir temperature, and turns CO2 into carbonate permanently. Kinetics put the viable window at initial rock temperature of 130 C or more (about 3.5-4.2 km on a 25-30 C/km gradient). The idea goes ahead only if a confined-core test shows CO2 uptake per m2 of fracture face that is at least 1/3 of the 125 kg/m2/yr design need.
patched_idea.conventional_core: In-situ CO2 mineralization in reactive rock: Carbfix (basalt; Matter 2016, measured) and 44.01 (Oman peridotite, 2025 shallow pilot, about 88% of a small injected mass mineralized in 45 days). The 44.01 figure shows that mineralization happens quickly. It is not a rate per unit of fracture area, so it does not show that the 125 kg CO2/m2/yr design rate is achievable. That anchor has to come from the desk calibration below.
patched_idea.graft: Shale/EGS completion technology: long horizontal laterals, 40-stage stimulation, and an injector-producer doublet as at Fervo Project Red/Cape. It is used to create reactive surface area and to recirculate the carrier water. Unchanged.
patched_idea.mechanism:
Natural fractures limit the area current mineralization pilots can reach, and freshwater supply limits scale (Carbfix uses about 25 t water per t CO2).

A stimulated horizontal doublet in hot olivine-rich rock creates about 8x10^5 m2 of geometric fracture face per well. Water is pumped through the fracture network, produced, re-carbonated and reinjected, so freshwater use is about zero.

Patched operating rule: the produced water stays hot. It is re-carbonated at reservoir temperature and at least 100 bar, where CO2 solubility is about 0.6-0.8 mol/kg at 150 C (Spycher-type model; modelled), and is reinjected without cooling. Surface heat co-production is dropped as a revenue line. Extracting heat would remove 15-30 MWth per doublet while conduction resupplies only about 3-6 MWth after 5 years (critic estimate, modelled). The fracture faces would then settle 30-60 C below the initial rock temperature, which would cost 4-8x in reaction rate.

The chemistry: forsterite dissolution consumes CO2 to make magnesite. The reaction's volume increase can either clog the rock or propagate cracks (Kelemen's 'reaction-driven cracking'). Whether new reactive surface keeps forming at centimetre spacing under in-situ effective stress is the single premise the economics rest on.

The idea is explicit about a tension in its own design. Hotter, deeper siting speeds the kinetics but raises effective stress to 67-80 MPa at 130 C sites. Magnesite crystallization pressure, RT/Vm x ln(supersaturation), reaches only about 27-63 MPa at ln(supersaturation) of 0.25-0.5 and about 108-126 MPa only at ln(supersaturation) of 1. Cracking at depth is therefore not assumed; it is what the gating test measures.
patched_idea.target: Large ophiolite and ultramafic bodies near CO2 sources or DAC: Oman/UAE (Samail; ADNOC/44.01), plus US and other ultramafic provinces. Only zones with initial rock temperature of 130 C or more qualify; shallow, cool peridotite is rejected. Basalt targets are secondary. The storage is durable, needs no caprock, and uses about 1.6 Gt olivine per Gt CO2.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
Computed with Palandri and Kharaka (2004) forsterite kinetics (subsurface_ideas.py; patch check in patch_gs3.py). All figures are modelled, not measured.

Design requirement: 0.1 Mt CO2/yr per doublet over 8x10^5 m2 of geometric face. That is 125 kg CO2 per m2 per year, or a reaction front of about 8.6 cm/yr into each face (about 69,000 m3 of rock per year at 70% olivine). Stoichiometry: at most 1.60 t forsterite per t CO2.

Reactive area needed, as a multiple of the geometric face area, at pH 5 and face temperature:
- 60 C: 3,900x
- 90 C: 513x
- 110 C: 158x
- 130 C: 54x
- 150 C: 21x

The isothermal loop keeps face temperature near the initial rock temperature. A 130-150 C site therefore needs about 20-55x surface multiplication from fracture branching or reaction-driven cracking. A '90 C' site cooled to about 60 C would need about 3,900x and is rejected.

Depth and stress (normal gradient 25-30 C/km, surface 25 C):
- Rock at 130 C sits at 3.5-4.2 km, with vertical effective stress of 67-80 MPa.
- Rock at 150 C sits at 4.2-5.0 km, with 80-96 MPa.

Water and energy:
- Carrier water is 28-38 t per t CO2 (0.6-0.8 mol/kg), recirculated hot.
- Circulation pumping takes 0.19-0.50 GJ/t (5-10 MPa loop pressure drop).
- CO2 compression to about 100 bar takes 0.40 GJ/t (it was 0.35 GJ/t at 60 bar).
- The total is about 0.6-0.9 GJ/t, or about 1-2.5% of world electricity per Gt/yr.

Cost: if uptake reaches only 1/10 of the requirement, the doublet count rises 10x and cost exceeds about $500/t before any re-stimulation (critic estimate).
patched_idea.who_gains: S3 and S7 in Gulf states with ophiolites (Oman, UAE): a storage business using frac and EGS skills. S6 (frac crews during shale downturns). S4 Gulf industry (ammonia, steel, cement) needing storage. S1 and S2: mineral permanence over more than 10,000 yr, no caprock dependence and no EOR. S10 investors: a cheap kill gate comes before any field capital is committed. S8 host countries, if benefit-sharing is designed in.
patched_idea.who_loses: S11 near sites: induced seismicity from stimulation and water handling. Deeper (3.5-5 km), more stressed targets raise the stakes, so remote siting and traffic-light protocols are needed. The anti-fracking part of S1, which may reject 'fracking for carbon' framing despite the climate benefit. Basalt and saline-aquifer storage competitors lose some share. Clogging or self-sealing risk falls on S10 investors if the gate is passed marginally. Geothermal co-revenue is forgone by design.
patched_idea.closest_known_work: Kelemen and Matter 2008 (PNAS): in-situ carbonation of peridotite, explicitly proposing hydraulic fracturing plus heating. Kelemen et al. 2011 (Annu Rev): recipes for enhanced in-situ storage. Natural Oman listvenites, which show complete carbonation of peridotite at kilometre scale over geological time. 44.01 Oman pilot (Nature 2025, about 88% in 45 days; a fraction of injected mass, not a rate per area). Soltanov/Matter SPE 2026 fit of the Oman pilot. Carbfix (Matter 2016). Nguyen et al. (ARMA 2026, LANL): induced shear fractures raise peridotite permeability up to 5 orders of magnitude and sustain carbonation. Dai et al. 2026: thermo-hydro-chemical model of fractured peridotite. Fervo Cape and Project Red horizontal EGS (drilling time down about 75%, S-1/A 2026).
patched_idea.cheapest_falsifying_test:
Bench test (3-4 months, LANL-type triaxial rig or a university lab).

Samples: 50 mm x 100 mm cores with a saw-cut or shear fracture (two faces, 0.01 m2 geometric area). Use both olivine-rich dunite and 30-60% serpentinized peridotite.

Conditions:
- Flow CO2-charged water at pCO2 of 60-100 bar and pore pressure of 35-45 MPa.
- Run triaxial at in-situ effective stress of about 67 MPa and about 80 MPa (the 130 C siting window), plus one 5 MPa run to isolate what confinement costs reaction-driven cracking.
- Use fluid temperatures of 130 C and 150 C (the isothermal design), plus 90 C to check the degraded case if reinjection runs cold.
- Run each for 60-90 days.

Measurements:
- Cumulative CO2 uptake per m2 of original face, by effluent mass balance plus TGA/XRD. The design target of 125 kg/m2/yr equals about 205 g in 60 days or 308 g in 90 days.
- Micro-CT before and after, to measure the new-crack surface multiplication (20-55x is needed at 130-150 C).
- Permeability throughout.

Kill if any of these holds:
- (a) Uptake is under 1/10 of target (12.5 kg/m2/yr; under about 20 g in 60 days) at every in-situ-stress condition.
- (b) Permeability falls more than 10x within 30 days at both temperatures under in-situ stress.
- (c) Micro-CT shows no surface multiplication above 5x under in-situ stress.

Count as passed only if uptake is at least 1/3 of target (about 68 g in 60 days) under in-situ stress.

Desk calibration: convert the Soltanov/Matter SPE 2026 fit of the 44.01 Oman pilot into kg CO2/m2/yr over the estimated contacted fracture area. Use that number, not the mineralized percentage, as the field anchor for the 125 kg/m2/yr requirement.

fix.change_summary:
I applied the critic's patch without changing the core (in-situ peridotite mineralization) or the graft (Fervo-style horizontal multistage doublets with closed-loop carbonated water).

1. **The falsifying test now tests the actual requirement.** The old gate killed only below 0.5 cm/yr of rim growth at 90 C, which is 17x below the design need. The new metric is CO2 uptake per m2 of original fracture face against the 125 kg/m2/yr requirement: about 205 g in 60 days for a 0.01 m2 two-face core. It kills below 1/10 of target and passes only at 1/3 of target or better.
2. **The test now runs at in-situ conditions.** Cores are confined at the in-situ effective stress of the new siting window (about 67-80 MPa), with a 5 MPa control.
3. **The test adds two diagnostics.** Micro-CT measures how much new crack surface forms, and serpentinized cores are included alongside olivine-rich ones.
4. **The face-cooling conflict is removed.** Surface heat co-production is dropped as revenue, and produced water is re-carbonated hot at 100 bar or more and reinjected at reservoir temperature.
5. **The siting rule is raised from 90 C to at least 130 C initial rock temperature.** On a 25-30 C/km gradient that means 3.5-4.2 km. I state the resulting stress-versus-crystallization-pressure tension openly instead of assuming cracking.
6. **The 44.01 '88% in 45 days' figure is relabelled.** It is evidence that mineralization is fast, not evidence for a rate per unit of fracture area. A desk calibration converts the SPE 2026 pilot fit into kg/m2/yr.

I re-ran the numbers in patch_gs3.py:
- **Area multiplication needed:** 54x at 130 C and 21x at 150 C, against 3,900x at 60 C.
- **Bench mass targets:** match the critic's.
- **Energy:** compression to 100 bar is 0.40 GJ/t, so the total is about 0.6-0.9 GJ/t.

The mechanism itself is unchanged; only operating parameters, siting and the test changed.

idea.title: Retire-and-store: dedicated CO2 storage in depleted oil fields whose hydrocarbon rights are permanently extinguished
idea.one_line: A conservation-easement-style covenant permanently extinguishes production rights in a depleted oil field that becomes a dedicated CO2 store. That gives S1 an enforceable no-EOR, keep-it-in-the-ground guarantee, gives S3 payment for marginal residual reserves, and costs about 6-15% of a $500/t carbon-removal credit.
idea.conventional_core: Dedicated geological CO2 storage in depleted oil reservoirs, which have the best-characterized traps, seals and data (TRL 9).
idea.graft: Conservation easements and land-trust reserve retirement (permanent, recorded restrictions that run with the property), applied to the subsurface hydrocarbon estate of the storage complex.
idea.mechanism:
Under OBBBA (2025), 45Q pays the same for EOR as for dedicated storage, so an operator storing CO2 in a depleted oil field will rationally choose EOR. That is S1's sharpest red line (Climate Action Network position 7) and a source of CDR-buyer distrust.

The covenant has four parts:
- Storage operator, mineral owners and a land trust record a perpetual extinguishment of hydrocarbon production rights within the storage complex.
- Owners are compensated from a buyer premium.
- The field is plugged for production and converted to Class VI dedicated storage, run with the same reservoir-engineering team.
- CO2 comes preferentially from DAC or BECCS, where the premium is affordable.
idea.target: Permian and Gulf Coast depleted oil fields near DAC hubs (e.g. Stratos) and BECCS sources. The aim is high-integrity carbon removal that S1 and Frontier-type buyers will accept.
idea.quantitative_claims:
Computed in subsurface_ideas.py.

Cost to the operator: forgone EOR margin of 2-3 bbl per t CO2 × $15-25/bbl netback (assumptions) = $30-75/t CO2. That equals 35-88% of the $85/t point-source 45Q credit, which makes it unaffordable for point-source CO2 without a premium. It equals only 6-15% of a $500/t DAC credit, which makes it affordable for removal.

Climate benefit of not producing the EOR oil: 0.86-1.29 t CO2 gross per t stored (0.43 t CO2/bbl assumed), or 0.17-0.65 t net after 50-80% market replacement.

Energy: compression only (floor 0.28 GJ/t to 150 bar; separation 0.47 GJ/t floor for the DAC source, per the verifier).
idea.who_gains: S1 (an enforceable no-EOR guarantee, plus barrels kept in the ground). S10 CDR buyers (Microsoft, Frontier): a removal quality tier. S3 depleted-field owners (paid for marginal residual reserves plus storage fees and pore-space lease). S11 mineral and pore-space owners (compensation). S6 (storage operations jobs). S2 (cleaner removal accounting).
idea.who_loses: EOR operators and CO2-for-EOR pipeline owners (lost CO2 supply). S7 producing states (forgone severance tax on retired barrels). Point-source capture projects, for which the premium is unaffordable. Some S3 groups, which may resist setting a 'stranded reserves' precedent.
idea.closest_known_work: Frontier and Microsoft CDR procurement rules that exclude EOR storage. 1PointFive Stratos dedicated Class VI wells. Lease buyouts and 'keep it in the ground' instruments (Ecuador's 2023 Yasuni Block 43 referendum; Arctic lease cancellations), from memory. Pore-space ownership statutes (North Dakota, Wyoming). Carbon takeback obligation (Allen, Jenkins et al. 2021). Supply-side leakage literature (replacement 50-80%, from memory and unverified).
idea.why_different: Today's 'no-EOR' assurances are contractual promises by the storage operator that apply only to the CO2 sold. This idea attaches a perpetual, recorded property restriction to the hydrocarbon estate itself, so the field cannot be produced later by anyone. It prices that restriction explicitly as a $30-75/t premium. It is mainly a socio-technical idea, and its physics is conventional.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test:
Three steps (about 6 weeks in total):
1. A cash-flow model for 3 depleted Permian San Andres units, comparing EOR plus 45Q with dedicated storage plus the covenant, to get the required premium in $/t.
2. A structured interview or survey experiment with about 20 S1 organisations (CAN members) and 5 CDR buyers, asking whether the covenant changes their acceptance and their willingness to pay.
3. A legal memo on whether Texas law allows perpetual extinguishment of a mineral estate.

Kill if most S1 respondents still reject storage in oil fields, or if the required premium exceeds about $100/t.
idea.family: Perpetual covenant extinguishing hydrocarbon rights in depleted fields converted to dedicated CO2 storage

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: Yasuni-ITT Initiative (Ecuador, 2007-2013) and the 2023 Yasuni Block 43 referendum
closest.overlap: Paying for a perpetual suspension of extraction from a specific oil field. Ecuador asked $3.6B over 13 years, about half the forgone revenue. Only $13.3M was ever delivered, the scheme was cancelled in 2013 and drilling began in 2016; the 2023 referendum later banned extraction. This is the direct precedent for 'pay to keep a named field's barrels in the ground'. It shows that a sovereign promise without a durable instrument can be reversed, which is the failure the covenant is meant to fix. It had no CO2 storage component, and the field was undeveloped, not depleted. Verified by fetch.

closest.title: Trust for Public Land purchase and retirement of PXP's Hoback Basin leases, Wyoming (2012), under the Wyoming Range Legacy Act (2009)
closest.overlap: A land trust bought existing oil and gas leases and permanently retired them, paid for by donors. This is exactly the 'graft' mechanism of conservation buyers extinguishing hydrocarbon rights. Fetching confirmed that the 2009 Act withdrew 1.2M acres from new leasing but left existing leases intact. The TPL deal itself (about $8.75M for about 58,000 acres) is from memory; its page could not be fetched (HTTP 403). There was no storage component, and the leases were undeveloped federal leases rather than a depleted private mineral estate.

closest.title: Federal lease cancellations and buyouts: Badger-Two Medicine, Montana (Solenex and others, 2016-2023); ANWR Coastal Plain lease cancellations (2023)
closest.overlap: Precedent for government-led permanent extinguishment of hydrocarbon rights, sometimes with lease buybacks. These were not market-priced, and none were tied to CO2 storage. From memory, not re-verified here.

closest.title: Harstad (2012) 'Buy Coal! A Case for Supply-Side Environmental Policy', Journal of Political Economy; supply-side and leakage literature, e.g. Erickson and Lazarus on oil supply elasticity
closest.overlap: The theoretical basis for buying and retiring fossil deposits as climate policy. It covers the leakage and market-replacement question behind the 0.17-0.65 t net benefit claim. From memory; the JPE page returned 403.

closest.title: Frontier, Microsoft, Puro.earth and Isometric CDR criteria excluding EOR; 1PointFive Stratos and other dedicated Class VI storage in the Permian
closest.overlap: These already deliver the 'no-EOR' quality tier for DAC and BECCS CO2: buyers will not pay for EOR-stored tonnes, and DAC hubs use dedicated saline or depleted-reservoir Class VI wells. That takes away much of the claimed buyer benefit, because premium removal tonnes already avoid EOR without a covenant. The covenant adds only a no-future-production guarantee for the surrounding hydrocarbon estate. The Isometric module text was not retrievable; this entry rests on known public criteria.

closest.title: Pore-space and mineral-estate law for CO2 storage: ND and WY pore-space statutes, Texas HB 1284 (2021) and Class VI primacy, Louisiana 2024 CCS law; Class VI area-of-review rules
closest.overlap: These existing regimes already restrict production that would penetrate a Class VI storage complex, and they define who owns pore space as distinct from minerals. They partly supply the protection the covenant would add, and they are where the Texas question (mineral estate dominance, and whether perpetual extinguishment is valid) gets decided. From memory.

closest.title: Carbon takeback obligation (Allen, Jenkins et al., 2021) and 'geological net zero' proposals
closest.overlap: These link fossil extraction to an obligation to store CO2 geologically. Related framing, but they impose the obligation on producers rather than retiring a reserve. From memory.

art.what_is_new:
I found no precedent for the specific combination proposed here. That combination has three parts:
(a) a perpetual, recorded conservation-easement-style restriction that extinguishes the hydrocarbon estate of a depleted field;
(b) attaching that restriction to the field's conversion into a dedicated Class VI CO2 store;
(c) pricing the restriction explicitly as a $30-75/t premium, bundled into a removal-credit quality tier.

Each part exists separately:
- Paid retirement of named oil reserves (Yasuni-ITT, TPL Hoback lease retirement, federal lease cancellations).
- Supply-side buyout theory (Harstad 2012).
- No-EOR CDR procurement rules and dedicated DAC Class VI storage (Frontier and Microsoft; Stratos).
- Pore-space and Class VI area-of-review law that already limits production through a storage complex.

Caveats:
1. My web-search budget ran out on the first query. The verdict rests on two verified fetches (Yasuni-ITT, and the Wyoming Range Legacy Act's lease-withdrawal terms) plus prior knowledge. I could not exclude a recent (2024-26) CDR registry methodology or startup that already sells 'retired-reserve' storage tiers. A targeted search on 'avoided extraction credit', 'mineral rights retirement carbon storage', and Isometric and Puro geological-storage permanence requirements should be run before relying on the NOVEL part.
2. The claimed buyer benefit is weaker than stated. Frontier and Microsoft tonnes already exclude EOR, so the covenant's marginal value is the keep-it-in-the-ground supply-side benefit, and that is subject to the unverified 50-80% leakage assumption. It is not the no-EOR guarantee itself.
3. Class VI area-of-review rules and state pore-space statutes already partly restrict future production in the storage complex.

phys.assumptions:
All figures below are as the script printed them. Tags: [src] = fetched this session, [recall] = from memory and not re-verified, [assume] = my assumption.

What the cost figures measure
- The headline cost is the covenant's incremental cost per tonne of CO2e it avoids. The counterfactual is the same DAC CO2 going to EOR, which also stores it.
- From a Monte Carlo of 200k draws: P10 $189, P50 $271, P90 $384 per t avoided.
- Identity used: $/t avoided = premium per bbl / (0.43 × (1 − replacement)). This does not depend on bbl/t.
- Alternative framing, storage side only (premium + T&S, excluding capture) per t of (stored + avoided): P50 $83/t CO2e.
- Full chain with DAC at about $450/t: P50 $412 per t CO2e.

Thermodynamic floors (verifier)
- The covenant does no separation itself.
- DAC source: 20.47 kJ/mol = 0.465 GJ/t (upstream). BECCS ethanol source: 0.0025 GJ/t.
- Ideal isothermal compression from 1 to 150 bar: 0.282 GJ/t (78 kWh/t). This matches the idea's 0.28 claim. Real CO2 is dense-phase above about 74 bar, so 0.282 is a conservative bound and nothing violates it.

Storage-step energy (electricity)
- Low/base/high: 0.31 / 0.41 / 0.53 GJ_e/t, i.e. 85-148 kWh/t for compression, pipeline boost and injection [recall: IPCC SRCCS 2005, NETL].
- Second-law efficiency against the compression floor is 92% / 69% / 53%.
- Dedicated storage saves the EOR recycle compression: about 0.27-0.54 GJ_e per t net CO2 at 2-3x gross/net injection [assume].
- Full chain including DAC: 5.3-10.5 GJ/t. The covenant adds about zero energy.

Checks on the idea's own numbers
- 2-3 bbl/t × $15-25/bbl = $30-75/t. That is 35-88% of the $85 45Q credit and 6-15% of a $500 DAC credit. The arithmetic checks.
- Net CO2 utilisation of 5-10 Mcf/bbl [recall] gives 1.9-3.8 bbl/t, so the idea's 2-3 bbl/t is inside the range.
- Gross avoided emissions: 0.86-1.29 t per t stored. Net after 50-80% replacement: 0.17-0.65 t. Both check. The 0.43 t CO2/bbl figure is [src] EPA's GHG equivalencies calculator.
- 45Q parity [src]: 26 USC 45Q as amended by P.L. 119-21 sets one $17 base rate for both storage and utilisation (×5 = $85) for facilities placed in service after 4 July 2025. This confirms the idea's premise.

Price inputs
- Oil [src]: EIA STEO, September 2026. Brent averaged $91/b in August 2026; the 2027 forecast is $74/b. I set WTI at Brent minus about $4 [assume].
- Royalty 12.5-25% [assume]. Texas severance tax 4.6% [recall]. EOR opex plus amortised conversion capex $22-40/bbl [assume].

The premium when every rights holder is counted
- At WTI $60/$70/$87, the working-interest netback is $15.8/$23.4/$34.4 per bbl, but royalty owners are owed another $12.0/$14.0/$17.4 per bbl.
- Monte Carlo: operator-only premium (the idea's framing) P10/P50/P90 = $38/$63/$92 per t stored. Premium including all owners: $67/$97/$134 per t stored.
- The all-owners premium is 13-27% of a $500 DAC credit, and 78-158% of the $85 45Q credit.

Dedicated-storage T&S cost
Case unit: 10,000 acres, 30 m net pay, 12% porosity. CoolProp CO2 density 763 kg/m3 at 40 C and 140 bar. Capacity is 11/28/44 Mt at 10/25/40% storage efficiency.
- Legacy wells: 500 at $75-300k each = $1.3-5.4/t.
- Deterministic T&S: $16.5 / $32.0 / $58.9 per t. Capex is annualised at 8% over 25 years. Electricity is $40/$60/$90 per MWh.
- The Monte Carlo uses $8-28/t, my recall of the US onshore range. That is lower than the deterministic base case, so treat the deterministic base as conservative.
phys.resource_needs:
Scale is limited by how much DAC and BECCS CO2 is near Permian and Gulf Coast depleted fields, not by pore space.

Scale cases (stored + net avoided, Gt/yr)
| Case | Stored | Net avoided | Storage energy (share of world primary) | Forgone EOR oil |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Low 2035 | 0.005 | 0.002 | 0.0003% | 34 kbbl/d |
| Base 2035 | 0.020 | 0.008 | 8.1 PJ/yr (0.0013%) | 137 kbbl/d |
| High 2035 | 0.080 | 0.030 | 0.0052% | 548 kbbl/d |
| Ceiling: all US purchased-CO2 EOR volume (~65 Mt/yr [recall]) | 0.065 | 0.024 | — | — |

- Even 0.1 Gt/yr stored would avoid only 0.038 Gt/yr, or 0.07% of world GHG.
- Pore space: the base case needs about 18 units of 28 Mt each over 25 years. US oil and gas reservoir capacity is about 186 Gt [recall NATCARB], so this does not bind.
- Materials: standard wells, compressors and monitoring wells, plus re-plugging about 500 legacy wells per unit.
- Land: no new surface land. Each covenant covers about 40 km2 of subsurface estate.
- Water: none incremental; less than EOR, because produced-water handling stops.
- Electricity: about 105-148 kWh per t stored.
phys.violations:
No physics violations.
- The compression floor is 0.282 GJ/t ideal-gas, and real CO2 in the dense phase needs less. The claimed 0.28 GJ/t matches it.
- Every energy case (0.31-0.53 GJ/t) is above the floor.

Economic understatement, which is not a physics problem:
- The idea prices the covenant at the operator's netback only ($30-75/t). It leaves out royalty owners, who also hold the estate being extinguished (about $12-17/bbl).
- Counting all private owners, the Monte Carlo premium is P50 $97/t, P90 $134/t. 46% of draws exceed the idea's own $100/t kill line (5% under the operator-only framing).
- At the August 2026 oil price ($91 Brent), the all-owners premium is $129/t at 2.5 bbl/t, well above the kill line.
- Excluding royalties is a modelling error. It is not heroic, but it makes the "6-15% of a $500 credit" headline optimistic; the corrected figure is 13-27%.
phys.key_uncertainties:
1. Market replacement of retired barrels (50-80%) is assumed and was not verified this session; the web-search budget was exhausted. Cost per t avoided scales with 1/(1 − replacement): $15/bbl gives $70/t at 50% replacement and $174/t at 80%. This is the dominant driver of the climate-benefit figure.

2. The oil price swings the premium about 2x: $69/t at WTI $60 versus $129/t at WTI $87, both at 2.5 bbl/t. Paying a fixed perpetual price exposes buyers and owners to oil-price risk. Pricing per bbl at the time of injection is more defensible than per t.

3. The target choice has a confound. Permian San Andres units, including residual oil zones, are the fields with the highest EOR option value, so they carry the largest premium. Post-CO2-flood fields or depleted gas fields would make the covenant cheap, but they also have little real oil to forgo. In those fields the benefit is mainly integrity and acceptance (S1 and buyers), not avoided emissions. The idea should state which value it sells.

4. Legal feasibility [recall, unverified]:
   - Texas has no compulsory unitization, so a perpetual extinguishment needs consent from every fractional mineral owner across the storage complex. Holdouts are likely.
   - Texas's rule against perpetuities must be checked, along with whether conservation-easement statutes can bind a severed mineral estate.
   - The CO2 plume or pressure front could reach adjacent leases outside the covenant.

5. The counterfactual may already be dedicated storage. Frontier and Microsoft rules already exclude EOR, and Stratos holds Class VI permits [recall]. If the DAC CO2 would have been stored without EOR anyway, the covenant's additional avoided emissions are only the option value of a later EOR project, which could be near zero. Oxy's "net-zero oil" positioning is the counter-case.

6. Scale assumptions are from memory: Stratos at 0.5 Mt/yr, US ethanol CO2 at about 45 Mt/yr and mostly in the Midwest, and the pace of DAC hubs after DOE funding changes. The base case of 0.02 Gt/yr stored is speculative.

7. T&S cost spread: the deterministic base is $32/t versus $8-28/t in the Monte Carlo. Legacy-well density and Class VI area-of-review corrective action could push it higher.

8. S7 forgone severance tax is $2.8-4.0 per bbl, about $7-10/t at 2.5 bbl/t. This loss is not compensated in the design.

stances.evidence: The covenant fixes only one of the Climate Action Network's red lines, number 7 (no EOR/EGR). It is the sharpest of them, and the map's EOR-parity entry shows NGO and watchdog opposition centres on it. At least three other CAN red lines are still hit. (4) CAN 'will not support' negative emissions or offsets 'as an alternative to stringent emission reductions', and this idea's revenue is a CDR credit sold to emitters. (8) DACCS has 'no place' in steep-reduction scenarios, and the idea prefers DAC as its CO2 source. (9) Storage liability is likely to shift to the public; a perpetual covenant makes the store perpetual too. Wikipedia's DAC article reports environmental-group 'disdain' that DAC lets companies keep polluting 'while greenwashing', and calls Oxy's $1.1bn Carbon Engineering purchase (2023) an attempt to extend the fossil industry's life. Project Drawdown's Jonathan Foley calls DAC a 'greenwashing exercise'. On the other side, S1 has backed keep-it-in-the-ground instruments: the 2023 Yasuni Block 43 referendum and Arctic lease cancellations (from memory, not re-verified). A recorded, perpetual retirement of reserves is new ground for that wing. Expected split: (a) pragmatic carbon-management NGOs, such as those inside the Carbon Capture Coalition, probably support it as the highest-integrity storage tier; (b) the CAN core probably still opposes it because DACCS and offsets remain. The idea's own kill test (about 20 CAN members) is the right measurement.
stances.red_line_hit: Mitigation deterrence and offsets (CAN 4), DACCS (CAN 8), and storage liability shifting to the public (CAN 9). It also pays fossil mineral owners. It neutralises the EOR red line (CAN 7) for the stored CO2 and the retired field only, not for EOR elsewhere.

stances.evidence: IPCC AR6 WGIII says CDR is needed for net zero and that CCS 'could allow fossil fuels to be used longer' (C.4.4). This idea separates storage from fossil extension, which removes the mechanism the IPCC flags. Oxford Net Zero (Allen et al.) backs storage obligations, and cleaner removal accounting fits the scientists' push for like-for-like permanence. Expected caveats from S2: (1) the claimed climate co-benefit of 0.17-0.65 t CO2 net per t stored depends on a supply-leakage range (50-80% market replacement) that is from memory and unverified. (2) Adverse selection: fields offered for retirement will be those with the least remaining EOR value, so the barrels kept in the ground may be well below 2-3 bbl/t. (3) A depleted field does not by itself make storage permanent; MRV for legacy wellbores still matters.
stances.red_line_hit: None categorical. The risk is overclaiming additionality for 'barrels kept in the ground'.

stances.evidence: Owners of genuinely depleted fields gain three income streams: payment for marginal residual reserves, storage fees and pore-space lease. This matches the S3 support for storage-revenue models seen in Equinor/Northern Lights and the takeback debate. EOR operators lose, and Occidental is the clearest case. It ran about 140 kb/d of CO2-EOR (2020, Wikipedia). It bought Carbon Engineering for $1.1bn (Nov 2023). It bought Holocene in Apr 2025, described as 'active in enhanced oil recovery'. Its DAC strategy therefore rests on CO2 for EOR. The industry also just won 45Q EOR parity in OBBBA (Jul 2025; Enverus estimated a 40% cut in some E&P costs), and a buyer-funded no-EOR tier works against that win in the voluntary market. API backs 'market-based' and 'predictable' frameworks. A voluntary, buyer-paid covenant fits that wording, so a formal API objection is unlikely, but members can be expected to resist the stranded-reserves precedent. Calculation (stakeholder_retire_store.py): royalties forgone at 12.5-25% royalty are $15-56/t CO2 (2-3 bbl/t at $60-75/bbl). They fall on mineral owners and are separate from the operator netback, so the $30-75/t premium probably understates what S3 and mineral owners together must be paid.
stances.red_line_hit: A recorded 'stranded reserves' precedent, perpetual loss of option value on reserves, and erosion of the EOR-parity market they just won.

stances.evidence: The idea is aimed at DAC and BECCS removal. For point-source industrial CO2 the premium is unaffordable: $30-75/t is 35-88% of the $85/t 45Q credit, a verified calculation. Cement, steel and chemicals are therefore neither helped nor hurt directly. Their documented interest is cheap access to storage for process emissions (the GCCA roadmap, Brevik/Northern Lights). Mild risks: if 'no-EOR covenant' becomes the buyer quality norm, it could later be demanded of industrial CCS. Separately, if retired depleted fields become DAC-dedicated stores, S4 might compete with DAC for nearby pore space, though DAC already competes for it.
stances.red_line_hit: None directly. There is a latent risk of a costlier storage-quality norm being extended to point-source CCS.

stances.evidence: The economics are the same as for S4. Gas or coal flue capture under the $85/t point-source credit cannot carry a $30-75/t premium, so utilities with capture projects would keep using EOR or ordinary Class VI storage. Utilities are buyers in neither the voluntary CDR market nor the covenant. The Carbon Capture Coalition (S5 members) lobbies for 45Q generally, and the idea leaves 45Q intact.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: Unions belong to the Carbon Capture Coalition and support carbon-management jobs. The idea keeps the reservoir-engineering team for Class VI operations, and DAC hub construction is unaffected. Production jobs from forgone EOR (well work, field operations) are lost. The volume is small: 10 Mt/yr of retired-EOR equivalent is about 68 kb/d, or 0.07% of world supply. Expect no organised union position unless retirement is framed as a precedent for retiring Permian production generally.
stances.red_line_hit: Small local loss of production jobs. It becomes a red line only if framed as a keep-it-in-the-ground policy for the Permian.

stances.evidence: US federal: there is no new public cost, because 45Q pays the same either way and the premium is buyer-funded. The current administration's energy-dominance framing (from memory) cuts against perpetually retiring domestic reserves, but nothing requires federal action. Texas: severance tax forgone is small. The Texas Comptroller lists 4.6% for primary oil, 2.3% for EOR, and a further reduction to 1.15% for EOR using in-state anthropogenic CO2. At 2-3 bbl/t and $60-75/bbl, that is about $1.4-5.2/t CO2 at EOR rates. A bigger obstacle (from memory, not verified this session): the state is a major Permian mineral owner through University Lands and the Permanent University Fund, which are managed for revenue, so state-owned minerals could probably not be extinguished without legislative action. Non-US governments: EU and UK policy favours dedicated storage. The NZIA obliges oil and gas licence holders to provide storage capacity, which suggests acceptance of storage-not-EOR models abroad.
stances.red_line_hit: Retiring domestic reserves (an energy-security and 'energy dominance' framing). Fiduciary or constitutional limits on state-owned mineral estates (from memory). The severance-tax loss is small (computed).

stances.evidence: Baum et al. 2024 surveyed 30 countries (N=30,284, fielded 2022). Global South publics supported every technology more than Northern publics, but worried more about mitigation deterrence and unequal risk. Both North and South rated engineered CDR (DACCS, BECCS) as the highest moral-hazard risk. The idea sells US-sited DAC/BECCS removals mostly to Northern corporate buyers, which matches the climate-justice concern about offsetting continued Northern emissions. On the other hand, keep-it-in-the-ground causes have strong S8 resonance (Yasuni 2023, from memory), and the idea involves no land grab because it uses depleted oil fields, not arable land; Frontier's criteria favour sinks that 'do not compete for arable land'. Expect Global South governments to be indifferent, and climate-justice advocates to split between welcoming a binding keep-it-in-the-ground precedent and rejecting offsets.
stances.red_line_hit: Offsets and mitigation deterrence by Northern emitters. No land-grab red line, because the sites are depleted fields.

stances.evidence: Consumers do not pay: the premium is borne by voluntary CDR buyers and there is no visible consumer price, which avoids the Canada 2025 'Axe the Tax' failure mode. The oil-supply effect is negligible. A 10 Mt/yr programme forgoes about 68 kb/d, or 0.066% of about 103 Mb/d world supply (computed), so no measurable fuel-price effect is expected. Public opinion data (Pew May 2024: 65% of US adults prioritise renewables over fossil fuels; Andre et al. 2024: 69% globally willing to contribute 1% of income) suggest mild latent approval, but there is no salience.
stances.red_line_hit: None (no price rises).

stances.evidence: Durable-CDR buyers form the demand side. Frontier ($1.8bn AMC; members include Stripe, Google, Shopify, Anthropic, JPMorgan and Salesforce) requires storage 'permanently (>1,000 years)', a path to under $100/t, and no competition for arable land. A no-EOR covenant offers verifiable integrity, addressing buyer reputational risk. Caveat: the premium is only 6-15% of a $500/t credit today but 30-75% at Frontier's under-$100/t target, so its relative cost rises as DAC gets cheaper. If royalty compensation ($15-56/t computed) is added, the all-in premium could exceed the idea's own $100/t kill threshold. Investors in EOR-heavy E&Ps, and insurers facing perpetual liability for a store that can never be produced, may be wary. Perpetuity has legal limits: under IRS 26 CFR 1.170A-14(g)(6), a 'perpetual' easement can still be 'extinguished by judicial proceeding'.
stances.red_line_hit: The premium does not scale down as CDR prices fall. Perpetual liability (insurers). EOR-exposed investors face a precedent for stranded reserves.

stances.evidence: Mineral and royalty owners are paid under the design, but the forgone royalty ($15-56/t CO2 at 12.5-25% royalty, computed) is separate from the operator netback used to size the $30-75/t premium. Unless royalty owners are paid explicitly they lose income and will object; this is the main design gap. Other legal points: IRS 1.170A-14(g)(4) already restricts mineral interests in conservation easements, but only against surface mining, so subsurface oil rights extinguishment has no direct federal precedent. Pore-space and split-estate law differs by state, and the Texas statute was not retrieved this session. For communities near facilities, retiring production removes flaring, traffic and produced-water disposal, a local benefit. CO2 transport and injection safety concerns persist (the Feb 2020 Satartia, Mississippi CO2-EOR pipeline rupture; eminent-domain opposition to the Summit Carbon pipeline in the Dakotas and Iowa; both from memory, not re-verified this session). Co-locating DAC at the storage field, as at Stratos, reduces pipeline exposure.
stances.red_line_hit: Uncompensated royalty loss. Local CO2 pipeline and injection safety. Eminent domain if pipelines are needed.

stake.coalition_notes:
How the coalition lines up:
- Most likely supporters: S10 durable-CDR buyers (Frontier, Microsoft), S2 scientists, owners of genuinely depleted fields within S3 (storage fees plus payment for residual reserves), and the pragmatic carbon-management wing of S1.
- Likely opponents: EOR-centred S3 operators. Occidental's DAC-for-EOR model and the 2025 OBBBA EOR-parity win are directly undercut. Texas as a mineral owner (University Lands/PUF, from memory) and S7 energy-dominance politics also oppose.
- The CAN core of S1 stays opposed, because the covenant removes only red line 7 (EOR). Red lines 4 (offsets), 8 (DACCS) and 9 (public liability) remain.
- Indifferent: S4, S5, S6 and S9. The premium is unaffordable for point sources ($30-75/t is 35-88% of $85/t), and the oil-supply and consumer-price effect is negligible (10 Mt/yr ≈ 68 kb/d ≈ 0.07% of world supply).
The idea therefore widens the coalition only at the margin, adding pragmatic S1 and buyers. It does not bridge to activists in general.

Numbers computed this session (climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/stakeholder_retire_store.py; all assumption-based, not measured):
1. Royalties forgone are $15-56/t CO2 at 12.5-25% royalty, 2-3 bbl/t and $60-75/bbl. This sits outside the operator netback, so the true all-in premium may be roughly $45-130/t and could breach the idea's own $100/t kill threshold. Add royalty owners to the cash-flow test.
2. Texas severance tax forgone is small: about $1.4-5.2/t at EOR rates of 2.3% and 1.15% (Texas Comptroller), and $5.5-10/t at the 4.6% primary rate. The S7 fiscal objection is therefore weak; the political and energy-security objection is the real one.
3. The premium's share rises as CDR gets cheaper: 6-15% of a $500/t credit, 17-42% of $180/t, and 30-75% at Frontier's under-$100/t target.

Design risks:
- Adverse selection: fields with the lowest EOR value will be offered first, which shrinks both the premium and the claimed 'barrels kept in the ground' benefit. The 0.17-0.65 t net figure rests on unverified 50-80% leakage.
- Perpetuity is legally soft. IRS 1.170A-14(g)(6) allows judicial extinguishment, and (g)(4) restricts mineral interests only against surface mining, so there is no direct federal precedent for extinguishing subsurface oil rights.

Source limits: the web-search budget was exhausted (200/200) at the start of this task, so the analysis relies on the documented-positions map plus pages fetched this session:
- Frontier homepage (criteria)
- 26 CFR 1.170A-14 (Cornell LII)
- Texas Comptroller crude oil tax page
- Wikipedia: Direct air capture; Occidental Petroleum; Conservation easement

Unverified items (from memory) include Yasuni, Satartia, Summit, University Lands/PUF, and the US administration's 'energy dominance' framing. The map's two entries on OBBBA 45Q EOR parity conflict: one cites the Global CCS Institute, the other says it is unverified from a primary source. Resolve this before relying on the S3 analysis.

critic.fatal_flaw:
None that cannot be designed around. The physics is conventional: storage energy of 0.31-0.53 GJ/t sits above the 0.282 GJ/t compression floor. Two problems are serious but not fatal.

1. Scale. About 0.02 Gt/yr stored and about 0.008 Gt/yr net avoided is roughly 0.01-0.07% of world GHG. This is a niche integrity instrument, not a climate solution, and it should be labelled that way rather than killed.

2. Texas mineral-estate law. Without compulsory unitization, a perpetual extinguishment needs every fractional mineral owner to agree. If Texas also cannot bind a severed mineral estate perpetually (rule against perpetuities), the instrument as written fails in Texas. That can be avoided by having the trust buy the mineral estate in fee, or by siting in states with pore-space and unitization statutes (ND, WY, LA). So it is not fatal, but the 6-week legal memo has to settle it before anything else.

Weakest point that comes close to fatal: additionality for the CDR-buyer pitch. Frontier and Microsoft tonnes already go to dedicated, non-EOR Class VI storage. For the target buyer, then, the covenant's only real product is avoided extraction, and that is an avoidance claim, not a removal.
critic.top_fixable_flaw:
The idea prices the covenant in the wrong unit and sells the wrong product.

Forgone oil depends on the field's remaining reserves, not on how many tonnes are stored. My check (critic_retire_store.py) used the TEA's own case unit: 10,000 acres, 30 m pay, 12% porosity, giving OOIP of about 535-611 Mbbl. At an assumed 8-18% incremental CO2-EOR recovery, the field holds about 43-110 Mbbl of EOR oil. Spread over 11-44 Mt of capacity, that is anywhere from 1.0 to 10 bbl per t stored. The fixed '2-3 bbl/t' therefore has no physical basis. A per-tonne premium either overpays (small reserve, large store) or underpays and invites holdouts (the reverse).

The bundle also mixes two claims:
- a removal (the DAC tonne, which is already non-EOR for Frontier-type buyers)
- an avoidance claim (barrels never produced, with 50-80% leakage)

Integrity bodies and S2 will reject selling these as one 'removal quality tier', and that bundling is what exposes the idea to the CAN-4 offset/mitigation-deterrence charge.

The real cost is a lumpy, all-owner, field-level buyout. At $28-52/bbl (all owners' netback plus royalty, from the TEA), it comes to about $1.4-5.7B per unit undiscounted, or roughly half that in present value if barrels would have come over 20-30 years. That works out to $130-605/t net avoided across 50-80% leakage. The idea's 6-15% figure hides all of this.
critic.suggested_patch:
Split the instrument in two, and price the retirement per field rather than per tonne.

**(1) Storage.** Keep DAC/BECCS storage as an ordinary Class VI removal credit sold to Frontier-type buyers. Add the covenant's no-future-production clause for the storage complex as a cheap permanence and MRV feature, not as a priced premium. Fields that are truly depleted (post-CO2-flood, or depleted gas) have little EOR option value left, so this costs little.

**(2) Retirement.** Sell barrel retirement as a separate, clearly labelled supply-side avoidance unit, using a reverse auction run per field:
- Owners bid a $/bbl price to extinguish an independently certified residual-EOR reserve (an SPE-PRMS-style audit of contingent resources).
- Every working-interest and royalty owner is paid, which closes the S11 and royalty gap.
- Payment is spread over the would-be production profile and indexed to strip price at each date, which removes the perpetual oil-price exposure.
- Credits are issued per bbl retired × 0.43 t × (1 − a conservative replacement factor, e.g. 0.8 until verified). That covers the leakage uncertainty and the adverse-selection worry that fields are offered because their EOR value is low.

**Legal structure.** Use fee acquisition of the mineral estate by a land trust or a charitable entity with mission lock, not a covenant. That avoids the perpetuity and severed-estate problems. Run the pilot first in a state with pore-space and unitization statutes (ND/WY/LA), not Texas.

**Pressure management.** Add a carve-out allowing fluid withdrawal. Any incidental oil produced is either reinjected or its credits are cancelled.

**Revised kill test:**
- The reverse-auction clearing price for 3 candidate units is above about $150/t net avoided at 80% replacement, or
- fewer than 1 in 3 units can assemble 100% owner consent, or
- the CAN-member survey shows the unbundled avoidance unit does not shift acceptance.

**Caveats.** The 8-18% recovery factor and the $/bbl ranges are assumptions or recalled from memory (the web-search budget was exhausted, so nothing new was verified). The field figures are undiscounted and are a sizing check, not a valuation.

patched_idea.title: Retire-and-store: dedicated CO2 storage in depleted oil fields plus a separately sold, per-field auction to retire their residual oil
patched_idea.one_line: Two separate instruments on one depleted field. (1) Ordinary Class VI DAC/BECCS storage, sold as removal, with a recorded no-future-production clause over the storage complex as a cheap permanence feature. (2) A land trust buys the field's residual-EOR mineral estate in fee through a per-field reverse auction, and the barrels retired are sold as a clearly labelled supply-side avoidance unit, credited conservatively. This is a niche integrity instrument, not a climate-scale solution.
patched_idea.conventional_core: Dedicated geological CO2 storage in depleted oil reservoirs (Class VI, TRL 9), which have the best-characterized traps, seals and data.
patched_idea.graft: Conservation easements and land-trust reserve retirement (permanent, recorded restrictions and mission-locked fee ownership that run with the property), applied to the subsurface hydrocarbon estate of the storage complex. The patch keeps this graft but implements it as fee acquisition rather than a bare covenant.
patched_idea.mechanism:
Problem: under OBBBA (2025), 45Q pays the same for EOR as for dedicated storage. A depleted-field storage operator therefore keeps an option to produce oil, which is S1's sharpest red line (CAN position 7) and a source of distrust. The patch splits the original single priced covenant into two products and prices retirement per field, not per tonne.

**(1) Storage (the removal product).** DAC or BECCS CO2 goes into Class VI dedicated storage and is sold as an ordinary removal credit to Frontier-type buyers. The storage operator, the mineral owners and a land trust record a no-future-production restriction covering the storage complex. This is a permanence and MRV feature (it stops later production from disturbing the plume or seal), not a priced premium. It is offered only for fields that are truly depleted, meaning post-CO2-flood or depleted-gas, where little EOR option value is left and the restriction is cheap.

**(2) Retirement (the avoidance product, never bundled with removal).**
- An independent SPE-PRMS-style audit certifies the field's contingent residual-EOR resource, in bbl, including an economic test at strip price.
- A per-field reverse auction follows. All working-interest and royalty owners jointly bid a $/bbl price to sell the mineral estate covering that resource.
- The winning field's mineral estate is bought in fee by a land trust or charitable entity with a mission lock. Fee ownership avoids the perpetuity and severed-estate problems of a covenant.
- Payment is spread over the would-be production profile and indexed to strip price at each date, which removes perpetual oil-price exposure.
- Every owner is paid, which closes the royalty and S11 gap.
- Avoidance credits are issued as bbl retired × 0.43 t CO2/bbl × (1 − replacement factor). The factor defaults to a conservative 0.8 until leakage is verified, which also covers the adverse-selection risk that owners offer fields because their EOR value is low.

**Pressure management.** A carve-out allows fluid withdrawal for pressure management. Any incidental oil produced is either reinjected or its avoidance credits are cancelled.

**Siting.** The pilot runs first in a state with pore-space and unitization statutes (ND, WY or LA), not Texas. The physics and reservoir engineering stay conventional, run by the same field team.
patched_idea.target: Depleted, post-CO2-flood oil units, and depleted gas fields, in ND, WY or LA for the pilot (Permian and Gulf Coast only after the legal memo), near DAC hubs or BECCS sources. The removal product is aimed at Frontier-type CDR buyers. The avoidance product is aimed at buyers and philanthropies seeking supply-side 'keep it in the ground' outcomes, explicitly labelled as avoidance.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
All figures are from retire_store_patch.py in the scratchpad. The inputs are the critic's case unit and assumptions: 8-18% incremental EOR recovery and $28-52/bbl all-owner netback including royalty, both recalled from memory and not verified. Results are undiscounted, or carry a crude 0.5 present-value factor for 20-30-year production. They are a sizing check, not a valuation.

**Field size.** The case unit is 10,000 acres, 30 m pay and 12% porosity. At So 0.7-0.8 and Bo 1.2, OOIP is about 535-611 Mbbl, so residual EOR oil is about 43-110 Mbbl. Across 11-44 Mt of storage capacity, that is 1-10 bbl per t stored. This is why retirement is priced per field and not per tonne. The original fixed 2-3 bbl/t and the '6-15% of a $500/t credit' figure are withdrawn.

**Retirement cost per field.** Undiscounted: $1.2-5.7B. With the 0.5 PV factor: about $0.6-2.9B.

**Cost per tonne net avoided** (0.43 t CO2/bbl):
- At 80% replacement: $326-605/t undiscounted, $163-302/t with PV.
- At 50% replacement: $130-242/t undiscounted, $65-121/t with PV.

**Break-even bid.** To clear the $150/t kill threshold at 80% replacement, owners would have to accept at most about $13/bbl in PV terms, or about $32/bbl at 50% replacement. That level is plausible only for fields with marginal EOR economics, and the conservative crediting factor is meant to cover exactly that adverse selection.

**Climate scale.** About 0.02 Gt/yr stored and about 0.008 Gt/yr net avoided, roughly 0.01-0.07% of world GHG. This is a niche integrity instrument.

**Energy.** Storage needs compression only: a floor of 0.28 GJ/t to 150 bar, and the critic's estimate of 0.31-0.53 GJ/t. Separation for a DAC source has a 0.47 GJ/t floor (verifier), with 5-10+ GJ/t measured in real plants.
patched_idea.who_gains: S1 gets a recorded no-production guarantee on storage fields and an honestly labelled keep-it-in-the-ground product, with no offset bundling. S10 CDR buyers get unchanged removal integrity plus a cleaner permanence feature, and supply-side buyers and philanthropies get an auditable avoidance unit. S3 depleted-field owners get paid at a market-discovered price for marginal residual reserves, on top of storage fees and pore-space lease. S11 royalty and pore-space owners: every owner is paid. S6 gets storage operations jobs. S2 gets removal and avoidance accounted separately, with explicit leakage.
patched_idea.who_loses: EOR operators and CO2-for-EOR pipeline owners, because retired fields drop out of the EOR supply. S7 producing states lose severance tax on retired barrels. Some S3 groups, which may resist a stranded-reserves precedent. Avoidance buyers, who pay $65-605/t net depending on replacement and discounting, which is expensive next to other avoidance options.
patched_idea.closest_known_work: Frontier and Microsoft CDR procurement rules that already exclude EOR storage, which is why the covenant is now a permanence feature rather than a premium. 1PointFive Stratos dedicated Class VI wells. Lease buyouts and keep-it-in-the-ground instruments (Ecuador's 2023 Yasuni Block 43 referendum; Arctic lease cancellations), from memory. Conservation land-trust fee acquisition. Pore-space ownership and unitization statutes (ND, WY), from memory. Supply-side leakage literature (replacement 50-80%, from memory and unverified). SPE-PRMS contingent-resource classification. Carbon takeback obligation (Allen, Jenkins et al. 2021).
patched_idea.why_different:
Today's no-EOR assurances are contractual promises by the storage operator that apply only to the CO2 sold. This idea goes further in three ways:
- It puts the hydrocarbon estate itself under mission-locked fee ownership or a recorded restriction, so nobody can produce the field later.
- It discovers the retirement price per field by reverse auction against a certified reserve, instead of guessing a per-tonne premium.
- It sells removal and avoidance as separate units, with explicit leakage crediting.

It is mainly a socio-technical idea, and its physics is conventional.
patched_idea.cheapest_falsifying_test:
About 6-8 weeks, in this order.

**1. Legal memo first** (ND, WY, LA, and Texas for comparison). Can a land trust hold severed mineral fee with a perpetual mission lock? Can unitization statutes bind holdouts?
