6. **Incumbent sunk cost.** Existing Chinese and Indian plants already have incinerators funded through CDM, China's HCFC phase-out plan and the Multilateral Fund, and that sunk cost favours incineration.
7. **Competing uses.** The R-23 refrigerant and etch-gas market (about 1 kt/yr reported) likely pays more per kg than VDF, but it is saturated.

Stakeholders:
- S4 gains modestly.
- S1/S2/S8 gain if collection actually improves.
- S7 (China) gains a credible compliance narrative.
- S9 is neutral.
- Operators who under-report HCFC-22 output lose from the mass-balance trail. That creates the main resistance, and it is also the case in which the idea most needs to work.

stances.evidence: Climate-focused NGOs back the core goal. NGOs campaigned against CDM HFC-23 projects as perverse incentives: 19 refrigerant plants were expected to get 18% of all CERs by 2012, against 12% for 2,372 wind projects. The EU banned HFC-23 CERs from May 2013 (Wikipedia, Clean Development Mechanism). Their objection was to over-reward, not to abatement. My script finds VDF revenue of about $1,100-5,100 per t HFC-23 ($0.08-0.35 per tCO2e). The CDM-era credit was about EUR 234,000 per t HFC-23 (20 EUR/t x GWP 11,700), so the over-production incentive is roughly 50-200x weaker. Anti-PFAS NGOs are the opposing wing. ChemSec (28 Aug 2026, 'Fluoropolymers and the cotton candy approach to PFAS lobbying') opposes any fluoropolymer exemption from the EU PFAS restriction. It cites a 2026 global inventory that found 'consistent patterns of PFAS contamination around all the plants', and it disputes industry claims about end-of-life destruction. CAN's 2021 red lines on offsets would apply if conversion were ever credited. Source: https://chemsec.org/fluoropolymers-and-the-cotton-candy-approach-to-pfas-lobbying/
stances.red_line_hit: Two red lines. (1) Fluoropolymer/PFAS lock-in: the idea ties HFC-23 abatement economics to PVDF demand. (2) Offsets: only if conversion is credited, which would re-create the CDM perverse incentive. The idea's own design (no credits, small revenue) avoids the second.

stances.evidence: Atmospheric scientists documented the gap that motivates the idea. Wikipedia's Fluoroform article cites 2024 research: the HFC-23 decrease is 'much less than has been reported' and does not meet Kigali. Stanley et al. 2020 and the 2024 Comm. Earth Environ. inversion are cited in the map; I did not re-fetch them (paywall redirect). The idea makes inversion-based MRV a design element, which matches this community's work. Expected caveat from S2, by analogy rather than documented for this idea: the simple baseline of destruction already required by Article 2J(6) since 1 Jan 2020 costs about EUR 0.2-0.5/tCO2e (CDM-era figure). They would therefore ask whether the excess comes from idle destruction or undeclared production before crediting any product incentive. Precedent, from memory and not re-verified here: after inversions exposed unexpected CFC-11 emissions from eastern China (Rigby et al. 2019), enforcement cut them within about two years (Park et al. 2021). That realized outcome shows MRV plus enforcement working without product revenue.
stances.red_line_hit: None. The risk is that S2 judges the product layer unnecessary if the attribution test shows undeclared HCFC-22 production.

stances.evidence: Oil and gas has no documented stake in fluorochemical by-products. The only touchpoint is methane used as a co-reactant: for about 14 kt/yr HFC-23, roughly 3 kt/yr CH4 at stoichiometry, which is negligible. The idea does not touch upstream emissions, pricing or EOR. The map shows S3 supports technology-led, non-fee approaches (OGCI, API 'market-based policies'). This idea is neither a fee nor a mandate on S3.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: The direct beneficiaries are fluorochemical producers, which often make both HCFC-22 and PVDF/VDF in the same clusters. Incumbent chemical makers backed Kigali and the US AIM Act because the phasedown created markets for their patented substitutes (map: AIM Act endorsed by the US Chamber, AHRI and the Alliance for Responsible Atmospheric Policy). The CDM showed HCFC-22 producers adopt HFC-23 abatement readily when it pays. Article 2J(6) already obliges destruction 'to the extent practicable' from 2020 (UNEP Ozone Secretariat text), so a revenue route turns a compliance cost into a small profit. Within S4 the support is conditional. Operators with undeclared HCFC-22 output or idle destruction units lose under a mass-balance trail. Capex for a high-temperature HF-handling reactor must be repaid by only about $1-5k per t HFC-23. The bench test (VDF selectivity at least 40%, by-product handling) is not yet done. The industry also faces PVDF regulatory risk: Wikipedia notes concern that EU PFAS rules could pose 'an existential risk' to PVDF.
stances.red_line_hit: An audit trail that exposes undeclared production or non-operation of destruction units. This applies to non-compliant operators only, and is the idea's purpose.

stances.evidence: Power utilities have no exposure. The energy input is about 2.19 GJ per t HFC-23 (task-brief calculation), roughly 30 GJ/yr per kt, which is negligible for any grid. There is no documented utility position on HFC-23.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: The idea runs at existing HCFC-22 sites and needs a small number of added reactor jobs. It causes no job losses in coal, oil or steel regions. VDF from this route substitutes for part of the HCFC-142b route, often at the same firms (idea brief), so jobs move rather than disappear. There is no documented union position on HFC-23 conversion. Unions in the Carbon Capture Coalition back capture-and-convert framings, but that is an analogy, not evidence.
stances.red_line_hit: None. There is occupational exposure to HF and fluorinated by-products, but this is a worker-safety issue, not a jobs one.

stances.evidence: Governments share a treaty obligation: Article 2J(6) requires each HCFC-22-producing party to destroy HFC-23 'to the extent practicable' from 1 Jan 2020 (UNEP Ozone Secretariat). China accepted Kigali on 17 Jun 2021 (Wikipedia, Kigali Amendment). A product-revenue route that produces auditable records gives China a way to show compliance against inversion-reported excess, and the battery supply chain has an energy-security interest in a second VDF route. Two splits. (a) A trail reconcilable against inversions is diplomatically sensitive for any government whose reported HCFC-22 or destruction data are under-stated. (b) The EU is developing a universal PFAS restriction that covers -CF2- polymers such as PVDF (Wikipedia, PVDF), so EU regulators may hesitate to endorse a scheme that anchors abatement to PVDF demand. Neither government position is documented for this specific idea; both are inferred from the treaty text and the restriction process.
stances.red_line_hit: Sovereignty and face: third-party mass-balance audits of national production data. EU: possible conflict with PFAS restriction policy.

stances.evidence: Wikipedia's Fluoroform article says HCFC-22 and HFC-23 production is now concentrated in developing countries, mainly China and India. Kigali brought in Article 5 countries through slower schedules and Multilateral Fund money (map). Climate-justice critics of the CDM objected that HFC-23 windfalls flowed to 'a few projects in advanced developing countries' (Wikipedia, CDM). This idea pays no credits, so that distributional objection does not apply. There are no land, food or resource-transfer implications. The Baum 2024 survey finds the moral-hazard concern centres on engineered CDR, which this idea is not.

stances.evidence: There is no consumer price channel. PVDF binder is a 1-2% solution used in electrode slurry (Wikipedia, PVDF), a trivial share of battery cost. The VDF volume, about 5-10 kt/yr at 40-80% selectivity (my script), is small against PVDF capacity (not verified). The map shows consumers punish visible prices (Canada's consumer carbon levy was removed from 1 Apr 2025), and this idea creates none.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: The decarbonisation is real and verifiable, about 204 Mt CO2e/yr at AR6 GWP100 14,600 for the 14 kt/yr pool (my script), but there is no tradeable asset. Without credits there is no carbon-market product for investors or buyers, which is deliberate. Investors' main concern would be PFAS liability around fluorochemical sites. From memory, not re-verified: 3M's roughly $10.3bn US water-utility PFAS settlement (2023). ChemSec, which engages institutional investors, reports contamination around all fluoropolymer plants (Aug 2026). Insurers would treat a new HF/fluorocarbon pyrolysis unit as added process-safety exposure at sites already carrying PFAS liabilities.

ChemSec (28 Aug 2026) cites a 2026 global inventory showing PFAS contamination around all fluoropolymer plants. A Lyon-area precedent, from memory and not verified this session (the Arkema Wikipedia page did not cover it): the PVDF-producing Pierre-Bénite site faced public PFAS controversy in 2022. Adding a high-temperature CHF3/CH4 pyrolysis unit means handling HF co-product (about 1.6-3.2 kt/yr across the global pool, my script). It could also form toxic perfluorinated by-products, which the idea's own falsification test flags as a failure condition. Mitigating factors: the unit sits at existing sites and substitutes for incineration or plasma destruction, which also has emission and by-product issues. It also cuts leakage from the HCFC-142b feedstock route. Most target sites are in eastern China, where documented community opposition is sparse in sources I could access; that is an absence of evidence, not support.

stake.coalition_notes:
Summary: this idea faces less opposition than any CO2 idea, because it targets an existing treaty obligation (Montreal Protocol Article 2J(6), destruction of HFC-23 since 2020). No major industry loses. S3, S5, S6 and S9 are neutral, S2 and S4 support, and the contest is between the climate wing of S1 and its anti-PFAS wing, plus S11.

Framing that holds the coalition:
(1) Present it as a compliance and enforcement device, never as a source of credits. The CDM HFC-23 history is exactly what S1, S8 and EU regulators remember. At about $1-5k per t HFC-23 against EUR 234k per t of CDM-era credit value, revenue is 50-200x too small to drive over-production. Say so explicitly.
(2) Present VDF as a substitute supply for the HCFC-142b route, not added PVDF output. This is the main counter to ChemSec and EEB-type PFAS objections. If net PVDF output rises, the anti-PFAS wing of S1, S11 and EU regulators will oppose.
(3) Lead with the simple baseline. Enforcing existing destruction, which costs pennies per tCO2e, plus inversion-based MRV may do the job on its own. The CFC-11 precedent (2018-2021, from memory, not re-verified) is a realized outcome where exposure plus enforcement worked without product revenue. The idea's own attribution test is therefore decisive for stakeholders too: if the excess comes from undeclared HCFC-22 production, S2 and S7 will prefer enforcement and the product layer adds little.
(4) The sensitive point is S7 (China): a mass-balance trail is valuable to everyone else and uncomfortable for any under-reporting jurisdiction.

Unverified this session:
- The 2024 Comm. Earth Environ. and Stanley 2020 primary texts (paywall redirect).
- ECHA's current treatment of fluoropolymers and batteries in the PFAS restriction (403).
- EUROBAT and EIA positions specific to HFC-23 or PVDF (pages lacked content).
- The Arkema Pierre-Bénite and 3M settlement details (from memory).
- PVDF capacity figures.
The web search budget was exhausted, so evidence came from targeted fetches only.

critic.fatal_flaw:
None that cannot be designed around. The physics is fine: dH is 2.19 GJ per t HFC-23 and the separation floor is about 1e-6 GJ per t CO2e. The cost is cents per t CO2e. The scale is small, about 0.08 Gt CO2e/yr in the base case, but it is real. The closest thing to a fatal flaw is behavioural, and it is a realized-outcome problem, not a physics one.

Article 2J(6) has applied since 2020, and China's 2021 control notice already allows 'resource utilisation'. Engineering-scale conversion already exists: the Sinochem Lantian / Zhonghao Chenguang unit, which won an award in 2024. Even so, measured 2023 emissions were still 14.0 kt (Adam et al. 2024, AGAGE inversion), about five times what was reported. So the policy experiment 'conversion is permitted and profitable' has in effect been run, and the gap did not close.

The marginal economics agree. My check is critic_non_co2_6.py in the scratchpad climate folder. Once the unit is built, the operating margin is about +$1,200 per t HFC-23 in the base case (+$4,000 low, -$1,300 high). That is $24 per t HCFC-22 at a 2% by-product rate, about 1% of the product price. Venting costs the operator nothing. An operator who vents today because a working destruction unit is still a hassle will not change for 1% of revenue, and one hiding undeclared HCFC-22 output will not change at all.

So 'revenue makes them capture every kilogram' should be treated as falsified unless shown otherwise. The idea survives only if the product layer is demoted and the enforcement and MRV layer becomes the core. That is a rescue by redesign, not a fatal flaw.
critic.top_fixable_flaw:
The 'auditable mass-balance trail' is circular. VDF sales document only the HFC-23 that was converted. They contain no information about the kilograms that were vented. To reconcile them, you need the plant's HCFC-22 output, and that is exactly the number an under-reporting operator falsifies. Invoices and production records under the operator's own control cannot catch that operator.

The trail therefore adds nothing to existing inversion MRV in the one case that matters: undeclared production or capture that is bypassed. The idea's falsification test 2 shows this is the most likely explanation. Adam et al. 2024 find that non-HCFC-22 sources explain only 0.4-1.5 kt of the eastern-China excess.
critic.suggested_patch:
1. **Anchor the balance on inputs the operator does not control.** HCFC-22 is made by CHCl3 + 2HF -> CHClF2 + 2HCl. Per t HCFC-22 that takes 1.381 t chloroform and 0.463 t HF, and yields 0.843 t HCl, all from executed stoichiometry. HF comes from fluorspar under Chinese quota, and chloroform is often bought from outside, so suppliers can report independently.
   - Rule: HFC-23 accounted for (converted plus destroyed, metered at the unit inlet with sealed flowmeters) must be at least the plant-specific by-product ratio times the HCFC-22 production implied by inputs.
   - Set the by-product ratio by one-off isotope or tracer verification at commissioning.
   - Cross-check each plant against city-scale or tall-tower inversion. Plant-cluster inversions already resolve eastern-China HFC-23.
2. **Make destruction and conversion equal compliance routes.** VDF is an optional cost offset where the bench test shows at least 40% selectivity without a halon promoter. The headline 2010 result used CBrF3, an ozone-depleting substance (ODS).
3. **Replace 'revenue makes them capture every kg' with a penalty on unaccounted HFC-23.** Charge each kg missing from the input-side balance at a few $/kg. That is about $0.1-0.3 per t CO2e, small enough to avoid recreating CDM-style perverse incentives, and it sits on top of the CFC-11-style enforcement path (Rigby 2019 to Park 2021).
4. **Re-run the case on the gap, not the plant.** Tie the 0.08 Gt/yr base case to what this input-side enforcement recovers, not to VDF sales. Keep the VDF route explicitly substitution-only, displacing HCFC-142b-route VDF, to hold the anti-PFAS wing of S1, S11 and EU regulators.

patched_idea.title: HFC-23 by-product to vinylidene fluoride for battery-grade PVDF, enforced by an input-side HCFC-22 balance
patched_idea.one_line: HCFC-22 plants must account for every kilogram of their HFC-23 by-product, either by destruction or by co-pyrolysis with methane to vinylidene fluoride (VDF), the PVDF battery-binder monomer. The balance is anchored on HF and chloroform inputs that the operator does not control. Kilograms missing from it carry a penalty of a few dollars each, and VDF sales serve only as an optional cost offset. The target is the gap between measured and reported HFC-23: about 11 kt/yr, or about 164 Mt CO2e.
patched_idea.conventional_core: Kigali Article 2J(6) by-product control: capture HFC-23 at HCFC-22 plants and incinerate or plasma-destroy it (TRL 9). Destruction stays a fully equal compliance route.
patched_idea.graft: Gas-phase co-pyrolysis of CHF3 with CH4 to CH2=CF2. Han, Kennedy, Mackie and Dlugogorski (J. Hazard. Mater. 2010) showed it at lab scale; the related HCFC-22 + CH4 work is in IECR 2010. It is matched to battery-supply-chain PVDF demand in the same industrial clusters, and it is now explicitly the second compliance route and cost offset, not the enforcement mechanism.
patched_idea.mechanism:
Measured HFC-23 emissions are about 5x reported (2023: 14.0 kt, Adam et al. 2024, AGAGE inversion), even though Article 2J(6) and China's 2021 notice already allow 'resource utilisation'. Revenue alone has therefore not closed the gap. The patched mechanism works in four steps.

1. **Input-side balance.** HCFC-22 is made by CHCl3 + 2HF -> CHClF2 + 2HCl. Executed stoichiometry gives 1.381 t CHCl3, 0.463 t HF and 0.843 t HCl per t HCFC-22. HFC-23 co-formation adds about 0.005-0.03 t HF per t HCFC-22 at 1.5-4% by-product. HF traces to quota-controlled fluorspar, and chloroform is often bought from outside, so both suppliers report independently. HCFC-22 output implied by inputs therefore does not rely on the operator's own production records.
2. **Compliance rule.** HFC-23 accounted for (destroyed plus converted to VDF, metered at the unit inlet with sealed flowmeters) must be at least the plant-specific by-product ratio times the input-implied HCFC-22. The ratio is about 31-81 kg HFC-23 per t HF purchased at 1.5-4% by-product, set by a one-off tracer or isotope verification at commissioning.
3. **Penalty, not revenue, drives capture.** Each kilogram missing from the balance is charged a few $/kg, assessed per plant.
4. **Independent cross-check.** Tall-tower and plant-cluster inversions that already resolve eastern-China HFC-23 check the result.

VDF conversion keeps its original role as the product that gives the operator a reason to prefer capture over a pure cost. A VDF sale is also a metered, third-party-visible disposition entry, but it is only the 'converted' term of the balance, not the balance itself. VDF made this way is substitution-only: it displaces HCFC-142b-route VDF, whose feedstock-use HCFC-142b (an ODS) leaks, and adds no new PFAS-family capacity.
patched_idea.target: The measured-minus-reported HFC-23 gap. Taking reported as about 1/5 of the 14.0 kt measured in 2023, the gap is about 11.2 kt/yr (164 Mt CO2e at AR6 GWP100 14,600). Eastern China dominates it, and Adam et al. 2024 attribute only 0.4-1.5 kt of the eastern-China excess to non-HCFC-22 sources. At plant level, one 100 kt/yr HCFC-22 plant at an ASSUMED 1.5-4% by-product rate makes 1.5-4 kt HFC-23 = 22-58 Mt CO2e/yr.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
Executed in patch_non_co2_6.py (scratchpad climate folder):
- **Input balance.** Per t HCFC-22: 1.381 t CHCl3, 0.463 t HF, 0.843 t HCl. Expected HFC-23 per t HF purchased: 31.5 / 41.7 / 61.4 / 80.5 kg at 1.5 / 2 / 3 / 4% by-product.
- **Penalty sizing.** $1, 2, 5 and 10 per kg HFC-23 = $0.07, 0.14, 0.34 and 0.68 per t CO2e. CDM CERs at $10-20/t CO2e were worth $146-292/kg HFC-23, so the penalty is 1-2 orders of magnitude below the level that drove CDM-era over-production. Being a penalty, it rewards no output in any case. It is set above the operator's avoided cost of destruction (CDM-era estimates: well under $1/t CO2e, i.e. a few $/kg; modelled, not measured), so venting stops being the cheaper option.
- **Scale, re-based on the gap rather than VDF sales (scenario shares ASSUMED).** Recovering 25%, 50% or 75% of the 11.2 kt gap = 2.8, 5.6 or 8.4 kt = 41, 82 or 123 Mt CO2e/yr. The critic's 0.08 Gt base case corresponds to about 50% recovery. The share depends on how much of the gap is bypassed capture at declared plants (reachable) versus wholly off-book production (only partly reachable through input tracing).
- **Unchanged from the original.** dH = +153 kJ/mol (2.19 GJ per t HFC-23, about 150 kJ per t CO2e), so energy is irrelevant. VDF stoichiometric yield is 0.915 t per t HFC-23.
- **VDF economics.** These are now only an offset. The critic's run gives a post-build operating margin of about +$1,200 per t HFC-23 (range -$1,300 to +$4,000), about 1% of HCFC-22 revenue at a 2% by-product rate. The VDF route is used only where bench selectivity is at least 40% without a halon promoter; the 2010 result used CBrF3, an ODS.
patched_idea.who_gains:
- S1/S2: the densest climate pollutant per tonne, abated, with independently verifiable accounting and no new PFAS capacity.
- S7 (China and other HCFC-22 producers): a credible, auditable answer to the inversion-reported excess, built on existing fluorspar quota data.
- S4 compliant fluorochemical producers: a level field against under-reporting competitors, plus an optional VDF cost offset.
- Battery and PVDF makers: a second VDF route that does not depend on HCFC-142b.
- S8: Montreal/Kigali-style enforcement with no new consumer cost.
- S9: neutral, since $0.1-0.7/t CO2e is negligible in product prices.
patched_idea.who_loses:
- Operators who vent, or who run undeclared HCFC-22 output: input tracing and penalties expose and charge them.
- HCFC-142b-route VDF capacity: some marginal value is lost, though often to the same firms.
- Incinerator and plasma vendors: minor, since destruction stays an equal route.
- Fluorspar, HF and chloroform suppliers: a new reporting burden.
patched_idea.closest_known_work:
- Han et al., J. Hazard. Mater. 2010 (CHF3 + CH4 to VDF with CBrF3) and the same group's IECR 2010 (HCFC-22 + CH4).
- The Sinochem Lantian / Zhonghao Chenguang HFC-23 resource-utilisation unit, which won an award in 2024 and shows conversion at engineering scale.
- Kigali Article 2J(6) and China's 2021 HFC-23 control notice.
- Measured excess: Stanley et al. 2020 and Adam et al. 2024.
- The enforcement precedent is the CFC-11 episode: inversion detection (Rigby et al. 2019) was followed by enforcement and measured decline (Park et al. 2021).
- CDM HFC-23 projects are the cautionary tale on over-rewarded by-products.
patched_idea.why_different: Prior work treats HFC-23 conversion as chemistry, or destruction as a pure compliance cost. Existing MRV reconciles operator-reported production against inversions, but cannot attribute below the region. Here, compliance is anchored on an input-side mass balance using supplier-reported HF and chloroform that the operator cannot falsify alone. A small per-kg penalty on unaccounted HFC-23 sits on top, and plant-cluster inversion cross-checks it. VDF conversion is retained as an equal compliance route and cost offset that turns a metered fraction into a saleable, substitution-only product. Revenue and penalty both stay at cents per t CO2e, so CDM-style perverse incentives cannot arise.
patched_idea.cheapest_falsifying_test:
Three tests, each needing months and a small budget:
1. **Attribution desk test.** Compare inversion-derived regional HFC-23 against HCFC-22 production implied by fluorspar/HF quota and chloroform trade data, alongside reported production and destruction. Falsified as a climate lever if input-implied production cannot be resolved per plant or province to within the gap: about ±20% of HF flows unattributable.
2. **Commissioning-ratio test at one cooperating plant.** Check whether the by-product ratio is stable enough (CV below about 15% across operating modes) for an input-side balance to flag a 20% shortfall.
3. **Bench co-pyrolysis of CHF3/CH4 without a halon promoter.** If VDF selectivity is below 40% at above 50% conversion, or by-product handling costs more than VDF revenue, the VDF route is dropped and destruction-only compliance remains. This test no longer decides the idea, only its offset.

fix.change_summary:
I applied the critic's four-part patch and kept the conventional core (Kigali Article 2J(6) by-product control) and the graft (CHF3 + CH4 co-pyrolysis to VDF for battery PVDF).

1. **Audit trail.** The circular output-side trail is replaced by an input-side mass balance on supplier-reported HF and chloroform. Executed stoichiometry gives 1.381 t CHCl3, 0.463 t HF and 0.843 t HCl per t HCFC-22, or 31-81 kg HFC-23 expected per t HF at 1.5-4% by-product. The by-product ratio is set at commissioning, and the balance is cross-checked by plant-cluster inversion.
2. **Equal routes.** Destruction and VDF conversion are now equal compliance routes. VDF is an optional cost offset, used only if bench selectivity is at least 40% without the CBrF3 (halon) promoter.
3. **Penalty replaces revenue.** "Revenue makes them capture every kg" is replaced by a per-kg penalty on unaccounted HFC-23. At $1-10/kg that is $0.07-0.68/t CO2e, sized above avoided destruction cost and 1-2 orders of magnitude below CDM credit values ($146-292/kg).
4. **Scale re-based.** Scale now comes from the measured-minus-reported gap: 11.2 kt = 164 Mt CO2e, so 41-123 Mt CO2e/yr at an ASSUMED 25-75% recovery. VDF is kept substitution-only.

Falsification tests now cover input-side attribution and ratio stability; the chemistry test decides only the offset. mechanism_changed is true because the incentive driver changed from product revenue to an input-anchored penalty, and the audit basis changed from VDF sales to supplier inputs, even though the product route and graft are retained.

phys2.assumptions:
Executed with OptiLex's physics.py verifier. Labels: [M] measured, [Mod] modelled, [A] assumption, [K] domain knowledge not re-checked this session; the web-search budget was exhausted, so new sources were limited to the cached Adam et al. 2024 text and Wikipedia.

**Floor and energy**
- **Separation floor.** HFC-23 from a 90% column vent: 0.80 kJ/mol = 0.011 GJ/t HFC-23 = 0.78 kJ/t CO2e. From a 1% fugitive stream: 0.189 GJ/t = 12.94 kJ/t CO2e.
- **Destruction energy [A, order of magnitude].** Plasma or incineration with support fuel at 5 / 15 / 40 GJ/t HFC-23 = 3.42e-4 / 1.03e-3 / 2.74e-3 GJ/t CO2e.
- **VDF reaction.** dH = +153.4 kJ/mol = 2.19 GJ/t HFC-23 = 150 kJ/t CO2e, which confirms the idea's figure.

**Stoichiometry.** The idea's numbers check out: 1.381 t CHCl3, 0.463 t HF and 0.843 t HCl per t HCFC-22, and 31.5 / 41.7 / 61.4 / 80.5 kg HFC-23 per t HF at 1.5 / 2 / 3 / 4% by-product.

**Detection Monte Carlo [Mod]**
- One 100 kt/yr plant with r = 2.5%.
- Flowmeter error CV 2%. Input-implied output CV_P is 2% or 5% (covers CHCl3 yield, inventory and diversion).
- Year-mean by-product-ratio variability CV_r is 5–25%.
- Commissioning bias b is 0 or 20%. This is where the commissioning ratio is set during a low-over-fluorination test, for example with fresh catalyst.
- Flag threshold: one-sided, 5% false-positive rate.

**Cost per t CO2e.** This is social cost; penalties are transfers and excluded.
- **Compliance cost:**
  - Low: the VDF full-cost low case, -$3,052/t HFC-23, from non_co2_6.py. Its selectivity is unverified.
  - Base: Zhao et al. 2023 lifecycle destruction cost, 7.32 CNY/kg = $1.02/kg = $0.070/t CO2e [Mod].
  - High: $3/kg = $0.205/t.
- **MRV programme [A]:**
  - About 50 HCFC-22 plants worldwide [K].
  - Tracer/commissioning test of $0.1–0.3M per plant, annualised at 10% over 10 years.
  - Supplier reporting and audit at $0.05–0.2M per plant per year.
  - 5–15 new tall-tower or flask sites at $0.3–1M/yr each.
  - Total: $4.8M / $12.6M / $27.4M per year, i.e. $0.19 / $0.18 / $0.24 per t.
- **Totals.** -$0.021 / +$0.252 / +$0.440 per t CO2e. The stress case (high MRV and high destruction cost at low abatement) gives $1.279/t.

**Scale [M: Adam et al. 2024]**
- Inputs:
  - Global emissions: 14.0 ± 0.9 Gg in 2023.
  - Reported: 2.8 Gg in 2021.
  - Outside eastern Asia: 8.3 ± 1.7 Gg in 2023.
  - Eastern-China excess over China's report: 3.5 ± 0.5 Gg (2021) and 4.3 ± 0.7 Gg (2022).
- **Low:** 50% of the eastern-China excess and nothing elsewhere = 1.8 kt = 0.026 Gt CO2e/yr.
- **Base:** 75% of the eastern-China excess plus 25% of the rest of the gap = 4.8 kt = 0.069 Gt (0.059 Gt at GWP20).
- **High:** 90% of the eastern-China excess plus 60% of the rest = 8.0 kt = 0.117 Gt.
- GWP100 is 14,600 (AR6). The base case is 0.19% of fossil CO2.
phys2.violations:
Nothing falls below the thermodynamic floor, and nothing is heroic on energy or cost. The cost is cents per t CO2e. There are five quantitative or factual errors.

**1. "Eastern China dominates the gap" is contradicted by the idea's own source.**
- Adam et al. 2024 put 8.3 ± 1.7 Gg of the 2023 emissions outside eastern Asia, which is 59% of the global total.
- The eastern-China excess is about one-third of the gap, as the paper itself says.
- So the inversion cross-check (step 4) is unavailable for most of the gap. The paper says Russia and India cannot currently be verified top-down.
- The idea's 50–75% gap-recovery scenarios (82–123 Mt) therefore need adoption and new monitoring well beyond China. The executed base is 0.069 Gt; 0.08 Gt is optimistic.

**2. The 0.4–1.5 kt non-HCFC-22 figure is mis-attributed.** In Adam et al. it is a global estimate covering HFC-32, HFC-125 and TFE/HFP production. It is not specific to eastern China.

**3. The detection claim is too tight.** The idea says a by-product-ratio CV below about 15% lets the input balance flag a 20% shortfall.
- At CV 15%, the Monte Carlo gives a minimum vented fraction detected with 80% probability of 0.34–0.36. The probability of detecting 20% venting is only 0.32–0.34.
- Flagging 20% needs CV ≤ about 5% (v_min 0.14–0.18).
- With a 20% commissioning bias, P(detect | 20% vented) = 0.04–0.05, which is just the false-positive rate. An operator who sets the commissioning ratio in a low-over-fluorination mode can vent about 20% risk-free.
- This is structural, not noise. The commissioning ratio needs periodic or continuous re-verification, for example online GC of the crude stream with an independent audit.

**4. The penalty is undersized at the low end.**
- The required penalty is avoided cost divided by detection probability.
- At the base avoided cost (Zhao lifecycle, $1.02/kg) and detection probability 0.3, the penalty must exceed $3.42/kg. At the high avoided cost ($3/kg) and P = 0.3–0.6, it must exceed $5–10/kg.
- So $1–2/kg does not make venting irrational, while $5–10/kg is robust and still only $0.34–0.68 per t CO2e (GWP100).

**5. Minor errors.**
- The HF increment for HFC-23 co-formation is 0.013–0.034 t per t HCFC-22, not 0.005–0.03.
- The CDM credit equivalence at the CDM-era GWP of 11,700 is $117–234/kg, not $146–292/kg. The conclusion is unchanged: the CDM credit is 50–200x the penalty.
phys2.resource_needs:
**Energy.** 0.009 / 0.071 / 0.320 PJ/yr, which is 1.4e-8 / 1.1e-7 / 5.2e-7 of world primary energy. Negligible.

**Materials from destruction**
- Each t HFC-23 needs 1.59 t Ca(OH)2 and yields 1.67 t CaF2.
- In the base case that is about 7.9 kt/yr of CaF2, which can be recycled as fluorspar-grade material.

**VDF offset.** Base case of 50% selectivity on half the volume gives about 1.1 kt VDF/yr. That is small next to a PVDF market of order 10^2 kt/yr [K], so it carries no market-saturation risk.

**Land and water.** Negligible.

**Institutional needs, which are the real constraint**
- Supplier reporting of chloroform and HF at about 50 plants.
- A commissioning tracer test at each plant.
- 5–15 new monitoring sites: about $5–27M/yr in total MRV.
- Coverage of the 8.3 Gg emitted outside eastern Asia, where networks are currently insensitive.
phys2.key_uncertainties:
**1. Input independence.** This is the crux [K, not re-verified this session].
- Major Chinese HCFC-22 producers are widely understood to be vertically integrated with their own chloromethanes (CHCl3) and anhydrous-HF units.
- Where that holds, the "supplier-reported inputs the operator cannot falsify" anchor collapses back to operator self-reporting.
- HF is also shared across multi-product fluorochemical sites (HFC-32/125/134a, fluoropolymers), so chloroform is the more specific anchor. Its dominant industrial use is HCFC-22 (Wikipedia, qualitative only).
- The claim that fluorspar is quota-controlled was not verified.

**2. By-product-ratio stability within a plant.** Executed detection power depends steeply on it: v_min(80%) is 0.14–0.18 at CV 5%, 0.24–0.26 at CV 10%, 0.34–0.36 at CV 15% and 0.52–0.53 at CV 25%. Commissioning bias can be gamed, as the CDM AM0001 ratio-gaming precedent shows in reverse.

**3. Composition of the gap.** It is unknown how much is bypassed capture at declared plants versus off-book production. Off-book production with self-made inputs is invisible to an input balance. Other sources are also possible: misunderstood emission factors and oxidation/ozonolysis, which Adam et al. flag.

**4. The 59% of emissions outside eastern Asia** (Russia, India, other or unknown) has no top-down verification today.

**5. Destruction costs** are modelled (Zhao 2023), not measured, and so are the MRV programme costs [A].

**6. VDF selectivity without a halon promoter** is unverified. The 2010 bench work used CBrF3. This affects only the low-cost case, -$0.021/t.

**7. Political willingness.** The policy precedent is the CFC-11 episode (Rigby 2019, then Park 2021), which suggests an enforcement response to inversion evidence is achievable. That case had province-level attribution, which exists here only for eastern China.

**Bottom line.** This is a strong-value, low-cost, small-scale lever: 0.03–0.12 Gt CO2e/yr at roughly $0–0.44/t. It is graded plausible rather than strong because the novel enforcement element (input-side balance) has weaker detection power and independence than claimed.

idea.title: Methane-intensity quality differential in gas and LNG contracts
idea.one_line: Treat measured upstream methane intensity like sulphur in crude oil. Gas contracts would carry an automatic, revenue-neutral price differential around a reference intensity, settled by independent measurement and not by certificates or offsets.
idea.conventional_core: Upstream and midstream methane abatement: LDAR, electric or zero-bleed pneumatics, vapour recovery and ending routine venting (TRL 9; IEA GMT 2026 puts more than 35 Mt CH4/yr avoidable at no net cost and about 85 Mt with existing technology, modelled).
idea.graft: The crude-oil quality escalator (sulphur and API-gravity de-escalators in benchmark crude pricing, e.g. the Platts Forties sulphur de-escalator, from memory). A physical quality attribute re-prices every cargo automatically.
idea.mechanism: Each LNG SPA or pipeline import contract carries a standard clause. The price adjusts by a published slope (e.g. $30/t CO2e, GWP100) times the gap between a reference intensity (e.g. 0.5%) and the supply portfolio's measured intensity. Measured intensity is the MORE CONSERVATIVE of two independent methods: operator OGMP 2.0 Level 5 reconciled data, and basin-level satellite or aircraft inversion. Low-leak cargoes earn a premium and high-leak cargoes take a discount, so the market average is roughly unchanged and consumers pay nothing on average. The EU Methane Regulation's 2027 import MRV gives buyers the legal reason to adopt the clause, and the clause turns it from a compliance cost into a price signal. Activist red lines are met: the reductions are measured physical cuts at source, not offsets. 'Carbon-neutral LNG' claims based on offsets are barred by the clause, and nothing is paid for volumes that are not measured. Grounding precedent: the EU Methane Regulation 2024/1787 (enacted), API's stated support for direct methane regulation, and the IMO 2020 sulphur cap (a fuel-quality standard the industry absorbed). It deliberately avoids a per-tonne fee, the S3 red line that killed the US Waste Emissions Charge.
idea.target: Methane in internationally traded gas. LNG is about 411 Mt/yr, about 21.2 bn MMBtu (IGU 2024, from memory, unverified), plus EU pipeline imports. This is a lever on part of the 35-85 Mt CH4/yr abatable fossil methane (IEA GMT 2026, modelled). That is about 1.0-2.5 Gt CO2e GWP100.
idea.quantitative_claims:
All from my script climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/coalition_ideas.py using the OptiLex verifier.
(1) 1 MMBtu of pure CH4 is 19.0 kg (HHV 55.5 MJ/kg).
(2) Cutting intensity from 1.0% to 0.2% avoids 0.152 kg CH4/MMBtu, which is 4.5 kg CO2e (GWP100) or 12.6 kg (GWP20). From 2.0% to 0.2% it avoids 10.2 / 28.2 kg CO2e.
(3) Paying $20/t CO2e for the 1.0%→0.2% step needs $0.09/MMBtu; $50/t needs $0.23/MMBtu. That is 0.8-2.3% of a $10-12/MMBtu LNG price.
(4) The revenue-neutral differential around a 0.5% reference at a $30/t slope is +$0.05/MMBtu at 0.2%, −$0.085 at 1.0% and −$0.26 at 2.0%.
(5) $0.10/MMBtu across all LNG is about $2.1 bn/yr of transfers. That would buy about 106 Mt CO2e/yr (3.6 Mt CH4) at $20/t or 42 Mt at $50/t.
(6) The recovered gas is itself worth $5.3/t CO2e at $3/MMBtu and $19.4/t at $11/MMBtu (GWP100).
(7) Source abatement is energy-positive: about 50 GJ of gas is recovered per t CH4. Removing the same CH4 from ambient air would cost 263 GJ/t CH4 in fan work alone (verifier: 1.93 ppm, 50% removal, 100 Pa).
(8) Settlement needs the two methods to agree within about 0.2 percentage points. Today's Permian methods disagree 7.3x: 0.44% by aircraft (2024) against 3.2% by TROPOMI inversion (2023). Different years are a confound.
idea.who_gains: S3: low-leak producers (Norway, best-practice US and Qatari operators) earn a premium for something they already do. S7: EU, Japan and Korea importers get a workable compliance path for the EU MR with no supply shock. S1 and S2 get measured cuts with no offsets. S9 pays about nothing on average because the scheme is revenue-neutral. S10 gets a priced, measurable risk. S11 near production sites gets VOC and air-quality co-benefits.
idea.who_loses: High-intensity exporters and operators, at about −$0.1 to −$0.3/MMBtu until they abate (e.g. flare-heavy Permian operators, some NOCs). Certificate vendors lose part of their market. S1 groups opposed to any LNG expansion may object that the clause legitimises LNG; the offset-claim ban is meant to answer that. Producers at negative-price hubs (Waha) gain little, because their gas has no value to recover.
idea.closest_known_work: MiQ certified gas and Project Canary/TrustWell differentiated gas (voluntary certificate premia). OGMP 2.0. EU Methane Regulation import MRV equivalence (2027). The Japan/Korea-led CLEAN LNG initiative (2023, from memory). The verified map's open problem on an EU MRV equivalence pathway.
idea.why_different: Certificates are optional premia paid by a few buyers, and they have not moved basin intensity at scale. This proposal makes intensity a contractual quality specification that re-prices every cargo symmetrically. It settles on the conservative of two independent measurements rather than self-reports, so it is revenue-neutral for consumers and penalises leakers without a government fee.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test: A 2-4 week desk study. For the Permian, Haynesville and Marcellus in the SAME years (2023-2025), compute methane intensity from public TROPOMI-based inversions and from Carbon Mapper/aircraft plume inventories. FALSIFIED as a settlement basis if the two methods disagree by more than 0.3 percentage points absolute or more than 2x for the same basin-year. In that case the clause cannot be settled and measurement R&D must come first. Second check: compile 2023-2026 certified-gas premium quotes. If premia stay below $0.02/MMBtu with no intensity response, the voluntary route is falsified, and only a mandated clause through EU MR adoption can work.
idea.family: Revenue-neutral measured methane-intensity price differential in gas/LNG contracts

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: Commission Recommendation (EU) 2026/1834 on optional model clauses under the EU Methane Regulation (20 July 2026). Verified: full text read.
closest.overlap: High on the contract vehicle, none on price. This is the EU's own standard clause set for gas and LNG supply contracts under Articles 27-29 of the Methane Regulation. It has four clauses. Clause 1 sets out the importer's status. Clause 2 waives confidentiality so methane data can flow to the Commission's transparency database and 'methane performance profiles'. Clause 3 obliges the seller to supply an MRV-equivalence document of compliance annually from 1 Jan 2027. Clause 4 exempts countries recognised as equivalent. No clause links price to methane intensity, and none involves a bonus or malus or independent measurement. Annex section 1 also has the Commission urging Member States to recognise 'certification' and 'trace and claim' compliance providers. So the official EU path leans towards the certificate model that this idea rejects. The idea's 'standard clause' would be an add-on to these model clauses, and nothing in them anticipates it.

closest.title: EU Methane Regulation 2024/1787, Articles 28-29 (MRV equivalence from 2027; intensity reporting from Aug 2028; maximum methane intensity values by delegated act, applying from 2030). Verified via the EC import guidance page (updated 22 Sep 2026) and the recitals of the 2026/1834 recommendation.
closest.overlap: It already makes methane intensity a regulated attribute of imported gas, and it will set a maximum intensity value. That makes it a pass/fail quality specification, which is half of the 'treat methane like sulphur' idea. It does not set a continuous price slope, symmetric premiums and discounts, or revenue neutrality. The Commission's intensity methodology (delegated act due by 5 Aug 2027) is unpublished. It could fix the reference intensity and the measurement basis the clause would need, or it could conflict with them.

closest.title: MiQ certification (A-F grades; certificates traded on Xpansiv CBL; homepage claims about 30 Bcf/d certified and a 3.5 million-certificate transaction settled in Mar 2026). Also Project Canary/TrustWell, EQT and others' 'responsibly sourced gas', and the S&P Global Platts assessment of MiQ certificate prices launched in about 2022 (from memory, not verified: the page returned 403).
closest.overlap: Measured-intensity grading already earns a price premium. The idea correctly names these as its closest work. The differences are that the premium is voluntary, paid one way and certificate-based, there is no discount for high-leak gas, and it is not built into every cargo's price. A Platts price for certificates already gives a public 'methane premium' reference, which a contractual slope could index to.

closest.title: LNG cargo-level GHG disclosure in SPAs: Pavilion Energy's SGHG (Statement of GHG) clauses in its 2021-22 SPAs with QatarEnergy, Chevron and BP, Cheniere Cargo Emissions Tags (2022), the GIIGNL MRV and GHG-Neutral LNG framework, and the JOGMEC/KOGAS-led CLEAN LNG initiative (2023). All from memory, not verified this session: the search budget was exhausted.
closest.overlap: These show that methane and GHG data can already be written into LNG SPAs and attached to each cargo, which is the plumbing the idea needs. As far as I recall none of them re-prices cargoes on a symmetric intensity slope. Some (GIIGNL 'GHG-neutral' and 'carbon-neutral LNG') rely on offsets, which the idea explicitly bans.

closest.title: Crude quality escalators and pipeline 'quality banks' (Platts sulphur and API de-escalators, the TAPS quality bank (FERC-regulated) and the CPC Blend quality bank). From memory, not verified.
closest.overlap: The source of the graft. A quality bank is the closest analogue to the revenue-neutral design: shippers of better-quality crude in a commingled stream are paid by shippers of worse-quality crude, so the stream average stays unchanged. The idea is in effect a methane-intensity quality bank. I found no precedent applying a quality bank or escalator to an emissions attribute, as opposed to a physical product attribute. Caveat: sulphur affects the refined product's value, but methane intensity does not affect the molecule's value. So the differential needs a contractual or regulatory basis, which is why the EU Methane Regulation hook is essential.

closest.title: Joint Importer-Exporter Energy Sector Methane Abatement Statement (COP28, 2023: US, EU, Japan, Canada, Norway, Singapore, UK) and its MMRV working group framework (2024). From memory: the DOE page now returns 404.
closest.overlap: A government-level aim to 'create an international market for gas that minimises methane emissions' through a common MMRV framework. It is a measurement-harmonisation effort without a pricing mechanism. Current US federal support looks uncertain: the page has been withdrawn, and the US Waste Emissions Charge was repealed in 2025.

closest.title: OGMP 2.0 Level 5 (reconciling source-level and site-level measurement), the EU/UNEP IMEO MARS satellite alerts, and the basin-level aerial and satellite intensity literature (e.g. Sherwin et al. 2024 Nature aerial survey; TROPOMI Permian inversions by Zhang 2020 and Varon 2023; MethaneSAT basin products). From memory.
closest.overlap: Measurement reconciliation already exists inside OGMP L5. The idea's distinctive settlement rule is the more conservative of operator L5 and an independent top-down inversion. I found no precedent for that rule in a pricing context. The literature already documents large disagreements between top-down and bottom-up estimates, often 2x or more against inventories. That supports the idea's own falsification test and suggests the 0.2-point agreement it requires is currently unlikely at basin level. Check the 0.44% Permian aircraft figure: it may be a point-source-only inventory rather than a total intensity, which would bias the 7.3x comparison.

art.what_is_new:
The rating is PARTIAL. Every component exists:
- **Measured-intensity grading:** MiQ, OGMP 2.0 Level 5.
- **Price premia for low-methane gas:** RSG/MiQ certificate markets, with Platts pricing the certificates.
- **Contract clauses carrying methane data:** Pavilion SGHG statements, Cheniere cargo tags, and the EU's own model clauses (Recommendation 2026/1834, verified).
- **A regulatory intensity threshold:** EU Methane Regulation Art. 29 maximum values from 2030.
- **Revenue-neutral quality settlement for physical attributes:** crude escalators and pipeline quality banks.

The novel part is the combination, and I found no precedent for it:
1. A continuous, symmetric bonus/malus price slope on methane intensity, embedded in every LNG or pipeline contract's price formula. Existing schemes are a voluntary one-way premium or a regulatory pass/fail cap.
2. Revenue neutrality around a reference intensity, i.e. a methane 'quality bank' for gas.
3. Settlement on the MORE conservative of operator OGMP L5 data and independent satellite or aircraft inversion, not on certificates or self-reports.
4. A contractual ban on offset-based 'carbon-neutral LNG' claims.

The EU model clauses, adopted 20 July 2026, are information-and-compliance clauses only. They contain no price term. They also encourage Member States to recognise certificate-based compliance providers, which this idea is built to avoid. So the clause would be an add-on to the official clause set, which helps it be adopted but means it gets no direct regulatory backing.

Three things limit the novelty and feasibility:
- The EU's pending intensity methodology (due Aug 2027) and maximum values could set the reference intensity and the measurement basis, and they may favour certificates.
- Methane intensity, unlike sulphur, does not change the product's value. The differential therefore rests on regulation, not refinery economics.
- The settlement rule depends on top-down and bottom-up methods agreeing at basin level. The existing literature, including the idea's own Permian comparison, suggests they do not yet. The proposed desk test is the right first step.

Verification note: the WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted (200/200), so the EU sources above were fetched and read directly. MiQ was checked via its homepage. The Platts, Pavilion, Cheniere, CLEAN, GIIGNL, quality-bank and Joint Statement items are from memory and marked unverified. A full search of 2024-2026 SPA press releases for any intensity-indexed price term was not possible. That gap is the main residual risk to the PARTIAL label, though it would not reach IMPORT unless such a clause is found.

phys.violations:
No thermodynamic violations. Four quantitative or design claims fail.

(A) SCALE IS OVERCLAIMED by about 8-20x. The claimed 1.0-2.5 Gt CO2e is 35-85 Mt CH4, which is the whole abatable fossil methane pool: oil, gas and coal. Gas traded as LNG plus EU pipeline imports carries only about 1.8-7.2 Mt CH4/yr of upstream emissions. The script's realistic range is 0.036 / 0.128 / 0.417 Gt CO2e (GWP100), and the high case needs basin-wide spillover.

(B) 'REVENUE-NEUTRAL' IS FALSE with a fixed 0.5% reference. In the illustrative base case the supply-weighted intensity is 0.97% (range 0.47-1.92%). The clause then becomes a net price cut paid by exporters to buyers: +$1.68 bn/yr (range −0.09 to +5.10). This is exactly the per-tonne-fee red line for S3 that the idea says it avoids. Neutrality needs the reference reset each period to the volume-weighted measured mean, which makes it a feebate.

(C) THE 'MORE CONSERVATIVE OF TWO METHODS' RULE IS BIASED. Even with two unbiased methods, taking the maximum adds +0.169 percentage points at a 0.3-point standard deviation. That is a systematic $0.029/MMBtu penalty at $30/t, and $0.048 at a 0.5-point standard deviation. Plume inventories are also structurally low because of detection limits. If they see 30-70% of emissions, the gap is 0.45-1.05 points for a 1.5% basin, above the idea's own 0.3-point falsification threshold. The 7.3x Permian gap (3.2/0.44) is therefore mostly a scope confound (point sources vs total), not only a different-year confound. In practice the rule will always settle on the satellite inversion.

(D) THE INCENTIVE IS DILUTED. Settling at basin level gives a best-practice operator in a leaky basin the basin's number. If exports are 12% of basin gas, the effective basin-wide incentive is only $3.6/t CO2e at a $30/t slope, below most abatement costs that are not already free.
phys.resource_needs:
Energy: net positive. At base scale about −0.16 EJ/yr = −0.027% of world primary energy (computed at 0.2 Gt), because recovered gas exceeds compression and measurement energy.

Materials: compressors and vapour-recovery units, electric or zero-bleed pneumatics, leak-detection equipment, and flare and combustor upgrades. These are commodity oilfield equipment with no critical-mineral constraint.

Measurement infrastructure: satellite constellations (TROPOMI, Carbon Mapper/Tanager, GHGSat; the MethaneSAT status is unverified), recurring aircraft basin surveys, site-level reconciliation to OGMP 2.0 Level 5, and an independent settlement body. Measurement and verification is assumed to cost $0.002-0.015 per MMBtu.

Capital: about USD 75 bn cumulative to 2030 for global oil and gas abatement (IEA NZR 2023, modelled). The share attributable to traded gas is much smaller.

Land and water: negligible.
phys.key_uncertainties:
1. MEASUREMENT AGREEMENT. Can the basin inversion be reconciled with operator-level Level 5 data, with plume inventories corrected for detection limits, to within about 0.3 percentage points? This decides whether the contract can be settled, and the idea's own 2-4 week desk test is the right first check. It should compare methods with the same scope (total emissions vs plumes above the detection limit), not only the same year.

2. REFERENCE DESIGN. A fixed reference is a fee paid by exporters, which S3 will resist. A rolling mean reference is neutral but its incentive decays as the mean falls. Which can be negotiated in bilateral SPAs, where sellers can simply raise the base price to offset an expected discount?

3. ATTRIBUTION. Associated gas (Permian) allocates methane between oil and gas, which can shift intensity about 2x (from memory). Pooled portfolio LNG cannot be traced to a basin.

4. EU MR DURABILITY. The 2027 MRV and 2030 maximum-intensity provisions are the legal anchor. Any 2025-26 softening under the US-EU trade deal could not be verified this session.

5. SUPPLIER INTENSITIES AND LNG SHARES. These are from memory. The weighted mean of 0.47-1.92% drives both the neutrality result and the scale.

6. ADDITIONALITY. Low-leak producers (Norway, Qatar on operator-reported data) earn premia for abatement they have already done. Qatar's intensity is mostly self-reported.

7. MARGINAL ABATEMENT COST. The high case assumes measures up to the $30/t slope; the true cost-curve tail is uncertain.

8. GWP CHOICE. GWP20 roughly triples the climate value: 0.355 Gt in the base case.

stances.evidence: Methane-focused NGOs (S1) supported the instruments this idea builds on. Sierra Club backed the US Waste Emissions Charge (map: IEA policy page), and EDF and CATF advocated for the EU Methane Regulation's import provisions (from memory, not re-verified this session). The clause meets CAN's offset red line: CAN 2021 'will not support any effort to promote negative emissions or offsets as an alternative'. The clause bars offset-based 'carbon-neutral LNG' claims and pays only for measured cuts at source. The anti-LNG wing objects. Sierra Club and Earthworks have campaigned against LNG export expansion and called certified or differentiated gas greenwashing (from memory; the Sierra Club and Earthworks pages returned empty or 404 when fetched today). For them, a contractual 'low-methane LNG' grade makes LNG look legitimate and helps lock in fossil use. That echoes CAN's principle that a technology's promise 'must not delay' action. Expect support from methane-specialist NGOs and opposition from groups campaigning against fossil expansion.
stances.red_line_hit: Possible fossil lock-in or greenwashing, if anyone markets a premium grade as 'clean LNG'. Offsets are avoided by design.

stances.evidence: IPCC AR6 WGIII C.4.5 and COP28 decision 1/CMA.5 para 28(f) call for substantially reducing methane by 2030 (map, verified). Abatement at source is energy-positive: about 50 GJ of gas recovered per t CH4, against 263 GJ/t in fan work alone to strip CH4 from ambient air (OptiLex verifier). Scientists' main reservation is measurement. The atmospheric-inversion literature consistently finds top-down (satellite or aircraft) estimates above operator self-reports. Permian estimates differ 7.3x: 0.44% from aircraft (2024) against 3.2% from TROPOMI (2023), with the different years as a confound. So scientists will back the principle of settling on the more conservative of two methods, but will question whether basin-level inversions can price an individual cargo.
stances.red_line_hit: No red line. The objection is a scientific-integrity concern: settling on an uncertain metric could award premiums for intensity that was never measured accurately.

stances.evidence: Low-intensity producers gain. OGCI members (Aramco, BP, Chevron, Equinor, ExxonMobil, Shell, TotalEnergies and others) self-report intensity below 0.20%, and the OGDC's 55+ companies, about 40% of world oil output, committed to <0.2% by 2030 (map). At a 0.5% reference they would earn about +$0.05/MMBtu. API says it supports direct methane regulation (map). MiQ's live counter shows 30 Bcf/d of gas and 660 kBOE/d of crude certified across 142 audits (miq.org, fetched 2026-10-05), so many producers already accept intensity grading. High-intensity operators lose. The industry's documented red line is a per-tonne charge: Western Energy Alliance and most of S3 helped kill the WEC through the Congressional Review Act in 2025 (map). My script (scratchpad/climate/stake_mi/stake_calc.py) shows the clause's discount is 37-54% of the repealed WEC's 2026 rate at the same intensity: -$0.085 against -$0.23/MMBtu at 1%, and -$0.26 against -$0.51 at 2%. For a Permian producer with a $1/MMBtu netback, the 2% discount is 25% of revenue, and 92% at 3.2% with a $0.5 netback. Expect opponents to call it a fee by another name. Exporting NOCs and governments resisted EU supply-chain rules: Qatar reportedly threatened in Dec 2024 to halt EU LNG over CSDDD penalties (from memory; I could not fetch Reuters).
stances.red_line_hit: A per-tonne charge set by contract rather than by a government fee, and attribution of basin-average intensity to individual cargoes that penalises clean operators in dirty basins.

stances.evidence: Heavy industry here is a gas consumer, and the differential is designed to be revenue-neutral. Even the largest discount is at most 0.7-1.0% of an EU retail gas price of €0.08-0.12/kWh, and industrial contracts are similar in scale (stake_calc.py). EU industry's documented priority is energy cost: VCI called carbon contracts for difference 'no panacea' and asked for lower energy prices (map). A clause that does not raise average prices and gives a compliance path under the EU Methane Regulation is unlikely to be opposed. Industry has no direct stake in upstream methane, so active support is unlikely.

stances.evidence: Utilities and LNG importers carry the EU Methane Regulation obligations. These are MRV equivalence from 1 Jan 2027, mandatory third-party verification for contracts concluded after 4 Aug 2024, and intensity reporting from 5 Aug 2028 (Commission import-requirements page, fetched 2026-10-05). A standard clause gives them a compliance path. In July 2026 the Commission issued a Recommendation on optional model clauses, EU/2026/1834 (energy.ec.europa.eu, fetched today). That shows importers asked for contract tools; its text could not be read because EUR-Lex was blocked by a WAF challenge. Japanese and Korean buyers (JERA, KOGAS) launched the CLEAN LNG initiative in 2023 to gather seller methane data (from memory, unverified). Gas-fired generators will resist anything that tightens supply.

stances.evidence: LDAR, replacing pneumatics and vapour recovery are labour-using work in producing regions. US unions and the BlueGreen Alliance have historically supported EPA methane rules (from memory; the page returned 404). The clause transfers margin from high-intensity to low-intensity operators and does not reduce volumes, so there is little direct risk to jobs. Exposure is concentrated on flare-heavy independents in basins with low netbacks such as Waha/Permian. Unions belong to the Carbon Capture Coalition (map) but have no documented position on methane price differentials.

stances.evidence: Importing governments wrote the legal hook. The EU Methane Regulation 2024/1787 (enacted) phases in importer MRV and adds a binding maximum intensity from 2030. Japan and Korea are aligned (from memory). But the EU puts supply security first. A Commission Recommendation (EU/2026/1835) temporarily suspends importer penalties for three years, and Member States 'should not apply any penalties that endanger the security of energy supply' (Commission import-requirements page, fetched 2026-10-05). So the claimed 'legal reason to adopt' is weaker than the idea assumes until about 2029. Exporting governments are hostile or mixed. The US Congress disapproved the WEC 52-47 and OBBBA pushed it back to 2034 (map). Qatar reportedly threatened EU supply over CSDDD (from memory). Norway, a low-intensity EEA supplier, would gain and may be exempt. EEA integration is 'not expected to apply' to its imports (Commission page). The COP28 consensus on methane (para 28(f)) gives every government nominal cover.

stances.evidence: Higher-intensity developing-country exporters would bear the discounts, with no Multilateral Fund-style transfer. For CBAM, India and South Africa objected that unilateral border measures are discriminatory (map; not re-verified). A buyer-bloc quality differential invites the same objection, and the countries short of OGMP Level 5 and aircraft-survey capacity are mostly in the Global South. In Baum et al. (2024; N=30,284 in 30 countries), Global South publics supported more climate technologies than Northern publics but worried more about unequal risk. Methane abatement is not CDR, so that study's moral-hazard finding does not apply here. Climate-justice advocates who oppose new LNG export projects in Africa may see a 'low-methane grade' as legitimising expansion (general documented stance, not re-verified). Countries that import LNG (India, Bangladesh, Pakistan) would be roughly neutral. The Kigali precedent suggests support would need finance and slower schedules.

Even if every supplier cut intensity to 0.2% while the reference stayed at 0.5%, buyers would pay +$0.05/MMBtu, about 0.1-0.2% of EU retail ($25-38/MMBtu at €0.08-0.12/kWh; stake_calc.py). The documented consumer pattern is that visible consumer carbon prices lose (Canada's fuel charge was removed 1 Apr 2025) while invisible charges in the industrial supply chain survive (map). This clause is invisible to households. Andre et al. (2024; 125 countries, N=129,902) found 69% willing to pay 1% of income, so the tiny cost is well within stated tolerance.

stances.evidence: Methane intensity is already a standard engagement metric. MiQ certificates trade on Xpansiv CBL, including a reported 3.5 million-certificate transaction (miq.org, fetched today). OGMP 2.0 Level 5 is the EU's producer-level route to MRV equivalence (Commission page). Turning intensity into a contractual price attribute makes transition risk priceable and comparable. Investor coalitions have long pushed methane disclosure (from memory, not re-verified). Insurers have no documented position, so low salience. The confound: certified-gas premia have stayed small and voluntary, so the investor case depends on the clause becoming a market standard.

stances.evidence: Communities near production sites (Permian, Marcellus) gain co-benefits: less flaring and fewer VOC and hazardous-air-pollutant emissions from LDAR and vapour recovery. That matches why local and environmental-justice groups backed EPA methane rules (from memory). Communities next to LNG export terminals (US Gulf Coast) do not benefit. The clause leaves liquefaction-plant pollution, flaring at terminals and safety risks untouched, and those communities have opposed terminal expansion (general documented pattern, not re-verified this session). If a low-methane grade helps sell more LNG, they could lose.
stances.red_line_hit: Local safety and air quality at LNG terminals, which the clause does not touch, and legitimisation of terminal expansion.

stake.coalition_notes:
Overall verdict: a credible support coalition of S2, S5, S10, importing S7, low-intensity S3 (OGCI/OGDC majors, Norway) and the methane-specialist part of S1. S4, S6 and S9 are mostly neutral, because the scheme is revenue-neutral and price effects are at most 0.7-1.0% of retail. The organised opposition is high-intensity US independents and their trade groups, exporting governments (US, possibly Qatar) and the anti-LNG wings of S1, S8 and S11. That is the same faction that killed the US Waste Emissions Charge.

Four findings that matter for the engine:
1. **It still prices tonnes.** Calculated with the OptiLex verifier constants (scratchpad/climate/stake_mi/stake_calc.py): the clause's implied rate is $894/t CH4 (GWP100 at $30/t CO2e). Its discount is 37-54% of the repealed WEC's 2026 rate at the same intensity. It avoids the S3 red line in legal form, a government fee, but not in economic substance, so expect it to be framed as 'a methane fee by contract'. Make the symmetry visible: low-intensity producers earn +$0.05/MMBtu at 0.2%.
2. **The regulatory hook is weaker than the idea assumes.** The Commission recommended suspending importer penalties for three years to protect supply security (EU/2026/1835; energy.ec.europa.eu, fetched 2026-10-05). EU buyers therefore have little compulsion to adopt a price clause before about 2029. In a tight LNG market sellers can refuse it.
3. **The novelty is narrower than claimed.** On 20 Jul 2026 the Commission issued a Recommendation on optional model clauses for methane in energy contracts (EU/2026/1834). That is the same contract-clause pathway. I could not read its text because EUR-Lex returned a WAF challenge, which I did not try to bypass. Before claiming novelty, check whether it already contains price-adjustment terms. If it does not, the idea's real contributions are the symmetric slope and settling on the more conservative of two measurement methods.
4. **Revenue neutrality is temporary.** It holds only while the reference equals the market average. As suppliers abate, the scheme becomes a small net premium (+$0.05/MMBtu at most) unless the reference ratchets down, and a ratchet looks like a tightening fee to S3.

Coalition-widening levers:
- Kigali-style finance: OGMP and measurement capacity for S8 exporters.
- A grace period for clean operators in dirty basins: settle at asset level where Level 5 data exist and use basin inversions only as a cap. This also eases the S3 attribution objection.
- An explicit ban on 'clean LNG' marketing claims, for the S1 anti-LNG wing.
- Pairing with terminal air-quality conditions, for S11.

**Evidence limits.** The web-search budget was exhausted at the start of this task. Several stances therefore rest on the provided map plus items marked 'from memory, not re-verified':
- Qatar's CSDDD threat
- the anti-certified-gas campaigns by Sierra Club and Earthworks
- CLEAN LNG
- BlueGreen Alliance's support for methane rules

Verified today: the EU import timeline and penalty suspension (Commission page), the existence of the model-clauses recommendation, and MiQ's 30 Bcf/d certified volume.

critic.fatal_flaw:
None found. Nothing in the physics is broken: source abatement has a 0 GJ/t floor and is net energy-positive. The scale is small, about 0.04-0.4 Gt CO2e (GWP100), but not zero. The stakeholder red lines identified can all be designed around. Two serious risks fall short of fatal.

(i) Cargo reshuffling. Clause buyers (roughly the EU plus Japan, Korea and Taiwan, about half of LNG demand, from memory) could be served by low-leak cargoes while high-leak cargoes go to buyers without the clause. The price signal survives only if clause demand is larger than the supply of low-intensity gas. On rough shares (Qatar plus Norway at about 20-30% of supply, from memory) it is, but this has to be checked.

(ii) EU leverage. The EU's suspension of importer penalties (Recommendation 2026/1835) removes most of the compulsion before about 2029. That weakens adoption but does not invalidate the mechanism.
critic.top_fixable_flaw:
The settlement rule, "the MORE conservative of operator OGMP L5 and basin inversion", takes away the abatement incentive it is meant to create.

Plume inventories miss sources below the detection limit, and inventories are structurally low against inversions. So the rule almost always settles on the basin-level satellite inversion. No single seller can move that number.

My script (scratchpad/climate/critic_coalition_1.py, verifier GWP 29.8, $30/t CO2e slope = $894/t CH4) gives the marginal reward for one tonne an operator abates under basin settlement. It equals the slope × the operator's share of basin production × the share of its gas sold under the clause:
- 2% of the Permian, 50% under the clause: $0.30/t CO2e.
- Even 10% of the basin, 100% under the clause: only $3/t CO2e.

That is 10-100x below the $5-37/t abatement costs in the TEA. The incentive becomes a public good inside each basin, so every operator free-rides.

The rule also has two other costs:
- **Bias.** Taking the maximum of two unbiased estimates adds +0.17 pp at a 0.3 pp standard deviation and +0.28 pp at 0.5 pp (Monte Carlo, true intensity 1.5%). That is a standing penalty on every cargo, and it supports S3's "fee by another name" objection.
- **Penalty on clean operators.** A clean operator in a dirty basin is charged the basin's number.

Separately, a LNG seller with a portfolio, or a liquefier that buys feedgas from many producers, cannot attribute its gas to an asset at all.
critic.suggested_patch:
Replace the max() rule with asset-level settlement plus basin reconciliation.

**1. Settled intensity per supply asset.** Settled intensity for a supply asset is I_i = L5_i × F_b, where F_b = max(1, basin inversion / Σ L5 reported in basin b). F_b is published each year with its uncertainty. If F_b is not significantly above 1 it is set to 1, so measurement noise does not create a one-sided penalty.

**2. Two new contract terms.**
- **Default intensity.** Any volume that cannot be traced to an L5-reporting asset is settled at a default: the basin inversion's 90th percentile, or a global default for portfolio cargoes without a basin. This makes laundering through a portfolio unprofitable.
- **Feedgas pass-through.** A liquefier must write the same differential into its feedgas purchase contracts, so the price signal reaches the producer.

**3. Set the reference per contract.** Set the reference at signing to the supply's measured intensity in the previous year, and lower it on a fixed published path (e.g. −0.05 pp/yr). The base price absorbs the level at negotiation. Only the slope moves money during the term. That keeps it revenue-neutral in expectation, so there is no standing fee to trigger S3's red line, and the marginal incentive is untouched.

**Effect.** An operator's own reported cut is worth slope × F_b × its share of gas under the clause: $15-37.50/t CO2e at 50% clause coverage and F_b of 1-2.5 (script). That is 50-100x the basin-settlement figure, and it removes the bias of the max() rule.

**Revised falsification test.** Check whether, in the same basin and year and over the same scope, the reconciliation factor F_b can be estimated to within ±25% (1σ). Also check whether clause-market LNG demand is larger than the supply of low-intensity gas, which is the reshuffling check.

patched_idea.title: Methane-intensity quality differential in gas and LNG contracts
patched_idea.one_line: Treat measured upstream methane intensity like sulphur in crude oil. Gas contracts would carry an automatic price differential, neutral at signing, settled per supply asset on operator measurement scaled up by an independent basin reconciliation factor, not on certificates or offsets.
patched_idea.conventional_core: Upstream and midstream methane abatement: LDAR, electric or zero-bleed pneumatics, vapour recovery and ending routine venting (TRL 9; IEA GMT 2026 puts more than 35 Mt CH4/yr avoidable at no net cost and about 85 Mt with existing technology, modelled).
patched_idea.graft: The crude-oil quality escalator (sulphur and API-gravity de-escalators in benchmark crude pricing, e.g. the Platts Forties sulphur de-escalator, from memory). A physical quality attribute re-prices every cargo automatically.
patched_idea.mechanism:
Each LNG SPA or pipeline import contract carries a standard clause. The price adjusts by a published slope (e.g. $30/t CO2e, GWP100) times the gap between the contract's reference intensity and the settled intensity of the supply.

SETTLEMENT (patched; replaces the earlier max-of-two-methods rule). Settled intensity for supply asset i in basin b is I_i = L5_i x F_b. L5_i is the asset's OGMP 2.0 Level 5 reconciled intensity. F_b = basin top-down inversion (satellite/aircraft) / sum of L5-reported emissions in the basin. F_b is published annually with its uncertainty and is set to 1 unless it is statistically significantly above 1, so measurement noise does not create a one-sided penalty. The independent measurement therefore still disciplines self-reports, because under-reporting in a basin raises everyone's F_b. But each operator keeps the private reward for its own cuts, so no operator can free-ride on its basin.

TWO TRACEABILITY TERMS. (a) Default intensity: volume that cannot be traced to an L5-reporting asset settles at the basin inversion's 90th percentile, or at a published global default for portfolio cargoes with no basin. This makes laundering through a portfolio unprofitable. (b) Feedgas pass-through: a liquefier or portfolio seller under the clause must write the same differential into its feedgas purchase contracts, so the signal reaches the producer who can abate.

REFERENCE PER CONTRACT. At signing the reference equals the supply's settled intensity in the prior year, so the differential starts at zero and the base price absorbs the level. The reference then falls on a fixed, published glide path (e.g. -0.05 pp/yr). During the term only the slope moves money: sellers who cut faster than the glide earn a premium, and those who don't pay a discount. There is no standing per-tonne fee, which avoids the S3 red line that killed the US Waste Emissions Charge.

INTEGRITY. Third-party verification of L5, plus aerial spot surveys at site level, guards against operators under-reporting to shift burden to others in the basin through F_b. 'Carbon-neutral LNG' claims based on offsets are barred by the clause, and nothing is paid for volumes that are not measured.

ADOPTION. The EU Methane Regulation's 2027 import MRV gives buyers the legal reason to adopt the clause, though the suspension of EU importer penalties in 2026 (per the critic) weakens compulsion before about 2029. Grounding precedent: EU Methane Regulation 2024/1787 (enacted), API's stated support for direct methane regulation, and the IMO 2020 sulphur cap (a fuel-quality standard the industry absorbed).
patched_idea.target: Methane in internationally traded gas. LNG is about 411 Mt/yr, about 21.2 bn MMBtu (IGU 2024, from memory, unverified), plus EU pipeline imports. This is a lever on part of the 35-85 Mt CH4/yr abatable fossil methane (IEA GMT 2026, modelled), which is about 1.0-2.5 Gt CO2e GWP100. The critic's realistic reach is 0.04-0.4 Gt CO2e/yr, because only traded gas under the clause is covered.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
Items (1)-(7) are from scratchpad/climate/coalition_ideas.py. Items (8)-(13) are from scratchpad/climate/patch_coalition_1.py. Both use the OptiLex verifier (GWP100 fossil CH4 29.8).
(1) 1 MMBtu of pure CH4 is 19.0 kg (HHV 55.5 MJ/kg).
(2) Cutting intensity from 1.0% to 0.2% avoids 0.152 kg CH4/MMBtu, which is 4.5 kg CO2e (GWP100) or 12.6 kg (GWP20). From 2.0% to 0.2% it avoids 10.2 / 28.2 kg CO2e.
(3) Paying $20/t CO2e for the 1.0%->0.2% step needs $0.09/MMBtu; $50/t needs $0.23/MMBtu. That is 0.8-2.3% of a $10-12/MMBtu LNG price.
(4) At a $30/t slope ($894/t CH4), each 0.1 pp of intensity gap is $0.017/MMBtu. With a reference of 0.5%, settlement at 0.2% gives +$0.05/MMBtu, at 1.0% -$0.085 and at 2.0% -$0.26. Under the patched per-contract reference, these are the in-term moves for intensity changes of the same size, not standing transfers.
(5) $0.10/MMBtu across all LNG is about $2.1 bn/yr of transfers. That would buy about 106 Mt CO2e/yr (3.6 Mt CH4) at $20/t or 42 Mt at $50/t.
(6) The recovered gas is itself worth $5.3/t CO2e at $3/MMBtu and $19.4/t at $11/MMBtu (GWP100).
(7) Source abatement is energy-positive: about 50 GJ of gas is recovered per t CH4. Removing the same CH4 from ambient air would cost 263 GJ/t CH4 in fan work alone (verifier: 1.93 ppm, 50% removal, 100 Pa).
(8) Marginal reward per t CO2e of an operator's own abatement. Old basin-settled max rule: $0.30 (2% basin share, 50% under the clause) and $3.00 (10% share, 100% under the clause). Patched asset settlement: $15 at F_b=1 and 50% clause coverage, $37.50 at F_b=2.5 and 50%, $30-75 at 100% coverage. That is 50-100x higher, and it now covers the $5-37/t abatement costs in the TEA.
(9) Settlement bias, Monte Carlo, true intensity 1.5%, L5 complete. Old max rule: +0.17 pp (sd 0.3) and +0.28 pp (sd 0.5). Ungated max(1,F): +0.13 / +0.20 pp. Significance-gated F_b (one-sided 95%): +0.03 / +0.05 pp. Trade-off: where L5 truly captures only 60%, the gated rule under-settles by -0.11 pp. That errs toward sellers and is acceptable, because it shrinks as inversion uncertainty falls.
(10) Clean operator in a dirty basin (L5 0.2%, basin inversion 3.0% against a sum-L5 of 1.2%, F_b 2.5). Old rule settles at 3.0% (-$0.43/MMBtu against a 0.5% reference). The patch settles at 0.5% ($0.00).
(11) Anti-laundering. With a basin inversion of 1.5% +/- 0.3 pp, the P90 default is 1.88%. Untraced volume pays $0.07-0.27/MMBtu more than traced volume at 1.5-0.3%, so tracing is worth more than its cost.
(12) Glide path -0.05 pp/yr. A seller holding intensity flat pays $0.0085/MMBtu more each year of the term ($0.043 by year 5), and a seller cutting faster earns the same amount. So the clause is neutral at signing and in expectation only if abatement tracks the glide. That is a disclosed, small, contracted ramp, not a fee.
(13) Reshuffling check. Rough inputs are from memory and unverified: clause buyers 35-50% of LNG (144-206 Mt) against low-intensity supply 20-30% (82-123 Mt). Clause demand is larger than low-intensity supply in all four combinations, so the price signal survives reshuffling on these guesses. This must be verified with GIIGNL/IGU trade shares.
(14) Measurement context: Permian methods disagree 7.3x, 0.44% by aircraft (2024) against 3.2% by TROPOMI inversion (2023). Different years and scopes are a confound. Under the patch this disagreement no longer has to be resolved between two settlement candidates. It enters through F_b and its uncertainty.
patched_idea.who_gains: S3: low-leak producers and operators (Norway, best-practice US and Qatari operators, and clean operators inside dirty basins, who are now settled on their own L5 and not on the basin number) earn a premium for cuts they control. S7: EU, Japan and Korea importers get a workable compliance path for the EU MR with no supply shock. S1 and S2 get measured cuts, checked against independent top-down data, with no offsets. S9: the clause is neutral at signing, with only a small contracted glide (about $0.01-0.04/MMBtu over 5 years for a non-abating seller). S10 gets a priced, measurable risk. S11 near production sites gets VOC and air-quality co-benefits.
patched_idea.who_loses: High-intensity operators that do not abate faster than the glide. Untraceable portfolio volumes, which settle at the P90 default (+$0.07-0.27/MMBtu). Operators in basins with large unreported emissions, through F_b. Certificate vendors lose part of their market. Liquefiers carry an administrative burden passing the clause through to feedgas contracts. S1 groups opposed to any LNG expansion may object that the clause legitimises LNG; the offset-claim ban is meant to answer that. Producers at negative-price hubs (Waha) gain little, because their gas has no value to recover. Residual risk: an operator can under-report L5 to push burden onto its basin peers through F_b, which is mitigated by third-party verification and site-level spot surveys.
patched_idea.closest_known_work: MiQ certified gas and Project Canary/TrustWell differentiated gas (voluntary certificate premia). OGMP 2.0 (whose Level 5 already requires reconciling source-level and site-level measurements). EU Methane Regulation import MRV equivalence (2027). The Japan/Korea-led CLEAN LNG initiative (2023, from memory). The verified map's open problem on an EU MRV equivalence pathway.
