patched_idea.why_different: Certificates are optional premia paid by a few buyers, and they have not moved basin intensity at scale. This proposal makes intensity a contractual quality specification that re-prices every cargo under the clause. Each operator is rewarded for its own measured cuts, while an independent basin top-down factor stops self-reports from drifting low. The levels are absorbed into the base price at signing, so it penalises leakers without a government fee or a standing charge on consumers.
patched_idea.cheapest_falsifying_test:
A 2-4 week desk study with two checks.
(1) For the Permian, Haynesville and Marcellus, in the same basin-year (2023-2025) and over the same source scope, estimate the reconciliation factor F_b: TROPOMI-based inversion divided by the bottom-up total (OGMP/EPA GHGRP plus Carbon Mapper plume inventories as a proxy for L5). FALSIFIED as a settlement basis if F_b cannot be estimated to within +/-25% (1 sigma) for any of the three basins. In that case gating would set F_b to 1, independent discipline would vanish, and measurement R&D must come first.
(2) Reshuffling: from GIIGNL/IGU trade data, check whether LNG demand from likely clause adopters (EU, Japan, Korea, Taiwan) is larger than supply already below about 0.2% intensity. If it is not, low-leak cargoes can be steered to clause buyers with no change in intensity, and the price signal is falsified.
Secondary check: compile certified-gas premium quotes for 2023-2026. If premia stay below $0.02/MMBtu with no response in intensity, the voluntary route is falsified, and only a mandated clause through EU MR adoption can work.

fix.change_summary:
I replaced the clause's settlement rule as the critic proposed. The old rule took the more conservative of the operator's OGMP L5 figure and the basin inversion. Because the basin inversion almost always won, each operator's cut became a public good shared across its basin: worth $0.30-3/t CO2e to the operator, and carrying a +0.17 to +0.28 pp upward bias. The new rule settles per asset as I_i = L5_i x F_b, where F_b is a basin top-down reconciliation factor set to 1 unless it is significantly above 1.

Three terms were added. Untraced or portfolio volume settles at a P90 default, to stop laundering. Liquefiers must pass the differential through to their feedgas contracts. The reference is set per contract at the prior year's intensity, with a fixed glide of -0.05 pp/yr, so the clause starts at zero at signing. A further line requires third-party L5 verification and spot surveys, so operators cannot under-report and shift burden to basin peers through F_b.

I checked the numbers in a new script (scratchpad/climate/patch_coalition_1.py, verifier GWP 29.8):
- The reward for an operator's own cut is $15-37.50/t CO2e at 50% clause coverage. That confirms the critic's figures.
- The gated F_b bias is +0.03 to +0.05 pp. There is a disclosed trade-off: it under-settles by -0.11 pp when L5 captures only 60% of emissions.
- A clean operator in a dirty basin moves from -$0.43 to $0.00/MMBtu.
- The P90 default makes untraced volume cost $0.07-0.27/MMBtu more.
- The glide costs a seller who does not abate $0.0085/MMBtu per year of term. This makes "revenue-neutral" true at signing and in expectation only, which is now stated.
- The reshuffling check passes on unverified share guesses.

The falsification test now asks whether F_b can be estimated to within ±25% (1σ) for the same basin-year and scope, and adds the reshuffling check. The core mechanism and the crude-oil sulphur-escalator graft are unchanged; only the settlement formula and contract terms inside that mechanism were revised.

idea.title: Clinker process-CO2 phasedown with storage-only compliance and process-first storage priority
idea.one_line: A Kigali-style tradeable phasedown applies only to limestone process CO2 per tonne of clinker. It can be met by permanent storage (never EOR), clinker substitution or direct separation, with no public subsidy, and it gives process CO2 and removals first claim on scarce storage.
idea.conventional_core: Retrofit amine CCS on existing kilns with ship or pipe transport to dedicated storage (Brevik plus Northern Lights, operating since 2025, measured), plus calcined clay/LC3 clinker substitution (TRL 9) and Leilac-type indirect calcination (pilot to 100 kt/yr).
idea.graft: The Kigali Amendment's scheduled phasedown of one emission class, which works because the incumbents sell the substitute (here stored-carbon clinker and LC3). Montreal-style border trade measures carry it to imports.
idea.target: Cement process CO2 of about 1.5 Gt/yr (IEA 2024). This verifier-consistent estimate gives 1.50 Gt at 4.0 Gt of cement and a clinker ratio of 0.71. These emissions have no fuel-switch route.
idea.quantitative_claims:
Calculations in coalition_ideas.py.
(1) Process CO2 is 0.526 t per t clinker (65% CaO, 1.5% MgO). That is 0.374 t per t cement at a 0.71 clinker ratio and 0.263 at 0.50. Globally it is 1.50 Gt/yr.
(2) Verifier floors at 90% capture: 0.110 GJ/t from 25% CO2 kiln flue, 0.124 from 20%, and 0.004 from a 95% Leilac-type stream. Isothermal compression to 150 bar adds 0.282 GJ/t, so the total floor is 0.39 GJ/t.
(3) Brevik-type amine at about 3 GJ_th/t and 120°C is about 0.72 GJ/t of exergy, about 15% second-law efficiency on separation.
(4) Capturing 90% of all process CO2 at 3 GJ/t needs 4.0 EJ/yr of heat (0.65% of world primary energy); the floor is 0.53 EJ (0.09%).
(5) At €100-150/t, abating process CO2 only costs €37-56 per t cement. At 0.15-0.30 t cement/m² that is €6-17/m², 0.28-0.84% of a €2,000/m² build cost.
(6) Storing ALL cement process CO2 for 100 years takes 150 Gt, 10% of the 1,460 Gt prudent storage limit (Gidden 2025). At general-purpose CCS rates of 8.7-15 Gt/yr the limit is exhausted in 97-168 years. Priority rules therefore cost Tier 1 almost nothing and bind only fossil-power CCS.
idea.who_gains: S4: cement keeps its kilns, quarries and market share, sells a premium product and is protected at the border. S3: storage operators (Equinor, Shell, Exxon) get guaranteed Tier-1 demand without the EOR controversy. S6: cement jobs stay. S8: LC3 counts toward compliance, so Global South producers with clay can comply cheaply. S1: storage cannot be used to extend fossil power's life, and no public money goes in. S9: under 1% of building cost. S7: no fiscal outlay.
idea.who_loses: Inland kilns far from storage pay more (trading or LC3) or close. Importers of high-clinker cement into border-adjusted markets lose. S11 near CO2 shipping and storage sites carries the risk. Fossil-power CCS developers (S5, S3) lose queue priority. S1 groups that reject CCS categorically will still object.
idea.closest_known_work: EU ETS plus CBAM, which prices all cement CO2 rather than scheduling process CO2. California SB 596 (2021; cement net-zero by 2045; from memory). Allen et al. carbon takeback and the EU NZIA 50 Mt injection obligation (upstream fossil focus). The GCCA Net Zero roadmap. Buy Clean/IDDI procurement. The verified map's open problems on a CCS eligibility rule and a storage-allocation commons.
idea.why_different: Existing instruments price all CO2 or subsidise CCS. This one is scoped to the single emission class where S1's objection to CCS is weakest. It bans the elements CAN objects to (subsidy, EOR, fossil-power life extension), credits clinker substitution equally, and is the first to tie compliance to a storage priority rule. The verifier result that cement uses only about 10% of prudent storage per century is what makes the priority rule cheap for incumbents.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test: Two parts over 4-6 weeks. (a) A plant-level marginal abatement curve for about 90 US and about 200 EU kilns from public data: clinker ratio, clay deposits, distance to operating or FID storage (Northern Lights, Porthos/Aramis, Gulf Coast Class VI). FALSIFIED economically if less than 50% of process CO2 can be cut by 2035 at ≤€150/t, which breaks the under-1% building-cost promise. (b) A structured elicitation with 10-15 NGOs (CAN members, Bellona, CATF, E3G) on the exact eligibility and priority rules. FALSIFIED politically if a majority would still campaign against it.
idea.family: Tradeable clinker process-CO2 phasedown with storage-only compliance and storage priority

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: EU ETS (clinker benchmark, linear reduction factor, CCS Directive storage rule) plus CBAM for cement (2026-2034 phase-in)
closest.overlap: This covers most of the mechanism already. There is a declining, tradeable cap: the linear reduction factor takes the cap close to zero around 2039-2040, which is steeper than the idea's -90% by 2050. It covers clinker producers' process and fuel CO2. Avoided surrender is granted only for CO2 stored under the CCS Directive, so EOR is effectively excluded. CBAM supplies the border adjustment (the idea's 'Montreal-style border trade measure') for imported cement and clinker. Difference: it prices all CO2 together, it is a mass cap rather than a process-CO2 intensity schedule, it does not bar subsidies (Brevik and Longship were state-funded), and it says nothing about storage priority.

closest.title: India Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) GHG-intensity targets for cement (notified 2025), plus the earlier PAT energy-intensity scheme; China national ETS extended to cement in 2025
closest.overlap: These are tradeable, declining, sector-specific intensity standards for cement, which is the 'Kigali-style tradeable phasedown per tonne of product' form. Clinker substitution lowers intensity per tonne of cement. Difference: they cover total GHG per tonne of product rather than limestone process CO2 per tonne of clinker, and they have no storage-only or anti-EOR compliance rule and no storage queue. Recalled from memory; not re-verified this session.

closest.title: California SB 596 (2021) Cement Sector Net-Zero Strategy (CARB)
closest.overlap: This is a statutory scheduled phasedown for one sector: GHG intensity 40% below 2019 by 2035 and net zero by 2045. It explicitly evaluates Portland limestone and blended cements. Verified: the bill text does not mention CCS eligibility, EOR or storage priority, and it covers all cement emissions, not process CO2 only.

closest.title: EU Industrial Carbon Management Strategy (COM(2024)62) and NZIA Art. 23 50 Mt/yr injection-capacity obligation; Germany Carbon Management Strategy (2024) and KSpG amendment
closest.overlap: This is closest to the 'process-first storage priority' graft. The EU strategy frames capture as mainly for hard-to-abate process emissions and removals. Germany's strategy and draft law aim state CCS support at hard-to-avoid industrial emissions and keep coal power out of CO2 pipeline access and support. That is a de facto 'fossil power last' rule. Difference: these are political prioritisations and access or subsidy exclusions, not tiered queue priority written into storage licences, and none ties storage priority to a sectoral compliance obligation. Recalled from memory; the fetches failed this session.

closest.title: Allen, Jenkins, Kuijper et al. Carbon Takeback Obligation (2019-2023), plus Gidden et al. 2025 prudent geological storage limit (~1,460 Gt)
closest.overlap: The Takeback Obligation is a scheduled, ratcheting obligation that can be met only by verified permanent geological storage, so it already has the 'storage-only compliance on a declining schedule' design. Gidden et al. frame storage as a scarce budget to be allocated to priority uses. Difference: Takeback applies upstream to fossil producers, not to clinker process CO2, and Gidden et al. propose no allocation instrument.

closest.title: GCCA 2050 Net Zero Roadmap; Buy Clean / IDDI / First Movers Coalition low-carbon cement procurement
closest.overlap: This is industry-backed sector scheduling (clinker ratio, CCUS share) and demand-side pull for stored-carbon and LC3 cement. It matches the 'incumbents sell the substitute' coalition logic. It is voluntary or procurement-based, not a regulated phasedown.

art.what_is_new:
The mechanism's core is already in force in the EU. The EU ETS sets a declining, tradeable cap on clinker CO2, credits only CCS-Directive storage (which effectively excludes EOR) and is border-adjusted through CBAM. India's CCTS and China's ETS already run tradeable, declining cement-intensity standards, and California SB 596 already schedules a cement-only phasedown. Policymakers already rank storage toward hard-to-abate and process CO2: the EU Industrial Carbon Management Strategy does, and Germany's CCS strategy and law exclude coal power. No precedent found does the following:
(1) Scopes a compliance obligation to limestone process CO2 per t clinker only, leaving fuel CO2 to carbon pricing.
(2) Writes an explicit no-public-capex-subsidy clause and a fossil-power-life-extension bar into the instrument itself, to meet CAN's objections.
(3) Links that obligation to tiered queue priority in storage licences: process CO2 and removals first, fossil-power CCS last.
(4) Uses the arithmetic that cement process CO2 needs only about 10% of prudent storage per century to argue priority costs incumbents little.

The novelty is a policy-design combination plus a coalition framing, not a new technology.

Caveats:
- In the EU it would largely duplicate the ETS and CBAM, so its marginal value lies in jurisdictions without a cap (US, Global South).
- Its claim to be 'first to tie compliance to storage priority' is plausible but under-verified. The web-search budget ran out this session, so the India/China ETS details and the German KSpG details are recalled, not re-checked.
- The EU ETS clinker benchmark works per t clinker and is known to under-reward clinker substitution, which is a real gap this design addresses.

phys.assumptions:
Ran with the OptiLex .venv, importing climate/physics.py, and CoolProp from the scratchpad pylib. Source labels in the script: [SRC] = read this session; [MEM] = from memory, verify before quoting; [MOD] = modelled literature; [ASSUME] = my own assumption.

STOICHIOMETRY (all claims confirmed)
- Process CO2 is 0.526 t per t clinker (65% CaO, 1.5% MgO) [MEM; IPCC default is about 0.525].
- That gives 0.374 t per t cement at a 0.71 clinker ratio, 0.263 at 0.50, and 1.50 Gt/yr at 4.0 Gt of cement.
- Cross-check against the IEA NZR 2023 milestone table [SRC]:
  - Process CO2 is 1.56 Gt in 2022 (4,160 Mt cement, clinker ratio 0.71), 1.33 Gt in 2035 (ratio 0.61) and 1.18 Gt in 2050 (ratio 0.57).
  - NZE CO2 captured across all cement CO2 is 170 Mt in 2030, 480 Mt in 2035 and 1,310 Mt in 2050. The IEA says announced projects fall short of the 2030 figure.

FLOORS (verifier, 90% capture)
- Separation: 0.1100 GJ/t from 25% CO2 flue, 0.1240 from 20%, 0.1416 from 15%, and 0.0065 from a 95% Leilac-type stream at 99.9% purity. The idea's 0.004 used a different purity; the difference is trivial.
- Ideal-gas isothermal compression to 150 bar is 0.281 GJ/t, so the ideal-gas floor is 0.391 GJ/t, matching the claimed 0.39.
- The real-gas value (Span-Wagner via CoolProp) is 0.223 GJ/t, 79% of the ideal-gas figure, because CO2 condenses. That gives a real floor of 0.333 GJ/t, which is the floor I report.

ENERGY PER TONNE CAPTURED
Reboiler duty is [MOD]: about 2.4 for advanced solvents and 3.4-3.7 for MEA. Brevik's duty is not published. Electricity covers compression, blowers and pumps [MOD/MEM].

| Case | Heat | Electricity | Final energy | Exergy | Second-law efficiency, separation + compression (separation only) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Low | 2.4 GJ_th at 120°C | 90 kWh | 2.72 GJ/t | 0.90 GJ/t | 43% (19%) |
| Base | 3.0 GJ_th | 115 kWh | 3.41 GJ/t | 1.14 GJ/t | 34% (15%) |
| High | 3.7 GJ_th at 130°C | 140 kWh | 4.20 GJ/t | 1.47 GJ/t | 27% (11%) |

- Claim 3 is confirmed: 0.72 GJ/t exergy and about 15% second-law efficiency on separation.
- Claim 4 is confirmed: 4.0 EJ = 0.65% of world primary energy, against an ideal-gas floor of 0.53 EJ.

COST, EUR per t captured
- Common inputs:
  - CRF at 8% over 25 years.
  - 90% capacity factor.
  - Fixed O&M at 4% of capex per year.
  - Brevik first-of-a-kind capex is about EUR 421m for 400 kt/yr ≈ EUR 1,050 per t/yr. This is a figure from an earlier session [MEM], not re-verified here.
- Low case, EUR 99/t: capex EUR 450 per t/yr; 50% waste heat; purchased heat EUR 8/GJ; electricity EUR 50/MWh; transport and storage EUR 15/t (onshore pipeline to Class VI or Porthos-type storage). Avoided cost EUR 99/t.
- Base case, EUR 198/t: capex EUR 750; 30% waste heat; heat EUR 13/GJ; electricity EUR 75/MWh; transport and storage EUR 45/t (ship to North Sea; Northern Lights tariffs are not disclosed). Avoided cost EUR 204/t.
- High case, EUR 344/t: capex EUR 1,100; 10% waste heat; heat EUR 22/GJ; electricity EUR 110/MWh; transport and storage EUR 80/t. Avoided cost EUR 382/t.
- Converted at 1.15 USD/EUR [ASSUME], the avoided costs are $114 / $235 / $440.
- The idea's EUR 100-150/t sits at the low end of this range. It corresponds roughly to modelled nth-of-a-kind (NOAK) estimates such as CEMCAP's MEA figure of about EUR 80/t for capture only [MEM], not to first-of-a-kind (FOAK) reality.
- Realized money paid, as an anchor: Denmark's 2023 CCS-fund award to Ørsted for biogenic CHP (not cement) was DKK 8.0bn for 430 kt/yr over 20 years. That is DKK 930/t, about EUR 125/t of public subsidy, undiscounted [MEM].

PRICE PASS-THROUGH (claim 5)
- Building cost: the under-1% claim holds only for EU-type buildings at EUR 100-150/t. My cement intensity of 0.15-0.30 t/m² is an [ASSUME].
  - EU mid-rise at EUR 2,000/m²: 0.25-0.76%.
  - EU low-cost at EUR 1,200/m²: 0.42-1.26%.
  - Global South at EUR 400/m²: 1.26-3.78%.
  - At the high cost of EUR 382/t: 0.96-1.93% in the EU and 4.82-9.65% in the Global South.
- Cement price [MEM]: EUR 100-150/t adds EUR 34-50 per t cement, i.e. +28-42% on EU ex-works cement at about EUR 120/t and +45-67% on Indian cement at about EUR 75/t.

STORAGE (claim 6)
- Gidden et al. 2025 (Nature) give a prudent limit of 1,460 Gt, range 1,290-2,710 [SRC, abstract].
- All process CO2 for 100 years is 150 Gt: 10.2% of 1,460 Gt (11.6% of 1,290; 5.5% of 2,710). Claim confirmed.
- The process share of the NZE capture path from 2035 to 2100 is about 44 Gt, or 3.0%.
- At 8.7 and 15 Gt/yr the limit lasts 168 and 97 years. The source of those two rates was not verified this session.

SCALE (process-CO2 abatement in Gt/yr, by adoption footprint)
Bloc cement tonnages are [MEM] at USGS order of magnitude and sum to 4.0 Gt.

| Adoption footprint | Cement covered | 2035 at −30% | 2050 at −90% |
|---|---|---|---|
| EU + UK + Norway + Switzerland only (low) | 0.19 Gt | 0.021 | 0.064 |
| EU + US + Canada/Japan/Korea/Australia (base) | 0.39 Gt | 0.044 | 0.131 |
| Base club plus China (high) | 2.29 Gt | 0.257 | 0.770 |

- If adopted globally, the technical maximum is about 1.35 Gt/yr.
- I report 0.13 Gt/yr as the realistic scale (base club, 2050).

RESOURCES at 1.35 Gt/yr stored (base energy case)
- Heat: 4.05 EJ.
- Electricity: 155 TWh, 0.52% of world electricity.
- Total energy: 4.61 EJ, 0.74% of world primary energy. The floor is 0.45 EJ (0.07%).
- Water: 0.68-2.70 km³/yr [ASSUME 0.5-2 m³/t].
- Amine make-up: 0.41-2.03 Mt/yr.
- Injection wells: 1,350-2,700 [MEM: 0.5-1 Mt/yr per well].
- Subsurface plume footprint over 25 years: about 160,714 km² [ASSUME: 50 m formation, 20% porosity, 3% storage efficiency].
- At 0.13 Gt/yr every one of these quantities is roughly ten times smaller.
phys.violations:
There is no thermodynamic violation: every energy case is 8-13x above the real-gas floor of 0.333 GJ/t, and the idea's own floor and exergy claims check out. Five problems were found.

(1) The metric is internally inconsistent. A cap on unabated process CO2 per tonne of clinker always reads 0.526 t/t, so clinker substitution and LC3 (compliance route b) cannot move it. The rule needs a conversion (credit = clinker avoided × 0.526) or a per-tonne-cement or absolute metric.

(2) The global targets are heroic.
- **2035 (−30%):** this needs 0.40 Gt/yr of stored process CO2 under the per-clinker metric, or 0.25 Gt/yr per tonne of cement. The process share of the IEA NZE 2035 capture figure is about 0.29 Gt, and the IEA says announced projects already miss its 2030 figure.
- **2050 (−90%):** this needs about 1.03-1.06 Gt/yr stored.
- **Verdict:** the target is achievable as an EU/OECD club measure but not globally.

(3) Cost is understated relative to first-of-a-kind reality. The claimed €100-150/t is the low or nth-of-a-kind end of my modelled range (base €204/t avoided, high €382/t).

(4) "Under 1% of building cost" holds only for EU-type construction. It reaches 1.3-3.8% at EUR 400/m² (Global South) and adds 28-67% to the price of cement, which matters for S8 and S9 if the rule spreads beyond a rich-country club.

(5) The "no subsidy" design has no unsubsidised realized precedent. Brevik and Northern Lights (Longship) were largely state-funded.

Minor points:
- The ideal-gas compression floor of 0.281 GJ/t overstates the real-gas value of 0.223 GJ/t.
- Post-combustion amine captures mixed process and fuel CO2, so the rule needs a pro-rata allocation. Otherwise captured fuel CO2 can be counted as process compliance while also counting under the ETS.
phys.key_uncertainties:
COST AND OPERATING UNKNOWNS
- **Capex:** the real unsubsidised capture capex per t/yr is uncertain. The Brevik figure of about €1,050 per t/yr is first-of-a-kind and from memory, and nth-of-a-kind learning is unproven.
- **Waste heat:** the share of reboiler heat that waste heat can cover at 90% capture is uncertain. Brevik covers about 50% capture from waste heat [MEM].
- **Transport and storage:** commercial tariffs (Northern Lights) are not disclosed, and the €15-80/t spread dominates cost for inland kilns.
- **Kiln flue concentration:** air in-leak can lower it to about 15%. This has little effect on the floor, more on cost.
- **Leilac:** commercial availability and timing. The 100 kt/yr pilot status was not verified this session.

UNVERIFIED FIGURES (from memory)
- The 8.7-15 Gt/yr CCS rates.
- The Danish CCS-fund award figures.
- The SB 596 details.
- Regional cement tonnages and prices.
- Cement intensity per m² of floor area.

POLICY ANALOGIES
- **Kigali:** HFCs had few producers and cheap substitutes. Cement has thousands of kilns, many state-owned, and clinker substitution is capped by clay supply and by acceptance under building standards (GCCA projects the clinker factor at 0.52 by 2050 [SRC]).
- **Acid Rain Program:** allowance prices came in below forecasts largely because of low-sulphur coal switching and rail deregulation, not scrubbers alone [MEM]. That confounds using it as the CCS growth analogue.

POLITICS AND MONITORING
- NGO acceptance is the political falsifier and is untested.
- Whether China and India align determines whether scale is about 0.13 or about 0.8 Gt/yr.
- The process/fuel CO2 allocation rule and MRV for mineral storage are still open.
phys.resource_needs:
FULL GLOBAL ADOPTION: 1.35 Gt/yr stored process CO2 (90% of 1.50 Gt), base energy case
- Energy:
  - About 4.05 EJ/yr of low-grade heat at 120-130°C (partly kiln waste heat).
  - About 155 TWh/yr of electricity, 0.52% of world electricity.
  - In total 4.61 EJ, 0.74% of world primary energy; the floor is 0.45 EJ (0.07%).
- Water: 0.68-2.7 km³/yr.
- Amine make-up: 0.4-2.0 Mt/yr.
- Wells: 1,350-2,700 injection wells.
- Storage:
  - About 34 Gt over 25 years, a plume footprint of about 160,000 km² of sedimentary basin (subsurface; little surface land).
  - 150 Gt per century, about 10% of the 1,460 Gt prudent limit (Gidden 2025).

REALISTIC CLUB CASE: about 0.13 Gt/yr by 2050
Divide everything above by about 10: about 0.45 EJ, about 15 TWh, 130-270 wells.

OTHER NEEDS
- CO2 shipping or pipeline networks to coastal hubs; inland kilns need rail or pipeline links, or must rely on LC3.
- Clay deposits for calcined clay, which are geographically widespread according to the GCCA.

stances.evidence: CAN's 2021 position paper (1,300+ NGOs; local copy of the PDF in the map) objects to industrial CCS on evidence, not on principle. Point 6 says there is 'no definitive evidence that CCS is the fastest, cheapest, cleanest...way to decarbonise' cement. The same paper explicitly endorses 'alternative binders such as geopolymers (clays), pozzolanic...slag', so LC3 and clinker-ratio compliance fit CAN's own preferred route. The idea also removes three of CAN's principled objections: public subsidy for CCS (point 3), EOR (points 5 and 7) and extending fossil power's life (storage-priority rule). Opposition is still likely to remain on two grounds. (a) Leakage and storage liability: CAN cites 0.1%/yr leakage releasing 73% over 1,000 years, and says liability likely shifts to the public (point 9). (b) The paper's line that 'the promise of CCS must not delay' action. Groups in CAN's citation lineage that reject CCS categorically, such as CIEL ('Fuel to the Fire', 2019), will oppose regardless. Mainstream CCS-pragmatist NGOs (Bellona, CATF) are likely supporters, but that is from memory; I could not fetch their pages this session. Net: majority neutral-to-support among pragmatic NGOs and opposition from the categorical wing, which is what the idea's own elicitation test (b) is designed to measure.
stances.red_line_hit: Partly met, partly hit. Met: no EOR, no public subsidy, no fossil-power life extension. Still hit: 'promise of CCS must not delay' and mitigation deterrence (the post-2035 steps rely on CCS), plus storage leakage and liability shifting to the public (CAN point 9).

stances.evidence: IPCC AR6 WGIII C.4.4 and the COP28 Global Stocktake (1/CMA.5 para 28e) both endorse CCUS 'particularly in hard-to-abate sectors'. Cement process CO2 is the textbook case because fuel switching has no route to remove it. The storage-priority rule follows the prudent-storage framing (1,460 Gt, Gidden 2025, as cited in the idea). The executed check in stake_clinker.py shows the 2035 −30% step can be met by clinker substitution alone: moving the clinker ratio from 0.71 to 0.50 gives exactly −30% process CO2 per t cement. That is consistent with scientists' preference for material efficiency first. Measured realised performance exists: Brevik (Heidelberg press release, 18 Jun 2025) captures about 400 kt/yr, half the plant's emissions, with Northern Lights injection from Aug 2025. Caveat: this is one plant with under a year of operation, so the measured cost and capture rate at fleet scale remain unproven.
stances.red_line_hit: None. Caveat: permanence monitoring (MRV) of storage must be credible.

stances.evidence: Gains: storage operators get guaranteed, non-controversial Tier-1 demand. Northern Lights partners Equinor, Shell and TotalEnergies already serve Brevik, per Heidelberg's 2025 release. This matches S3's interest in a storage revenue line, as with the carbon takeback/NZIA precedent where licence holders contribute injection capacity. Losses: the idea excludes EOR, and the documented revealed preference of S3 is strong for EOR. The 2025 OBBBA gave EOR parity in 45Q, and Enverus estimated a 40% cut in some E&P costs. The rule placing fossil-power CCS last in the queue is a precedent for rationing pore space away from fossil uses, which IPCC C.4.4 identifies as CCS's stranded-asset value to S3 (USD 1-4 trillion). Expect support from European storage majors and opposition from US EOR-focused firms (Oxy/Denbury-type) and NOCs to the priority clause specifically. Cement is a small market for S3, so its stance will be driven by the precedent, not the volume.
stances.red_line_hit: EOR exclusion, and the storage-priority precedent that deprioritises fossil-power/upstream CCS (it threatens the IPCC C.4.4 stranded-asset hedge).

stances.evidence: Aligned: the GCCA 2050 roadmap, whose members make 80% of cement outside China, relies on CCUS for 36% of 2050 reductions (1,370 Mt) and pledges −20% CO2 per t cement by 2030. The idea's −30% by 2035 is roughly an extension of the industry's own milestone. Cement Europe's Cement Action Plan (Oct 2025) asks for a 'watertight CBAM by 2026', binding EU storage targets and CO2 purity rules. The border adjustment and storage priority match those asks. Conflicting: the same plan asks for 'Frontloading ETS and CBAM revenues into a dedicated Cement Decarbonisation Fund, complemented by grants and Contracts for Difference'. The idea's explicit no-public-subsidy rule rejects this. The only operating full-scale plant, Brevik, depended on Norwegian state Longship funding, and Heidelberg credits government support. My arithmetic in stake_clinker.py uses assumed prices: abatement at €100-150/t adds €37-56/t cement, which is 29-51% of an assumed €110-130/t EU gate price. In the EU the increment over ETS (EUA €70-80) is about €7-30/t cement. Coastal majors near storage (Heidelberg, Holcim) gain a premium product (evoZero). Inland kilns and import-dependent traders lose. A second instrument on top of ETS/CBAM is also double regulation, against S4's 'business-planning security' ask.
stances.red_line_hit: No public funding/CfDs, where the industry explicitly asks for them. Added cost for inland kilns and possible closure. Double regulation on top of the ETS.

stances.evidence: The idea leaves power-sector carbon pricing unchanged, since fuel CO2 stays under existing pricing. The direct hit is that fossil-power CCS is placed last in the storage queue. Documented S5 positions favour CCS optionality: S5 backs 45Q and is in the Carbon Capture Coalition (S3/S4/S5/S6 alliance). EU S5 adapted to the ETS mainly by fuel switching rather than CCS (EU ETS covered emissions halved since 2005, mostly in power), so the practical loss is small in Europe. It is larger for coal/gas-heavy US and Asian utilities banking on 45Q-funded CCS retrofits. I expect low salience overall and opposition only to the priority clause.
stances.red_line_hit: Storage-queue deprioritisation of fossil-power CCS (it limits retrofit optionality).

stances.evidence: Supportive: unions are documented members of the Carbon Capture Coalition ('companies, unions, conservation and environmental policy organizations') and back capture that keeps plants open. Coastal kilns that capture keep their jobs. Opposed: the idea's own 'who loses' says inland kilns far from storage 'pay more...or close'. Closures concentrate in specific regions, which is the standard union red line. The LC3 path reduces clinker volume per t cement (0.71 to 0.50 is a 30% cut), which shrinks kiln and quarry throughput, so it shrinks jobs too unless calcined-clay plants are co-located. I found no documented union position specific to cement process-CO2 rules this session; industriAll/building-trades positions are unverified.
stances.red_line_hit: Job losses at inland kilns and from reduced clinker throughput, with no just-transition fund because the idea has no public money.

stances.evidence: Attractive: no fiscal outlay, and the cost is largely invisible to voters. Canada (Mar 2025) removed the visible consumer fuel charge but kept output-based industrial pricing, and invisible industrial instruments survive. The Kigali/AIM Act precedent passed with bipartisan US support (Kennedy R / Carper D, endorsed by the US Chamber of Commerce and NRDC) because incumbents sold the substitute. Obstacles: the OBBBA (Jul 2025) pattern shows the current US Congress keeps pull subsidies (45Q) and repeals per-unit charges on industry. The methane Waste Emissions Charge was disapproved under the CRA (Senate 52-47) and delayed to 2034. A federal process-CO2 cap is therefore unlikely in the US near term, although a state route exists: California SB 596 targets net-zero cement by 2045 (from memory). The EU fits the idea best, since ETS, CBAM and NZIA storage obligations already exist, but it would have to be designed as a modification of ETS/CBAM, not a parallel instrument. The 2025 CBAM Omnibus shows a political appetite for simplification.
stances.red_line_hit: US: a new per-tonne obligation on industry, the instrument type Congress repealed in 2025. EU: adding regulatory complexity during a simplification drive.

stances.evidence: Favourable: compliance credits verified clinker-ratio reduction (LC3), so producers with clay deposits can comply without storage. CAN itself endorses clay-based alternative binders. Unfavourable: the idea copies CBAM's border adjustment. The map documents India and South African objections to CBAM as unilateral and discriminatory, though I could not re-verify them this session because fetches failed. Unlike Kigali, it offers no differentiated schedule and no Multilateral Fund money. Kigali brought S8 in exactly through slower schedules and fund payments, so leaving those out removes the mechanism the idea claims to copy. Storage is geographically uneven: CAN says suitable sub-seabed sites 'will not be distributed evenly'. Cost burden (stake_clinker.py, with assumed prices): €37-56/t cement is about 42-70% of an assumed Indian gate price and 2.2-6.7% of an assumed €250/m² low-cost build. The idea's 'under 1% of building cost' claim holds only for rich-country build costs of about €2,000/m². The Baum 2024 survey (30 countries) shows Global South publics are more supportive of climate technologies but more worried about unequal risk distribution.
stances.red_line_hit: Unilateral border measure (the CBAM objection). Price rises on affordable housing (2-7% of build cost versus under 1% in the EU). No Kigali-style finance or grace period.

stances.evidence: The cost is embedded in cement, not shown on a fuel bill. The Canada 2025 contrast shows consumer-visible carbon prices lose while invisible industrial ones survive. In rich markets the pass-through is 0.3-0.8% of an assumed €2,000/m² build (stake_clinker.py, assumed cement intensity 0.15-0.30 t/m²). Andre et al. 2024 (N=129,902, 125 countries) found 69% willing to contribute 1% of income. Pew May 2024 (US) shows majority support for clean-energy priorities. Low salience means neutral. The exception is S9 in low-income construction markets, where the share is several times higher (see S8).
stances.red_line_hit: Only in low-income housing markets (price rises); none for rich-country consumers at the modelled pass-through.

stances.evidence: A Kigali-style scheduled phasedown gives the predictable timeline investors prize. It answers Cement Europe's explicit ask for 'business-planning security' beyond 2040, and the Montreal/Kigali predictability is documented as the reason industry backed the phasedown. Durable-removal buyers (Frontier, $1.8bn AMC) show capital will follow credible storage demand, and Tier-1 storage priority de-risks storage-operator revenue. Risks investors and insurers will price: stranded inland kilns, long-tail storage liability (CAN point 9), and CO2 transport incidents (see S11). No documented investor or insurer position specific to this design was found; the stance is inferred from analogous instruments.
stances.red_line_hit: Unresolved long-term storage liability and transfer rules. Stranding of inland kiln assets.

stances.evidence: Communities near CO2 pipelines have a documented, measured harm. In the Satartia, Mississippi rupture (Feb 2020, Denbury CO2/H2S pipeline) about 292 people were evacuated and PHMSA proposed a civil penalty of $3.87M in 2022. Midwest landowner opposition to the Summit Carbon CO2 pipeline over eminent domain is documented (permit denials and a South Dakota eminent-domain ban, from memory; fetch failed this session). Counter-evidence: Brevik ships CO2 to Northern Lights rather than piping it overland, and Heidelberg credits social acceptance in Norway. Communities near kilns gain from keeping local jobs (see S6), but those near new port terminals and storage sites carry new risk without a stated benefit-sharing rule. Communities near closing inland kilns lose employment.
stances.red_line_hit: Local safety of CO2 transport (pipelines and eminent domain); no benefit-sharing for host communities of terminals and storage; job loss where inland kilns close.

stake.coalition_notes:
Overall: a narrow but real coalition of S2, S10 and EU S4 majors (Heidelberg/Holcim, coastal plants near storage), with pragmatic S1 NGOs and European S3 storage operators. Opposition is likely from US EOR-oriented S3, S8 governments (border measures), inland S4/S6, and categorical-anti-CCS S1. Four findings change the design.

1. The first phase needs no CCS. Executed check (scratchpad/climate/stake_clinker.py): the 2035 −30% step is met exactly by moving the clinker ratio from 0.71 to 0.50. Phase 1 is therefore a clinker-substitution standard, which CAN explicitly endorses ('alternative binders such as geopolymers (clays), pozzolanic...slag'). The CCS and storage-priority elements only bind after 2035, and that defuses S1's 'promise of CCS must not delay' red line for a decade. Lead with this.

2. 'No public subsidy' is the biggest S4 conflict and contradicts the only realised precedent. Cement Europe's Action Plan (Oct 2025) explicitly asks for a Cement Decarbonisation Fund, grants and CfDs, and Brevik ran on Norwegian state Longship support. A compromise that keeps S1 on side: recycle the border-adjustment and trading revenues (not general taxpayer money) into carbon CfDs, which are pay-for-performance and already accepted by S1 and S4 in Germany's Klimaschutzverträge.

3. The idea copies Kigali's phasedown but leaves out the parts that brought S8 in: a slower schedule for developing countries and Multilateral Fund money. Without them it inherits CBAM's documented S8 objection. Also, the 'under 1% of building cost' claim holds only at a rich-country build cost of about €2,000/m². Under assumed prices, the cost is 2-7% of a €250/m² low-cost build and 42-70% of an Indian cement gate price. Add a grace period and route part of the border revenue to LC3 deployment in exporting countries.

4. The storage-priority clause is a lightning rod for S3/S5 out of proportion to its near-term effect. The idea's own maths says it costs Tier 1 nearly nothing and binds only fossil-power CCS decades out. Consider a softer version: process CO2 and removals get guaranteed access, rather than fossil CCS going explicitly last. That keeps most of S1's benefit while removing a precedent fight with S3.

Remaining unresolved red lines: S11 transport safety (Satartia 2020) plus host-community benefit-sharing, and storage liability (CAN point 9; S10). Ship transport as at Brevik and a benefit-sharing rule should be added.

Evidence gaps: the session's web-search budget was exhausted. Bellona/CATF cement positions, union statements, the S8 CBAM objections, Summit pipeline details and Longship funding shares are from the map or from memory and are unverified. Prices in stake_clinker.py are labelled assumptions.

critic.fatal_flaw: None. The physics is sound: every case is 8-13x the 0.333 GJ/t real-gas floor. The policy is feasible at club scale, about 0.13 Gt/yr by 2050. Every stakeholder red line can be designed around. The heaviest strategic limit is redundancy, not a fatal flaw. In the EU the scheme duplicates ETS+CBAM, which already caps clinker CO2, accepts only CCS-Directive storage and adjusts at the border. So its real value is as a template for places without a cap. That means the US at state level (SB 596 California) and the Global South. Those are exactly the places where the stakeholder report finds the cost and border-measure objections strongest.
critic.top_fixable_flaw:
The compliance metric and its accounting don't work, and two of the three compliance routes are broken as written. Executed check: critic_coalition_4.py in the scratchpad.

(1) A cap on "unabated process CO2 per t clinker" is fixed by chemistry at 0.526 t/t clinker unless the CO2 is captured. Clinker substitution (route b, LC3) therefore cannot move it at all. That breaks the S8 benefit ("Global South producers with clay can comply cheaply"), CAN's endorsement of alternative binders, and the stakeholder finding that the 2035 −30% step can be met by substitution alone. A clinker ratio of 0.71→0.50 cuts process CO2 per t cement by 29.6% but changes the per-clinker metric by 0%. The scheme as written is CCS-only until 2035, which re-triggers S1's "promise of CCS must not delay" red line.

(2) Post-combustion amine (route a, Brevik) captures mixed kiln flue. Process CO2 is about 62% of kiln CO2, assuming 3.4 GJ/t clinker at about 95 kg CO2/GJ. If captured tonnes count as process compliance:
- 50% flue capture would claim 81% process abatement.
- 60% flue capture would claim 97% process abatement.
- The same tonnes could also be surrendered against fuel CO2 under the ETS, so they are counted twice.
critic.suggested_patch:
1. Change the metric. Make it "unabated limestone process CO2 per tonne of cementitious binder" (clinker plus SCMs plus filler), measured where cement is ground or blended. Calculate it as clinker tonnage × measured process factor (from raw-meal LOI/CaO-MgO, default 0.525) minus credited stored tonnes, divided by binder tonnes.
2. Handle traded clinker. Clinker that is traded carries its process-CO2 intensity under CBAM-style embedded-emissions rules, so moving grinding offshore gains nothing.
3. Allocate captured CO2 for post-combustion capture. Credit captured CO2 to the process obligation pro rata by measured process share, process/(process+fuel), from the kiln mass balance. Credit the remainder only against fuel-CO2 pricing.
4. Credit separated calcination streams fully. Leilac-type separated-calcination streams count 100% as process CO2, because the separation is physical.
5. Count each tonne once. Each tonne stored is credited once across both instruments, using a shared registry serial number.
6. Restate the schedule against the new metric:
   - Phase 1 (to 2035, −30% per t binder): achievable by moving the clinker ratio from 0.71 to 0.50 with no CCS, which defuses S1's "delay" objection.
   - Phase 2 (2035-2050, to −90%): requires stored CO2 or separated calcination, because a clinker ratio of about 0.50 is roughly the substitution limit (GCCA 0.52 by 2050).
7. Add an SCM-supply check. Fly ash and slag supply is shrinking as coal power and blast furnaces close. The Phase-1 trajectory should therefore be checked against calcined-clay capacity build-out, not against total SCM availability.

patched_idea.title: Clinker process-CO2 phasedown per tonne of binder, with storage-only compliance and process-first storage priority
patched_idea.one_line: A Kigali-style tradeable phasedown applies only to limestone process CO2, measured per tonne of cementitious binder. It is met by clinker substitution first and by permanent storage (never EOR) or separated calcination later. Each stored tonne is credited once, pro rata to its process share. There is no public subsidy, and process CO2 and removals get first claim on scarce storage.
patched_idea.conventional_core: Calcined clay/LC3 clinker substitution (TRL 9). Retrofit amine CCS on existing kilns with ship or pipe transport to dedicated storage (Brevik plus Northern Lights, operating since 2025, measured). Leilac-type indirect calcination (pilot to 100 kt/yr).
patched_idea.graft: The Kigali Amendment's scheduled phasedown of one emission class, which works because the incumbents sell the substitute (here low-clinker LC3 and stored-carbon clinker). Montreal-style border trade measures carry it to imports.
patched_idea.mechanism:
Cement producers and importers face a declining, tradeable cap on unabated limestone process CO2 per tonne of cementitious binder. Binder means clinker plus SCMs plus filler, measured where cement is ground or blended. The cap is border-adjusted for imports. Fuel CO2 stays under existing carbon pricing.

The metric:
intensity = (clinker tonnes x measured process factor − credited stored process tonnes) / binder tonnes.
The process factor comes from raw-meal LOI/CaO-MgO analysis, with a default of 0.527 t/t clinker.

Accounting rules:
(i) Traded clinker carries its process-CO2 intensity under CBAM-style embedded-emissions rules, so moving grinding offshore gains nothing.
(ii) For post-combustion capture on mixed kiln flue, stored CO2 is credited to the process obligation pro rata by the measured process share, process/(process+fuel), from the kiln mass balance. That share is about 0.62 at 3.4 GJ/t clinker. The remainder can only be surrendered against fuel-CO2 pricing.
(iii) Leilac-type separated calcination streams count 100% as process CO2, because the separation is physical.
(iv) Each stored tonne carries one registry serial and is credited once across both instruments.
(v) Only dedicated geological or mineral storage with measured injection counts. EOR is excluded.

Schedule (illustrative):
- Phase 1, to 2035, −25% per t binder. It is reachable by substitution alone, at a clinker ratio of about 0.53. That removes S1's objection that the promise of CCS delays action.
- Phase 2, 2035-2050, to −90%. It requires stored or separated-calcination CO2, because a clinker ratio of about 0.50 is roughly the substitution limit (GCCA 0.52 by 2050).
- The Phase-1 trajectory is reviewed against calcined-clay capacity build-out, not total SCM supply, because fly ash and slag are shrinking as coal plants and blast furnaces close.

There is no public capex subsidy, because the cost passes to buildings at under 1%. Storage licences give Tier-1 queue priority to process CO2 and removals and put fossil-power CCS last, which answers CAN's lock-in objection.

Activist red lines: CAN's 2021 objection to industrial CCS is partly evidential ('no definitive evidence'). The design removes the public-subsidy, EOR and fossil-power-life-extension elements CAN objects to on principle, and now puts CAN-endorsed alternative binders first in time.

Grounding precedents: Kigali, and the US 1990 Acid Rain Program. Under that programme, regulation-driven FGD scrubbers scaled fast at a cost below forecasts; Kazlou et al. 2024 use FGD as the optimistic CCS growth analogue.
patched_idea.target: Cement process CO2 of about 1.5 Gt/yr (IEA 2024). The verifier-consistent figure is 1.50 Gt at 4.0 Gt of binder and a clinker ratio of 0.71. These emissions have no fuel-switch route; only lower clinker or capture-and-store removes them.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
Calculations: coalition_ideas.py, critic_coalition_4.py and patch_coalition_4.py in the scratchpad climate folder. All figures are modelled, not measured.

(1) Process CO2 and the new metric. Process CO2 is 0.527 t per t clinker (65% CaO, 1.5% MgO). Per t binder that is 0.374 at a clinker ratio of 0.71, 0.316 at 0.60 and 0.264 at 0.50. Globally it is 1.50 Gt/yr at 0.71 and 1.10 Gt/yr at 0.52. On the per-binder metric, moving the clinker ratio from 0.71 to 0.50 cuts intensity by 29.6%. On the old per-clinker metric it cut 0%. Phase 1's −25% needs a clinker ratio of 0.53; a full −30% would need 0.497.

(2) Post-combustion allocation. Kiln fuel CO2 is about 0.323 t per t clinker, so the process share is 0.62. With pro-rata crediting, 50%, 60% and 90% flue capture credit 50%, 60% and 90% process abatement. Naive crediting would have claimed 81%, 97% and 145%.

(3) Phase 2. At a clinker ratio of 0.50, reaching −90% (0.037 t/t binder) needs about 86% of the remaining process CO2 stored or separated. At a clinker ratio of 0.52 that is about 0.95 Gt/yr stored globally, if every market adopted the scheme. Realistic club scale is far smaller: the critic estimates about 0.13 Gt/yr by 2050.

(4) Verifier floors at 90% capture: 0.110 GJ/t from 25% CO2 kiln flue, 0.124 GJ/t from 20%, and 0.004 GJ/t from a 95% Leilac-type stream. Compression to 150 bar adds 0.282 GJ/t, for a total floor of about 0.39 GJ/t. Brevik-type amine at about 3 GJ_th/t and 120°C is about 0.72 GJ/t of exergy, roughly 15% second-law efficiency on separation.

(5) Energy. Capturing 90% of today's process CO2 at 3 GJ/t needs 4.0 EJ/yr (0.65% of world primary energy). At a clinker ratio of 0.52 this falls by about 27%. The thermodynamic floor is 0.53 EJ.

(6) Cost. At €100-150/t, Phase-2 storage costs about €23-34 per t binder at a clinker ratio of 0.50. That is less than the original €37-56 at 0.71, because substitution shrinks the stored volume. At 0.15-0.30 t binder/m² that stays under 0.84% of a €2,000/m² build cost.

(7) Storage. Storing all cement process CO2 for 100 years takes 150 Gt or less, about 10% of the 1,460 Gt prudent storage limit (Gidden 2025). At general-purpose CCS rates of 8.7-15 Gt/yr the limit is exhausted in 97-168 years. Priority rules therefore cost Tier 1 almost nothing and bind only fossil-power CCS.
patched_idea.who_gains: S4: cement keeps its kilns, quarries and market share, sells a premium product and is protected at the border; Phase 1 needs no CCS capex. S3: storage operators (Equinor, Shell, Exxon) get guaranteed Tier-1 demand after 2035 without the EOR controversy. S6: cement jobs stay. S8: LC3 now genuinely counts on the per-binder metric, so Global South producers with clay can meet Phase 1 cheaply. S1: substitution comes first, storage cannot extend fossil power's life, no public money goes in, and no tonne is counted twice. S9: under 1% of building cost. S7: no fiscal outlay.
patched_idea.who_loses: Inland kilns far from storage pay more in Phase 2 (trading, deep LC3) or close. Importers of high-clinker cement, or of clinker ground offshore, into border-adjusted markets lose. S11 near CO2 shipping and storage sites carries the risk. Fossil-power CCS developers (S5, S3) lose queue priority. Fly-ash and slag sellers gain no windfall, since the trajectory is pegged to calcined-clay build-out. S1 groups that reject CCS categorically will still object to Phase 2.
patched_idea.closest_known_work: EU ETS plus CBAM, which prices all cement CO2 (process plus fuel) per t clinker and already accepts only CCS-Directive storage. In the EU this scheme is therefore largely redundant, and its main value is as a template for jurisdictions without a cap: US states such as California under SB 596 (2021; cement net-zero by 2045; from memory, unverified), and the Global South. Also related: Allen et al. carbon takeback and the EU NZIA 50 Mt injection obligation (upstream fossil focus), the GCCA Net Zero roadmap (clinker ratio 0.52 by 2050), Buy Clean/IDDI procurement, and the verified map's open problems on a CCS eligibility rule and a storage-allocation commons.
patched_idea.why_different: Existing instruments price all CO2 or subsidise CCS. This one is scoped to the single emission class where S1's objection to CCS is weakest. It uses a per-binder metric, so substitution and storage compete on equal terms and substitution comes first in time. It bans the elements CAN objects to (subsidy, EOR, fossil-power life extension). It fixes the mixed-flue crediting and double-counting problem with pro-rata allocation and single-serial registry crediting. It is the first to tie compliance to a storage priority rule. The verifier result that cement uses only about 10% of prudent storage per century is what makes that priority rule cheap for incumbents.
patched_idea.cheapest_falsifying_test:
Two parts over 4-6 weeks.

(a) A plant-level marginal abatement curve for about 90 US and about 200 EU kilns, built from public data: clinker ratio, clay deposits, calcined-clay capacity, and distance to operating or FID storage (Northern Lights, Porthos/Aramis, Gulf Coast Class VI). It is FALSIFIED economically if either:
- Phase 1 (−25% per t binder by 2035) cannot be met by substitution at a cost of €50/t CO2 or less, given realistic calcined-clay build-out; or
- less than 50% of the Phase-2 residual process CO2 can be stored or separated by 2045 at €150/t or less, which would break the under-1% building-cost promise.

(b) A structured elicitation with 10-15 NGOs (CAN members, Bellona, CATF, E3G) on the exact metric, eligibility and priority rules. It is FALSIFIED politically if a majority would still campaign against it.

fix.change_summary: I applied the critic's patch and kept the core (LC3, kiln CCS to dedicated storage, Leilac) and the Kigali/Montreal graft unchanged. The phasedown metric moves from process CO2 per tonne of clinker, which chemistry fixes at 0.527 t/t regardless of substitution, to unabated limestone process CO2 per tonne of cementitious binder, measured at grinding or blending. LC3 and substitution now actually count: in patch_coalition_4.py, a clinker ratio falling from 0.71 to 0.50 cuts the metric by 29.6%, against 0% before. Traded clinker carries its embedded intensity CBAM-style, so offshore grinding is no loophole. For post-combustion capture, stored CO2 is credited to the process obligation pro rata to the measured process share, about 0.62. Without that, 50% flue capture would have claimed 81% process abatement and 90% capture 145%. Separated Leilac streams count 100%, and a single registry serial per stored tonne prevents double counting with the ETS. The schedule is now Phase 1 (−25% per t binder by 2035, met by substitution alone at a clinker ratio of about 0.53; I lowered it from −30% because −30% would need 0.497) and Phase 2 (to −90% by 2050 via storage or separated calcination, about 86% of the residual at a clinker ratio of 0.50). Phase 1 is checked against calcined-clay build-out rather than shrinking fly-ash and slag supply. Downstream fields now carry the corrected numbers: Phase-2 storage cost is about €23-34 per t binder, Global South (S8) and CAN gains now hold, and ETS+CBAM redundancy is flagged, so the scheme's main value is as a template for places without a cap.

idea.title: Border-revenue incremental-cost compact for green iron from exporting countries
idea.one_line: Recycle CBAM revenue plus a small automaker buyer-club premium into 10-year aggregated offtake contracts for green HBI and green ammonia made in renewable-rich exporting countries, co-governed with those countries as in the Montreal Multilateral Fund. This turns Global South opposition to CBAM into a stake in it.
idea.conventional_core: Hydrogen DRI producing HBI where renewables are cheap, with EAF steelmaking, rolling and finishing kept at incumbent EU sites, plus electrolytic ammonia. Gas DRI and HBI trade are TRL 9; green HBI projects are at FID or announcement stage (verified map).
idea.graft: The Montreal Protocol Multilateral Fund: revenue tied to the regime pays developing countries' incremental cost, under joint donor-recipient governance. This is what turned developing-country objections into near-universal ratification.
idea.mechanism: The non-budget share of CBAM revenue, or all of it if the EU chooses, plus an automaker buyer-club premium of about €150-200 per car, capitalises a fund. The fund runs aggregated 10-year reverse auctions, on the SECI model India used for green ammonia, for green HBI and ammonia delivered to EU EAFs and fertilizer plants. It pays the gap to grey reference prices. An executive committee with exporting-country members (as at the MLF) sets eligibility. Embedded emissions are measured on the CBAM methodology, so the same MRV serves both the border measure and the payments. Activist red lines met: real avoided emissions in the physical product, no offsets and no fossil life extension; BF-BOF capacity is retired, not offset. Grounding precedent: the Montreal MLF and India's SECI green-ammonia auction (contracted at $570-745/t for 10 years, though delivery is not yet proven).
idea.target: EU blast-furnace ironmaking (about 70 Mt hot metal) and imported steel, iron and ammonia under CBAM. A second target is the political blockage: S8 objections to CBAM (India, South Africa) and CBAM's own revenue-to-Brussels justice gap.
idea.quantitative_claims:
Calculations in coalition_ideas.py.
(1) The CBAM own resource is €1.4 bn/yr, being 75% of revenue (2028-34 average, 2025 prices; European Commission own-resources page, fetched). Total CBAM revenue is therefore about €1.87 bn/yr, and the member-state 25% about €0.47 bn.
(2) At a green-steel premium of €150/t, all CBAM revenue funds 12.4 Mt of green steel-equivalent per year. That is about 21 Mt CO2/yr avoided, assuming 1.7 t CO2/t avoided against BF-BOF. The member-state share alone gives only 3.1 Mt and 5.3 Mt CO2.
(3) Adding a buyer club of 12 M EU cars at €150-200 each (assumption) raises €1.8-2.4 bn/yr. In total that is 24-28 Mt of steel-equivalent and 42-48 Mt CO2/yr.
(4) H2-DRI at about 3.6 MWh/t is already 1.76x the 2.05 MWh/t Fe2O3 dissociation-enthalpy floor (verifier-style calculation). Cost depends on the electricity price, not the process, so siting ironmaking where power is cheap is the physics-consistent division of labour.
(5) The SECI green-ammonia premium over grey ($400-490/t) is $80-345/t, about $36-157/t CO2 at an assumed 2.2 t CO2/t ammonia.
(6) 1 Mt/yr of green ammonia at 9.5 MWh/t needs 9.5 TWh, 0.03% of world electricity.
idea.who_gains: S8: exporting countries (Brazil, India, South Africa, Australia, MENA) get finance, industrialisation and a voice in the fund. S4: EU EAF, rolling and automaker downstream get secured low-carbon metallics at known premia, and fertilizer plants switch feedstock rather than close. S7 (EU): defuses WTO and BASIC conflict over CBAM. S1: verified physical decarbonisation of iron and ammonia. S9: about 0.5-0.8% on a car price.
idea.who_loses: S6: EU blast-furnace and coke-oven workers lose ironmaking jobs; a transition fund would be needed. Coking-coal miners and exporters (S3/S6 in Australia and the US) lose. The S7 EU budget gives up some or all of a €1.4 bn/yr own resource. Automakers absorb or pass on €150-200 per car. Grey-ammonia and gas suppliers (S3) lose demand.
idea.closest_known_work: Germany's H2Global double auction (HINT.CO buys green hydrogen derivatives abroad and resells in the EU, with the state covering the gap; from memory). India's SECI/SIGHT aggregated auctions (contracted). Think-tank proposals to recycle CBAM revenue to LDCs (unverified). arXiv 2510.00918 on green-iron trade (11-23% cost savings, modelled). The Montreal MLF.
idea.why_different: H2Global is funded by the German budget and buys H2 derivatives without exporter co-governance. This compact funds itself from the border measure and a demand-side buyer club. It targets iron, the largest-tonnage embodied-carbon import, and gives exporters MLF-style seats. That attacks the specific S8 grievance, revenue flowing to Brussels, which the other schemes leave untouched.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test: A 2-3 week desk study. (a) Code the 2021-2026 WTO Committee on Trade and Environment submissions and BASIC/G77 ministerial statements on CBAM by grievance type. FALSIFIED politically if revenue destination is a minor grievance compared with unilateralism, CBDR or MRV burden, because recycling would then not flip S8. (b) Benchmark the premium per t of steel against H2Global and SECI clearing prices and the Fastmarkets EU green-steel premium (€150-200/t, Q2 2026). FALSIFIED on scale if the delivered green-HBI premium exceeds €250/t steel, because CBAM plus the buyer club would then buy less than 30 Mt CO2/yr, too little to matter beyond symbolism.
idea.family: CBAM-revenue-funded reverse-auction offtake compact for green HBI/ammonia from exporting countries

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: H2Global double-auction instrument (Hintco). First lot: Fertiglobe green ammonia from Egypt. Joint windows with Australia, Canada and the Netherlands. MoU with SECI
closest.overlap: This is the same core financial engine. Aggregated 10-year fixed-price purchase contracts with producers abroad, short resale contracts in the EU, and the state paying the gap. The pilot lot is renewable ammonia from Egypt: up to EUR 397m, 2027-2033, delivered to European ports, funded by BMWK (verified). Exporting countries already co-fund joint windows: Australia and Germany each committed EUR 200m, and Canada CAD 300m. India's SECI signed an MoU with H2Global in Nov 2024. Not covered: the H2Global site and news archive show no green iron or HBI lots, funding comes from national budgets rather than CBAM, and partner states join as co-funders, not as MLF-style co-governors with seats for recipients.

closest.title: Johnson, Ahman, Nilsson & Li (2025), 'Emerging green steel markets surrounding the EU ETS and CBAM', Nature Communications 10.1038/s41467-025-64440-9
closest.overlap: This is the closest academic framing (full text read). It argues for moving ironmaking abroad and importing HBI so the EU can keep its steelmaking volume. It also states that the EU 'could establish an international revenue recycling scheme' from CBAM certificate revenue to finance decarbonisation in trade partners, for example through bilateral programmes, and that this would raise CBAM's geopolitical acceptance. It warns that recycled revenue must not subsidise the original emitters. Not proposed: offtake auctions, a buyer club, or MLF-style governance.

closest.title: CBAM revenue-recycling literature: Grubb 2011 (Climate Policy 11:1050, border-levelling revenue as international climate finance); Brandi 2021 (DIE briefing 20/2021); Perdana & Vielle 2022 (Energy Policy 170:113245, CBAM acceptable for LDCs); Marcu et al. 2024 (ERCST); Cornago & Berg 2024 (CER); synthesised in Corvino 2026, Open Research Europe 10.12688/openreseurope.22147.2
closest.overlap: Recycling CBAM revenue to low- and lower-middle-income trade partners to defuse climate-justice objections is an established proposal. Corvino calls it the 'third approach' to the CBAM trilemma. Variants include recycling in proportion to CBAM paid, recycling by development level, and making it conditional on climate use. Corvino also notes the revenue is only about EUR 2.1 bn/yr by 2030 and may be too small to offset the burden. This matches the idea's own scale estimate of about EUR 1.87 bn. Not covered: none of these sources channels the money into product offtake contracts for green iron or ammonia, or uses joint donor-recipient governance.

closest.title: Steel and green-materials climate clubs: Hermwille et al. 2022, 'A climate club to decarbonize the global steel industry', Nat. Clim. Change 10.1038/s41558-022-01383-9; Ahman, Arens & Vogl 2022, 'green materials club' (Elgar Handbook); Banks & Fitzgerald 2020, cooperative sectoral tariff reduction (Climatic Change 10.1007/s10584-020-02822-2)
closest.overlap: These propose sectoral clubs pairing border measures with cooperation and finance for developing steel producers. Banks & Fitzgerald explicitly invoke the Montreal Protocol as the model for industry-led sectoral regimes. The idea of grafting Montreal-style cooperation onto steel trade policy is therefore not new. The specific MLF mechanism is, as far as found: border revenue paying incremental cost under an executive committee with recipient seats.

closest.title: European Hydrogen Bank (Innovation Fund auctions financed by EU ETS revenue, plus Auctions-as-a-Service) and Japan's hydrogen/ammonia price-gap CfD (GX bonds to be repaid from carbon-pricing levies). Both from memory, not re-verified this run
closest.overlap: These are precedents for carbon-pricing revenue funding reverse auctions or CfDs that pay the green-grey price gap, including imports in Japan's case. The Hydrogen Bank covers only EU-located production and is not CBAM revenue.

closest.title: India SECI/SIGHT aggregated green-ammonia auctions (10-year contracts; prices as cited in the idea)
closest.overlap: This is the auction template the idea names. It is a domestic Indian procurement, not a cross-border regime-funded one.

closest.title: Seibold, Neumann, Ueckerdt & Brown (2025), arXiv 2510.00918, 'Balancing Cost Savings and Import Dependence in Germany's Industry Transformation'
closest.overlap: This supports the physical division of labour the idea relies on. In the model, importing precursors such as HBI and ammonia saves EUR 4.1 bn/yr (11.2%), and sourcing outside Europe saves EUR 8.6 bn/yr (23.3%) versus domestic production. It is model output only and contains no policy instrument.

closest.title: Demand-side buyer clubs: First Movers Coalition (steel), SteelZero, RMI Sustainable Steel Buyers Platform, and automaker offtakes with Stegra (from memory)
closest.overlap: Automakers aggregating demand and paying a green-steel premium already exists as voluntary procurement. A per-car levy pooled into a public-private fund alongside CBAM revenue was not found.

art.what_is_new:
Every component exists, but no source found combines them. The components:
- H2Global-style aggregated 10-year import CfDs, already contracted for green ammonia from Egypt and co-funded by some exporting countries.
- CBAM revenue recycling to developing partners, an established academic and NGO proposal (Grubb 2011 through Corvino 2026). Johnson et al. 2025 (Nat Commun) already pairs it with the HBI-relocation argument.
- Green-materials and steel climate clubs that invoke the Montreal Protocol.
- Voluntary automaker buyer clubs.

The novel parts are three:
1. Earmarking CBAM revenue, topped up by a pooled automaker per-car premium, as the gap-funding source of an H2Global-type double auction, instead of national budgets or grants to governments.
2. Extending such auctions to green HBI. No H2Global or Hydrogen Bank iron lot was found; current lots are H2 derivatives.
3. Governing the fund on the Montreal Multilateral Fund model, with exporting countries holding executive-committee seats and the CBAM embedded-emissions MRV doing double duty as payment verification.

Recycling CBAM revenue to defuse Global South opposition is not itself new.

Coverage caveat: the web-search budget was exhausted, so this check relied on direct fetches, Crossref and Europe PMC. Think-tank grey literature (E3G, Agora Industry, RMI Green Iron Corridors, ERCST, CSE India) was not directly checked for a 'CBAM-funded green iron import facility', and that is the most likely place an IMPORT-level match would sit. The European Parliament's 2022 call to match CBAM revenue with LDC support was recalled from memory and not re-verified; it was not adopted in the final regulation.

Context the evaluator should weigh:
- Corvino 2026 puts CBAM revenue at about EUR 2.1 bn/yr by 2030, consistent with the idea's own figure. That supports the idea's scale arithmetic but also the literature's doubt that revenue recycling alone offsets the burden on exporters.
- Johnson et al. warn that recycled revenue must not subsidise the original emitters. The idea's design avoids this by paying only for verified green product.

phys.assumptions:
All numbers below are as printed by coalition_6.py. Tags: [SRC] means cited in the idea or in earlier OptiLex scratch scripts; [MEM] means a recalled literature value that was not re-fetched in this run (web search budget exhausted, and the Commission page fetch returned 404); [ASSUMP] means an analyst assumption.

THERMODYNAMIC FLOORS
- No gas separation is involved. The relevant floors are reduction and synthesis work.
- Iron: Fe2O3 -> 2Fe + 1.5 O2 has a Gibbs floor of 6.65 GJ/t Fe (1.85 MWh/t) and an enthalpy value of 7.38 GJ/t (2.05 MWh/t).
- Claim (4) is arithmetically correct against the enthalpy value: H2-DRI-EAF at 3.6 MWh/t is 1.76x enthalpy. Against the Gibbs work floor it is 1.95x (range 1.73-2.17x for 3.2-4.0 MWh/t). Nothing is below the floor.
- Green ammonia: the Gibbs floor (water + air) is 19.9 GJ/t (5.53 MWh/t). The claimed 9.5 MWh/t is 1.72x that floor. N2 separation work is negligible (0.036 GJ/t NH3).
- The floor per t CO2 avoided is 3.95 GJ/t (Gibbs reduction floor at 0.98 t Fe per t steel, divided by 1.65 t CO2 avoided).

FUNDING POOL (claims 1-3)
- CBAM total revenue of EUR 1.87 bn/yr is implied by EUR 1.4 bn being 75% [SRC idea]. This could not be re-fetched in this run.
- A bottom-up cross-check gives EUR 0.8-2.1 bn/yr: about 90 Mt CO2 embedded in CBAM imports [ASSUMP], EUA EUR 75-100, mean CBAM phase-in factor 57.4% for 2028-34 (computed from the regulation schedule), and a 30-50% chargeable share after exemptions and deductions [ASSUMP]. The Commission figure is consistent with this.
- Buyer club: EU27 has about 10.7 M new cars/yr [MEM, ACEA]. The idea's 12 M looks like an EU+EFTA+UK-scale number.
  - At 10.7 M cars the pool is EUR 1.60-2.14 bn/yr; at 12 M it is EUR 1.80-2.40 bn/yr.
  - Per car, EUR 150-200 is 0.33-0.67% of a EUR 30-45k car, slightly below the idea's 0.5-0.8%.

GREEN-HBI PREMIUM (bottom-up, per t liquid steel, imported green HBI into an EU EAF vs EU BF-BOF, no carbon price)
- Inputs, low/base/high:
  - Electrolyser system capex $900 / $1,700 / $2,500 per kW ([MEM, IEA GHR]: Chinese vs Western).
  - Capacity factor 0.65 / 0.55 / 0.45 from hybrid solar-wind [ASSUMP].
  - Power $22 / 35 / 50 per MWh [ASSUMP].
  - Electrolyser use 50 / 53 / 56 kWh/kg.
  - WACC 7 / 9 / 12% over 20 years, plus 2.5% O&M.
  - H2 use 55 / 60 / 65 kg/t HBI (stoichiometric is 54) [SRC].
  - H2 storage $0.25-0.80/kg.
  - DR-grade pellets $140-175/t, against a BF ore blend at $110/t.
  - Coking coal plus PCI 0.5 t at $230.
  - Shaft furnace $350/t-yr.
  - Shipping $15-35/t.
  - 0.92 t HBI vs 0.94 t hot metal per t liquid steel, with the scrap share cancelling.
- Results:
  - LCOH is $2.29 / $4.87 / $9.24 per kg.
  - Premium is EUR 23 / 204 / 507 per t liquid steel.
  - For reference: GEI 2024 modelled $167-231/t at about $5/kg H2; Fastmarkets assessed the EU low-carbon flat premium at EUR 150-200/t in 2026.
- Fund premium cases used: EUR 100 / 200 / 350 per t.
  - Base is the bottom-up base and the top of the Fastmarkets range.
  - High is a Western-capex tail, and the bottom-up high case is higher still.

AVOIDED CO2 AND COST
- Avoided CO2 is 1.85 / 1.65 / 1.50 t per t steel: EU BF-BOF at about 1.9-2.0 t/t, minus residuals from pellets, lime, electrodes, EAF grid power (0.6 MWh at 0.2-0.25 t/MWh) and shipping. The idea uses 1.7.
- Cost per t CO2, with 3% MRV and administration overhead and EUR/USD at 1.16:
  - EUR 56 / 125 / 240 per t CO2.
  - $65 / 145 / 279 per t CO2.
- Energy is gross electricity at 3.2 / 3.6 / 4.0 MWh/t steel: 6.2 / 7.9 / 9.6 GJ/t CO2. This displaces roughly 17-20 GJ/t steel of coal in BF-BOF.

SCALE
- Pool is all CBAM revenue plus the buyer club:
  - Low: EUR 4.27 bn buys 42.7 Mt steel and avoids 78.9 Mt CO2/yr.
  - Base: EUR 3.74 bn buys 18.7 Mt steel and avoids 30.8 Mt CO2/yr.
  - High: EUR 3.47 bn buys 9.9 Mt steel and avoids 14.9 Mt CO2/yr.
- Claim (3), 42-48 Mt CO2/yr, reproduces arithmetically but uses optimistic inputs: EUR 150/t, 1.7 t/t and 12 M cars.
- Ceilings: EU BF ironmaking is about 116 Mt CO2/yr. Global BF-BOF is about 2.23 Gt.

ETS PHASE-OUT
- If the fund pays the gap to a grey reference that includes ETS cost, the base gap (EUR 200) falls as free allocation phases out:
  - With EUA rising from EUR 75 to EUR 115: 197 (2026), 186 (2028), 124 (2030), 44 (2033), 10 (2034).
  - With EUA flat at EUR 70, the gap is still 84 in 2034.
- Breakeven EUA at full phase-out is EUR 54 / 121 / 233 per t (low/base/high).
- So the fund is a 2027-2033 bridge, not a permanent subsidy.

AMMONIA (claims 5-6)
- The SECI premium of $80-345/t over grey gives $33-192/t CO2 at 1.8-2.4 t CO2/t NH3. Delivery to the EU adds $40-80/t of shipping.
- 1 Mt NH3 needs 9.5 TWh, 0.032% of world electricity (claim 6 is correct).
- A full switch of EU ammonia (about 16 Mt) needs 152 TWh and avoids about 32 Mt CO2.
phys.resource_needs:
At the base volume of 18.7 Mt steel-equivalent per year:

- **Electricity in exporting countries:** 52/60/68 TWh/yr for low/base/high. That is 0.17-0.23% of world electricity.
- **Electrolysers:** 8/11/16 GW at capacity factors of 0.65/0.55/0.45. Installed electrolysis worldwide is only about 2-5 GW today [MEM, IEA GHR], so this is several times today's global fleet.
- **EU EAF power:** 11 TWh/yr, 0.42% of EU electricity.
- **DR-grade pellets:** 24 Mt/yr. That is 38-49% of today's seaborne DR-grade supply of about 50-65 Mt [MEM, IEEFA: 3-4% of seaborne ore]. This is the binding material constraint. Easing it needs one of:
  - beneficiation or new DR-grade mines (Brazil, Canada, Sweden, MENA), or
  - an electric smelting furnace or melter step that can use BF-grade ore.
- **Land:** about 18 GWp of solar at roughly 1.5 ha/MWp, about 269 km2, plus wind.
- **Water:** 1.03 Mt H2/yr needs 15-26 Mm3/yr. Desalination takes 0.09 TWh, which is negligible.
- **Ammonia lane:** 9.5 TWh per Mt NH3.
- **Fiscal:** EUR 1.87 bn/yr of CBAM revenue (all of it) plus EUR 1.6-2.4 bn/yr from the car buyer club.
phys.violations:
No physics violations: every energy claim is above its floor. H2-DRI-EAF is 1.73-2.17x the Gibbs reduction floor, and green ammonia is 1.72x its floor.

The arithmetic is correct but the inputs are optimistic:

1. **Claim (2)-(3) premium.** The idea uses EUR 150/t from the Fastmarkets assessed premium. That premium mostly prices scrap-EAF and mass-balance "green" steel, not primary H2-DRI, so it understates the gap the fund must pay. My bottom-up base is EUR 204/t, which puts funded abatement at 30.8 Mt CO2/yr. That is right at the idea's own falsification line of 30 Mt. The high case (EUR 350/t) gives 14.9 Mt.
2. **Car numbers.** 12 M cars is above the EU27's roughly 10.7 M. The cost per car of 0.5-0.8% is overstated; the computed range is 0.33-0.67%.
3. **Avoided CO2.** The idea's 1.7 t/t sits at the upper-middle of my 1.5-1.85 range (base 1.65).
4. **CBAM revenue.** The EUR 1.4 bn own-resource figure could not be re-verified in this run. The bottom-up cross-check (EUR 0.8-2.1 bn) is consistent with it.

Not heroic, but binding constraints:
- DR-grade pellet supply: 38-49% of today's seaborne DR-grade supply.
- Electrolyser build-out: 8-16 GW, several times today's global fleet.
- Contract-length mismatch: the fund pays 10-year contracts, but its gap to grey closes by about 2033-34 at EUA ≥ EUR 121. 10-year contracts signed around 2028 therefore over-pay late unless they are indexed to the ETS.
phys.key_uncertainties:
1. **Green-HBI premium.** This is dominated by LCOH, which spans $2.29-9.24/kg across electrolyser capex, capacity factor and WACC; the bottom-up premium is EUR 23-507/t. Emerging-market cost of capital (7-12%) is decisive, and so is whether Chinese-built electrolysers at about $900/kW are used.
   Realised-outcome signals, all recalled and not re-verified in this run, point to premia at the high end for EU-sited H2-DRI:
   - Stegra's 2025 funding shortfall.
   - ArcelorMittal shelving its German H2-DRI plans in 2025 despite approved aid.
   - India's SECI green ammonia is contracted but not yet delivered.
   
   Those are confounded by high EU power prices, which this idea deliberately avoids by siting the ironmaking abroad.
2. **CBAM revenue path.**
   - The EUR 1.4 bn own-resource figure is not re-fetched.
   - Revenue depends on EUA prices, the phase-in schedule, the de minimis exemptions from the 2025 omnibus, foreign carbon-price deductions and trade diversion.
   - The EU budget would have to give up an own resource it has already earmarked.
3. **EUA path 2028-2034.** This sets how fast the fund's gap shrinks. At EUA ≥ EUR 121 the ETS alone closes the EUR 200 gap by 2034.
4. **DR-grade ore supply and DRI-grade beneficiation timelines.**
5. **The political falsifier is untested.** Is revenue destination actually a major S8 (Global South) grievance compared with unilateralism, common-but-differentiated responsibilities (CBDR) and the MRV burden?
6. **WTO and state-aid compatibility** of earmarking border revenue to specific exporters' producers.
7. **Avoided CO2 depends on the EU grid intensity** for the EAF step and on whether BF capacity is actually retired rather than redeployed.
8. **The scale is small:** 0.015-0.079 Gt/yr, with a base of 0.031 Gt/yr. Its value is as a political template that could be extended toward the roughly 2.2 Gt/yr global BF-BOF ceiling, not as a direct climate lever.

stances.evidence: This is the closest documented match of any group, because NGOs have already asked for CBAM revenue to go abroad. A joint NGO statement (Carbon Market Watch, WWF EPO, CAN Europe, E3G, EEB; 13 Dec 2021) said 'All revenues generated through the sale of CBAM certificates should be earmarked in full to fund climate action outside the EU'. The same statement opposed sending the revenue to the EU budget (https://caneurope.org/publications/joint-ngo-statement-on-the-carbon-border-adjustment-mechanism/). CAN Europe's consultation response (28 Oct 2020) proposed '50% for climate action within the EU and 50% for developing countries', and opposed export rebates and free allocation running alongside CBAM (https://caneurope.org/publications/supporting-document-consultation-carbon-border-adjustment-mechanism/). The idea also clears CAN's 2021 CCUS red lines: it delivers physical avoided emissions in the product, with no offsets, no EOR and no fossil life extension. Pay-for-performance contracts for difference are already generally supported by S1 (see the map entry on Klimaschutzverträge). Two caveats. Some S1 will see the scheme as EU-import procurement dressed up as climate finance, because the money buys goods delivered to EU plants rather than funding the recipient country's own decarbonisation. NGO concern about water and land use for export hydrogen in arid or poor regions is plausible but was not verified this session.
stances.red_line_hit: Support turns to opposition if eligibility admits gas-DRI or blue ammonia with CCS ('fossil-linked technologies including CCS', CAN 2021 red line 3), or if the buyer-club premium is marketed as an offset. There is a possible land and water conflict at export hydrogen sites (unverified).

stances.evidence: The physics supports the division of labour, but the economics come from models, not realised outcomes. Verpoort et al. (Nature Energy 2024) estimate the energy-cost 'renewables pull': with a €40/MWh electricity-price gap, relocation saves 18% for steel, 32% for urea and 38% for ethylene. They find that trading intermediates such as HBI 'could save costs while keeping substantial value creation in renewable-scarce importing regions', which is exactly the split proposed here (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41560-024-01492-z). Seibold et al. (arXiv 2510.00918, Oct 2025, modelled) find that importing HBI, ammonia and methanol beats importing hydrogen. It cuts German industry costs by €8.6 bn/yr (23.3%) with non-European sourcing, or €4.1 bn/yr (11.2%) from European partners only (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00918). The verifier-style check puts H2-DRI at about 1.76x the Fe2O3 dissociation floor, so cost is driven by the electricity price. IPCC AR6 WGIII treats hydrogen DRI as a key steel mitigation option (from memory, not re-fetched this session). Expect S2 caution that green HBI is not yet proven at scale, and that SECI ammonia contracts are awarded but not yet delivered.
stances.red_line_hit: None categorical. Scientists would object if the MRV allows grid-average or certificate-based hydrogen accounting that overstates avoided CO2.

stances.evidence: The direct effect on oil and gas is small: grey-ammonia gas demand in the EU falls, and coking coal, which is S3-adjacent (Australian and US exporters), loses its EU market. The deciding question for S3 is technology eligibility. The documented pattern is that S3 backs pull subsidies that keep its assets in play: S3 supported 45Q, especially EOR parity after OBBBA 2025, and API backs 'market-based policies'. S3 opposes measures that exclude it, as with the per-tonne methane fee repealed under the CRA in 2025.
