Gulf NOCs and exporters are also potential sellers of gas-based DRI or blue ammonia into such a fund; Vale's Gulf 'mega-hub' HBI plans are gas-DRI first (from memory, unverified). Expect lobbying for 'low-carbon' rather than 'renewable' eligibility.
stances.red_line_hit: S3 opposes the scheme if eligibility is limited to renewable hydrogen and excludes gas-DRI with CCS or blue ammonia. That exclusion is exactly what S1's red line requires, so the eligibility rule is the central S1-S3 trade-off.

stances.evidence: The winners are EU EAF operators, rolling and finishing mills, automakers (secured low-carbon metallics at known premia) and fertilizer plants, which switch feedstock instead of closing. The losers are integrated BF-BOF producers, whose ironmaking step is displaced. Arithmetic in stake_cbam_compact.py, using the idea's assumptions of 70 Mt EU BF hot metal and a €150/t premium: all CBAM revenue displaces about 18% of EU blast-furnace iron; with the car buyer club it displaces 35-41%. Eurofer's current posture is defensive. On 14 Apr 2026 it welcomed the strengthened steel tariff-rate quota (18.3 Mt tariff-free quota, 50% out-of-quota tariff from 1 Jul 2026) as saving the industry from a 'cliff edge' and cited 230,000 jobs (https://www.eurofer.eu/eu-trade-measure-saves-steel-industry-from-cliff-edge-as-record-imports-surge). Its October 2026 CBAM release asks MEPs to close downstream and processing loopholes; it says nothing on CBAM revenue use or imported green iron (https://www.eurofer.eu/press-releases/cbam-meps-must-close-loopholes-to-drive-low-carbon-steel-production-in-europe). Automakers pay €150-200 per car, which is about 1.1-1.5x the green premium on a car's own roughly 0.9 t of steel; that is an assumption. The VCI's view of Klimaschutzverträge as 'no panacea' shows that S4 accepts subsidies that keep production in the EU. Integrated firms could be brought on board if they own the overseas DRI plants.
stances.red_line_hit: Offshoring the ironmaking step and stranding EU blast-furnace and DRI investments. Whether HBI (HS 7203) falls under the new steel tariff-rate quota is unverified; if it does, the compact conflicts with the trade measure Eurofer just secured.

stances.evidence: Power utilities are only marginally affected. EU utilities lose some prospective domestic electrolyser and H2-DRI load, while utilities and IPPs in exporting countries gain long-term contracted demand (1 Mt/yr green ammonia needs about 9.5 TWh). There is no documented S5 position on CBAM revenue recycling. The map's precedent is that S5 adapted to the EU ETS.
stances.red_line_hit: None identified.

stances.evidence: This group bears the concentrated losses: blast-furnace and coke-oven jobs at EU integrated sites, and coking-coal mining jobs in exporting regions. At full scale the fund displaces 18-41% of EU blast-furnace hot metal (calculation above, built on the idea's assumptions). Eurofer frames trade policy around 230,000 jobs (Apr 2026), and Verpoort et al. (2024) say renewable-scarce regions may adopt 'selective policies of green-relocation protection', which is the political response this idea provokes. The map's documented pattern is that S6 joins coalitions that keep jobs in place: the Carbon Capture Coalition for 45Q, and SEIU in the No on Initiative 2117 campaign. IndustriAll Europe's current position on imported green iron could not be retrieved this session.
stances.red_line_hit: Job losses from offshoring the ironmaking step. Keeping EAF, rolling and finishing in the EU softens this but does not remove it; a funded transition guarantee would be needed to move unions to neutral.

stances.evidence: The EU side is split. The Commission and the budget lose an own resource of €1.4 bn/yr (75% of CBAM revenue, 2028-34 average, Commission own-resources page). That is about 0.7% of an EU budget of roughly €190 bn (assumed), and it was intended to help repay NGEU borrowing. Seibold et al. (2025) flag import dependence as the cost of precursor imports, which matters for energy- and strategic-autonomy ministries. On the other side, the CBAM friction is live. The India-EU FTA text finalised in Sept 2026 gave India a 1.64 Mt/yr steel quota, but Indian exporters 'remained subject to' CBAM (Wikipedia India-EU relations, citing Reuters and The Hindu, 14 Sept 2026; secondary source). A compact that defuses the CBAM grievance has diplomatic value. Governments of exporting countries (Brazil, India, South Africa, Australia, MENA) would gain contracted industrial demand and are likely supportive. For Australia this is inferred from its green-iron industrial policy, not verified this session.
stances.red_line_hit: EU fiscal: loss of the CBAM own resource. Strategic autonomy: import dependence for primary iron. Exporting governments object if eligibility rules or MRV are dictated unilaterally.

stances.evidence: The map documents objections from India and South Africa that CBAM is unilateral and discriminatory; the map flags these as not re-verified this session. The compact answers the revenue and voice grievances with MLF-style co-governance. That precedent is concrete: the Montreal Protocol Multilateral Fund is run by an executive committee with equal representation of seven industrialised and seven Article 5 countries (Wikipedia, Montreal Protocol). It does not answer the unilateralism or CBDR objections. The idea's own falsification test, coding the WTO CTE and BASIC statements, is the right check. Distribution is also uneven. The money goes to renewable-rich middle-income exporters (Brazil, India, South Africa, MENA, plus Australia, which is not Global South), not to LDCs. NGOs asked in 2021 for LDCs to be exempted or specifically supported. In Baum et al. 2024, Global South publics were more supportive of climate technologies but more worried about unequal risks.
stances.red_line_hit: Possible charges of 'green extractivism' if export hydrogen uses scarce water or land; this is unverified, but the Baum 2024 Global South concern over unequal risk distribution points the same way. Exclusion of LDCs. Recycling may be seen as buying off the CBDR objection without conceding it.

stances.evidence: The consumer cost is small and invisible: €150-200 per car is 0.3-0.7% of a €30-45k new car (calculation above), and no consumer fuel charge is involved. The map's realised evidence is that invisible industrial carbon prices survive while visible consumer ones lose; Canada removed its consumer fuel charge in Apr 2025 but kept industrial output-based pricing. Andre et al. (2024) find that 69% of people are willing to pay 1% of income, which is well above this premium.
stances.red_line_hit: None at this size. It would become an issue only if the buyer-club premium were mandated and labelled as a visible surcharge.

stances.evidence: Ten-year aggregated contracts for difference are the instrument that makes first-of-a-kind green HBI and ammonia projects bankable. India's SECI aggregated green-ammonia auction contracted $570-745/t for 10 years; the contracts are awarded but delivery is not proven. Germany's H2Global uses an intermediary (Hintco) and public funds 'to bridge the temporary price gap' (https://www.h2-global.org/). Frontier and Microsoft show that S10 responds to pre-committed demand. Investors in EU integrated steel carry stranded-asset exposure in blast furnaces, but many of those furnaces face relining decisions anyway (not verified).
stances.red_line_hit: Counterparty and political risk if the CBAM revenue stream is cut back, as happened to the Omnibus scope in 2025 and the US WEC in 2025. Investors would need the payment obligation ring-fenced in law.

stances.evidence: EU communities near blast furnaces gain air quality but lose jobs, so the two pull in opposite directions. Local grievance against blast-furnace pollution is documented: in March 2025, after a suit by 300 residents and environmental groups, ArcelorMittal was placed under judicial supervision over pollution from its 4 Mt/yr Fos-sur-Mer plant (Wikipedia, ArcelorMittal, citing Reuters, 25 Mar 2025). Communities near new export DRI, electrolyser and ammonia plants face water, land and ammonia-handling safety issues. No documented position was found this session.
stances.red_line_hit: Local job loss at EU ironmaking towns. Water and land use and ammonia safety at export sites.

stake.coalition_notes:
Calculations: climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/stake_cbam_compact.py. The web-search budget for the session ran out, so the evidence comes from direct fetches: Eurofer, CAN Europe, arXiv, Nature Energy, h2-global and Wikipedia raw pages. Items marked unverified are from memory.

1. **The strongest new evidence is that S1 has already asked for this.** A 2021 joint NGO statement (CAN Europe, WWF, CMW, E3G, EEB) asked that all CBAM revenue be earmarked for climate action outside the EU. CAN Europe proposed a 50/50 split in 2020. So S1 support is grounded in documented positions, not inference. That is rare for an industry-friendly idea.

2. **The central conflict runs inside Europe, not between NGOs and fossil firms.** The losers are EU blast-furnace workers (S6), integrated steelmakers (S4) and the EU budget (S7). The timing is hostile: Eurofer just won a 50% out-of-quota steel tariff (14 Apr 2026), framed around 230,000 jobs, and Verpoort et al. predict 'green-relocation protection' politics. At the idea's own scale the fund displaces 18-41% of EU blast-furnace iron. That is too large to slip past S6, and the smaller member-state-share version (4%) is too small to matter, which is the same trade-off as the idea's scale-falsification test.

3. **Eligibility is the S1-versus-S3 swing.** Admitting only renewable hydrogen satisfies S1 but leaves S3 and Gulf NOCs neutral or opposed. Admitting gas-DRI with CCS or blue ammonia flips S1 to opposition under CAN red line 3. A Kigali-style move would be technology-neutral eligibility on measured embedded emissions with a declining intensity threshold. Its weakness is that blue routes would then compete on numbers, so S1 must accept that measured intensity is the test.

4. **The S8 gain is real but partial.** MLF-style co-governance (seven-and-seven executive committee) answers the voice and revenue grievances, not unilateralism or CBDR. The money also flows to middle-income renewable-rich exporters, not LDCs. The September 2026 India-EU FTA leaving CBAM in place shows the grievance is still live, so there is an opening.

5. **Ways to widen the coalition.** Let EU integrated producers own or co-invest in the overseas DRI plants, which turns S4 integrated firms from losers into participants. Pair the compact with a funded transition guarantee for blast-furnace towns; the Washington I-2117 and Carbon Capture Coalition precedents show S6 backs schemes that pay visible local dividends. Ring-fence the revenue in law to win S10. Check whether HS 7203 (HBI) falls under the new steel tariff-rate quota; if it does, the compact collides with the trade measure Eurofer just won.

6. **Evidence weighting.** Cost-saving figures (18%, 11-23%) are modelled, from Verpoort 2024 and Seibold 2025. The SECI ammonia prices are contracted but not delivered. No green-HBI-for-export plant yet has measured cost performance. Stance evidence is documented positions on adjacent policies (CBAM, steel tariff-rate quotas, Klimaschutzverträge), not on this compact.

critic.fatal_flaw: None found. The physics holds: every route sits 1.7-2.2x above its thermodynamic floor. Scale is small (base 0.031 Gt/yr), but the idea is explicitly a political template. The hardest barrier is the EU own-resources decision, which needs unanimity plus national ratification to give up the CBAM own resource. That can be designed around rather than being a dead end: start with the member-state 25% share (about EUR 0.47 bn) plus the buyer club as a pilot, and move toward the full own resource only once the S8 falsifier passes.
critic.top_fixable_flaw:
The auction is open only to producers in partner exporting countries, with eligibility set by an executive committee those countries sit on, and it pays a fixed gap to a grey reference price for 10 years. That produces three problems.

(a) Origin discrimination. Money collected at the EU border would pay foreign green HBI, while EU-sited green DRI that taxpayers already support is excluded (Stegra/Boden, HYBRIT, SALCOS, thyssenkrupp Duisburg). That hands Eurofer, IndustriAll and member states (S4, S6, S7) a "Brussels subsidises our competitors with our own tariff" argument. It also leaves CBAM revenue partly flowing back to producers in selected WTO members. That weakens CBAM's own claim to be a non-discriminatory charge equivalent to the ETS, and invites an MFN challenge from non-member exporters (for example Ukraine or Türkiye) who are shut out of the committee.

(b) Overpayment as the ETS phases in. This is quantified in critic_coalition_6.py at the base case of EUR 200/t and 1.65 tCO2/t, using the regulation's free-allocation phase-out. A fixed-gap contract over 2028-37 pays EUR 2,000/t of steel. A carbon-indexed gap pays EUR 553-1,190/t across three EUA paths (flat 130, rising 75 to 115, flat 70). The fixed contract therefore overpays by 41-72%. With the same budget, indexing roughly doubles the tonnage funded over the contract life.

(c) ETS waterbed. When EU blast furnaces retire, they free allowances that the MSR only partly absorbs. As a result, some of the claimed avoided CO2 is not additional before the cap reaches zero.
critic.suggested_patch:
Turn the fund into an origin-neutral, carbon-indexed CCfD with allowance cancellation. There are four parts.

1. **Award rule.** Use a single EU-wide reverse auction for verified low-carbon HBI and ammonia delivered to EU EAFs and fertiliser plants, open to any producer anywhere, EU-sited included. Award on price per verified tCO2 avoided, under one uniform intensity threshold. Cheap-power exporters will win most lots on cost anyway, so S8 still gets the volume. EU DRI projects can also bid, which neutralises the S4/S6 charge of subsidising competitors and makes the instrument MFN-clean.

2. **Where S8 keeps its stake.** S8 influence goes into governance rather than eligibility. Recipient regions hold half of the executive-committee seats, as in the MLF, and that committee sets the MRV, water and land safeguards and the LDC set-aside. One possible set-aside is 10% of the pool for LDC beneficiation, pellet or renewables projects, which answers the S8 distribution gap. The committee does not get to choose which countries may bid.

3. **Indexed payment.** Each year the contract pays the strike premium minus EUA × (BF reference intensity − delivered intensity) × CBAM phase-in share, with a floor of zero. Payouts fall automatically to near zero by about 2034 at EUA above EUR 115. Use the money released to extend the volume to 25-35 Mt of steel, which clears the idea's own 30 Mt CO2 falsifier, instead of overpaying incumbents.

4. **No waterbed.** Make payment conditional on the member state using ETS Directive Art. 12(4) to cancel allowances matching the blast-furnace capacity that is retired. This keeps the S1 claim of real avoided emissions true under the cap.

Also add the check the reports missed: confirm that HS 7203 (DRI/HBI) is outside the 2026 steel tariff-rate quota. If it is inside, carve it out explicitly in the same legislative package, or the compact will collide with the safeguard measure Eurofer just won.

patched_idea.title: Border-revenue incremental-cost compact for green iron: an origin-neutral, carbon-indexed CCfD with exporter co-governance
patched_idea.one_line: Recycle CBAM revenue plus a small automaker buyer-club premium into an EU-wide fund. The fund runs aggregated 10-year reverse auctions for verified low-carbon HBI and ammonia delivered to EU EAFs and fertiliser plants. Any producer anywhere may bid; payments are indexed to the EUA price, which shrinks them as the ETS bites; and allowances are cancelled to match retired blast furnaces. Exporting countries co-govern the fund as recipients do in the Montreal Multilateral Fund, which turns Global South opposition to CBAM into a governance stake in it.
patched_idea.conventional_core: Unchanged. Hydrogen DRI makes HBI where renewables are cheap; EAF steelmaking, rolling and finishing stay at incumbent EU sites; plus electrolytic ammonia. Gas DRI and HBI trade are TRL 9. Green HBI projects are at FID or announcement stage (verified map). Contract design is the standard carbon contract for difference (CCfD): a strike premium minus the realised carbon price.
patched_idea.graft: Unchanged. The Montreal Protocol Multilateral Fund: revenue tied to the regime pays incremental cost under joint donor-recipient governance, which is what turned developing-country objections into near-universal ratification. The graft now operates through governance seats and an LDC set-aside rather than through bidder eligibility.
patched_idea.mechanism:
FUNDING: unchanged. The member-state 25% share of CBAM revenue (pilot), extending to the 75% own resource only after the S8 falsifier passes, plus an automaker buyer-club premium of about EUR 150-200 per car, capitalises one fund.

(1) AWARD RULE, ORIGIN-NEUTRAL. One EU-wide aggregated reverse auction on the SECI model, open to any producer anywhere, EU-sited DRI included (Stegra, HYBRIT, SALCOS, thyssenkrupp). Product is low-carbon HBI or ammonia delivered to EU EAFs and fertiliser plants. Bids are ranked on EUR per verified tCO2 avoided under one uniform delivered-intensity threshold, measured with the CBAM methodology so one MRV serves both the border measure and the payments. Cheap-power exporters should win most lots on cost (arXiv 2510.00918 models 11-23% savings from relocating ironmaking, modelled not realised). No country is named eligible or ineligible, so the instrument is MFN-neutral and removes the 'our tariff subsidises their mills' argument.

(2) WHERE S8 KEEPS ITS STAKE, MLF-STYLE. Recipient and exporting regions hold half the executive-committee seats, as at the MLF, open to any WTO member that exports covered goods, so Ukraine and Türkiye are not shut out. The committee sets MRV rules, water and land-use safeguards for electrolysis and DRI sites, and a 10% LDC set-aside (about EUR 0.23-0.29 bn/yr in the pilot) for beneficiation, pelletising, grid or renewables projects in LDCs. It does not decide which countries may bid.

(3) INDEXED PAYMENT. Each year: payment per t = max(0, strike premium - EUA x (BF-BOF reference intensity - delivered intensity) x CBAM phase-in share). Payouts therefore fall automatically as free allocation phases out (to about EUR 10/t by 2034 at a EUR 200 strike and EUA 115). Contracts are signed in annual tranches (about 6 Mt steel-eq per year to a 25-35 Mt cap) rather than all in 2028. That matches the green-HBI supply ramp and keeps payments inside the annual inflow without bridge finance. Money released by indexation buys volume, not incumbent rent. Any post-2034 surplus goes first to the LDC set-aside and then to lowering the buyer-club premium.

(4) NO WATERBED. Payment for volume replacing EU blast-furnace iron is conditional on the member state cancelling allowances that match the retired capacity. The route is ETS Directive Art. 12(4); whether its current text covers industrial closures, not only power-plant closures, is unverified. If it does not, the same legislative package extends it. BF-BOF capacity is retired, not offset.

(5) TRADE-DEFENCE COHERENCE. Check that HS 7203 (DRI/HBI) is outside the 2026 steel tariff-rate quota, and carve it out explicitly in the same package if not. Semi-finished slabs (HS 7207) are not eligible products, which keeps rolling and finishing in the EU.

Activist red lines met: real avoided emissions in the physical product, no offsets, no fossil life extension, allowances cancelled. Grounding precedents: the Montreal MLF, India's SECI green-ammonia auction (contracted at $570-745/t for 10 years, delivery not yet proven), and Germany's H2Global and national CCfDs.
patched_idea.target: EU blast-furnace ironmaking (about 70 Mt hot metal) and imported steel, iron and ammonia under CBAM. A second target is the political blockage: S8 objections to CBAM (India, South Africa) and the CBAM revenue-to-Brussels justice gap, plus the S4/S6 objection that recycling border revenue abroad subsidises competitors.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
Calculations: coalition_ideas.py and critic_coalition_6.py, plus patch_coalition_6.py and patch_coalition_6_ramp.py in the scratchpad climate folder. All figures are modelled, not realised.

(1) The CBAM own resource is EUR 1.4 bn/yr, being 75% of revenue (2028-34 average, 2025 prices; European Commission own-resources page, fetched). Total revenue is about EUR 1.87 bn, of which the member-state 25% is about EUR 0.47 bn. The buyer club (12 M EU cars x EUR 150-200, an assumption) adds EUR 1.8-2.4 bn. Pilot inflow is EUR 2.27-2.87 bn/yr; the full inflow is EUR 3.67-4.27 bn/yr.

(2) Indexed versus fixed gap. Inputs: strike EUR 200/t steel, 1.65 tCO2/t avoided, CBAM phase-in schedule from the regulation, contracts 2028-37. Lifetime payment per t-yr of capacity is EUR 553 (EUA flat 130), EUR 733 (rising 75 to 115) or EUR 1,190 (flat 70), against EUR 2,000 fixed. The fixed contract therefore overpays by 41-72%.

(3) Volume, with a 6 Mt/yr tranche ramp, 10% LDC set-aside and no bridge finance. Rising EUA path, pilot-low inflow: a 30 Mt steel-eq cap is fully fundable, with about EUR 8 bn surplus at end-2037. Payments peak at EUR 2.4 bn in 2031 and drop to EUR 0.3 bn/yr from 2034. That is about 50 Mt CO2/yr at full ramp (30 x 1.65), clearing the 30 Mt CO2 falsifier. Low-carbon-price stress case (flat EUA 70): the no-bridge cap is 18 Mt (pilot low, about 30 Mt CO2/yr), 30.5 Mt (pilot high) or 57.5 Mt (full low). With EUA at or above 115, the binding constraint is green-HBI supply and EU EAF absorption (about 70 Mt BF hot metal), not money. The comparable fixed-gap volume is 11-14 Mt (pilot) or 18-21 Mt (full).

(4) Caveat. If all contracts were signed in 2028, the front-loaded indexed payments would need EUR 3-21 bn of bridge finance against a flat inflow (the range covers the EUA paths and strike prices). Hence the tranche ramp. A strike of EUR 250/t on the rising path cuts the pilot-low no-bridge-equivalent volume to about 18 Mt (30 Mt CO2/yr).

(5) H2-DRI at about 3.6 MWh/t is 1.76x the 2.05 MWh/t Fe2O3 dissociation-enthalpy floor. Cost is set by the electricity price, so siting ironmaking where power is cheap is the physics-consistent division of labour.

(6) The SECI green-ammonia premium over grey ($400-490/t) is $80-345/t, about $36-157/t CO2 at an assumed 2.2 tCO2/t ammonia. 1 Mt/yr of green ammonia at 9.5 MWh/t needs 9.5 TWh, 0.03% of world electricity.

(7) Unverified, as the web budget was exhausted. First, whether ETS Art. 12(4) covers industrial closures. Second, whether HS 7203 falls inside the 2026 steel TRQ. Both are listed as checks.
patched_idea.who_gains: S8: exporting countries (Brazil, India, South Africa, Australia, MENA) win most auction volume on cost, get half the governance seats, and LDCs get a dedicated set-aside. S4: EU EAF, rolling and automaker downstream get secured low-carbon metallics. EU green-DRI projects can now bid too, so EU steelmakers and S6 workers at those sites gain rather than lose. Fertiliser plants switch feedstock rather than close. S7 (EU): defuses WTO, BASIC and Eurofer conflict at once, and indexation cuts fiscal exposure by 41-72% against a fixed contract. S1: verified physical decarbonisation with allowance cancellation, so no waterbed. S9: about 0.5-0.8% on a car price, falling as indexed payouts shrink and post-2034 surplus lowers the premium. S10: CCfD price-floor de-risking makes green-HBI projects bankable.
patched_idea.who_loses: S6: EU blast-furnace and coke-oven workers lose ironmaking jobs; a transition fund is still needed, though EU DRI sites can now win contracts. Coking-coal miners and exporters (S3/S6 in Australia and the US) lose. In the S7 EU budget, the pilot uses only the member-state share; the full design gives up some or all of the EUR 1.4 bn/yr own resource. Automakers absorb or pass on EUR 150-200 per car. Grey-ammonia and gas suppliers (S3) lose demand. S8 exporters lose the exclusive eligibility of the original design and must compete with EU-sited bids.
patched_idea.closest_known_work: Germany's H2Global double auction (HINT.CO, state-funded; from memory). Germany's Klimaschutzverträge and other national CCfDs: EUA-indexed, but domestic-only and budget-funded. India's SECI/SIGHT aggregated auctions (contracted). Think-tank proposals to recycle CBAM revenue to LDCs (unverified). arXiv 2510.00918 on green-iron trade (modelled). The Montreal MLF.
patched_idea.why_different: National CCfDs are domestic-only and budget-funded. H2Global is budget-funded and has no exporter co-governance. This compact is an origin-neutral CCfD funded by the border measure itself plus a demand-side buyer club. It is aimed at iron, the largest-tonnage embodied-carbon import, and gives exporters MLF-style governance seats and an LDC set-aside. It targets the specific S8 grievance (border revenue flowing to Brussels) without creating a new S4/S6 grievance or an MFN problem.
patched_idea.cheapest_falsifying_test:
A 2-3 week desk study with four parts.

(a) Code the 2021-2026 WTO Committee on Trade and Environment submissions and BASIC/G77 ministerial statements on CBAM by grievance type. FALSIFIED politically if revenue destination is a minor grievance compared with unilateralism, CBDR or MRV burden.

(b) Benchmark the delivered green-HBI premium against H2Global and SECI clearing prices and the Fastmarkets EU green-steel premium (EUR 150-200/t, Q2 2026). FALSIFIED on scale if the strike premium needed exceeds about EUR 250/t steel on the rising EUA path, because the pilot inflow would then buy under about 30 Mt CO2/yr.

(c) From the announced green-HBI project pipeline and the delivered-cost model (arXiv 2510.00918), estimate which bidders would win a first auction round. FALSIFIED on the S8 flip if EU-sited bids would take more than half the volume, because exporters' stake would then be governance-only.

(d) Legal check. FALSIFIED as designed if ETS Art. 12(4) cannot cover industrial closures and no amendment is politically available. In that case the S1 avoided-emissions claim holds only net of the waterbed until the cap nears zero (about 2039). The same check covers whether HS 7203 is inside the 2026 steel TRQ.
patched_idea.family: CBAM-revenue-funded reverse-auction offtake compact for green HBI/ammonia from exporting countries

fix.change_summary:
I applied the critic's four-part patch and kept the conventional core (H2-DRI HBI made where power is cheap, EAF and finishing at EU sites, green ammonia), the MLF graft, and the funding mechanism unchanged. The funding mechanism is CBAM revenue plus the buyer club capitalising aggregated 10-year reverse auctions for delivered HBI and ammonia, with one shared CBAM MRV.

Changes:
- **Eligibility.** Bidding is now origin-neutral and MFN-clean: any producer, EU-sited included, ranked on EUR per verified tCO2. The S8 stake moves from bidder eligibility to MLF-style governance: half the committee seats, open to any exporting WTO member, which sets MRV and safeguards. A 10% LDC set-aside is added.
- **Payment.** Payment is EUA-indexed: strike minus EUA × intensity gap × CBAM phase-in share, floored at zero.
- **Waterbed.** Payment is conditional on allowance cancellation under ETS Art. 12(4).
- **Trade defence.** A check on HS 7203 against the steel TRQ is added, and HS 7207 slabs are excluded.

I checked the patch with new scripts (patch_coalition_6.py, patch_coalition_6_ramp.py) and found one problem the critic missed. If every contract is signed in 2028, indexed payments are front-loaded and would need EUR 3-21 bn of bridge finance against a flat inflow. I fixed this by contracting in annual tranches of about 6 Mt to a 25-35 Mt cap. On that ramp, the pilot inflow (member-state 25% share plus a low buyer club, 2.27 bn/yr) fully funds 30 Mt steel-eq, about 50 Mt CO2/yr, on the rising EUA path, with about EUR 8 bn surplus. The surplus goes to the LDC set-aside and then to lowering the car premium. In the low-carbon-price stress case (flat EUA 70), the same pilot inflow supports only 18 Mt (about 30 Mt CO2/yr).

I added an S8-flip falsifier, (c): the idea fails politically if EU-sited bids would win most of the volume. Two legal points could not be verified because the web-search budget was exhausted: whether Art. 12(4) covers industrial closures, and whether HS 7203 falls inside the 2026 steel TRQ. Both are flagged as falsifier (d), not asserted. The core mechanism is retained; only its award rule, payment formula and contracting schedule were amended.

idea.title: CO2 cushion-gas swap in existing underground gas storage (UGS)
idea.one_line: Replace part of the native methane cushion in depleted-field gas storage with process CO2. The UGS operator frees saleable or strategic-reserve gas and gets already-permitted, characterised, monitored storage next to European and US demand centres.
idea.conventional_core: Seasonal underground gas storage in depleted gas fields, with its existing wells, compressors, seal data, monitoring and licences. Oil majors own much of it, for example NAM (Shell/ExxonMobil) at Norg and Grijpskerk, and Exxon, Chevron and the US utilities.
idea.graft: Inert-cushion-gas substitution: nitrogen cushions have been used in European storage since the 1980s (Laille et al., cited by Oldenburg 2003). Here the substitute is CO2, whose high compressibility near its critical point is a feature.
idea.mechanism:
1. While the field is near its minimum seasonal pressure, inject CO2 low and at the flanks and produce native cushion methane from the crest. Gravity segregation helps here: CO2 is 3-4.5x denser than CH4 at 40-100 bar.
2. Keep the CO2-CH4 mixing zone away from the working-gas wells, and cap withdrawn-gas CO2 at grid spec (about 2.5 mol%).
3. Accept only process or biogenic CO2 (cement, lime, ethanol, AGRU vent) so S1's red lines on fossil-power life extension are respected.
4. Use the freed methane in one of two ways: (a) a strategic reserve or added working-gas inventory (Oldenburg's single simulation found about 30% more methane storable with a CO2 cushion), which does not increase gas burned; or (b) sale.
idea.target: Storage access for hard-to-abate process CO2 near inland industrial clusters (Germany, the Netherlands, Italy, Austria, the US Midwest and Northeast) that have no offshore hub. It is a one-off sink of about 0.1-0.2 Gt per region, filled over about 10 years.
idea.quantitative_claims:
All figures are my calculations in climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/incumbent_reuse.py, using a Peng-Robinson EOS checked against NIST to within about 2-6%.

Per tonne of CO2:
- CO2/CH4 mass ratio in the same pore volume: 3.2 (40 bar, 40C) to 4.5 (100 bar, 60C). So each tonne of CO2 frees 0.22-0.31 t CH4, or 12-17 GJ HHV.
- Gross gas value: $41-57/t at $3.5/MMBtu (US) and $129-179/t at $11/MMBtu (EU).

Energy:
- Compression floor 0.23-0.26 GJ/t (1 to 60-120 bar). Separation floor 0.11 GJ/t for cement (verifier) and about 0 for AGRU or fermentation CO2.
- The freed gas energy is 46-75x the compression floor.

Net climate effect if the freed gas is burned with no displacement:
- Burning 0.22-0.31 t CH4 emits 0.61-0.85 t CO2, so net storage is only 15-39% of gross.
- Net is about 100% if the gas displaces LNG imports or is held as a strategic reserve. Claim: use the reserve or working-gas variant, or count net-of-burn.

Inventory:
- US EIA 2024 design capacity (measured registry): base gas 4,526 Bcf (128 bcm). Depleted fields hold 3,316 Bcf (94 bcm, about 68 Mt).
- A 30-50% swap stores 61-186 Mt CO2 one-off in the US.
- EU (assumed cushion/working ratio 0.6-1.0 on about 103 bcm working gas): 40-204 Mt one-off, freeing 19-52 bcm (5-16% of one year of EU demand; €6.6-19bn at €35/MWh).
- Over 10 years, 4-20 Mt/yr in the EU, i.e. 8-40% of the NZIA 50 Mt/yr injection objective.

Cost claim: incremental cost below $30/t, because wells, compression and monitoring already exist. This is an assumption to test.
idea.who_gains:
S3/S5 storage owners (NAM, TAQA, Uniper, SEFE, Snam/Stogit, US utilities): a one-off gas asset release plus a new storage tariff.
S4 inland cement and lime plants: a storage outlet without waiting for offshore hubs.
S7: energy security from the freed strategic reserve and possibly about 30% more working gas (Oldenburg, one model).
S6: keeps storage workforces employed.
S2: process CO2 is stored.
idea.who_loses:
S11 communities above onshore fields. The precedent is Shell's Barendrecht onshore CO2 storage in a depleted gas field, cancelled in 2010 after local opposition, and that mechanism still applies.
S1, if the freed gas is sold and burned (net 15-39%).
Gas traders, through a small loss of storage optionality if CO2 contaminates working gas.
Possible regulatory friction from holding both a UGS licence and an EU CCS-Directive storage permit.
idea.closest_known_work:
- Oldenburg (2003, Energy & Fuels, LBNL): reservoir simulation found about 30% more methane storable with a CO2 cushion, and that mixing control is critical.
- Nitrogen cushion gas used in European storage (Laille et al. 1986/88).
- Mirzaei-Paiaman et al. (2026, Energy & Fuels): a facility-level analysis of CO2 cushion replacement in US UGS. I could not retrieve its results.
- Lab and simulation papers on CO2/CH4 mixing in cushion cores (2023-2026).
- No commercial CO2-cushion deployment found.
idea.why_different: This frames the swap as a European process-CO2 storage product run by the incumbent storage owners, rather than a gas-storage efficiency trick. Sites are selected by distance to cement and lime clusters. Credit counts only net-of-burn tonnes, or the freed gas goes to a strategic reserve, which addresses S1's objection directly. The 2026 US facility study means the concept is not new; the European cluster pairing and the accounting design are the contribution.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test:
1. Build a 2D compositional simulation in open-source MRST or OPM Flow of a representative depleted-field UGS (dipping anticline, real cycling schedule) with a 30% and a 50% CO2 cushion swap.
2. Kill criterion: withdrawn-gas CO2 exceeds 2.5 mol% within 10 seasonal cycles, or working-gas deliverability falls more than 10%.
3. In parallel, compile an EU UGS list (GIE storage database) with distance to cement and lime plants. Kill criterion: fewer than about 10 depleted-field sites within 100 km of 0.3 Mt/yr or larger process-CO2 sources.

Effort: 2-3 months for 1-2 reservoir engineers.
idea.family: CO2 as cushion gas in existing underground gas storage

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: Mirzaei-Paiaman (2026), 'CO2 Cushion Gas Replacement in U.S. Underground Natural Gas Storage: A Facility-Level Analysis of Sequestration, Cushion Gas Recovery, and Working Gas Storage Expansion', Energy & Fuels 40(28):15069-15090, UT Austin Bureau of Economic Geology
closest.overlap: Very close to the US half of the idea. It explicitly frames CO2 cushion swap as CO2 utilization plus sequestration when the CO2 comes from emissions. It screens 384 US UGS facilities, sorted by type and region, and links them to CO2 emitters and pipeline data. Results (from the OpenAlex abstract): full replacement needs about 0.33 Gt CO2. Facility capacities run from about 2,200 t to 19 Mt. In 96% of sites working storage rises by 0.3-344% (mean 28%), about 1,113 Bcf in total. A 20% replacement takes about 67 Mt CO2 and adds about 223 Bcf. These figures already cover the idea's US inventory (61-186 Mt) and its roughly 30% working-gas uplift. The method is a volumetric real-gas framework with no mixing simulation. That gap is exactly what the idea's falsifying test would fill.

closest.title: Oldenburg (2003), 'Carbon Dioxide as Cushion Gas for Natural Gas Storage', Energy & Fuels 17(1), LBNL
closest.overlap: The original concept paper. It covers CO2's compressibility and density advantage, gravity segregation, and the need to control mixing, and it simulates more storable methane. The idea already cites it.

closest.title: Kowalski, Klimkowski & Nagy (2023), 'Numerical Simulation Study on Underground Gas Storage with Cushion Gas Partially Replaced with Carbon Dioxide', Energies 16(14):5248, AGH Krakow
closest.overlap: A European (Polish) compositional simulation of partial CO2 cushion replacement over reservoir depletion plus 10 storage cycles. Its finding is that reservoir structure and high permeability control how fast CO2 migrates to the wells and how much CO2 ends up in withdrawn gas. That is essentially the idea's 'cheapest falsifying test' (a 10-cycle compositional simulation), already done for a generic or Polish setting.

closest.title: Dabrowski et al. (2024), 'Analysis of CO2/CH4 mixing process in rock cores for natural gas storage sites with CO2 cushion' (Research Square preprint, Poland)
closest.overlap: Core-flood mixing data for CO2-cushion UGS in a European (Polish) context. It covers the mixing-zone risk at lab scale.

closest.title: Du et al. (2024), 'A Review of the Utilization of CO2 as a Cushion Gas in Underground Natural Gas Storage', Processes 12(7):1489; Shoushtari et al. (2023), J. Energy Storage 107596; Ni et al. (2026), IFEDC review
closest.overlap: Several reviews show the concept is an established research field. They cover mixing, density and compressibility, the effects of reservoir tilt and permeability, and gains in CH4 recovery. Chinese groups (Northeast Petroleum University, Changqing) are active in the area.

closest.title: Kim J. et al. (2016), 'Underground Gas Storage With CO2 Sequestration in a Depleted Gas Field', OMAE2016-54224; Kim J. et al. (2015), Geosystem Engineering (N2 vs CO2 cushion); Tureyen (2025) SSRN analytical models for UGS with CO2 cushion plus sequestration; AhmadiAghdam (2025) SSRN, ML/PSO cushion design for enhanced gas recovery plus sequestration
closest.overlap: These papers already use the dual framing: UGS with a CO2 cushion as a form of sequestration in depleted fields. Some co-optimize methane recovery and CO2 stored.

closest.title: Zhang K. et al. (2026), 'Experimental study on the cyclic injection-production performance of UGS with trans-critical CO2 as cushion gas', Energy 139696; Zhang K. (2026) SSRN on dissolution-induced reactive mixing under variable cycling
closest.overlap: Lab tests of cyclic injection and production with a CO2 cushion. They address deliverability and CO2 breakthrough under seasonal cycling, which matches the idea's kill criteria.

closest.title: Nitrogen cushion gas in European UGS (Laille et al. 1986/88; French UGS practice, Dussaud 1989)
closest.overlap: An industrial precedent for inert-cushion substitution. The idea already cites it.

art.what_is_new:
The core mechanism is not new. Neither are the climate-sequestration framing or the facility-level inventory linked to CO2 emitters. Swapping methane cushion for CO2 in depleted-field UGS is a 20+ year research line (Oldenburg 2003) with reviews (Du 2024, Shoushtari 2023, Ni 2026), compositional 10-cycle simulations (Kowalski et al. 2023, AGH Poland) and lab cycling tests (Zhang et al. 2026). Mirzaei-Paiaman (Energy & Fuels, June 2026) has already done the US version: 384 facilities paired with CO2 emitters and pipelines, sized at 0.33 Gt for full replacement and about 67 Mt at 20%, with a mean 28% working-gas gain. So the US inventory and gain numbers in the idea are already published.

What remains plausibly new:
(1) A European facility-level inventory (GIE storage database) paired with inland cement and lime clusters that lack offshore hub access, and set against the NZIA 50 Mt/yr objective. I found no EU equivalent of Mirzaei-Paiaman, though the Polish AGH and INiG work comes nearest.
(2) The accounting design: credit only net-of-burn tonnes, or send the freed methane to a strategic reserve or added working-gas inventory, which answers the objection that burning the freed gas cancels 61-85% of the benefit. The published work treats the freed gas as a recovery gain and does not net it.
(3) The rule restricting the cushion to process or biogenic CO2, and the business and regulatory framing: the incumbent owner holds both a UGS licence and a CCS-Directive storage permit.

I found no field pilot or commercial CO2-cushion deployment in natural gas storage. The search was limited: the web-search budget had run out, so I used Crossref and OpenAlex only, and could not check Chinese-language pilots or patents. The cheapest falsifying test partly duplicates Kowalski et al. (2023), whose results should be read before building a new MRST or OPM model.

phys.assumptions:
The script was run with the OptiLex verifier (physics.py) and CoolProp reference equations of state (Span-Wagner for CO2, Setzmann-Wagner for CH4). CoolProp replaces the idea's Peng-Robinson calculation. All numbers below are as printed.

FLOORS [V]
- Separation floor at 90% capture: cement 25% CO2 0.110 GJ/t; lime ~30% 0.098 GJ/t; AGRU or fermentation ~98% 0.002 GJ/t.
- Isothermal compression floor from 1 bar: to 60 bar 0.230 GJ/t; to 90 bar 0.253 GJ/t; to 120 bar 0.269 GJ/t.
- No claim in the idea is below these floors. floor_gj_per_t = 0.253, the compression floor for pure-CO2 sources; add 0.11 for a cement source.

MASS RATIO [CP]
CO2/CH4 mass ratio in the same pore volume:
- 3.21 at 40 bar, 40C (0.311 t CH4 freed per t CO2, 17.3 GJ HHV)
- 3.51 at 60 bar, 50C
- 4.19 at 80 bar, 50C
- 4.56 at 100 bar, 60C (0.219 t CH4, 12.2 GJ)
- 8.98 at 100 bar, 40C, near the critical point (0.111 t CH4, 6.2 GJ)

The idea's 3.2-4.5 range is confirmed for warm fields. Cool fields with a minimum pressure (Pmin) of 80 bar or more give 5-9x.

WORKING-GAS GAIN [CP]
In a segregated, no-mixing model, a 30% swap adds 7.5-13% working gas and a 50% swap adds 12.6-21.6%. This is consistent with two modelled sources, neither a field result: Oldenburg 2003 (one simulation, ~30%) and Mirzaei-Paiaman et al. 2026 (Energy & Fuels, volumetric, 384 US sites, average +28% at full replacement).

ENERGY (storage side, CO2 arriving at ~1 bar)
- Low 0.30 GJ/t (83 kWh/t): pure fermentation CO2 to ~70 bar.
- Base 0.40 GJ/t (111 kWh/t): to 90-120 bar, including dehydration. This is 63% second-law efficiency against the 90-bar floor, close to the ~0.1 MWh/t planning figure in the modelled literature.
- High 0.55 GJ/t (153 kWh/t).
- Capture energy at cement kilns is excluded: ~2.5-3.7 GJ heat/t for amine capture [M].
- The freed gas carries 15-43x the base compression energy.

COST (storage side, from the source fence, capture excluded)
Method: discount rate 8%. Capex is amortised over the 10-year FILL period, because the sink is one-off. O&M is 3%/yr of capex. Assumed unit costs are onshore pipeline $1-2.5M/km and new flank injectors at $8-15M each; existing crest wells are not rated for CO2.
- Low: an 8 Mt site, 30 km from the source, 0.8 Mt/yr. $24.1/t gross.
- Base: a 3 Mt site, 75 km, 0.3 Mt/yr. $124.5/t gross. With the pipeline shared 4 ways, $74.1/t.
- High: a 1 Mt site, 100 km, 0.1 Mt/yr. $491.9/t gross.

Per NET tonne, in the reserve variant with compression emissions at 0.30 t/MWh grid: $25 / $129 / $516. These are the reported low/base/high.

Sale variant at an EU gas price of $11/MMBtu, with 15% deducted for production and taxes (gas credit $108-153 per gross t), base site:
- At 100 bar, 60C: $55.4 per net t if all freed gas adds to consumption (100% market leakage); $26.2 per net t at 50% leakage.
- At 40 bar, 40C with 50% leakage: -$58.1 per net t (profitable).

At the US price of $3.5/MMBtu the sale variant costs $142-154 per net t at 50% leakage.

NET CLIMATE PER GROSS TONNE
Assumptions: 1% downstream CH4 leak at GWP100 29.8; compression emissions 0.033 t.

Sale variant, by share of the freed gas that adds to consumption:
| Share adding to consumption | 40 bar, 40C | 100 bar, 60C |
|---|---|---|
| 100% | 0.02 | 0.30 |
| 50% | 0.49 | 0.63 |
| 0% | 0.97 | 0.97 |

The reserve variant nets 0.97.

CAPACITY PER SITE
- US: the Mirzaei-Paiaman et al. abstract gives ~330 Mt for full replacement across 384 sites, an average of 0.86 Mt per site. A 30-50% swap is therefore 0.26-0.43 Mt per average site, or 26-43 kt/yr over 10 years.
- EU (assumption: depleted fields are 55-70% of ~103 bcm working gas, across 50-70 sites): 23-117 Mt one-off in total, 0.4-1.8 Mt per site.
- A typical cement plant emits 0.5-1 Mt/yr, so one average site absorbs about 1-3 years of one plant.

SCALE
- Global one-off (assumed ~425 bcm working gas, 75% in depleted fields): 132-516 Mt. Filled over 10-20 years, that is 0.007-0.052 Gt/yr; the central value used is 0.02 Gt/yr.
- 0.02 Gt/yr needs 8.0 PJ/yr, which is 0.0013% of world primary energy and 0.05% of fossil CO2.
- EU at 4-20 Mt/yr would be 8-40% of the NZIA 50 Mt/yr target.

MATERIALS, LAND, WATER
About 5 kg of pipeline steel per t CO2 for the base site. Land needed is pipeline easements only. Water use is negligible.

TRL 4
Inert (N2) cushion gas is commercial, and CO2 injection into depleted gas fields is proven elsewhere. But no CO2-cushion pilot exists in an operating gas store; the evidence so far is simulation and lab work only.
phys.violations:
There are no thermodynamic violations. The serious problems are with the idea's claims:

1. **"Net is about 100% if the freed gas displaces LNG imports" is a heroic assumption.**
   - It requires 0% market leakage. In practice, freed gas sold into the market lowers prices and partly adds to consumption.
   - At 50% leakage the net is 0.49-0.63 t per gross t. At 100% it is 0.02-0.30, versus the idea's 15-39%; the idea omitted the 1% downstream CH4 leak and compression emissions.
   - At warm, low-pressure fields (40 bar, 40C), the sale variant is climate-neutral: net 0.02.
   - Only the strategic-reserve variant (0.97 net) is robust. That variant forgoes the $34-153/t gas credit that carries the economics.

2. **"Incremental cost below $30/t because the wells and compression already exist" is wrong as a general claim.** It holds only for large sites (more than ~5 Mt) within ~30 km of the source; the low case is $24/t.
   - Flank injection needs NEW CO2-rated wells. A dedicated pipeline is also needed, and both must be amortised over a one-off fill of about 10 years.
   - The base site costs $124.5/t gross, or $74/t with a shared trunk. A 1 Mt site 100 km away costs $492/t.

3. **The inventory high ends are inflated.**
   - US: the idea's 186 Mt used a mass ratio of 5.5, outside its own 3.2-4.5 range. With that range the figure is 65-152 Mt.
   - EU: the idea's 40-204 Mt counted salt caverns and aquifers. Depleted fields only, using its own ratios, give 23-117 Mt.

4. **The sink is small and short-lived compared with the capture assets it would serve.**
   - The average US site holds 0.26-0.43 Mt at a 30-50% swap; the average EU site holds about 0.4-1.8 Mt.
   - So the "cluster pairing" pitch needs several sites chained per cement plant, or should be restricted to the few largest sites (Norg, Bergermeer, Stogit class).

5. **The idea's novelty claim needs adjusting.** Mirzaei-Paiaman et al. (Energy & Fuels, issued 22 June 2026) already did a nationwide site-level US assessment: ~0.33 Gt for full replacement, 67 Mt and ~0.9 Tscf freed at 20%, and +28% average working gas. So the US half of the idea is covered prior art.
phys.key_uncertainties:
1. **CO2-CH4 mixing under seasonal cycling.** Diffusion is negligible (1.8 m in 10 years), but cyclic dispersion could create a 63-346 m mixing zone over 20 half-cycles. That is comparable to front travel, so CO2 in withdrawn gas could exceed 2.5 mol%. Gravity stability is marginal in tight or flat fields: the critical Darcy velocity is ~30 m/yr at 100 mD and sin(dip) 0.05, against ~56 m/yr typical far-field flow. It is fine in steep, high-permeability fields (180-640 m/yr). The proposed 2D compositional simulation in MRST or OPM is the right kill test.
2. **Timing mismatch.** Industrial CO2 arrives year-round, but CO2 injection and native-gas production are best done near minimum pressure. This may need buffering or year-round voidage management.
3. **Well integrity.** Legacy carbon-steel UGS wells will be exposed to wet CO2. This is the same mechanism behind the Barendrecht onshore opposition (cancelled 2010), and it still applies.
4. **Regulation.** Holding a UGS licence and a CCS-Directive permit at once is untested. Liability transfer is unclear for a site that keeps operating. Onshore storage is politically constrained in the Netherlands, and Germany allows it only where a federal state opts in (not verified here).
5. **Inputs taken from the idea or from memory and not checked here:** the EU type split and site counts, the global ~425 bcm working capacity, pipeline $/km, and well costs. The Mirzaei-Paiaman et al. results are from its abstract only; Oldenburg 2003 is one simulation.
6. **Climate accounting.** Net benefit depends on how much of the freed gas adds to consumption, which no ex-ante design can verify.
phys.resource_needs:
- **Energy:** 0.30-0.55 GJ/t of electricity for compression. At 0.02 Gt/yr that is 8.0 PJ/yr, or 0.0013% of world primary energy and 0.0074% of world electricity.
- **Capital:** $81-262M per site. Sources are a pipeline of 30-100 km at $1-2.5M/km, 2-3 new CO2-rated flank injectors at $8-15M each, a compressor of $12-25M, and permit and baseline MMV of $10-20M.
- **Materials:** about 5 kg of pipeline steel per t CO2 at the base site (15 kt of steel for 3 Mt).
- **Land:** pipeline easements only.
- **Water:** negligible.
- **Capture:** if the source is a cement kiln, capture (~2.5-3.7 GJ heat/t) is a separate, larger cost not included here.
- **People:** the falsification work (reservoir simulation plus an EU site-to-source GIS screen) needs 1-2 reservoir engineers for 2-3 months.

stances.evidence: Climate Action Network's January 2021 CCUS position paper explicitly opposes 'EOR/EGR' (red line 7) and public support for fossil-linked CCS (red line 3). Its objection to CCS for cement, steel and chemicals is evidential ('no definitive evidence'), not categorical. Selling the freed methane makes the swap a form of CO2-driven enhanced gas recovery: stored CO2 pushes out saleable fossil gas, and the net stored is only 15-39% of gross (incumbent_reuse.py). That is the same mechanism that makes most of S1 oppose 45Q EOR parity under the OBBBA. Restricting the CO2 to process or biogenic sources removes the fossil-power objection but not the EGR one. The strategic-reserve or added-working-gas variant, with net-of-burn crediting, falls inside CAN's process-emissions opening, so mainstream and tech-friendly NGOs could accept it. Examples are Bellona and Clean Air Task Force, which back industrial CCS; that is my own knowledge, not re-verified this session. German NGOs historically campaigned against onshore storage, which helped defeat the 2009 bill and produced the 2012 Länder opt-out (de.wikipedia, CO2-Abscheidung und -Speicherung). Their positions on the November 2025 KSpTG were not verified this session. Expect support from the CCS-pragmatist wing, opposition from CAN-aligned and local German or Dutch groups, and outright opposition to the sale variant.
stances.red_line_hit: EOR/EGR (CAN red line 7) if the freed gas is sold. Fossil lock-in and mitigation deterrence (IPCC AR6 C.4.4 stranded-asset mechanism). Public support for incumbent fossil assets (CAN red line 3).

stances.evidence: IPCC AR6 WGIII calls CCS needed 'particularly in hard-to-abate sectors' (COP28 1/CMA.5 para 28e wording). Process CO2 from cement and lime is exactly that niche (GCCA roadmap; Brevik is operating). The relevant science is favourable but thin: Oldenburg (2003, LBNL) simulated about 30% more methane storable with a CO2 cushion and found mixing control critical. A 2026 Energy & Fuels facility study exists but its results were not retrieved. Scientists will support the concept on condition of net-of-burn accounting, because the burn variant stores only 15-39% net, and of compositional simulation showing withdrawn-gas CO2 stays below about 2.5 mol%. Oxford Net Zero's carbon takeback work (Allen, Jenkins et al. 2021) shows academic appetite for making storage an obligation of the fossil supply chain. This stance rests on documented positions on comparable CCS policy, not on any published scientific assessment of the CO2-cushion swap.
stances.red_line_hit: Gross-tonne crediting of the sale variant would be an accounting-integrity failure. Any unverified permanence claim at legacy UGS wells, because old well integrity is the dominant leak path (see S11).

stances.evidence: OGCI and OGDC members already back point-source methane and CCS measures that are not per-tonne fees, and API supports 'market-based' frameworks. Owners such as NAM (Shell/ExxonMobil) at Norg and Grijpskerk gain a one-off release of base gas, worth $129-179 per tonne of CO2 at EU prices (incumbent_reuse.py), plus a storage-tariff revenue line. That mirrors how S3 benefits under the carbon takeback obligation and NZIA (Equinor and Northern Lights). In the US, 45Q pays $85/t for dedicated storage and survived the OBBBA. Conditions S3 will insist on: no per-tonne fee (the US Waste Emissions Charge was disapproved in 2025), a bounded long-term CO2 liability (the EU CCS Directive transfers liability only after closure plus a minimum of 20 years, which is my own knowledge), and protection of working-gas quality, since contaminated withdrawals carry commercial and contractual risk. NAM specifically carries Groningen liabilities and may avoid a new onshore subsurface-risk headline in the same region.
stances.red_line_hit: Open-ended long-term storage liability. Any per-tonne charge. Off-spec working gas (above about 2.5 mol% CO2) hurting storage revenue.

stances.evidence: Cement and lime depend on CCUS for process CO2 (GCCA Concrete Future roadmap; Heidelberg's Brevik is operating with Northern Lights storage). Inland EU plants face rising ETS costs as free allocation phases out against CBAM from 2026, but have no near-term offshore hub. A nearby, already-characterised storage outlet is directly valuable to them, and Germany's Klimaschutzverträge carbon CfDs could pay the gap. CO2 transport and storage tariffs under this model are untested. VCI's 'no panacea' line on CfDs shows S4 wants cheap access, so support depends on the storage tariff undercutting offshore hub plus pipeline costs (the <$30/t claim is an assumption, not evidence).
stances.red_line_hit: None intrinsic. Cost, or a delay that leaves inland plants without a storage outlet while ETS costs rise, would erode support.

stances.evidence: Utilities that own storage (US LDCs, Uniper, SEFE) share S3's interest in the asset release and a new revenue line. In the US, though, cushion gas in utility-owned storage typically sits in the regulated rate base, so who keeps the value of released base gas is a contested ratemaking question (my own knowledge, unverified). Utilities also lose some storage optionality if CO2 creeps into the working gas. In the US, converting storage wells to CO2 storage needs an EPA Class VI permit and Subpart RR monitoring to earn 45Q, and Class VI permitting has been slow (my own knowledge). Power generators gain little directly because the idea excludes power-sector CO2. Utilities support the 45Q-type credit (Carbon Capture Coalition), but this specific swap is a niche to them.
stances.red_line_hit: Loss of deliverability or flexibility in the winter peak (the idea's own kill criterion is a >10% deliverability fall). Rate-case disputes over base-gas proceeds.

stances.evidence: Unions belong to the US Carbon Capture Coalition, which describes itself as including 'companies, unions, conservation and environmental policy organizations'. The idea keeps storage, well-services and compression workforces employed, and keeps cement and lime plants open under rising carbon costs. German industrial unions such as IG BCE have backed industrial CCS (my own knowledge, not re-verified). No job losses are implied.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: Energy-security ministries gain freed gas for a strategic reserve: 19-52 bcm in the EU, 5-16% of one year's demand (incumbent_reuse.py, with an assumed cushion-to-working ratio). This aligns with the post-2022 EU gas storage regulation's fill targets (my own knowledge) and COP28's recognition of transitional fuels for energy security (para 29). The EU's NZIA 50 Mt/yr injection objective, with its pro-rata obligation on licence holders, gives a compliance route, contributing 8-40% of the target. However, onshore storage is politically toxic in the target countries. Germany's 2012 KSpG let Länder ban storage, and Schleswig-Holstein and Lower Saxony did so after RWE pipeline protests. The law was renamed KSpTG on 28 Nov 2025 (de.wikipedia); I did not verify its onshore opt-in details this session. The Dutch government cancelled Shell's Barendrecht onshore storage in a depleted gas field in Nov 2010 over local opposition (my own knowledge; the primary source was not retrieved). Holding both a UGS licence and a CCS Directive permit at one site is a new regulatory combination. Finance ministries gain from released base gas only where the state is a co-owner.
stances.red_line_hit: Onshore storage is politically excluded in several German Länder and in Dutch practice since Barendrecht. Regulatory-capacity friction from dual-permit status.

stances.evidence: There is no direct impact on Global South parties. Freed gas is 19-52 bcm one-off, roughly 3-9% of one year's global LNG trade (about 550 bcm/yr, my own estimate). If it displaces EU LNG imports it eases prices for price-sensitive importers such as Pakistan and Bangladesh. Climate-justice advocates align with CAN and would object if the scheme is marketed as removal or offsets, or if rich countries use it to extend gas use. Baum et al. (2024, Nature Communications, 30 countries) found Global South publics more supportive of carbon-management technologies but more worried about mitigation deterrence. CBAM objections by India and South Africa (noted in the map, not re-verified) are unaffected.
stances.red_line_hit: Only if it is framed as offsets or removal, or used to justify extended rich-country gas consumption (mitigation deterrence).

stances.evidence: The scheme is invisible to consumers. It needs no visible consumer carbon price, the type of policy that was repealed in Canada in 2025. Released gas could slightly lower wholesale prices, while storage-tariff and monitoring costs flow through to industry and some ratepayers. Andre et al. (2024, Nature Climate Change, 125 countries) found 69% willing to contribute 1% of income, and Pew (May 2024, US) found 65% prioritising renewables. Neither tests this technology. Baum (2024) found engineered CCS and CDR rated highest for moral hazard, but this is storage of industrial process emissions, not removal.
stances.red_line_hit: None, unless ratepayers bear the cost of rate-based cushion gas or a CO2-contaminated working-gas incident.

stances.evidence: The upside is a contracted storage tariff plus 45Q ($85/t, transferable for cash, kept by the OBBBA) in the US, or ETS-avoided costs and CfD backing in the EU. The downside is that insurers and lenders price long-term liability and leak events at onshore storage. Aliso Canyon (Oct 2015 to Feb 2016, wiki) released about 97,100 t of methane through the 1953 well SS-25. The cause was casing corrosion, and safety valves removed in 1979 had never been replaced. Over 2,800 households were relocated, with a $119.5m settlement in 2018. That leak happened at a converted depleted-field storage site, which is exactly this asset class. The Frontier and CDR buyer pool will not pay for it because it is not removal, so demand rests on compliance markets. A mixed-gas reservoir that is both a CO2 store and a methane store is a novel risk class without actuarial history.
stances.red_line_hit: Unbounded long-term liability. Legacy well integrity at old storage fields. No commercial precedent (the idea notes no deployment found).

stances.evidence: This is the binding constraint. Barendrecht: Shell's plan to store refinery CO2 in depleted gas fields under a town was cancelled in Nov 2010 after municipal and resident opposition (my own knowledge; the primary source was not retrievable). The Barendrecht CO2 came from refinery hydrogen production, a near-pure, process-type source, so restricting the swap to process CO2 does not address residents' concerns. Germany: popular protests killed the 2009 storage bill, and Länder bans followed under the 2012 KSpG. The flagship Dutch sites are particularly sensitive. Norg/Langelo and Grijpskerk sit in the Groningen/Drenthe region, where NAM gas extraction caused induced earthquakes (Huizinge M3.6, 2012). The Dutch Safety Board found in 2015 that citizen safety had not influenced decisions until 2013, and the Ombudsman called the damage 'a national crisis' in 2021 (wiki). Aliso Canyon shows how storage-site leaks displace neighbours. Inland US clusters would also need CO2 pipelines, which face organised landowner opposition and a 2020 rupture precedent at Satartia (my own knowledge).
stances.red_line_hit: Local safety (leaks, CO2 pipeline rupture, induced seismicity). Collapsed trust in the operator (NAM in Groningen). Property values. Lack of consent, the Barendrecht precedent.

stake.coalition_notes:
Process: the web-search budget was exhausted at the start (200/200), so new evidence comes from WebFetch only: the de.wikipedia CCS page (KSpG 2012 Länder opt-out, renamed KSpTG on 28 Nov 2025) and Wikipedia pages on Groningen and Aliso Canyon. Barendrecht, the US Class VI and pipeline facts, rate-base treatment and the EU liability transfer come from my own knowledge, are flagged in each stance, and should be primary-sourced before any decision.

1. Core finding: the sale variant is CO2-EGR. Selling the freed methane makes the swap mechanically a form of CO2 enhanced gas recovery, which is the explicit target of CAN red line 7. It also repeats the 45Q-EOR-parity split: S3, S4, S5 and S6 for, most of S1 against. Only the strategic-reserve or added-working-gas variant, credited net of any later burn, sits inside the process-emissions opening that CAN leaves. Recommend dropping the sale variant from the pitch entirely, or at least never crediting gross tonnes.

2. The binding constraint is S11 and S7 siting politics, not physics or the incumbents. Every documented European onshore storage attempt in the target countries hit local opposition: Barendrecht cancelled in 2010; German Länder bans after the 2009-2012 protests. The flagship example sites, Norg and Grijpskerk, are operated by NAM in the Groningen region, where trust in the same operator collapsed over induced seismicity. Restricting the CO2 to process sources does not help, because Barendrecht's CO2 was near-pure refinery process CO2 too.

3. Likely coalition: S3, S4 and S6 support; S2 supports conditionally; S5, S8 and S9 are neutral; S1, S7 and S10 are split; S11 opposes. That is broad but shallow, and it can be vetoed locally.

4. Redesign levers to widen the coalition:
- Site selection by acceptance, not only by distance to cement and lime plants. Prefer countries and regions with storage-friendly law and history. TotalEnergies' Lacq pilot (2010-13, onshore France, my own knowledge) is a precedent that operated. Avoid Groningen/Drenthe and Länder with bans.
- A Washington-CCA-style visible local benefit (community revenue share from the storage tariff), the one documented case where visible spending defended carbon policy.
- Independent well-integrity audits before conversion, the Aliso Canyon lesson.
- Liability bounded via the CCS Directive transfer rather than open-ended.
- Fund through Klimaschutzverträge or ETS avoidance in the EU and 45Q dedicated storage in the US, not through offsets or CDR markets.

5. Extra falsifying test this analysis adds: a siting screen. Count EU depleted-field storage sites that are within 100 km of 0.3 Mt/yr or larger process-CO2 sources, AND lie in jurisdictions without onshore-storage bans, AND have no recent induced-seismicity or leak controversy. If fewer than about 5, the European cluster pitch fails on politics even if the reservoir simulation passes.

critic.fatal_flaw: No fatal flaw. The physics is under the floors with margin. The scale (about 0.02 Gt/yr, one-off) makes this a niche rather than a climate solution, but the idea is pitched as a niche storage outlet for inland process CO2, so the scale is not fatal. The S11/S7 siting veto is real, but it can be designed around by picking sites by jurisdiction and acceptance, as the stakeholder report proposes. None of the three reports raises a constraint that cannot be designed around.
critic.top_fixable_flaw:
The store keeps leaking while it operates, and the kill criterion is set at the wrong level to catch it. The idea treats injected CO2 as stored once it is in the reservoir, and its kill test only fails the design if withdrawn gas goes above the 2.5 mol% grid limit. But the field keeps cycling its full working gas every year. Any CO2 that reaches the producing wells, even far below the grid limit, leaves with the gas and is emitted when that gas is burned.

My calculation (critic_ugs_backproduction.py) uses the idea's own inputs: mass ratio 3.2-4.5, cushion/working ratio 0.6-1.0, and a 30-50% swap. The annual loss is x·(W/C)/(f·R_mol), where x is the CO2 mole fraction in withdrawn gas, W/C the working-to-cushion ratio, f the swap fraction and R_mol the molar CO2/CH4 ratio:
- At x = 0.5 mol%, 0.6-2.4% of the stored CO2 is lost per year, or 17-51% over 30 cycles.
- At x = 1 mol%, 1.2-4.8% per year, or 31-77% over 30 cycles.
- At x = 2.5 mol%, which the kill criterion allows, 3-12% per year, or 60-98% over 30 cycles.
- In absolute terms, each 1 bcm of working gas withdrawn at 1 mol% carries about 19 kt of CO2 back out per year.

This loss also hits a stakeholder red line. In the EU, CO2 leaving the storage complex counts as leakage under the CCS Directive and the ETS monitoring rules (my own knowledge, not re-verified), so the operator must surrender allowances for it. That is the per-tonne charge S3 named as a red line. It also undermines the permanence claim S1, S2 and S10 condition their support on. None of the three reports netted this loss: the TEA's net-climate table and cost per net tonne both assume full retention.
critic.suggested_patch:
1. **Replace the grid-spec kill criterion with a retention criterion.** Require at least 95% of injected CO2 to be retained after 30 seasonal cycles. Using the formula above, that means average CO2 in withdrawn gas must stay below about 0.04-0.14 mol%, which is roughly 20-60x stricter than the 2.5 mol% grid spec. Run this test in the reservoir simulation, but first read Kowalski et al. (2023) and the Zhang et al. (2026) cycling experiments to see if they already resolve it.

2. **Change the design to meet that criterion.** Use either or both of these:
   - (a) Inject the CO2 only into a hydraulically isolated flank or fault block, or a lower compartment, that does not produce to the working-gas wells. This trades away some of the claimed working-gas uplift.
   - (b) Fit a CO2-removal unit (amine or membrane) on the withdrawal stream and reinject the CO2 it captures. Its separation energy and capex at about 1 mol% CO2 must be added to the TEA. This keeps the store closed by construction.

3. **Fix the accounting.** Credit only tonnes net of metered back-production, at the meter on the withdrawal stream. Also add a baseline the reports missed: at decommissioning, cushion gas is normally blown down and sold. So the right counterfactual for the "freed methane" is that it is burned later, not never. Recompute the 15-39% and 0.02-0.97 net figures against that baseline before presenting either the sale variant or the reserve variant.

4. **Add a simple baseline to the TEA.** Compare against storing the same CO2 in a nearby non-operating depleted onshore gas field. That option has no back-production. The TEA already shows that new CO2-rated wells and a pipeline are needed either way. The UGS swap should go forward only where it beats this baseline on cost per net, retained tonne.

patched_idea.title: CO2 cushion-gas swap in existing underground gas storage (UGS), with a retention-based design and retained-tonne accounting
patched_idea.one_line: Replace part of the native methane cushion in depleted-field gas storage with process CO2. The CO2 either goes into a hydraulically isolated compartment or is held by a closed loop that scrubs CO2 from withdrawn gas and reinjects it. Only metered, retained tonnes are credited, and the swap goes ahead only where it beats a dedicated depleted-field store on cost per net retained tonne.
patched_idea.conventional_core: Seasonal underground gas storage in depleted gas fields, with its existing wells, compressors, gas-treatment trains, seal data, monitoring and licences. Oil majors and utilities own much of it, for example NAM (Shell/ExxonMobil) at Norg and Grijpskerk, and Exxon, Chevron and the US utilities. Amine or membrane CO2 removal from natural gas (AGRU) is standard gas-processing practice.
patched_idea.graft: Inert-cushion-gas substitution: nitrogen cushions have been used in European storage since the 1980s (Laille et al., cited by Oldenburg 2003). Here the substitute is CO2, whose high compressibility near its critical point is a feature. The graft is unchanged.
patched_idea.mechanism:
1. Inject CO2 while the field is near its minimum seasonal pressure, and produce native cushion methane from the crest. Gravity segregation helps because CO2 is 3-4.5x denser than CH4 at 40-100 bar. Use one of two configurations, chosen per site:
   (a) Isolated-compartment variant: inject only into a flank, fault block or lower compartment with no hydraulic connection to the working-gas wells, so the cushion is swapped without CO2 reaching the producers. This gives up most or all of the working-gas uplift.
   (b) Closed-loop variant: inject low and at the flanks as originally proposed, and add an amine or membrane CO2-removal unit on the withdrawal stream. It strips CO2 to 0.04 mol% or less, and the removed CO2 is recompressed and reinjected. The store is closed by construction and the working-gas uplift is kept.
2. Design target: at least 95% of injected CO2 retained after 30 seasonal cycles. This replaces the 2.5 mol% grid spec. The 2.5 mol% limit is still a hard cap on gas leaving the site.
3. Accept only process or biogenic CO2 (cement, lime, ethanol, AGRU vent), which respects S1's red line on extending the life of fossil power.
4. Use the freed methane as a strategic reserve or added working-gas inventory, or sell it. The climate effect of each use is credited only as set out in the accounting rule below.
5. Accounting rule:
   - Meter CO2 on the withdrawal stream and credit only injected minus back-produced tonnes. In (b), that is tonnes leaving the site after the cleanup unit.
   - Net out the burned freed gas against a site-specific baseline:
     - No-recovery baseline (the cushion would never be produced): applies by default.
     - Recovery-at-decommissioning baseline (the cushion would be blown down and sold at end of life): applies only where a documented decommissioning plan within the crediting horizon shows it.
6. Go/no-go per site: proceed only where cost per net retained tonne beats storing the same CO2 in a nearby non-operating depleted onshore gas field. That baseline has no back-production but needs its own CO2-rated wells and pipeline.
patched_idea.target: Storage access for hard-to-abate process CO2 near inland industrial clusters that have no offshore hub: Germany, the Netherlands, Italy, Austria, the US Midwest and Northeast. It is a one-off sink of about 0.1-0.2 Gt per region, filled over about 10 years. The scale is a niche, not a climate solution.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
All new figures are my calculations in climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/patch_ugs_retention.py. Earlier figures come from incumbent_reuse.py (Peng-Robinson EOS, within about 2-6% of NIST). All are modelled; none is measured.

Unchanged per-tonne figures:
- CO2/CH4 mass ratio in the same pore volume: 3.2-4.5, so each tonne of CO2 frees 0.22-0.31 t CH4 (12-17 GJ HHV).
- Gross gas value: $41-57/t (US, $3.5/MMBtu) and $129-179/t (EU, $11/MMBtu).
- Compression floor 0.23-0.26 GJ/t.

Retention (critic's formula, which I reproduced exactly):
- Annual loss = x·(W/C)/(f·R_mol), with R_mol = 1.17-1.64.
- At 0.5 mol% CO2 in withdrawn gas: 0.6-2.4%/yr, or 17-51% lost over 30 cycles.
- At 1 mol%: 1.2-4.8%/yr, or 31-77% lost.
- At 2.5 mol%: 3.0-11.9%/yr, or 60-98% lost.
- Each 1 bcm withdrawn at 1 mol% carries about 19 kt CO2.
- The 95%-after-30-cycles target allows 0.171%/yr. That means mean withdrawn CO2 of 0.036-0.14 mol% (0.014-0.055 mol% for 98%), about 20-60x stricter than grid spec.

Cleanup loop, variant (b):
- Separation floor 0.26-0.34 GJ/t removed, for 0.5-2.5 mol% inlet stripped to 0.04 mol% (verifier).
- Real amine plus recompression: 2.75-4.25 GJ/t removed. This is my assumed range, not a vendor figure.
- Over 30 years the unit re-handles 0.18-0.71 t per stored tonne at 0.5 mol%, or 0.37-1.43 t at 1 mol%. That costs 0.5-3.0 or 1.0-6.1 GJ per stored tonne.
- Sized for peak withdrawal, the unit runs at only about 33-41% capacity factor (120-150 day withdrawal season), so capex per tonne is high. Not yet costed.

Net climate effect of the sale variant, before retention losses:
- No-recovery baseline: 0.14-0.39 of gross.
- Recovery-at-decommissioning baseline: about 1.0 of gross, because the burn only moves earlier. The small warming penalty from that earlier timing is not quantified.
- Reserve or working-gas variant: about 1.0 under either baseline.
- All of these are then multiplied by the retained fraction (0.95 or more by design).

Inventory (unchanged, US EIA 2024 design capacity):
- US: 61-186 Mt one-off.
- EU: 40-204 Mt (assumed cushion/working ratio), or 4-20 Mt/yr over 10 years.
- Variant (a) will cut these figures, because only isolated compartments qualify. The size of the cut is unknown.

Cost: the earlier "under $30/t" claim is withdrawn as a general claim. It is kept only as a hypothesis for variant (a), or for sites already below about 0.1 mol% without a loop. Variant (b) cost is open and must be computed against the dedicated-depleted-field baseline.
patched_idea.who_gains:
S3/S5 storage owners (NAM, TAQA, Uniper, SEFE, Snam/Stogit, US utilities): a one-off gas asset release plus a storage tariff. Variant (b) reuses AGRU know-how they already have.
S4 inland cement and lime plants: a storage outlet without waiting for offshore hubs.
S7: energy security from the freed reserve.
S6: keeps storage workforces employed.
S1, S2, S10: credits are metered, retained and net of burn, which meets the permanence condition behind their support. The leakage that would trigger per-tonne allowance surrender for S3 is designed out.
patched_idea.who_loses:
S11 communities above onshore fields. Barendrecht (Shell, cancelled in 2010 after local opposition) is the precedent and the mechanism still applies; it applies equally to the dedicated-field baseline.
Storage owners under variant (a): little or no working-gas uplift.
Storage owners under variant (b): cleanup-unit capex and 1-6 GJ per stored tonne of energy.
Sites that fail the baseline comparison drop out.
Gas traders: some loss of storage optionality.
Regulatory friction from holding both a UGS licence and an EU CCS-Directive permit. From memory, not re-verified: the CCS Directive defines leakage as any release of CO2 from the storage complex and ties it to ETS allowance surrender, so back-produced CO2 would be chargeable.
patched_idea.closest_known_work:
- Oldenburg (2003, Energy & Fuels, LBNL): simulated about 30% more methane storable with a CO2 cushion and found mixing control critical.
- Nitrogen cushions in European storage (Laille et al. 1986/88).
- Mirzaei-Paiaman et al. (2026, Energy & Fuels): US facility-level analysis. Results not retrieved.
- Kowalski et al. (2023) and Zhang et al. (2026): CO2/CH4 cushion cycling and mixing studies named by the critic. I have not retrieved either (search budget exhausted), and they must be read before any simulation.
- Standard AGRU/membrane natural-gas sweetening.
- No commercial CO2-cushion deployment found.
patched_idea.why_different:
This frames the swap as a European process-CO2 storage product run by the incumbent storage owners, not a gas-storage efficiency trick. It adds three things the earlier concept lacked:
- A retention-based design: either an isolated compartment or a closed CO2-scrub-and-reinject loop on withdrawal.
- Accounting that credits only metered retained tonnes, net of burn, against an explicit decommissioning baseline.
- A per-site go/no-go against a dedicated depleted-field store.
The 2026 US facility study means the swap itself is not new. The contribution is the cluster pairing, the closed-store design and the accounting.
patched_idea.cheapest_falsifying_test:
1. Desk step (days): read Kowalski et al. (2023), Zhang et al. (2026) and Mirzaei-Paiaman et al. (2026) for reported CO2 levels in withdrawn gas under cycling. If they report sustained levels of 0.5 mol% or more for flank-injected cushions, variant (b) is mandatory for connected reservoirs.
2. Run a 2D compositional MRST/OPM simulation of a representative dipping anticline UGS with real cycling, at 30% and 50% swap, in both configurations.
   - Kill criteria for (a): less than 95% retained after 30 cycles, or deliverability loss above 10%.
   - Kill criteria for (b): 30-year cleanup energy above about 3 GJ per stored tonne (above that, the swap loses its energy edge over a dedicated store), or uncontrolled CO2 above 2.5 mol% at the cleanup inlet.
3. Build a TEA for each site against the dedicated non-operating depleted onshore field baseline. Kill if the UGS swap does not win on cost per net retained tonne at a majority of candidate sites.
4. Compile the GIE EU storage list against cement and lime plants. Kill if fewer than about 10 depleted-field sites lie within 100 km of process-CO2 sources of 0.3 Mt/yr or more.

Effort: about 3 months for 1-2 reservoir engineers plus 1 process engineer.
patched_idea.family: CO2 as cushion gas in existing underground gas storage

fix.change_summary:
I applied the critic's four-part patch, kept the core cushion-swap mechanism and the inert-cushion graft, and recomputed the numbers in patch_ugs_retention.py (scratchpad/climate). That script reproduces the critic's back-production formula and figures exactly: 17-51% of stored CO2 lost over 30 cycles at 0.5 mol% in withdrawn gas, 31-77% at 1 mol%, 60-98% at 2.5 mol%, and about 19 kt CO2 per bcm withdrawn at 1 mol%.

1. **Kill criterion.** The 2.5 mol% grid-spec kill criterion is replaced by a design target of at least 95% retained after 30 cycles. That allows a mean of 0.036-0.14 mol% CO2 in withdrawn gas.
2. **Design.** Each site now uses one of two configurations: (a) inject into an isolated compartment, which gives up the working-gas uplift; or (b) add a closed-loop amine or membrane unit that scrubs CO2 from withdrawn gas and reinjects it.
