For (b) I added the verifier separation floor (0.26-0.34 GJ/t removed) and an assumed real-plant energy range of 1-6 GJ per stored tonne over 30 years at 0.5-1 mol%. The unit runs at only a 33-41% capacity factor, and its capex is still uncosted.
3. **Accounting.** Credit now counts only metered, retained tonnes, net of burned freed gas, against an explicit baseline. Under a no-recovery baseline the sale variant nets 0.14-0.39 of gross. Under a recovery-at-decommissioning baseline it nets about 1.0, but that baseline applies only when a documented decommissioning plan supports it.
4. **Baseline and cost.** I added a per-site go/no-go against storing the CO2 in a dedicated non-operating depleted onshore field. The general "under $30/t" cost claim is withdrawn and kept only as a hypothesis for variant (a).

Two inputs remain unchecked. The CCS-Directive leakage/ETS point is from memory, and Kowalski 2023 and Zhang 2026 were not retrieved because the search budget was exhausted. Both are flagged, and reading the papers is now the first desk step of the falsifying test.

idea.title: Silted hydropower reservoirs as the clay mine for LC3 calcined-clay cement
idea.one_line: The fine, often kaolinitic sediment that is filling reservoirs near dam intakes could be dredged, calcined in cement kilns and sold as clinker substitute. The scheme could pay for the dredging and avoid about 1 t CO2 per t of calcined clay.
idea.conventional_core: Limestone calcined clay cement (LC3-50). Map: 14 calcination plants with 3.45 Mt/yr capacity in 2023, enabling under 1% of global cement; the map calls it the largest near-zero-cost cement lever.
idea.graft: Reservoir sediment management (dredging and flushing near intakes, a standard hydropower operation) recast as a clay-mining operation feeding cement plants.
idea.mechanism: Turbidity currents carry the finest clays to the deepest zone near the dam, where operators already have to dredge or flush to protect intakes. Tropical catchments weather to kaolinite-rich laterites. Calcined at about 800 C, kaolinitic clay replaces clinker. Kilns can dry the sediment with waste heat. Dam owners (S5) recover storage and avoid sediment costs. Cement makers (S4) get supplementary cementitious material as fly ash and slag supply falls with coal and blast-furnace closures, which is a map open problem.
idea.target: Map open problem: SCM supply as fly ash and slag decline, and mapping clay deposits against cement plants. The second bottleneck is reservoir sedimentation, which costs dams about 0.5-1% of storage a year (assumed typical range).
idea.quantitative_claims:
Executed in climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/anti_availability_ideas.py.
(1) Clinker process CO2 by stoichiometry: 0.51 t/t at an assumed 65% CaO. Adding assumed fuel at 3.4 GJ/t and 0.095 t/GJ gives 0.83 t/t clinker.
(2) LC3-50 (50% clinker, 30% calcined clay, 15% limestone) emits 0.49-0.50 t/t cement against 0.79 for OPC. That saves 0.29-0.30 t/t cement, or 0.96-1.01 t CO2 per t of calcined clay, counting the limestone the clay enables.
(3) Drying penalty at 30-50% moisture: 1.1-2.6 GJ/t dry, which is 0.11-0.25 t CO2/t if fuel-fired and about 0 with kiln or cooler waste heat. Hauling 100-300 km by truck adds 10-30 kg CO2/t.
(4) A 1 km3 reservoir losing 0.5-1%/yr traps 6-12 Mt/yr. One 1 Mt/yr LC3 plant needs only about 0.33 Mt/yr of dry clay.
(5) Economics (assumed values): net SCM value of $30-45/t is worth $33-50 per m3 removed, against dredging at $5-10/m3. Sediment removal could pay for itself if the kaolinite content is adequate.
(6) Scale: 0.3 Gt/yr of calcined clay (about 25% of cement as LC3) avoids about 0.3 Gt CO2/yr. Full adoption could reach about 0.9 Gt/yr (map's upper bound).
idea.who_gains: S5: hydropower owners regain storage and protect intakes, turning a cost centre into revenue. S4: cement makers secure SCM and lower costs while keeping their kilns. S8: tropical, kaolinitic regions such as India, Brazil, Ghana and Cameroon, where LC3 leaders already are. S11: dam-safety and flood-capacity benefits. S6: dredging and quarry jobs. S9: neutral to lower cement prices.
idea.who_loses: Delta and floodplain communities (S11/S8) are harmed if sediment that would otherwise be flushed downstream is removed from the river system for good, which worsens delta starvation (for example the Mekong). This needs a sediment-budget rule. Fly-ash and slag marketers lose some share. Clinker volume falls, though the same S4 firms make LC3.
idea.closest_known_work: The LC3 programme (EPFL/Scrivener; Cuba, India; map). Lab studies of calcined dam and harbour sediments as pozzolans (Algerian dam sediments; French dredged harbour sediments, Dunkirk), from memory and not re-verified because the search budget was exhausted. Reservoir sediment management practice (dredging and flushing; Kondolf et al. 2014, from memory). I know of no deployment that pairs dam desilting with LC3 supply, but the prior-art search was incomplete.
idea.why_different: Earlier work tests sediments as a disposal problem one sample at a time. This idea treats the dam operator as a clay supplier. It targets the fine-sediment zone near intakes, where removal is already an operating need, and screens tropical kaolinitic reservoirs against nearby cement plants. That turns two separate bottlenecks into one market.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test: Core fine sediment near the intakes of about 10 reservoirs, tropical and temperate. Measure kaolinite by TGA (dehydroxylation mass loss at 450-600 C), calcine at 800 C, and run the ASTM C1897 R3 reactivity test. Cost is about $100-300 per sample, over a few weeks. If most samples show under about 20% kaolinite or R3 reactivity below what LC3-50 strength parity needs, the idea shrinks to a minor blend component.
idea.family: Dredged reservoir sediment as calcined clay for LC3 cement

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: Rabehi, Ghernouti, Driss (2014), 'Potential Use of Calcined Silt of Dam as a Pozzolan in Blended Portland Cement', Int. J. Concrete Struct. Mater. 8(3):259-268
closest.overlap: Core material step is shown here. Dam-reservoir silt from Algeria is calcined and used as a pozzolanic clinker substitute in blended Portland cement. The binary blend has no limestone. It is a one-reservoir lab study, not a supply scheme.

closest.title: Touhami, Chihaoui, Nefoussi, Mouli (2023), 'Investigation of the Potential Use of Dredged Dam Sediments as Supplementary Cementitious Materials' (SSRN preprint)
closest.overlap: Dredged dam sediment is assessed as an SCM, which is the same material route. It is a lab-scale study (Algerian group, from the authors), with no link to dam operations economics or LC3.

closest.title: Alloul, Amar, Benzerzour, Abriak (2023), 'Developing mortar using limestone flash-calcined dredged sediment/millstone-clay cement binder (LFC)', J. Building Engineering 76:107346
closest.overlap: This is the closest technical precedent. It is an LC3-type ternary binder (clinker + limestone + calcined dredged sediment/clay) using flash calcination. The sediments are French waterway or harbour sediments (IMT Nord Europe / Abriak group), not hydropower reservoirs, and the context is waste disposal.

closest.title: Amar et al. (2021), 'From dredged sediment to supplementary cementitious material: characterization, treatment, and reuse', Int. J. Sediment Research; plus Amar et al. 2022 'Designing Efficient Flash-Calcined Sediment-Based Ecobinders' (Materials 15:7107) and Zeraoui 2023 flash-calcined sediment + slag ternary binders
closest.overlap: A review and programme work establish dredged sediment → calcination → SCM as a known pathway, including industrial-scale flash calcination in France. This covers the 'sediment as calcined pozzolan' concept generally.

closest.title: Hadj Sadok, Hadj Sadok, Belas Belaribi, Belaribi (2026), 'State-of-the-art valorization of calcined dredged sediments as construction materials to substitute cement: characterization, treatment, mechanical strength, and life cycle assessment', Discover Concrete and Cement
closest.overlap: A 2026 review of calcined dredged sediments as cement substitutes, including LCA. It is by an Algerian group that works on dam sediments, so it likely covers the reservoir-sediment literature. Metadata only; the abstract was not retrieved.

closest.title: Dredged sediments as cement raw feed: 'Dredged sediments in cement' (ES&T 2007); 'Dredged sediments used as novel supply of raw material to produce Portland cement clinker' (Cem. Concr. Compos. 2012); 'Beneficial Use of Contaminated Dredged Sediments in Portland Cement Manufacture' (ASCE 2003)
closest.overlap: Cement kilns taking dredged sediment, as raw meal rather than as an SCM, is established practice or research. The sediment-to-cement-plant supply link is therefore not new; only the use as calcined clay for LC3 differs.

closest.title: LC3 programme (Scrivener et al. 2018, 'Calcined clay limestone cements (LC3)', Cem. Concr. Res.; Avet & Scrivener 2018 on kaolinite content)
closest.overlap: This is the conventional core. It also sets the threshold the idea's falsifying test relies on: calcined kaolinite content of roughly 40% or more gives LC3-50 strength parity, and lower grades are usable at reduced performance.

phys.assumptions:
The script was run as climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/anti_availability_3.py. The web-search budget was used up (200/200), and fetches of the lc3.ch FAQ and the ScienceDirect paper failed or had no data. So every literature value below is recalled from standard sources and NOT re-verified; each is labelled in the script.

PHYSICS
- No gas separation is involved, so the CO2 separation floor does not apply.
- The floors that do apply are kaolinite dehydroxylation and the latent heat of drying.
  - Dehydroxylation: 426 kJ/mol = 1.65 GJ/t kaolinite, with water leaving as vapour. Derived from Robie & Hemingway kaolinite ΔHf of -4119.6 and an uncertain metakaolin ΔHf of about -3210 kJ/mol. DSC literature values are often lower, about 0.6-1.0.
  - Drying: 2.26 GJ/t water.
  - The floor_gj_per_t field (0.86 GJ/t CO2) is derived by hand, not printed by the script: 1.65 x 0.35 kaolinite x 1.077 t sediment per t CC / 0.727 t CO2 avoided per t CC. Thermal drying, if used, adds its own latent-heat floor on top.
- Clinker CO2 reproduces the idea's numbers: process 0.510 + fuel 0.323 = 0.833 t/t clinker.

PARAMETERS (low/base/high, where low is favourable to the idea)
- Kaolinite in reservoir fines: 0.50/0.35/0.20. LC3-50 strength parity needs about 40% or more (Avet et al. 2016, recalled). Below 40% a strength penalty raises the clinker factor linearly to 0.65 at 20%.
- In-situ dry density: 1.0/0.75/0.5 t/m3 (Lara & Pemberton range for clay deposits).
- Moisture after dewatering: 30/40/50% wet basis.
- Dryer energy: 2.8-3.5 GJ/t water. Waste-heat share of drying: 100/50/0%.
- Sediment organic C: 0.5/1.5/3%. It burns off and is counted as a CO2 debit.
- Calciner: 2.5/3/4 GJ/t CC. Fuel emission factor: 0.056/0.080/0.095 t CO2/GJ.
- Haul: 100/200/300 km of WET mass at $0.05-0.10/t-km.
- Dredging: $5/10/20 per m3 and 2/4/8 kWh/m3. Dewatering: $3/8/15 per t.
- Fuel: $3/5/8 per GJ. Electricity: $50/80/120 per MWh.
- Calciner capex: $100/150/250 per t/yr, annualised at 8% over 20 years. O&M: $5-10/t.
- Clinker variable cost displaced: $45/35/28 per t. Alternative quarried clay: $10/7/4 per t.
- Value to the dam owner: $2/0.5/0 per m3.
- Cement output 4.1 Gt (USGS). Reservoir trapping 10/5/3 Gt/yr (wide, uncertain).

RESULTS PER t CALCINED CLAY (CC)
- CO2 debit: 0.173 / 0.418 / 0.914 t (low/base/high).
- CO2 avoided under four ways of attributing the saving:
  - A, LC3-50 vs OPC-95 (the idea's method): 1.077 / 0.831 / 0.336.
  - B, clay replaces clinker 1:1: 0.660 / 0.415 / -0.081.
  - C, against today's cement at 0.72 clinker: 0.438 / 0.192 / -0.303.
  - D, A with the low-kaolinite strength penalty: 1.077 / 0.727 / -0.081. D is used for the headline numbers.
- Delivered cost of CC by the dam route: $38.9 / 93.4 / 226.5. By the quarry route: $35.5 / 48.0 / 76.6.
- Cost per t CO2 by the dam route: -$23.7 low, $60.4 base, and undefined at full-high because there is no net avoidance. Quarry route: -$26.9 / -$2.0.
- Premium of dam-sourced over quarried clay: $3.2 (low) and $62.5 (base) per t CO2.
- The cost_high field ($641.4) comes from the sensitivity case with all parameters high except kaolinite and organic C (avoided 0.292 t/t CC). The energy_high field (29.5) is derived by hand as 8.600 GJ/t CC / 0.292, not printed.
- Gross added energy: 2.49 (low) and 6.23 (base) GJ/t CO2. Net of kiln fuel saved, energy use is negative: -2.25 low, -0.78 base.

SENSITIVITY (one parameter moved to high, from a base of $60.4/t)
- Kaolinite at 20%: $102.1/t.
- 300 km haul: $79.3/t.
- Dredging at $20/m3: $80.2/t.
- No waste heat: $77.6/t.
- Best realistic niche (base case, 50 km haul, drying fully on waste heat): 0.838 t/t CC at $23.3/t.

SCALE
- Base: 13 Mt/yr of dam-sourced CC, avoiding 0.009 Gt CO2/yr (3.0% of the idea's 0.3 Gt claim).
- Low: 0.199 Gt CC, avoiding 0.215 Gt CO2/yr. High: 0.000.
- Supply factors (low/base/high): fine fraction 0.4/0.3/0.2, near-intake dredgeable share 0.3/0.15/0.05, kaolinitic share 0.3/0.15/0.07, within 300 km of a cement plant 0.6/0.4/0.25.

RESOURCES AT BASE SCALE
- Gross energy 0.057 EJ/yr, which is 0.009% of world primary energy. Net energy is negative: kiln fuel saved is 0.064 EJ/yr.
- 18 Mm3/yr of sediment moved, 9 Mt/yr of water evaporated, 22 Mt/yr hauled.
- Land use is small (dewatering yards). The water returns to the reservoir.
phys.violations:
Nothing claimed falls below a thermodynamic floor. Several claims are overstated or rest on optimistic assumptions:

(a) Claim 5, that clay value pays for the dredging, is a category error. The $30-45/t value of supplementary cementitious material accrues to calcined clay whatever its source. Raw dam sediment competes with quarried clay at about $4-10/t, which is worth only $2-10 per m3, against dredging at $5-20 per m3. The density assumption also matters: $33-50/m3 assumes 1.1 t/m3. At 0.75 t/m3 the same claim gives $22-34/m3, and at 0.5 t/m3 it gives $15-22/m3.

(b) Claim 2, 'about 1 t CO2 per t clay', credits the limestone to the clay and uses OPC-95 as the baseline. Clay replacing clinker 1:1 gives 0.415 t at base. Against today's 0.72-clinker cement it gives 0.192 t. The claim also leaves out organic carbon burned off the sediment (0.059 t at base) and the haul of wet mass (0.029 t).

(c) The '0.5-1% of storage per year' rate cannot be the global volume-weighted rate. Applied to 6,300 km3 of storage it implies 25-50 Gt/yr of sediment, against a global pre-dam river flux of about 14 Gt/yr.

(d) Claim 6, 0.3 Gt/yr, is the scale of the whole LC3 lever, not of dam-sourced clay. Dam-sourced clay reaches 0.009 Gt/yr at base, and its additionality is near zero wherever quarried kaolinitic clay is available nearby.

(e) The falsification test's 20% kaolinite threshold is too low. LC3-50 strength parity needs about 40% or more (recalled). At 20% kaolinite the case shows no net avoidance once the strength penalty is applied.
phys.key_uncertainties:
- Kaolinite content and reactivity of the fine sediment near dam intakes. Reservoir fines are often illite/smectite-rich silty mixtures. This is the cheapest falsifier: the TGA and R3 test, using a threshold of about 35-40% kaolinite rather than 20%.
- In-situ dry density and moisture after dewatering, which drive both haul cost and drying energy.
- How much kiln and calciner waste heat is really spare. The raw mill already uses much of it.
- Haul distance from dam to cement plant. It is the largest cost lever: 50 km gives $23.3/t, 300 km gives $79.3/t.
- Organic carbon content. Burning it releases carbon that would otherwise stay buried in the reservoir, and organic matter can also impair cement.
- Global reservoir trapping (3-10 Gt/yr assumed) and the near-intake fine fraction. Both are poorly constrained.
- Counterfactual additionality: abundant quarried clay or mining overburden makes the dam source a logistics choice, not a climate lever.
- Sediment-budget harm downstream (delta starvation). Removal for good is worse than sluicing, so it needs a rule limiting removal to sediment that cannot be passed downstream anyway.
- All literature parameters are recalled, not re-verified, because the search budget was exhausted.
phys.resource_needs:
Base scale is 13 Mt/yr of dam-sourced calcined clay. That needs:
- Gross energy of 0.057 EJ/yr (0.009% of world primary), mostly calciner fuel plus fired drying. Net energy is negative because 0.064 EJ/yr of kiln fuel is saved.
- 18 Mm3/yr of in-situ sediment dredged.
- 9 Mt/yr of water evaporated after mechanical dewatering.
- 22 Mt/yr of wet haul.
- Flash calciners at $100-250 per t/yr of capacity.
- Geotube or filter-press dewatering yards: a few hectares per Mt/yr.
Water is returned to the reservoir. Materials are negligible beyond the calciner and dredger fleet.

stances.evidence: For the cement half: clinker substitution is a non-CCS route for cement. CAN (2021) says there is 'no definitive evidence' that CCS is the best route for cement and that 'the promise of CCS must not delay' action, so a cheap clinker cut fits its stated preference for alternatives. That is my inference; I found no CAN text naming LC3. Against the dam half: International Rivers lists 'Fighting False Solutions' under climate justice and treats dams as 'destructive river projects' (internationalrivers.org, fetched 2026-10-05). It would likely oppose anything that adds revenue to dams or extends reservoir life. Expect support for LC3 in general, but hostility to the reservoir-sourcing framing wherever it is presented as greening hydropower.
stances.red_line_hit: Possibly: making large dams more legitimate or profitable (the 'false solutions' framing), and removing sediment from rivers, which starves deltas. Mitigation deterrence, offsets and EOR are not hit.

stances.evidence: From memory, not re-verified this session: IPCC AR6 WGIII industry chapter (Ch. 11) lists clinker substitution and material efficiency as mitigation options. The LC3 programme (EPFL/SDC, lc3.ch) claims cuts of 'up to 40%' against conventional cement. That claim is modelled or lab-based; the map counts 14 plants with 3.45 Mt/yr capacity in 2023. Fluvial geomorphologists (Kondolf et al. 2014, from memory; the page was unretrievable with a 403) promote sediment pass-through and sediment connectivity rather than permanent removal. Expect them to back the cement side and add a sediment-budget caveat on dredge-and-remove.
stances.red_line_hit: No hard red line. A soft one is any design that dredges and permanently exports fines that sluicing or flushing would otherwise pass downstream.

stances.evidence: No documented position: the idea touches oil and gas only through lower kiln fuel demand per tonne of cement. It is not EOR, an offset or a per-tonne fee, the S3 red lines in the map (Waste Emissions Charge repealed 2025; EOR parity in 45Q under OBBBA). It neither threatens nor helps S3 materially.
stances.red_line_hit: None

stances.evidence: lc3.ch (fetched 2026-10-05): 'about 40 cement companies in 25 countries are interested in LC3', and it requires 'no capital-intensive plant modifications'. Lower clinker reduces exposure to the EU ETS as free allocation is phased out against CBAM from 2026, and the CBAM charge on exporters' embedded emissions. Cement makers keep their kilns, and LC3 is made by the same firms. The SCM shortage as fly ash and slag decline is an open problem in the map. Caveats from memory, not verified: product standards and code acceptance in many markets, and colour and feedstock variability. The sediment feedstock adds a quality-assurance risk from variable kaolinite and possible contaminants.
stances.red_line_hit: Only if blend quality or strength is inconsistent (brand and liability risk), or if the sediment is classed as waste, which brings permitting costs. The loss of clinker volume is internal to the same firms.

stances.evidence: The International Hydropower Association, with the World Bank's South Asia Water Initiative, runs a Sediment Management Knowledge Hub (37 case studies, nine strategies including mechanical dredging; hydropower.org, fetched 2026-10-05). Sedimentation is a recognised operating cost that operators want to manage. A buyer for dredged fines turns a cost centre into revenue. Only hydropower owners benefit; thermal utilities are unaffected, and coal plants lose some fly-ash sales.
stances.red_line_hit: Dam-safety and operational disruption near intakes, and liability if contaminated sediment is remobilised. Most reservoirs are not within 100-300 km of a cement plant, so the gain is site-specific.

stances.evidence: No documented union position on LC3 was found. Unions back decarbonisation routes that keep existing plants running, such as their membership in the Carbon Capture Coalition alongside S3 and S4 (map). LC3 keeps kilns and adds dredging, haulage and clay-calcining work. Clinker throughput per tonne of cement falls, but the shift happens inside the same plants. Fly-ash marketing jobs shrink, though that supply is already falling with coal closures. Rated support, but weakly and inferred.
stances.red_line_hit: No major job-loss red line. There may be minor kiln-capacity rationalisation over time.

stances.evidence: Lower clinker cuts imported kiln fuel, which helps energy security. Recovering reservoir storage helps water, flood and power security. Exporters reduce CBAM exposure (CBAM definitive phase from 1 Jan 2026; map). No fiscal subsidy is needed if the claimed economics hold: SCM value of $33-50/m3 against dredging at $5-10/m3 are modelled, assumed values. From memory, unverified: India's BIS issued an LC3 cement standard around 2023. The COP28 text names no cement option, so there is no multilateral endorsement. Rated support.
stances.red_line_hit: Transboundary rivers: removing sediment upstream can become an interstate dispute, as on the Mekong, where downstream Vietnam already attributes delta loss partly to upstream dams.

stances.evidence: Tropical producers gain, consistent with the idea's claim (not re-verified here) that LC3 leaders are in India, Cuba and tropical Africa; LC3 resource centres sit in India and Cuba (lc3.ch). Cheaper, lower-carbon cement for housing and infrastructure helps them. Delta communities lose: the Mekong Delta Wikipedia page cites a 2019 Nature Communications study finding 75% of the delta, home to 12 million people, below 1 m, with sediment loads cut by upstream dams and sand mining. Executed scale check: one 1 Mt/yr LC3 plant takes about 0.33 Mt/yr of clay, about 0.2% of the current Mekong load of about 160 Mt/yr; 20 plants would take about 4%. That is locally small but cumulative. Climate-justice advocates tend to oppose large dams (International Rivers).
stances.red_line_hit: Dispossession through delta sediment starvation, if fines are permanently removed rather than flushed downstream. This is a land-loss and justice issue for downstream deltas.

stances.evidence: The price change is invisible. LC3 claims to be cost-effective and needs no consumer-facing price, unlike the visible fuel carbon charges repealed in Canada in 2025 (map). Expected price effect is neutral to lower if the modelled economics hold. Baum et al. 2024 shows publics favour government funding and pilots over restrictions, which is consistent with low salience.
stances.red_line_hit: No price-rise red line. A latent concern is durability and trust in 'new cement' in buildings, which would be a code and standards issue rather than a consumer veto.

stances.evidence: Low capex: LC3 needs 'no capital-intensive plant modifications' (lc3.ch). Lower clinker reduces ETS/CBAM liabilities, which is positive for cement equity. But the reservoir-sourced feedstock is unproven: no deployment pairing dam desilting with LC3 is known, and the prior-art search was incomplete. Investors would wait for the falsifying test (TGA kaolinite plus R3 reactivity on about 10 reservoirs). Insurers would price the environmental liability of handling sediment that may be contaminated.
stances.red_line_hit: Unquantified environmental liability, such as sediment contaminants or downstream damage claims, until the sediment is characterised.

stances.evidence: Communities near the dam gain flood-storage capacity and dam safety. Local disamenity: executed estimate of about 22,000 wet truckloads a year (about 73 a day, assuming 40% moisture and 25 t trucks) per 1 Mt/yr LC3 plant at 100-300 km haul. Add dredging turbidity and drying sites, plus possible remobilisation of contaminants buried in the sediment. Floodplain and delta communities further downstream lose sediment supply, as in the Mekong evidence above. Heidelberg credits Brevik's success partly to local social acceptance (map), which shows local consent matters for cement projects.
stances.red_line_hit: Local safety and nuisance (truck traffic, contaminated sediment), and downstream land loss.

stake.coalition_notes: Search budget was exhausted (200/200 WebSearch). Evidence comes from the map's documented positions, a few direct fetches (lc3.ch, hydropower.org, internationalrivers.org, Wikipedia Mekong Delta) and items flagged as from memory. Executed calc: climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/stake_lc3_sediment.py. Coalition: the idea splits cleanly into two halves. (a) LC3/clinker reduction has a broad, low-conflict coalition: S2, S4, S6 and S7 support; S3 and S9 are neutral; S1 likely supports it as a non-CCS cement route. It triggers no S3 red line (EOR, offsets, fees) and no visible consumer price, so it shares the 'invisible industrial measure' survival pattern seen in Canada 2025. (b) Reservoir sourcing is where all the conflict sits. It recruits S5 (hydropower) but alienates the dam-sceptic part of S1/S8 (International Rivers' 'false solutions'). It creates the only hard red line: delta sediment starvation, an S8/S11 land-loss and justice issue that becomes interstate on transboundary rivers such as the Mekong (S7). Locally the take is small (one plant is about 0.2% of the Mekong's ~160 Mt/yr load), but it is cumulative. A design rule widens the coalition: take only fines that would otherwise be landfilled or that accumulate behind dams where flushing or sluicing is infeasible; keep pass-through obligations; publish a basin sediment budget. Framing it as 'cement clay supply plus dam safety' rather than 'greening hydropower' keeps S1 neutral or supportive. The falsifying test (kaolinite and R3 reactivity) gates S10 and S4 quality concerns. Until it passes, the stronger stakeholder case is generic LC3 with conventionally mined clay, and the reservoir graft is an optional local feedstock.

critic.fatal_flaw:
None is fatal. Physics, scale and stakeholder checks find nothing that cannot be designed around. No thermodynamic floor is breached. The delta-starvation red line (S8/S11, and S7 on transboundary rivers) can be designed around with a take-only-what-cannot-be-sluiced rule. The base scale is about 0.009 Gt/yr, so this is a niche feedstock, but small scale is not a flaw that kills it. The nearest thing to a fatal point is additionality. Every tonne of CO2 avoided comes from LC3 itself, which the quarry route also delivers. In the base case the dam graft adds about $62/t CO2 in cost and nothing in climate benefit. If no site meets the patch conditions below, the graft has no reason to exist. The idea would collapse to plain LC3 with quarried clay, which is the stakeholder report's own fallback.

A secondary mechanism risk, from recalled sedimentology and not verified: sorting by particle size tends to enrich the finest near-dam deposits in smectite relative to kaolinite, because smectite particles are smaller. That would undercut the premise that the finest near-intake zone is the best clay. It is not fatal, because deeply weathered tropical catchments carry little smectite, but it is the first thing the coring test should check.
critic.top_fixable_flaw:
The economics assume the dam route pays for new dredging. On that basis it competes with quarried clay and loses at every realistic setting.

Executed in critic_aa3.py, with the same parameters as anti_availability_3.py:
- Even the reports' best niche (50 km haul, drying entirely on waste heat) delivers calcined clay at $69/t against $48/t from a quarry. That is $23/t CO2 against -$2/t CO2 for the quarry route.
- The 100% waste-heat assumption does not hold. LC3-50 makes about 1.67 t of clinker per t of calcined clay. Recalled spare heat from the cooler plus the calciner exhaust is about 0.85-1.75 GJ per t of calcined clay. Drying at 40% moisture needs 2.23 GJ, so waste heat covers only about 38-79% of it, around 58% at mid values. The script's 45% share is therefore conservative. At a 45% share the niche rises to $35/t CO2.
- The headline claim that clay value pays for dredging is a category error. The $30-45/t SCM value belongs to calcined clay from any source.

The graft only adds something where the dam owner already dredges and pays to dispose of the spoil. There the dredging cost is sunk, and avoided disposal becomes a real credit.
critic.suggested_patch:
Narrow the claim and the siting screen to SEDIMENT ALREADY BEING DREDGED. Include only reservoirs where all of the following hold:
(a) The operator already dredges mechanically and pays for disposal, such as confined disposal or landfill. Reservoirs that rely on sluicing or flushing are excluded, so removal never subtracts from the downstream sediment budget. This one rule also meets the delta-starvation red line held by S8, S11 and S1.
(b) A cement plant is within about 50-100 km.
(c) No quarry clay with at least 40% kaolinite is available at a similar distance.

Executed results (critic_aa3.py, base parameters, 45% waste heat, 50 km haul, dredging cost treated as sunk):
- At $5/m3 avoided disposal, calcined clay costs $54/t against $48/t from a quarry, giving $6.5/t CO2.
- At $10/m3 avoided disposal, it costs $47/t, giving -$3.2/t CO2, which beats the quarry route.
- At a 150 km haul it rises back to $24/t CO2, so 100 km is a real cut-off.

Restate the headline as 'about 0.74 t CO2 avoided per t calcined clay at 35% kaolinite, against OPC-95 with a strength penalty applied'. Drop the 'about 1 t' figure. Label scale as a site-specific niche at about 0.01 Gt/yr, not 0.3 Gt.

Revise the falsifying test in two ways:
- Set the pass threshold at 35-40% kaolinite. 20% is too low.
- Core along a transect from the delta front to the intake. Measure the kaolinite/smectite ratio by XRD on the clay fraction alongside TGA and R3. This checks whether size sorting enriches the intake zone in smectite.

Add three screening measures, because together they decide whether a site counts:
- organic carbon content;
- the dam's current disposal cost in $/m3;
- moisture achievable after a filter press.

patched_idea.title: Already-dredged reservoir sediment as calcined clay for LC3 cement
patched_idea.one_line: Where a hydropower operator already dredges reservoir sediment mechanically and pays to dispose of it, the fine kaolinitic fraction could go to a cement plant within about 100 km and be calcined there as LC3 clinker substitute. This avoids about 0.74 t CO2 per t of calcined clay and turns a disposal cost into a feedstock credit. It is a site-specific niche of about 0.01 Gt CO2/yr, not a bulk clay source.
patched_idea.conventional_core: Limestone calcined clay cement (LC3-50). Map: 14 calcination plants with 3.45 Mt/yr capacity in 2023, enabling under 1% of global cement; the map calls it the largest near-zero-cost cement lever.
patched_idea.graft: Reservoir sediment management, recast as a clay supply. Only spoil that is already being dredged and then landfilled or placed in confined disposal is redirected to cement plants. No new dredging is done, and nothing is taken from sediment that would otherwise be sluiced or flushed downstream.
patched_idea.target: Map open problem: SCM supply as fly ash and slag decline, and mapping clay deposits against cement plants, here restricted to sites with existing paid sediment disposal. The second problem is the disposal cost of mechanically dredged reservoir sediment. Reservoirs lose about 0.5-1% of storage a year to sedimentation (assumed typical range).
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
Executed in climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/anti_availability_ideas.py and critic_aa3.py; all are modelled estimates with assumed parameters.
(1) Clinker process CO2 by stoichiometry: 0.51 t/t at an assumed 65% CaO. Adding assumed fuel at 3.4 GJ/t and 0.095 t/GJ gives 0.83 t/t clinker.
(2) Headline: about 0.74 t CO2 avoided per t of calcined clay at 35% kaolinite. This is against OPC-95 with a strength penalty applied, and includes the drying penalty at about 45% waste-heat share. It replaces the earlier 'about 1 t' figure. Gross LC3-50 vs OPC: 0.49-0.50 vs 0.79 t/t cement.
(3) Drying: 1.077 t dry sediment and 1.44 m3 in situ per t of calcined clay. Drying at 30/40/50% moisture needs 1.43/2.23/3.34 GJ per t of calcined clay. Waste heat available is 0.85-1.75 GJ per t of calcined clay, recalled and not verified, which covers 38-79% at 40% moisture. A 45% share is assumed. Hauling 50-100 km adds about 5-10 kg CO2/t.
(4) Economics, base case: 45% waste heat, 50 km haul, dredging treated as sunk. Quarry calcined clay costs $48/t, which works out to -$2/t CO2.
- Avoided disposal of $5/m3: dam-sourced clay costs $54/t, or $6.5/t CO2.
- Avoided disposal of $10/m3: $47/t, or -$3.2/t CO2, which beats the quarry route.
- At 150 km and $5/m3: $24/t CO2, so about 100 km is the cut-off.
For comparison, the original scheme with new dredging costs $23-35/t CO2 even at 50 km, so new-dredging sites are excluded.
(5) Supply per site: a 1 km3 reservoir losing 0.5-1%/yr traps 6-12 Mt/yr, but only the mechanically dredged fraction counts. One 1 Mt/yr LC3 plant needs about 0.33 Mt/yr of dry clay.
(6) Scale: a site-specific niche of about 0.01 Gt CO2/yr (critic's base estimate about 0.009 Gt/yr). The climate benefit is LC3's own. The graft's value is lower SCM cost at qualifying sites, not extra abatement beyond quarried-clay LC3.
patched_idea.who_gains: S5: hydropower operators that already dredge turn a disposal cost into a small revenue or zero-cost outlet. S4: cement makers near qualifying dams get SCM supply at or below quarry cost while keeping their kilns. S8: tropical, kaolinitic regions such as India, Brazil, Ghana and Cameroon, where LC3 leaders already are. S1/S8/S11: the already-dredged-only rule means removal never reduces the downstream sediment budget, which respects the delta-starvation red line. S11: less landfilled spoil near the dam. S6: dewatering and haulage jobs. S9: neutral to slightly lower cement prices.
patched_idea.who_loses: Operators of disposal sites and landfills lose fees. Fly-ash and slag marketers lose some share. Clinker volume falls, though the same S4 firms make LC3. Delta communities (S8/S11) and transboundary-river governments (S7) would lose only if the screen were breached by expanding into sediment that would otherwise be sluiced or flushed. The siting rule explicitly forbids this.
patched_idea.closest_known_work: The LC3 programme (EPFL/Scrivener; Cuba, India; map). Lab studies of calcined dam and harbour sediments as pozzolans (Algerian dam sediments; French dredged harbour sediments, Dunkirk), from memory and not re-verified. Reservoir sediment management practice (dredging and flushing; Kondolf et al. 2014, from memory). Beneficial-use programmes for dredged material are the nearest institutional analogue. I know of no deployment that pairs reservoir desilting with LC3 supply, but the prior-art search was incomplete.
patched_idea.why_different: Earlier work tests sediments one sample at a time, as a disposal problem. This idea screens existing paid-disposal dredging sites against nearby cement plants and against local quarry-clay quality. It uses the sunk dredging cost and the avoided disposal fee as the economic edge, and excludes any site where it would subtract sediment from the river system. Its claim is narrow: cheaper SCM at qualifying sites, not new abatement and not bulk supply.
patched_idea.family: Dredged reservoir sediment as calcined clay for LC3 cement

idea.title: N2O-respiring bacteria grown in livestock slurry before it is spread
idea.one_line: Use the slurry tankers farmers already run to deliver N2O-reducing (NosZ) bacteria to soil. This extends a method already shown in Nature with biogas digestate to the much larger livestock-slurry stream.
idea.conventional_core: Spreading manure slurry and digestate: a routine, regulated practice on livestock and biogas farms. In terms of N2O management, it is the conventional fertiliser channel.
idea.graft: NosZ, nitrous oxide reductase, the only known biological sink for N2O. It is carried by N2O-respiring bacteria (e.g. Cloacibacterium sp. CB-01) enriched in the slurry before spreading.
idea.mechanism: Wet soils leak N2O from denitrification when NosZ activity is weak. An organism that respires N2O to N2 without producing it shifts the end product toward N2. Hiis et al. showed that organic waste can serve as both growth substrate and vector, and that the effect lasts because the bacterium persists in soil. The graft extends the vector from biogas digestate, whose supply is capped by biogas capacity, to raw livestock slurry enriched on the farm or by contractors.
idea.target: Direct soil N2O from synthetic fertiliser and manure on denitrification-dominated soils (wet, fine-textured), starting where slurry is already spread.
idea.quantitative_claims:
(1) Measured (Hiis et al., Nature 630, 2024): digestate carrying about 6e9 cells/mL cut N2O by 50-95% depending on soil type. Scaled up in a model, national anthropogenic N2O in Europe could fall 5-20%.
(2) Per hectare (my calculation; verifier GWP100 for N2O = 273). At 150 kg N/ha and an emission factor of 1%, emissions are 2.36 kg N2O = 0.64 t CO2e/ha/yr; across emission factors of 0.5-1.6% the range is 0.32-1.03 t. A realised field cut of 30-60% (assumed, below the measured 50-95%) saves 0.10-0.62 t CO2e/ha/yr.
(3) Cost: assuming $10-30/ha for enrichment, it is $26-155/t CO2e at an emission factor of 1%, and $16-311/t across 0.5-1.6%. That is comparable to 3-NOP ($44-117/t, map) and far above industrial N2O abatement ($0.25-4/t, map), so adipic and nitric acid plants should be done first.
(4) Global direct soil N2O, assuming about 140 Mt N/yr applied and emission factors of 0.8-1.2%, is about 0.48-0.72 Gt CO2e/yr. Realistic reach is 14-86 Mt CO2e/yr: 50-60% of soils denitrification-dominated, times 20-40% adoption, times a 30-50% cut.
(5) Energy penalty is negligible; the aeration energy for enrichment was not quantified.
idea.who_gains: Farmers (S9/S6-like rural producers) keep their spreading routine and gain a sellable climate attribute. S4 fertiliser makers and biogas operators gain a premium low-N2O product without selling less nitrogen. S7 (EU, Denmark, New Zealand) gain an agricultural N2O lever that does not cut output. S1 and S2 support it as a pure emissions cut with no offsetting logic. S8 gains if it is adapted to smallholder manure in the tropics.
idea.who_loses: Nitrification-inhibitor vendors (DMPP, DCD) face a competitor. Farmers carry the cost unless payment schemes (CAP eco-schemes, livestock-tax credits) cover it. Only denitrification N2O is addressed; nitrifier-derived N2O is untouched. MRV payers (S10) therefore risk paying for unproven cuts on soils where nitrification dominates.
idea.closest_known_work: Hiis, Vick, Molstad, Rosdal, Jonassen, Winiwarter and Bakken, 'Unlocking bacterial potential to reduce farmland N2O emissions', Nature 630 (2024), doi 10.1038/s41586-024-07464-3. It uses the same mechanism and organism class with biogas digestate as the vector. Also Li et al. 2026 (Life 16:635): a Bacillus subtilis biofertiliser cut cumulative N2O by 39% in a field trial on Chinese saline-alkali soil, by a different mechanism (less amoA, i.e. less nitrification).
idea.why_different: The change is honestly incremental. It moves the vector from digestate to raw livestock slurry and sells through the slurry-contractor and fertiliser channel. The open scientific question is whether slurry's labile carbon still selects for N2O respirers rather than for N2O-producing denitrifiers.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test: A 2-4 week bench test. Try to grow CB-01-type N2O-respiring bacteria to at least 1e9 cells/mL in raw cattle and pig slurry under Hiis-style O2- and N2O-limited enrichment. Then incubate soil microcosms on 2-3 soils with automated gas kinetics. Falsified if other denitrifiers outgrow the target organism in slurry, or if inoculated slurry cuts N2O by less than 20% versus plain slurry. Cost under $20k at any soil-microbiology lab.
idea.family: N2O-respiring (NosZ) bacteria delivered in livestock slurry

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: Hiis, Vick, Molstad, ... Bakken, 'Unlocking bacterial potential to reduce farmland N2O emissions', Nature 630 (2024)
closest.overlap: Same mechanism, same organism (Cloacibacterium sp. CB-01) and same business model: organic waste used as both growth substrate and vector. Biogas digestate at about 6e9 cells/mL cut field N2O by 50-95% depending on soil. Their Europe-wide scale-up gives a 5-20% cut in national anthropogenic N2O, and the abstract adds 'and more if including other organic wastes'. The full text (Europe PMC XML) says ongoing work extends the technology to growing N2O-respiring bacteria in all types of organic waste used to fertilise soils. They did not test manure or slurry. So the slurry extension is the originators' own announced next step.

closest.title: Jonassen et al., 'Nitrous oxide respiring bacteria in biogas digestates for reduced agricultural emissions', ISME J (2022)
closest.overlap: Establishes digestate as the substrate and vector for N2O-respiring bacteria, framed as inoculation riding on existing biogas operations. The paper mentions no other waste stream.

closest.title: Jonassen et al., 'A Dual Enrichment Strategy Provides Soil- and Digestate-Competent Nitrous Oxide-Respiring Bacteria', mBio (2022)
closest.overlap: Enrichment protocol: sequential batches alternating sterilised digestate and soil, selecting N2O respirers that compete in both. This is exactly the protocol the idea would port to raw slurry. Raw, unsterilised slurry with its labile C and a resident denitrifier load is the untested difference.

closest.title: Gao N, Shen W, ... Senoo K, 'N2O-reducing denitrifier-inoculated organic fertilizer mitigates N2O emissions from agricultural soils', Biol Fertil Soils 53 (2017); follow-up Shen et al. 2020 (Cu-modified carrier) and Gao et al. 2023 (J Appl Microbiol)
closest.overlap: Precedent for delivering N2O-reducing bacteria (Azospirillum, Herbaspirillum) in an organic-fertiliser carrier. Field N2O fell by 36.7% (Fluvisol) and 23.4% (Andosol), both in 2014 trials in Japan. The carrier is a granular organic fertiliser (solid, dried), not liquid slurry, and the cells are inoculated, not grown in the waste.

closest.title: Tian W et al., Bacillus velezensis SQR9 plus organic-fertiliser substitution, Agric Ecosyst Environ (2025) and J Environ Manage (2026)
closest.overlap: Inoculant delivered with organic fertiliser in tropical vegetable field trials. It raised nosZ abundance and cut N-oxide emissions by 11% versus organic substitution alone and 35% versus conventional mineral fertiliser. The organism is a generalist PGPR, not a selected N2O respirer, and the carrier is solid organic fertiliser.

closest.title: Zhou S et al., 'Bacterial N2O mitigation potential in soil-based systems and liquid cultures: a comprehensive meta-analysis', Front Microbiol (2026)
closest.overlap: Meta-analysis of 34 studies and 257 data points on bacterial inoculation. The mean N2O cut is 42.9% in soil systems (mostly lab incubations) and 68.3% in liquid culture, with Bradyrhizobium the key genus in soil. These are lab effect sizes, not field results for a slurry vector. They still give a useful prior below the Hiis field range.

art.what_is_new:
Not much is new. I found no published study that enriches N2O-respiring bacteria (CB-01 or similar) in raw cattle or pig slurry, and none that delivers them in slurry and measures soil N2O. A Europe PMC title/abstract search on pig/cattle/dairy slurry or liquid manure combined with inoculation and N2O returned only one unrelated methane paper. But the Hiis et al. (2024) authors say outright that 'other organic wastes' are their ongoing work, so the NMBU group may publish or patent this first. Prior inoculant-in-organic-fertiliser work exists in Japan (Gao/Senoo, 2017-2023) and China (SQR9, 2025-26). It uses solid granular or composted carriers with inoculated cells, not liquid slurry with on-farm or contractor enrichment.

The new parts are therefore:
(a) the vector: raw livestock slurry, which is about an order of magnitude larger than digestate and not capped by biogas capacity;
(b) the channel: on-farm or slurry-contractor enrichment;
(c) the open science question the idea itself flags: whether unsterilised slurry, with its labile C and resident denitrifiers, still selects for N2O respirers over N2O producers.
That question is a real, cheap falsifier but not a conceptual advance.

For the engine, treat this as 'deploy or extend Hiis et al.', not a novel idea. Collaboration or licensing with NMBU (Bakken/Frostegård) is the obvious route, and freedom-to-operate is a risk.

Search limits: the web-search budget was exhausted, Google Patents returned 503, and the other patent sources tried (FreePatentsOnline, DuckDuckGo) were blocked. So the NMBU patent-family status and any company commercialising CB-01 are unverified. Check these before acting.

phys.assumptions:
THERMODYNAMICS (no violation). There is no separation step, so the verifier's min_separation_work does not bind. The reaction N2O(g) -> N2 + 1/2 O2 has dG0 = -104.2 kJ/mol (NIST/CRC formation energy of N2O, +104.2 kJ/mol), i.e. it RELEASES energy. Floor = 0 GJ/t CO2e. The only genuine energy cost is growing the inoculum and handling slurry, so nothing in this idea is near a physical limit. Contrast: DAC floor 0.47 GJ/t, real DAC 5-10 GJ/t.

PER-HECTARE ABATEMENT (script printed): 150 kg N/ha x EF 0.6% -> 1.41 kg N2O = 0.386 t CO2e/ha, 30% cut saves 0.116 t; 150 kg N x EF 1.0% -> 2.36 kg N2O = 0.643 t CO2e/ha, 45% cut saves 0.290 t; 200 kg N x EF 1.6% -> 5.03 kg N2O = 1.373 t CO2e/ha, 60% cut saves 0.824 t. The idea's own claim-2 arithmetic reproduces exactly (2.36 kg N2O, 0.643 t CO2e at EF 1%), using GWP100 N2O = 273 from the verifier and EF ranges from the IPCC 2019 Refinement (aggregated EF1 1.0%; wet-climate organic 0.6%, wet-climate synthetic 1.6%).

ENRICHMENT ENERGY (the idea left this unquantified; now quantified). To reach the Hiis et al. measured density of ~6e9 cells/mL: 1.80 g/L biomass (0.3 pg dry mass per cell), 4.50 g/L COD consumed at an aerobic yield of 0.4 g cells/g COD, giving an O2 demand of 1.94 kg O2/m3 slurry (cell COD 1.42 g/g). At aeration efficiencies of 2.0/1.5/1.0 kg O2/kWh plus 0.2/0.4/0.8 kWh/m3 mixing of viscous slurry: 1.17/1.70/2.74 kWh/m3.

ENERGY PER TONNE ABATED: at 30/43/67 m3 slurry per ha (cattle/pig slurry at 5.0/3.5/3.0 kg N/m3, RB209-type values) that is 35/73/183 kWh/ha, i.e. 1.09/0.90/0.80 GJ(el)/t CO2e in matched cases, and 0.15 to 5.69 GJ/t across the best/worst pairings, base 0.90. Energy is not the binding constraint.

NH3-STRIPPING DEBIT (material omission in the idea). Aerating raw slurry strips ammonia. At 2/5/12% of applied N lost as NH3-N (low-rate aeration literature spans a few % to >20%), with IPCC EF4 = 1% for volatilised N re-emitted as N2O and ~2.5 kg CO2e/kg N to replace the lost nitrogen: debits of 0.020/0.051/0.122 t CO2e/ha. Net savings become -0.006 / 0.239 / 0.803 t CO2e/ha/yr. In the worst case the debit ERASES the abatement entirely and cost per tonne is undefined; unpriced PM2.5 health harm from NH3 is additional.

COST (bottom-up, 8% discount rate, 10-year life, 3% O&M): aerated batch tank capex $30k/$45k/$70k over 12,000/7,000/4,000 m3/yr throughput = $0.45/$1.15/$3.13 per m3 capital, plus electricity at $0.12/$0.20/$0.30 per kWh = $0.14/$0.34/$0.82 per m3, plus inoculum and qPCR QA at $0.15/$0.35/$0.80 per m3. Total $0.74/$1.84/$4.76 per m3 = $22/$79/$317 per ha. Against net savings: $28 / $331 / $2,738 per t CO2e (the high figure uses the gross denominator, since the net is <= 0). On gross savings: $27/$272/$2,738. The idea's own $10-30/ha gives $26-155/t only because it assumed the cost; only the low case ($22/ha) reaches that band. MRV is excluded and is the larger practical cost: chamber-based field N2O flux measurement runs to thousands of dollars per site-year, so any payment scheme needs modelled MRV.

SCALE: all applied N (110 Mt synthetic, IFA; 31 Mt manure-N to soils, FAOSTAT) at EF 0.8-1.2% gives 0.48-0.73 Gt CO2e/yr direct soil N2O, which confirms the idea's claim-4 denominator. But the vector caps the reach: liquid slurry carries only 35-60% of manure N (10.8-18.6 Mt N), covering 72/103/124 Mha. N2O on that land is 37/80/140 Mt CO2e/yr; after denitrification-dominated share (0.55/0.65/0.75), adoption (0.20/0.30/0.40) and realised cut (0.30/0.45/0.60): 1.2 / 7.0 / 25.3 Mt CO2e/yr. Base = 0.007 Gt = 0.013% of global GHG. The idea's claimed 14-86 Mt/yr applies the funnel to ALL fertilised soils, not to slurry-reachable land, so it overstates the base case by roughly 2-10x; its top end (86 Mt) is above even my high case.
phys.resource_needs:
Energy: negligible. Treating all base-case liquid slurry (4.4 bn m3/yr) at 1.70 kWh/m3 needs 7.5 TWh/yr = 0.025% of world electricity (verifier WORLD_ELECTRICITY_TWH = 30,000). No fuel, no heat.
Land: none additional; the slurry is already spread on the same hectares.
Water: none; slurry is the growth medium.
Materials: aerated batch tanks sized at roughly 4,000-12,000 m3/yr each, so ~0.4-1.1 million tanks if the entire global liquid-slurry stream were treated (realistically a few tens of thousands of contractor units in the EU, Denmark, New Zealand, the US dairy belt and China). Plus freeze-dried or liquid starter cultures and qPCR QA capacity. Where farms already have aerated or separated slurry handling, marginal capex is far lower, which is where the $28/t low case lives.
Nitrogen: aeration strips 2-12% of slurry NH3-N, which must be replaced with mineral N (debited above) and worsens local air quality.
phys.violations:
None. No claim falls below a thermodynamic floor. The conversion is exergonic (dG0 = -104.2 kJ/mol), there is no gas separation, and the computed enrichment energy (0.15-5.69 GJ/t CO2e, base 0.90) is a real positive cost well above zero, so no free-lunch claim is being made. The measured anchor (Hiis et al., Nature 630, 2024: ~6e9 cells/mL, 50-95% N2O cut by soil type, 5-20% of national anthropogenic N2O in a European model) is a published realized-outcome result, and the idea deliberately assumes a lower 30-60% field cut, which is the right direction.

Claims that need correction rather than rejection: (a) the stated $26-155/t rests on an ASSUMED $10-30/ha, which my bottom-up build reproduces only in the low case; base is $79/ha and $331/t. (b) The claimed 14-86 Mt CO2e/yr reach applies the adoption funnel to all fertilised soils instead of slurry-reachable land; vector-limited reach is 1.2-25.3 Mt, base 7.0. (c) "Energy penalty is negligible" is correct per tonne of slurry but the idea admitted it was unquantified; it is now 1.17-2.74 kWh/m3 and is a real line item in the cost. (d) The NH3-stripping debit from aerating raw slurry was entirely absent and can zero out the abatement at the low end.
phys.key_uncertainties:
1. THE CENTRAL ONE, correctly identified by the idea itself: whether raw slurry's labile carbon selects for N2O-respiring NosZ organisms rather than for N2O-PRODUCING denitrifiers under the Hiis-style O2- and N2O-limited enrichment. Digestate is already carbon-depleted by the digester, which is plausibly why the enrichment worked there; raw slurry is not. This is a binary technical risk, not a parameter, and the proposed sub-$20k bench test is the right and cheapest way to settle it.
2. NH3 stripping during aeration: my 2-12% range is assumed, not measured for this specific low-rate N2O-limited regime. If real losses are at the top of that range, net abatement is near zero and the idea fails on net-GHG grounds, not on biology. This should be measured in the same bench test (headspace NH3 alongside the gas kinetics) at near-zero marginal cost.
3. Realised field cut vs incubation cut. The 50-95% figure is dominated by soil incubations; field N2O is episodic (freeze-thaw, rainfall, hot moments) and field-scale cuts for nitrification inhibitors have historically come in below incubation values. My 30-60% is an assumption inherited from the idea.
4. Nitrification-derived N2O is untouched, so the denitrification-dominated share (0.55-0.75 assumed) sets the ceiling, and no cheap field diagnostic currently tells a farmer which regime their soil is in. This is the MRV hole that S10 (investors, insurers) would be asked to underwrite, and it is the reason to treat this as a regulated-practice or eco-scheme lever rather than a carbon-credit product.
5. Persistence beyond one season is MEASURED in Hiis et al. as the organism's distinguishing trait, but repeat-dose economics (does one application cover 2-3 years?) would swing cost per tonne by 2-3x and is unresolved.
6. Opportunity cost is unambiguous and the idea states it honestly: industrial N2O abatement at nitric and adipic acid plants runs $0.25-4/t, i.e. two to three orders of magnitude cheaper. Those plants should be abated first; this idea only matters because soil N2O has almost no other lever that does not cut farm output.
7. Stakeholder read, which is where this idea's real value sits: it is one of the few agricultural N2O levers that does not reduce nitrogen sales or yields, so S4 (fertiliser makers), S6/S9 (farmers) and S7 (EU, Denmark, New Zealand, all facing agricultural N2O targets) can all accept it, and S1/S2 get a genuine emissions cut with no offsetting logic. Its weakness is not politics but arithmetic: 7 Mt CO2e/yr base is a rounding error against 53 Gt total GHG, so it belongs in a portfolio, never as a headline climate solution.

stances.evidence: Mostly supportive in principle. It is a direct cut in emissions with no CCS, EOR or removal logic, so CAN's 2021 red lines 3-8 on CCS, EOR, DACCS and BECCS do not apply. The closest documented precedent is the Danish Society for Nature Conservation co-signing Denmark's June 2024 green tripartite agreement, which pairs a livestock CO2e tax with technology deductions and land conversion. This is from my own knowledge; the primary text was not retrievable this session. Two documented concerns split the group. (a) Groups working on food and factory farming (for example Food & Water Watch and Sierra Club campaigns against biogas from factory farms under California's LCFS; from my own knowledge, not re-fetched) attack technical fixes that make intensive livestock look green instead of reducing herds. This idea's vector is slurry and digestate from intensive livestock and biogas systems, so that critique applies. (b) If the money comes from carbon credits sold to other emitters, it hits CAN red line 4 ('will not support … offsets as an alternative'). Supported as a regulated or subsidised practice; opposed as an offset.
stances.red_line_hit: Offsets, if financed through voluntary or compliance credits. Greenwashing intensive livestock, from food and animal-welfare NGOs. Neither applies if it is funded as a farm subsidy or a deduction under an emissions tax.

stances.evidence: The mechanism is published in a top journal: Hiis et al., Nature 630 (2024). Digestate enriched with a NosZ-only bacterium cut N2O by 50-95% across soils. These were pot and incubation experiments plus a model scale-up; I found no multi-season field trials, and the paper page could not be fetched this session. IPCC AR6 WGIII lists soil N2O measures such as nitrification inhibitors as agricultural mitigation. N2O is also the largest remaining ozone-depleting emission (Ravishankara et al., Science 2009; from my own knowledge), a co-benefit scientists value. Scientists' support will depend on field replication, and on how the cut performs on soils where nitrification dominates, which the idea itself flags. An inventory caveat that scientists will raise: the IPCC 2019 Tier 1 direct emission factor is a fixed 1% (0.5% dry, 1.6% wet climates). A country using Tier 1 cannot report this cut at all without Tier 2/3 methods.
stances.red_line_hit: None. The only risk is overclaiming beyond the lab evidence.

stances.evidence: It does not touch oil and gas volumes, prices or assets, and it does not reduce nitrogen fertiliser demand, which is made from natural gas, so gas demand is unchanged. One small upside: Shell owns Nature Energy, Denmark's largest biogas producer (acquired 2023, about $2bn; from my own knowledge). Higher-value digestate would modestly help an S3-owned biogas line. No documented S3 position on soil N2O exists.
stances.red_line_hit: None

stances.evidence: Fertiliser producers (Yara, CF, Fertilizers Europe) gain. The idea cuts emissions per kg of N without reducing N sales, which matches the industry's 'nitrogen use efficiency' framing over any input cap (an inference from their public NUE framing, not a fetched position). Makers of nitrification and urease inhibitors face a direct competitor. These include BASF (DMPP/Vizura) and Koch Agronomic Services (Agrotain/Centuro), both S4 chemical companies, so S4 divides by product line. The expected response is commercial: licensing or acquiring the organism rather than lobbying against it. That is an inference; no documented position exists.
stances.red_line_hit: Lost market for inhibitor vendors only.

stances.evidence: No effect on power generation. Biogas and biomethane operators, some owned by utilities or majors, could sell an upgraded low-N2O digestate. That is a small revenue line, and the Hiis et al. digestate vector already serves it. This is an inference, not a documented position.
stances.red_line_hit: None

stances.evidence: No job losses, and it keeps the existing slurry-spreading and contractor work. Danish unions (3F, FH) co-signed the 2024 tripartite agreement, which favours technical deductions over cutting output (from my own knowledge, not re-fetched). For farmers, the closest S6-like group, the documented pattern is support for technical fixes over herd cuts. Examples: Dutch nitrogen protests against halving livestock and the rise of the BBB party (Wikipedia, fetched), and Federated Farmers' long opposition to agricultural emissions pricing in NZ (Wikipedia 'Climate change in New Zealand', fetched). The farmers' red line is cost without payment. My calculation: at EF 1% and a 30-60% cut, the abatement is worth only $3-7/ha at Denmark's effective 2030 livestock-tax rate (DKK 120/t, about $17/t) and $8-17/ha at the 2035 rate (DKK 300/t). That is below the assumed enrichment cost of $10-30/ha. It breaks even only near EU ETS-level prices (about $81/t, i.e. $16-31/ha). Unsubsidised adoption is unlikely.
stances.red_line_hit: Unfunded mandates and added cost or MRV burden on farmers.

stances.evidence: Governments need agricultural N2O cuts that do not reduce output. Examples: Denmark's livestock CO2e tax (agreed 2024, from 2030, with a 60% basic deduction; from my own knowledge), the EU's 2040 target debate, and NZ's 2024 coalition moving away from pricing toward technology (from my own knowledge). All parties to COP28 endorsed reducing non-CO2 gases. There are two documented frictions. (1) Regulation: the EU Fertilising Products Regulation 2019/1009 CMC 7 lists only Azotobacter, mycorrhizal fungi, Rhizobium and Azospirillum as microbial biostimulants (from my own knowledge; EUR-Lex fetch failed). A Cloacibacterium-type organism would need national authorisation or an amendment. (2) Inventory: Tier 1 emission factors cannot record the cut, so governments get no reported credit until Tier 2/3 methods exist. A precedent for regulatory risk: NZ fertiliser cooperatives voluntarily suspended DCD in 2013 after residues were found in milk, which threatened dairy exports (from my own knowledge).
stances.red_line_hit: None. Barriers are authorisation and inventory accounting, not opposition.

stances.evidence: Benefits are limited at first. Most tropical smallholders handle solid manure, not liquid slurry or digestate, and the idea's 'adapted to smallholder manure' is untested. Climate-justice groups such as ETC Group and GRAIN have documented opposition to corporate 'climate-smart agriculture', soil-carbon offsets and proprietary microbes (from my own knowledge, not re-fetched). CB-01 is a natural isolate, not an engineered organism, which reduces but does not remove the biopiracy and patent concern if a firm owns the strain. The Baum et al. 2024 survey showed Global South publics more supportive of all climate technologies; it did not test this one.
stances.red_line_hit: Possible: patents on the organism, or offset credits generated in the North to excuse emissions.

stances.evidence: Price effect is negligible: $10-30/ha is under 1% of typical arable input costs (an inference). There is a documented backlash risk from technical fixes in the food chain: the Nov 2024 Arla/Bovaer (3-NOP) trial in UK supermarkets triggered boycott calls and milk-dumping despite EFSA and FSA approval (Wikipedia 3-NOP page, fetched). This idea sits further from food (soil, not feed or milk), so that risk is lower but not zero; 'bacteria in slurry' framing could attract the same misinformation.
stances.red_line_hit: None on price. A minor food-additive-style misinformation risk.

stances.evidence: Buyers of agricultural N2O credits, such as those issued under Verra VM0042 for improved agricultural land management (from my own knowledge), face MRV risk. Soil N2O is highly variable across sites and seasons, and the idea admits it does nothing for N2O produced by nitrification. Without per-soil diagnostics, buyers would pay for unproven tonnes. Durable-removal buyers such as Frontier members do not buy avoided emissions, so that demand pool does not apply. Investors in inhibitor makers face a competitor. Insurers: no exposure.
stances.red_line_hit: MRV and integrity risk if credited.

stances.evidence: Slurry spreading already happens, so odour, traffic and ammonia are unchanged. The bacterium reduces N2O to N2 but does not cut nitrate leaching or ammonia, so local water and air-quality complaints (for example those behind the Dutch nitrogen crisis) are not addressed. Communities may raise questions about spreading bacterial cultures enriched on farms, and evidence on the strain's safety for humans and animals should be published first. The genus Cloacibacterium was first isolated from wastewater; I have not verified its pathogenicity status.
stances.red_line_hit: Minor biosafety perception risk; no documented opposition.

stake.coalition_notes: This idea has an unusually wide no-veto coalition. It hits none of the hard red lines that split S1 from S3, S4 and S5: no CCS, EOR, removal-as-substitute, SRM or per-tonne fee on industry. It reduces nobody's output or sales, apart from inhibitor vendors within S4. The only groups with real opposition potential are food and factory-farm NGOs within S1, if it is framed as making intensive livestock green, and S1/S8 groups, if it is monetised as offsets. The binding constraints are economic and institutional, not political. (1) My calculation (scratchpad climate/stake_nosz.py; EF 1%, 150 kg N/ha, 30-60% cut) puts its value at $3-7/ha at Denmark's effective 2030 livestock-tax rate and $8-17/ha in 2035, below the assumed enrichment cost of $10-30/ha. It breaks even only near EU ETS-level prices (about $81/t, $16-31/ha), so it needs a subsidy channel such as CAP eco-schemes or a tax deduction. (2) National inventories using the fixed IPCC Tier 1 emission factor cannot report the cut, so governments get no credit without Tier 2/3 methods. (3) The EU Fertilising Products Regulation's CMC 7 microbe list probably excludes this organism (from my own knowledge, not verified). Best route: present it as a deduction under an emissions tax or a subsidised farm practice, not a credit; publish strain-safety data before scaling; and run field MRV on the soils where denitrification dominates. Limits of this analysis: the web-search budget was exhausted, and the Danish tripartite terms, NZ DCD 2013, ETC/GRAIN and EU FPR CMC 7 positions come from my own knowledge, not fetched sources. Fetched this session: the Bovaer backlash and Dutch protests (Wikipedia). The Nature paper page was paywalled.

critic.fatal_flaw: No fatal flaw. The conversion is exergonic, there is no separation step, no stakeholder red line is hit, and the mechanism is published with a measured anchor. Two things are often mistaken for fatal and are not: (a) scale — 7 Mt CO2e/yr base is a portfolio line, not a climate solution, but that is a sizing fact, not a defect; (b) the N2O supply question I checked and withdrew — because N2O respiration yields only 9.2 g dry weight per mol electrons, growing a 6e9 cells/mL inoculum BY N2O respiration would route ~9.5 kg N2O/m3 (111 t CO2e/ha, 383x the abatement, 0.26% leak budget, $700-4,200/t in gas alone) through the vessel. That would be fatal, but the paper's abstract states CB-01 "had grown aerobically to about 6 × 10^9 cells per millilitre", so production uses O2 and the issue does not arise. N2O is used only in the one-off lab selection step. The one result that WOULD be fatal is in the bench test: if CB-01 cannot exceed ~1e9 cells/mL in non-sterile slurry without heat treatment, the idea reduces to "pay to pasteurise slurry" at 7-36 GJ/t CO2e (below), i.e. DAC-class energy for 0.007 Gt of reach. Kill it on that result, not before.
critic.top_fixable_flaw: All three reports model the process as "grow CB-01 in the slurry" and inherit Hiis et al.'s effect sizes, but every reported result in that paper grew CB-01 in a STERILISED vector and applied it at a rate no slurry programme can legally match. The Methods state the digestate was autoclaved at 121 °C for 20 min, air-sparged 48 h to oxidise Fe2+, then autoclaved again; re-fertilisations used autoclaved digestate; the dead-cell control was the same digestate at 70 °C for 2 h. So the idea's self-declared central uncertainty is mis-framed: the question is not whether raw slurry's labile carbon "selects for" N2O respirers (production is aerobic growth of an already-isolated strain, not a selection), but whether a pure-culture-grown strain can reach target density against a live resident community — a case Hiis never ran, not even in digestate. Three quantified consequences nobody costed. (1) If heat treatment proves necessary, pasteurising raw slurry from 10 to 70 °C costs 240 MJ/m3 = 35.6 GJ/t CO2e with no heat recovery, 7.1 GJ/t at 80% recovery, versus the TEA's 0.90 GJ/t base and real DAC at 5-10 GJ/t — it inverts "energy penalty is negligible" into the binding constraint. (2) Dose: the demonstrated loading was 6.6e13 cells/m2, delivered as 480 mL per 0.043 m2 bucket = 11.2 L/m2 = 112 m3/ha carrying 191 kg NH4-N/ha, already above the EU Nitrates Directive 170 kg manure-N/ha ceiling. Raw slurry at 3.0-5.0 kg N/m3 permits only 34-57 m3/ha under that cap, so matching the demonstrated cells/m2 requires 1.2-2.0e10 cells/mL — 2.0 to 3.3x the density achieved in sterile digestate. Every report quotes cells/mL; the acting quantity is cells/m2, and it is short. (3) Field evidence is weaker than all three reports state: 50-95% comes from 0.043 m2 field buckets and incubations; the single true field-plot test used 0.5 m2 plots with digestate harrowed into the top 10 cm, and over days 10-290 "the effect of CB-01 was not statistically significant", with a wide CI. The 30-60% realised annual field cut is therefore an assumption with no field support, and its interval should include ~0 on cold, dry or nitrification-dominated ground. Separately, two numbers need correcting in opposite directions: the TEA assumed 0.3 pg dry mass per cell where the paper measures 108 fg, and the paper's measured aerobic yield (4e14 cells/mol O2) gives 0.48 kg O2/m3, not 1.94 — so aeration is 0.44-1.28 kWh/m3 and the NH3-stripping debit is ~4x smaller than the TEA's worst case (it no longer zeroes the abatement on its own). And the Europe headline is the wrong one: the authors' own liquid-manure scenario (60% cut, all European liquid manure, GAINS 2030) gives -2.7% of European anthropogenic N2O and -4.0% for EU27. The "5-20%" that the idea and the reports quote is a broader, per-country range, not the slurry case this idea targets.
critic.suggested_patch: Stop growing the organism in the bulk slurry; decouple the cells from the nitrogen carrier. Produce a concentrated, QA'd inoculum by aerobic growth in a small heat-treated side-stream (separated slurry liquid fraction or digestate, 1-5% of the load) at contractor depots or a central supplier, then dose it into the tanker at loading, specified as cells per m2 of field, not cells per mL of slurry. This single change fixes four problems at once, with the numbers: heat-treating 2% of the volume at 50% recovery costs 0.36 GJ/t CO2e instead of 17.8, so the sterility requirement stops being a kill criterion; cell loading becomes independent of the 170 kg N/ha cap, so the demonstrated 6.6e13 cells/m2 is reachable at 34-57 m3/ha; only the covered side-stream is aerated, cutting the NH3 debit ~50x; and the vessel is sized to cells rather than slurry volume, which removes a duty-cycle error the TEA missed — annual throughput compressed into a ~3-week spreading campaign with multi-day batches implies 760-2,300 m3 of working volume, not the ~50-100 m3 implied by $30-70k of capex. The cost case then shifts from "free substrate" to growth medium plus shelf-life, which must be priced explicitly rather than assumed at $10-30/ha. Precedent that dosing works without in-situ growth: Gao/Senoo's inoculated solid organic-fertiliser carriers cut field N2O 23-37% in 2014 Japanese trials. Then add five measurements inside the existing sub-$20k bench test, all cheap: (i) the actually untested step — growth of CB-01 in non-sterile raw slurry versus heat-treated raw slurry versus a sterile-digestate control, run side by side, tracking CB-01's share of the community by qPCR and 16S, with a pass bar of 1e10 cells/mL and no pasteurisation; (ii) headspace NH3 during aeration, which the TEA flagged as absent; (iii) a four-log dose-response expressed in cells/m2, since every cost line scales linearly with cells and the minimum effective loading is unknown; (iv) 1-6 month viability and N2O-reducing activity of the stored concentrate, which the central-production route depends on entirely; (v) surface-applied versus incorporated microcosms, because the demonstrated protocol harrowed the vector into the top 10 cm while trailing-hose broadcast leaves it on the surface. Finally, re-anchor the reports: quote -2.7% of European anthropogenic N2O (-4.0% EU27) at 100% liquid-manure adoption and a 60% cut as the authors' own slurry-specific figure, drop "5-20%" for this case, label 50-95% as bucket and incubation values, and treat freedom-to-operate as live — the paper itself says ongoing work extends the technology to all organic wastes used to fertilise soils, so the originators have publicly staked this exact extension. License or co-author with NMBU rather than race them.

patched_idea.title: N2O-respiring bacteria dosed into slurry tankers from a concentrated side-stream inoculum
patched_idea.one_line: Keep the slurry tanker as the delivery channel for NosZ-carrying N2O-reducing bacteria, but decouple the cells from the nitrogen they ride on: grow a concentrated, QA'd inoculum in a small heat-treated side-stream and meter it into the tanker at loading, with the dose specified in cells per m2 of field rather than cells per mL of slurry.
patched_idea.conventional_core: Spreading manure slurry and digestate: a routine, regulated practice on livestock and biogas farms, and the conventional fertiliser channel for N2O management. Metering a concentrated biological product into a tank at loading is equally conventional - it is how silage inoculants and seed inoculants are already handled by the same contractors.
patched_idea.graft: NosZ, nitrous oxide reductase, the only known biological sink for N2O, carried by N2O-respiring bacteria (e.g. Cloacibacterium sp. CB-01) that respire N2O to N2 without producing it.
patched_idea.mechanism: Unchanged mechanism of action: wet soils leak N2O from denitrification when NosZ activity is weak, and adding an organism that reduces N2O to N2 without generating it shifts the end product toward N2; Hiis et al. showed the effect persists because the bacterium survives in soil. The delivery engineering is what the patch changes, and it also corrects a mis-framing that the earlier version inherited. Every reported result in Hiis et al. grew CB-01 in a STERILISED vector (digestate autoclaved 121 C/20 min, air-sparged 48 h, autoclaved again; re-fertilisations autoclaved; the dead-cell control heat-treated at 70 C/2 h), and the organism grew aerobically - so production is aerobic propagation of an already-isolated strain, not an in-situ selection by slurry's labile carbon. The open question is therefore not whether slurry carbon selects for respirers over producers, but whether a pure-culture-grown strain can reach and hold target density against a live resident community, a case the paper never ran even in digestate. Accordingly: produce the inoculum by aerobic growth in a small heat-treated side-stream (separated slurry liquid fraction or digestate) at contractor depots or a central supplier, concentrate it, and dose it into the tanker at loading. Growing the cells outside the bulk slurry makes the sterility requirement affordable, makes the cell loading independent of the nitrogen application cap, confines aeration (and its NH3 stripping) to a covered side-stream, and sizes the vessel to cells rather than to slurry volume.
patched_idea.target: Direct soil N2O from denitrification on wet, fine-textured soils where slurry is already spread, in regions with an N2O policy lever (EU, Denmark, New Zealand). Explicitly NOT nitrifier-derived N2O, and not cold or dry ground. Delivery mode matters and is untested: the demonstrated protocol harrowed the vector into the top 10 cm, whereas trailing-hose broadcast leaves it on the surface.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
(1) MEASURED ANCHOR, correctly labelled. Hiis et al., Nature 630 (2024): digestate carrying ~6e9 cells/mL cut N2O 50-95% - but those are 0.043 m2 field-bucket and lab-incubation values. The single true field-plot test (0.5 m2 plots, vector harrowed into the top 10 cm) found no statistically significant CB-01 effect over days 10-290, with a wide CI. The slurry-specific scaled figure is the authors' own liquid-manure scenario: -2.7% of European anthropogenic N2O, -4.0% for EU27, at 100% adoption across European liquid manure with a 60% cut (GAINS 2030). The '5-20%' quoted previously is a broader per-country range and is dropped for this case.
(2) DOSE IS THE BINDING NUMBER (my calculation). 480 mL of 6e9 cells/mL on 0.043 m2 = 6.7e13 cells/m2 = 6.6e17 cells/ha = 71 kg dry cell mass/ha at the paper's measured 108 fg/cell (not the 0.3 pg the earlier TEA assumed). Under the EU Nitrates Directive 170 kg manure-N/ha ceiling, slurry at 3-5 kg N/m3 permits only 34-57 m3/ha, so in-slurry growth at 6e9 cells/mL delivers just 31-52% of the demonstrated loading; matching it in slurry would need 1.2-1.9e10 cells/mL, i.e. 1.9-3.2x the titre achieved in sterile digestate.
(3) THE SIDE-STREAM MUST BE SIZED FROM THE DOSE, NOT FIXED AT 1-5%. A 1-5% side-stream of a 42.5 m3/ha load (0.42-2.12 m3/ha) carries the demonstrated loading only at 3.1e11-1.6e12 cells/mL - 50-260x the paper's titre, beyond liquid-culture density. Feasible combinations: ~10% of the load at 1.6e11 cells/mL, or 1-5% only if the minimum effective dose proves 3-20x below the demonstrated one. This makes the dose-response the gating measurement for the whole idea, not an optional extra.
(4) ENERGY IS DOSE-DETERMINED, NOT NEGLIGIBLE. Reference abatement 0.257 t CO2e/ha (150 kg N/ha, EF 1%, 40% cut, GWP100 N2O = 273 from the verifier) on 42.5 m3/ha. Heat-treating the WHOLE load 10->70 C costs 240 MJ/m3 = 39.6 GJ/t CO2e with no heat recovery, 19.8 at 50%, 7.9 at 80% - DAC-class, which is why bulk heat treatment is a kill criterion. A 2-5% side-stream costs 0.16-1.98 GJ/t depending on recovery, which is affordable. Aeration, using the paper's measured yield of 4e14 cells/mol O2: 0.48 kg O2/m3 at 6e9 cells/mL (0.24-0.96 kWh/m3), about 4x below the earlier TEA's 1.94 kg O2/m3, so the NH3-stripping debit no longer zeroes the abatement on its own; at 1e11 cells/mL it rises to 8 kg O2/m3 (4-16 kWh/m3). Concentration is the new energy risk: at the full demonstrated dose, 110 m3 of 6e9 cells/mL broth per hectare through a disc-stack centrifuge at 1-4 kWh/m3 costs 1.5-6.2 GJ/t CO2e - again DAC-class - falling to 0.31 GJ/t at one tenth the dose and 0.03 GJ/t at one hundredth.
(5) VESSEL DUTY CYCLE. A contractor covering 2,000 ha in a 3-week campaign with 48 h batches needs 13,200 m3 of broth per season at 1e11 cells/mL = ~1,260 m3 working volume at the full dose; at one hundredth of the dose, 12.6 m3. Capex cannot honestly be quoted before the dose-response is measured, which retires the earlier $30-70k figure.
(6) COST, now built up rather than assumed. $10-150/ha covering growth medium, side-stream heat treatment, aeration, concentration, cold chain, shelf-life and dosing hardware gives $16-1,554/t CO2e across EF 0.5-1.6% and realised cuts of 30-60%; the central band ($30-60/ha, EF 1%, 40% cut) is $117-233/t. The earlier $26-155/t rested on a $10-30/ha free-substrate case that the decoupled route does not support. This sits at or above 3-NOP ($44-117/t) and far above industrial N2O abatement ($0.25-4/t), so nitric and adipic acid plants stay first in the portfolio.
(7) REACH, slurry-specific. Global direct soil N2O is 0.48-0.72 Gt CO2e/yr (verifier: ~140 Mt N/yr, EF 0.8-1.2%). Slurry-spread share 25-35% x adoption 20-40% x realised cut 30-50% = 7-50 Mt CO2e/yr. The realised-cut interval should be read as including ~0 on cold, dry or nitrification-dominated ground, because no statistically significant field-plot effect exists yet. This is a portfolio line, not a climate solution.
patched_idea.who_gains: Farmers keep their spreading routine unchanged and gain a sellable climate attribute, now without carrying a fermentation asset. Slurry contractors and inoculant manufacturers gain a new metered product line and capture the manufacturing margin. S4 fertiliser makers and biogas operators gain a low-N2O premium product without selling less nitrogen. S7 (EU, Denmark, New Zealand) gain an agricultural N2O lever that does not cut output. S1 and S2 support it as a pure emissions cut with no offsetting logic. S8 gains only if a dose low enough to ship as a shelf-stable concentrate is found, since smallholder manure systems cannot host side-stream fermentation.
patched_idea.who_loses: Nitrification-inhibitor vendors (DMPP, DCD) face a competitor.
