Farmers now buy a product rather than grow it, so more of the value accrues to the supplier and less to the farm - weakening the original 'free substrate' selling point. Only denitrification N2O is addressed; nitrifier-derived N2O is untouched. MRV payers (S10) risk paying for cuts that have never been demonstrated at field-plot significance, particularly on nitrification-dominated soils. S11 near depots take an odour and bioaerosol exposure from aerated side-streams, small but non-zero.
patched_idea.closest_known_work: Hiis, Vick, Molstad, Rosdal, Jonassen, Winiwarter and Bakken, 'Unlocking bacterial potential to reduce farmland N2O emissions', Nature 630 (2024), doi 10.1038/s41586-024-07464-3 - same mechanism and organism, sterilised digestate as vector, aerobic production. Gao and Senoo's inoculated solid organic-fertiliser carriers cut field N2O 23-37% in 2014 Japanese trials, the main precedent that dosing a grown inoculum works without in-situ growth in the carrier. Li et al. 2026 (Life 16:635): a Bacillus subtilis biofertiliser cut cumulative N2O 39% in a field trial on Chinese saline-alkali soil, by a different mechanism (reduced amoA, i.e. less nitrification). Freedom to operate is live: the paper states that ongoing work extends the technology to organic wastes used to fertilise soils, so the originators have publicly staked this exact extension - license or co-author with NMBU rather than race them.
patched_idea.why_different: Honestly incremental, and the increment has moved. It is no longer 'use slurry instead of digestate as the growth vector' - that framing assumed an in-situ selection the paper never performed. It is: separate the cell factory from the nitrogen carrier, so that the cell loading is set by a measured cells/m2 specification instead of being capped by the 170 kg manure-N/ha limit, and so that the sterility the published results depended on costs 0.16-1.98 GJ/t rather than 7.9-39.6. The live scientific question is the minimum effective cells/m2 and whether a pure-culture-grown strain holds density against a live resident community.
patched_idea.cheapest_falsifying_test: A 4-8 week bench programme at a soil-microbiology lab, $25-45k, ordered so that the cheapest kill comes first. (a) Dose-response, four logs, reported in cells per m2 on 2-3 contrasting soils with automated gas kinetics. This is the gate: every energy and cost line above scales with cells, and the calculations show the full demonstrated loading (71 kg dry cells/ha) is infeasible to manufacture and concentrate at acceptable energy. Falsified for practical purposes if a cut above 20% requires more than roughly one tenth of the demonstrated loading. (b) Density against a live community: growth of the strain in non-sterile raw slurry versus heat-treated raw slurry versus a sterile-digestate control, run side by side, tracking the strain's share of the community by qPCR and 16S. If no route reaches target density without bulk pasteurisation, the idea reduces to paying to pasteurise slurry at 7.9-39.6 GJ/t CO2e and should be killed. (c) Shelf life: 1-6 month viability and N2O-reducing activity of the stored concentrate, which the central-production route depends on entirely. (d) Headspace NH3 during aeration of the side-stream, previously unquantified. (e) Surface-applied versus incorporated soil microcosms, since the demonstrated protocol incorporated the vector and trailing-hose broadcast does not. Only after (a) and (b) pass is a replicated multi-site field trial with per-plot flux chambers justified, because the published field-plot evidence is not significant.

fix.change_summary: I applied the critic's patch without touching the mechanism (NosZ-mediated reduction of N2O to N2 by introduced N2O-respiring bacteria) or the graft, changing only the delivery engineering and the numbers. The inoculum is now grown aerobically in a small heat-treated side-stream and metered into the tanker at loading, with the dose specified in cells per m2 of field; the mechanism text also corrects the mis-framing the critic identified, since every published result used a sterilised vector and aerobic growth of an already-isolated strain, so the real uncertainty is holding density against a live resident community rather than whether slurry carbon selects for respirers. Executed calculation confirmed most of the patch but refuted one of its numbers: a 1-5% side-stream can carry the demonstrated loading (6.7e13 cells/m2 = 6.6e17 cells/ha = 71 kg dry cell mass/ha at the paper's 108 fg/cell) only at 3.1e11-1.6e12 cells/mL, which is 50-260x the titre the paper reports, so the side-stream fraction must be sized from a measured minimum effective dose rather than fixed, and the four-log dose-response becomes the gating test instead of a supporting one. The energy verdict is therefore dose-determined, not negligible: side-stream heat treatment costs 0.16-1.98 GJ/t CO2e against 7.9-39.6 for the whole load, aeration is ~4x cheaper than the old TEA assumed (0.48 kg O2/m3 at the paper's measured 4e14 cells/mol O2), but concentrating the full demonstrated dose by centrifuge costs 1.5-6.2 GJ/t CO2e, which is DAC-class and only falls to 0.03-0.31 GJ/t if the effective dose is 10-100x lower. I also re-anchored the claims as the critic asked - the authors' own slurry-specific -2.7% of European anthropogenic N2O (-4.0% EU27) replaces the broader "5-20%", the 50-95% figures are labelled as bucket and incubation values, the single true field-plot test is reported as not statistically significant so the realised-cut interval now includes ~0, cost is rebuilt explicitly at $117-233/t in the central band rather than $26-155/t on a free-substrate assumption, the capex figure is retired pending the dose-response (a 2,000 ha contractor needs ~1,260 m3 of working volume at full dose versus 12.6 m3 at one hundredth), and freedom to operate is flagged as live with licensing or co-authorship with NMBU recommended.

idea.title: Swap carbonate aglime for silicate fines in tropical estates, and apportion alkalinity with river-geochemistry mixing models
idea.one_line: Replace part of the carbonate lime and dolomite on Brazilian cane and soy and Southeast Asian palm estates with quarry silicate fines. Credit the avoided carbonate CO2 at once, and credit silicate removal only when a carbonate-versus-silicate source-apportionment model shows it above detection. This fixes the measured failure in the Sabah palm trial.
idea.conventional_core: Agricultural liming of acidic tropical soils (TRL 9; Brazil uses tens of Mt of lime a year, about 35-50 Mt, recalled). Ground magnesium limestone and dolomite on palm estates. Brazil's remineralizer (rochagem) law recognises silicate rock powders as inputs (recalled).
idea.graft: End-member mixing and source apportionment from global river weathering budgets (Gaillardet et al. 1999 style), imported into field ERW MRV. It uses Ca/Na, Mg/Na and Sr/Ca ratios, 87Sr/86Sr, δ13C-DIC and nitrate to split alkalinity between carbonate fertilizer and silicate rock, and between carbonic-acid and nitric-acid weathering.
idea.mechanism: In heavily N-fertilised tropical soils, nitrification makes nitric acid. Carbonate lime dissolved by nitric acid releases CO2 (IPCC Tier 1 counts all of it as emitted). Silicate weathered by nitric acid releases none, and silicate weathered by carbonic acid removes CO2. Swapping part of the lime for silicate fines therefore avoids an emission and may add removal. The measurement problem is that carbonate weathering swamps the silicate signal. Larkin et al. (2022) applied andesite at 50 t/ha/yr for 3 years on a Sabah oil-palm estate and measured catchment CDR of 3.8±0.8 t CO2/ha (treated) against 3.7±0.6 (untreated). The signal was driven mainly by the estate's carbonate fertilizer. Mixing models separate the two sources, so the credit can be split into avoided carbonate CO2, read from purchase records and confirmed by tracer chemistry, and measured silicate CDR.
idea.target: Corporate cane, soy and palm estates, each a single counterparty with drain or catchment outlets, located within about 50 km of basalt or andesite quarries producing fines. Examples: Paraná and São Paulo basalt, and Sabah/Sumatra palm estates. Partners: estate agronomy teams, quarries, an isotope lab.
idea.quantitative_claims:
IPCC 2006 Tier 1: 0.44 t CO2/t limestone and 0.48 t/t dolomite. A West and McBride-type net estimate (recalled) is about 0.22 t/t, 49% of Tier 1. Brazil at 35-50 Mt lime/yr: 15-22 Mt CO2/yr at Tier 1, 8-11 Mt on the net estimate. A 30% swap is about 2.5-7 Mt/yr avoided.

Computed substitution logistics: at 10-30% CaCO3-equivalence, 3-10 t of rock replaces 1 t of lime. Trucking at 30-100 km costs 10-100 kg CO2 per t lime replaced, against 216-440 kg avoided. Using existing quarry fines avoids 18-26 kWh/t of Bond grinding (P80 100-50 µm, Wi 20).

Silicate CDR is credited only if measured. The Illinois field rate of about 0.05 t CO2/t rock is the optimistic reference; in tropical andesite (Larkin 2022) the signal was not detectable. Process energy is near zero beyond haulage.
idea.who_gains: S4 quarries and aggregates producers: fines become a product. S8/S9: estates and farmers get a liming, K, Mg and Si input that may be cheaper per hectare near quarries. S7 (Brazil): less reliance on imported potash (partial K substitution) and lower reported agricultural emissions. S2: a measurement method that resolves the main confound in tropical ERW. S1: credits are tied to measured signals rather than models.
idea.who_loses: Agricultural limestone and dolomite suppliers lose part of their market. Estates face agronomic risk if silicate neutralizes acidity too slowly in Al-toxic Cerrado or Ultisol soils, so the swap must stay partial (25-50%). S11: dust and trace metals if mafic fines are poorly characterised.
idea.closest_known_work: Larkin et al. 2022 (Frontiers in Climate) ran the catchment method on a palm estate but did not swap out the carbonate, and that is why the method failed. The map's open problem proposes Midwest aglime substitution 'credited on the difference'. Brazilian ERW firms (InPlanet, Terradot; recalled) apply remineralizers on top of liming. Hubbard Brook's 1999 wollastonite catchment addition is the measurement precedent. What is different: the swap plus a tracer-based apportionment is aimed at the specific failure Larkin measured. The nitric-acid question also decides whether the avoided-lime credit is real.
idea.why_different: It turns the dominant noise source in tropical ERW, carbonate fertiliser, into a lever: remove it, and measure what remains.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test: A 12-16 week soil-column experiment (about $10-20k) on a urea-fertilised tropical Oxisol or Ultisol. Treatments: control, GML, basalt fines, GML+basalt, and a blind known-proportion spike. Measure leachate cations, alkalinity, Sr isotopes, δ13C-DIC, nitrate, headspace CO2 flux and pH. It is falsified if (a) the mixing model misassigns the known silicate fraction by more than ±50%, or (b) GML under urea shows no net CO2 efflux (the avoided-emission claim then shrinks toward zero), or (c) basalt at swap rates raises pH by less than 0.2 units in 16 weeks, so farmers would need lime anyway. Larkin's archived stream chemistry, if obtainable, gives a zero-cost first pass.
idea.family: Swap carbonate aglime for silicate fines with mixing-model source apportionment

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: Larkin et al. 2022, 'Quantification of CO2 removal in a large-scale enhanced weathering field trial on an oil palm plantation in Sabah, Malaysia' (Frontiers in Climate)
closest.overlap: Very high, and it contradicts the idea's framing. I fetched the paper. It already applied the proposed graft in the exact target setting: a two-end-member cation-ratio mixing model (Na, Ca and Mg fractions of total cations) plus 87Sr/86Sr to split silicate from carbonate weathering. It found over 90% of stream cations were carbonate-derived in most catchments, and it identified the ground Mg-limestone fertiliser applied in 2018-19 as the driver. Treated catchments gave 3.8±0.8 t CO2/ha and untreated 3.7±0.6; one plot showed about 1 t/ha extra. Apportionment was done in that trial, not missing from it. What Larkin did not do was remove or reduce the carbonate.

closest.title: Eion Carbon: olivine sold as a replacement for agricultural lime (US row crops)
closest.overlap: Commercial precedent for the swap itself. The company says it replaces the ag lime farmers normally apply with olivine to manage pH and remove CO2. Its MRV uses before-and-after soil sampling, not isotope or cation tracers, and the site does not mention crediting avoided lime CO2. It works in temperate US cropland, not tropical estates.

closest.title: Isometric, Enhanced Weathering in Agriculture protocol v1.2
closest.overlap: The protocol behind current ERW credits (used by Brazilian and US projects). It already deducts 'non-carbonic acid neutralization', such as nitric acid from nitrification of ammonium fertiliser, as a CO2e loss. Per the fetched text, it does not credit displaced agricultural lime and does not specify isotope or cation source apportionment. That leaves room for the 'avoided carbonate CO2' half of the proposed split credit, but a removal registry would likely refuse to count an avoided emission as removal.

closest.title: Kantola et al. 2017 (Biology Letters); Beerling et al. 2018 'Farming with crops and rocks' (Nature Plants) [recalled; the page was behind a CAPTCHA and not verified]
closest.overlap: From memory, these early ERW-cropland papers propose crushed basalt as a partial substitute for agricultural lime, noting the avoided liming CO2 alongside silicate CDR. Concept-level precedent for the swap plus avoided-emission argument.

closest.title: West & McBride 2005 (Agric. Ecosyst. Environ.); Hamilton et al. 2007 (Global Biogeochemical Cycles) [recalled]
closest.overlap: Source of the net lime emission factor of about 0.059 t C per t CaCO3, about 0.22 t CO2/t, matching the idea's 49%-of-Tier-1 figure. Also the origin of the point that lime dissolved by nitric acid (from N fertiliser) releases CO2 while carbonic-acid dissolution is a sink. This is the nitric-acid mechanism the idea relies on.

closest.title: Dietzen & Rosing 2023, 'Quantification of CO2 uptake by enhanced weathering of silicate minerals applied to acidic soils' (Int. J. Greenhouse Gas Control) [recalled; 403 on fetch]
closest.overlap: From memory, this analyses silicate weathering by strong (nitric) acid in acidic agricultural soils and compares basalt with lime. It argues that much of the benefit in acidic soils comes from avoided lime emissions rather than direct removal. That directly anticipates the idea's two-part logic.

closest.title: InPlanet and Terradot: Brazilian ERW with basalt remineraliser on sugarcane and other crops; Brazil remineraliser law 12.890/2013 and Embrapa rochagem agronomy
closest.overlap: Basalt fines are already deployed commercially on Brazilian cane under the remineraliser framework (Terradot runs a Brazil 'Sentinel Site'). Neither company's site mentions displacing lime, crediting avoided lime CO2, or isotope-tracer MRV. Rock is applied on top of liming, as the idea itself notes.

closest.title: Gaillardet et al. 1999 river mixing models; Hubbard Brook 1999 wollastonite catchment addition
closest.overlap: The general source-apportionment and catchment-addition methods being imported. Both are well established, and Larkin 2022 already carried the method into field ERW.

art.what_is_new: Every component exists. The swap is sold commercially by Eion in the US and was proposed in early ERW papers. The carbonate-versus-silicate apportionment using 87Sr/86Sr and cation ratios was already applied in the very Sabah palm trial the idea cites, where it is the method that showed the signal was over 90% carbonate. The nitric-acid accounting for lime is established (West & McBride 2005, Hamilton 2007) and is a deduction in the Isometric protocol. The idea's premise needs correcting: Larkin's method did not fail for lack of apportionment. Apportionment worked and showed the carbonate fertiliser swamped the silicate signal. What appears new: (1) a deliberate partial swap of GML or dolomite for nearby quarry silicate fines on tropical cane, soy and palm estates, aimed specifically at removing Larkin's confound so tracer apportionment can detect silicate CDR. (2) A split credit: avoided carbonate CO2, taken from purchase records and confirmed by tracers, kept separate from measured silicate removal. Isometric v1.2 does not credit lime displacement, though removal registries may refuse an avoided-emission component as removal. (3) The cheap soil-column falsification test, with a blind known-proportion spike to check mixing-model accuracy. Treat this as engineering of known parts, worth doing for MRV, not a new mechanism. Caveat: WebSearch was exhausted (200/200) during this run. I verified Larkin 2022, Isometric v1.2, Eion, InPlanet and Terradot by direct fetch. Kantola 2017, Beerling 2018, Dietzen & Rosing 2023, West & McBride 2005 and Hamilton 2007 are cited from memory. I could not check for 2024-26 papers on lime-displacement crediting or Sr-isotope ERW MRV in Brazil, so such work may exist.

phys.assumptions:
The script labels each input as [P] primary source checked this session, [R] recalled, or [A] assumption.

**Physics floor.** There is no gas separation step. The avoided emission has a floor of 0 GJ/t. Silicate weathering is spontaneous, so its CDR also has a floor of 0 beyond rock handling. The air-capture floor is printed only for comparison: 0.47 GJ/t.

**Emission factors.** Tier 1 values recomputed from stoichiometry: limestone 0.440 and dolomite 0.477 t CO2/t, which confirms the claims of 0.44 and 0.48. The model uses a 50/50 limestone/dolomite blend [A].

The net lime emission depends on f_s, the share of lime dissolved by strong (nitric) acid. Carbonic-acid dissolution is credited as a sink of one CO2 per carbonate, giving E = EF_Tier1 x (2 f_s - 1). Setting f_s = 0.75 reproduces the West & McBride-type ~49% of Tier 1 [R]. Computed values:

| f_s | Net emission (t CO2/t lime) |
|---|---|
| 0.5 | +0.000 |
| 0.6 | +0.092 |
| 0.75 | +0.229 |
| 0.9 | +0.367 |
| 1.0 | +0.459 |

phys.resource_needs:
At the base case:
- **Lime replaced:** 4.7 Mt/yr.
- **Rock fines:** 24 Mt/yr, against Brazilian aggregates output of roughly 500-700 Mt/yr [R], so supply is not binding.
- **Process energy:** 4.2 PJ/yr, which is 6.7e-06 of world primary energy. It is diesel haulage and spreading, plus partial regrinding.
- **Land:** zero new, since it uses existing estates.
- **Water:** none beyond rainfall.
- **MRV:** lysimeters or drain sampling, Sr-isotope and δ13C-DIC analyses, and an isotope lab partnership, at $50-200k per estate-year [A].
- **Agronomy:** the swap moves 3-10 t of rock per t of lime. That roughly triples spreading passes and tonnage.
phys.violations:
There are no thermodynamic violations: no claimed energy is below a floor, and the floor is 0. The stoichiometric claims are confirmed:
- Tier 1 factors: 0.440 and 0.477.
- Brazil emissions: 16-23 Mt at Tier 1 and 8-11 Mt net.
- Bond grinding: 18-26 kWh/t.

Haulage of 10-100 kg CO2 per t of lime replaced is consistent: the script gives 6-100 kg.

Claims that are overstated or need heroic assumptions:

1. **The 2.5-7 Mt/yr headline needs every Brazilian estate to be within haul range of silicate fines.** Restricted to estates within ~50 km of a quarry, the base case is ~1 Mt/yr for Brazil plus 0.1 Mt for SE Asia, so 0.0011 Gt.

2. **"Process energy near zero beyond haulage" assumes quarry fines are already agronomic powder.** Typical quarry fines are mm-scale, with P80 ~1-2 mm [R]. Regrinding from 1.5 mm to 100 um costs 14.8 kWh/t of rock, which at Malaysian grid intensity cancels the avoided credit.

3. **The avoided-emission credit is not a robust "credit at once".** It is positive only if the strong-acid share of lime dissolution exceeds ~0.53 (base logistics). At f_s 0.60 the cost is $717/t. In the high case the net is -113 kg CO2 per t of lime replaced.

4. **Silicate CDR is implausible to detect at swap rates.** Swapping 30% of 1.5 t lime/ha puts 1.5-4.5 t rock/ha/yr on the field, giving 0.03-0.23 t CO2/ha/yr even at Illinois-like 0.02-0.05 t/t. The primary check of Larkin 2022 shows the scale of the problem: 50 t/ha/yr for 3 years gave a treated-versus-control difference of 0.1 t/ha, with combined 1-sigma uncertainty of about 1.0 t/ha. Apportionment would have to cut uncertainty more than 10x. Treat the removal credit as roughly zero for planning.
phys.key_uncertainties:
1. **Strong-acid share (f_s) is the dominant uncertainty.** It sets the sign and size of the avoided credit. The break-even is 0.53, and the cost swings from $123/t at f_s 0.95 to $717/t at 0.60. It is unmeasured in Brazilian or Malaysian estates. A further caveat is that the carbonic-acid sink treatment is a choice: if ocean re-precipitation is counted, the counterfactual lime "sink" shrinks and the avoided credit rises toward Tier 1. The proposed soil-column test (b) targets exactly this and is the right first experiment.

2. **Agronomic equivalence.** Basalt or andesite CCE of 0.1-0.3 [A/R], and the slow neutralization in Al-toxic Oxisols, decide whether farmers actually drop lime. If pH lags, there is also a possible N2O penalty from more acidic soils, which the script did not model.

3. **Rock particle size and price.** Whether the fines need regrinding, and whether they are free or cost $15/t, swing the base cost from $57 to $234/t.

4. **Tracer power is likely weaker than assumed [R, recalled, not verified this session].**
   - For C4 sugarcane, soil-respired CO2 has δ13C near -12‰, closer to carbonate's ~0‰, which weakens δ13C-DIC discrimination. It works better for C3 soy and palm.
   - Paraná flood basalts reportedly have variable, sometimes radiogenic 87Sr/86Sr (~0.705-0.71+), which may overlap marine and Neoproterozoic carbonate (~0.707-0.709). Highly weathered Oxisols add a basement Sr background.

5. **Brazil lime tonnage and SE Asian GML use are recalled or assumed.** The national lime association's figures could not be fetched, and the session's web-search budget was exhausted, so only Larkin 2022 was checked against a primary source. Larkin 2022 [P] confirms 3.8±0.8 vs 3.7±0.6 t CO2/ha, with the signal driven primarily by carbonate fertilizer.

6. **MRV cost per estate is an assumption.** It adds $2-100 per t of lime replaced and favours very large single-counterparty estates.

7. **This is a niche reduction, not a removal pathway.** Scale is ~0.001 Gt/yr in the base case, with a global ceiling of ~0.02-0.07 Gt even at Tier 1 with zero logistics. Its value lies mainly in the MRV method, which resolves the carbonate confound for tropical ERW, and in the low case, where nearby fines are cheaper than delivered lime (-$79/t). It is not a material climate lever.

stake.coalition_notes:
Overall, the idea is low-conflict and modest in scale. It avoids an estimated 2.3-6.6 Mt CO2/yr, about 0.1-0.3% of Brazil's gross emissions (computed), and does not touch the major high-carbon industries (S3, S5, S6 neutral). The sharpest conflicts sit inside S4: silicate quarries win and aglime producers lose, with $160-600M/yr of lime sales displaced at an assumed price. At avoidance-credit prices, that loss exceeds the climate value created ($23-200M/yr at $10-30/t).

A broad coalition would need four conditions:
1. Keep credits measurement-gated and sold for removal or inventory accounting, not as offsets for continued emissions. This is CAN's offset red line and Baum 2024's moral-hazard finding.
2. Include smallholders and cooperatives, not only corporate estates, to answer S8 and climate-justice concerns about benefit capture by agribusiness and deforestation-linked estates.
3. Prefer an inventory or government route: Brazil reports lower liming emissions, and the National Fertilizer Plan funds remineraliser use. This sidesteps the voluntary-market avoidance-credit problem and the agribusiness red line against caps (the SBCE excludes agriculture).
4. Bring the aglime producers in, for example by having lime firms blend and sell silicate-limestone mixes (25-50% partial swap), which the agronomy needs anyway for aluminium-toxic soils. This turns the main S4 loser into a distributor.

Confound to flag to S2 and S10: the Larkin non-detection used coarse rock (p80 1,767 µm), so carbonate swamping is not the only reason for the null result. The swap alone may not make silicate CDR detectable, and the avoided-carbonate credit hinges on the nitric-acid share under urea, which is still modelled.

Realised-market evidence: Frontier's Brazilian ERW offtake with Terradot is 170,890 t contracted against 167 t delivered, so buyers exist but delivery and MRV is the bottleneck this idea targets.

Several positions were recalled rather than re-verified this session because the web-search budget was exhausted: Brazil Law 12.890, the National Fertilizer Plan, SBCE, MAPA's toxic-element limits, EUDR, and the La Via Campesina and MST positions.

critic.fatal_flaw:
The idea's distinctive claim, that tracer apportionment plus a carbonate swap makes silicate CO2 removal measurable, fails on arithmetic.

**Prior art removes the premise.** Larkin 2022 already ran the 87Sr/86Sr and cation-ratio apportionment. That is the method which showed the signal was over 90% carbonate, so "apportionment fixes the Sabah failure" is not new.

**Silicate removal stays undetectable at swap rates.** A 30% swap of 1-2 t lime/ha puts only 1-6 t rock/ha/yr on the field, about 10-50x less than Larkin's 50 t/ha/yr. At Illinois-like rates of 0.02-0.05 t CO2/t rock, that gives 0.02-0.30 t CO2/ha/yr of silicate CDR (my critic_gs3.py).

**The swap barely shrinks the background.** It cuts Larkin's carbonate background only to about 2.6±0.4 t/ha. A treated-versus-control 2-sigma detection would need more than about 1.2 t/ha. The silicate signal is 4-60x below detection.

**Even a 100% swap fails.** The natural catchment carbonate and silicate background would still exceed the added signal, and Larkin's coarse rock (p80 1,767 µm) is a further confound.

**What survives.** The removal leg is dead, and with it the novelty. What remains is lime-for-silicate substitution with an avoided-lime credit. Eion sells this commercially, and Beerling 2018 and Dietzen & Rosing 2023 propose it. It is worth about 0.001 Gt CO2e/yr in the base case, with a ceiling of 0.02-0.07 Gt.

**Verdict.** This is not a physics violation, and the avoided-lime remnant is not dead. It is fatal as framed (measured silicate removal). It could be kept only as a small avoided-emission or MRV project, using the patch below.
critic.top_fixable_flaw:
The avoided-lime credit is the only part that survives, but neither its accounting nor its counterfactual is defined, and the TEA's sign risk follows from one accounting choice.

**The TEA formula is one convention among several.**
- The TEA's E = EF×(2f_s−1) books carbonic-acid lime dissolution as a durable sink of 1 CO2 per carbonate. That gives a break-even at f_s 0.53 and $717/t at f_s 0.6.
- Counted over ocean timescales, CaCO3 re-precipitates in the ocean, so carbonic-acid lime nets about 0 and nitric-acid lime about +1. The avoided factor is then EF×f_s: 0.23-0.41 t/t across f_s 0.5-0.9. It stays positive at every f_s and is 1.1-2.5x the TEA's value.
- The IPCC inventory route counts the full Tier 1 factor of 0.44/0.48 regardless of f_s.

So whether the credit is "fragile" is a matter of convention, and the idea does not pick one.

**Two unaddressed risks could cancel the credit.**
- **N2O from pH lag.** At 60-120 kg N/ha and EF1 of 1%, a 10-20% rise in N2O from slower neutralisation costs 0.03-0.10 t CO2e/ha. That is set against only 0.10-0.21 t/ha of avoided lime CO2 (critic_gs3.py), so it could cancel 25-100% of the benefit.
- **Lime added back.** If basalt's in-season CCE is low, farmers will add the lime back. The avoided emission then vanishes.
critic.suggested_patch:
**1. Drop the measured-silicate-removal credit.** Keep tracers only as a research add-on.

**2. Re-scope the product** as an inventory-grade avoided-liming-emission reduction. Sell it through Brazil's national inventory or Fertilizer Plan route and supply-chain (Scope 3) claims, not as removal credits. This also answers the S1 and S10 red lines on offsets and avoidance-versus-removal.

**3. Make the credit a measured quantity.** Credit = verified lime tonnes not applied × EF. Choose the EF convention up front:
- Tier 1 for inventory purposes.
- EF×f_s on the ocean-durable basis for a conservative voluntary claim, never 2f_s−1.
- Determine f_s per estate from leachate NO3−, Ca+Mg and alkalinity balance under urea.

**4. Net out N2O.** Deduct measured or modelled N2O change (static chambers on swap versus lime plots), plus extra haul and spreading diesel.

**5. Add an agronomic and additionality gate.** Credit only if topsoil pH and Al saturation in swap plots stay within 0.1 pH units (and the matching Al band) of the lime controls by month 6. Lime purchase records must show no make-up liming.

**6. Change the soil-column test to match.** Add N2O flux as a primary endpoint, and add falsifier (d): the N2O increase exceeds 50% of the avoided lime CO2.

**7. Bring in lime producers.** Have them sell 25-50% silicate-limestone blends so the main S4 loser becomes the distributor.

**Expected scale:** about 1 Mt CO2/yr, so present it as a niche co-benefit, not a climate lever.

idea.title: Verified ration balancing: co-op dairy methane intensity measured from the bulk-milk spectra the plant already takes
idea.one_line: Scale India's cooperative ration-balancing programme, which measurably raises milk yield and cuts methane per litre. Verify it at near-zero marginal cost with mid-infrared (MIR) methane predictions run on each village society's daily bulk-milk sample, and pay a per-litre premium through the co-op's existing payment rail.
idea.conventional_core: NDDB-style ration balancing for smallholder cows and buffaloes: local feeds are rebalanced by trained village resource persons using software (TRL 9; field-measured).
idea.graft: Milk mid-infrared spectra as a methane proxy. Canada already uses MIR-predicted methane in national genetic evaluation (JDS 2026 abstracts). It is applied here to pooled society-level bulk milk rather than individual cows.
idea.mechanism: Garg et al. (Animal Feed Sci Tech 2013; 1,131 buffaloes and 540 cows under field conditions) found that balanced rations raised milk yield by 2-14%. They also raised feed-conversion efficiency and cut enteric CH4 per kg milk by 15-20% (P<0.05). Per-cow methane measurement is too costly for smallholders. Every society's milk is already sampled daily at the chilling centre or plant. A calibrated MIR model applied to bulk milk would give a society-level methane-intensity trend. Payments are made per litre through the co-op, and only absolute per-animal reductions beyond a baseline are credited.
idea.target: Indian dairy co-op unions (and East African dairy hubs) with FTIR-equipped plant labs. Partners: a dairy union lab, an animal-nutrition institute holding SF6 or GreenFeed reference data.
idea.quantitative_claims:
Measured: 15-20% lower CH4 per kg milk and 2-14% more milk (Garg 2013). Computed (assumed 50-70 kg CH4/yr per lactating animal, biogenic GWP100 27): 0.20-0.38 t CO2e per animal-year on an intensity basis, worth $3-11 per animal-year at $15-30/t. The absolute per-animal reduction is likely smaller and unverified.

Computed MRV cost: monthly per-cow MIR at $0.5-1.5 per sample is $6-18 per animal-year, which exceeds the carbon value. Daily bulk-milk MIR at society level (200-500 animals) is $0.4-2.7 per animal-year, so only the pooled design pays.

Scale: 10-30 M animals gives 1.5-11 Mt CO2e/yr (intensity basis, an upper bound). Energy: no process energy; feed efficiency improves.
idea.who_gains: S8/S6 smallholder dairy households: more milk and lower feed cost (the main driver; carbon is a small add-on). S4 dairy processors gain a verified Scope 3 reduction without a Bovaer-style mandate backlash. S7 gains an inventory improvement and livestock-mission outcomes. S2 gains low-cost, population-scale methane data from tropical breeds. Mineral-mixture makers gain sales.
idea.who_loses: Sellers of excess protein concentrate lose some sales, because ration balancing often cuts over-fed crude protein (71% of animals were over-supplied in Garg 2013). If the herd grows with productivity, absolute emissions may not fall. That is a rebound risk the credit design must exclude.
idea.closest_known_work: NDDB's Ration Balancing Programme (Garg 2013; scale recalled at millions of animals). Canadian Lactanet/MIR methane index for Holsteins. European MIR-CH4 equations (e.g. the Austrian and Swiss 2026 JDS studies on silage/TMR diets). A 2026 faecal-NIRS study suggests MIR may miss additive-driven changes. What is different: MIR applied to pooled bulk milk as programme MRV for results-based payments in tropical buffalo and crossbred systems on crop-residue diets, where no calibration yet exists.
idea.why_different: It reuses a measurement stream the co-op already generates daily, rather than adding chambers or GreenFeeds. It credits absolute rather than per-litre reductions to avoid rewarding herd growth.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test: About 3-4 months, with lab access only. Collect paired milk samples from animals with existing SF6 or GreenFeed methane measurements before and after ration balancing (an NDDB- or ICAR-type dataset), or from about 60 animals measured with a hand-held laser methane detector. Apply published MIR-CH4 equations, then recalibrate locally with cross-validation. It is falsified if the cross-validated prediction error exceeds the 15-20% treatment effect, or if bulk-milk spectra cannot separate balanced from unbalanced societies at p<0.05 with about 20 societies per arm.
idea.family: Dairy ration balancing verified by MIR methane prediction on bulk-milk samples

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: Bleu-Blanc-Coeur 'Eco-Methane' results-based payment scheme (France, since 2011), as described in Le Gloux et al. 2023, J Dairy Sci, 'Taking the diet of cows into consideration in designing payments to reduce enteric methane emissions on dairy farms' (PMC10570405)
closest.overlap: Very high on the MRV-plus-payment concept. Each farm's enteric CH4 per litre is computed from milk productivity and the milk fatty-acid ratio (FA <=C16 / total FA), measured by infrared spectroscopy on routine milk analysis. A Tier 3 equation is used: CH4 = 11.368 x Productivity^-0.4274 x (FA<=C16/total FA). Farms are paid per t CO2eq reduced against 11 forage-system baselines (about EUR 15/t CO2eq in 2017, funded by private donors). The scheme covered more than 600 farms, with an average 11% reduction in 2017. The paper says it is recognised by the UN as eligible for carbon credits. So the core of the idea already exists and has run for over a decade: milk-spectra-derived methane used as low-cost MRV for diet-change payments through the dairy chain. Differences: the scheme is intensity-based (g CH4/L), works at the level of a single French farm's milk, targets linseed and omega-3 diets in temperate Holstein systems, and has no ration-balancing or smallholder pooling element.

closest.title: Garg MR et al. 2013, Anim Feed Sci Technol, 'Effects of feeding nutritionally balanced rations ... enteric methane emissions of milking animals under field conditions' (NDDB Ration Balancing Programme)
closest.overlap: This is the intervention itself and its field-measured effect: more milk, better feed-conversion efficiency and lower CH4 per kg milk. It runs at NDDB scale through village resource persons. My recollection is millions of animals; I did not verify that figure. I found no evidence that RBP is verified by milk spectra or paid through carbon or results-based finance.

closest.title: Bittante G & Bergamaschi M 2019, Animals, 'Enteric Methane Emissions of Dairy Cows Predicted from Fatty Acid Profiles of Milk, Cream, Cheese, Ricotta, Whey, and Scotta'
closest.overlap: Direct precedent for pooled-milk prediction. It shows that methane yield and intensity predicted from vat (pooled) milk fatty acids are usable stand-ins for the reference individual samples. Cream, cheese and whey were also tested; they were accurate on average but imprecise. This is a temperate Italian system using FA equations, not a tropical buffalo/crossbred calibration or a payment programme.

closest.title: Ramirez Mauricio MA et al. 2026, J Dairy Sci, 'Impact of farming systems and welfare indicators on enteric methane emissions calculated from infrared-predicted milk fatty acids in Parmigiano Reggiano Consortium farms'
closest.overlap: Applies MIR-predicted fatty acids and then methane at consortium scale: 940 farms, 174k cows and 1.26M test-day records. This is the population-scale MIR-methane monitoring layer the idea relies on, but it uses individual test-day samples, has no payment, and covers Italian systems only.

closest.title: Lactanet Canada MIR-based methane efficiency genomic evaluation (Rojas de Oliveira H et al. 2024, JDS Communications, 'Development of genomic evaluation for methane efficiency in Canadian Holsteins')
closest.overlap: Routine national use of MIR-predicted methane on routine milk samples. It uses individual cows for genetic selection, not pooled samples and not MRV for diet-change payments. The idea already cites this.

closest.title: European individual-cow MIR-CH4 calibration literature: Vanlerberghe/Dehareng 2012 Animal; Shetty 2017 JDS (Danish Holstein); Coppa/Bittante 2018 JDS (daily CH4, yield and intensity per unit of milk and cheese); Rovere/Bittante 2020 JDS (laser methane detector reference); 2022 JDS GreenFeed methodological guidelines; Austrian 2026 JDS nested cross-validation (10.3168/jds.2026-28551); 2026 JDS biological validation across lactation (10.3168/jds.2026-29014)
closest.overlap: Supplies the calibration methods, including laser methane detectors as a cheap reference, which matches the idea's proposed falsification test. All of it is temperate and Holstein/Brown Swiss/Fleckvieh, at the individual-cow level. I found no buffalo, zebu-crossbred or crop-residue-diet MIR-CH4 calibration in Europe PMC; buffalo MIR work covers only fatty acids such as linoleic acid (Yao 2023 Foods).

closest.title: Carbon-market methodologies for enteric methane via feed (recalled, not verified this session because search was exhausted): Verra VM0041 (enteric CH4 reduction via feed ingredients); Gold Standard methodologies for adjusted feed intake and smallholder dairy (developed with ILRI/SNV for East Africa)
closest.overlap: Provide crediting pathways for feed-based enteric reductions and smallholder dairy intensity improvements, generally using modelled Tier 2/3 emissions rather than milk-spectra measurement. They are relevant to the idea's 'absolute vs intensity' crediting rule.

art.what_is_new:
The core concept is not new. Using routine milk infrared analysis to estimate per-litre enteric CH4 and paying farmers per tonne reduced through the dairy chain is France's Eco-Methane scheme (Bleu-Blanc-Coeur, since 2011, more than 600 farms, about EUR 15/t, UN-recognised for credits). Pooled (vat) milk fatty acids are known to track herd-level methane intensity (Bittante & Bergamaschi 2019).

Genuinely new elements:
- Applying the approach to India's ration-balancing intervention rather than linseed/omega-3 feeding.
- Pooling at village-society level across many smallholders (200-500 animals per sample) rather than one commercial farm's tank.
- Tropical buffalo and crossbred animals on crop-residue diets, where no MIR-CH4 calibration was found.
- A rule crediting absolute per-animal reductions to block rebound from herd growth. Eco-Methane's indicator is per-litre intensity, so this is a real design difference.

Two caveats for the idea's authors:
(1) Eco-Methane is the obvious template and should replace 'Canadian Lactanet' as the headline closest work.
(2) In Indian co-ops, society milk is usually tested at the village collection unit with ultrasonic analysers, not FTIR. Society milk is commingled in bulk-milk-cooler and tanker loads before reaching the FTIR-equipped plant lab, so 'a measurement stream the co-op already generates daily' at society resolution may not exist. Separate society samples would need to be retained and shipped.

Search was constrained: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so evidence came from the Europe PMC and Crossref APIs. The carbon-standard methodologies (VM0041, Gold Standard) and NDDB RBP scale are recalled, not verified.

phys.assumptions:
The script ran successfully. Source tags: [M] measured, [R] recalled, [A] assumed. My web search budget was used up and the NDDB and ScienceDirect fetches failed (404 and 403). So every [R] value comes from recall and was not re-checked in this run.

Thermodynamic floor:
- This is not a gas separation. The idea changes rumen fermentation per litre of milk, so the floor is 0 and no floor can be violated.

Abatement per lactating animal-year:
- Enteric CH4 per animal [R]: 35 / 52 / 70 kg/yr (low / base / high). This follows Indian inventory and IPCC Tier 2 ranges for indigenous cows, crossbreds and buffalo. The idea's 50-70 kg sits in the upper half.
- Cut in CH4 per kg milk [M]: 15 / 17.5 / 20% (Garg et al. 2013, field data).
- Milk gain [M]: 2-14%. I paired the high gain with the low absolute case.
- Biogenic CH4 GWP100 = 27 and GWP20 = 79.7 [R] (IPCC AR6).
- Absolute per-animal change: -3.1% / -10.9% / -18.4%.
- Intensity basis: 0.142 / 0.246 / 0.378 t CO2e per animal-year.
- Absolute basis: 0.029 / 0.153 / 0.348 t CO2e per animal-year. Base on GWP20: 0.452 t.
- The idea's own claims reproduce exactly:
  - Intensity basis 0.202-0.378 t (claimed 0.20-0.38).
  - Carbon value $3.0-11.3 per animal-year (claimed $3-11).

MRV cost:
- FTIR in an existing union plant lab [A]: $0.3 / 0.8 / 1.5 per sample.
- Monthly per-cow sampling: $3.60 / $9.60 / $18.00 per animal-year.
- Daily society sampling at 200-500 animals: $0.22-2.74 per animal-year, which reproduces the idea's claim.
- Weekly society sampling at 300 animals: $0.05 / 0.14 / 0.26 per animal-year.
- One-off tropical calibration study [A]: $0.3-1.5M, annualised at 8% over 10 years across 10M animals. That adds only $0.004-0.022 per animal-year.

Delivery cost and farmer benefit:
- Delivery [A]: $2 / 5 / 10 per animal-year (resource-person visits, software, overhead).
- Farmer net benefit: Rs 3 / 8 / 20 per day over 300 days at 88 INR/USD, giving $10.2 / 27.3 / 68.2 per animal-year. This is conservative against the recalled NDDB figure of Rs 10-25 per day [R].

Cost per tonne (absolute basis, GWP100):
- Gross cost to a payer: $7 / $39 / $251 per t.
- Net of farmer benefit: -$189 / -$139 / +$34 per t.
- MRV alone in the base case: $6.4/t.
- The high-cost case applies a 5% absolute-cut floor, giving 0.047 t, because the computed absolute cut there is only 3.1%.

Energy:
- Resource-person motorcycle travel at 0.75 MJ/km [A]: 4 visits per animal-year, 1-3 km each.
- FTIR at about 1.7 Wh per sample.
- Result: 3-9 MJ per animal-year = 0.020 / 0.039 / 0.059 GJ/t CO2e. This is before crediting the feed saved per litre, which probably makes it net-negative.

Scale (base, absolute basis):
- 10M animals: 1.53 Mt/yr. 30M animals: 4.59 Mt/yr (= 0.0046 Gt). 80M animals: 12.24 Mt/yr. On an intensity basis the 30M figure is 7.37 Mt.
- 30M animals is 1.8% of India's roughly 256 Mt CO2e/yr of enteric methane [R].
- Global ceiling at 150M smallholder dairy animals [A]: 0.023 Gt/yr.
phys.resource_needs:
- **Energy:** a negligible share of world supply, about 3-9 MJ per animal-year, and probably net-negative once feed saved per litre is counted.
- **Equipment:** existing FTIR milk analysers in union plant labs (about $50-150k each [A]). The idea's premise needs checking here: many Indian village societies test fat and SNF with ultrasonic analysers, not FTIR. So society samples may have to be routed to a plant lab.
- **Consumables:** mineral mixture, plus a local resource-person workforce of about 1 per few hundred to 1,000 animals [A].
- **Calibration:** a one-off dataset of about 150-300 animals with SF6 or GreenFeed reference methane on tropical diets, roughly $0.3-1.5M [A].
- **Land and water:** none added.
phys.violations:
There are no thermodynamic violations (there is no separation step, so the floor is 0), and none of the quantitative claims needs heroic assumptions.

Problems found:

1. **The headline numbers are on an intensity basis.** The idea says it will credit absolute reductions, but its 0.20-0.38 t per animal-year is the intensity figure. On an absolute basis the script gives 0.029 / 0.153 / 0.348 t. With a 14% milk gain, the absolute cut is only 3.1%. The idea flags this itself, but its scale range (1.5-11 Mt) mixes the two bases. The base absolute figure for 10-30M animals is 1.5-4.6 Mt.

2. **The falsification criterion is wrong.** It treats a cow-level cross-validated MIR error above the 15-20% treatment effect as falsifying. In a pooled design, random cow-level error of 15-20% shrinks to 0.87-1.15% across 300 animals. The real test is systematic: does the slope or bias of MIR-predicted versus measured CH4 change hold up when the diet itself changes?

3. **The power claim depends on enrolment share.** "~20 societies per arm" holds only for a before/after diff-in-diff design or for at least 60% of a society's animals enrolled. At 30% enrolment with a cross-sectional SD of 12%, power is 0.28 and 83 societies per arm are needed. With a diff-in-diff SD of 6%, 21 per arm give power 0.79.

4. **Pooled MRV is only marginally affordable on daily sampling.** Daily sampling costs $0.6-1.5 per animal-year against $1-10 of carbon value. Weekly sampling ($0.05-0.26) makes MRV clearly affordable.
phys.key_uncertainties:
1. **MIR as a methane proxy (decisive, TRL about 4).** MIR methane equations largely detect methane through milk fatty-acid profiles. Ration balancing changes the diet directly, so predicted CH4 may track the diet change rather than real methane. This is the same mechanism as the 2026 faecal-NIRS finding that MIR misses additive-driven changes. There is no calibration for buffalo milk, crossbreds or crop-residue diets. Bulk milk that mixes cow and buffalo, plus adulteration or added water, will shift the spectra.

2. **Size and durability of the effect.** The 15-20% intensity cut comes from one programme's field study (Garg 2013; 1,131 buffaloes and 540 cows). The methane sub-sample method and how long the effect lasts were not re-verified in this run. Self-selection of enrolled farmers is a confound.

3. **Additionality.** If farmers gain $10-68 per animal-year, a carbon add-on of $1-10 may not change adoption. Adoption is probably limited by delivery, not by money. That weakens the case for crediting, though not for the programme itself.

4. **Rebound.** If productivity gains feed herd growth, absolute emissions may not fall. Society-level bulk-milk data alone cannot separate per-animal from herd effects, so an animal census per society is needed.

5. **Unverified recalled inputs.** NDP-I programme scale, the Rs 10-25/day farmer benefit and the per-animal CH4 factors are recalled, not fetched (search budget used up).

6. **Small scale.** About 0.005 Gt/yr at 30M animals, with a global ceiling of about 0.02 Gt/yr. It is a strong development and stakeholder win (S6/S8/S4/S7) with a negative net cost to society, but it is not a major climate lever.

stances.evidence: No documented S1 position on ration balancing itself, so this is inferred from the closest comparables. CAN (2021) opposes offsets 'as an alternative to stringent emission reductions'. Paying credits to dairy processors for Scope 3 claims, or selling them as offsets, hits that line directly. A domestic, results-based payment with no offset sale is a pay-for-performance design of the kind S1 has accepted, as with Germany's carbon contracts for difference. Livestock-focused NGOs criticise intensity metrics because intensity can fall while absolute emissions rise. The idea's own claims are on an intensity basis (15-20% per kg milk; NDDB reports 13.7%), and its absolute effect is 'likely smaller and unverified'. Support therefore depends on crediting absolute reductions only. Fossil-focused NGOs may also object that 1.5-11 Mt CO2e/yr of agricultural methane diverts attention from fossil methane, which they see as the larger and cheaper target. My knowledge of the IATP and Changing Markets critiques of intensity metrics could not be re-fetched this session (search budget exhausted).
stances.red_line_hit: Offsets/Scope-3 claims substituting for reductions (CAN 2021); intensity-based crediting that rewards herd growth (rebound)

stances.evidence: IPCC AR6 WGIII lists improved livestock feeding and management among agricultural methane options, and COP28 1/CMA.5 para 28f calls for substantially reducing methane by 2030. The core intervention has field-measured results. The NDDB page reports 2.865 M animals in 33,374 villages and 18 states under NDP-I, 13.7% less enteric CH4 per kg milk, 11.8% lower feed cost per kg milk and +0.27 kg/day milk. These are measured programme averages, although the CH4 figure is likely model-estimated rather than chamber-measured. Scientists will value the population-scale tropical MIR-CH4 data. They will also demand cross-validation against SF6 or GreenFeed reference measurements, because no MIR calibration exists for buffalo on crop-residue diets and a 2026 faecal-NIRS study suggests MIR can miss diet-driven changes. Support is for the research and verification step, not yet for crediting.
stances.red_line_hit: Crediting before calibration is validated would be MRV overclaiming

stances.evidence: No direct business exposure. The documented S3 position on methane is to back fossil-methane abatement on its own terms (OGCI, OGDC <0.2% intensity, API support for direct regulation) and to oppose per-tonne fees (Waste Emissions Charge repealed under the CRA in 2025). Agricultural methane programmes neither help nor hurt this. Some S3 actors may welcome attention to agricultural methane, which S1 would read as deflection. Some majors might buy the credits as offsets, which would turn S1 against the scheme.
stances.red_line_hit: None for S3

stances.evidence: Among S4 only food and dairy processors are affected; steel, cement and chemicals are neutral. The closest comparable is the Arla Bovaer trial: in Nov 2024 Arla announced a trial on about 30 farms with Morrisons, Tesco and Aldi. It drew calls to boycott Arla products, especially Lurpak, and protesters poured milk down sinks (Wikipedia, 3-NOP). Ration balancing uses local feeds and no additive, so it avoids the additive-safety framing that drove that backlash. It also raises milk and fat yield, which suits the processor's own procurement goals, and gives processors a verified Scope 3 lever. Co-op processors already run the bulk-milk testing labs, so marginal cost is small. Concentrate-feed sellers, a small part of S4, lose some protein sales because 71% of animals were over-supplied (Garg 2013).
stances.red_line_hit: None, provided the scheme is voluntary (S4 red line is mandates and visible additive programmes)

stances.evidence: There is no interaction with electricity generation or demand. The co-op chilling and lab energy involved is negligible.
stances.red_line_hit: None

stances.evidence: The workers involved here are smallholder dairy households and co-op staff, not fossil-industry unions. NDDB reports a measured net income gain of Rs25.5/day per animal (Rs16.3 from feed cost, Rs9.2 from milk and fat). By my calculation that is about Rs6,900-9,300 (US$82-111) per animal-year. The ration-balancing work also creates paid local resource-person jobs. No jobs are lost in high-carbon regions. Fossil-region unions are indifferent.
stances.red_line_hit: None

stances.evidence: India is absent from the Global Methane Pledge's 159-country participant list (globalmethanepledge.org, fetched 2026-10-05). Its usual reason, from my own knowledge and not re-verified this session, is protecting smallholder agricultural livelihoods. That makes any methane target or fee for livestock a red line. However, the Indian government itself (through NDDB under NDP-I) funded ration balancing as a productivity and livelihood programme. So it is supported as a livelihoods policy, not as methane regulation. Framing it as climate MRV or international crediting could trigger sovereignty and Article 6 concerns, such as who owns the reductions and whether they count toward India's NDC through corresponding adjustments. Elsewhere, governments pulled back from farm emissions pricing under farmer pressure (New Zealand, 2024, from my own knowledge, primary source not fetched), which shows voluntary, income-positive designs are the only politically durable form. Revenue cost is low: the programme's government money goes to extension, not subsidy per tonne.
stances.red_line_hit: Livestock methane targets/pricing on smallholders (India); international crediting without sovereign control (Article 6 corresponding adjustments)

stances.evidence: The money flows to Global South smallholders, so the justice concern is reversed: they are paid and face no mandate. The main gain is the measured feed-saving and milk gain, about $82-111 per animal-year. My calculation puts the carbon payment of $3-11 per animal-year at only about 3-13% of that gain. Even if the carbon credit fails, farmers still keep the core benefit. Baum et al. 2024 found Global South publics more worried that technologies undermine mitigation or spread risk unequally. This scheme uses no land, carries no technology risk and leaves no stranded-asset debt, so it avoids those concerns. Justice advocates will object if Northern processors or oil majors use the credits to claim offsets while smallholders get a token per-litre share, and if MRV data or credit ownership sits with buyers rather than co-ops.
stances.red_line_hit: Possible extraction of carbon value by Northern buyers (offset use) and data/ownership not held by farmers

stances.evidence: My calculation puts the premium on the farm-gate price at about Rs0.08-0.62 per litre, roughly 0.1-1.1% of a Rs56-68/L retail price. It is funded by carbon or Scope 3 buyers, not consumers. Programme feed cost per kg milk fell 11.8% (NDDB), which puts downward pressure on prices if anything. Unlike the Bovaer backlash (Arla, 2024), there is no new additive in the food chain for consumers to object to.
stances.red_line_hit: None (no price rise; no additive)

stances.evidence: Investors are pushing food and dairy companies to disclose and cut methane, for example through the Dairy Methane Action Alliance (from my own knowledge; the EDF launch page returned 404). A cheap, measured Scope 3 lever is therefore welcome. The value at stake is small: 1.5-11 Mt CO2e/yr on an intensity basis, worth $3-11 per animal-year. Carbon-credit buyers will discount it until the MIR-CH4 calibration is cross-validated and absolute rather than intensity reductions are shown. Existing Verra VM0041 (v2.0, active since 21 Dec 2021) covers feed ingredients, but it is not clear that whole-ration balancing qualifies. Without an approved methodology, investment-grade credits are unlikely. Insurers have no exposure.
stances.red_line_hit: Unverified MRV / non-additionality (NDDB already funded RBP, so additionality vs existing programme is questionable)

stances.evidence: There is no new facility, emission source or safety hazard. The scheme uses existing chilling-centre and dairy-plant sampling, and the benefits go to the same villages (NDDB: 33,374 villages under NDP-I). Locally it reads as an income programme.
stances.red_line_hit: None

stake.coalition_notes:
This idea has a broad but shallow coalition.

**Strong support:** S2 (for validation), S4 dairy processors, S6/S8 smallholders, S9 and S11.
**Neutral:** S3 and S5.
**Split:** S1, S7 and S10.

Three design choices decide which way the split groups fall.

1. **Absolute vs intensity crediting.**
   - The measured evidence is all intensity-based: NDDB NDP-I reports 13.7% less CH4 per kg milk across 2.865 M animals, and Garg 2013 reports 15-20%.
   - S1, and later S10, will accept only absolute per-animal reductions with herd-growth safeguards.
   - That cuts the credited volume below the 1.5-11 Mt CO2e/yr upper bound.

2. **Domestic results-based payment vs exportable offsets.**
   - Selling the credits to Northern buyers or oil majors as offsets hits CAN's 2021 red line ('offsets as an alternative') and S8's extraction concern.
   - It also risks India's red line on sovereignty and Article 6 corresponding adjustments.
   - A domestic or insetting design avoids all three: co-op processors pay a per-litre premium for verified Scope 3 reductions inside their own supply chain, and the government can count the reductions in India's inventory.

3. **Framing.**
   - India is not in the Global Methane Pledge (absent from the 159-country participant list), yet the government itself funded the Ration Balancing Programme as a livelihood measure.
   - Present it as productivity plus verification, not as methane regulation.

Economics support the livelihood framing.
- Farmers' measured net gain from NDDB's reported Rs25.5/day is about $82-111 per animal-year.
- The carbon payment adds only about 3-13% on top of that, so the farmer case does not depend on the credit.
- The consumer price effect is at most about 0.1-1.1%, and even that is paid by buyers, not consumers.

The idea dodges the Bovaer backlash. Arla's UK trial with Tesco, Morrisons and Aldi (Nov 2024) drew boycott calls and milk-pouring protests, but ration balancing involves no additive.

**Weaknesses:**
- **Additionality.** NDDB already ran the programme with public money, so buyers will ask what the carbon money adds beyond scaling it from about 2.9 M to 10-30 M animals.
- **Methodology fit.** Verra VM0041 covers feed ingredients; it is unclear whether whole-ration balancing qualifies.
- **Calibration.** No MIR calibration exists yet for buffalo on crop-residue diets.

**Sourcing limits:** The web search budget was exhausted this session. The following points come from my own knowledge and were not re-fetched:
- India's stated livelihood reasons for not joining the pledge.
- New Zealand's 2024 retreat from farm-emissions pricing.
- The Dairy Methane Action Alliance.
- NGO critiques of intensity metrics by IATP and Changing Markets.

**Sources fetched:**
- https://www.nddb.coop/services/animalnutrition/programmes/ration-balancing-programme
- https://www.globalmethanepledge.org/
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3-Nitrooxypropanol
- https://verra.org/methodologies/vm0041-methodology-for-the-reduction-of-enteric-methane-emissions-from-ruminants-through-the-use-of-feed-ingredients-v2-0/

**Calculation:** climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/dairy_stakeholder_econ.py. Assumptions: Rs84 per USD, 1,500-3,000 L per animal-year, Rs56-68/L retail.

critic.fatal_flaw: None. There is no physics floor. Scale is small (about 0.005 Gt CO2e/yr) but that is not disqualifying for a stakeholder-satisfying option. Every stakeholder red line can be designed around: credit only absolute reductions, keep payments domestic as insetting, frame it as livelihoods and not methane regulation. The one structural limit is that bulk-milk spectra cannot by themselves produce the absolute per-animal number the crediting rule requires. That breaks the MRV design as written but can be fixed (see patch). It does not invalidate the idea.
critic.top_fixable_flaw:
The bulk-milk MIR signal cannot be the crediting quantity. There are three reasons.

1. **The proxy is confounded by the treatment.** MIR-CH4 equations infer methane mostly from milk fatty-acid shifts, and ration balancing changes the diet, which shifts fatty acids whether or not methane changes. The predicted drop is therefore partly guaranteed by design. That is the same failure mode as the 2026 faecal-NIRS additive finding.

2. **The society pool dilutes and drifts.** My calculation (critic_gs4.py in the scratchpad):
   - At 30% enrolment, a 15-20% per-kg cut in enrolled animals shows up as only about 4.6-6.6% in the pooled intensity.
   - Normal swings of 10-20% in buffalo versus cow milk share move the pooled value by about 2-8%, if predicted intensity differs 20-40% between species. Those are the same size as the signal, so pooled spectra cannot attribute a change to the programme.

3. **Bulk milk only gives a litre-weighted intensity.** Absolute per-animal reduction needs head counts and per-animal yield, which no milk spectrum contains. So the rule against herd-growth rebound cannot be enforced from the stream the idea says it reuses.

On top of this, society milk is commingled before it reaches the FTIR plant lab (prior-art finding), so the "existing data stream" premise is also weak.
critic.suggested_patch:
Swap the roles of model and measurement, following Eco-Methane's architecture but with an absolute basis.

**(a) Crediting quantity.** Compute per-animal absolute CH4 (kg/yr) with an IPCC Tier 2 model. Its inputs are the ration records the RBP software already logs per ear-tagged animal (in NDDB's INAPH system): DMI, digestibility and therefore Ym, plus recorded milk yield. Multiply by the INAPH census of enrolled animals. Subtract a baseline fixed on the same animals before balancing, and cap the credit at zero growth in society herd size.

**(b) Role of MIR.** Society-level MIR becomes an audit and haircut factor only. Credits for a society are discounted if its MIR-predicted intensity trend falls short of what the Tier 2 model implies, beyond a pre-set tolerance. The MIR reading is also adjusted for the society's daily buffalo/cow milk-volume split, which collection-unit records already hold.

**(c) Sampling.** Retain a dedicated weekly society sample, sealed at the collection unit before commingling, rather than relying on plant-level bulk. This cuts MRV to about $0.05-0.26 per animal-year (physics report). Credit only societies with at least 60% of animals enrolled, so the pooled signal is at least about 9-12%.

**(d) Falsification test, rewritten.** The test is no longer cross-validated cow-level error versus effect size. It is: on about 60 animals with laser-methane-detector, GreenFeed or SF6 reference measurements before and after ration balancing, regress MIR-predicted change on measured change. The proxy is falsified for audit use if the slope's 95% CI excludes 0.7-1.3, or if bias exceeds 5 percentage points. Run cows and buffalo separately on crop-residue diets.

**(e) Headline numbers.** Restate claims on the absolute basis only: 0.03-0.35 t CO2e per animal-year, and 1.5-4.6 Mt/yr at 10-30M animals. Name Eco-Methane as the closest prior art.

patched_idea.title: Verified ration balancing: co-op dairy methane credited from per-animal ration records, audited by society-level milk MIR spectra
patched_idea.one_line: Scale India's cooperative ration-balancing programme, which measurably raises milk yield and cuts methane per litre. Credit absolute per-animal methane cuts computed from the ration records the programme already logs per ear-tagged animal. Audit those credits with mid-infrared (MIR) methane predictions on a sealed weekly milk sample from each village society, and pay through the co-op's existing payment rail.
patched_idea.conventional_core: NDDB-style ration balancing for smallholder cows and buffaloes: trained village resource persons use software to rebalance local feeds (TRL 9; field-measured).
patched_idea.graft: Milk MIR spectra as a methane proxy. Canada already uses MIR-predicted methane in national genetic evaluation (JDS 2026 abstracts). Here it is applied to a pooled society-level milk sample. It serves as an independent audit and haircut signal on model-computed credits, not as the crediting measurement itself.
patched_idea.mechanism:
Garg et al. (Animal Feed Sci Tech 2013; 1,131 buffaloes and 540 cows under field conditions) found that balanced rations raised milk yield by 2-14%. They also improved feed-conversion efficiency and cut enteric CH4 per kg milk by 15-20% (P<0.05). Per-cow methane measurement is too costly for smallholders, so the MRV has three layers.

(a) **Crediting quantity.** Absolute CH4 per animal (kg/yr) comes from an IPCC Tier 2 model. Its inputs are the per-animal ration records the RBP software already logs in NDDB's INAPH system: dry-matter intake (DMI), diet digestibility and hence the methane conversion factor Ym, plus recorded milk yield. This is multiplied by the INAPH census of enrolled animals. A baseline fixed on the same animals before balancing is subtracted. Credit is capped so that society herd size shows zero growth, which excludes herd-growth rebound.

(b) **Role of MIR: audit only.** A calibrated MIR-CH4 model gives a society-level, litre-weighted methane-intensity trend. Before use, that trend is adjusted for the society's daily buffalo/cow milk-volume split, which collection-unit records already hold. If the MIR trend falls short of the intensity change the Tier 2 model implies, beyond a pre-set tolerance, the society's credits are discounted. MIR alone never creates credit, because ration changes shift milk fatty acids whatever happens to methane.

(c) **Sampling.** A dedicated weekly society sample is sealed at the collection unit before commingling and sent to the union's FTIR lab. Plant-level bulk milk is commingled and is not used. Only societies with at least 60% of animals enrolled are credited, so the expected pooled intensity signal is about 9-12% (0.6 × 15-20%) rather than being diluted below the noise from shifts in species mix.

Payments go per enrolled animal or per litre through the co-op's existing payment rail. They are domestic insetting or results-based payments framed as livelihood support, not methane regulation.
patched_idea.target: Indian dairy co-op unions (and East African dairy hubs) that run INAPH-type animal registries and FTIR-equipped union labs. Partners: a dairy union lab, plus an animal-nutrition institute holding SF6, GreenFeed or laser-methane-detector reference data.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
**Measured.** 15-20% lower CH4 per kg milk and 2-14% more milk (Garg 2013, field conditions).

**Computed, absolute basis only** (patch_gs4.py in the scratchpad; assumes 50-70 kg CH4/yr per lactating animal, biogenic GWP100 = 27):
- The absolute per-animal cut is 3-18% of enteric CH4. Low end: a 15% intensity cut with 14% more milk. High end: a 20% cut with 2% more milk.
- That is 0.04-0.35 t CO2e per animal-year, central about 0.18.
- It is worth $0.6-10 per animal-year at $15-30/t.

**Scale.** 10-30 M enrolled animals gives 0.4-10 Mt CO2e/yr across the full range, centrally about 1.8-5.3 Mt/yr. The critic's 1.5-4.6 Mt/yr sits near the central case; the full range is wider. These are modelled figures, not measured ones.

**MRV cost (computed).** One sealed weekly society sample at $0.5-1.5 per MIR analysis, spread over 200-500 animals, costs $0.05-0.39 per animal-year. That is below the carbon value except at the very bottom of the reduction range. Per-cow monthly MIR would cost $6-18 per animal-year, which is uneconomic.

**Pooled audit signal.** About 9-12% at the 60% minimum enrolment.

**Energy.** No process energy; feed efficiency improves.
patched_idea.who_gains:
S8/S6 smallholder dairy households gain more milk and lower feed cost. That is the main driver; carbon is a small add-on.

S4 dairy processors gain a Scope 3 reduction that is model-computed and independently audited, without a Bovaer-style mandate backlash.

S7 gains an inventory improvement on Tier 2 activity data, plus livestock-mission outcomes.

S2 gains population-scale, paired ration-record and milk-spectra data from tropical breeds on crop-residue diets.

Mineral-mixture makers gain sales.
patched_idea.who_loses:
Sellers of excess protein concentrate lose some sales, because ration balancing often cuts over-fed crude protein (71% of animals were over-supplied in Garg 2013).

Societies below 60% enrolment are excluded from credits until they reach it.

Rebound risk from herd growth is handled by the zero-herd-growth cap, but this makes credits smaller than intensity-based claims would be.
patched_idea.closest_known_work:
NDDB's Ration Balancing Programme (Garg 2013; recalled at a scale of millions of animals) and its INAPH registry.

Eco-Methane is the closest prior art for the MRV architecture: modelled methane with a milk-based check. This version differs by crediting on an absolute basis with a herd-growth cap.

Other related work:
- The Canadian Lactanet MIR methane index for Holsteins.
- European MIR-CH4 equations (e.g. the Austrian and Swiss 2026 JDS studies on silage/TMR diets).
- A 2026 faecal-NIRS study suggesting spectral proxies can miss diet- or additive-driven changes. This is why MIR is demoted to an audit role here.
patched_idea.why_different:
Credits come from ration records the programme already keeps per animal, on an absolute, herd-capped basis. A cheap pooled spectral audit can haircut those credits but never inflate them.

It targets tropical buffalo and crossbred systems on crop-residue diets, where no MIR-CH4 calibration yet exists.

It avoids both costly per-animal chambers and the confound of using a diet-sensitive proxy as the crediting quantity.
patched_idea.cheapest_falsifying_test:
About 3-4 months, with lab access only. Take about 60 animals with laser-methane-detector, GreenFeed or SF6 reference measurements before and after ration balancing, using an NDDB- or ICAR-type dataset or new handheld-laser measurements. Run cows and buffaloes separately, on crop-residue diets. Collect paired individual milk samples, apply published MIR-CH4 equations, then recalibrate locally with cross-validation.

Regress the MIR-predicted change on the measured change. The proxy is falsified for audit use if the slope's 95% CI excludes 0.7-1.3, or if bias exceeds 5 percentage points.

In parallel, compare Tier 2 predictions from the logged ration records against the reference measurements. The crediting model is falsified if it overstates the measured absolute reduction by more than 30%.

fix.change_summary:
I kept the conventional core, NDDB ration balancing, and the graft, MIR methane prediction on pooled society milk. I swapped the roles of measurement and model, as the critic suggested.

- **Crediting quantity.** Credits are now an absolute per-animal IPCC Tier 2 estimate built from the per-animal ration records the RBP/INAPH software already logs. It uses a fixed same-animal baseline and a zero-herd-growth cap. This enforces the anti-rebound rule that bulk-milk spectra could not.
- **Role of MIR.** MIR is demoted to an audit and haircut factor, adjusted for the buffalo/cow volume split. This removes the "treatment confounds proxy" problem.
- **Sampling.** Plant-level commingled bulk milk is replaced by a weekly sample sealed at the collection unit. Only societies with at least 60% enrolment are credited, so the pooled signal is about 9-12%.
- **Falsification test.** Rewritten as a slope/bias test (slope 95% CI within 0.7-1.3, bias at most 5 percentage points), run on cows and buffaloes separately. I added a check that the Tier 2 model does not overstate measured reductions.
- **Eco-Methane.** Named as the closest prior art.

I recomputed the numbers on the absolute basis (patch_gs4.py). They are 0.04-0.35 t CO2e per animal-year and $0.6-10 per animal-year at $15-30/t. Scale is 0.4-10 Mt/yr across the full range, centrally about 1.8-5.3 Mt/yr. The critic's 1.5-4.6 Mt/yr is close to the central case but narrower than the full range. MRV cost is $0.05-0.39 per animal-year, slightly above the critic's $0.05-0.26 at the upper bound.

I set mechanism_changed=true. The causal mechanism (ration balancing cuts methane per litre) is unchanged, but the verification mechanism changed: the crediting quantity is now modelled, not MIR-measured.

phys2.assumptions:
The script ran cleanly. Source tags used: [M] is field data as reported on the idea card. The Garg 2013 primary was not re-fetched, because the session web-search budget is exhausted and ScienceDirect returned 403. [R] is a recalled literature value, [P] is earlier OptiLex scratchpad research, and [A] is an assumption.

**Card arithmetic reproduces exactly** (section 1 of the output).
- Absolute cut per animal: -3.1% (15% intensity cut, milk +14%), -10.9% (17.5%, +8%) and -18.4% (20%, +2%).
- That is 0.042, 0.177 and 0.348 t CO2e per animal-year (GWP100 = 27), worth $0.63-10.43 per animal-year at $15-30/t.
- Scale: 0.42-10.43 Mt across the full range, with a central 1.77-5.30 Mt.
- MRV for one weekly sealed sample: $0.052-0.390 per animal-year. Per-cow monthly MIR: $6-18.

**Own low/base/high, absolute basis, GWP100.**
- Methane per in-milk animal is 35, 52 or 70 kg per year [R]. IPCC 2006 Tier 1 defaults for the Indian subcontinent are about 58 for dairy cattle and 55 for buffalo; indigenous cows run lower. The card's 50-70 sits in the upper half.
- Garg 2013 pairings as above [M].
- The balanced ration applies for 0.65, 0.8 or 1.0 of the year [A]. RBP targets in-milk animals and calving intervals are about 14-18 months; the card implicitly assumes 1.0.
- Result: **0.019, 0.122 and 0.348 t CO2e per animal-year** (GWP20: 0.056, 0.361 and 1.027).

**Cost per tonne.** Gross programme cost is $7, $43 and $549 per t (low/base/high). Components, per animal-year:
- Delivery (village resource persons, software, supervision): $2, $5 or $10 [A].
- MRV: $0.5-1.5 per sample [A]. A dedicated $100k FTIR analyser annualised at 8% over 10 years adds only $0.29 per sample at 52,000 samples a year.
- One-off costs: a $0.2-1.5M calibration study plus $0.2-1M for methodology approval, annualised at 8% over 10 years across 10-30M animals.
- Registry and payment administration: 5% of a $25/t payment.

Carbon layer only (MRV + one-offs + administration): $1.4, $2.6 and $23.7 per t.

Net of the farmer benefit the cost is negative ($-218, $-332 and $-740 per t). That uses Rs 8, 15 or 25.5 per day over 270 in-milk days; Rs 25.5 per day is the NDDB NDP-I programme-reported average [P], and USD/INR is 88 [A]. The farmer benefit is $25-78 per animal-year. Carbon at $15-30/t is worth $0.29-10.43, which is 0.4-43% of the private gain.

**Energy.** Moped travel for village resource persons (4 visits, 1-3 km each, 0.75 MJ/km) plus about 2 Wh of FTIR per sample gives 3-9 MJ per animal-year. That is 0.025-0.074 GJ/t, before counting the feed saved per litre, which probably makes it net negative.

**Scale.** NDP-I reached 2.865M animals [P]; the card's 10-30M is 3.5-10.5x that.
- 30M animals: 0.57, 3.67 or 10.43 Mt/yr.
- Base at 30M is 1.4% of India's enteric methane (taken as about 256 Mt CO2e, from about 9.5 Mt CH4 [R]).
- Global smallholder ceiling of 150M animals: 0.0184 Gt (base) to 0.0522 Gt (high), or 0.035% of global GHG.

**Pooled audit signal.** The litre-weighted signal at 60% enrolment is 9.5-12.1%, against the card's 9-12%, so the claim holds.

The thermodynamic floor is not applicable because there is no separation step, so no claim can sit below it.
phys2.violations:
No physically impossible claim, since there is no separation floor to fall below. The card's arithmetic is correct, but three issues remain.

**1. The crediting model is mis-specified as written. This is the key finding.** I ran the IPCC 2006 Tier 2 energy-requirement equations (section 3) with the 2019 Refinement's single Ym bin of 6.5% for cows under 5,000 kg of milk.
- Raising milk at constant diet digestibility (DE) and Ym gives an absolute methane **increase**: +0.8% at 2% more milk, +3.1% at 8% and +5.5% at 14%.
- Reaching the card's 17.5% intensity cut needs DE to rise from 55% to 59.1-61.7%, or Ym to fall from 6.5% to 5.43-5.80%.
- So "IPCC Tier 2 from ration records" only credits a cut if it is replaced by an intake-based model. That model would need recorded dry-matter intake, gross-energy content and a diet-specific Ym equation, and that Ym equation is load-bearing and unvalidated for tropical buffalo and crossbreds on crop-residue diets.
- The recorded intake is the software's prescribed ration, not measured intake, so farmer compliance is unobserved.
- Caveat: my Tier 2 absolute levels (91 kg CH4/yr for a 350 kg crossbred cow; 109 kg for a 450 kg buffalo) are above Indian inventory values. Only the relative direction is the finding.

**2. Per-animal-year credits are mildly optimistic.** Applying the cut to the whole year's methane overstates it if balancing applies only during lactation. With an active fraction of 0.8, the base case falls from 0.177 to 0.122 t.

**3. The audit design leaves the grouping unspecified.**
- Haircuts for a single society are underpowered. With a 6% season-to-season residual SD, power to detect a 9% effect is 0.18 with one society per arm and 0.66 with five per arm.
- Power reaches 1.00 at 20 societies per arm, or with five per arm if the residual SD is 3% or less.
- The audit therefore needs control societies (difference-in-differences) and a cluster level, neither of which the card specifies.
- The residual error from species mix after the volume-split correction is small: 0.2-2.4%.

**Additionality.** RBP is privately profitable many times over, so it fails strict offset additionality. The card's framing as insetting or results-based livelihood payments is the defensible one.
phys2.resource_needs:
- **Energy:** about 3-9 MJ per animal-year, effectively 0% of world supply. The feed saved per litre probably makes it net negative.
- **Materials:** existing union FTIR milk analysers (about $100k each if one must be bought, which adds $0.29 per sample), tamper-evident sample vials, and mineral mixture.
- **Land and water:** none added, and better feed conversion should lower feed and land per litre.
- **Labour:** village resource persons, about one per few hundred to 1,000 animals. That means scaling the NDP-I workforce, which covered 2.865M animals, by 3.5-10.5x.
- **One-offs:** a reference-methane calibration (laser detector, GreenFeed or SF6) on about 60 animals for the falsifying test and about 300 for production, at $0.2-1.5M. Methodology development and approval add $0.2-1M.
- **Data:** access to NDDB's INAPH animal registry with ration records, and buffalo/cow volume splits from collection-unit records.
phys2.key_uncertainties:
1. **The Ym-diet equation** is the decisive term in the crediting model. With IPCC's single bin, Tier 2 credits zero or negative change; a diet-specific equation is unvalidated for these animals and feeds. The card's falsification test (Tier 2 overstating by more than 30%) is the right check and should run first.

2. **Garg 2013's effects are not re-verified here.** These are the 15-20% cut in methane per kg of milk and the 2-14% milk gain. They need checking for:
   - whether the methane estimate itself was measured (SF6) or modelled;
   - whether the pairing of intensity cut and milk gain holds per site;
   - whether the effects persist beyond the study period.

3. **Baseline methane per animal** (35-70 kg/yr) and the share of the year on the balanced ration (0.65-1.0) together span about 2.5x.
