4. **The MIR proxy under diet change.** Milk fatty acids shift with the ration whatever happens to methane, and no tropical buffalo calibration exists. The audit role limits the damage, but a biased proxy could still wrongly haircut real reductions.

5. **Seasonal diet noise in society-level spectra.** Per-society audits need a residual SD of 3% or less, or cluster-level difference-in-differences with controls.

6. **Compliance and rebound.** Prescribed rations are not measured intake. The zero-herd-growth cap may be hard to enforce where the animal census is incomplete.

7. **Scale is inherently small.** Even the 150M-animal global ceiling is 0.018-0.052 Gt/yr. This is a cheap, co-benefit-led, livelihood-first measure, not a climate lever at Gt scale.

8. **Unverified scale inputs.** The NDP-I reach (2.865M animals) and the Rs 25.5 per day benefit come from earlier OptiLex research and were not re-fetched this run. India's enteric total (about 9.5 Mt CH4) is recalled.

idea.title: Pay plantation companies to fully rewet deep-peat blocks, measured by InSAR-detected subsidence arrest against paired drained blocks
idea.one_line: Rewetting drained tropical peat avoids about 35-70 t CO2e/ha/yr, so a carbon price of $4-26/t beats palm-on-peat margins. Pay the plantation owner per centimetre of subsidence arrested, measured by Sentinel-1 InSAR against adjacent still-drained blocks. This replaces REDD+-style counterfactual baselines with physics.
idea.conventional_core: Peatland rewetting by canal blocking. Indonesia's BRG/BRGM programme has run since 2016. Indonesia's water-table regulation (PP 57/2016, recalled) sets a 0.4 m water-table requirement.
idea.graft: Satellite InSAR ground-deformation monitoring, imported from oil-and-gas and CCS reservoir surveillance (e.g. In Salah CO2-storage uplift monitoring), with Hoyt et al. 2020 as the peat-science precedent. It is used as a payment-grade MRV signal, because peat subsidence is mostly carbon oxidation.
idea.mechanism: Hooijer et al. (Biogeosciences 2012) measured large-scale subsidence in Acacia and oil-palm plantations: about 5 cm/yr after year 5 at a 0.7 m water table, with 92% of subsidence from oxidation after 18 years. That equals about 73 t CO2e/ha/yr. Better water management inside a working plantation cuts this by at most 20%, so real abatement requires taking deep-peat blocks out of drained production. Subsidence converts to CO2 through bulk density and carbon content, so a paired-block InSAR time series measures the avoided emission directly. Payment flows to the concession holder, with a share for communities or paludiculture, such as sago or jelutong.
idea.target: The 4.3 Mha of industrial plantations on peat in Sumatra, Borneo and Peninsular Malaysia (oil palm 3.1 Mha, pulpwood 1.1 Mha; Miettinen 2016). The first targets are deep-peat, low-yield and flood-prone blocks near the end of their drainability. Partners: a palm or pulp company with a no-peat commitment, BRGM, and an InSAR group.
idea.quantitative_claims:
Measured: Hooijer 2012 gives 73 t CO2e/ha/yr after year 5 and 178 t in years 1-5. Plantation water management alone saves at most 20%.

Computed check: 3-5 cm/yr subsidence × 0.75-0.92 oxidative share × 80-100 kg/m3 bulk density × 55-57% C gives 36-96 t CO2/ha/yr, consistent with Hooijer.

Assumed residual CH4 after rewetting: 20-60 kg/ha/yr, i.e. 0.5-1.6 t CO2e/ha/yr. Net avoided: about 35-70 t CO2e/ha/yr.

Computed break-even: at an assumed palm-on-peat net margin of $300-900/ha/yr, the break-even carbon price is $4-26/t CO2e.

Scale: rewetting 0.5, 1 or 2 Mha gives 18-35, 35-70 or 70-140 Mt CO2e/yr. Process energy is near zero (earth or plank canal blocks). Verifier DAC-equivalent for 50 Mt: 0.3 EJ/yr at 6 GJ/t (0.048% of world primary energy) against a 0.023 EJ floor.

Assumed InSAR detection: about 0.5-1 cm/yr precision per pixel-year, against a 3-5 cm/yr drained signal. That is an SNR of about 3-10 before spatial averaging over blocks of 100 ha or more.
idea.who_gains: S7 Indonesia and Malaysia: fire and haze suppression (the 2015 fires cost about $16bn per the World Bank, recalled) and avoided subsidence-driven coastal flooding of undrainable peat. S11 and S8: haze health, plus community payment shares and paludiculture jobs. S4: plantation companies are paid more than their margin on a depleting asset that will become undrainable. S10: insurers face lower fire-risk exposure. S3: subsurface-monitoring and InSAR service firms gain a new market. S1/S2: abatement is measured physically rather than against REDD+ baselines.
idea.who_loses: S4 plantation and pulp output on rewetted blocks falls, with lower mill throughput. S6 plantation and mill workers on those blocks lose jobs unless paludiculture or restoration work replaces them. Some of the 3.5 Mha of smallholder peat holdings face pressure if rewetting raises water tables on neighbouring land, so hydrological units must be negotiated as a whole. Downstream refiners lose a marginal amount of supply.
idea.closest_known_work: Indonesia's BRG/BRGM canal blocking (no payment-by-measurement). Katingan Mentaya and other peat REDD+ projects under Verra VM0007's peat module, which protect forest against modelled baselines. Hoyt et al. 2020 (Nature Geoscience) used InSAR to estimate SE Asian peat subsidence and emissions as science, not payment; numbers not re-verified this run. Deltares drainability assessments. What is different: (1) the seller is the company holding already-drained plantation land, not a forest protector; (2) payment is indexed to measured subsidence relative to paired drained blocks, not a counterfactual deforestation baseline; (3) full rewetting is required, because Hooijer shows 0.4 m-type management saves at most 20%.
idea.why_different: It is the largest per-hectare abatement in land use (tens of t CO2e/ha/yr), on land already converted. It brings an oil-and-gas measurement tool to land MRV, and it pays a high-carbon industry to stop rather than offset.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test: Computation only, about 2-3 months. Process Sentinel-1 SBAS or PS-InSAR for 2017-2025 over known BRG canal-blocked areas and adjacent drained concessions. Cross-check against published subsidence-pole and dipwell records where available. It is falsified if InSAR cannot separate rewetted from drained subsidence by more than 2σ (about 1-2 cm/yr) at a 100 ha block scale, or if canal-blocked blocks show no subsidence slowdown compared with drained ones. That outcome would mean rewetting did not raise water tables, or that InSAR coherence over vegetated peat is too poor for payment-grade MRV.
idea.family: Paid full rewetting of deep-peat plantation blocks measured by InSAR subsidence against paired drained blocks

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: Tay, Jovani-Sancho, Evans, Callaghan et al. (EGU 2025): Validating L-band InSAR for tropical peat motion monitoring, framed as an approach to peat MRV
closest.overlap: Very close on the measurement half. It names InSAR peat motion as a proxy for peat CO2 emissions in Southeast Asian drained peatlands and pitches it for MRV. It validates ALOS-2 L-band against high-rate ground-truth peat cameras, and the authors include the UKCEH/APRIL plantation-subsidence group. It does not propose a payment scheme or a paired-block design.

closest.title: Hoyt, Chaussard, Seppalainen & Harvey 2020, Nature Geoscience: widespread subsidence and carbon emissions across SE Asian peatlands (ALOS PALSAR InSAR)
closest.overlap: Converts InSAR subsidence to peat CO2 emissions at regional scale, as science rather than payment. The idea already cites it. I could not open the paper (paywall), so its numbers were not re-checked this run.

closest.title: Conroy & Hanssen (ESSOAr 2025/2026): an upper bound on carbon emissions of drained peat soils from satellite radar interferometry (Netherlands)
closest.overlap: Estimates InSAR land motion per parcel at daily resolution. It splits motion into reversible and irreversible parts, converts the irreversible part to CO2e (upper bound 21.5 t CO2e/ha/yr, western Netherlands grassland on peat), and says the method can evaluate the efficacy of installed subsidence-mitigation measures. That is the 'measure the effect of rewetting' use, on temperate agricultural peat rather than tropical plantations. Its caveat: InSAR gives only an UPPER BOUND, because reversible shrink-swell (bog breathing) is mixed into the signal.

closest.title: Terra Motion (UK), APSIS InSAR peatland apps marketed for MRV and peatland carbon-loss estimation
closest.overlap: A commercial InSAR service already sold to show restoration outcomes and carbon-positive results for peatland MRV, aligned with NatureScot guidance (UK blanket bog). This means the 'new market for InSAR firms' already partly exists. Not tropical, and not used as the payment index.

closest.title: Verra VM0027, Methodology for Rewetting Drained Tropical Peatlands (WWF-Germany; active 2014-2023, now inactive)
closest.overlap: Direct precedent for crediting the rewetting of drained tropical peat. It quantifies avoided oxidation from water-table depth modelled with SIMGRO, not from subsidence. It was made inactive because no project registered within five years, which is evidence that demand and design failed under a modelled-baseline approach.

closest.title: Verra VM0007 (REDD+ Methodology Framework) peat modules, PRC/WRC rewetting, e.g. Katingan Mentaya
closest.overlap: Credits peat rewetting and conservation using modelled or water-table-proxy baselines. The seller is a forest/ecosystem-restoration concession, not a plantation operator. Recalled from memory, not re-verified this run.

closest.title: Couwenberg & Hooijer 2013, Mires and Peat: subsidence-based soil carbon emission factors for oil palm and Acacia plantations
closest.overlap: Establishes the physics the idea relies on: in steady-state drained plantations, net C loss = subsidence × carbon density below the water table. 4.2 cm/yr × 0.043 g C/cm3 gives about 18 t C/ha/yr, or about 66 t CO2e/ha/yr. This independently supports the idea's 36-96 t figure. Caveat: the method assumes steady-state continuous land use, and the steady-state assumption breaks in the transition after rewetting.

closest.title: Evans et al. 2019 (Geoderma), subsidence in Acacia plantations and forest in Sumatra; Evans et al. 2021 (Nature), overriding water-table control on managed peatland GHG
closest.overlap: Plantation-scale subsidence-pole networks (APRIL concessions) and the water-table-to-emissions relationship. These are the dipwell/pole ground truth the falsifying test needs, and they come from inside a working pulp company.

closest.title: Umarhadi & Siegert 2026 (Environ. Res. Commun.), Izumi et al. 2022 (Remote Sensing), Sari et al. 2023: Sentinel-1 SBAS/PS-InSAR of tropical peat subsidence and CO2
closest.overlap: Show that C-band Sentinel-1 InSAR over Indonesian peat works but suffers decorrelation. Izumi 2022 explicitly frames InSAR as a tool for 'assessing peat restoration'. Umarhadi & Siegert mapped ex-Mega Rice Project Blocks B and C at about 1.6-1.7 ± 1.6-2.3 cm/yr, a pixel scatter similar to the idea's assumed 0.5-1 cm/yr. That makes C-band SNR at 100 ha marginal, and L-band (ALOS-2, NISAR) preferable.

closest.title: Asia Pulp & Paper's 2015 retirement of about 7,000 ha of plantation on peat after Deltares drainability assessment; Indonesia BRG/BRGM canal blocking since 2016
closest.overlap: A plantation operator voluntarily taking deep-peat blocks out of production on drainability grounds, and a state rewetting programme. Neither has payment by measurement. Recalled from memory, not re-verified this run.

closest.title: Profitability of Direct Greenhouse Gas Measurements in Carbon Credit Schemes of Peatland Rewetting (Ecological Economics 2018)
closest.overlap: Analyses whether measurement-based (rather than proxy-based) crediting of peat rewetting pays for its own MRV cost. This is the economic question behind 'payment-grade' InSAR. Only the title was seen; contents not read this run.

art.what_is_new:
Every component already exists. Rewetting tropical peat for carbon credits exists (VM0027, now inactive; VM0007 peat modules). Converting subsidence to CO2 exists (Couwenberg & Hooijer 2013; Hoyt 2020). Using InSAR for peat MRV is already proposed for SE Asia (Tay et al., EGU 2025, L-band) and sold commercially in the UK (Terra Motion APSIS). InSAR is already used to evaluate subsidence-mitigation measures on drained peat (Conroy & Hanssen 2025, Netherlands). Plantation operators have retired peat blocks before (APP, about 7,000 ha, recalled).

I found no precedent for the combination: an operating or proposed contract that pays the tropical plantation concession holder directly, indexed to InSAR-measured differential subsidence against paired, still-drained control blocks, with full rewetting required rather than 0.4 m-style water management. That paired-control, payment-indexed design is the genuinely new part. It replaces modelled water-table baselines, which is probably why VM0027 never registered a project.

Four caveats should be added to the idea:

1. **Rewetting causes uplift.** InSAR captures reversible shrink-swell as well as oxidation, so Conroy & Hanssen treat it only as an UPPER BOUND on emissions. Right after rewetting, the surface rebounds and swells, which can look like 'arrest' or even negative subsidence without carbon actually being saved. Payment needs a multi-year irreversible-trend estimator, or a holdback period.
2. **C-band is marginal at 100 ha.** Sentinel-1 decorrelates over vegetated tropical peat; Umarhadi & Siegert report about ±1.6-2.3 cm/yr scatter. The falsifying test should use ALOS-2 and NISAR L-band data (NISAR launched in 2025, data free), not Sentinel-1 alone.
3. **The steady-state assumption breaks.** The subsidence-to-carbon conversion assumes a steady state, which holds under drainage but not during the post-rewetting transition. Residual CH4 cannot be seen by InSAR at all and needs a separate default factor.
4. **The In Salah 'graft' is cosmetic.** InSAR-to-carbon on peat is already established within peat science itself, so the oil-and-gas lineage is not where the novelty lies.

Search limits: the web-search budget was exhausted before this run started. Findings come from Crossref, direct fetches (Verra, Terra Motion) and recall. The VM0007 peat modules, the APP retirement and Hoyt's figures were not re-verified, and a commercial tropical InSAR-MRV vendor or a recent Verra/ICVCM peat-subsidence module could have been missed.

phys.assumptions:
Script: global_south_6.py, run with the OptiLex verifier. Labels: [M] means the primary source was read this run; [R] means recalled and not re-verified; [A] means assumed.

Subsidence-to-CO2 conversion [M]. Hooijer et al. 2012 (Biogeosciences 9:1053; PDF text extracted this run) uses 92% oxidation, 55% C and a bulk density of 0.075 g/cm3.
- The script reproduces 69.6 t CO2/ha/yr at 5 cm/yr, against 73 in the paper, which is 13.9 t CO2/ha per cm.
- The idea's 36-96 t range reproduces exactly (36.3-96.1).
- Hooijer's abstract does state that improved plantation water management cuts impacts by "20 % at most, relative to current conditions". His plantation regression, CL = 21 + 69×WD, gives 30% for 0.7→0.4 m. The claim's direction holds.

Residual emissions after rewetting [M]. Hooijer's drained-forest relation CL = 98×WD gives a residual of 4.9, 14.7 or 29.4 t CO2/ha/yr at mean water tables of 0.05, 0.15 or 0.30 m. The idea assumes zero residual CO2 after rewetting, and this relation says otherwise.

Net abatement cases (low/base/high):
- Drained baseline: 40 t (IPCC 2013 Wetlands Supplement Tier 1 oil palm, 11 tC/ha/yr [R]), 60 t [A], 73 t (Hooijer, after year 5 [M]).
- Rewetted CH4: 134, 41 or 20 kg/ha/yr (IPCC rewetted tropical, 41 kg, range 7-134 [R]), at GWP100 biogenic 27.
- DOC avoided: 1.5 t (half of IPCC's 0.82 tC [R/A]).
- Leakage (palm displaced elsewhere): 50%, 30% or 10% [A].
- Result: net 4.2, 32.0 or 62.2 t CO2e/ha/yr. Monte Carlo net P10/P50/P90 is 16.9, 26.1 and 36.2. The idea claims 35-70.

Cost inputs per ha (low/base/high, all [A]):
- Forgone net margin: $300 / 700 / 1300 per yr. Basis: 15-20 t FFB/ha at $170-220/t with a 10-30% net margin; pulpwood margins are lower.
- Capex: $300 / 1200 / 3000 one-off, for canal blocks plus revegetation or paludiculture. Annualised at 6%/25 yr, 8%/20 yr and 10%/15 yr.
- O&M and fire patrol: $20 / 50 / 100 per yr.
- MRV: $2 / 6 / 15 per yr.
- Overhead (community share, registry, intermediaries): 10%, 20% or 30%.
- Totals: $384 / 1098 / 2585 per ha/yr.

Cost results:
- Paired $/t: low 6.2 (cheapest cost with the best abatement), base 34.3. The worst cost with the worst abatement gives 609.3.
- Monte Carlo (n=20000): P10 29.3, P50 48.0, P90 81.1. I report P90 81.1 as the high figure, because the 609 corner pairs every pessimistic input at once.
- The idea's $4-26/t break-even reproduces arithmetically ($4.3 and $25.7). It omits capex, O&M, MRV, overhead, residual CO2 and leakage.

Energy: process energy covers canal-block works (5 GJ per 20 ha, one-off) plus patrol fuel (0.05 GJ/ha/yr), giving 0.0010, 0.0020 and 0.0147 GJ/t CO2e. This is avoided emission rather than a gas separation, so no separation floor applies (reported as 0). For reference, the DAC floor is 0.47 GJ/t, and the DAC-equivalent for 50 Mt is 0.300 EJ/yr, or 0.048% of world primary energy at 6 GJ/t, against a 0.0233 EJ floor. The idea's own yardstick numbers reproduce exactly.

Scale:
- Net Mt CO2e/yr (low/base/high): 0.5 Mha gives 2 / 16 / 31; 1 Mha gives 4 / 32 / 62; 2 Mha gives 8 / 64 / 124.
- The idea claims 18-35, 35-70 and 70-140, which are about 10-50% too high at base.
- Rewetting all 4.3 Mha (Miettinen 2016 [R]) has a ceiling of 0.138 Gt/yr at base and 0.267 at high. 1 Mha at base is 0.06% of 53 Gt total GHG.
- The headline scale of 0.032 Gt/yr is for 1 Mha at base.

InSAR SNR for a paired 100 ha block (all [A]):
- Pessimistic C-band (5% coherent pixels, 0.8 cm/yr correlated noise): SNR 0.9, ±16 t/ha/yr.
- Base: SNR 5.3, ±7.9 t/ha/yr.
- Optimistic L-band: SNR 15.9, ±3.9 t/ha/yr.
- Converting subsidence to tonnes adds ±26% relative uncertainty (bulk density ±25%).
phys.violations:
No thermodynamic violation is possible, because this is an avoided emission with no separation step. The idea's claims are overstated in four places, though none needs heroic assumptions:

1. **Net 35-70 t CO2e/ha/yr is too high.** It assumes zero residual CO2 after rewetting and zero leakage. Hooijer's own drained-forest relation gives 5-29 t/ha/yr residual at a mean water table of 0.05-0.30 m. With 10-50% leakage, the verified net is 4.2 / 32.0 / 62.2.
2. **The $4-26/t break-even is incomplete.** It includes only the forgone margin. With capex, O&M, MRV, overhead and corrected abatement, the base is $34.3/t and the Monte Carlo median is $48.0/t.
3. **Scale is overstated by roughly 10-50%.** 1 Mha gives 32 Mt/yr at base, not 35-70.
4. **InSAR "payment-grade" MRV is unproven.** C-band Sentinel-1 coherence under palm canopy may give SNR below 1 for a 100 ha pair. L-band (ALOS-2, NISAR) makes it robust.
phys.resource_needs:
**Energy:** negligible, 0.001-0.015 GJ/t CO2e, about 0% of world supply.
**New land:** none. It reuses converted plantation land.
**Water:** none withdrawn; rainfall is retained.
**Materials:** earth, timber or plank canal blocks, at roughly 1 block per 20 ha [A].
**Main resource cost is forgone output:** 1 Mha (72% palm at 3.5 t CPO/ha) removes 2.5 Mt CPO/yr, 3.2% of the world's ~79 Mt [R]. 2 Mha removes 5.0 Mt, 6.4%. That is large enough to raise palm prices and drive expansion elsewhere, which is the leakage term.
**Money:** about $384-2585/ha/yr, base $1098, so a 1 Mha programme costs about $1.1bn/yr at base.
**MRV:** InSAR time series, preferably L-band (NISAR, ALOS-2), plus dipwells and subsidence poles for ground truth.
phys.key_uncertainties:
1. **Achievable water table after canal blocking in working concessions.** This dominates the result: residual oxidation is 98 t CO2/ha/yr per metre of mean water-table depth (Hooijer [M]). Evidence from BRG-blocked areas on dry-season water tables is mixed [R], so a field number is needed.
2. **Leakage.** Removing 3-6% of world palm supply invites expansion elsewhere, including onto forest. That could erase 10-60% of the abatement, and the paired-block MRV does not measure it.
3. **InSAR feasibility.** C-band coherence over vegetated peat, seasonal peat swelling and shrinking, and spatially correlated atmospheric error all reduce precision. The paired-block design removes regional atmosphere but not differences in peat depth or drainage age between blocks. The idea's cheapest falsifying test, a retrospective 2017-2025 InSAR study, is the right first step. NISAR L-band data (launched 2025 [R]) should be included.
4. **Converting subsidence to CO2.** The bulk density of the oxidising surface layer ranges from 0.075 to 0.15 g/cm3 (Hooijer [M]), giving ±26% on tonnes. In rewetted blocks, compaction lag and swelling can be mistaken for oxidation.
5. **Margins.** Palm margins vary with FFB price, yield on deep peat and stand age. Integrated mill and refinery losses are not counted.
6. **Permanence and reversal.** Payments must continue indefinitely, or blocks get re-drained.
7. **Fire co-benefit not counted.** Avoided peat fires (2015 fires cost about $16bn [R]) would add substantial upside not counted in these numbers.

**Unverified this run:** Hoyt et al. 2020 (abstract inaccessible), IPCC Wetlands Supplement factors, Miettinen 2016 areas and world CPO output are all recalled. The web search budget was exhausted; only Hooijer 2012 was read from the primary source.

stances.evidence: Peat protection has long been a core NGO campaign target (Greenpeace/WWF/Wetlands International peat campaigns around the 2015 fires; recalled, not re-verified). Physically measured abatement answers S1's main complaint about forest offsets: the 2023 Guardian/Die Zeit/SourceMaterial investigation judged about 94% of Verra rainforest credits phantom, with deforestation threat overstated by about 400% on average (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verra_(organization), fetched 2026-10-05). Against that, CAN 2021 says it 'will not support any effort to promote negative emissions or offsets as an alternative' to cuts (map). If buyers use these tonnes as offsets, the idea crosses that line. Some NGOs will also object to paying the companies that drained the peat, which reverses 'polluter pays'.
stances.red_line_hit: Offsets, if credits are sold to fossil emitters as compensation. Also rewarding past illegal drainage or burning (polluter-pays inversion).

stances.evidence: The idea rests on measured science. Hooijer et al. 2012 measured plantation subsidence (73 t CO2e/ha/yr after year 5, 92% from oxidation), and Hoyt et al. 2020 estimated peat emissions from InSAR. IPCC AR6 WGIII rates peatland protection and restoration among the larger, cheaper AFOLU options (recalled from SPM C.9; not re-fetched this session). S2 will flag two conditions: permanence (re-drainage or fire reverses the gains) and the residual CH4 after rewetting. Both are measurable, which suits a scientist audience. The proposal's own falsification test (InSAR separating blocks by >2 sigma) is the kind of check S2 would require.
stances.red_line_hit: None categorical. Permanence and reversal risk must be priced in, for example with buffer pools and multi-decade contracts.

stances.evidence: Oil and gas companies are barely exposed. Their possible gains are a new market for InSAR and subsurface-monitoring services (the In Salah precedent) and a supply of high-integrity nature credits. Fossil firms, Shell among them, have historically been large buyers of nature-based credits (recalled, not verified this session). Nothing here threatens S3's core business or touches their red lines (per-tonne fees on their own emissions, per the map).
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: The affected heavy industry is palm and pulp, not steel or cement. Firms with no-deforestation, no-peat, no-exploitation (NDPE) commitments are natural sellers. APP spent about $100m on fire management after Singapore named it over the 2015 haze (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia_Pulp_%26_Paper, fetched), and RSPO requires drainability assessments before replanting on peat (recalled). Computed (my script, assumed yields of 2-3.5 t CPO/ha on peat and a 72% palm share): rewetting 1 Mha removes 1.4-2.5 Mt CPO/yr, which is 1.8-3.2% of about 79 Mt world supply. Mills lose throughput. The industry association GAPKI and pulp firms resisted PP 57/2016's 0.4 m water-table rule and its zoning of peat for protection, arguing it would cut output and jobs (recalled, not re-verified). Support depends on the payment exceeding margin, which at $26/t is $910-1,820/ha/yr against an assumed $300-900/ha margin.
stances.red_line_hit: Mandatory rewetting without compensation, and lost mill throughput or stranded processing capacity.

stances.evidence: Power utilities are not directly affected. Indirect link: Indonesia's biodiesel mandates (B35-B40, with B50 planned; recalled) tie palm supply to transport fuel, not to power.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: Computed (my script, assumed 0.1-0.2 workers/ha): rewetting 1 Mha of plantations, 0.72 Mha of it palm, puts about 72-144k plantation jobs at risk, plus mill jobs. The proposed replacement livelihoods earn less. Monoculture jelutong is 'considered less efficient than crops like smallholder oil palm' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paludiculture, fetched), and only Liberica coffee on rewetted peat is reported to give higher returns. The map shows that S6 support follows where payments go (unions in the Carbon Capture Coalition, SEIU funding the 'No' campaign on Washington's I-2117). The proposal routes payment to the concession holder, not to workers.
stances.red_line_hit: Job losses in plantation and mill regions with no wage-replacement or redeployment guarantee.

stances.evidence: Producer governments (Indonesia, Malaysia) have large gains available. Indonesia's environment minister put the cost of the 2015 haze at Rp300-475 trillion (US$35-47bn); a disputed Harvard-Columbia study estimated more than 100,000 excess deaths (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Southeast_Asian_haze, fetched). Indonesia created BRG in 2016 and has a FOLU Net Sink 2030 target (recalled). Against that, palm oil is a strategic export and biodiesel feedstock, and the computed 1.8-3.2% world supply loss per Mha would fall on Indonesia and Malaysia. Indonesia has also asserted control over carbon exports and requires domestic registry or authorisation (Article 6 corresponding adjustments) before credits leave the country (recalled). It would reject a foreign-buyer offset model that bypasses its own system. Importing governments (EU, Singapore) would back it as haze and deforestation policy.
stances.red_line_hit: Sovereignty over carbon credits (no export without national authorisation), and loss of palm export or biodiesel revenue.

stances.evidence: Money would flow to Global South producers and haze-affected populations, and climate-justice voices favour real reductions over offsets. But indigenous and climate-justice groups have a documented record of opposing REDD+-type schemes. The International Indigenous Peoples Forum on Climate Change said REDD 'will not benefit Indigenous Peoples' (2007), and there are concerns about 'carbon cowboys' and weak FPIC (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reducing_emissions_from_deforestation_and_forest_degradation, fetched). Paying concession holders could entrench contested concession boundaries over customary land.
stances.red_line_hit: Land grabs or entrenching concession claims over customary land. Selling Southern land-carbon so Northern emitters can offset ('carbon colonialism').

stances.evidence: Computed: 1 Mha removes about 1.8-3.2% of world palm supply. That is a modest price nudge for consumers of a substitutable vegetable oil, spread globally (an assumption; elasticities not modelled). Local consumers gain haze-health benefits. The map's evidence (Canada's 'Axe the Tax') shows consumers object to visible price rises, and this would not be visible.
stances.red_line_hit: Only if scaled to 2 Mha+ (3.7-6.4% of supply), where cooking-oil price effects in producer countries could become politically salient.

stances.evidence: For insurers, fire and haze risk falls (2015 cost US$35-47bn per the Indonesian government, fetched). For plantation investors, the payment monetises a depleting asset that will become undrainable (a Deltares drainability argument). Buyers of carbon credits have been burned by the 2023 Verra scandal (94% phantom, fetched), so payment indexed to physical InSAR measurement suits S10 durable-integrity demand, as with Frontier-style buyers, though this is lower-durability carbon than geological storage.
stances.red_line_hit: Reputational risk if fire or re-drainage reverses the abatement (permanence), or if it becomes seen as another offset scandal.

stances.evidence: Communities near the peat stand to gain the most from haze relief (more than 500,000 respiratory cases reported by Oct 2015, fetched) and from lower flood risk. But per the idea itself, 3.5 Mha of smallholder peat holdings sit in shared hydrological units, so raising water tables can flood neighbouring smallholder crops. Paludiculture alternatives also earn less (Paludiculture page, fetched). Canal blocking without consent has produced local disputes (recalled; Mongabay search returned nothing to verify).
stances.red_line_hit: Flooding neighbouring smallholder land or restricting customary use without FPIC and compensation.

stake.coalition_notes:
Research limits: the session's 200-search WebSearch budget was used up before this task, so the new evidence comes from 8 WebFetch calls (Wikipedia pages on the 2015 haze, Verra, REDD+, APP and paludiculture). Items marked 'recalled' are unverified. That covers GAPKI's opposition to PP 57/2016, Indonesia's carbon-export rules, the B40/B50 mandates, FOLU Net Sink 2030 and IPCC AFOLU rankings. Computed figures come from climate/runs/2026-10-05/scripts/peat_stakeholder.py and rest on assumed yields, labour intensity and world supply. Per 1 Mha rewetted: 1.8-3.2% of world palm supply lost, about 72-144k plantation jobs at risk, and a programme cost of $0.35-1.8bn/yr at $10-26/t.

Coalition shape: support from S2 and S10, with S1, S4, S7, S8 and S11 split, S3, S5 and S9 neutral, and S6 opposed. The idea avoids every fossil red line (no EOR, no mitigation deterrence for fossil producers). Its exposures are all on the land and labour side.

Three design choices would move the split groups:
(1) Sell the measured tonnes as results-based payments or contribution claims, not offsets, preferably through Indonesia's own registry or authorisation with Article 6 corresponding adjustments. This clears CAN's offset red line and S7's sovereignty red line together.
(2) Earmark part of the payment for worker transition and smallholder compensation per hydrological unit, with FPIC. This addresses S6, S8 and S11, the only groups opposed or with hard red lines.
(3) Target low-yield, deep, near-undrainable blocks first. This minimises supply loss (S7, S9) and margin loss (S4).

The idea's main strength across stakeholders is that it swaps the modelled baselines discredited by the 2023 Verra findings for measured physics. That is the argument most likely to unite S1, S2 and S10. The main risk is the 'paying polluters' framing (S1) and payment going to concession holders rather than workers or communities (S6, S8). The closest coalition precedent from the map is Montreal/Kigali: there, incumbents' own gain plus funding for the Global South bought broad support. Here, incumbents' gain plus community payment shares would play that role.

critic.fatal_flaw:
No fatal flaw. There is no physics problem: this is an avoided emission with no separation step. The scale is small (about 0.03-0.14 Gt/yr) but real. Every stakeholder red line in the reports can be designed around. Two near-fatal risks are worth flagging.

1. Legal additionality (recalled, not re-verified this run). PP 71/2014 and PP 57/2016 assign a "protection function" to at least 30% of each peat hydrological unit (KHG), including peat 3 m or deeper. Ministerial rules (P.17/2017) then ordered pulp concessions to restore protection-zone peat. The idea's first targets ("deep-peat, near-undrainable blocks") may therefore already be legally required to be rewetted. Paying for them would be paying for compliance. S7 (governments) would not fund that, and S1 (activists and NGOs) would see it as rewarding illegal drainage.
   - Design-around: either target cultivation-function peat only, or reframe as results-based enforcement finance paid through BRGM and the national registry.
   - This must be checked before any pilot. It does not kill the concept.
2. Leakage. Taking 3% or more of world crude palm oil supply out of production is the main threat to the climate claim (10-50% erosion). It sets a ceiling on scale rather than making the idea fail.
critic.top_fixable_flaw:
The new part of the idea, paying the concession holder per cm of subsidence relative to paired drained blocks, lets the seller set its own baseline. The payment is control subsidence minus treated subsidence, and the same company manages the water levels on the control block. So the contract rewards draining the controls harder. That raises real emissions, and it reads as abatement.

Computed with Hooijer's plantation regression, CL = 21 + 69×WD (script: scratchpad/climate/critic_peat6.py):
- Lowering the control water table from 0.7 m to 0.9 m adds 13.8 t CO2/ha/yr (about 1.0 cm/yr more subsidence). That is 43% of the 32 t base net abatement.
- At 1.0 m it adds 20.7 t (65%).

The design is also biased in the other direction at the same time:
- Hydrological spillover from the rewetted neighbour raises the water table on 10-50% of an adjacent 1 km × 1 km control (assuming a 100-500 m edge buffer). That shrinks the measured difference, which makes the seller want to over-drain the controls even more.
- Swelling after rewetting can hide residual oxidation. At a mean water table of 0.15-0.30 m, that is 15-29 t/ha/yr, or 1-2 cm/yr. A flat or rising surface would then be paid as full arrest.

Last, paired drained controls have to keep emitting for the contract to work, and they run out as the programme scales. At 1-2 Mha there are no controls left.
critic.suggested_patch:
Swap the seller-controlled paired design for a before/after-control/impact (BACI) baseline with three changes.

1. **Each block's own baseline.** Use the block's pre-rewetting irreversible subsidence trend from archival InSAR as the baseline: ALOS-2 L-band from 2014 onward, Sentinel-1 from 2017 onward, then NISAR. Freeze it at contract signature, and cap payment at that frozen rate.

2. **Independent control pool.** Use the control pool only to correct for regional trends such as climate-year and ENSO effects, not as the counterfactual. The pool must:
   - be drawn from third-party concessions the seller does not own or manage;
   - sit in different hydrological units, or at least 1-2 km from any treated boundary;
   - have its dipwell water tables monitored, with any control whose water table falls below 0.7 m excluded.

3. **Paid tonnes:**

   paid tonnes = (frozen pre-trend − post-rewetting irreversible trend, after a 2-year swell holdback and a seasonal model of reversible "bog breathing") × site-specific bulk density × C fraction − dipwell-based residual (98 t CO2/ha/yr × mean water-table depth in m) − CH4 default (IPCC rewetted tropical, 41 kg/ha/yr) − jurisdictional leakage deduction (20-30%) − 20% reversal buffer

   Sell these tonnes only as results-based contribution claims through Indonesia's registry, with an Article 6 corresponding adjustment.

4. **Revised falsifying test.** Rerun it on this estimator. It passes if BACI separates BRG-blocked areas from their own pre-trend by more than 2σ at the 100 ha scale with L-band data. It fails if post-blocking dipwell water tables in canal-blocked peat do not average below 0.3 m.

This removes the gaming incentive and the shrinking supply of controls together. The cost is about $2-5/ha/yr of extra dipwell MRV, which is small against the base cost of $1,098/ha/yr.

patched_idea.title: Pay plantation companies to fully rewet deep-peat blocks, measured by InSAR subsidence arrest against each block's own frozen pre-rewetting trend (BACI with independent controls)
patched_idea.one_line: Rewetting drained tropical peat avoids about 35-70 t CO2e/ha/yr physically, and about 6-46 t/ha/yr is creditable after deductions. Pay the concession holder per tonne of InSAR-measured subsidence arrest against the block's own archival pre-rewetting trend, frozen at signature. Third-party controls correct only for regional trends. Break-even is about $7-47/t (central $12-36/t) against palm-on-peat margins. This replaces REDD+ counterfactual baselines with physics, and the seller cannot set its own baseline.
patched_idea.conventional_core: Peatland rewetting by canal blocking. Indonesia's BRG/BRGM programme has run since 2016. PP 57/2016 sets a 0.4 m water-table requirement (recalled).
patched_idea.graft: Satellite InSAR ground-deformation monitoring, imported from oil-and-gas and CCS reservoir surveillance (e.g. In Salah CO2-storage uplift monitoring), with Hoyt et al. 2020 as the peat-science precedent. It is used as a payment-grade MRV signal, because peat subsidence is mostly carbon oxidation. It now runs inside a before/after-control/impact (BACI) design rather than a seller-managed paired-block comparison.
patched_idea.mechanism:
Hooijer et al. (Biogeosciences 2012) measured large-scale plantation subsidence: about 5 cm/yr after year 5 at a 0.7 m water table, 92% of it oxidation after 18 years, about 73 t CO2e/ha/yr. Water management inside a working plantation cuts this by at most 20%, so real abatement means taking deep-peat blocks out of drained production. Subsidence converts to CO2 through bulk density and carbon fraction, so an InSAR time series measures the emission.

The estimator is a BACI design.

(1) Baseline. Each block's baseline is its own pre-rewetting irreversible subsidence trend from archival InSAR: ALOS-2 L-band from 2014, Sentinel-1 from 2017, then NISAR. It is frozen at contract signature, and payment is capped at that frozen rate. Draining harder after signing can no longer raise the baseline.

(2) Control pool. Controls only correct for regional and climate-year effects (ENSO, rainfall anomalies); they are not the counterfactual. They are drawn from third-party concessions the seller neither owns nor manages, in different hydrological units or at least 1-2 km from any treated boundary. Dipwell water tables are monitored, and any control drained below 0.7 m is excluded. This removes both the over-drained-control incentive and the spillover bias. Because controls are not consumed, the programme can scale to 1-2 Mha without running out of them.

(3) Paid tonnes, per ha/yr:
[(frozen pre-trend emission) − max(post-rewetting irreversible-trend emission, dipwell residual of 98 t CO2/ha/yr × mean water-table depth in m) − CH4 default (IPCC rewetted tropical, 41 kg/ha/yr)] × (1 − jurisdictional leakage deduction of 20-30%) × (1 − 20% reversal buffer).
Trend emissions are subsidence × site-specific bulk density × C fraction × oxidative share. The post-trend is estimated after a 2-year swell holdback, with a seasonal model removing reversible 'bog breathing'. Taking the larger of the InSAR post-trend and the dipwell residual guards against swelling masking residual oxidation without counting that oxidation twice.

(4) Legal additionality screen. Blocks in the legally mandated protection function (at least 30% of each KHG, and peat 3 m or deeper under PP 71/2014 and PP 57/2016, recalled) are either excluded, or paid only as results-based enforcement finance through BRGM and the national registry, never as private offsets.

Tonnes are sold only as results-based contribution claims through Indonesia's registry, with an Article 6 corresponding adjustment. Payment goes to the concession holder, with a share for communities or paludiculture (sago, jelutong).
patched_idea.target: The 4.3 Mha of industrial plantations on peat in Sumatra, Borneo and Peninsular Malaysia (oil palm 3.1 Mha, pulpwood 1.1 Mha; Miettinen 2016). First targets are low-yield, flood-prone, deep cultivation-function blocks with at least 3 years of archival InSAR pre-trend; protection-function peat goes through the enforcement-finance channel. Partners: a palm or pulp company with a no-peat commitment, BRGM and the national registry, an InSAR group with L-band access, and a dipwell-network operator.
patched_idea.quantitative_claims:
Measured (Hooijer 2012, plantation-scale): about 73 t CO2e/ha/yr after year 5 and 178 t in years 1-5. Plantation water management alone saves at most 20%.

Computed check (earlier run): 3-5 cm/yr × 0.75-0.92 oxidative share × 80-100 kg/m3 × 55-57% C gives 36-96 t CO2/ha/yr, consistent with Hooijer.

Computed, patched estimator (scratchpad/climate/patch_peat6.py). Assumptions: pre-trend 3-5 cm/yr; post irreversible trend 0.5-1 cm/yr; mean water table 0.15-0.30 m; bulk density 80-100 kg/m3; C fraction 0.56; oxidative share 0.85; CH4 41 kg/ha/yr at GWP100 28; leakage 20-30%; 20% buffer.
- Central case (4 to 1 cm/yr, water table 0.2 m, 25% leakage): 62.8 t pre-emission, 19.6 t post-emission (dipwell-bound), about 42 t/ha/yr physical avoided, 25 t/ha/yr paid.
- Full range: 6-46 t/ha/yr paid.

Break-even (palm-on-peat net margin of $300-900/ha/yr, assumed): central $12-36/t, full range $7-142/t. The upper end applies only to the worst blocks, so high-margin, shallow-signal blocks are deprioritised. These figures are higher than the unpatched $4-26/t because leakage, the buffer and the conservative residual are now deducted.

Scale (paid tonnes): 0.5, 1 and 2 Mha give about 13, 25 and 51 Mt/yr (ranges 3-23, 6-46 and 13-91). Physical abatement is roughly 1.7x higher. Process energy is near zero. Verifier DAC-equivalent for 50 Mt: 0.3 EJ/yr at 6 GJ/t, against a 0.023 EJ floor.

MRV cost: extra dipwell monitoring of $2-5/ha/yr is about $0.08-0.20 per paid tonne (central case).

Gaming closed: under the old paired design, lowering a seller-managed control from 0.7 m to 0.9 m inflated payment by 13.8 t/ha/yr, 43% of base (critic's computation). Under BACI the seller has no lever on its baseline or controls.

Assumed InSAR detection: about 0.5-1 cm/yr per pixel-year (C-band; L-band expected to be better over vegetated peat), against a 2-4 cm/yr pre-vs-post difference. SNR is about 2-8 before averaging over blocks of 100 ha or more.
patched_idea.who_gains: S7 Indonesia and Malaysia: fire and haze suppression (2015 fires cost about $16bn per the World Bank, recalled), avoided subsidence-driven flooding, enforcement finance for protection-zone peat, and registry-controlled Article 6 credits. S11 and S8: haze health, community payment shares, and paludiculture and dipwell-monitoring jobs. S4: plantation companies are paid above margin on a depleting asset heading for undrainability, under a baseline they cannot dispute after signing. S10: lower fire-risk exposure, and credits with a reversal buffer. S3: InSAR and subsurface-monitoring firms gain a new MRV market. S1/S2: abatement is measured physically against the block's own history, with no reward for drainage gaming or for legally required compliance.
patched_idea.who_loses: S4: plantation and pulp output on rewetted blocks falls, with lower mill throughput, and payments come in lower per hectare than the unpatched design implied because of the leakage and buffer deductions. S6: plantation and mill workers on those blocks lose jobs unless paludiculture or restoration work replaces them. Smallholders on neighbouring peat (3.5 Mha in total) may face higher water tables, so whole hydrological units must be negotiated. Downstream refiners lose a marginal amount of supply. Companies holding illegally drained protection-zone peat get no private offset revenue for it.
patched_idea.closest_known_work:
Indonesia's BRG/BRGM canal blocking (no payment-by-measurement). Katingan Mentaya and other peat REDD+ projects under Verra VM0007's peat module, which protect forest against modelled baselines. Hoyt et al. 2020 (Nature Geoscience) used InSAR to estimate SE Asian peat subsidence and emissions as science, not payment; not re-verified this run. Deltares drainability assessments. BACI designs come from ecological impact assessment.

What is different:
(1) The seller is the holder of already-drained plantation land, not a forest protector.
(2) Payment is indexed to measured subsidence arrest against the block's own frozen archival trend, with independent controls for regional correction only, instead of a counterfactual deforestation baseline.
(3) Full rewetting is required, because Hooijer shows 0.4 m-type management saves at most 20%.
patched_idea.why_different: It is the largest per-hectare abatement in land use (tens of t CO2e/ha/yr), on land already converted. It brings an oil-and-gas measurement tool to land MRV, in a BACI design the seller cannot game. It pays a high-carbon industry to stop rather than to offset.
patched_idea.cheapest_falsifying_test:
Computation plus existing field data, about 2-3 months. Build archival pre-trends from ALOS-2 L-band (2014 onward) and Sentinel-1 (2017 onward) over known BRG canal-blocked areas. Apply the BACI estimator with third-party drained controls from other hydrological units. Cross-check against published subsidence-pole and dipwell records.

It is falsified if:
(a) BACI cannot separate blocked areas' post-trend from their own pre-trend by more than 2σ at the 100 ha scale with L-band data; or
(b) post-blocking dipwell water tables in canal-blocked peat do not average shallower than 0.3 m, meaning rewetting did not rewet; or
(c) the seasonal and swell model leaves residual reversible motion as large as the irreversible signal.

fix.change_summary: I applied the critic's patch and kept the core (canal-blocking rewetting) and the graft (InSAR subsidence as payment-grade MRV). The patch replaces the seller-managed paired-drained-block counterfactual with a BACI design, which removes the incentive to over-drain the controls and stops the supply of controls running out. Each block's own archival pre-rewetting trend (ALOS-2 L-band, Sentinel-1, NISAR) becomes its baseline, frozen and capped at signature. Third-party controls now correct only for regional and ENSO trends: they come from other hydrological units, sit at least 1-2 km from treated boundaries, and are dropped if their dipwell water table falls below 0.7 m. Paid tonnes now carry a 2-year swell holdback, a seasonal model for reversible motion, a dipwell-based residual, the IPCC CH4 default, a 20-30% leakage deduction and a 20% buffer. Sales go through Indonesia's registry with an Article 6 corresponding adjustment. I added the critic's legal-additionality screen: protection-function peat is excluded, or paid only as enforcement finance through BRGM. I made one small correction to the critic's formula. It subtracted both the InSAR post-trend and the dipwell residual, which counts residual oxidation twice. I use the larger of the two instead, which still guards against swelling masking oxidation. I recomputed the numbers in scratchpad/climate/patch_peat6.py. Central case: about 42 t/ha/yr physically avoided and about 25 t/ha/yr paid (range 6-46). Break-even rises from $4-26/t to a central $12-36/t (range $7-142/t). Paid scale is about 13, 25 or 51 Mt/yr at 0.5, 1 or 2 Mha. Extra MRV costs about $0.08-0.20 per tonne. I rewrote the falsifying test around the BACI estimator, using the critic's dipwell water-table criterion of 0.3 m or shallower.

idea.title: Rich/lean amine tankage plus off-peak electric regeneration for cycling gas plants
idea.one_line: Borrow refinery intermediate tankage to decouple absorption from regeneration at an NGCC with capture running 25-40% of the time. Store rich amine while the turbine runs, keeping full output at peak prices. Regenerate around the clock in a stripper sized for average flow, using an electric boiler or heat pump in the cheap, renewable-surplus hours when the gas plant is off.
idea.conventional_core: NGCC post-combustion amine capture (NZT Power, Calpine Baytown; NETL Rev 4A cost basis).
idea.graft: From refining: intermediate tankage that decouples units with different run schedules, in this case between absorber and stripper. The off-peak electric reboiler is a sub-element of the same decoupling, not a second mechanism.
idea.mechanism: The absorber is sized for full flue-gas flow and runs only with the turbine. Rich solvent goes to a nitrogen-blanketed tank, and lean solvent is drawn from a second tank. The stripper, reboiler and CO2 compressor are sized for the daily average CO2 rate and run 24 h. When the turbine is off, regeneration heat comes from an electric boiler or heat pump on low-price power. The turbine therefore sells its full output at peak prices with no steam extraction, and expensive regeneration equipment runs at a high capacity factor.
idea.target: The capacity-factor penalty on gas-plant capture. NETL's $61/t at 85% CF rises to about $99-110/t at 40% CF (map). This is the map's first open problem.
idea.quantitative_claims: My calculation, all assumptions labelled in the script. Basis: 742 MW NGCC with 270 t/h captured at full load; capture capex of $717M from NETL Rev 4A H-class ($970 to $1,936/kW, 2018$); 35% of it in regeneration and compression (assumed); scaling exponent 0.65. (a) Verifier floor at 4% CO2 and 90% capture: 0.219 GJ/t. (b) At 40% CF and one daily block, the buffer is 1,555 t CO2/day. That needs 71 kt of 30 wt% MEA (cyclic capacity 0.5 mol/kg) or 41 kt of 5 m PZ (0.86 mol/kg), i.e. 39-67k m3 per tank. Added capex (amine $38-49M, two tanks at $150-300/m3, 90 MWth e-boiler) is $69-97M, against a regeneration-train capex saving of $113M. At 25% CF it is $52-73M against $149M. At 60% CF it is $75-106M against $71M, so the sign flips near 50-60% CF. That is consistent with Cohen et al. 2011, who found only 15-30 min of storage optimal at high capacity factor. (c) Energy arbitrage: lost peak output of about 0.30 MWh/t at $100-150/MWh against e-boiler regeneration of 0.93 MWh/t at $0-20/MWh saves $11-45 per t. Over 0.95 Mt/yr at 40% CF that is $11-43M/yr. Combined with annualised capex savings of $1.6-4.3/t, the reduction is about $13-49/t against an approximately $100/t CF-adjusted baseline. (d) Climate guard: off-peak electric regeneration at 0.93 MWh/t adds 0.09 t CO2 per t captured if marginal grid emissions are 100 g/kWh, 0.37 at 400 and 0.84 at 900. It must run only in hours under about 100 g/kWh, or with a heat pump (0.43 MWh/t at COP 2.5).
idea.who_gains: S5: capture no longer costs peak-hour output, and the plant becomes a flexible load-shifter. S3: gas-plant capture remains bankable as capacity factors fall, which preserves gas demand. S7: firm low-carbon capacity at lower cost per tonne. S6: jobs in industrial clusters such as Teesside. S10: lower stranded-capex risk.
idea.who_loses: S1: may see this as entrenching gas (lock-in), and it does nothing about upstream methane. S11: very large solvent tanks (two tanks of 40-70k m3) add a perceived chemical-storage hazard. S9: capacity-payment pass-through. Solvent vendors could gain or lose depending on inventory.
idea.closest_known_work: Cohen, Rochelle & Webber, Energy Procedia 2011 (doi 10.1016/j.egypro.2011.02.159). For a 500 MW coal plant, solvent storage gave a 9-29% profit advantage at $30-100/t CO2, and only 15-30 min of storage was optimal. Aburime et al., CCST 2022 (doi 10.1016/j.ccst.2021.100024), modelled AMP capture with solvent storage at an NGCC; I could not retrieve the details. Energy 2025 covers predictive control of solvent storage. The map lists this as an open problem.
idea.why_different: The prior work assumed high-capacity-factor plants that shift a little stripping into peak hours. This idea targets 25-40% capacity factor, sizes for a full daily cycle, downsizes the regeneration train to average flow, and moves regeneration energy to an electric source in the gas plant's off-hours. The calculation shows it pays only below about 50-60% CF and only on low-carbon off-peak power.
idea.cheapest_falsifying_test: Computation, about 3-4 weeks: an hourly dispatch-and-storage optimisation for a real cycling CCGT using 2024-25 GB or ERCOT hourly prices and marginal emission factors, plus a vendor-checked regeneration capex share. The idea fails if net present value is not positive at a 40% capacity factor, or if fewer than about 1,500 h/yr fall below 100 g/kWh (the climate guard). Parallel bench test: oxidative and thermal degradation of rich MEA and PZ held 24-72 h at 40-50 C under a nitrogen blanket. It fails if hold-up adds more than about 0.5 kg amine per t CO2 of make-up.
idea.family: Rich/lean solvent tank storage for cycling gas plants with capture; stripper sized to average and regenerated electrically off-peak

art.label: PARTIAL

closest.title: Cheng, Patankar, Chakrabarti & Jenkins (Princeton ZERO Lab), 'Modeling the operational flexibility of NGCC power plants coupled with flexible CCS via solvent storage and flexible regeneration', IJGGC 118 (2022)
closest.overlap: This is the closest academic precedent. It covers an NGCC with rich-solvent storage and regeneration that is decoupled in time from absorption, evaluated inside a capacity-expansion and dispatch model of decarbonising grids, where gas runs at falling capacity factors. I verified the title, authors and scope through Crossref and OpenAlex. I could not retrieve the abstract or full text, so I have not confirmed whether stripper capacity was optimised independently, down to average flow, or whether electric regeneration heat was allowed.

closest.title: Colorado State University ARPA-E FLECCS Phase 1, 'Synergistic Heat Pumped Thermal Storage and Flexible Carbon Capture System' (OSTI 2202638, 2023); follow-up by Markey et al., 'Economic impact of thermal energy storage on natural gas power with carbon capture in future electricity markets', IJGGC 2024
closest.overlap: This directly precedes the off-peak electric regeneration element. At an NGCC, a heat pump stores low-cost off-peak electricity as heat that later powers CCS solvent regeneration (ION solvent, target over 99% capture). The buffer is heat, not solvent, so absorber and stripper stay coupled. It removes the steam-extraction penalty at peak using grid-charged heat, which is the idea's arbitrage logic. Markey 2024: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijggc.2024.104098

closest.title: Zantye, Arora & Hasan, 'Renewable-integrated flexible carbon capture: a synergistic path forward to clean energy future', Energy & Environmental Science (2021)
closest.overlap: This combines renewable or surplus power with flexible capture at existing fossil plants, using solvent storage to run regeneration when renewable power is cheap and to absorb renewable intermittency. It is conceptually the same as storing rich solvent and regenerating it on renewable-surplus electricity. As I recall it, the case was coal, not a low-capacity-factor NGCC (from memory; only the one-line abstract was retrievable). Related earlier work: Zantye et al., Comput. Chem. Eng. 2019 (multistage stochastic scheduling with flexible capture).

closest.title: Aburime et al., 'AMP-based post-combustion capture process with solvent storage for decarbonisation of NGCC', Carbon Capture Sci. & Tech. 2 (2022)
closest.overlap: Solvent storage at an NGCC that defers regeneration to low-price periods. The abstract reports about 1% profit gain over plain capture, viable above €25/t CO2. That is a far smaller benefit than the idea claims. It assumes a high-capacity-factor plant and no electric heating.

closest.title: Patiño-Echeverri & Hoppock, 'Reducing the energy penalty costs of postcombustion CCS systems with amine-storage', ES&T 46 (2012); Bandyopadhyay & Patiño-Echeverri, Renewable Energy 85 (2016)
closest.overlap: Amine storage that postpones about 92% of capture energy use to low-price hours, with an explicit capital-versus-arbitrage threshold analysis. The abstract finds it pays only where price variability is large, which matches the idea's sign-flip analysis. The 2016 paper reframes coal-plus-flexible-amine-CCS as a wind-integration load. Both are coal cases.

closest.title: Cohen, Rochelle & Webber, Energy Procedia 2011 and IJGGC 2012; Oates, Versteeg, Hittinger & Jaramillo, 'Profitability of CCS with flue gas bypass and solvent storage', IJGGC 27 (2014)
closest.overlap: These are the standard solvent-storage economics papers, for coal at high capacity factor. Cohen found the optimum is short storage of 15-30 min. Oates is recalled as finding storage rarely profitable in ERCOT; I could not retrieve that abstract. They establish the baseline the idea claims to extend into the low-capacity-factor regime.

closest.title: Qiu et al., 'Economic and flexible operation of solvent-based carbon capture system with solvent storage based on absorption-desorption decentralized predictive control', Energy (2025)
closest.overlap: Recent work on controlling absorber and stripper as separately scheduled units linked by solvent tanks, for economic flexibility. This is the operating-control side of the decoupling. No abstract was retrievable.

closest.title: Abreu, Suresh Babu, Drewry & Rochelle, 'Optimization of operating profit with variable load for CO2 capture by aqueous piperazine on a 460 MW NGCC', I&EC Research (2025); Hersbach, Mastrandrea & Wara, The Electricity Journal (2025)
closest.overlap: These are context, not precedents. Abreu et al. optimise PZ capture profit on an NGCC at 50-95% load under SPP prices, with no storage. Hersbach et al. show NGCC CCS is cost-effective only at high capacity factor and is weakened by upstream methane. This confirms the problem the idea targets and the S1 objection about upstream methane (doi 10.1016/j.tej.2025.107494).

art.what_is_new:
The idea is PARTIAL, leaning towards IMPORT; every mechanism in it has a precedent. Rich and lean solvent storage that decouples absorber from stripper has been studied since about 2009, including at NGCCs: Aburime 2022, Cheng/Jenkins 2022, Qiu 2025. Running regeneration on off-peak or renewable electricity also has precedents. CSU's ARPA-E FLECCS project uses heat-pumped thermal storage to power regeneration at an NGCC, and Zantye/Hasan 2021 uses renewable-integrated flexible capture with solvent storage.

From memory, and not verified this session, early flexibility literature also cites downsizing the regenerator and compressor to average flow as a benefit of storage: Chalmers & Gibbins around 2009 and IEAGHG flexibility reports around 2012. Cheng/Jenkins 2022 may also already optimise regeneration capacity separately; I could not get its abstract.

What appears new is the operating point and the way the pieces are combined:
1. It targets a gas plant that runs only 25-40% of the time, the opposite of the high-capacity-factor plants with 15-30 min of storage in Cohen, Oates and Patiño-Echeverri.
2. It stores a full day's capture (about 1,500 t CO2/day, 40-70k m3 tanks) so the regeneration train is sized to daily-average flow and runs 24 h.
3. It supplies regeneration heat with an electric boiler or heat pump specifically in the hours when the gas plant is off. Earlier work either used turbine steam at off-peak or buffered heat rather than solvent.
4. It adds an explicit climate guard: electric regeneration only below about 100 g/kWh marginal grid intensity, or with a heat pump. I found no precedent for this.

The sign-flip near 50-60% capacity factor and the $13-49/t saving are the idea's own calculations, not verified prior art. Before committing, retrieve the full text of Cheng/Jenkins 2022 and the CSU FLECCS final report. If either optimises regeneration-train size at low capacity factor with grid-electric heat, the label should move to IMPORT.

Search caveat: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so this hunt relied on the Crossref, OpenAlex and OSTI APIs. Publisher pages (ScienceDirect, ACS, RSC) and the ARPA-E project pages could not be read. Patent databases were not reached; Aker, MHI, Shell/Cansolv and Fluor patents on solvent storage are a known gap.

phys.assumptions:
The script ran successfully. All figures below are as printed. Each input is labelled in the script as [idea], [lit], [assume] or [calc].

The web-search budget for the session was used up, so the NETL Rev 4A figures ($61/t at 85% capacity factor (CF); $970 and $1,936/kW) come from the idea and the map and were not re-checked. One fetch of the OSTI page returned only the abstract. Literature values were taken from memory: reboiler duty of 2.3-3.6 GJ_th/t; steam-extraction penalty of 0.065-0.075 MWh_e per GJ; compression to about 150 bar at 0.10 MWh/t; e-boiler capex of $60-150/kWth; MEA cyclic capacity of 0.5-1.2 mol/kg; PZ cyclic capacity of 0.86-1.0 mol/kg. They are order-of-magnitude and flagged.

(a) Floor at 4% CO2, 90% capture: 9.64 kJ/mol = 0.219 GJ/t (61 kWh/t). This confirms the idea's number. No claim falls below the floor. Resistive regeneration at 3.35 GJ_th/t = 0.93 MWh_e/t has a second-law efficiency of 0.065 against the floor. The exergy of 125 C reboiler heat is 0.84 GJ/t, 3.8x the floor.

Plant basis: 270 t/h checks out at 50% net efficiency (300 t/h generated). At 53% it would be 254 t/h. Capture capex is $717M, matching the idea's arithmetic.

(b) Buffer at 40% CF is 1,555 t CO2/day, confirmed. Inventory is 71 kt of MEA solution at 0.5 mol/kg, 44 kt at 0.8 and 29 kt at 1.2; PZ is 41 kt at 0.86. Capex at 40% CF, with a crude-type tank at $150-250/m3 and a stainless or lined tank at $500/m3:
- Favourable: added $46M against a regeneration-train saving of $145M, net +$98M.
- Base: added $58M against $113M, net +$54M.
- Unfavourable (MEA at 0.5 mol/kg, tanks at $500/m3, regeneration share 25%): added $137M against $80M, net -$56M.
At 60% CF the nets are +$42M, +$7M and -$94M; at 25% CF they are +$156M, +$105M and +$2M. The sign flip near 50-60% CF is reproduced only in the base case.

(c) Arbitrage at 40% CF. A stripper sized for average flow still regenerates 40% of tonnes during turbine-on hours, so only 60% of tonnes can be shifted. The idea's saving of $11-45/t applied to all tonnes therefore overstates the benefit.
- Favourable ($150 peak, $10 delivered off-peak): $35.2/t if every tonne were shifted, $21.1/t with only 60% shiftable.
- Base ($110 peak, $35 delivered off-peak including network charges): $0.7/t and $0.4/t.
- Unfavourable ($80 peak, $60 off-peak): -$39.3/t and -$23.6/t.
The break-even peak/off-peak price ratio is 3.08 for resistive heating and 1.41 with a heat pump at COP 2.5.

(f) Cost. The CF-adjusted baseline is $99-106/t captured (central $102), which confirms the idea's $99-110. Results:
- Favourable: $74/t captured, $76/t avoided.
- Base: $98/t captured, $116/t avoided after 0.15 t/t of grid emissions at 250 g/kWh.
- Unfavourable: $132/t captured, $179/t avoided.
The capex saving is +$7.3, +$4.1 and -$5.9/t (CRF 7.07%, 10% in the unfavourable case). The idea's claimed reduction of $13-49/t is reproduced only in the favourable case, at about $28/t.

(g) Scale. Base is 0.1 Gt/yr: the share of gas-power CCS on cycling plants by around 2040 (low 0.02, high 0.4). This idea makes capture cheaper; it does not add capture capacity of its own.
phys.resource_needs:
Electricity at base scale (0.1 Gt/yr) is 62 TWh/yr of off-peak power, 0.21% of world electricity. The low case (0.02 Gt) needs 12 TWh (0.04%) and the high case (0.4 Gt) 247 TWh (0.82%).

Solvent inventory at base scale is about 2.24 Mt of MEA, a one-time fill at 71 kt of solution per plant. The low case needs 448 kt and the high case 8.97 Mt. This is a real materials constraint at the high end. From memory, global ethanolamine production is roughly a few Mt/yr, so it needs checking. The PZ market is far smaller, which matters if PZ is chosen.

Tankage at base scale is 14.2 Mm3 (low 2.8, high 56.9). Per plant that is two tanks of 34-67k m3, about 0.5-1 ha each plus bunding. Land outside the tank farm and process water are minor. The e-boiler is 75-108 MWth per plant at 40% CF, and the plant's existing export connection must also be able to import that power.
phys.violations:
No thermodynamic violations: every energy claim is above the 0.219 GJ/t floor. Several quantitative claims are overstated.

1. **Arbitrage counts every tonne.** The claimed saving of $11-45/t, about $11-43M/yr, applies to all captured tonnes. With the stripper sized for daily average flow, only (1 - CF) of tonnes, 60% at 40% CF, are regenerated off-peak. This scales the saving by 0.6.
2. **Off-peak price is wholesale, not delivered.** Off-peak power at $0-20/MWh is a wholesale price. Delivered prices, including GB network charges and levies, are plausibly $30-60/MWh. At $35 delivered, the arbitrage is about $0.4/t, because the break-even peak/off-peak price ratio is 3.08 for a resistive boiler.
3. **The favourable case contradicts itself.** Cheap power and a marginal emission factor below 100 g/kWh are assumed for all off-hours. If only 1,500 h/yr qualify, the stripper and e-boiler must be about 3.5x larger and storage must grow from daily to multi-day, which wipes out the capex saving. At 3,000 h it is 1.75x.
4. **Cyclic capacity sets the capex.** MEA at 0.5 mol/kg is the conservative Rochelle-type equilibrium definition, while operating capacity can reach about 1.2 mol/kg. Inventory spans 29-71 kt, and net capex at 40% CF spans +$98M to -$56M.
5. **The climate guard under-reports grid emissions.** Including compression, grid emissions are 0.10-0.41 t CO2/t at 100-400 g/kWh. At 250 g/kWh, net avoided cost rises to $116/t, above the no-storage baseline of $102/t captured.

None of this needs heroic assumptions. It holds in the favourable case, marginal in the base case and negative in the unfavourable case.
phys.key_uncertainties:
1. **Price spread and emissions at the same hours.** What matters is the delivered off-peak price and the marginal emission factor in the hours when the CCGT is off. Where cycling gas plants sit off for 60% of hours, the marginal unit is often another gas plant (about 350-400 g/kWh), unless renewables are being curtailed. This single factor decides the sign. The idea's own falsifying test, an hourly GB/ERCOT dispatch model, is the right test.
2. **Regeneration-train capex share.** The idea assumes 35%; the script tests 25-45%. The real figure needs a vendor breakdown. The NETL Rev 4A figures were not re-verified here because the search budget ran out.
3. **Solvent and storage.** Cyclic capacity and solvent choice (MEA vs PZ) set inventory and tank size. The required tank material (lined carbon steel vs stainless) could raise tank cost 3x.
4. **Degradation and emissions from hold-up.** A stoichiometric ceiling, in which all dissolved O2 is consumed in the tank, gives at most 0.26-0.59 kg MEA/t and 0.21-0.48 kg PZ/t. That is near the idea's 0.5 kg/t fail threshold, so the bench test is informative. Separately, NO2 picked up in the absorber can form nitrosamines, MNPZ in PZ; longer hold-up could increase accumulation, which matters to S11.
5. **Baseline.** The baseline is NETL's $61/t at 85% CF, scaled by an assumed 55-65% capital plus fixed-O&M share. Outcomes are modelled only: Cohen et al. 2011 and Aburime et al. 2022 are simulations, and no plant has run daily-cycle solvent storage. NZT Power, with final investment decision taken in Dec 2024 and operation targeted around 2028, is the first relevant realized data point. Gas-plant capture itself has no operating record at scale yet.
6. **Integrated maturity.** The parts are mature but the combination is not. Amine capture, tanks and e-boilers are TRL 8-9; the integrated daily-cycle concept is about TRL 4.
7. **Scale depends on gas CCS.** The 0.1 Gt/yr base depends entirely on gas-CCS deployment policy (UK dispatchable power agreements, US 45Q). For S1, the gas lock-in objection is unaffected by the calculation.

stances.evidence: Closest documented position is CAN's 2021 CCUS paper (1,300+ NGOs). It calls for phasing out public support for fossil-linked technologies 'including CCS' (red line 3) and opposes EOR (red line 7). Its only opening is for hard-to-abate industry, and that opening rests on evidence, not principle. Gas power is not industrial process emissions. COP28's 'particularly in hard-to-abate sectors' qualifier does not obviously cover it either. IPCC AR6 WGIII C.4.4 (high confidence) says CCS lets fossil fuels be used longer and reduces stranded assets, which is the lock-in mechanism S1 objects to; the idea's own 'who_gains' entry claims exactly that ('preserves gas demand'). Wikipedia's CCS article records environmental-justice groups preferring shutdown to CCS retrofit. A minority of S1 (conservation and policy groups in the Carbon Capture Coalition) accept CCS, so opposition is not unanimous. S1's natural simple baseline: batteries, demand response and less gas at 25-40% CF instead of capturing it. Caveat: the search budget ran out this session, so I could not retrieve current Sierra Club or NRDC statements on gas-plant CCS.
stances.red_line_hit: Fossil lock-in and mitigation deterrence; public subsidy for fossil-linked CCS (CAN #3); EOR, if US CO2 goes to EOR under OBBBA's 45Q parity (CAN #7); upstream methane not addressed.

stances.evidence: IPCC AR6 WGIII treats CCS as one option in mitigation pathways and is explicit about the stranded-asset trade-off (C.4.4). Its verdict on this idea will turn on two quantities. (1) The climate guard. My calculation (stake_tankage.py; assumptions labelled) gives 0.05 t CO2 added per t captured for the e-boiler at 50 g/kWh marginal grid intensity, 0.09 at 100, 0.19 at 200 and 0.37 at 400. A heat pump at COP 2.5 roughly halves these. (2) Upstream methane, which the idea ignores. Fuel use is about 6.3 GJ/MWh, and the 90%-capture stack residual is about 0.035 t/MWh. At 0.2% upstream leakage, methane adds 0.008 tCO2e/MWh (GWP100) or 0.021 (GWP20). At 1% it adds 0.038 (GWP100), about equal to the stack residual, or 0.105 (GWP20). At 2% it adds 0.076 or 0.21. These are modelled, not measured. Scientists would likely accept it as a cost reduction for gas CCS that already exists, conditional on hourly-matched low-carbon regeneration power and verified upstream methane.
stances.red_line_hit: None categorical. It becomes net-harmful if regeneration runs on high-carbon marginal power or upstream leakage is about 1% or more.

stances.evidence: Documented support for comparable measures: S3 backed 45Q, and OBBBA (4 Jul 2025) kept it and gave EOR and utilisation parity (Enverus estimated a 40% cut in some E&P costs). OGCI and OGDC (55+ companies, about 40% of global oil production) commit to CCS and methane targets. API supports 'market-based' and 'predictable' frameworks. The idea keeps gas-fired capacity bankable as capacity factors fall, which protects gas demand, and it involves no per-tonne fee. A per-tonne fee is S3's documented red line: the US Waste Emissions Charge was disapproved under the CRA in 2025.
stances.red_line_hit: None. It would only become one if paired with a methane fee or upstream MRV mandates; the EU Methane Regulation importer requirements already apply in the EU.

stances.evidence: Not directly affected; the idea targets power, not process emissions. Indirect gain: shared CO2 transport and storage in clusters (East Coast Cluster/Teesside; UK commitment of up to £21.7bn over 25 years for the Teesside and Merseyside clusters, per a gov.uk press release fetched this session) lowers per-tonne infrastructure costs for cement and chemicals. Chemical makers and solvent vendors gain from amine inventories 6-12x a conventional plant's. Mild competing interest: S4 (VCI) wants low electricity prices, and the idea adds off-peak electric demand.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: The idea attacks S5's main cost problem, the capacity-factor penalty: NETL's $61/t at 85% CF rises to about $99-110/t at 40% CF. It also removes the loss of peak-hour output. The comparable flagship is NZT Power: UK cluster funding of up to £21.7bn over 25 years, with O&M contracts creating '100 local jobs and apprenticeships' (NZT news, 27 Mar 2026). That support is conditional on a revenue contract such as the UK dispatchable power agreement (not verified from a primary source this session). In the US the regulatory driver is gone: EPA signed a partial repeal of the power-plant GHG standards on 14 Sep 2026, with a supplemental proposal for full rescission (EPA page, fetched this session). From memory and not verified this session, the 2024 rule required CCS only for baseload units above 40% CF, so the 25-40% CF target segment was never covered. US utilities would therefore support it only where 45Q at $85/t covers costs. Operators will discount the first-of-a-kind operating risk (amine degradation during hold-up, a novel control scheme).
stances.red_line_hit: None. The operational and liability risk of large solvent tanks is a cost concern, not a red line.

stances.evidence: Unions are members of the Carbon Capture Coalition, which describes itself as including 'companies, unions, conservation and environmental policy organizations'. The UK cluster announcement claims 4,000 direct jobs and 50,000 supported in the 2030s; these are government claims, not realised figures. NZT reports apprenticeships and local O&M contracts (2026). The idea keeps gas plants and their workforce running, adds tank-farm construction and 24-h stripper operation, and causes no job losses.
stances.red_line_hit: None.

stances.evidence: UK and EU: supportive in pattern. The UK committed up to £21.7bn over 25 years to Teesside and Merseyside CCUS. COP28 decision 1/CMA.5 para 28 endorses CCUS and para 29 recognises 'transitional fuels' for energy security. US federal: 45Q survived OBBBA, which was bipartisan in effect, but EPA is repealing the power-sector CO2 standards (partial repeal signed 14 Sep 2026), so there is no regulatory pull. Fiscal cost: 45Q at $85/t on about 0.95 Mt/yr is about $81M/yr per plant, a target for fiscal watchdogs (Taxpayers for Common Sense opposed EOR parity). The idea's lower per-tonne cost helps the fiscal case relative to conventional gas CCS.
stances.red_line_hit: Fiscal cost of open-ended per-tonne credits, for fiscal hawks; none for energy-security-focused governments.

stances.evidence: Of little direct relevance: it is a cost tweak for rich-country cycling gas fleets on high-renewable grids with cheap off-peak hours. Baum et al. 2024 (N=30,284, 30 countries): Global South publics support climate technologies more but worry more that they undermine mitigation and spread risk unequally. Climate-justice advocates align with S1 against gas lock-in. Gas-producing developing-country governments, which backed COP28's 'transitional fuels' language, would welcome anything that keeps gas demand bankable. These two S8 subgroups pull in opposite directions, so the net is neutral.
stances.red_line_hit: Mitigation deterrence (justice advocates); no land, food or border-tax issue.

stances.evidence: Costs reach bills through capacity or contract pass-through: UK cluster support is levy- and tax-funded, and US 45Q is taxpayer-funded. Against conventional gas CCS the idea lowers cost: $13-49/t × 0.95 Mt/yr ≈ $12-47M/yr per plant (modelled, idea basis). Against no CCS it raises cost. Canada 2025 shows visible consumer carbon costs lose and invisible industrial ones survive, and this cost would be invisible. Off-peak electric demand may slightly firm off-peak prices.
stances.red_line_hit: Price rises only if pass-through is visible; otherwise low salience.

stances.evidence: Investors gain from lower stranded-capex risk on the regeneration train (downsized to average flow) and better economics at low CF. But this is first-of-a-kind. Cohen et al. 2011 found only 15-30 min of storage optimal at high CF, and the idea's own calculation flips sign near 50-60% CF, so returns hinge on dispatch assumptions and on whether policy demand exists. The US power-plant rule is being repealed; 45Q survives. Record of comparable plants (realised, from scratch capex_intensity.py notes): Petra Nova (2017) averaged about 1.15 Mt/yr against 1.4 Mt/yr design before mothballing. Boundary Dam 3 captured 0.72 Mt in 2025 against 1 Mt/yr design. Gorgon failed to inject about two-thirds of captured CO2 in one year (Wikipedia). Insurers would price the 41-71 kt solvent inventory, 6-12x a conventional 0.5-1 h hold-up, as a liability.
stances.red_line_hit: Policy-dependence and first-of-a-kind technology risk; not a categorical red line.

stances.evidence: Local safety concerns are documented for amine CCS. Wikipedia's CCS article: volatile nitrosamines and nitramines from amine systems 'are carcinogenic when inhaled or drunk in water'. In the Satartia, Mississippi CO2 pipeline rupture (2020), about 200 people were evacuated and 45 hospitalised. Environmental-justice critiques note CCS-suitable facilities sit disproportionately in burdened communities. The idea adds two tanks of about 40-70k m3 holding 41-71 kt of solvent, about 6-12x a conventional plant's inventory (my calc; 0.5-1 h hold-up assumed). Holding rich amine at 40-50 C raises degradation-product inventory. Counter-evidence: Teesside-type industrial host communities show engagement, with local MP visits (May 2026), apprenticeships and 100 local O&M jobs. Acceptance likely splits by site: established industrial clusters accept, while EJ fenceline communities, e.g. on the US Gulf Coast, oppose.
stances.red_line_hit: Local safety: large chemical inventory, amine/nitrosamine emissions and degradation products, and CO2 pipeline risk.

stake.coalition_notes:
I rate the coalition for idea graft_near_6 as moderate and incumbent-led. S3, S5, S6 and S7 (UK/EU) support it, and S10 splits. It mirrors the 45Q constituency that survived OBBBA. S1, the climate-justice part of S8, and EJ-sited S11 contest it. It does not reach the broad S1 to S3 overlap seen for methane abatement or Kigali.

Main fragility: there is no US demand driver for capture on cycling gas plants. EPA signed a partial repeal of the power-plant GHG standards on 14 Sep 2026. From memory and not verified, the 2024 rule never required CCS below about 40% CF anyway. Viable markets are therefore the UK (cluster funding of up to £21.7bn over 25 years) or US plants under 45Q.

Conditions that would neutralise objections without costing S3 or S5 support:
1. Dedicated geological storage only, with no EOR. This avoids CAN red line #7 and the fiscal watchdogs' EOR-parity critique.
2. An auditable hourly climate guard. Regenerate only in hours under about 100 g/kWh marginal grid intensity, or use a heat pump. The e-boiler adds 0.09 t CO2 per t captured at 100 g/kWh and 0.37 at 400.
3. Bundle with verified upstream methane performance on the gas supply (OGDC/OGCI targets under 0.2%; EU Methane Regulation importer rules). At 1% upstream leakage, methane equals the stack residual under GWP100 and is about 3x it under GWP20 (my calc, modelled). This is what S2 will check first.
